en: The First Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the Origin of the Veda.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Then, indeed, Aupadhenava, Vaitaraṇa, Aurabhra, Pauṣkalāvata, Karavīrya, Gopurarakṣita, Suśruta, and others spoke to the Blessed One, Dhanvantari, the King of Kāśi named Divodāsa, who was staying at his hermitage and surrounded by a multitude of sages and the best of immortals.

O Blessed One, having observed human beings afflicted by the onslaught of various pains from physical, mental, and incidental diseases—struggling like those without a protector even though they have one, and crying out—we feel pain in our own minds. Desiring their happiness and for the sake of the alleviation of their diseases, as well as for the purpose of maintaining our own lives, we wish to hear the Ayurveda being taught here, for the welfare pertaining to this world and the next depends upon it. Therefore, we have approached the Blessed One to become your disciples.
The Blessed One said to them: "Welcome to you all; you are not to be questioned further, my children, for you are all to be taught."

In this world, indeed, the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), having created living beings, composed the auxiliary branch (upāṅga) of the Atharvaveda known as Āyurveda, consisting of one hundred thousand verses and one thousand chapters; subsequently, observing that the lifespan and intellect of human beings had diminished, he further arranged it into eight divisions.

Namely: surgery (śalya), minor surgery (śālākya), internal medicine (kāyacikitsā), the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), toxicology (agadatantra), alchemy (rasāyanatantra), and aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇatantra).
Now follows the summary of its characteristics according to each individual part.

In this context, "foreign body" (*śalya*) refers to various grasses, wood, stones, dust, iron, clods of earth, bones, hair, nails, pus, and discharges; it is for the purpose of extracting such foreign bodies lodged within the womb of a malignant ulcer, and for the purpose of applying instruments, surgical tools, alkali, or fire, as well as for the definitive diagnosis of ulcers.
Śālākya is the branch [of medicine] intended for the pacification of diseases located in the supraclavicular region, specifically those residing in the ears, eyes, mouth, nose, and so forth.

The science of medicine (kāyacikitsā) is for the purpose of pacifying diseases affecting all parts of the body, such as fever, diarrhea, hemorrhaging, consumption, insanity, epilepsy, leprosy, urinary disorders, and dysentery.

The science of spirits (*bhūtavidyā*) is for the purpose of pacifying the influence of planetary spirits (*graha*)—such as those possessed by gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, piśācas, nāgas, and so forth—by means of rites for peace (*śāntikarma*), the extraction of strength, and other methods.

The branch known as Kaumārabhṛtya is for the purpose of purifying defects in the nourishment and nursing of children, as well as for the alleviation of diseases arising from corrupted breast milk or the influence of malevolent spirits (grahas).

The science of antidotes (agadatantra) is for the purpose of identifying the poisons from the bites of snakes, insects, spiders, rats, and so forth, and for the purpose of neutralizing various combinations of poisons.
The science known as Rasāyana establishes youth, promotes longevity, intelligence, and strength, and is capable of removing diseases.

The section on aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa-tantra) is for the purpose of providing nourishment, clarity, and growth to those with diminished, vitiated, or depleted semen, and for the purpose of generating sexual excitement.
Thus, this Ayurveda is taught as having eight branches; herein, for whom should what be said?
They said, "May the Blessed One teach us all, making the knowledge of surgery (śalya) the very foundation."
He said, "So be it."
They said again to the Blessed One: "Having observed the consensus of our united minds, Suśruta will question the Blessed One; and we too shall retain in our memory that which is taught to him."
He said, "So be it."
My dear Suśruta, the purpose of Āyurveda here is indeed the liberation from disease for those afflicted by illness, as well as the protection of the healthy.
Āyurveda is so called because life (āyus) exists in it, or because by means of it one attains life.
Accept this, which is being stated as his foremost and primary limb, and which is not contradicted by perception, scripture, inference, or analogy.

This is indeed the first limb [of medicine], prior to the healing of wounds from injuries and the rejoining of the head of the sacrifice. For it is heard in scripture that when the head of the sacrifice was severed by Rudra, the gods approached the two Aśvins and said: "O Blessed Ones, you shall become our most excellent physicians; the head of the sacrifice must be rejoined by you. They replied, "So be it."
Then, for the sake of those two, the gods propitiated Indra with a share of the sacrifice;
thus the head of the sacrifice was restored to them.

Moreover, among all eight systems of Ayurveda, this very one is considered superior because it performs the processing of undigested matter (āma) and the vital essence (śukra), because it employs instruments, surgical tools, alkalis, and cautery, and because it is common to all systems.
This [treatise] is eternal, meritorious, conducive to heaven, conducive to fame, conducive to long life, and provides a means of livelihood.

Then Brahmā spoke; from him Prajāpati learned it, from him the two Aśvins, and from the two Aśvins Indra. From Indra, this [knowledge] was obtained by me; and here, for the sake of the welfare of all creatures, it must be bestowed by me upon those who seek it.
And there is a verse on this point:
"For I am Dhanvantari, the primordial god who removes old age, disease, and death from the immortals;
having returned to earth with my limbs joined by other limbs, I have arrived here once more to provide instruction."
In this treatise, the conjunction of the five great elements and the embodied soul is called the *puruṣa*.

Action resides in that [conjunction]; why? Because the world is twofold. For the world is indeed twofold: stationary and moving. It consists of two natures: fiery and lunar; or, because of the predominance of those [elements], it consists of five natures. Therein, the fourfold collection of beings is known as the sweat-born, the womb-born, the egg-born, and the soil-born. Among these, the *puruṣa* is primary, while the other is its instrument. Therefore, the *puruṣa* is the locus of action.
The conjunctions with that suffering are called diseases.
These are of four kinds: adventitious, physical, mental, and natural.
Among these, the adventitious ones have their cause in injury.
Bodily diseases, however, have food and drink as their root cause, and they arise from the imbalance of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), blood (śoṇita), or their combination (sannipāta).
Mental [afflictions], however, arise through the divisions of desire and aversion, such as anger, grief, fear, joy, dejection, envy, malice, wretchedness, parsimony, lust, greed, and so forth.
But those consisting of hunger, thirst, old age, death, and sleep are innate.
These [organs] have the mind and the body as their substrata.
For them, the proper application of purificatory and palliative therapies, along with diet and conduct, are the means of subduing [the disease].

Furthermore, food is the root of living beings, and it is dependent upon the six tastes for strength, complexion, and vitality. Tastes, in turn, reside in substances; substances, moreover, are medicinal herbs.
These are of two kinds: stationary and mobile.
Among them, the stationary beings are fourfold: shrubs, trees, creepers, and herbs.

Among these, those that bear fruit without flowers are shrubs; those that possess both flowers and fruit are trees; those that have tendrils or grow as stalks are creepers; and those that reach their end with the ripening of their fruit are herbs.
Mobile beings, moreover, are of four kinds: those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those born from a sprout.

Among these, domestic animals, humans, beasts of prey, and so forth are womb-born; birds, snakes, reptiles, and so forth are egg-born; worms, insects, ants, and so forth are sweat-born; and *indragopa* beetles, frogs, and so forth are sprout-born.

Among those, from stationary beings (sthāvara) there are useful products such as bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, tubers, exudations, and natural juices; from mobile beings (jaṅgama) there are skin, claws, hair, blood, and so forth.
Earthen substances include gold, silver, gems, pearls, red arsenic, clay, potsherds, and so forth.
Those produced by time are the specific divisions of the year, such as wind, calm, heat, shade, moonlight, darkness, cold, warmth, rain, day, night, fortnight, month, season, and solstice.
These, by their very nature, are the causes for the accumulation, provocation, pacification, and remediation of the humors (doṣas), and they are purposeful.
And there are verses on this subject:
This fourfold classification of bodily disorders,
as well as the causes for their provocation and pacification, has been stated by physicians.
Indeed, those diseases that are adventitious fall into two categories:
some are in the mind and others are in the body; their treatment is likewise twofold.
For those diseases that have fallen upon the body, the treatment is like that for physical ailments;
however, for mental ones, the desired group of objects such as sound and the rest is held to bring happiness.

Thus, this fourfold set—the person (*puruṣa*), disease (*vyādhi*), medicine (*auṣadha*), and the time for action (*kriyākāla*)—has been explained in brief. Therein, by the mention of "person," the collection of substances originating from him, such as the primary elements (*bhūta*) and so forth, as well as the variations of his limbs and minor members, such as skin, flesh, bone, vessels, and sinews, are described. By the mention of "disease," all diseases whatsoever caused by the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), blood (*śoṇita*), and their combination (*sannipāta*) are explained. By the mention of "medicine," there is the instruction on substances, tastes (*rasa*), qualities (*guṇa*), potencies (*vīrya*), and post-digestive effects (*vipāka*). By the mention of "action," procedures such as excision (*chedya*) and oleation (*sneha*) and so forth are explained. By the mention of "time," there is the instruction regarding the timing for all these actions.
And there is a verse on this point: This seed of therapeutics has been proclaimed in brief;
its detailed exposition shall consist of one hundred and twenty chapters.

And that [work], consisting of one hundred and twenty chapters, having been divided according to the requirements of the subject matter into five sections—the Sūtra, Nidāna, Śārīra, Cikitsita, and Kalpa—we shall explain the remaining topics in the Uttara-tantra.
And there is a verse on this point: "Whoever shall read this eternal [work] proclaimed by the Self-Existent One and revealed by the Lord of Kāśī,
that performer of meritorious deeds, honored by kings upon earth, shall go to the same world as Śakra when there is no destruction."
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Origin of the Veda," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Second Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter concerning the initiation of the disciple.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

A physician should initiate as a student one who belongs to any of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes, and who is endowed with lineage, youth, good character, valor, purity, proper conduct, humility, capability, strength, intelligence, fortitude, memory, wisdom, and practical understanding; whose body, tongue, lips, teeth, gait, face, eyes, and nose are straight; whose mind, speech, and gestures are serene; and who is capable of enduring hardships. He should not, however, initiate one who possesses qualities contrary to these.

For the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa, however, on an auspicious lunar day, karana, muhurta, and nakshatra, having smeared a four-cubit square sacrificial mound (sthandila) with cow dung in a pure, level place facing an auspicious direction, having strewn it with Darbha grass, and having worshipped the deities with flowers, parched grain, food offerings, and gems; and having likewise honored the Brahmins and physicians there, having drawn lines and sprinkled water, having established the Brahma priest to the south, and having kindled the sacred fire.

One should offer oblations of clarified butter with a *sruva* ladle according to the procedure for wooden-offerings (*dārvīhaumika*), using fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of four kinds—khadira, palāśa, devadāru, and bilva—or of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*, namely *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *madhūka*), smeared with curds, honey, and ghee; these offerings should be made with the *mahāvyāhṛtis* accompanied by the *praṇava*. Thereafter, one should perform the *svāhā*-utterance for each deity and for the *ṛṣis*, and cause the disciple to do so as well.

A Brāhmaṇa is entitled to perform the initiation ceremony for members of the three [higher] castes; a Rājanya for two; and a Vaiśya for a Vaiśya alone. Some say that one may also teach a Śūdra who is endowed with noble lineage and good qualities, provided he is not initiated and the sacred mantras are excluded.

Then, having circumambulated the fire three times, he should speak to the disciple in the presence of the fire: "Having abandoned desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, egoism, envy, harshness, calumny, falsehood, laziness, and infamy; being pure, with trimmed nails and hair, wearing saffron-colored garments, and devoted to truth, vows, celibacy, and respectful salutation; you must necessarily remain intent upon going to, staying in, sitting in, eating in, and studying according to my approval, and conduct yourself for my pleasure and welfare. If you act otherwise than this, it will be unrighteousness for you; your knowledge will be fruitless and shall not attain renown."
Or, if while you are conducting yourself correctly I were to perceive otherwise, I would become a partaker of sin and my knowledge would be fruitless.

One must certainly provide medical treatment with one's own medicines for Brahmins, teachers, the poor, friends, renunciants, those who have approached for help, the virtuous, the helpless, and those who have sought refuge—treating them like one's own kinsmen; in this way, it is right. However, one must not treat hunters, fowlers, outcasts, or evildoers; in this way, one’s knowledge shines forth, and one attains friends, fame, virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
And here are the verses [of Bhava]:
"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the two days of its passing away, and likewise on the same days of the bright fortnight; at the two twilights of the day;
during unseasonable lightning and the roar of thunder; and during distresses affecting one's own kingdom or the sovereign."

One should not study while traveling to a cremation ground, during battle, at great festivals, or when witnessing portents; nor should one study on other such occasions where those who have performed the purificatory rites do not study, nor ever while being impure.
Thus ends the second chapter, named "The Initiation of the Disciple," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Third Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter concerning the transmission of study.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
It was previously stated that there are one hundred and twenty chapters in five sections.

Among them, the Sūtrasthāna consists of forty-six chapters; the Nidāna section has sixteen; the Śārīra section has ten; the Cikitsita section has forty; and the Kalpa section has eight. Thus, the latter [four] total sixty-six chapters.

The origin of the Vedas, the method of instruction for disciples, as well as the rules for study and the giving [of knowledge], the teaching and the receiving [of it], the conduct according to the seasons, and then the mechanical [rites].
The chapters on the application of surgical instruments, the preparation of caustics,
the procedures for cauterization and leeches, and the description of blood;
The chapters on the humors, tissues, and wastes, as well as consciousness;
the piercing of the ear, poultices for unripened swellings, medicinal pastes, and the management of wounds.

The inquiry regarding what is beneficial and harmful for wounds, the discharge from wounds individually, the rules concerning what should and should not be done, and the chapter on the enumeration of diseases.

The determination of the methods of surgical instruments, as well as the knowledge of those who have lost consciousness; the extraction of foreign bodies, the knowledge of wounds, and the interpretation of messengers and dreams.
The five faculties, as well as the shadow, the natural state, and likewise the transformation;
the warder-off, the one with a disciplined army, the afflicted, the sequence, and the two belonging to the ground.
The group of substances known as "Mixed" (miśraka) is that which pertains to purification and pacification;
furthermore, there is another group of substances consisting of the knowledge of substances and their specific properties.
This chapter concerns the knowledge of tastes for the purpose of emesis and purgation,
as well as the rules for liquid substances and the rules for food and drink.
Because it indicates, because it strings together, because it extracts, and because it flows with a continuous stream of meaning,
they call this collection of forty-six chapters the Sūtrasthāna.
Diseases of wind (vātavyādhi), hemorrhoids, urinary stones, fistula-in-ano, leprosy, urinary disorders, abdominal enlargements, obstructed labor, abscesses, and erysipelas.
Granthi, vṛddhi, kṣudra, śūka, bhagandara, and diseases of the mouth— these sixteen [chapters] constitute the Nidāna-sthāna by virtue of their exposition of causes and symptoms.
Reflection on the elements, purification from passion, the descent into the womb,
and the prophecy concerning the embryo as well as what is remembered regarding the body.
The detailed description of each vital point (marman), the enumeration of the vessels (sirā),
venesection, the arteries (dhamanī), and likewise the description of the pregnant woman.
These ten bodily constituents have been taught by the Great Sage for the sake of understanding the body, both for physicians and for yogins.
The two types of ulcer treatment, acute fractures, diseases of Vāta,
severe Vāta disorders, hemorrhoids, urinary stones, and fistula-in-ano.

The treatment for the great types of leprosy (kuṣṭha), as well as urinary disorders (meha) such as those caused by honey-like urine (mākṣika) and gravel-like urine (piḍaka), and likewise the treatment for diabetes (makṣumeha) and for those suffering from abdominal enlargements (udarin).
The treatment for obstructed labor, abscesses, erysipelas, glandular swellings,
scrotal enlargements, venereal diseases, as well as minor ailments.
The treatment of the defects of the hair-follicles, as well as that of those suffering from diseases of the mouth;
the prevention of swellings before they arise, and likewise the Miśraka (miscellaneous) section.
That which is aphrodisiac, which brings about the pacification of all diseases when one is emaciated,
which promotes intelligence and longevity, and which wards off natural ailments.
It is proclaimed that sudation, which dispels affliction, is an elixir;
it is also employed for oleation, emesis, and purgation.

The treatment of complications for those two, the classification of enema-nozzles and enema-bags, the successful management of complications of enema-nozzles and enema-bags, and likewise the section on urethral and vaginal enemas.
The procedure known as Nirūha-asti, likewise that known as Ātura-asti,
and finally the Dhūma-nasya procedure— these are recorded as the forty [chapters].
Expiation, pacification, medical treatment, and rites for peace are synonyms; because they are taught therein, this section is called the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsā-sthāna).
The protection of food, both stationary and otherwise,
the knowledge of snakebites and their poisons, and the medical treatment for those very same conditions.
The Dundubhi, Mūṣikā, Kīṭā,
and Kalpa— these eight kalpas are fully described according to their application as antidotes for poison.
Thus, this [work] consisting of one hundred and twenty chapters has been described.
Hereafter, the Uttara-tantra is spoken of by its own name alone.
Since this treatise was composed concerning complications, it is designated as "Opadravika" (The Section on Complications); it is so called because of its preeminence.
Regarding the joints, the eyelids, the white [sclera], the black [iris], and everywhere in the fields of vision—
these chapters are for the purpose of specific identification of each individual disease.
The classification of treatments for vāta-abhiṣyanda,
as well as for that caused by pitta, kapha, and blood; likewise,
the prohibitions regarding scarification and incision, and the procedures for excision in the eyelids and the pupil.
The ritual manual, the striking [of the drum], those arising from the ear, and their medical treatment.
The diagnosis of disorders arising from the nose and their prevention,
the treatment for chronic catarrh, and the classification of diseases of the head.
The treatment of those diseases is called the Śālākya-tantra;
it includes the knowledge of the forms of the nine grahas and the ritual for the warding off of Skanda.
Furthermore, separately for Apasmāra and Śakuni, for Revatī,
and likewise for Pūtanā and Andhā, there are Maṇḍikā and Śītapūtanā.
The medical treatment of Naigameṣa and the origin of the seizing spirits (grahas) along with their birth—
this is proclaimed as the Kaumārabhṛtya-tantra within the section on the body (śārīra).
For those suffering from fever, diarrhea, emaciation, abdominal tumors, heart disease, anemia,
internal hemorrhaging, fainting, and those ailments arising from alcohol consumption;
The prohibition of emesis and hiccup in cases of thirst; [the treatment] for dyspnea and cough;
and the treatment for hoarseness of voice, worms, and upward movement of wind (udāvarta), each separately.
Regarding cholera, loss of appetite, urinary obstruction, and dysuria—
thus the remainder of internal medicine (kāyacikitsā) is proclaimed here.
The prohibition of non-human [possession], as well as another [section] on epilepsy,
and the prohibition of insanity— this is defined as the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā).

The classifications of tastes, the regimen for health, the methodological principles, and those pertaining to the Tantras— these are to be known as the "classifications of the humors" (doṣabheda), which constitute the chapters that adorn the treatise.
Because of its excellence, the great seers call this tantra "Uttara" (the Later);
it is excellent because it contains a compendium of many meanings, and it is also called "Uttara" because it comes last.
The Śālākya-tantra, the Kaumārabhṛtya, the treatment of bodily diseases (Kāyacikitsā),
and Bhūtavidyā— these four constitute the section known as the Uttara-tantra.
The aphrodisiac therapy, the procedure for rejuvenation (rasāyana),
the science of poisons (viṣatantra), the ritual preparations (kalpas), and the knowledge of surgery (śalyajñāna) in its entirety;
Thus, having studied this eight-limbed tantra revealed by the Primordial God according to the prescribed rule, those who apply it become givers of life upon the earth.
For this must certainly be studied, and having studied it, the medical practice must necessarily be mastered; for a physician who knows both [theory and practice] is worthy of a king.
And there are verses on this point:
"But he who knows only the scriptures and is unestablished in practical actions, becomes bewildered when encountering a patient, like a coward entering a battle."
But he who is proficient in ritual acts yet excluded from the scriptures due to audacity does not receive honor among the virtuous; he deserves execution by the king.
Both of these are unskilled and incapable in their own duties;
possessing only half of the Veda, they are like two birds with only one wing.
Herbs that are like nectar become like weapons, lightning, and poison when offered by those who lack knowledge; therefore, one should avoid them.

Those quack physicians who are ignorant of the application of oleation and other such treatments, as well as surgical procedures like incision, destroy people out of greed due to the king's own fault.
But the wise man who knows both is capable of accomplishing his purpose;
he is able to carry out his task in battle like a chariot with two wheels.

Now, my dear child, this very thing should be studied; therefore, attend closely to what I am saying. Then, at the time of study, the teacher should instruct the disciple—who is pure, who has arranged his upper garment, and who stands before him unperturbed—according to his ability, whether it be a word (*pada*), a quarter-verse (*pāda*), or a stanza (*śloka*). These words, quarters, and stanzas should further be synthesized in sequence. Thus, one should join them one by one and recite them oneself, neither too fast nor too slow, without hesitation, without nasalizing, with distinct syllables, without distorting the phonemes, and without gesturing with the eyes, eyebrows, lips, or hands; one should recite them in well-refined tones that are neither too high nor too low.
And no one should pass between those two while they are studying.
And there are these verses on the subject:
"Pure, devoted to the guru, skillful, and free from drowsiness and sleep,
a disciple reciting according to this rule shall reach the end of the scripture."
One who has completed his studies should strive for excellence of speech, comprehension of meaning, eloquence, skill in action, the practice thereof, and its perfection.
Thus ends the third chapter, named "The Transmission of Study," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the discourse.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari himself has said:
Even a study that has been mastered, if its meaning is not articulated, results in nothing but exhaustion—like a load of sandalwood carried by a donkey.
And there is a verse on this point:
Just as a donkey carrying a load of sandalwood knows the weight but not the sandalwood,
so too those who have studied many scriptures but are deluded regarding their meanings carry them like a donkey.

Therefore, this one hundred and twenty chapters, along with its words, quarters, and verses, must be described and studied. Why? Because the subtle distinctions regarding substances, tastes, qualities, potencies, post-digestive effects, defects, tissues, impurities, receptacles, vital points (*marma*), vessels, ligaments, joints, bones, the formation of the fetus, and the classification of the collection of substances—as well as the extraction of lost foreign bodies, the determination of wounds, the varieties of fractures, and the curability, maintainability, or incurability of diseases—these and thousands of other such particulars, when contemplated, would confound even the intellect of one possessed of pure and vast intelligence, let alone that of one with little intelligence. Therefore, it must necessarily be described and studied word by word, quarter by quarter, and verse by verse.

Furthermore, regarding those matters established in other treatises that are introduced here by virtue of their meaning, one should follow the explanations from those who are experts in those very [other] sciences; for it is not possible within a single treatise to encompass all treatises.
And there are verses on this point:
"One who studies a single treatise will not attain certainty regarding the science;
therefore, a physician should understand the science through extensive learning."

He who, having received the scripture uttered from the mouth of his guru and having studied it repeatedly, performs the medical treatment—he alone is a true physician; others, however, are merely thieves.
One should designate these as the roots of the remaining systems of surgery (Śalyatantra): the Aupadhenava, the Aurabhra, the Sauśruta, and the Pauṣkalāvata.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "The Exposition," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Fifth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the preliminary procedures for treatment.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
Action is threefold—prior action, primary action, and subsequent action—and we shall explain these with respect to disease.
In this treatise, because the ritual action of the scripture is primary, we shall first explain that very ritual action along with its necessary requisites.
And that surgical procedure is of eight kinds, namely: excision, incision, scarification, puncturing, probing, extraction, drainage, and suturing.

Therefore, a physician desiring to perform any other medical procedure must first prepare the following: instruments, surgical tools, caustics, cautery, probes, horns, leeches, gourds, rose-apple-shaped applicators, cotton swabs, threads, leaves, bandages, honey, ghee, muscle fat, milk, oil, saturating agents, decoctions, ointments, pastes, fans, cold and warm water, cauldrons, and so forth; as well as attendants who are gentle, steady, and strong.

Then, on an auspicious lunar day, karana, muhurta, and nakshatra, having honored the fire, the Brahmins, and the physicians with curd, unbroken rice, food, drink, and jewels, and having performed the offerings, auspicious rites, and recitation of benedictions, the physician—having seated the patient facing east after he has eaten lightly and being secured by a splint—should face west and, avoiding the vital spots (marmans), veins, ligaments, joints, bones, and arteries, insert the instrument in the direction of the hair until the pus is seen; he should extract the instrument in a single stroke quickly, and even in cases of large abscesses, the site for the instrument is said to be two or three finger-breadths apart.
In this regard, the qualities of a wound are that it be long, wide, even, well-proportioned, and independent;
and concerning this, there are the following [verses]: "Long, wide, well-proportioned, and independent."
Furthermore, a wound treated at the appropriate time is commended for the performance of ritual action.
Courage, swiftness of action, sharpness of the instrument, absence of perspiration and trembling,
and lack of confusion are praised in a physician performing surgical procedures.
Or, while not being purified by means of a single wound, one should not, out of a sense of cleverness, create other wounds in the interim.
And there is a verse on this point:
"In whatever direction one perceives the movement, and wherever the swelling is located,
one should make an incision right there so that the morbid humor does not remain."
In that regard, it is taught that the incision is made transversely on the eyebrows, cheeks, temples, forehead, eye-sockets, lips, gums, armpits, flanks, and groins.

The wise physician should perform incisions on the hands and feet shaped like the lunar disc, and likewise in the anus and the penis, in the form of half-moons. Otherwise, however, there will be excessive cutting of vessels and ligaments, intense pain, delayed healing of the wound, and the appearance of fleshy nodules.
In cases of obstructed labor, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, urinary stones, fistula-in-ano, and diseases of the mouth, one should perform the medical procedure on an empty stomach.

Then, having applied the surgical instrument and comforted the patient with cold water, one should press the wound all around with a finger, rub it, wash it with a decoction, and taking water boiled [with herbs], insert a medicinal wick (varti) composed of sesame paste, honey, and clarified butter, enriched with medicinal drugs, neither too oily nor too dry. Then, having covered it with the paste and applied a thick poultice (kavalikā), one should bind it with a cloth bandage. One should fumigate it with incenses that destroy pain and demons, and provide protection with mantras that destroy demons.

Then, one should fumigate [the area] with powders of guggulu, aguru, sarjarasa, vacā, and white mustard seeds, mixed with salt and nimba leaves and combined with clarified butter; and with the remainder of the clarified butter, one should touch the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the [deity].
Taking water from a water-pot, one should perform the rite of protection while sprinkling [it]. We shall explain that for the purpose of counteracting *kṛtyās* as well as the fear of *rākṣasas*:
"I shall perform the rite of protection; may Brahmā grant his approval to that."
May Nāgas, Piśācas, Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas—
whoever may rush toward you— be forever slain by Brahmā and the other gods.
May those night-stalkers who roam upon the earth and in the atmosphere,
as well as those dwelling in the quarters and in the homesteads, protect you when they are saluted with reverence.
May the sages protect you with the power of Brahmā, as well as the divine royal seers,
the mountains, all the rivers, and all the oceans.
May Agni protect your tongue, and Vāyu likewise your vital breaths;
may Soma protect your diffused breath (vyāna), and Parjanya protect your downward breath (apāna).
May the lightnings protect the *udāna* breath, and the thunders the *samāna*.
May Indra, the lord of strength, protect my strength; and may Manu likewise protect my intellect.
May the Gandharvas protect your desires; may Indra guard your vital strength;
may King Varuṇa protect your wisdom; and may the Ocean protect the circle of your navel.
May the Sun protect your eye, the Quarters your ears, and the Moon your mind;
may the stars always protect your form, and the nights your shadow.
May the waters nourish your semen, as well as the hair and the herbs;
may space protect your orifices, and may the earth protect your body.
May Vaiśvānara protect your head; Viṣṇu, your prowess; Puruṣottama, your manly strength; Brahmā, your self; and Dhruva, your two eyebrows.
These deities indeed reside eternally within your body in particular;
may they protect you constantly, and may you attain a long life.
May the Blessed Brahmā grant you well-being, and may the gods likewise grant you well-being;
may the Moon and the Sun grant you well-being, and may Nārada and Parvata grant you well-being;
may Agni and Vāyu grant you well-being, and may the gods together with Indra grant you well-being.
May the protection bestowed by your grandfather increase your well-being and longevity;
may your calamities be pacified, and may you always remain free from affliction.
Thus, svāhā!
By these mantras, which are the very essence of the Vedas and which destroy misfortune and disease,
and by me having thus performed this protection, may you attain a long life.
Then, having caused the patient to enter the chamber where protection has been established, he should instruct the attendant.
Then, on the third day, having loosened it, he should bind it in this very same manner with a cloth band; and he should not release it the following day in haste.
A wound that is not bandaged after being released on the second day heals slowly and remains intensely painful.
From this point forward, one should prescribe decoctions, ointments, bandages, diets, and modes of conduct after having considered the strength of the doshas, the time, and other such factors.
And one should not, in haste, cause it to heal while internal defects remain; for even with a slight lapse in care, it may form an internal abscess and become disturbed once again.
On this subject, there are also these verses:
Therefore, one should ensure that the wound is well-healed both internally and externally.
Even when healed, one should avoid indigestion, physical exercise, sexual intercourse,
and the like, as well as joy, anger, and fear, until firmness has been fully restored.

A wise man should release [the cattle] during the winter, the cool season, and the spring; likewise, he should release them every three days in autumn and summer, and every two days during the rainy season.
In cases of excessively fatal diseases, a physician should not wait for this [standard] procedure;
rather, he should act with immediate countermeasures, as if a house were on fire.
Whatever intense pain arises from the falling of a weapon and consumes the body of a living being,
that finds relief when sprinkled with lukewarm ghee mixed with *yaṣṭīmadhuka*.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, named "The Extraction of Foreign Bodies," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Sixth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the seasonal regimen (*ṛtucarya*).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Time, indeed, is the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, without beginning, middle, or end; upon it depend the success or failure of human tastes, as well as the life and death of men. He does not dissolve even a subtle fraction [of existence]; thus he is "Kāla. He either sums up all beings or drives them along, and for this reason he is called Kāla.

The Blessed Sun, by means of his specific movements, effects the division of that year-soul into nimeshas, kāṣṭhās, kalās, muhūrtas, days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons, solstices, years, and yugas.

In this context, the twinkling of an eye (*akṣinimeṣa*) consists of the mere utterance of a short syllable; fifteen twinklings of the eye make a *kāṣṭhā*; thirty *kāṣṭhās* make a *kalā*; twenty *kalās* plus one-tenth of a *kalā* make a *muhūrta*; thirty *muhūrtas* make a day and night (*ahorātra*); fifteen days and nights make a fortnight (*pakṣa*), which is of two kinds: the bright (*śukla*) and the dark (*kṛṣṇa*); these two constitute a month (*māsa*).

In this regard, a year consists of twelve months beginning with Māgha; by grouping them into two-month periods, there are six seasons: namely, the cool season (śiśira), spring (vasanta), summer (grīṣma), the rainy season (varṣā), autumn (śarad), and winter (hemanta). Of these, the months of Tapas and Tapasya constitute the cool season; Madhu and Mādhava, the spring; Śuci and Śukra, the summer; Nabhas and Nabhasya, the rainy season; Iṣa and Ūrja, the autumn; and Sahas and Sahasya, the winter.

These two solstices—the southern and the northern—of the moon and the sun, characterized by cold, heat, and rain, bring about the divisions of time. Of these two, the southern [solstice] consists of the rainy season, autumn, and winter; during these, the Lord Soma waxes full, and the tastes become sour, salty, and sweet and grow powerful. Furthermore, the strength of all living beings increases progressively.

And as for the north, there are the seasons of late winter, spring, and summer; during these, the blessed sun draws strength, and bitter, astringent, and pungent tastes become powerful, while the strength of all living beings gradually diminishes further and further.
And there is a verse on this point:
"The moon moistens the earth, and the sun dries it;
yet relying upon both of them, the wind protects all living beings."

Now, indeed, two solstices (ayana) together constitute a year; five of those receive the designation of a "yuga. This very time, beginning with a blink of an eye (nimeṣa) and ending with a yuga, revolving like a wheel, is called the "Wheel of Time" (kālacakra), according to some.

In this context, however, there are six seasons—rainy, autumn, winter, spring, summer, and the monsoon—which serve as the causes for the accumulation, provocation, and pacification of the *doṣas*. These are explained in terms of two-month periods beginning with Bhādrapada: namely, Bhādrapada and Āśvayuja are the rainy season; Kārtika and Mārgaśīrṣa are autumn; Pauṣa and Māgha are winter; Phālguna and Caitra are spring; Vaiśākha and Jyeṣṭha are summer; and Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa are the monsoon.

During the rainy season, the medicinal herbs are young and of little potency, and the waters are turbid and mostly composed of earthy sediment. When these are consumed by living beings whose bodies are drenched by the rain-soaked earth while the sky is covered with clouds, their digestive fire is suppressed by the cold wind, leading to a burning sensation (*vidāha*). This burning produces an accumulation of *pitta*. In autumn, when the clouds have thinned from the sky, that accumulated *pitta* dries up in the mud as it is melted by the rays of the sun, thereby generating *pitta*-derived diseases.

Those very same medicinal herbs, through the transformation of time, become potent and powerful in the winter; likewise, the waters become clear, unctuous, and exceedingly heavy. When these are consumed by embodied beings whose bodies are supported by frosty winds due to the mild rays of the sun, they—being undigested because of their oiliness, coldness, heaviness, and coating quality—bring about an accumulation of *śleṣman* (phlegm). That accumulated [phlegm], melted by the rays of the sun in spring, gives rise to diseases characterized by *śleṣman* in those beings whose bodies are somewhat stiffened.

Those very same medicinal herbs become sapless, parched, and excessively light during the summer, and so too do the waters. When these are consumed by living beings whose bodies have been withered by the heat of the sun, they cause an accumulation of *vāyu* (wind) due to their dryness, lightness, and clarity. That accumulated *vāyu*, when the rains arrive and the earth is excessively saturated with water, provokes *vātika* diseases in living beings whose bodies are moistened by cold winds and rain. Thus has the cause for the accumulation and provocation of the *doṣas* been explained.
In that regard, the elimination of the humors (doṣas) accumulated during the rainy season, winter, and summer, as well as those aggravated during autumn, spring, and the monsoon, must be performed.

Among those, the pacification of bile-related diseases occurs naturally in winter, that of phlegm-related diseases in summer, and that of wind-related diseases in autumn; thus have these accumulations, aggravations, and pacifications been explained.

In that regard, one should observe the signs of spring in the forenoon, summer at midday, the rainy season in the afternoon, the monsoon at dusk, autumn at midnight, and winter at dawn; in this manner, one should understand even a single day and night to be like a year, characterized by cold, heat, and rain, through the accumulation, provocation, and pacification of the bodily humors (doṣas).
In that regard, when the seasons are unimpaired, the medicinal herbs and the waters become unimpaired; and when these are consumed, they promote life, longevity, strength, vigor, and vitality.
Furthermore, their misfortunes are caused by unseen forces; indeed, cold, heat, wind, and rain become adverse, destroying medicinal plants and waters.
From the consumption of these, there will arise the manifestation of various diseases or even a pestilence.
In that regard, there is the consumption of non-toxic medicinal herbs and water.

Sometimes, even when the seasons are not disturbed, the populations of the countryside are afflicted by sorcery, curses, the wrath of *rakṣas* demons, or unrighteousness; or that region is assailed by winds carrying the scent of poisonous herbs and flowers. There, due to the specific nature of the local humors (*doṣa*), people suffer from coughs, vomiting, catarrh, headaches, and fevers; or [they are afflicted] by the movements of planets and constellations, or by the appearance of ominous signs and marks on houses, wives, beds, seats, vehicles, mounts, jewels, and utensils.

In that regard, one must remain devoted to abandoning unsuitable places, performing rites for peace, expiatory ceremonies, auspicious recitations, burnt offerings, oblations, worship, joining the palms in reverence, salutations, austerity, observances, compassion, charity, the undertaking of initiation, and toward deities, Brahmins, and teachers; in this way, it becomes successful.
Hereafter, we shall describe the characteristics of the seasons when they have not undergone any abnormality.
A cold wind blows from the north; the quarters of the sky are filled with dust and smoke;
the sun is obscured by frost, and the reservoirs of water are frozen over with ice.
In the month called Himasāhvaya (Mārgaśīrṣa), the ravens, rhinoceroses, buffaloes, rams, and elephants become arrogant,
while the *rodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, and *puṃnāga* trees are in full bloom.
In the winter season, the cold is excessive and the quarters of the sky are agitated by wind and rain;
the wise should understand that all other characteristics are to be known as being like those of the late autumn (hemanta).
On Mount Malaya, marked by the red lac from the feet of the wives of the accomplished Vidyādharas,
and perfumed by the embrace of sandalwood creepers;
In spring, the southern wind blows, generating joy for those filled with desire, kindling the god of love, and shattering the jealous pride of couples.
In spring, the quarters of the sky became stainless and were adorned with forests blooming with *kiṃśuka*,
lotus, *bakula*, mango, *aśoka*, and other flowers.
Charming with the songs of flocks of cuckoos and bees,
embraced by the southern breeze, they were beautiful-faced and radiant with new sprouts.
In summer, the sun has fierce rays, the wind from the southwest is unpleasant,
the earth is scorched, the rivers are diminished, and the quarters of the sky seem as if they are ablaze.
Deer with pairs of wheels appearing blurred from the agitation of drinking water;
with shrubs, grasses, and creepers destroyed; and trees marked by the loss of their leaves.
In the rainy season, the sky was covered by clouds driven by the western winds,
flashing with lightning and emitting tumultuous sounds.
The earth is rich with tender, dark-green grass, radiant with *śakragopa* insects,
and adorned with *kadamba*, *nīpa*, *kuṭaja*, *sarja*, and *ketaki* trees.
There, during the rainy season, the rivers have their banks and trees submerged by water;
the ponds are resplendent with blossoming white and blue lotuses.
The earth was filled with unmanifested tracts and chasms, yet adorned with abundant crops;
the sky was obscured by clouds thundering and raining incessantly, such that the sun and planets were hidden from view.
In autumn, the sun is tawny and warm, and the sky is as pure as a white cloud;
likewise, the lakes shine with lotuses brushed against by the shoulders of swans.
The ground was strewn with mud and withered trees, and it was adorned with uneven and level stretches,
as well as with *bāṇa*, *saptāhva*, *bandhūka*, *kāśa*, and *asan* flowers.

In embodied beings, the humors (doṣas) become aggravated during the seasons, whether those seasons are endowed with their own characteristic qualities, or are contrary to them, or even when they are irregular.
One should eliminate phlegm in spring and eliminate bile in autumn;
one should pacify wind during the rainy season, before the aggravation of the disorders occurs.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, named "The Regimen According to the Seasons," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Seventh Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the procedure for surgical instruments.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

Among the one hundred and one machines, understand that the hand alone is the most important of all machines. Why? Because without the hand, there is simply no operation of machines, since the functioning of machines is dependent upon it.
In that context, "shafts" (śalya) are those things that cause affliction to the mind and body; the instruments (yantra) are the means for their extraction.
These are of six types, namely: swastika-instruments, pincer-instruments, lock-instruments, tube-instruments, probe-instruments, and accessory instruments.

In that regard, there are twenty-four *svastika* instruments, two *saṃdaṃśa* instruments, two *tāla* instruments, twenty tubes (*nāḍī*), twenty-eight probes (*śalākā*), and twenty-five secondary instruments (*upayantra*).
These are generally made of iron, or of materials resembling it, in the absence of such.

In that regard, the mouths of various kinds of predatory beasts, wild animals, and birds are generally similar to the mouths of machines; therefore, one should have them constructed based on that similarity, according to traditional authority, instruction, observation of other machines, and logical reasoning.
One should have the mechanical devices made well-balanced, with surfaces both rough and smooth, very firm, well-formed, and easy to grasp.

In that regard, the *svastika* instruments, measuring eighteen finger-breadths in length, are prescribed for the purpose of extracting splinters lodged in bone. They are fashioned with the faces of a lion, tiger, wolf, hyena, bear, leopard, cat, jackal, *airāvaka*, crow, heron, osprey, vulture, hawk, partridge, crane, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *añjalikarṇa*, *avabhañjana*, and *nandīmukha*; they are secured by pegs shaped like lentils (*masūra*) and have curved handles at their base resembling elephant goads (*aṅkuśa*).

The *sanigraha* and *anigraha* are two types of forceps (*saṃdaṃśau*) sixteen finger-breadths in length; they are prescribed for the purpose of extracting foreign bodies located within the vessels, muscles, veins, and ligaments.

The *tālayantra* (pincer instrument), twelve finger-breadths in length, resembling the pincers of a fish and having one or two blades, is for the purpose of extracting foreign bodies from the ears, nose, and channels.

Tubular instruments (nāḍīyantra) are also of many types and serve many purposes; they may have a single opening or two openings, and are used for the purpose of extracting foreign bodies lodged in channels, for examining diseases, for suction, and for facilitating surgical procedures. They should correspond in circumference to the orifice of the channel and be of appropriate lengths. Among them, we shall describe later the instruments for fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, ulcers, enemas (vasti), urethral enemas (uttarabasti), scrotal hernia, abdominal dropsy, fumigation, intestinal obstruction, strangulation, anal stenosis, as well as the gourd (alābu) and horn instruments.

There are also various types of probes (*śalākāyantra*) for various purposes, with widths and lengths as appropriate. Two each are taught with heads shaped like a *gaṇḍūpada* worm, a snake’s hood, an arrow-shaft, and a fishhook, for the purposes of probing, spreading, moving, and extracting [foreign bodies]. Two have mouths the size of a lentil leaf and slightly curved tips, for the purpose of extracting splinters located within the channels. Six are made of cotton with a turban-like head for wiping; three are spoon-shaped with a hollow mouth for applying alkaline medicine; three others have faces like a jackal’s mouth; and three have faces like a hook—these six are intended for cauterization (*agnikarma*). One has a mouth the size of a jujube stone fragment with a hollow and sharp lip, for extracting polyps from the nose. One is for applying collyrium (*añjana*), being the size of a pea in circumference with bud-like tips at both ends.
For the purpose of purifying the urinary tract, there is one [instrument] which is circular in size, measuring the tip of a stalk of a *mālatī* flower.

The instruments for inducing vomiting are also as follows: a rope, a braid of hair, a cloth, leather, the inner bark of trees, a creeper, a garment, a stone, a mallet, the hand, the sole of the foot, the fingers, the tongue, the teeth, the nails, the mouth, the tail of a horse, a bracelet, a branch, expectoration, purging, exhilaration, magnets, alkali, fire, and medicinal drugs.
One should apply these, as appropriate, throughout the entire body, as well as to its specific parts, the joints, the abdominal cavity, and the vessels.

The mechanical operations, however, are twenty-fourfold: striking, filling, binding, arranging, turning, moving, revolving, opening, pressing, clearing the path, drawing out, taking away, cutting, raising, lowering, breaking, churning, sucking, searching, splitting, straightening, washing, blowing, and wiping.
Furthermore, the wise physician should analyze the functions of the instruments with his own intellect;
for it is certain that darts possess innumerable variations.

In that regard, there are twelve defects of the instrument: being too thick, lacking substance, too long, too short, not grasping [the bone], grasping unevenly, crooked, loose, too high, having a soft peg, having a soft tip, and having a soft noose.
A mechanical device (yantra) eighteen finger-breadths in length, free from these defects, should be known by physicians as excellent; indeed, one should employ it in medical procedures.

A visible foreign body should be extracted using instruments with lion-like faces and so forth, while a concealed one should be removed slowly using those with heron-beak faces and so forth, in accordance with the medical treatises and logical reasoning.
For it does not recoil, it penetrates well, and having seized the barb, it extracts it.
Therefore, among mechanical devices, the *kaṅkamukha* (heron-beaked) is the most important, and it is effective in all positions.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, named "The Procedure for Instruments," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Eighth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the application of surgical instruments.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

There are twenty types of surgical instruments, namely: the *maṇḍalāgra* (round-topped), *karapatra* (saw), *vṛddhipatra* (scalpel), *nakhaśastra* (nail-clippers), *mudrikā* (ring), *utpalapatra* (lotus-leaf-shaped), *ardhadhāra* (half-edged), *sūcī* (needle), *kuśapatra* (grass-leaf-shaped), *āṭīmukha* (crow-beak-shaped), *śarārimukha* (hawk-beak-shaped), *antarmukha* (inward-pointing), *trikūrcaka* (three-bristled), *kuṭhārikā* (small axe), *vrīhimukha* (rice-ear-shaped), *ārā* (awl), *vetasapatra* (cane-leaf-shaped), *baḍiśa* (fish-hook), *danta* (tooth-shaped), and *śaṅku* (probe).

Among these, the *maṇḍalāgra* and *karapatra* are used for excision and incision; the *vṛddhipatra*, *nakhaśastra*, *mudrikā*, and *utpalapatra-ardhadhārā* are for excision and division; the *sūcī*, *kuśapatrāṭīmukha*, *śarārimukha*, *antarmukha*, and *trikūrcaka* are for bloodletting; the *kuṭhārikā*, *vrīhimukha*, and *ārāvetasapatra* are for piercing; the *sūcī*, *baḍiśa*, and *dantaśaṅku* are for extraction; and the various *sūcīs* (needles) are for probing, searching, and suturing. Thus, the application of surgical instruments (*śastra*) in eight types of procedures has been explained.

Now, the method for grasping these instruments according to their respective requirements will be explained in the section on surgical procedures (*karma*). Among them, one should grasp the lancet (*vṛddhipattra*) at the portion common to both the handle and the blade; all other types of lancets should be grasped in this same manner. The circular-headed lancet (*maṇḍalāgra*) and the lancet should be applied repeatedly for scraping with the hand slightly turned upward. For bloodletting (*visrāvaṇa*), one should especially use a triple-pronged instrument (*trikūrcaka*) for children, the elderly, the delicate, the timid, women, kings, and princes. One should hold the handle concealed by the palm with the thumb and index finger; the rice-mouthed lancet (*vrīhimukha*) or the small axe (*kuṭhārikā*) should be held in the left hand and struck with the middle finger of the other hand while it is pressed against the thumb. The saws (*ārā*), the leaf-shaped instruments (*karapatra*), and the probes (*eṣaṇī*) should be grasped at the base; as for the remaining instruments, they should be grasped according to their specific requirements.
Their forms are for the most part explained by their very names.

In this regard, regarding the instruments for nails and surgical probes, the needles will be described as being eight finger-breadths (aṅgula) long. A ring [measuring] the size of the proximal phalanx of the index finger is ten finger-breadths long; it has a mouth like that of a *śarāri* bird and is called a "scissors" (*kartarī*). The remaining instruments, however, are six finger-breadths long.
These weapons are easy to grasp, made of good metal, well-edged, handsome in appearance, with well-proportioned tips, and not jagged; such is the excellence of weapons.
In this regard, there are eight defects of a surgical instrument: being curved, blunt, jagged, having a rough edge, being excessively thick, excessively thin, excessively long, or excessively short.

One should therefore take up an instrument possessing qualities contrary to these; however, this does not apply to the saw (*karapatra*), for that indeed has a rough edge for the purpose of cutting bone.

In that regard, the *dhārā* (edge) of instruments for piercing is like a lentil (*māsūrī*); for scraping, it is half a lentil; for puncturing and draining, it is like a hair (*kaiśikī*); and for excising, it is half a hair.
The hook (baḍiśa) and the tooth-pike (dantaśaṅku) have curved tips;
the probes (eṣaṇī) are shaped like sharp thorns, the first barley-leaf, or the head of a woodlouse.
Their irrigation is of three kinds: with alkaline water, with water, and with oil.

Among these, irrigation with alkaline water is for cutting out arrows, splinters, and bones; irrigation with water is for cutting, piercing, and lancing flesh; and irrigation with oil is for venesection and cutting tendons.
For the purpose of sharpening them, there is a smooth stone the color of mung beans; for the purpose of establishing the edge, there is a board made of śālmalī wood.

And there is a verse on this point: When the blade is well-sharpened, capable of cutting hair, well-proportioned, and firmly grasped with the correct measure, then one should employ it in the various tasks.
The secondary instruments (anuśastra), however, are: bamboo-sap, crystal, glass, kuruvinda stone, leeches, fire, alkali, the nail, gojī, śephālikā, leaf-shoots, and the hair of the fingers.

A wise physician should employ the fourfold group beginning with *tvaksāra* (bamboo) for those who are children, those who are fearful of weapons, or when weapons are unavailable, as well as for excision.

One should employ the nail on those [foreign bodies] that are removable, excisable, or fissurable, provided they are capable of being so treated; the procedure for alkaline substances, fire, and leeches shall be explained hereafter.
Whatever diseases may be located in the mouth or in the eyelids,
one should cause them to drain by means of the leaves of *gojī*, *sephālikā*, and *śāka*.
If these desired instruments cannot be obtained, then the fingers and sprouts of a child are beneficial;
however, a wise man should have these tools made from pure iron by a skilled smith who has mastered his craft.
Success always attends the physician who knows the proper application;
therefore, one should constantly cultivate familiarity with the handling of surgical instruments.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Application of Surgical Instruments," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Ninth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules for training (Yogyāsūtrīya).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Even if a disciple has mastered the meaning of all the treatises, one should still cause them to undergo the preparatory training (*yogyā*). One should instruct them in the course of action regarding [procedures such as] affectionate treatments, incisions, and so forth. For even one who is very well-versed in learning becomes unfit for clinical procedures if they have not undergone this training.

In that regard, one should demonstrate the various types of incision on flowers, fruits, gourds (*alābu*), *kālindaka*, *trapusa*, *ervāruka*, *karkārūka*, and so forth; and one should instruct on excision (*utkartana*) and dissection (*parikartana*). One should demonstrate the suitability for puncture (*bhedyayogyā*) on inflated skins such as bellows (*dṛti*), bladders (*vasti*), and pouches (*prasevaka*) filled with water or mud; on hair-bearing stretched leather; and on the veins of dead animals and lotus stalks. One should demonstrate the suitability for scarification (*lekhyasya*) on wood, bamboo, or reed tubes damaged by wood-worms (*ghuṇa*), and on the openings of dried gourds. One should demonstrate the suitability for extraction (*eṣyasya*) on the marrow of the fruit of the *panasa*, *bimbī*, and *bilva* trees, and on the teeth of dead animals. One should demonstrate the suitability for draining (*visrāvyasya*) on a board of *śālmali* wood smeared with beeswax. One should demonstrate the suitability for suturing (*sīvyasya*) between the edges of fine, thick cloth or between the edges of soft leather. And one should demonstrate the suitability for bandaging (*bandhanayogyā*) on the various major and minor limbs of a mannequin made of cloth (*pusta*).

[The physician should practice] on soft skin and flesh-muscles, as well as on lotus stalks, for the purpose of joining ear-joints; on soft pieces of flesh, for the application of cautery and caustic; and on the side-holes of water-filled jars, the mouth of a gourd, and so forth, for the purpose of inserting catheters, enemas, and applying pressure to wounds.
And on this point, you two [the authors] have said:
"In such cases as these, a wise man who performs the appropriate ritual upon substances that are fit and worthy according to the rule does not become confused in his actions."

Therefore, one seeking skill in the applications of the scalpel, caustics, and fire should employ whatever is appropriate in each case, according to its similarity to the specific procedure required here.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, named "The Chapter on the Training of Disciples," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Tenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on entering the surgical ward (viśikhānupraveśanīya).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

A physician who has mastered the tantras, who has meditated upon the meaning of the tantras, who has observed the practical applications, who has completed his training, who recites the scriptures, who is authorized by the king, whose nails and hair are trimmed, who is pure, dressed in white garments, carrying an umbrella, holding a staff, wearing sandals, whose appearance is not arrogant, who is well-disposed, whose speech is auspicious, who is free from deceit, who is a friend to all beings, and who possesses good assistants, may enter at night.

Then, having approached the patient's house in accordance with favorable signs from messengers, omens, and auspicious portents, he should sit down, observe the patient, touch him, and question him; for some say that diseases are generally to be known by these three means of cognition. However, that is not correct, for there are sixfold means of cognizing diseases, namely: by the five [senses] beginning with hearing, and by questioning.

Among these, the specific qualities perceivable by the sense of hearing will be described in the chapters on diseases such as "Knowledge of Wound Exudations" (*Vraṇāsrāva-vijñānīya*) and others, beginning with: "The wind, expelling blood along with foam, issues forth with a sound," and so forth. The specific qualities of touch perceivable by the sense of touch—such as cold, heat, smoothness, roughness, softness, and hardness—are found in conditions like fever and swelling. Those perceivable by the sense of sight include the increase or decrease of bodily bulk, signs of longevity, strength, and changes in complexion. Those perceivable by the sense of taste are the specific tastes found in urinary disorders (*prameha*) and the like. Those perceivable by the sense of smell are the specific odors of both wounds and non-wounds, as seen in the signs of impending death (*ariṣṭa*) and other such cases.

One should ascertain [the patient's condition] through questioning regarding place, time, caste, suitability, the origin of the disease, the intensity of the pain, strength, the digestive fire, the passage or non-passage of wind, urine, and feces, and specific details such as the duration of the illness;
one should learn these from those who resemble oneself in their means of acquiring knowledge.
And there is a verse on this point:
"For disorders caused by wrong views,
as well as those poorly explained and poorly treated, may lead even a physician into delusion."
One should manage those that are incurable but not undertake treatment; generally, one should avoid treating disorders that have persisted for a full year.
Among those, even curable diseases generally become most difficult to treat for the following:

Vedic scholars, kings, women, children, the elderly, the timid, royal servants, gamblers, the powerful, physicians, the clever, those afflicted by chronic illness, cowherds, the poor, the wretched, the irascible, and those who lack self-control or are without a protector. Having thus diagnosed, one who administers treatment attains virtue, wealth, pleasure, and fame.
And there is a verse on this point:
One should avoid living together with women and engaging in jesting with them; furthermore, the best of physicians should not give them anything other than food, even if it has been offered.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Entry into the Surgical Ward," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The eleventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the method for cooking alkaline preparations (kṣārapāka).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Among primary and secondary surgical instruments, the alkali (kṣāra) is the most important, because it performs the functions of cutting, piercing, and scraping; because it destroys the three doṣas; and because it is employed for specialized therapeutic procedures.
In that regard, it is called *kṣāra* because of its dissolving (*kṣaraṇa*) or its cutting (*kṣaṇana*).

Due to the combination of various medicinal herbs, it destroys the three *doṣas*; due to its whiteness, it is *saumya* (lunar in nature). Although it is *saumya*, its power to burn, digest, and cleave is not contradictory; for it abounds in the qualities of fiery (*āgneya*) herbs. It is pungent, hot, sharp, digestive, liquefying, purifying, healing, drying, astringent, and scraping. When consumed excessively, it destroys worms, undigested matter (*āmadoṣa*), phlegm (*kapha*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), poisons, and fat, as well as virility.
It is of two kinds: that which is to be removed and that which is water.

In that regard, the procedure of *pratisāraṇīya* (rubbing with medicinal paste) is prescribed for leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), *kiṭibha*, ringworm (*dadru-maṇḍala*), vitiligo (*kilāsa*), fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), tumors (*arbuḍa*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), malignant ulcers (*duṣṭavraṇa*), sinus tracts (*nāḍī*), corns (*carma-kīla*), moles (*tilaka-alaka*), *nyaccha*, freckles (*yaṅga*), external abscesses caused by mosquitoes (*maśaka-bāhya-vidradhi*), worms (*kṛmi*), poisons (*viṣa*), and so forth; as well as in the seven diseases of the mouth—specifically sublingual swelling (*upajihvā*), epiglottis swelling (*adhijihvā*), inflammation of the gums (*upakuśa*), and *danta-vaidarbha*—and in the three types of *rohiṇī*. It is stated that the application of the instrument follows immediately after these [treatments].

Pānīya, however, is beneficial for treating goiters, abdominal tumors, loss of digestive fire, indigestion, anorexia, constipation, gravel, urinary stones, internal abscesses, worms, poison, and hemorrhoids.

It is, however, harmful for those suffering from internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), fever, or a Pitta constitution; for children, the elderly, and the weak; and for those afflicted by vertigo, intoxication, fainting, or blurred vision, as well as others of a similar condition.
If one should burn that like alkali and strain it, its detailed procedure is explained elsewhere.
Now, the other [type] is threefold: mild, moderate, and sharp.

Desiring to prepare it, one should, in the autumn, having fasted while pure on an auspicious day, consecrate a large, dark *muṣkaka* tree that grows on a mountain ridge—uninjured, of middle age, and born in an auspicious location. On the following day, having split it and cut it into pieces, and having carved it out, one should pile it up in a windless place, mix in lime-dust, and set it ablaze with dried reeds. Then, when the fire has subsided, one should collect the ashes separately and the lime-dust.

Then, by this very procedure, one should burn the roots, fruits, leaves, and branches of *kuṭaja*, *palāśa*, *aśvakarṇa*, *pāribhadraka*, *bibhītaka*, *āragvadha*, *tilvaka*, *arka*, *snuhī*, *apāmārga*, *pāṭalā*, *naktamāla*, *vṛṣa*, *kadala*, *citraka*, *pūtīka*, *indravṛkṣa*, *āsphotā*, *aśvamāraka*, *saptacchada*, *agnimantha*, *guñjā*, and the four kinds of *kośātakī*.

Then, having stirred one *droṇa* of the resulting alkali with six *droṇas* of water or with the aforementioned urines twenty-one times, one should boil it slowly in a large cauldron while stirring it gently with a ladle until it has been strained.
When it becomes clear, red, sharp, and slimy, one should take it, strain it through a large cloth, separate the other [impurities], and place it back on the fire according to the rule.
From that very salt-water, one should remove a *kuḍava* or a half-*kuḍava*.

Then, having made pieces of *kaṭa*, sugar, ashes, sugar, milk-curd (*kṣīrapāka*), and conch-shell navel (*śaṅkhanābhi*) red-hot like fire, one should pour them into that very same iron vessel containing the alkaline water, grind them, and having added eight *palas*—the prescribed measure for the conch-nave and the other ingredients—to those two *droṇas* of liquid, one should cook it while stirring constantly and vigilantly. One should strive so that it becomes neither too thick nor too thin. Then, having removed it from the heat once the cooking is complete, one should place it in a covered iron jar with its mouth sealed; this is the medium consistency.
This very [mixture], cooked without any addition, is the soft *saṃvyūhima*.

For the additive (*pratīvāpa*), equal parts of finely powdered *dantī*, *dravantī*, *citraka*, *lāṅgalakī*, *pūtika-pravāla*, *tālapattrī*, *viḍa*, *suvarcikā*, *kanakakṣīrī*, *hiṅgu*, *vacā*, and *ativiṣā*—measuring one *śukti* each—are added according to availability.
That same [preparation], when cooked with this additive, is called *sapratīvāpa*; it is *pākya* (requiring cooking) and is sharp (*tīkṣṇa*).
Their application should be according to the strength of the disease.
But when its strength has diminished, one should pour in alkaline water for the purpose of restoring its strength.
And on this point, the masters have said: "Neither too sharp nor mild, white, smooth, and slimy;
non-driping, auspicious, and swift—thus is alkaline fluid (kṣāra) traditionally held to possess eight qualities."
Excessive softness, coldness, heat, sharpness,
sliminess, oiliness, thickness, under-ripeness, and deficiency of constituent substances are said to be defects.

In that regard, having seated the patient afflicted with a disease curable by caustic (*kṣāra*) in a place free from wind and sunlight that is not crowded, and having prepared the necessary materials according to the procedure described in the *Agropaharaṇīya* [chapter], one should then examine that area of his, rub it, scrape it, and scarify it; then, applying the caustic with a probe, one should wait for the duration of a hundred breaths.
When that disease has subsided, blackness is the sign of being burnt;
in that case, the group of sour substances combined with ghee and madhuka is the pacifier.
If, however, due to its deep-rooted nature it does not slough off even when cauterized with alkali,
one should apply this entire medicinal plaster to that area.
Having ground equal parts of the seeds of *amlakāñjika*, sesame seeds, and *madhuka* together, one should smear him with that.
A paste of sesame mixed with madhuka and smeared with ghee promotes the healing of wounds;
however, when combined with substances that are sour, sharp, and hot in potency, it acts as an irritant.
"How can an alkali, which is equal to the fire of Agni, be extinguished?
If you think thus, my son, listen to what I am saying."
In that [taste], pungency is predominant, with saltiness as its secondary flavor;
it is joined with sourness and possesses both sharpness and salinity.
It attains extreme sweetness and abandons its sharpness;
through this sweetness it reaches tranquility, like a fire drenched with water.
In that case, when properly cauterized, there is alleviation of the disorder, lightness, and absence of discharge.
When [the Moon] is weak and combust, there is itching, urticaria, numbness, and the aggravation of diseases.
If it is excessively cauterized, there may occur burning, suppuration, redness, discharge, body ache, fatigue, thirst, and fainting, or even death.
A wound cauterized with alkali should be treated according to the specific humor involved and according to the specific disease.

Now, these are not fit for alkaline therapy (kṣārakṛtya): namely, the weak, the young, the old, the timid, those with swelling in all limbs, those suffering from abdominal enlargement (udara), those with internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), pregnant women, women in their menses, those with high fever, those with urinary disorders (prameha), the dehydrated, those emaciated by chest wounds, those afflicted by thirst and fainting, the impotent, and women whose vaginal canals are displaced downward or upward.

Likewise, one should not apply [the treatment] to vital spots (marmas), veins (sirās), ligaments (snāyu), joints (sandhi), cartilage (taruṇāsthi), sutures (sevanī), arteries (dhamanī), the throat, the navel, the interior of the nails, the penis, the channels (srotas), or regions with little flesh, nor to the eyes, except in cases of diseases of the eyelids (vartmaroga).

In that regard, even among diseases treatable by alkali (kṣāra), it does not cure one whose limbs are swollen, who suffers from bone pain, who has an aversion to food, and who is afflicted by pain in the heart and the joints.
And there is a verse on this point:
When applied by one of small intelligence, it becomes like poison, fire, a weapon, a thunderbolt, or death;
yet when properly applied by the wise, it destroys even terrible diseases without delay.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Calcination of Alkaline Preparations," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Śrī Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Twelfth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the procedure for cauterization (agnikarma).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Fire is explained as being superior to alkaline cautery (kṣāra) in therapeutic procedures, because diseases burnt by it do not recur, and because it can cure those conditions that are incurable by medicine, surgery, or alkaline cautery.

Now, these are the instruments for cauterization (*dahanopakaraṇa*), namely: long pepper (*pippalī*), goat dung (*ajāśakṛt*), cow-tusk (*godanta*), reed-shaft (*śaraśalākā*), jambu-fruit-stone (*jāmbavauṣṭha*), other metals (*itaraloha*), honey (*kṣaudra*), molasses (*guḍa*), and oils (*sneha*).

Among these, long pepper, goat dung, cow-tusk, and reed-shafts are for [lesions] located in the skin; jambu-fruit-stone and other metals are for those located in the flesh; honey, molasses, and oils are for those located in the vessels (*sirā*), ligaments (*snāyu*), joints (*sandhi*), and bones (*asthi*).

In that regard, one may perform cauterization (agnikarma) during all seasons except autumn and summer; even then, it may be performed in cases of urgent illness treatable by cauterization, provided one has first applied a regimen counteracting those specific seasons.

In all diseases and during all seasons, one should perform the ritual for one who has eaten slimy food; however, in cases of urinary stones, fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, and diseases of the mouth, it should be performed for one who has not eaten.

In this regard, some say that there are two types of thermal therapy (agnikarma): that which burns the skin and that which burns the flesh; however, in this [treatise], fire is prohibited even for the application to vessels, ligaments, joints, and bones.

In that regard, when the skin is burnt, there is the appearance of a sound, a foul odor, and contraction of the skin; when the flesh is burnt, there is a pigeon-like color, slight swelling and pain, and the wound becomes dry and contracted; when the vessels and ligaments are burnt, there is a blackish elevation of the wound and cessation of secretion; and when the joints and bones are burnt, there is a rough, reddish, hard, and stable wound.

In that regard, for diseases of the head and *adhimantha*, one should cauterize the regions of the eyebrows, forehead, and temples; for diseases of the eyelids, having covered the pupil with moist lac, one should cauterize the hair follicles of the eyelids.

One should perform cauterization (agnikarma) in cases where the wind (vāyu) resides in the skin, flesh, vessels, ligaments, joints, or bones and causes extremely severe pain; in ulcers characterized by elevated, hard, and fleshy growths; in cases of glandular swellings (granthi), hemorrhoids (arśas), tumors (arbuda), fistula-in-ano (bhagandara), scrofula (apacī), elephantiasis (ślīpada), corns (carma-kīla), moles (tilaka), dark spots (alaka), and hernia (antra-vṛddhi); and in procedures such as the incision of joints or veins, as well as in cases of excessive discharge of pus or blood from channels.
In that regard, the "ring," "dot," "scratching," and "rubbing" are specific types of cauterization.
And there is a verse on this point: Having properly observed the location of the disease, the vital points (*marmans*) of the patient, and their relative strength or weakness;
and having duly considered the illness as well as the season, the physician should then proceed with the application of thermal therapy (*agnikarman*).
In that case, once it has been properly cauterized, an ointment consisting of honey and clarified butter should be applied.

Now, one should avoid applying cauterization (agni) to those who have a pitta constitution, those with internal hemorrhage, those with a perforated abdomen, those from whom a foreign body has not been extracted, the weak, the young, the elderly, the timid, those afflicted by many wounds, and those for whom cauterization is contraindicated.

Henceforth, we shall describe the characteristics of burns caused by other means. In that regard, fire burns a substance by depending on whether it is oily (*snigdha*) or dry (*rūkṣa*).
