Those things which are exclusively beneficial and those which are exclusively harmful have already been taught; however, regarding the wholesome and unwholesome for Vāyu, that which is wholesome for Vāyu is unwholesome for Pitta.
However, other combinations become equivalent to poison.

For example, one should not eat together: creepers, fruits, mushrooms, bamboo shoots, sour fruits, salt, horse gram, oil-cake, curd, oil, *virohi* grain, flour, dried vegetables, or the meat of goats, sheep, wine, *jāmbava* fruit, *cilicima* fish, catfish, iguanas, and wild boars; nor should one eat these with milk.
A wise physician, having carefully observed the disease, the patient's suitability, the location, the time, the body,
and factors such as the digestive fire, should apply them according to the course of the disease.
Because of the great variety of different states, physicians do not accept that disease and the like are established as substances; rather, they seek [the means] for the preservation of health.
Regarding the taking of either one of two things— poison or milk—
they say that milk is exclusively beneficial, while poison is exclusively harmful.
Thus, O dear Suśruta, know that these substances such as water and the rest, when their tastes are properly combined, are exclusively beneficial; it is not otherwise.

Therefore, we shall describe other things that are harmful due to their combination: one should not consume the meat of domestic, marshy, or aquatic animals together with sprouted grains, fat, honey, milk, molasses, or black gram; nor should one eat *rohiṇī* potherb or *jātuka* potherb with milk and honey; nor *balākā* crane with *vāruṇī* wine and fermented grain-porridge (*kulmāṣa*); nor *kākamācī* with long pepper and black pepper; nor should *nāḍībhaṅga* potherb, chicken, and curd be eaten together; nor honey followed by hot water; nor raw meat with bile; nor wine, *kṛśara*, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) together; nor sesame-cakes with *sauvīraka* vinegar; nor sugarcane products with fish; nor *kākamācī* with molasses; nor radish with honey; nor boar's flesh with molasses; nor radish with milk; and [the following are also incompatible]: mango, rose-apple (*jāmbava*), the porcupine (*śvāvit*), the wild boar (*śūkara*), and the monitor lizard (*godhā*).

And all fish may be eaten with milk, especially the cilicima; the plantain fruit with palm-fruit juice, milk, curd, or buttermilk; and the lakucha fruit with milk, curd, or black gram soup—either before the milk or after the milk.

Therefore, we shall describe those things that are contrary to ritual action (*karmaviruddha*). One should not eat pigeons fried in mustard oil; nor should one eat the *kapiñjala* partridge, peacock, quail, partridge, or monitor lizard cooked with castor root or *dārvī* wood, or cooked in castor oil. One should not eat ghee kept for ten nights in a bronze vessel, nor honey when it is hot or with hot substances. One should not eat *kākamācī* greens prepared in a fish-cooking pan or a ginger-cooking pan, nor *upodikā* vegetables prepared with sesame paste. One should not eat a crane or a vulture roasted on charcoal with pig fat, nor a porcupine roasted on charcoal. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, we shall state those things that are contrary to the rules of measure: one should not consume honey and water, or honey and ghee, in equal quantities by measure; nor should one consume two fats, such as honey and fat, or water and fat, especially when followed by a drink of rainwater.

Henceforth, we shall describe pairs of tastes that are antagonistic by virtue of their taste (*rasa*), potency (*vīrya*), and post-digestive effect (*vipāka*). Among them: sweet and sour are antagonistic in taste and potency; sweet and salty, as well as sweet and pungent, are antagonistic in all three respects; sweet and bitter are antagonistic in taste and post-digestive effect; sweet and astringent are antagonistic in all three respects. Sour and salty are antagonistic in taste; sour and pungent are antagonistic in taste and post-digestive effect; sour and bitter, as well as sour and astringent, are antagonistic in all three respects. Salty and pungent are antagonistic in taste and post-digestive effect; salty and bitter, as well as salty and astringent, are antagonistic in all three respects. Pungent and bitter are antagonistic in taste and potency; pungent and astringent are antagonistic in all three respects; and bitter and astringent are antagonistic in taste.
One should avoid states of being characterized by degrees of intensity—such as those that are excessively dry, excessively oily, excessively hot, or excessively cold—and so forth.
And there are verses on this point:
"Whatever [qualities] such as these are contrary to vigor, they are exclusively harmful; one should know the remainder to be either beneficial or harmful."
A man who lacks self-control and consumes foods of conflicting tastes and potencies encounters disease, weakness of the senses, and death.
Whatever food, having provoked a disorder, is consumed but not eliminated from the body,
or which is transformed improperly within the bodily constituents such as the rasa, leads to the arising of disease.
Purgation counteracts diseases born of incompatible food,
as do emesis, pacification, or the prior adoption of wholesome practices.
For one who is moderate in diet, or for one with a small digestive fire, or for a young person, or for those who are unctuous,
habituated to exercise, and strong, even incompatible food may prove ineffective.
Now we shall describe the qualities of wind (vāta): Wind is primarily sweet, unctuous, and salty; it is heavy, produces a burning sensation, and increases blood-bile (raktapitta).
For those who have wounds, those afflicted by poison, those with ulcers, and those with phlegmatic constitutions—
it especially and constantly increases their diseases.
It is recommended for those with vāta disorders and for those exhausted by the depletion of kapha;
however, it specifically increases the moisture of their ulcers.
The southern wind is sweet, non-burning, slightly astringent in aftertaste,
light, excellent for the eyes, and increases strength.
It pacifies *raktapitta* (bleeding disorders) and does not aggravate *vāta*;
it is clear, dry, harsh, rough, and depletes unctuousness and strength.
The western wind is sharp, it dries up phlegm and fat;
it causes the immediate destruction of life and withers embodied beings.
The northern wind is unctuous, mild, and sweet;
it has an astringent aftertaste, is cool, and does not aggravate the humors.
Therefore, it is moistening and strength-increasing for those in their natural state,
and it is especially esteemed for those who are emaciated, suffering from wasting diseases, or afflicted by poisons.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, named "The Wholesome and Unwholesome," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the inquiry concerning wounds.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

Vāta, pitta, and śleṣman alone are the causes of the body's origin. When these very elements remain unimpaired and are situated in the lower, middle, and upper parts [of the body], this body is sustained by them, just as a house is supported by three pillars; therefore, some call it "three-pillared.
And when these same elements become impaired, they are the cause of its dissolution.
Thus, by means of these very [elements], with blood as the fourth, the body exists, persists, and undergoes dissolution, never being separated from them.
And there is a verse on this point: "There is no body without phlegm, nor without bile, nor without wind;
nor indeed without blood—the body is constantly sustained by these."

In this regard, from the verbal roots *vā* (in the sense of moving or blowing), *tap* (in the sense of heating), and *śliṣ* (in the sense of embracing), the forms *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* arise through the application of suffixes prescribed for the formation of nouns (*kṛt-pratyaya*).

Hereafter, we shall describe the locations of the humors (doṣas) in brief: among them, vāta resides in the pelvis and the rectum; above that and below the navel is the colon (pakvāśaya); the middle between the colon and the stomach is the location of pitta; and the stomach (āmāśaya) is the location of śleṣman.
Beyond this, they are divided into five types.

Among them, we shall describe the locations of *vāta* in the chapter on *vātavyādhi*; those of *pitta* are the liver, spleen, heart, eyes, skin, and that which was mentioned previously; and those of *śleṣman* are the chest, head, throat, joints, and that which was mentioned previously. These indeed are the locations of the *doṣas* when they are not deranged.
Just as the moon, the sun, and the wind sustain the body of the world through emission, intake, and diffusion,
so too do phlegm, bile, and wind sustain the bodily frame.

In this regard, what is to be investigated is whether fire is something other than bile (*pitta*), or whether bile itself is fire. To this it is replied: indeed, no fire is perceived apart from bile. Because bile is of fiery nature (*āgneya*), when its functions of burning, cooking, and so forth proceed, it is treated metaphorically as fire, being called "internal fire" (*antaragni*). For we observe—through the depletion of the qualities of fire, through the consumption of substances similar to that [fire], through the application of cooling treatments when [fire] is excessively increased, and through traditional scripture—that there is indeed no fire apart from bile.

And that bile, situated within the stomach (pakvāśaya) by means of a specific quality caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), digests the four kinds of food and drink and separates them into the humors (doṣa), nutrient fluid (rasa), urine, and feces; remaining in that very place, it also provides assistance through its own power and its fiery function to the other locations of bile and to the body as a whole. Regarding that bile, the designation is "the digestive fire" (pācaka-agni). As for the bile in the liver and spleen, the designation is "the coloring fire" (rañjaka-agni), which is said to be the cause of the coloring of the nutrient fluid. The bile situated in the heart is designated as "the accomplishing fire" (sādhaka-agni), which is said to be the accomplisher of desired objects and intentions. The bile in the eyes is designated as "the perceiving fire" (ālocaka-agni), which is appointed to the apprehension of forms.

That which is the bile (pitta) in the skin is designated as the "illuminating fire" (bhrājako 'gniḥ); it is the digester of the substances used in actions such as anointing, pouring, immersion, and ointment, and it is the illuminator of colors.
Bile (pitta) is sharp, liquid, foul-smelling, blue, and likewise yellow;
it is hot, pungent in taste, and when vitiated, it becomes sour.

Hereafter, we shall explain the locations of phlegm (śleṣman). Among them, the stomach (āmāśaya) is situated above the receptacle of bile (pittāśaya); because it is the opposite of bile and because its movement is upward—just as the moon is to the sun—it serves as the support for the four kinds of food. There, the food becomes moistened by watery qualities, its mass is broken down, and it becomes easily digestible.
Due to its sweetness, its sliminess, and likewise its moistness,
phlegm (śleṣman), which is sweet and cold, arises in the stomach (āmāśaya).

Remaining there, it benefits the remaining phlegmatic sites and the body as a whole through its watery function by means of its own power. Situated in the chest, together with the essence of food, it maintains the three junctions and provides support for the heart through its own vitality. Situated at the root of the tongue and in the throat, due to its gentle nature, it functions in the correct perception of tastes for the sense organ of the tongue. Situated in the head, because it is responsible for lubrication and satiation, it benefits the sense organs through its own vitality. As for the phlegm situated in the joints, because it binds all the joints together, it provides strength to the tips of all the joints.
Kapha is white, heavy, unctuous, slimy, and cold;
when undigested it is sweet, but when digested it becomes salty and flows out.
The seat of blood is the liver and the spleen; this has been previously mentioned, and situated therein, it provides nourishment to the remaining seats of blood.
Blood is neither hot nor cold, sweet, unctuous, and red in color;
it is heavy, has a fleshy odor, and its burning sensation is like that of pitta.
These indeed are the locations where the doshas are accumulated;
the cause of their accumulation has been stated previously.

Regarding the signs of the doshas that have thus accumulated: they consist of stiffness and fullness of the abdominal cavity, a yellowish appearance, diminished heat in the limbs, heaviness, laziness, and aversion to the factors that caused the accumulation.
Among these, the first is the time for action.
Hereafter, we shall describe the factors that cause provocation.

In this regard, Vāyu becomes aggravated by specific factors such as violent conflict, excessive physical exercise, sexual intercourse, over-study, falling, running, compression, trauma, jumping, leaping, swimming, staying awake at night, carrying heavy loads, riding elephants, horses, chariots, or marching on foot; and by the consumption of pungent, astringent, bitter, dry, light, and cold-potency foods; dried vegetables, parched grain, *varaka*, *koddālaka*, *koradūṣa*, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra* millet, mung beans, lentils, *āḍhakī*, *hareṇu*, *lāya*, and *niṣpāva* beans; fasting, irregular eating, or overeating; and by the suppression of the urges of flatus, urine, feces, semen, vomiting, sneezing, eructation, and tears.
It becomes aggravated especially during cold clouds and winds, at the end of the summer heat,
at dawn, in the afternoon, and when the food has been digested.

Pitta becomes provoked by anger, grief, fear, fatigue, fasting, sexual intercourse, pungent, sour, salty, sharp, hot, light, and burning substances; and by sesame oil, oil-cakes, horse-gram, mustard seeds, linseed, green leafy vegetables, the meat of the monitor lizard, fish, goats, and sheep; as well as by curd, buttermilk, inspissated milk, whey, fermented gruel, *sauvīraka* liquor, various preparations of *surā* wine, sour fruits, *kaṭvara*, and similar items.
It is aggravated by hot things during the hot season and especially at the end of the rainy season;
it also flares up at midday, at midnight, and when food is being digested.

Kapha becomes aggravated by daytime sleep, lack of exercise, laziness, and the consumption of sweet, sour, salty, cold, unctuous, heavy, slimy, and obstructive foods; by old *hāyanaka*, *yavaka*, and *naiṣadha* grains; by *itkaṭa*, black gram (*māṣa*), large black gram (*mahāmāṣa*), wheat, sesame, and preparations of flour; by curd, milk, *kṛśarā*, and *pāyasa*; by products of sugarcane, meat from marshy or aquatic regions, fat, lotus roots, lotus stalks, *kaseruka*, water chestnut (*śṛṅgāṭaka*), and sweet climbing fruits; and by eating in equal proportions or by overeating, and so forth.
It becomes aggravated during the cold season by cold things, especially in the spring, as well as in the forenoon, at dusk, and immediately after eating.

The blood undergoes provocation specifically through factors that also provoke pitta—namely, frequent consumption of liquid, unctuous, and heavy foods, as well as particular conditions such as sleeping during the day, anger, fire, heat, physical exertion, injury, indigestion, incompatible foods, and eating before the previous meal has been digested.
Since blood never becomes aggravated without the involvement of the *doṣas*,
one should therefore determine the time for its provocation according to the specific *doṣa* involved.
From their provocation, there arise piercing pain in the abdomen, shifting sensations, sour eructations, thirst, burning heat, aversion to food, and nausea;
this is the second time for medical intervention.

Henceforth, we shall describe their spreading (prasara). When these [doshas] have become aggravated by these specific pathologies and are increased—like a mixture of stale leaven, water, and flour—their spreading occurs.
Among them, because it possesses mobility, vāyu is the cause of spreading, even though it lacks consciousness;
for it is predominantly composed of rajas, and rajas is the impeller of all states of being.

Just as a great accumulation of water, having overflowed its banks and breached the embankment, rushes forth in all directions mixed with other waters, so too the humors (doṣas)—whether individually, in pairs, collectively, or combined with the blood—spread in many ways at various times.

Namely: wind, bile, phlegm, blood; wind-and-bile, wind-and-phlegm, bile-and-phlegm, wind-and-blood, bile-and-blood, phlegm-and-blood; wind-bile-blood, wind-phlegm-blood, bile-phlegm-blood, wind-bile-phlegm, and wind-bile-phlegm-blood—thus they manifest in fifteen ways.
Whether in the whole body, in a half, or even in a single limb, wherever the humor (doṣa) is intensely provoked,
it pours down disorder there like a cloud raining upon the sky.
He does not become excessively angry, nor does he remain hidden in his ways;
being without opposition, he becomes enraged only when the time is right and a cause is encountered.

In that regard, the treatment for vāyu located in the seat of pitta is like that for pitta; for pitta located in the seat of kapha, it is like that for kapha; and for kapha located in the seat of vāyu, it is like that for vāyu—this is the classification of therapeutic procedures.

When the Vāyu is thus aggravated and spreading, its symptoms are wandering in wrong channels and distension; those of Pitta are burning, parching, a general sense of heat, and a sensation of fuming; and those of Śleṣman are anorexia, indigestion, malaise, and vomiting. This constitutes the third period for medical intervention.
Beyond this, regarding their localization in specific sites:
thus provoked, they reach various parts of the body and produce various diseases.

When they take up residence in the abdomen, they produce conditions such as abdominal tumors (gulma), abscesses (vidradhi), enlargement of the abdomen (udara), loss of digestive fire (agnisanga), flatulence (ānāha), choleraic poisoning (visūcikā), and diarrhea (atisāra). When located in the bladder, they produce urinary disorders (prameha), urinary stones (aśmarī), urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta), and defects of the urine (mūtradoṣa). When located in the testes, they produce scrotal enlargements (vṛddhi). When located in the penis, they produce obstructed prepuce (niruddhaprakasha), balanitis (upadaṃśa), and disorders of the seminal ducts (śūkadoṣa). When located in the anus, they produce fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) and hemorrhoids (arśas). When located above the clavicles, they produce diseases of the upper body. When situated in the skin, flesh, and blood, they produce minor diseases (kṣudraroga), leprosy (kuṣṭha), and erysipelas (visarpa). When located in the fat (medas), they produce glandular swellings (granthi), scrofula (apaci), tumors (arbuda), goiter (galagaṇḍa), and carbuncles (alajī). When located in the bones, they produce abscesses (vidradhi), osteomyelitis (anuśayi), and so forth. When located in the feet, they produce elephantiasis (ślīpada), gout (vātaśoṇita), and rheumatic nodules (vātakaṇṭaka). When located throughout the entire body, they produce fever (jvara), general body ailments (sarvāṅgaroga), and the like.
For those who are thus afflicted, there is the manifestation of premonitory symptoms; we shall describe these according to each specific disease.
Among these, when the premonitory symptoms have appeared, it is the fourth stage for medical intervention.

Hereafter, we shall describe the manifestation of disease, namely the clear appearance of symptoms in cases such as swelling, tumors, nodules, abscesses, and erysipelas, as well as in fever, diarrhea, and so forth.
This constitutes the fifth period for medical intervention.

Beyond this, when these [afflictions] have burst open and reached the state of an ulcer, or when fevers, diarrhea, and so forth persist for a long duration, it is the sixth stage for medical intervention;
if left untreated in those cases, they become incurable.
And there are verses on this point:
He who understands the accumulation, the provocation, the spread, the localization, the manifestation, and the differentiation of the humors (doṣas) shall be a physician.
Faults that have been removed through accumulation do not find higher rebirths;
yet those very same faults become even more powerful in those higher rebirths.
Whether by all three humors, or by two, or even by one alone,
when they are combined, the provoked humor pursues the aggravated humor.
In a case of combined morbidity (*saṃsarga*), that which is most severe should indeed be treated first;
likewise, in a case of the three humors combined (*sannipāta*), one should act without contradicting the remaining morbidities.
Because the substance of the wound does not perish even when healed,
as long as the body is maintained, it is therefore called a "vraṇa" (wound) by the wise.
The twenty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of the discharge from wounds (*vraṇāsrāvavijñānīya*).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
Skin, flesh, vessels, ligaments, bones, joints, cavities, and vital points—these are the eight substrates of ulcers;
herein is the location of all ulcers.
Among these, a wound that involves only the first single layer of tissue and does not breach the skin is easily treated; the remaining types, which burst spontaneously, are difficult to manage.
Among these, elongated, square, circular, and triangular are the summary classifications of wound shapes; all others are deformed shapes that are difficult to treat.

All wounds heal quickly when treated by self-disciplined individuals and skilled physicians; however, those treated by undisciplined individuals and the ignorant become corrupted due to the aggravation of the bodily humors (doṣas).

In that regard, the characteristics of a vitiated ulcer (*duṣṭavraṇa*) are as follows: it is excessively constricted, excessively dilated, excessively hard, excessively soft, elevated, depressed, excessively cold, or excessively hot; it possesses one or another of the colors such as black, red, yellow, or white; it is terrifying; it is filled with putrid pus, flesh, veins, sinews, and so forth; it exudes putrid pus through abnormal openings, has an offensive odor from its cavities, and is unpleasant to look at; it is accompanied by extreme pain and is afflicted by burning, suppuration, redness, itching, swelling, and pustules; it discharges highly corrupted blood and persists for a long duration. These are the signs of a vitiated ulcer.
Having analyzed that [disease] into six types according to the predominance of the humors, one should strive for its remedy accordingly.

Hereafter, we shall describe all types of discharges (*srāva*). Among them, when the skin is abraded or incised, or when boils are burst or lacerated, the discharge is clear like water, slightly malodorous, and yellowish in appearance. When vessels (*sirā*) are freshly severed, there is an excessive flow of blood; when they are matured, pus flows out like water through irrigation channels. In this case, the discharge is thin, intermittent, slimy, hanging, dark-brown, and resembles hoarfrost. When located in the tendons (*snāyu*), it is unctuous, thick, resembling nasal mucus (*siṅghāṇaka*), and mixed with blood. When located in the bone, the bone—whether struck, cracked, split, or opened by the humors (*doṣa*)—becomes devoid of substance due to being consumed by the humors, appearing as if washed by lime-water (*śukti*); the discharge here is mixed with marrow, accompanied by blood, and unctuous.

When it has reached the joints (saṃdhi), being oppressed, it does not move; yet through contraction, extension, raising, lowering, running, coughing, and straining, it flows out. Here, the discharge is slimy, hanging down, mixed with foam, pus, and blood. When located in the visceral cavity (koṣṭha), it flows out as blood, urine, feces, pus, and lymph. When it has reached the vital points (marman), it is not mentioned because it is obstructed within the skin and other tissues.

In that regard, the discharges (āsrāva) occurring from the skin and other tissues, in their respective order, due to *vāta* resemble dryness, a dark-brown hue, frost, curd-whey, alkaline water, meat-washings, and water with broken rice grains; due to *pitta*, they resemble the urine of a camel, cow's urine, ash-water, conch-shell powder-water, honey-liquor, and oil; and like *pitta*, due to blood, they possess an excessively foul odor; and due to *kapha*, they resemble butter, green vitriol, marrow, flour-paste, coconut water, and boar fat; and due to the combination of all three (*sannipāta*), they resemble coconut water, cucumber juice, clear fermented gruel (*kāñjika*), water from boiled wood, water from *priyaṅgu* fruit, liver, and mung-bean soup.
There are two verses on this point:
A discharge resembling water with parched grain (pulāka) from the colon (pakvāśaya) is incurable;
however, a discharge resembling alkaline water flowing from the receptacle of blood (raktāśaya) should be rejected as fatal.
Arising from the stomach, resembling water from a *kalā* plant, and born at the junction of the three channels—
the physician should first examine these discharges and then perform the treatment.

Hereafter, we shall describe the pains of all wounds (*sarvavraṇavedanā*). Where there arise pricking, tearing, beating, cutting, stretching, churning, tossing, throbbing, burning, breaking, bursting, splitting, uprooting, trembling, various types of aches (*śūla*), dislocation, scattering, filling, stiffening, numbness, contraction, and hook-like pains; or where various causeless pains repeatedly manifest—such specific sensations one should know as *vātika* (wind-born). Where there is burning, parching, general heat, and a sensation of fuming, where the limb is as if being cooked over glowing coals, where there is an increase in heat, and where the pain in a wound is like that of having been sprinkled with caustic lye—one should know such specific sensations as *paittika* (bile-born). One should understand that which arises from blood to be similar to that of bile (*pitta*).

One should recognize that [affection] as being caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika) where there is itching, heaviness, numbness, a coating sensation, slight pain, stiffness, and coldness; one should recognize that as being caused by the combination of all [humors] (sānnipātika) where there is the arising of all [types of] pain.

Hereafter, we shall describe the colors of ulcers: those that are ash-colored, like the color of a pigeon’s bone, rough, reddish, or black belong to the ulcer born of Vāta; blue, yellow, green, dark-brown, black, red, tawny, or reddish-brown belong to those arising from blood and Pitta; white, unctuous, or pale belong to the ulcer born of Kapha; and that which possesses all these colors belongs to the Sānnipātika (combined) type.
And there is a verse on this point:
"The description of pain and color has been stated not only for wounds; the physician should observe all types of swellings and disorders in the same manner as wounds."
The twenty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done.
As the Blessed One, Dhanvantari, has said:

Among those, wounds in individuals who are of stable age, physically firm, possessed of vital strength (*prāṇa*), and endowed with mental fortitude (*sattva*) are easily treated; or, in a single person, wherever these four qualities are present, the wounds are most readily curable.

Among these, wounds heal quickly in those of middle age because their bodily tissues are fresh; in the elderly, because of their firm and abundant muscle tissue, the surgical instrument does not encounter vital structures such as veins or ligaments when applied; in those possessed of vitality, exhaustion does not arise due to the assault of pain or the constraints of diet and regimen; and in those endowed with mental fortitude, no distress occurs even from harsh medical procedures. Therefore, these [patients] are the most easily treated.
These same qualities, when reversed, should be observed in those who are aged, emaciated, weak, or timid.
Wounds located on the buttocks, anus, genitals, forehead, cheeks, lips, back, ears, scrotum, abdomen, sternum, and the interior of the mouth are easily healed.

Those [fistulas] located at the eyes, teeth, nose, outer corners of the eyes, ears, navel, abdomen, perineum, buttocks, sides, flanks, chest, armpits, breasts, and joints; those discharging frothy pus, blood, or wind; and those containing internal foreign bodies are difficult to treat. Likewise, those in the lower parts that discharge upward, those situated at the hairline, the nails, the vital points (*marmans*), the calves, or the bones, as well as fistula-in-ano (*bhagandara*) that is inward-facing or situated at the perineum, the sacrum, or the bones, are difficult to cure.
The ulcers of those suffering from leprosy, those afflicted by poison, those with consumption, and those with diabetes,
as well as those who have ulcer upon ulcer, are cured only with great difficulty.

Avapāṭikā, niruddhaprakaśa, sanniruddhaguda, abdominal tumors (jaṭhara-granthi), worms born from wounds, those arising from catarrh, and those originating in the visceral cavity; skin diseases (tvag-doṣa) or urinary disorders (prameha) appearing in those with ulcers; gravel (śarkarā), sandy urine (sikatā-meha), Vātakuṇḍalikā, Aṣṭhīlā, dental tartar (danta-śarkarā), Upakuśa, Kaṇṭhaśālūka, and inflamed gums (dantaveṣṭa) damaged by toothpicks; erysipelas (visarpa), bone injuries, chest wounds, ulcers, and tumors—these and similar conditions are palliable (yāpya).
Curable diseases turn into palliable ones, and palliable ones likewise turn into incurable ones;
however, incurable diseases take away the lives of men who do not undergo treatment.
One should recognize that [an action] is sustainable when it maintains its activity;
however, once that activity has ceased, it perishes immediately.
The treatment that has been obtained sustains a patient suffering from a palliable disease,
just as a well-applied prop supports a house about to collapse.

Hereafter, we shall describe those [ulcers] that are incurable: those that protrude like a mass of flesh, those characterized by excessive salivation, those with internal pain from putrefaction, and some with upturned lips like those of a horse's anus; others have hard, horn-like growths of soft flesh rising upward; others discharge foul blood, or a thin, cold, and slimy secretion, being elevated in the center; some have depressed cavities at their margins covered with a network of sinews like hemp-cotton and are hideous to behold; they discharge fat, marrow, brain matter, and mastulunga, and when arising from the humors (*doṣa*), they carry yellow or black urine, feces, and wind while located within the abdominal cavity (*koṣṭha*); these same types, when appearing at the openings of ulcers on both sides, discharge pus and blood, spreading in all directions with minute openings and fleshy bubbles, especially in those whose flesh has been wasted away.

Those located in the head and throat that carry sound and wind, which discharge pus and blood in those with wasted flesh, and are accompanied by complications such as anorexia, indigestion, cough, and dyspnea; or where the cranial bone is fractured and the brain matter is visible; or in one for whom the symptoms of the three doṣas appear along with cough and dyspnea—[these are incurable].
And there are verses on this point:
An incidental ulcer (āgantuvraṇa) that exudes fat, adipose tissue, marrow, or brain matter may heal;
however, one arising from the [vitiated] humors (doṣasambhava) will not heal.
When a disorder spreads through a region that is not vital (amarmopahita) and is devoid of vessels, joints, and bones,
that is a characteristic of an incurable condition.
Having gradually attained growth and slowly pervaded the constituent elements, a disease—
like an old tree— is impossible to uproot.
On account of its stability, its magnitude, and its conformity with the sequence of the elements,
it destroys the potencies of medicinal herbs, just as an evil planet neutralizes mantras.
Therefore, one who is the opposite of this is said to be easily cured;
just as a small shrub that has not taken deep root is easy to uproot.
A wound that is not afflicted by the three doshas, characterized by dark lips, covered with pustules, even, painless, and free from discharge, is said here to be "pure."
One should declare that a wound is healing when its interior has the color of a pigeon, is free from moisture,
firm, and covered with small pustules.
One should declare a wound to be properly healed when its track has closed, it is free of knots, swelling, and pain, and its surface is level with and the same color as the surrounding skin.
Due to the provocation of the humors (doṣas), from physical exertion, from injury, from indigestion,
or even from joy, anger, or fear, a wound— even one that has healed— will burst open again.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Rules for What Should and Should Not Be Done," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the enumeration of diseases.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Diseases are of two kinds: those curable by surgery and those curable by oleation and other therapeutic measures. Among these, oleation and other such measures are not prohibited in cases curable by surgery, nor is surgical intervention performed in cases curable by oleation and other such measures.

Furthermore, in this treatise, because it is common to all systems of thought (*sarvatantra-sāmānya*), a general classification of all diseases is made according to their broad characteristics. It was previously stated that "diseases are conjunctions with suffering.
That suffering is threefold: internal (*ādhyātmika*), external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*).
That [diagnosis] applies to seven types of diseases.

Furthermore, those seven types of diseases are as follows: those arising from the power of primary causes (*ādibalapravṛtta*), those arising from the power of birth (*janmabalapravṛtta*), those arising from the power of the humors (*doṣabalapravṛtta*), those arising from the power of the bodily constituents (*saṃghātabalapravṛtta*), those arising from the power of time (*kālabalapravṛtta*), those arising from the power of destiny (*daivabalapravṛtta*), and those arising from the power of inherent nature (*svabhāvabalapravṛtta*).

Among these, those diseases that arise from the power of the primary humors (*doṣa*) and are connected to defects in the semen and ovum, such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and so forth, are also of two kinds: those born from the mother and those born from the father.

Those that arise from the power of birth and are produced due to the mother’s misconduct—such as being lame, blind from birth, deaf, mute, stammering, or dwarf—are also of two kinds: those caused by [defective] nutritional fluids (*rasa*) and those caused by misconduct during pregnancy (*dauhṛda*). Those that arise from the power of the humors and are produced through illness or improper diet and conduct are also of two kinds: those originating in the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and those originating in the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*).
Furthermore, they are of two kinds: physical and mental;
these are the internal [sufferings].

Those arising from the force of a collective impact—namely, those external [factors] resulting from a conflict between the weak and the strong—are also of two kinds: those caused by weapons and those caused by predatory beasts.
These are the physical (ādhibhautika) [sufferings].

Those [afflictions] that arise through the power of time (*kālabala*)—having cold, heat, wind, rain, and so forth as their causes—are also of two kinds: those produced by a corrupted season (*vyāpannartukṛta*) and those produced by an uncorrupted season (*avyāpannartukṛta*).

Those that arise through the power of fate (*daivabala*)—such as those resulting from hostility toward the gods, curses, spells (*atharvaṇakṛta*), or calamities (*upasarga*)—are also of two kinds: those caused by lightning and thunderbolts, and those caused by *piśācas* and other such beings; furthermore, they are again of two kinds: those arising from contagion (*saṃsargaja*) and those that are accidental (*ākasmika*).

Those functions that proceed by the power of their own nature—such as hunger, thirst, old age, death, sleep, and so forth—are also of two kinds: those produced by time (*kālakṛta*) and those not produced by time (*akālakṛta*). Among these, those resulting from protection are produced by time, while those resulting from lack of protection are not produced by time. These are the super-natural (*ādhidaivika*) afflictions;
herein all diseases are included.

Furthermore, wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman) alone are the root of all diseases, because they possess those symptoms, because this is observed in experience, and because of traditional scripture (āgama).

Just as the entire range of transformations existing in manifold forms is not distinct from the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, even so, the entire range of transformations existing in manifold forms exists without being distinct from wind, bile, and phlegm.
Their differentiation arises from the combination of humors (doṣa), tissues (dhātu), and wastes (mala), from specific locations (āyatana), and from causal factors (nimitta).

When the bodily constituents (dhātus) are excessively afflicted by the humors (doṣas), the designation "this disease is born from rasa," "this is born from blood," "this is born from flesh," "this is born from fat," "this is born from bone," "this is born from marrow," or "this is born from semen" is applied.

In that regard, disorders arising from defects of the *rasa* (plasma) include lack of appetite, anorexia, indigestion, body aches, fever, nausea, satiety, heaviness, heart disease, anemia, obstruction of the channels, emaciation, bad taste in the mouth, lassitude, and the premature appearance of wrinkles and gray hair; disorders arising from defects of the *rakta* (blood) include leprosy, erysipelas, pustules, scabies, blue moles, black moles, freckles, vitiligo, warts, alopecia, splenic enlargement, abscesses, abdominal tumors, gout, hemorrhoids, tumors, body aches, menorrhagia, and hemoptysis; and disorders arising from defects of the *māṃsa* (flesh) include inflammation of the anus, mouth, and penis; as well as fleshy growths, tumors, hemorrhoids, inflammation of the tongue, epiglottis, uvula, tonsils, and throat; and swellings of the flesh, lips, throat, goiter, and cervical lymphadenitis.

Diseases arising from defects of the bone include: enlargement of glands, goiter, tumors, disorders of the fat tissue, inflammation of the lips, diabetes, excessive obesity, and excessive perspiration; those arising from defects of the marrow include: darkness of vision, fainting, vertigo, diseases with thick roots at the joints, ulcers, and ophthalmia; those arising from defects of semen include: impotence, lack of sexual excitement, seminal calculi, spermatorrhea, and other seminal disorders; defects of the excretory channels (mala-āyatana) include skin diseases, obstruction, or excessive or improper discharge; and defects of the sensory organs (indriya-āyatana) include non-functioning or impaired functioning of the senses. This has been stated in brief; we shall describe their causes and symptoms in detail for each individual disease.
And there is a verse on this point:
"When the humors (doṣas) become provoked and course through the body,
wherever they encounter an obstruction due to a local deficiency, there a disease arises."

Furthermore, it must be investigated here whether the connection between the *vāta* and other humors on one hand and fever and other diseases on the other is permanent or intermittent. If the connection were permanent, then all living beings would be eternally afflicted by illness. On the other hand, if it were otherwise—that is, if the *vāta* and others, while existing in one place, could manifest their signs elsewhere—then the claim that the *vāta* and others are the roots of fever and other diseases would be untenable.

To this it is replied: fevers and the like do not exist apart from the humors (*doṣa*), yet their connection is not eternal. For instance, lightning, wind, thunderbolts, and rain do not exist apart from space; even though space exists, these phenomena do not occur at all times, yet they arise from that very source due to specific causes. Likewise, waves, bubbles, and so forth are merely particular states of water. In the same way, there is neither a permanent fusion nor a fixed delimitation between the humors and fevers, and so on; nevertheless, they arise solely through specific causes.
And there is a verse on this point:
"The modifications, the measurements, and the numbers of these [humors] individually,
as well as all their afflictions, will be explained in detail in the subsequent Tantra."
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of Diseases," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter concerning the eightfold surgical procedures.

As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari said: Fistula-in-ano, glandular swellings caused by phlegm (kapha), moles and dark spots, ulcerated margins, tumors, hemorrhoids, and skin tags located in the bone or flesh are to be excised.
A splinter, a concretion, a mass of flesh, a uvula,
a decayed tendon, flesh, or vein, a wart, and a centipede-like growth;
Adhruṣa, upadaṃśa, māṃsakandī, and adhimāṃsaka; abscesses (vidradhi) are to be incised, except for those caused by all three doṣas; likewise, the three types of glandular swellings (granthi).

First, those which are visarpa (erysipelas), vṛddhi (scrotal enlargement), along with vidārikā (scrotal abscess), pramehapiḍakā (boils caused by urinary disorders), swelling, diseases of the breast, and avamanthaka (a type of facial tumor).
The kumbhīkā, the anuśayī, the nāḍīs, the two types of vṛnda, the puṣkarikā, the alajī,
the various minor diseases (kṣudraroga), and the two types of pustules (puppuṭa) arising from the palate and the teeth.
Tuṇḍikerī, gilāyu, and those previously mentioned as suppurating, as well as the bladder, stones, and any [growths] born of fat (medas).
The four Lekhya types are Rohiṇī, Kilāsa, Upajihvikā,
Medoja, Dantavaidarbha, Granthi, Vartma, and Adhijihvikā.
Hemorrhoids, skin patches, fleshy growths, and elevations of the flesh; various types of vessels to be punctured, urinary hernia, and ascites.
Fistulas that are discharging, accompanied by foreign bodies, or following an abnormal course;
the three types of gravel (śarkarā); dental tartar; earwax; and urinary calculi (aśmarī)—these are to be extracted.
Foreign bodies, retained fetal parts, and accumulated feces in the rectum—
these five types of abscesses (vidradhi) should be drained, with the exception of those caused by all three doshas combined.
Skin diseases, painful swelling localized in one part of the body,
diseases of the earlobes, elephantiasis, and blood vitiated by poison [are treated with this].
Arbuda, visarpa, and the three types of granthi; upadaṃśa, the three types of breast diseases, and vidārikā.
Suṣira, galaśālūka, kaṇṭaka, kṛmidantaka,
dentaveṣṭa, sopakuśa, śītāda, and dantapuppuṭa.
The diseases of the lips arising from pitta, blood, and kapha, as well as many minor diseases (kṣudraroga),
those originating in the fat (medas), and those that have burst open— these ailments should be properly incised and then sutured.
Those wounds that are fresh, as well as those located in movable joints,
which are not afflicted by alkali, fire, or poison, and which do not follow the path of the wind;
Nor are there internal blood or splinters; in them, there is thorough purification [of what is impure], such as dust, hair, nails, and whatever bone may be mobile.
Since these [impurities], if not extracted, would cause the wound to suppurate excessively and produce various kinds of pain, one should therefore cleanse them.
Then, having elevated the wound and restored it to its natural position,
one should suture it with a fine thread or with the inner bark of the *aśmantaka* tree.
One should slowly sew a vellitaka bandage using threads made of hemp or linen, or with sinew, hair, or fibers from mūrvā, guḍūcī, or tāna.
One may sew it with a gophaṇikā stitch, or sew it with a tunnasevanī stitch,
or even with a straight knot, or otherwise as is appropriate.
In a region with little flesh or at a joint, a round needle two finger-breadths long is recommended;
however, in a fleshy part, a triangular needle three finger-breadths long is also esteemed.
Curved like a bow, beneficial for use over vital points (marmas), the scrotum, and the abdomen—
these are the three types of needles, sharp-tipped and well-proportioned.
One should have [the needles] made with a circumference like the tip of a *mālatī* flower stalk;
one should apply the needle in the work neither too far nor too close.
For a wound on the lip, there is no tearing away when it is close at hand, but it is done from a distance.
Then, one should apply a well-sewn plug covered with linen cloth, dusting it all over with the powders of *priyaṅgu*, *añjana*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, and *rodhra*.
Alternatively, having bound the wound appropriately with either the powder of *śallakī* fruit or with a fine linen cloth,
one should prescribe the regimen of conduct.
This eightfold action has been proclaimed in brief;
its full details will be explained in their entirety within the sections on therapeutics.
Deficiency, excess, and lateral deviation, as well as the cutting off of one's own limbs—
these four are recorded as the complications in the eightfold medical procedure.
[They arise] through ignorance, greed, harmful speech, application, fear, delusion, and other such states.
When a physician employs a poor instrument, then he leaves behind residual disorders.
One who desires to live should avoid from afar that physician who repeatedly applies caustics, surgery, fire, and medicines in an improper manner, for he is like a venomous snake or a deadly enemy.
That alone is proper; for [if applied otherwise], it would injure the vital joints, the vessels, the tendons, and even the bones.
A person treated by a fool might be deprived of life in an instant, or perhaps in some other way.
Dizziness, delirium, falling down, fainting, convulsions, prostration, and fever;
drooping of the limbs, syncope, upward movement of wind (ūrdhvavāta), and various other sharp pains caused by Vāta [occur].
Blood resembling meat-water flows, and likewise there is a cessation of the functions of all the sense organs;
this is generally stated to be the symptom when the five [specific] vital points (marmas) are wounded.
When veins are cut or pierced, blood flows profusely like cochineal insects, and the Vayu,
entering through the wound, produces various diseases as previously described.
One should diagnose that person as having been pierced in a ligament who suffers from hunching of the body, physical exhaustion, incapacity for activities, and intense pains,
and whose wound heals only after a long time.
Excessive increase of swelling, tumultuous pains, loss of strength, and splitting pain and swelling in the joints;
and the cessation of joint function when the joints are neither fixed nor mobile—these are the signs [of injury].
One should diagnose a person as having a bone-piercing wound (asthividdha) when they suffer from terrible pains day and night, find no relief in any condition,
and experience thirst, aching of the limbs, and a rough swelling.
One should discern these signs according to their respective locations when the vital points (*marmans*) are struck:
he who has been struck in a vital point of the flesh does not perceive touch and becomes pale in complexion.
One who, while performing medical treatment, strikes himself with a weapon as a result of his own inferior practice— that self-slayer and quack physician— one desiring long life should avoid.
The faults incurred when a surgical instrument is applied obliquely have been described previously;
therefore, avoiding those faults, one should perform the application of the instrument.
A sick man may even suspect his mother, father, sons, and kinsmen,
yet he places his trust in the physician.
The physician releases himself by means of his own self and does not harbor any suspicion toward him;
therefore, the physician should protect the patient just like a son.
For the sake of dharma, wealth, and fame, one should undertake the highest service to the virtuous;
by performing beneficial actions, one shall attain residence in heaven.
A certain transformation is accomplished by one action, another by two, likewise some by three,
and yet another even by four actions.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Eightfold Surgical Procedure," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The twenty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the diagnosis of lost foreign bodies (*pranaṣṭa-śalya-vijñānīya*).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
The verbal root *śal* (or *śval*), meaning "to go swiftly," has the form *śalya* [derived from it].
That is of two kinds: innate and adventitious.
Because that which causes affliction to the entire body is taught here as a "salya" (foreign body/spear-head), it is therefore called the *Śalya-śāstra* (the Science of Surgery).

In that regard, the bodily [suffering] consists of hair, nails, and so forth; the bodily constituents (dhātu), the impurities of food, and the corrupted humors (doṣa); and furthermore, all those things that produce suffering, whether adventitious or distinct from physical thorns.

For there is authority regarding [arrows] made of iron, bamboo, wood, grass, horn, and bone; yet among these, specifically those made of iron are intended for the purpose of slaughter. Even among iron [arrows], the arrow (*śara*) alone is authorized because it is suitable for the act of piercing, because iron is difficult to ward off, because its tip is minute, and because it serves a long-range purpose. It is of two kinds: barbed (*karṇin*) and smooth (*ślakṣṇa*). Generally, their forms are explained as being like the leaves, flowers, and fruits of various trees, and they resemble the mouths of predatory beasts and birds.
Regarding all arrows, whether large or small, there are five specific modes of movement: upward, downward, oblique, horizontal, and straight.

Due to the exhaustion of their momentum or because of obstruction, they remain in the skin and other sites of wounds, or in various regions of the body such as the channels, the flow of vessels, the cavities of the bones, the muscles, and so forth.
In this regard, attend to the description of the signs of a foreign body (*śalya*).
That [diagnosis] is twofold: general and specific.

One should recognize that a wound which is dark-brown, covered with pustules, accompanied by swelling and pain, repeatedly discharging blood, elevated like a bubble, and having soft flesh, as being "this person has a foreign body."
This definition has been stated as a general one.

The specific symptoms are as follows: when located in the skin, there is discoloration, swelling, and hardness; when located in the muscle, there is an increase in swelling, non-healing of the wound tract caused by the foreign body, intolerance to pressure, and pricking pain (coṣa) and inflammation (pāka); when located within the muscle mass (peśī), the same symptoms occur except for the pricking pain and swelling; when located in the vessels (sirā), there is distension of the vessels, vessel pain, and swelling of the vessels; when located in the tendons (snāyu), there is displacement of the network of tendons, inflammation, and severe pain; when located in the channels (srotas), there is loss of the specific functions and qualities of those channels; when located in the arteries (dhamanī), wind (vāyu) exits with a sound, propelling frothy blood, accompanied by body ache, thirst, and nausea; when located in the bone, various types of pain manifest along with swelling; when located in the marrow cavity of the bone, there is a sense of fullness in the bone, a throbbing sensation (todana), and intense piercing pain (saṃharṣa); and when located in the joints, the symptoms are like those of the bone, along with the cessation of movement.

When the shaft has entered the abdominal cavity, there is flatulence and distension, and urine, feces, or food may be seen emerging from the mouth of the wound. When it has struck a vital point (*marman*), the patient exhibits convulsive movements;
in the case of shafts with minute trajectories, these very symptoms become indistinct.

Whether large or small, these [wounds] heal especially well when situated favorably on the bodies of those with pure constitutions—specifically within the channels of the throat, the skin, the flesh, and the interstices of the bones; however, once displaced by the provocation of the humors (doṣa), physical exertion, trauma, or indigestion, they cause affliction once again.

In that regard, when the skin is lost [to injury], one should recognize the presence of a foreign body (*śalya*) at the spot where redness or pain occurs after the skin has been lubricated and fomented, and rubbed with clay, black gram, barley, wheat, or cow dung; or, after it has been smeared with solidified ghee, clay, or sandalwood paste, one should recognize the foreign body at the spot where the ghee quickly spreads due to the heat of the foreign body, or where the paste quickly dries up. When the flesh is lost, one should treat the patient with specific procedures such as oleation and fomentation that are not contraindicated. However, in the case of a person who has been emaciated, one should recognize the foreign body at the spot where it—having become loose, unattached, and agitated—produces redness or pain. One should examine in this very same manner for foreign bodies situated within the abdominal cavity, bone joints, muscle bellies, or interstices.

When the foreign body is lost within the veins, arteries, channels, or ligaments, one should place the patient on a vehicle equipped with a broken wheel and travel quickly along a rough road; wherever inflammation or pain occurs, there one should know the foreign body is located. When it is lost in a bone, one should treat the bones with oleation and sudation, and then apply intense pressure and bandaging; wherever inflammation or pain occurs, there one should know the foreign body is located. When it is lost in a joint, one should treat the joints with oleation and sudation, and then apply intense extension, flexion, bandaging, and pressure; wherever inflammation or pain occurs, there one should recognize the foreign body. However, when it is lost in a vital organ (*marman*), the examination must be conducted according to the specific nature of those vital organs as previously described.

Furthermore, one should recognize the presence of a *śalya* (foreign body) wherever there is agitation or pain resulting from physical exercises such as mounting an elephant’s shoulder, a horse’s back, a mountain, or a tree; practicing archery; rapid travel; wrestling; walking long distances; jumping, swimming, or leaping; or from yawning, belching, coughing, sneezing, spitting, laughing, or breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), or from the discharge of wind, urine, feces, or semen.
And there are verses on this point:
In that place where there is pricking and so forth, numbness, and heaviness;
where it frequently feels as if it is being struck, squeezed, or even pierced.
Furthermore, one should point out the location of the arrow in that very place which the patient frequently guards and repeatedly massages.
It should have little affliction, be non-swollen, free from pain, and devoid of complications;
it should be clear, soft at the edges, without fissures, and not protruding.
Having examined it from all sides with the probe, the physician should certainly determine that it is free of the shaft by means of extension and contraction according to the path.
An arrow made of bone is shattered, while one made of horn or iron generally breaks internally; this is the certainty.
If those made of wood, bamboo, or grass are not discarded,
they quickly cause embodied beings to cook their own blood and flesh.
Gold, silver, copper, brass, tin, and lead—
these all dissolve from long-term storage due to the heat and intensity of bile.
Those things which are naturally cool and soft, as well as others considered to be like them,
become liquefied within this body and attain unity with the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
Horn, ivory, hair, bone, bamboo,
wood, reeds, and earthen objects do not disintegrate within the body when they become embedded as foreign bodies.
He who knows how to extract the two kinds of foreign bodies— whether loose or embedded— found within the five types of wounds such as those caused by arrows and the like, is worthy to serve the king.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Lost Foreign Bodies," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The twenty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the extraction of foreign bodies (śalyāpanayanīya).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
A foreign body (śalya) is of two kinds: fixed and unfixed.
In this regard, we shall briefly describe fifteen causes for the purpose of extracting an embedded shaft (śalya):

namely, natural disposition (svabhāva), ripening (pācana), breaking (bhedana), splitting (dāraṇa), pressing (pīḍana), cleansing (pramārjana), blowing out (nirdhmāpana), emesis (vamana), purgation (virecana), washing (prakṣālana), massage (pratimarśa), inducing evacuation (pravāhaṇa), suction (ācūṣaṇa), the magnet (ayaskānta), and exhilaration (harṣa).

In that regard, a shaft deeply embedded in the flesh falls out due to tears, sneezing, belching, coughing, urine, feces, or wind—occurring through their own natural force—from the eyes or other orifices; or it falls out when the wound, though not yet inflamed, has been ripened and putrefied by the pressure of pus and blood or by its own heaviness. One should cause a suppurated shaft that does not burst spontaneously to burst or incise it. Once incised, if it is not expelled, one should press it out with compressing instruments or with the hands.
Minute foreign bodies lodged in the eyes should be removed by irrigation, insufflation, or wiping with the hands, soft cloth, or cotton wool.
Minute foreign bodies that are not mixed with remnants of food or phlegm should be blown out using breath, coughing, or blowing through a tube.
Foreign bodies consisting of food particles should be removed by means of emetics, finger-probing, or digital massage.
Purgatives are for disorders located in the colon;
washouts are for disorders located in the site of a wound;
and straining is prescribed for obstructions of flatus, urine, feces, or the fetus.
One should extract [foreign matter] from breast milk corrupted by wind, water, poison, or blood by means of sucking with the mouth or using horns;
[one should extract] a loose, unattached foreign body from the ear that does not have a large wound opening by means of a magnet;
and a grief-thorn lodged in the heart, arising from many causes, one should extract with joy.
For all shafts, whether large or small, there are only two means of extraction: the reverse method and the direct method.
In that case, one should bring [the fire] hitherward in reverse order, and thitherward in direct order.
Having cut away the protruding part, one should eliminate the opening that is to be excised.

One should also strive to remove, by means of the hand itself and in the proper manner, those [foreign bodies] that have entered the openings for excision, as well as those fallen into the abdomen, chest, armpits, groin, or the intercostal spaces, provided they can be reached by the hand.
If it cannot be removed by hand, one should cut it with a surgical instrument and remove it using a mechanical forceps.
And there is a verse on this point:
One should sprinkle him who is fainting with cool water;
one should protect his vital organs and repeatedly reassure him.

Then, having extracted the foreign body (śalya), made the wound free of blood, and applied fomentation (sveda) using fire, ghee, and other appropriate means, one should cauterize it, smear it with ghee and honey, bandage it, and prescribe the regimen of conduct (ācārika). [If the foreign body is lodged in a vein or a ligament, it should be released and removed using probes and similar instruments. If the opening is constricted by swelling, one should press out the swelling; if the opening is weak, one should bind it with kuśa grass and other materials.]

One should extract a splinter situated near the heart by means of cold water and other such methods; however, if it is difficult to remove by those means or if it is obstructed from another direction, one should incise the area and pull it out.

If [the shaft] has entered a cavity between the bones or is caught by the teeth of a bone, one should seize it with both feet and extract it with a mechanical device (*yantra*). Or, if this is impossible, when the patient is firmly held by strong men, one should cause the shaft to be grasped with a device, split the tip of the shaft (*śalyavāraṅga*), bind one end to the bowstring, and tie the other end to the bridle of a horse restrained by its five limbs (*pañcāṅgya*). Then, one should strike it with a whip so that, as the horse raises its head with force, it extracts the shaft. Alternatively, having bent down a sturdy tree branch and bound [the shaft] to it as before, one should extract it.

Having displaced it by means of a blow from one of the following—an improper instrument, a sharp-pointed object, a tumor-like growth, a stone, or a mallet—one should [extract it] using a surgical instrument along its natural path.
By means of the [proper] instrument, their ears were pressed down so that they possessed ears, with the regions of the cheeks rendered free from obstruction and the tips protruding forward.

When a waxen [plug] is stuck in the throat, one should insert a tube into the throat and a probe heated by fire; having secured it with that, one should sprinkle it with cold water and, once it has become firm, extract it.
Some say that one should use a stick smeared with lac and beeswax that has not yet been heated, according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Having observed a bone splinter or another foreign object lodged transversely in the throat, one should have the patient drink a mass of hair tied together with a single strong thread and mixed with liquid food until the throat is full; once the stomach is full, one should induce vomiting. While the patient is vomiting, if one perceives that the object is caught in a certain part, one should suddenly pull the thread. Alternatively, one may remove it with a soft brush made of tooth-cleaning wood or push it inward.
To the one whose throat is wounded, one should give honey and ghee to lick, or the powder of triphalā mixed with honey and sugar.
One should press down upon his belly filled with water while he is head-downward, or shake him, or cause him to vomit, or bury him up to his mouth in a heap of ashes.
If a morsel of food becomes a thorn stuck in the throat, one should strike the shoulder with the fist without hesitation or awareness, or have the patient drink oil, wine, or water.

When the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated by the pressure on the neck from the noose-like cords of the arms and hands, it provokes the phlegm (śleṣman), obstructs the channels, and causes the flow of saliva, the emergence of froth, and the loss of consciousness; for such a person, one should apply oil massage, induce sudation, administer a strong head-purgative (śirovirecana), and provide meat broth that subdues the wind.
And there are verses on this point:
Having observed the specific shapes of the foreign bodies and their locations, as well as the various types of instruments, the wise physician should then properly extract the foreign body.
Therefore, a physician, being composed and employing proper skill, should extract those arrows that have barbs and are difficult to remove.
If the splinter is not extracted by these means,
the physician should remove it with clever ingenuity and the application of instruments.
A foreign body that has not been extracted causes swelling, suppuration, and severe pain;
it may even lead to deformity or death. Therefore, one should extract it with great effort.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Extraction of Foreign Bodies," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of wounds that are contrary and those that are not contrary.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari said:
Just as flowers, smoke, and clouds indicate the future occurrence of fruits, fire, and rain,
so too do portents (ariṣṭas) announce the impending death.

Due to their subtlety, or through negligence, or likewise because of a rapid transgression, these [signs] do not appear to the ignorant when they have emerged; this is not, however, because of their non-existence in one who is about to die.
Death, when portended by ominous signs, is certainly averted— so it is said— by stainless Brahmins who are devoted to elixirs, ascetic penances, and the chanting of prayers.
Just as the affliction of the stars ripens in many ways according to the time,
so too do many people speak of the ripening of misfortune (ariṣṭa).
In this world, one who attempts to treat those whose life-span has expired meets with failure;
therefore, a skilled physician should diligently observe the signs of impending death.
Any alteration in the specific qualities of odor, color, taste, and so forth, occurring by their very nature,
is declared to be the sign of ripening in a patient with an ulcer.
The odor caused by the wind and other [humors] is pungent, sharp, and fleshy;
that caused by blood has the smell of iron, while a combination of these is the result of the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (sānnipātika).
Those which are similar in smell to parched grain, sesame oil, or slightly putrid should be known as having their natural odor; anything other than these is a corruption of the odor.
The wounds of those about to die are known to be fragrant with the scents of madhuka, aguru, ghee, jasmine, lotus, sandalwood, and campaka flowers, or to possess a divine fragrance.
Those with the smell of dogs, horses, mice, crows, putrid meat, lice, mud, and the earth are censured.
Those [ulcers] that have the color of soot, saffron, or *kaṅkuṣṭha* due to the provocation of *pitta*,
which neither burn nor suppurate— the physician should avoid them.
Those [tumors] that are itchy, firm, white, and oily due to the cause of phlegm (kapha),
yet which throb or burn, the physician should avoid them.
One should avoid those black-colored discharges that flow from the body, which are born of wind (vāta) and cause pain in the vital points (marmas), even if they do not produce much pain.
Those ulcers that make a hissing sound, produce a gurgling noise, and seem as if they were burning,
and which, situated in the skin and flesh, emit wind with a sound;
And those wounds which do not arise in vital spots yet cause excessive pain,
which burn intensely within while being cold on the outside;
The spears, banners, chariots, lances, horses, elephants, cattle, and bulls burn excessively on the outside while remaining cool within.
And those which appear in the form of palaces,
or which shine as if strewn with powder, though they are not actually powdered;
Those afflicted by the wasting of vital breath and flesh, by dyspnea, cough, and loss of appetite,
and those whose wounds in the vital organs (marmas) have become profuse with pus and blood;
A wise physician, desiring to protect his own reputation, should avoid those ulcers that do not heal despite being properly initiated with medical treatments.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Favorable and Unfavorable Ulcers," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the interpretation of dreams, both contrary and non-contrary.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
The sight and conversation of messengers, as well as their dress and gestures;
the constellation, the time, the lunar day, omens, auspicious signs, and the wind.
The physician’s complexion, as well as the movements of his speech, body, and mind,
indicate whether the condition of the patient is auspicious or inauspicious.
Those who belong to heretical sects, stages of life, or castes are favorable for the successful accomplishment of a rite;
those same individuals, when acting in a contrary manner, serve as messengers leading to the failure of the rite.

Eunuchs, women, many [persons], those who do not share a single purpose, and those who are envious; they shall obtain donkey- and camel-drawn chariots, or they may encounter a succession of calamities.
Those messengers who approach the physician— carrying nooses, staffs, and weapons, and dressed in garments other than white— are also censurable.
Wearing damp, tattered, left-side-turned, soiled, and disheveled garments;
with deficient or redundant limbs; agitated, deformed, and of fierce appearance.
Those who speak harsh and cruel words, uttering inauspicious things;
those who cut grass or wood, or touch their noses or breasts.

Those who touch the hem of one's garment, the ring finger, the hair, the nails, the body hair, or the fringe; or those who touch the stream of urine, the obstruction, the heart, the cheeks, the head, the chest, or the belly with their hands.
Those who carry skulls, stones, ashes, bones, husks, and charcoal, scratching the earth,
breaking clods of soil, and letting out slight cries;
With their limbs smeared with oil and mud, wearing red garlands and unguents,
they took ripe fruit or something else of that same nature, though devoid of essence.
Those who scratch one nail with another, or likewise the foot with the hand,
or those whose hands are covered in leather sandals, or those afflicted by deformed diseases;
Moving to the left, weeping, panting, and with distorted eyes,
they stood in the southern direction with palms joined in reverence, positioned on uneven ground.

Those messengers who approach a physician are also censured; likewise, one who sees a fire burning toward the south in an impure place, or one kindling it, cooking, or intent upon a cruel act. (1.29.15ef)
Nor one who is naked, or lying on the ground, or impure due to the discharge of natural urges,
or with disheveled hair, or anointed with oil, or perspiring, or even one who is distressed.
Those messengers who approach a physician for a rite dedicated to the ancestors,
a rite dedicated to the gods, or upon the sight of an omen are also censured.
At midday or at midnight, during the two twilights, and under the asterisms of Kṛttikā,
Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Mūla, the three Pūrvās, and Bharaṇī;
Those messengers who approach a physician on the fourth, ninth, or sixth lunar days, or on the junction days (sandhi), are also censured.
Messengers who have arrived before a physician at midday, perspiring and tormented by heat near a fire, are censured in cases of bile-related diseases.
These very [remedies] are traditionally held to bring success in treatments for diseases of phlegm (kapha).
By this, the remainder is explained; having understood it, one should distribute it accordingly.
In cases of hemorrhaging, bile disorders, diarrhea, as well as urinary diseases,
and in obstructions of waterways, the arrival of a messenger or a physician is highly recommended.
Having thus understood this distinction, the wise man should comprehend the remainder:
[the deity] is white-robed, pure, fair or dark-complexioned, and pleasant to behold.
A messenger who belongs to one's own caste or one's own lineage is considered effective in his task;
he is auspicious if he arrives by bullock-cart, appears pleased, and moves with graceful gait on foot.
One who possesses mindfulness, knows the proper time for action, is independent, and is resourceful;
who is adorned, auspicious, and capable of accomplishing the task—such a messenger is traditionally prescribed.
He who approaches a physician— who is healthy, seated facing the east on a clean and level spot, and himself pure— is considered capable of accomplishing the task.
Meat, a water-pot, an umbrella, a Brahmin, an elephant, and a bull— these,
when seen at the time of departure, are honored if they are white in color.
A woman with sons, a cow with her calf, an ornamented increasing vessel,
a maiden, fish, raw fruit, a svastika, sweetmeats, and curd.
A vessel of gold and unbroken rice, gems, and beautiful flowers; a king, a fire that is not yet extinguished, a horse, a swan, a blue jay, and likewise a peacock.
The sounds of the Brahma-drum, the clouds, the conch, the flute, and the chariot;
the roars of lions, bulls, and cows; and the neighing of horses and the trumpeting of elephants.
The cry of swans and that of the *kauśika* bird are auspicious when heard on the left; likewise, for one setting out on a journey, words that are pleasing to the heart are excellent.
Or they may be trees endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruit, yielding milk and free from disease;
or they may be situated within celestial dwellings, beneath banners, on archways, or upon altars.
When the quarters are tranquil, birds that speak sweetly while following behind,
whether on the left or the right, portend the successful accomplishment of one's undertakings.
On a tree that is withered, struck by lightning, leafless, entwined by creepers, or thorny; or else upon stones, ashes, bones, excrement, husks, charcoal, or dust.
Those who dwell on shrines, anthills, or uneven ground, those with a harsh and blazing voice,
and those who speak while facing the cardinal directions that are ablaze— these do not accomplish one's purpose.
Birds with names beginning with the letter *pu* are auspicious when on the left, while those designated as female are auspicious on the right.
For dogs and jackals, movement from the right to the left is praised;
for mongooses and blue jays, the left is favorable; but for rabbits and snakes, neither direction is auspicious.
It is said that both the sight and the cry of the Bhāsa and the owl are not auspicious;
likewise, neither the sight nor the cry of the iguana and the chameleon is favorable.
For men, seeing a horse that resembles undesirable messengers— such as a horse resembling kulattha beans, sesame seeds, cotton, husks, stones, or ashes— is inauspicious.
Likewise, a vessel filled with glowing coals, oil, or mud; or one full of spirits other than *prasanna*, or red mustard seeds, is not desired.
The meeting on the road of withered wood, dry palāśa leaves,
and likewise of those who have fallen, the wretched, the blind, and the enemies, is not desired.
A wind that is gentle, cool, favorable, and fragrant is auspicious;
one that is harsh, hot, foul-smelling, and contrary is censured.

In cases such as cysts and tumors (granthy-arbuda), the term "excision" (cheda) is always honored; likewise, in cases of abscesses, abdominal enlargements, and tumors (vidradhi-udara-gulma), the term "incision" (bheda) is used.
In cases of hemorrhagic fever, bilious fever, and diarrhea, the term "ruddha" (obstructed) is recommended;
thus one should determine the underlying cause according to the specific disease.
Likewise, there are sounds of being reviled, cries of "Alas! Alas!", and the noises of lamentation and weeping;
as well as the sound of vomiting wind and excrement, and indeed the braying of donkeys and camels.
That which is forbidden, as well as broken, sneezed upon, stumbled over, struck,
or accompanied by the physician's dejection during the journey, is not commended.
This [examination] should be performed upon entry and likewise when the patient is present;
however, it need not be repeated at every door or throughout the house.
Hair, ashes, bones, wood, stone, chaff, cotton, thorns,
a bed with upturned legs, liquor, water, fat, oil, sesame seeds, and grass.
Eunuchs, the mutilated, the crippled, the naked, the shaven-headed, and those clad in white garments—
these are not desired to be seen when setting out on a journey or upon returning home.
Likewise, the shifting of vessels from their place of storage,
the uprooting of what was buried, breaking, falling, and exiting [the house].
Or the physician may sit on a low seat, or the patient may be facing downward;
while conversing with the physician, [the patient] may lean against a limb, a wall, or a bedsheet.
One should wipe or shake the hands, the back, and likewise the head;
having drawn back the physician's hand, one should place it upon one's own head and chest.
The sick man who asks a physician while facing away from him rubs his own body;
he does not recover, nor does the physician succeed, in whose house he is not honored.
Or even in whose house the physician is honored, he succeeds;
for auspicious results follow from auspicious messengers and the like, while inauspicious results follow from inauspicious ones.
Therefore, the physician should certainly observe the messengers and others of the patient;
next, I shall describe dreams that portend either death or well-being.
That which his friends see, or that which he himself sees when thus afflicted by disease—
his body smeared with oil [and dragged] by young camels, snakes, and donkeys.
If one should travel facing south on boars or even on buffaloes,
[he sees] a dark woman wearing red garments, laughing with her hair disheveled.
Or if a woman, having bound him, drags him while dancing toward the south;
or if he is dragged toward the south by outcasts (antāvasāyin).
Or even those who are embraced by hungry ghosts (pretas) or likewise by renunciants,
and he who is repeatedly sniffed at by beasts of prey with distorted faces.
One might drink honey and oil, or sink into the mud;
or with limbs smeared with mud, one might dance and likewise laugh.
He who is naked and wears a red garland upon his head,
or whose lineage is that of Nala or Tāla, or who has one growing upon his chest;
Whether one might be swallowed by a fish, or a man were to enter his mother's womb,
or whether he might fall from a mountain peak into a pit shrouded in darkness.
Whether one is carried away by a current, or undergoes tonsure,
or is defeated, or bound, or overcome by crows and other such creatures;
