He who sees the falling of stars and the like, the extinction of lamps and the eyesight,
as well as the trembling of deities and likewise of the earth;
He who has vomiting or purging, or whose teeth fall out,
sees the Śālmalī tree, the Kiṃśuka tree, a sacrificial post, an anthill, or the Pāribhadraka tree.
He who ascends a *kovidāra* tree rich in flowers, or a funeral pyre,
or cotton, sesame oil, oil-cakes, iron, salt, or sesame seeds;
Whether he eats cooked food, drinks liquor, or remains healthy, he incurs disease;
being diseased, he meets with death.
Just as one's own natural dream is forgotten or obstructed,
so too those dreams produced by daytime thoughts become fruitless.
For those suffering from fever, friendship with dogs is prescribed; for those suffering from wasting diseases, friendship with monkeys;
in cases of insanity, association with Rākṣasas; and in epilepsy, with Pretas.
Drinking water is [contraindicated] for those suffering from excessive urination; oil for those with skin diseases (kuṣṭha);
the growth of plants within the abdominal cavity for those with abdominal tumors (gulma); and [the application of oil] to the head for those with headaches.
For one suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍuroga), eating fried cakes (śaṣkulī) leads to vomiting; traveling on foot leads to dyspnea and thirst; and even consuming turmeric with food [leads to the same].
One who suffers from *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) perishes if he drinks blood;
having seen such dreams, one should rise early in the morning and exert effort.
One should give beans, sesame seeds, iron, and likewise gold to the Brahmins;
one should also recite auspicious mantras as well as the three-footed Gāyatrī.
Having seen [an ill omen], however, he should sleep during the first watch of the night after contemplating something auspicious;
or else, being composed and observing celibacy, he should recite a portion of one of the Vedas.
One should likewise dwell for three nights in a temple of the gods and constantly honor Brahmins; thus one is liberated from evil dreams.
Henceforth, I shall describe the auspicious visions seen in dreams:
[dreaming of] gods, twice-born brahmins, bulls, living friends, and kings.
One should behold a well-kindled fire, virtuous people, and pure waters for the sake of attaining auspiciousness and for the removal of disease.
Meat, fish, white garlands, garments, and fruits—
one obtains these for the sake of gaining wealth and for the removal of disease.
One should ascend a great palace, a fruit-bearing tree, an elephant, or a mountain for the sake of obtaining wealth and for the removal of disease.
One should cross over rivers, streams, and oceans that are agitated and turbid with foul water for the sake of attaining auspiciousness and for the removal of disease.
Whether it be a serpent, a leech, or even a bee that bites him,
a wise man should predict for that person good health and the acquisition of wealth.
A sick man who sees such auspicious dreams as these should be known as long-lived; one should perform ritual actions for him.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Auspicious and Inauspicious Dreams," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirtieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the disorders of the objects of the five sense organs.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
When there occurs a transformation of either the body or the character from their natural state, that indeed is a fatal sign (ariṣṭa);
understand it from me in brief, and then in detail.
He hears various sounds, even in the absence of divine beings,
and the resonances of oceans, cities, and clouds, despite their non-existence.
One perceives those sounds by their own names and conceives of them as being like other words;
one also hears the sounds of village and forest creatures in a distorted manner.
He who takes delight in the words of enemies, becomes angry at the words of friends,
and does not listen when addressed unexpectedly— they say that such a person has reached the end of his life.
He who perceives heat as if it were cold, and cold as if it were heat;
and he who, having developed a cold eruption, is tormented by a burning sensation.
One whose body is excessively hot and who trembles from even slight cold,
who does not feel the pain of blows or even the amputation of a limb;
He who considers his limbs as if covered with dust, or indeed,
he whose limbs exhibit changes in color or the appearance of streaks;
If blue flies swarm upon one who has just bathed and anointed himself,
or if someone suddenly becomes fragrant without cause, they say that person's life has come to an end.
He who perceives tastes incorrectly,
or he for whom tastes consumed in their proper sequence lead instead to the increase of the bodily humors (doṣas).
One whose humors and digestive fire have been brought into equilibrium by the improper administration [of therapies],
or who no longer perceives tastes and food, is declared to be one whose life has departed.
One perceives fragrance as foul odor, or foul odor as fragrance;
or one grasps the odor incorrectly, even when the lamp is extinguished and free from defect.
Or one who does not perceive odors should be declared dead;
likewise, the pairs such as heat and cold, the seasons, and the directions [are no longer perceived].
The man who perceives other entities through distortion,
and who sees even the celestial lights during the day as if they were ablaze;
Whoever sees the sun blazing at night, or the moon’s radiance by day,
or the qualities of Indra’s bow and lightning when there is no obstruction of clouds;
Or those dark clouds accompanied by lightning in a cloudless sky,
and the atmosphere crowded with celestial chariots, vehicles, and palaces.
And he who sees the wind personified and the intermediate space,
as well as the earth as if covered by veils of smoke and mist;
He who sees the world as if ablaze, or as if flooded with water,
and he who sees the earth marked with lines in the pattern of a checkerboard.
They say that he who does not see the goddess Arundhatī together with the stars, nor Dhruva, nor the celestial Gaṅgā, has reached the end of his life.
And he who does not see his own reflection in moonlight, in a mirror, or in warm water;
or who sees it as lacking a limb, or deformed, or belonging to another being.
Of dogs, crows, kaṅkas, vultures, pretas, yakṣas,
rākṣasas, piśācas, uragas, nāgas, and even of the transformed spirits (bhūtas).
Or he who sees a smokeless fire with the luster of a peacock’s neck—
the death of the sick man shall occur, and the healthy one shall contract a disease.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Misapprehension of the Objects of the Five Senses," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the abnormalities of the shadow (chāyā-vipratipatti).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
Whichever shadow— whether dark-brown, reddish, blue, or even yellow— rushes toward a man, he is undoubtedly about to die.
He from whom splendor, fortitude, mindfulness, and glory suddenly depart,
or who is suddenly possessed by them, is undoubtedly one whose life-force has departed.
If one's lower lip has fallen away and the upper lip is thrust upward,
or if both lips resemble the color of a jambu fruit, his life is difficult to preserve.
One whose teeth are reddish, or dark-brown, or falling out,
or even resembling wagtails, should be declared to have reached the end of his life.
He whose tongue is black, stiff, or coated, or indeed swollen,
or rough, shall surely give up his life before long.
A man whose nose is crooked, cracked, or dry, or which quivers,
or has sunken in, does not live.
A man whose eyes are constricted, uneven, fixed, bloodshot, drooping,
or excessively watering is certainly one whose life has departed.
He whose hair is parted with a line, whose eyebrows are drawn together and drooping,
and whose eyelashes cut into his eyes— he goes to death before long.
He who does not swallow food remaining in his mouth, nor holds his head steady,
being of deluded mind with one-pointed gaze, shall instantly lose his life-breaths.
Whether strong or weak, if one who has fallen into delusion is frequently roused up,
the physician should declare that he is ripe [for recovery].
That man who always lies on his back, who moves his feet about,
or who habitually stretches them out, does not live.
A wise man should avoid that mortal whose breath is cold from his hands and feet, whose breathing is interrupted, or who has the gasping breath of a crow.
He whose sleep is never interrupted, or who remains perpetually awake,
or who becomes deluded when desiring to speak— such a person should be rejected by one who knows.
One who licks his upper lip, one who makes spitting sounds,
or one who converses with ghosts— one should designate him as having the form of a ghost.
If blood flows from one's own hair follicles in a man who is not afflicted by poison, he shall lose his life immediately.
But he in whose heart the vātāṣṭhīlā moves upward,
causing pain and an aversion to food, is undoubtedly on the verge of death.
A swelling arising from the feet, caused by no other affliction, kills a man;
one arising from the mouth kills a woman; and one arising from the private parts kills both.
One should declare that person to be wasted away who suffers from diarrhea, fever, hiccups, vomiting, swelling of the scrotum and penis,
or who is afflicted with asthma or cough.
Excessive sweating, burning sensations, severe hiccups,
and labored breathing will undoubtedly deprive even a strong man of his life.
One whose tongue becomes dark-brown, whose left eye sinks in,
and whose mouth becomes foul-smelling— one should avoid such a person.
The mouth is filled with tears, both feet perspire,
and the eyes become agitated for one who is about to go to the realm of Yama.
He whose limbs suddenly become excessively light or heavy should be known as one who is going to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Those men who smell the scent of mud, fish, fat, oil, and ghee,
or those who emit the scent of fragrant perfumes, shall go to the abode of Yama.
Lice swarm upon their foreheads, crows do not eat their offerings, and they find no pleasure in anything; such people go to the abode of Yama.
For one whose fever, diarrhea, and swelling mutually weaken each other,
and whose strength and flesh are wasted away, that condition cannot be cured.
When hunger and thirst are not alleviated by heart-pleasing, sweet, and wholesome foods and drinks for one who is emaciated, death has arrived for him.
Diarrhea, headache, and severe abdominal pain,
along with thirst and loss of strength— death has approached him.
Through adverse treatment, by actions performed in the past,
and because of the impermanence of living beings, life comes to its end in death.
Pretas, bhūtas, piśācas, and various kinds of rākṣasas constantly approach a human being who is facing death.
Those medicinal potencies counteract [the disease] with a desire to kill;
therefore, all actions become utterly futile for those whose life-span has expired.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Misinterpretation of Chāyā," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the perversion of natural constitution.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
The transformation of certain parts of the body that are established in their own nature leads to death.

For example: whiteness appearing as blackness in white things, blackness in black things, other colors in red things; firmness in soft things, softness in firm things; motionlessness in moving things, movement in motionless things; contraction in broad things, breadth in contracted things; shortness in long things, length in short things; the property of falling in things that do not have the property of falling, and the property of not falling in things that have the property of falling; and furthermore, the sudden onset of coldness, heat, oiliness, roughness, stiffness, discoloration, and exhaustion of the limbs.

The sudden displacement, elevation, wandering, tossing, falling, release, exit, entry, heaviness, or lightness of parts of the body from their own positions; the appearance of sprout-like discolorations (*vyaṅga*) on the skin; the visible appearance of veins on the forehead or the bridge of the nose; the eruption of pustules (*piḍaka*); perspiration on the forehead at dawn; the flow of tears without ocular disease; the sight of dust resembling powdered cow-dung or its settling upon the head; the increase in the excrement of pigeons, herons, crows, and similar birds; the disappearance of such signs in those who do not eat, or their appearance in those who do eat; the onset of pain in the root of the breasts, the heart, and the chest; swelling in the center with flaccidity at the extremities, or the reverse; and likewise, edema in half of the body.

Wasting away of the limbs or the wings [of the body], loss, impairment, deficiency, or distortion of the voice; the appearance of discolored spots on the teeth, face, nails, or body; that person whose phlegm, feces, or semen sink in water; or he in whose visual field (dṛṣṭimaṇḍala) broken and distorted forms are perceived; one who appears as if his hair and limbs were smeared with oil; and a man who is weak, afflicted by aversion to food and diarrhea, coughing and overcome by thirst, emaciated, possessed of vomiting and aversion to food, expectorating froth, pus, and blood, with a destroyed voice and seized by pain, and whose hands, feet, and face are swollen—such a person, being emaciated, having an aversion to food, with sagging calves, shoulders, hands, and feet, and overcome by fever and cough, [is near death].

He who, having eaten in the forenoon, vomits it up undigested in the afternoon, or suffers from diarrhea while overcome by fever and cough, dies of asthma while moaning like a goat; and that man who falls to the ground with his testicles sagging, his penis stiffened, his neck broken, and his organ lost, whose heart was previously drying up though his body remains moist; and he who strikes a clod with a clod, a piece of wood with a piece of wood, or tears at blades of grass; who bites his lower lip or licks his upper lip; who pulls out his ears or his hair; who hates gods, brahmins, teachers, friends, and physicians; whose planets—whether direct or retrograde—are afflicted by moving into censurable positions and tormenting his birth-star (*janmarkṣa*); or whose *horā* is struck by a meteor or a thunderbolt.
Or it is the manifestation of signs and marks of reproach regarding one's house, wife, bed, seat, carriage, vehicle, jewels, gems, and utensils.
And there are verses on this point:
When a disorder, though being properly treated, continues to increase,
that is a sign of one whose strength and flesh have wasted away and whose life has reached its end.
If a great disease suddenly subsides for a person,
yet no result from his diet is observed, he perishes.
The physician who correctly understands these signs of impending death shall be esteemed by the king in the examination of what is curable and incurable.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Deviation from Natural State," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the incurable (avāraṇīya).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
O child, listen with a single-minded focus to me regarding those incurable diseases that afflict men through calamities, which cannot be overcome except by means of *rasāyana*.

Diseases of wind (vāta), urinary disorders (prameha), leprosy (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (arśas), fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara), urinary stones (aśmarī), obstructed labor (mūḍhagarbha), and likewise abdominal enlargement (udara) as the eighth.
These eight great diseases are by their very nature difficult to treat,
accompanied by wasting of the vital breath and flesh, dyspnea, thirst, emaciation, vomiting, and fever.
Furthermore, those afflicted by these complications— fainting, diarrhea, and hiccups—
should be especially avoided by a physician desiring success.
A person who is swollen, has numb skin, is broken-limbed, afflicted by tremors,
flatulence, and pain— such a man, suffering internally from the disease of wind (vāta), shall perish.
When afflicted by the aforementioned complications, or when excessively discharging urine,
or when severely tormented by carbuncles, prameha kills the man.

It destroys the leprosy of a leper in this world— [leprosy] which has burst open, from which secretions flow from the limbs, whose eyes are bloodshot, whose voice is impaired, and which has transcended the curability of the five therapeutic measures (pañcakarma).
The disease of hemorrhoids destroys one who is afflicted by thirst, anorexia, and colic; who has excessive bleeding;
and who is accompanied by swelling and diarrhea.
One should avoid that person from whom wind, urine, feces, worms,
and even semen flow out through a fistula-in-ano.
Accompanied by gravel and urinary calculi,
a stone (aśmarī) quickly destroys one who has a swollen scrotum, obstructed urine, and is afflicted with pain.
Attachment to the inner membrane (garbhakoṣa), the placenta (makkalla),
and the closure of the birth canal (yonisaṃvṛti) may kill the woman in the case of a retained fetus, as well as the complications previously described.
One should avoid treating a patient afflicted with abdominal disease who suffers from side-pains, aversion to food, swelling, and diarrhea,
or one who has been purged and whose abdomen continues to distend.
The man who faints and lies unconscious, or even falls down;
who is afflicted by cold yet has heat within, dies from fever.
The fever that kills a man is characterized by bristling body hair, bloodshot eyes, a piercing pain in the chest, and constant labored breathing through the mouth.
Fever destroys a man who is afflicted by hiccup, labored breathing, and thirst; who is delirious with wandering eyes; who breathes incessantly; and who is emaciated.
Fever destroys a man whose eyes are turbid, who is fainting, who is excessively drowsy,
and whose blood and flesh are wasted away.
Dysentery especially destroys an elderly man who is afflicted by labored breathing, pain, thirst, emaciation, and fever.
Consumption (yakṣmā) destroys a man in this world who has white eyes, who loathes food, who is oppressed by upward breathing, and who voids much urine with great difficulty.
For one suffering from gulma who is destined for death, there occur labored breathing, piercing pain, thirst, aversion to food, abdominal knots, mental confusion, and physical debility.
An abscess (vidradhi) destroys a man who is bloated, suffering from obstructed evacuation, afflicted with vomiting, hiccups, and thirst, and overwhelmed by pain and dyspnea.
A man whose teeth and nails are pale, whose eyes are pale,
and who perceives white masses [of objects], perishes from jaundice.
He who vomits blood frequently, whose eyes are red,
and who perceives the quarters of the sky as red, perishes from rakta-pitta (blood-bile).
A man whose flesh and strength are wasted, whether looking downward, forward, or upward,
and who remains wakeful, will undoubtedly perish from insanity.
But epilepsy shall destroy one who frequently suffers from it, whose body is emaciated, whose eyebrows are twitching, and whose eyes are distorted.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Incurable," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the army in array.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
The physician must provide protection for King Yuktasena as he seeks to conquer his enemies; how this is to be done will now be explained.
A king who desires victory and is intent on an expedition must, with great effort, protect himself especially from his own ministers, just as he would from poison.

Enemies defile the roads, water, shade, food, fodder, and fuel; one should recognize this and likewise purify it. Its symptoms and medical treatment will be explained in the Section on Formulas (Kalpasthāna).
The Atharvans declare that there are one hundred and one types of death;
among these, one is connected with time (kāla), while the remainder are known as adventitious (āgantuka).

The physician and the priest, both experts in the science of tastes and mantras, should constantly guard the king with diligence against death caused by internal humors, external accidents, or natural demise.
Brahmā proclaimed the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the eight-limbed Āyurveda;
therefore, a self-possessed physician should abide by the opinion of the royal chaplain.
There will be a confusion of all castes, the destruction of righteous deeds,
and even the extermination of the subjects, caused by the king's misfortune.
Among men and kings alike, there is only equality in physical form;
yet [in them] reside command, renunciation, forgiveness, fortitude, and superhuman valor.
Therefore, desiring his own welfare, a wise physician should constantly regard the king as a god through auspicious deeds of speech, mind, and body.
And in the great military camp, situated immediately adjacent to the royal palace,
it should always be kept present, equipped with all necessary provisions.
Those afflicted by the diseases of poison, thorns, and illness approach him as he stands there, exalted like a banner through the renown of his glory, with undeluded minds.
Skilled in his own field and not excluded from the meanings of other treatises,
the physician shines like a banner, honored by the king and those learned in that science.
The physician, the patient afflicted by disease, the medicine, and the attendant—
these are the four pillars of medical treatment, serving as the causes for accomplishing the therapeutic act.
With three feet that possess qualities, a physician who possesses the fourth quality as well can cure even a great disease in a short time.
Three feet, though possessed of all qualities, are useless if they lack a physician,
just as the Udgātṛ, Hotṛ, and Brahman priests are useless in a sacrifice without the Adhvaryu.
But a single physician endowed with excellence can always rescue patients,
just as a helmsman [rescues those] on water using a boat provided with rowers.
One who has mastered the meaning of the treatises, has observed the practical application of the rites, is personally skillful,
light-handed, pure, brave, and possesses ready equipment and medicines.
The wise physician who possesses presence of mind, is resolute, confident, and devoted to truth and righteousness is said to be the fourth quarter.
One who possesses longevity, strength, treatability, wealth, and self-control;
who is a believer and abides by the physician’s instructions—such a patient is said to constitute one quarter [of a cure].
Produced in an auspicious place, extracted on an auspicious day,
of the proper measure, pleasing to the mind, and endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste.

Medicine that destroys the doshas, does not cause exhaustion, and produces no adverse effects even when there is a change in condition, and which is administered after careful consideration at the proper time, is said to constitute one quarter [of the ideal treatment].
Affectionate, free from disgust, strong, and diligent in protecting the patient;
one who follows the physician’s instructions and is tireless—such a person is known as the attendant (pāda).
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "On the Array of the Army," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the management of the patient (Āturōpakramaṇīya).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari said:

A physician treating a patient must first examine the life-span; once the existence of life is confirmed, he should examine the disease, the season, the digestive fire, age, the body, strength, the mind, suitability, constitution, the medicine, and the location.

In that regard, one should recognize a man as long-lived by his large hands, feet, sides, back, nipples, teeth, face, shoulders, and forehead; his long fingers, joints, breath, gaze, and arms; his broad eyebrows, the space between the breasts, and chest; his short shanks, penis, and neck; his deep character, voice, and navel; his not-too-high-set breasts; his well-developed, large, hairy ears; and his posterior fontanelle. Furthermore, one should recognize him by his body drying up gradually from the head downward when bathed and anointed, and his heart drying last of all.
One should attend to such a person exclusively.
By these characteristics being the opposite, one has a short lifespan; by those being mixed, a medium lifespan.
And there are verses on this point:
He whose joints, veins, and sinews are hidden, whose limbs are compact, whose senses are steady,
and who possesses increasingly excellent fields [of merit], is said to be long-lived.
He who is free from disease from the time of conception and gradually develops his body,
knowledge, and discernment, is, in brief, long-lived.
Now learn from me the knowledge of the middle lifespan;
for one who has distinct, long lines below the two eyes, [he lives for a medium duration].
The feet, ears, and nose-tip are fleshy, measuring two, three, or even more [finger-breadths];
and there are upward-pointing lines on the back of the head.
For one who possesses [these], the maximum lifespan is seventy years;
now learn from me the knowledge regarding the minimum lifespan beyond this point.
He whose joints are short and whose penis is very large, and likewise whose chest is broad with folds, but whose back is not long— [he is a man of great fortune].
If the ears of an embodied being protrude upward from their natural position and the nose is elevated,
and if the gums of the teeth become visible even when he is laughing or speaking,
and if he looks about with a wandering gaze, he shall live for twenty-five years. (1.35.11ef)
Furthermore, for the sake of understanding the lifespan, we shall now teach the measurements and essential qualities of the major and minor limbs.
In this context, the major limbs (aṅga) are the trunk, the thighs, the forearms, and the head; their constituent parts are the minor limbs (pratyaṅga).

Therein, according to one's own fingers (svairaṅgula): the big toe and the fore-toe are two fingers long; the middle, ring, and little toes are each successively shorter by a fifth part compared to the fore-toe. The forefoot and the sole of the foot are four and five fingers long respectively, while the heel is five and four fingers long and wide. The foot is fourteen fingers long, and the circumference of the foot, ankle, calf, and middle of the knee are each fourteen fingers. The calf is eighteen fingers long, and from above the knee it is likewise thirty-two fingers, making fifty fingers in total for the length of the leg. The thighs are equal in length to the calves. Two fingers [in measurement] are the scrotum, chin, teeth, nostril-aperture, ear-root, and the distance between the eyes; four fingers are the distance between the penis and the mouth, the nose, the ears, the forehead, the height of the neck, and the distance between the eyes.

The breadth of the face is twelve *aṅgulas*. The length of the penis, navel, heart, neck, space between the breasts, and mouth, as well as the thickness of the wrist and forearm, are [twelve *aṅgulas* each]. The circumference of the *indrabasti* (the pubic region), the distance from the shoulder-blade to the elbow, and the hand are sixteen *aṅgulas*. The arm measures thirty-two *aṅgulas*, and the thighs have a circumference of thirty-two *aṅgulas*. The distance from the wrist to the elbow is sixteen *aṅgulas*. The palm is six *aṅgulas* in length and four *aṅgulas* in breadth. The thumb and the forefinger at their base, the ear, and the distance between the outer corners of the eyes are five *aṅgulas*. The middle finger is four and a half *aṅgulas*; the forefinger and ring finger are three and a half *aṅgulas*; and the little finger and thumb are three *aṅgulas* and a half. The face and neck together measure twenty-four *aṅgulas* in width and circumference; the boundary of the nostrils is three parts of an *aṅgula* in width.

The circumference of the pupil is three parts of the eye; the ninth part of the pupil is the vision (*dṛṣṭi*). The distance from the hairline to the top of the head is eleven finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); from the top of the head to the hairline at the nape is ten finger-breadths; the distance between the ear and the nape is fourteen finger-breadths. A woman’s hips are as wide as a man’s chest; the chest is eighteen finger-breadths in width, and a man’s waist is of that same measure. One hundred and twenty finger-breadths is the height of a man.
And there are verses on this point:
"In the twenty-fifth year, a man [attains full vigor], while a woman does so in the sixteenth; a skilled physician should recognize that their vital energies have reached equilibrium at those times."
This body has been described according to its own finger-breadths; whether it be a man or a woman, it is endowed with this measurement.
One obtains a long life and attains great wealth through superior [means];
with middling [means], middling life and wealth; and with inferior [means], the lowest.

Now we shall describe the essential constituents (*sāra*). One should recognize the essence of *sattva* (mental vigor) as being endowed with memory, devotion, wisdom, courage, and purity, and characterized by a commitment to virtue. One should recognize the essence of semen (*śukra*) by smooth, compact, white bones, teeth, and nails, abundant desire, and progeny; by its presence, one is not emaciated and possesses supreme strength, a smooth and deep voice, good fortune, and large eyes. One should recognize the essence of marrow (*majjā*) by a large head and shoulders; the essence of bone (*asthi*) by firm teeth, jawbones, bones, and nails; the essence of fat (*medas*) by unctuous urine, sweat, and voice, and a large body that is unable to endure exertion; the essence of flesh (*māṃsa*) by a body with no gaps between the limbs and hidden joints, and well-developed musculature; and the essence of blood (*rakta*) by unctuous, copper-colored nails, eyes, palate, tongue, lips, palms, and soles, and by skin and hair that are very clear and soft. Thus one should know them.
Among these, each preceding one is more important than the following in terms of longevity and good fortune.
By specifically examining the proportions of the major and minor limbs, as well as the strength [of the patient], a highly skilled physician succeeds in his medical treatments.

All these specific types of diseases previously mentioned are of three kinds: curable (*sādhya*), palliable (*yāpya*), and incurable (*pratyākhyeya*). In this regard, one should further examine them in three ways: whether it is a secondary complication (*aupasargika*), a primary disease (*prākkevala*), or a different characteristic (*anyalakṣaṇa*). Among these, a secondary complication is a disease that arises at a later time and afflicts a disease already produced; it is rooted in that [primary disease] and is termed a "complication" (*upadrava*). A primary disease is one that has arisen previously, appearing as something new [in itself] and being without complications. A different characteristic is that which indicates a future disease; it is termed a "prodromal sign" (*pūrvarūpa*).

In that case, one should treat a condition accompanied by complications without causing mutual conflict; or, if there is a powerful complication, one should first counteract it alone according to its own nature; however, if the symptoms differ, one should strive against the primary disease.
And there is a verse on this point:
Since no disease exists without the humors (doṣas), therefore a wise physician should treat a disease even when it has not been explicitly mentioned, by means of the symptoms of the humors.
The seasons have been previously mentioned.
Having provided relief from cold in the cold season and warding off heat in the hot season,
one should perform the task at hand and not let the proper time for action pass by.
Whether the time for action has not yet arrived or has already passed, an action that is omitted,
deficient, or excessive will not succeed even when the goal is to be accomplished.
For that action is effective which pacifies what has been provoked and does not produce another disease; it is not that which, while removing one disease, provokes another.
The fire that digests food has been described previously.

It is of four kinds: one is unimpaired by the *doṣas*, while the other three, having undergone transformation, are as follows: the irregular (*viṣama*) due to *vāta*, the sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) due to *pitta*, the dull (*manda*) due to *śleṣman*, and the fourth is the balanced (*sama*), resulting from the equilibrium of all [the *doṣas*].

Among these, that which properly digests food consumed at the appropriate time is *sama* (balanced), being balanced with the *doṣas*. That which sometimes digests properly and sometimes produces distension, colic, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), diarrhea, heaviness of the abdomen, rumbling in the intestines, and tenesmus is *viṣama* (irregular). That which quickly digests even a large amount of food consumed is *tīkṣṇa* (sharp); when this same fire increases excessively, it is called *atyagni* (hypermetabolic); it repeatedly and very rapidly digests even a large amount of food, and at the conclusion of digestion, it produces dryness of the throat, palate, and lips, as well as burning sensations and heat. That which takes a long time to digest even a small amount of food consumed, causing heaviness of the abdomen and head, cough, dyspnea, excessive salivation, vomiting, and lassitude of the limbs, is *manda* (dull).
An irregular digestive fire produces diseases born of wind (vāta), a sharp fire those caused by bile (pitta),
and likewise, a dull fire produces disorders arising from phlegm (kapha).

In that regard, one should provide protection when the digestive fire is balanced; when it is irregular, one should treat it with specific measures consisting of unctuous, sour, and salty substances; when it is sharp, one should treat it with sweet, unctuous, and cold substances as well as purgatives; likewise in the case of excessive fire, and especially with buffalo milk, curd, and ghee; and when it is sluggish, one should treat it with pungent, bitter, and astringent substances as well as emetics.
The venerable gastric fire is the lord that digests food;
because of its subtlety, it is impossible to discern as it takes up the essences.
By the three vital airs— prāṇa, apāna, and samāna—
which are established in their respective locations, [the body] is inflated and also cooked on all sides.
Age, however, is threefold: childhood, youth, and old age. Among these, those under sixteen years of age are children.
They too are of three types: sucklings, those who eat both milk and solid food, and those who eat solid food.
Among them, those up to one year old subsist on milk; those up to two years old subsist on milk and rice; beyond that, they subsist on solid food.
The middle stage of life lies between the sixteenth and seventieth years.
Its subdivisions are growth, youth, full maturity, and decline.

In that regard, growth lasts until the twentieth year; youth until the thirtieth; and until the fortieth, there is the full perfection of all elements, faculties, powers, and vigor. Beyond that, up to the seventieth year, there is slight decline.

After the seventieth, with the elements, faculties, powers, vigor, and enthusiasm wasting away day by day, afflicted by wrinkles, gray hair, and baldness, overcome by ailments such as coughing and labored breathing, incapable of any activity, and sinking like an old house rained upon, they call it "old age."

In this regard, as one passes through successive stages of life, there are progressively greater specificities in the dosage of medicine, except in cases of decline; therefore, one should treat according to the initial state even at later stages.
And there are verses on this subject:
"In the child, phlegm increases; in the middle-aged, bile indeed increases;
in the elderly, wind increases most excessively. Having observed this, one should apply treatment accordingly."
One should avoid the use of fire, alkaline treatments, and purgatives for children and the elderly;
however, in cases where these are necessary, one should perform treatment gently and with mild measures.
The body is taught to be gross, emaciated, or of medium size, as previously described.
The physician should always cause those who are stout to lose weight and those who are thin to gain weight;
furthermore, he should constantly maintain the health of those who are of medium build.
Strength should be understood as possessing the qualities already mentioned, while weakness should be examined through its inherent nature, defects, old age, and so forth.
Since all activities proceed from one who possesses strength, strength alone is the primary factor among the clinical considerations.
Some men who are emaciated possess vitality, while others who are stout have little strength;
therefore, a physician should infer strength from stability and physical exercise.
But courage indeed causes one to be free from despondency in situations involving misfortune, prosperity, action, and so forth.
One endowed with *sattva* endures everything by steadying the self with a composed mind;
one characterized by *rajas* endures when steadied by others, but one characterized by *tamas* does not endure at all.

However, those things which are habituated—such as place, time, caste, season, disease, exercise, water, daytime sleep, tastes, and so forth—which do not cause affliction even though they may be contrary to one's constitution (prakṛti).
That taste which, when consumed, conduces solely to one's well-being—
whether it be physical exercise or something else— should be designated as *sātmya* (habitual suitability).
We shall explain the constitution and the medicine further below.
Regarding the regions: they are the marshy (*ānūpa*), the arid (*jāṅgala*), and the intermediate (*sādhāraṇa*).

Among these, the marshy region is characterized by abundant water, low-lying and uneven terrain, rivers, and dense monsoon forests; it has soft, cool winds, many great mountains and trees, is populated mostly by people with soft, delicate, and well-nourished bodies, and is preponderant in diseases of phlegm (*kapha*) and wind (*vāta*). The arid region is like the open sky, consisting mostly of sparse and small thorny trees, having little rain, few springs or wells, hot and harsh winds, very few mountains, and is populated mostly by people with firm and thin bodies; it is preponderant in diseases of wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*). The intermediate region possesses the characteristics of both.
And there are verses on this point:
Since cold, rain, heat, and wind are equal during the *sādhāraṇa* season, the equilibrium of the bodily humors (*doṣas*) in a living being occurs; therefore, it is considered *sādhāraṇa*.
Aquatic creatures brought onto dry land would not be so powerful; likewise, faults that are latent in one's own country become like a provoked fire when they reach a foreign land.
For one who conducts oneself appropriately, there is no fear arising from the location,
provided that the qualities of that place— such as its food, sleep, and activities— are favorable.
However, it is the opposite when there is a favorable location, constitution, and suitability;
when the disease is of recent onset; and when there is the excellence of the physician and other factors, as well as strength, mental fortitude, and longevity.
A disease that arises solely from the digestive fire (agni) of the body is the easiest to cure;
otherwise, it would be incurable, while one characterized by a mixture of both is difficult to treat.
If the desired result is not obtained from a treatment, one should employ another treatment;
however, when the momentum of the previous treatment has subsided, a confusion of treatments is not beneficial.
If that very same action is beneficial even when its qualities are not attained immediately,
then it must certainly be performed, even if the illness is most difficult to cure.

The wise one who maintains this single form of discipline according to the power of time and other factors cuts through the bonds of death and the floods of disease of the world with the axe of medicine.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of the Patient," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the classification of the stages (bhūmi).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

One should examine the ground for medicinal plants as follows: it should not be disturbed by chasms, gravel, stones, unevenness, anthills, cremation grounds, execution sites, temples, or sand; it should be free from salinity, non-fissile, with water nearby, moist, vegetative, soft, firm, and level; and it should be black, pale-yellow, or red in color.

Even when grown on such ground, one should collect the medicine from the northern side of the plant, provided it has not been damaged by worms, poison, weapons, sun, wind, fire, or water, nor by the obstruction of paths; it should be of uniform quality, well-nourished, and possess deep-reaching roots. This is the general specific method for examining the soil.

Specifically, among these: The earth characterized by the quality of stone (*aśmavatī*) is stable, heavy, dark or black, abounding in large trees and grain, rich in its own [earthly] qualities, unctuous, cool, near water, abounding in unctuous crops, grasses, and tender trees, white, rich in the qualities of water, and of various colors. The earth characterized by the quality of fire (*agniguṇabhūyiṣṭhā*) is light, contains stones, is sparse with few pale trees and sprouts, rough, the color of ash or a donkey, thin, dry, with hollows, and abounding in trees of little sap. The earth characterized by the quality of wind (*anilaguṇabhūyiṣṭhā*) is soft, level, possesses chasms, has water of indistinct taste, is everywhere devoid of substantial trees, abounds in great mountain-like trees, and is dark. The earth characterized by the quality of space (*ākāśaguṇabhūyiṣṭhā*) is similar [to the preceding].

Regarding this, some teachers say that one should collect roots, leaves, bark, milky sap, heartwood, and fruits respectively during the rainy season, the monsoon, autumn, winter, spring, and summer; however, that is not correct, because the world consists of both lunar (saumya) and fiery (āgneya) elements.
One should collect lunar medicinal substances during the lunar seasons and fiery ones during the fiery seasons; in this way, their qualities remain unimpaired.
Lunar medicinal substances collected during the lunar seasons grow in ground abounding in lunar qualities, and thus they become exceedingly sweet, unctuous, and cold.
By this, the remainder is explained.

In that regard, one should collect purgative substances from ground where the qualities of earth and water predominate; emetic substances from ground where the qualities of fire, ether, and wind predominate; substances acting on both routes from ground where both sets of qualities predominate; and palliative substances from ground where the quality of ether predominates; in this way, they become more potent.

All [medicinal substances] should indeed be fresh, with the exception of honey, ghee, jaggery, long pepper (*pippalī*), and *viḍaṅga* (which may be old); all of these should be accompanied by milk and be potent. In the absence of these, one should take those that have not exceeded one year [of age].
And there are verses on this point:
"From cowherds, ascetics, hunters, and others who roam the forest,
as well as from those who subsist on roots— the manifestation of medicinal substances is sought from them."
In the case of substances such as *palāśa* leaves and salt, which are prepared by means of all their constituent parts, there is no fixed time; rather, every [time] is prescribed therein.
The earth is held to be of six kinds, endowed with fragrance, color, and taste;
therefore, by virtue of the nature of the earth, those who possess seeds are endowed with the six tastes.
It is said that the taste of water is indeed unmanifest and determined by certainty;
yet that very same unmanifest taste becomes manifest through the taste of earth.
That ground, endowed with all auspicious characteristics, is considered common;
yet the substances located therein possess those qualities in particular.
One should specify that a substance— whether new or old— is indeed fit for acceptance if it is not affected by a foul odor and has not deteriorated in its taste and other qualities.
Viḍaṅga, pippalī, honey, and fresh ghee are beneficial;
as for the rest, one should take them when they are fresh and free from defects.
One should collect the blood, hair, nails, and so forth from mobile beings in their youth,
as well as their milk, urine, and excrement, once they have digested their food.
A medicine storehouse is desired in a clean location facing an auspicious direction, with medicines placed upon a platform, earthenware vessels, wooden boards, or pegs.
The thirty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on miscellaneous topics (Miśraka).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari said:
Mātuluṅga, agnimantha, bhadradāru, mahauṣadha,
ahiṃsrā, and rāsnā— this application as a plaster conquers swelling caused by vāta.
Dūrvā grass, the root of Nala, Madhuka, and Chandana, along with all the cooling groups of drugs— this medicinal paste removes swelling caused by Pitta.

This same procedure is prescribed for disorders born of external causes and those born of blood; likewise, an anti-toxin treatment is beneficial for disorders born of poison, and a pitta-alleviating treatment is likewise beneficial.
Ajagandhā, aśvagandhā, kālā, along with saralā,
ekaiṣikā, and ajaśṛṅgī— this application as an ointment removes phlegmatic swellings.
These three groups, along with *lodhra*, *pathyā*, *piṇḍītaka*, and *anantā*— this ointment removes swelling caused by the combination of all three humors (*sānnipātika*).
For the pacification of Vāta, it should be unctuous, sour, and salty, and lukewarm; for Pitta, it should be cool and mixed with milk; and for Kapha, it should be rich in alkali and urine, and warm.
The fruits of hemp, radish, and śigru, as well as sesame, mustard seeds, flour,
fermenting agent (kiṇva), and linseed— these substances are heating and promote digestion.

*Cirabilva*, *agnika*, *dantī*, *citraka*, and *hayamāraka*, as well as the excrement of pigeons, vultures, and herons, are scarifying agents; or whatever substances are alkaline, or indeed alkali itself, is the supreme scarifier. (1.37.10ef)
For substances that are slimy, [the treatments are] the application of bark, wool, and pressing;
and, in brief, the powders of barley, wheat, and black gram.
Śaṅkhinī, aṅkoṭha, sumana, karavīra, and suvarcalā are purifying decoctions; so too is the group beginning with āragvadha.
Ajagandhā, ajaśṛṅgī, gavākṣī, and lāṅgalāhvayā;
pūtīka, citraka, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, elā, and hareṇu.
The three pungents (kaṭutrika), alkali of barley (yavakṣāra), salts, realgar (manaḥśilā),
green vitriol (kāsīsa), trivṛt, dantī, yellow orpiment (haritāla), and alum (surāṣṭrajā).
One should specify these substances for the purificatory wicks (varti);
with these very same medicinal drugs, one should also prepare purificatory pastes (kalka).
One should indeed prepare oils and clarified butters from kāsīsa, kaṭurohiṇī, the root of jātī, and haridrā, as well as from the previously mentioned ingredients.
Having ground the best *arka*, the milk of *snuhī*,
the best alkalis, the root of *jātī*, the two types of *haridrā*, *kāsīsa*, and *kaṭurohiṇī* [into a paste].
One should also prepare other purifying ghees (saṃśodhana-ghṛta) as previously indicated,
using mayūraka, rājavṛkṣa, nimba, kośātakī, and sesame seeds.
Bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārī, yellow orpiment, and realgar—
these purifying substances should be employed in the oil for the purpose of purification.
One should prepare a purifying powder from green vitriol, rock salt, yeast, *vacā*, the two types of turmeric, and other ingredients used for purification.

A purifying medicinal extract (rasakriyā) should be prepared from the heartwoods of the *sāla* tree and others, as well as from *paṭola* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), for the purpose of purification during cleansing therapies.
A wise person should perform the fumigation of wounds using *śrīveṣṭaka*, resin (*sarjarasa*), *sarala*, *devadāru*, and also the heartwoods (*sāra*) of these trees.
A decoction prepared from the barks of non-hot (non-irritating) astringent trees—
whether boiled and then cooled or used as a fresh decoction— is recommended for the purpose of healing wounds.
Vartīs prepared from soma, amṛtā, aśvagandhā, as well as in the kākolyādi group and in the sprouts of milk-exuding trees, are known as healing (ropaṇa) agents.
A paste (kalka) consisting of samaṅgā, somasaralā, somavalka,
candana, and the kākolyādi group is excellent for healing wounds.
The physician should employ pṛthakparṇī, ātmaguptā, the two types of haridrā, white mālatī, and the kākolyādi group in a healing ghee (ropaṇa-ghṛta).
Kālānusārya, aguru, the two types of haridrā, devadāru,
priyaṅgu, and rodhra should be added to the oil for the purpose of healing.
A powder consisting of kaṅgukā, triphalā, rodhra, kāsīsa, śravaṇāhvayā,
and the bark of dhava and aśvakarṇa is desired for healing [wounds].
Priyaṅgu, resin of the Sarja tree, and Pushpakāsīsa,
as well as the powder of Dhava-bark, are recommended for the purpose of healing.
One should prepare a medicinal extract (rasakriyā) from the bark of the Nyagrodha group as well as from Triphalā,
in the proper sequence, for the purpose of healing.
Apāmārga, asvagandhā, tālapatrī, and suvarcalā,
as well as the group of drugs beginning with kākolī, are recommended for use in rubbing ointments.
Green vitriol, rock salt, fermenting agent, Kuruvinda salt, realgar,
hen’s eggshells, and jasmine buds.
The fruits of śirīṣa and kārañja, as well as the powders of metallic minerals,
are recommended for the subsiding of elevated flesh in wounds.
A wise physician should employ the entire group, or half of it, or even as much as is available, in the procedures as they have been prescribed.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, named the Miśraka Chapter, in the Sūtrasthāna of the Śrī Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the collection of substances that promote firmness.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
In brief, there are thirty-seven groups of substances.

They are as follows: vidārigandhā, vidārī, viśvadevā, sahadevā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, pṛthakparṇī, śatāvarī, sārivā, kṛṣṇasārivā, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, mahāsahā, kṣudrasahā, the two types of bṛhatī, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, haṃsapādī, vṛścikālī, and ṛṣabhī.
This group of drugs beginning with Vidārīgandhā removes pitta and vāta;
it destroys consumption, abdominal tumors, body aches, upward dyspnea, and cough.

Āragvadha, madana, gopaghoṇṭā, kaṇṭakī, kuṭaja, pāṭhā, pāṭalā, mūrvā, indrayava, saptaparṇa, nimba, kuruṇṭaka, dāsīkuruṇṭaka, guḍūcī, citraka, śārṅgeṣṭā, the two types of karañja, paṭola, kirātatiktaka, and suṣavī.
This group, beginning with *āragvadha*, removes phlegm and poison;
it destroys urinary disorders, skin diseases, fever, vomiting, and itching, and it purifies wounds.

Varuṇa, ārtagala, śigru, madhuśigru, tarkārī, meṣaśṛṅgī, pūtīka, naktamāla, moraṭā, agnimantha, the two types of saireyaka, bimbī, vasuka, vāsī, citraka, śatāvarī, bilva, ajaśṛṅgī, darbha, and the two types of bṛhatī.
Indeed, this group beginning with Varuṇa wards off phlegm and fat;
it destroys headaches, abdominal tumors, and internal abscesses.
Vīratara, sahacara, dvaya, darbha, vṛkṣādanī, gundrā, anala, kuśa, kāśa, aśmabheda, agnimantha, moraṭā, vasuka, vasi, bhallūka, kuraṇṭaka, indīvara, kapotavaṅkā, and śvadaṃṣṭrā.
This group of drugs beginning with vīratara removes disorders of the wind (vāta),
and it cures urinary calculi, gravel, dysuria, and pain caused by trauma.

Sālasāra, rājakarṇa, khadira, kadara, kālaskandha, kramuka, bhūrja, meṣaśṛṅgī, tiniśa, candana, kukkuṭacandana, śiṃśapā, śirīṣa, asana, dhava, arjuna, tāla, śāka, naktamāla, pūtīka, aśvakarṇa, aguru, and kālīyaka.
This group, beginning with *sālasāra*, destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*),
removes urinary disorders and jaundice, and dries up phlegm and fat.
Rodhra, sāvara-rodhra, palāśa, kuṭannaṭa, aśoka, phaṃjī, kaṭphala, elavāluka, śallakī, jiṅginī, kadamba, sālā, and kadalī.
This group, beginning with *rodhra*, has been described as removing fat and phlegm;
it cures disorders of the female reproductive tract, is astringent, improves the complexion, and destroys poison.
Arka, alarka, the two types of karañja, māgadantī, mayūraka, bhārgī, rāsnā, indrapuṣpī, kṣudraśvetā, mahāśvetā, vṛścikālī, alavaṇā, and tāpasavṛkṣa.
This group beginning with *arka* indeed removes phlegm, fat, and poison;
it pacifies worms and skin diseases, and specifically purifies wounds.

Surasā, śvetasurasā, phaṇijjha, kārjaka, bhūstṛṇa, sugandhaka, sumukha, kālamālaka, āsamarda, kṣavaka, kharapuṣpā, viḍaṅga, kaṭphala, surasī, nirguṇḍī, kulāhala, undurukarṇikā, phañjī, prācībalā, kākamācī, and viṣamuṣṭika.
This group beginning with surasā indeed removes phlegm and destroys worms;
it cures catarrh, loss of appetite, dyspnea, and cough, and it purifies ulcers.
Muṣkaka, palāśa, dhava, citraka, madana, vṛkṣaka, śiṃśapā, vajravṛkṣa, and triphalā.
This group beginning with Muṣkaka indeed destroys fat, removes defects of the semen,
cures urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, and anemia, and is supreme in destroying gravel.

Long pepper, long pepper root, chaba pepper, leadwort, ginger, black pepper, elephant pepper, hareṇuka, costus, bishop’s weed, indrayava, pāṭhā, cumin, mustard, mahānimba fruit, asafoetida, bhārgī, sweet flag, ativiṣā, vacā, viḍaṅga, and katurohiṇī.

The Pippalyādi group subdues kapha and cures catarrh, disorders of vāta, and loss of appetite; it is digestive, destroys abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic, and promotes the digestion of undigested food (āma).

Cardamom, tagara, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, dhyāmaka, bark, leaf, nāgapuṣpa, priyaṅgu, hareṇukā, vyāghranakha, śukti, caṇḍa, sthauṇeyaka, śrīveṣṭaka, coca, coraka, vāluka, guggulu, sarjarasa, turuṣka, kunduruka, aguru, spṛkkā, uśīra, bhadradāru, kuṅkuma, and punnāgakeśara.
Elādikā destroys wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha), as well as poison;
it clarifies the complexion and eliminates itching, pustules, and urticaria.
Vacā, mustā, ativiṣā, abhayā, bhadradāru, and nāgakeśara.
Haridrā, dāruharidrā, kalaśī, kuṭaja seeds, and madhuka.
These two groups, beginning with vacā and haridrā respectively, purify the breast milk,
alleviate diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra), and especially promote the digestion of the bodily humors (doṣa).
Śyāmā, mahāśyāmā, trivṛt, dantī, śaṅkhinī, tilvaka, kampillaka, ramyaka, kramuka, putraśreṇī, gavākṣī, rajavṛkṣa, the two types of karañja, guḍūcī, saptalā, chagalāntrī, sudhā, and suvarṇakṣīrī.

This group of drugs beginning with Śyāmā has been described; it removes abdominal tumors and poisons, relieves flatulence and abdominal enlargement, promotes the passage of stool, and likewise destroys upward-moving wind (udāvarta).
Bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā, kuṭaja fruit, pāṭhā, and madhuka.
The Bṛhatyādi group of drugs is digestive, pacifies pitta and vāta,
and cures phlegm, anorexia, heart disease, dysuria, and pain.
Patola, candana, kucandana, mūrvā, guḍūcī, pāṭhā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
The group beginning with *paṭola* destroys pitta, kapha, and loss of appetite;
it pacifies fever, heals wounds, and removes vomiting, itching, and poison.
Kākoli, kṣīrakākoli, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, medā, mahāmedā, chinnaruhā, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, tugākṣīrī, padmaka, prapauṇḍarīka, ṛddhi, vṛddhi, mṛdvīkā, jīvantī, and madhuka.
This *kākolyādi* group destroys *pitta*, blood, and *vāta*;
it is vitalizing, nourishing, aphrodisiac, and likewise increases breast milk and *śleṣman*.
Bitumen, rock salt, bitumen from Śilāja, the two types of kāsīsa, asafoetida, and blue vitriol.
The group of drugs beginning with ūṣaka destroys phlegm (kapha) and dries up fat (medas);
it is a destroyer of urinary calculi (aśmarī), gravel (śarkarā), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), and abdominal tumors (gulma).
Sārivā, madhuka, candana, kucandana, padmaka, the fruits of kāśmarī, the flowers of madhūka, and uśīra.
The group of drugs beginning with sārivā (sārivādi) alleviates thirst, removes blood-bile (raktapitta),
pacifies pitta-fever, and specifically destroys burning sensations.
Añjana, rasāñjana, nāgapuṣpa, priyaṅgu, nīlotpala, nalada, nalina-keśara, and madhuka.
Indeed, this group of substances beginning with *añjana* destroys hemorrhagic disorders (*raktapitta*),
pacifies poison, and likewise eliminates internal burning sensations.
The fruits of the *parūṣaka*, grape, *kaṭphala*, pomegranate, *rājādana*, *kataka*, and *śāka*, as well as the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
This group, beginning with *parūṣaka*, destroys wind (*vāta*),
removes urinary disorders, is beneficial for the heart, quells thirst, and bestows appetite.
Priyaṅgu, samaṅgā, dhātakī, punnāga, nāgapuṣpa, candana, kucandana, mocarasa, rasāñjana, kumbhīka, srotoñjana, padmakesara, yojanavallī, and dīrghamūla.
Ambaṣṭhā, dhātakī flowers, samaṅgā, kaṭvaṅga, madhuka, the pulp of bilva, sāvara, rodhra, palāśa, nandīvṛkṣa, and lotus filaments.
The two groups beginning with priyaṅgu and ambaṣṭhā destroy chronic diarrhea;
they are healing for pitta, beneficial, and also promote the healing of wounds.

Nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, madhuka, kapītanaka, kakubha, āmrakośāmra, coraka, patra, the two kinds of jambu, piyāla, madhūka, rohiṇī, vañjula, kadamba, badarī, tindukī, sallakī, rodhra, sāvararodhra, bhallātaka, palāśa, and nandīvṛkṣa.
The group of drugs beginning with Nyagrodha heals wounds, is astringent, cures fractures,
removes blood-bile (rakta-pitta), destroys burning sensations and morbid secretions, and alleviates disorders of the female reproductive tract.
Guḍūcī, nimba, kustumburu, candana, and padmaka.
This [formula] beginning with *guḍūcī* destroys all fevers, stimulates the digestive fire,
and cures nausea, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, and burning sensations.
The blue lotus, the red lotus, the kumuda, the saugandhika, the kuvalaya, the puṇḍarīka, and the madhuka.
This group of drugs beginning with *utpala* destroys burning sensations, bile, and blood disorders; it removes thirst, poisons, heart disease, vomiting, and fainting.
Musta, haridrā, dāruharidrā, harītakī, āmalaka, bibhītaka, kuṣṭha, haimavatī, vacā, pāṭhā, kaṭurohiṇī, śārṅgaṣṭā, ativiṣā, drāviḍī, bhallātaka, and citraka.
This group of drugs beginning with *mustā*, known by this name, destroys phlegm (*śleṣman*),
removes disorders of the female reproductive tract (*yonidoṣa*), purifies breast milk, and likewise acts as a digestive stimulant (*pācana*).
Harītakī, āmalaka, and bibhītaka constitute triphalā.
Triphalā destroys kapha and pitta, cures urinary disorders and skin diseases, is beneficial for the eyes,
stimulates digestion, and destroys irregular fevers.
Pippalī, marica, and śṛṅgavera constitute trikaṭuka.
Trikaṭu destroys phlegm and fat, cures urinary disorders, skin diseases, and ailments of the skin; it is digestive-stimulant and also overcomes abdominal tumors, chronic catarrh, and weak digestion.
Āmalakī, harītakī, pippalī, and citraka.
This group, beginning with *āmalakī*, removes all fevers;
it is beneficial for the eyes, stimulates digestion, is aphrodisiac, and destroys phlegm and loss of appetite.
Cotton, tin, copper, silver, black iron, gold, and iron dross.
This supreme formulation known as Gaṇasvarvādi removes parasites and worms;
likewise, it cures thirst, poison, heart disease, anemia, and urinary disorders.
Lākṣā, revata, kuṭaja, aśvamāraka, kaṭphala, the two types of haridrā, nimba, saptacchada, mālatī, and trāyamāṇā.
Kāṣāya is bitter and sweet; it destroys the afflictions of phlegm and bile, removes skin diseases and worms, and purifies malignant ulcers.
We shall now describe the five groups of five roots (pañcamūla) hereafter.
Among them, the minor group (kanīya) consists of trikaṇṭaka, the two types of bṛhatī, pṛthakparṇī, and vidārigandhā.
The minor group of five roots (kanīya-pañcamūlaka) is astringent, bitter, and sweet;
it subdues wind, pacifies bile, promotes corpulence, and increases strength.
Bilva, agnimantha, ṭiṇṭuka, pāṭalā, and kāśmarya constitute the "great" [pañcamūla].
The Great Five-Roots (mahat-pañcamūla) is known to be slightly bitter, subduing phlegm and wind, light in digestion, stimulating the digestive fire, and having a sweet aftertaste.
Of these two, the "ten roots" (daśamūla) is now described.
Indeed, this *gaṇa* removes dyspnea and alleviates phlegm, bile, and wind;
it is a digestive for undigested matter (*āma*) and a destroyer of all fevers.
Vidarī, sārivā, rajanī, guḍūcī, and ajaśṛṅgī constitute the group known as vallī (creepers).
Karamarda, trikaṇṭaka, sairīyaka, śatāvarī, and gṛdhranakhi constitute the group known as "thorny" (kaṇṭaka).
For these two indeed remove blood-bile (raktapitta) and destroy the three types of swelling;
they also remove all urinary disorders (meha) and destroy defects of the semen.
Kuśa, kāśa, nalada, darbha, and kāṇḍekṣuka are known as the names of grasses.
The last one, when applied with milk, will destroy it very quickly.
Of these, the first two groups are known to remove wind (vāta), the last two destroy bile (pitta),
and the other two are proclaimed to pacify phlegm (śleṣman).
We shall explain the *trivṛt* and other such matters elsewhere.
These groups have been described in brief;
however, their detailed classification I shall explain in the sections on therapeutics, having understood the relative strength and weakness of the humors.
A wise physician, having categorized these [substances] into ointments, decoctions, oils, clarified butters, and drinks, should prepare them according to the proper method.
One should collect the medicinal herbs according to the prescribed rules and store them in a house that is not affected by rain, dust, or moisture throughout all seasons.
Having carefully examined the specific types and combinations of defects, one should administer [remedies] individually,
in combination, as a whole group, or as separate and combined units.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Collection of Substances," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on purification and pacification therapies.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

Madana, kuṭaja, jīmūtaka, ikṣvāku, dhāmārgava, kṛtavedhana, sarṣapa, viḍaṅga, pippalī, karañja, prapunnāḍa, kovidāra, karbudāra, ariṣṭa, aśvagandhā, vidula, bandhujīvaka, śvetā, śaṇapuṣpī, bimbī, vacā, mṛgervāru, and citrā are emetics that act as upward-purgatives (*ūrdhvabhāgahara*).
Among these, the fruits of those beginning with *kovidāra* [are used], while the roots of those beginning with *kovidāra* [are used for the others].

Vivṛtā, āsyā, adantī, dravantī, saptalā, śaṅkhinī, viṣāṇikā, gavākṣī, chagalāntrī, sruc, suvarṇakṣīrī, citraka, kiṇihī, kuśa, kāśa, tilvaka, kampillaka, ramyaka, pāṭalā, pūga, harītakī, āmalaka, bibhītaka, nīlinī, caturaṅgula, eraṇḍa, pūtīka, mahāvṛkṣa, saptacchada, arka, and jyotiṣmatī—these are the drugs that eliminate downward (the lower part of the body).

In that regard, [the ingredients are] the roots of those beginning with *tilvaka*; the bark of those beginning with *tilvaka* and ending with *pāṭalā*; the powder of the fruit of *kampillaka*; the fruits of those beginning with *pūga* and ending with *eraṇḍa*; the leaves of *pūtīka* and *āragvadha*; and the milks of the remaining [plants].
Koṣātakī, saptalā, śaṅkhinī, devadālī, and kāravellikā are emetics that act on both parts [of the body];
these are their fresh juices.

Pippalī, viḍaṅga, apāmārga, śigru, siddhārthaka, śirīṣa, marica, karavīra, bimbī, girikarṇikā, kiṇihī, vacā, jyotiṣmatī, karañja, arka, alarka, laśuna, ativiṣā, śṛṅgavera, tālīśa, tamāla, surasa, arjaka, iṅgudī, meṣaśṛṅgī, meṣaśṛṅgī, mātuluṅgī, suraṅgī, pīlu, jātī, śāla, tāla, madhūka, lākṣā, hiṅgu, salts, wine, cow dung, meat broth, and urine—these are the head-purgatives (śirovirecana).

In that regard, there are the fruits of those beginning with *karavīra* and ending with *arka*; the roots of those beginning with *tālīśa* and ending with *arjaka*; the leaves of those beginning with *tālīśa* and ending with *arjaka*; the barks of *iṅgudī* and *meṣaśṛṅgī*; the flowers of *mātuluṅgī*, *surabhī*, *pīlu*, and *jātī*; the heartwood (*sāra*) of *śāla*, *tāla*, and *madhūka*; the two resins (*niryāsa*), namely *hiṅgu* and *lākṣā*; the salts, which are specific varieties of earth; the liquors, which are products of fermentation and mixture; and the excrement, juices, urine, and impurities.

Beyond this, we shall describe the groups for the pacification of Vāta. In that regard, the group that pacifies Vāta consists of equal parts of the following: Bhadradāru, Kuṣṭha, Haridrā, Varuṇa, Meṣaśṛṅgī, Balā, Atibalā, Ārtagala, Kacchurā, Sallakī, Kuberākṣī, Vīrataru, Sahacara, Agnimantha, Vatsādanī, Eraṇḍa, Aśmabheda, Kālarka, Arka, Śatāvarī, Punarnavā, Vasuka, Vaśira, Kāñcanaka, Bhārgī, Kārpāsī, Vṛścikālī, Pattūra, Badara, Yava, Kola, Kulattha, and so forth, as well as the Vidārigandhādi group and the first two Pañcamūla groups. This is the group that pacifies Vāta.

In brief, the group that pacifies pitta consists of: sandalwood, red sandalwood, hrīvera, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, payasyā and its like, dāru, śatāvarī, gundrā, śaivala, kahlāra, kumuda, utpala, kanda (as well as ādā), dalī, dūrvā, mūrvā, and so forth; as well as the kākolyādi group, the sārivādi group, the rañjanādi group, the utpalādi group, the nyagrodhādi group, and the tṛṇapañcamūla.

Kāleyaka, aguru, tilaparṇī, kuṣṭha, haridrā, śītaśiva, śatapuṣpā, saralā, rāsnā, prakīrya, udakīrya, iṅgudī, sumana, kākādanī, lāṅgalakī, hastikarṇa, muñjātaka, lāmajjaka, and so forth; as well as the two groups of five roots—those of the creepers (*vallī-pañcamūla*) and those of the thorny shrubs (*kaṇṭaka-pañcamūla*); and the groups beginning with *pippalyādi*, *bṛhatyādi*, *muṣkakādi*, *vacādi*, *surasādi*, and *āragvadhādi*: this, in brief, is the group that pacifies phlegm (*śleṣman*).
In that regard, one should administer all medicinal drugs after carefully considering the strength of the disease, the digestive fire, and the patient's physical power.

Among these, a medicine administered in an amount exceeding the strength of the disease pacifies that specific disease but brings about another disease; exceeding the strength of the digestive fire, it is digested with indigestion or causes flatulence; exceeding the strength of the person, it brings about exhaustion, fainting, and intoxication. Likewise, a purifying (saṃśodhana) treatment administered in excess produces similar effects. Administered in an amount inferior to these [strengths], it becomes ineffective.
Therefore, one should perform [the rites] equally.
And there are verses on this point:
"In a disease that is curable by purification (śodhana), if the patient should be weak due to the morbid humors (doṣa),
a wise physician should administer a mild evacuation of those humors."
When the doshas have moved, the digestive tract is soft, and one need not consider the strength of men in this case;
for even in one who is weak due to lack of disease, purification (śodhana) should then be administered.
Purification therapy administered even to one who is weak, provided that the disorder has manifested spontaneously and the patient has a soft bowel, will result in the destruction of the disease.
In moderate cases of diseases such as fevers and the like, one añjali of decoction is desired;
a powder should be given in the measure of a cat's paw (biḍālapadaka), and a paste (kalka) should be given in the measure of an akṣa.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Purification and Palliation," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The fortieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of substances, tastes, properties, potencies, and post-digestive transformations.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Some teachers state that substance (*dravya*) is primary. Why? Because of its stability. Indeed, in this world, substance is stable, whereas tastes and the other qualities are not; for instance, those tastes and qualities present in an unripe fruit do not exist when it is ripe. Furthermore, because of permanence: substance is permanent, while qualities are impermanent; for example, the same substance such as a medicinal paste may possess a matured taste and smell or a deteriorated taste and smell. Also, because of its persistence in its own genus: just as an earthy substance does not change into the nature of another element, so it is with the remaining [elements]. Moreover, because of being perceived by the five senses: substance is grasped by all five senses, whereas tastes and the others are not. And because of being a substratum: tastes and the others reside supported by substance. Finally, because of the capacity for action: action resides supported by substance.

For example, in instructions such as "having gathered vidārigandhādi and having crushed it, one should boil it," there is no primary concern with the tastes (rasa) and so forth; this is because of the authority of the treatise (śāstra). For in the treatise, the substance (dravya) is primary in the instruction of formulations (yoga), as in the case of "mātuluṅga and agnimantha," etc., where the tastes and so forth are not what are taught. Furthermore, because tastes and so forth depend on sequence: tastes and so forth indeed depend on the sequence of substances, as in "when [the fever] is young, [use] young [substances]; when it is full-blown, [use] full-blown [substances]. Also, because diseases are cured by even a portion of substances: diseases are cured even by a single part of a substance, as in the case of "with the milky sap of the mahāvṛkṣa. Therefore, the substance is primary.
The definition of substance (dravya), however, is that which possesses action and qualities and is an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).

"No," say others; "the tastes (rasas) are primary. Why? Because of scripture (āgama). For scripture is said to be the authoritative treatise (śāstra), and in the treatise, the tastes are the subject of discourse. As it is said: 'Food is dependent on taste, and upon that depend the vital breaths (prāṇas). Furthermore, because of instruction: for the tastes are taught, as in: 'Sweet, sour, and salty pacify Vāta. Also, because of inference: for a substance is inferred by its taste, as when one says, 'This is sweet. And because of the words of the sages (ṛṣi): the word of the sages is the Veda, as in: 'One should bring something sweet for the sake of the sacrifice. Therefore, the tastes are primary; the term 'quality' (guṇa) is applied to them."
We shall explain the definition of the tastes elsewhere.
Others say "no," asserting that potency (*vīrya*) is primary. Why? Because it is by virtue of potency that medicinal actions are accomplished.

Here, medicinal actions—such as purification of the upper, lower, or both parts of the body; pacification (*saṃśamana*); collection (*saṃgrāhaka*); stimulation of the digestive fire (*agnidīpana*); softening (*pīḍana*); scraping (*lekhanā*); nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*); rejuvenation (*rasāyana*); aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*); causing swelling (*śvayathukara*); liquefaction (*vilayana*); burning (*dahana*); splitting (*dāraṇa*); intoxication (*mādana*); life-destroying (*prāṇaghna*); and the neutralization of poison (*viṣapraśamana*)—occur due to the predominance of potency.
And that potency (*vīrya*) is of two kinds: hot and cold, because the world consists of fire and moon.
Some say it is eightfold: cold, hot, unctuous (*snigdha*), dry (*rūkṣa*), clear (*viśada*), slimy (*piccila*), mild (*mṛdu*), and sharp (*tīkṣṇa*).
These potencies, by the excellence of their own strength and qualities, overcome the taste (*rasa*) and perform their own specific actions.

Just as the great five roots (*mahat-pañcamūla*), being astringent with a bitter aftertaste, pacify *vāta* due to their hot potency (*uṣṇa-vīrya*), so too do horse gram (*kulattha*)—which is astringent—and onion (*palāṇḍu*), which is pungent, increase *vāta* because of their cold potency (*śīta-vīrya*), as does sugarcane juice, which is sweet due to its oily nature. Pungent long pepper (*pippalī*) pacifies *pitta* due to its mild and cold potency; sour emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*) and rock salt (*saindhava*) [increase *pitta*]; bitter black nightshade (*kākamācī*) increases *pitta* due to its hot potency; and sweet fish [do the same]. Furthermore, pungent radish (*mūlaka*) pacifies phlegm (*śleṣman*) due to its dry potency, as does sweet honey (*madhu*). This has been stated merely as an illustration.
And there are verses on this point:
"If those tastes which pacify vāta lack dryness,
lightness, and coldness, they will not destroy the wind."
If those tastes which pacify pitta possess sharpness,
heat, and lightness, they do not perform that [pacifying] function.
If those tastes which pacify phlegm (kapha) do not possess oiliness, heaviness, and coldness, they do not perform that function.
Therefore, vigor is the foremost.

"No," say others, "the *vipāka* (metabolic transformation) is primary. Why? Because of the nature of correct and incorrect transformation; for all substances consumed here are transformed correctly or incorrectly, thereby producing either benefit or harm. Regarding this, others say that there is a transformation for each individual taste.

Some maintain that there are three kinds [of taste]: sweet, sour, and pungent. But that is not correct; for there is no sour post-digestive transformation (vipāka) other than the raw state (āma) resulting from the qualities of the elements. Indeed, bile (pitta), when it is "burnt" (vidagdha) due to the dullness of the digestive fire, attains acidity. If this were so, there would also be a distinct salty post-digestive transformation, for phlegm (śleṣman), when burnt, attains salinity.

Some say that what is sweet becomes sweet, what is sour becomes sour, and so it is for all [tastes]; they provide an illustration, saying: "Just as milk that has entered a cooking pot remains sweet while being boiled, so too rice, barley, mung beans, and the like, once scattered [into it], do not abandon their own nature even at a later time.
Others say that the weak come under the control of the strong. Such instability [of taste] means that this is not a tenable conclusion.
For in the traditional scripture (*āgama*), digestion (*pāka*) is indeed of two kinds: sweet (*madhura*) and pungent (*kaṭuka*).
Of these two, that which is called sweet is heavy (*guru*), and that which is called pungent is light (*laghu*).

In this regard, there is a twofold nature among earth, water, fire, air, and ether due to their similarity in qualities (*guṇasādharmya*): heaviness and lightness. Earth and water are heavy; the remaining [elements] are light. Therefore, digestion is indeed of two kinds.
And there are verses on this point: "When substances are being cooked, if the qualities of water and earth predominate therein,
that cooking is called sweet."
When, among those substances being cooked, the qualities of fire, wind, and space predominate,
the resulting transformation is called pungent.
This is a summary of the arguments of those proponents who perceive distinctness;
regarding this, the wise maintain that there is a causal totality for all four [conditions] as well.
That substance, when consumed in its own form, by its potency,
or by its taste and post-digestive transformation, either destroys or produces the *doṣas*.
There is no ripening without potency; there is no potency without taste;
there is no taste without substance; and substance is considered the most excellent.
The birth of both substance and taste is traditionally held to be mutually dependent,
just as the birth of the body and the embodied soul is mutually dependent.
The eight qualities known as "vigor" (vīrya) are also considered to reside in substances;
these do not exist in tastes, for qualities are said to be devoid of [further] qualities.
Since substances indeed undergo transformation within other substances, and not the six tastes, substance is therefore to be known as preeminent; the remaining factors are dependent upon it.
Medicines that are beyond investigation, inconceivable, and established by their very nature should be employed by the wise according to the authoritative tradition (āgama).
A wise person should never examine medicinal herbs by means of logical reasons, for they are established by their very nature as having the characteristics and results of direct perception.
Even with a thousand reasons, one such as Ambaṣṭha would not induce purgation;
therefore, a wise person should abide by the authoritative tradition (āgama) and not by mere reasons.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Substances, Qualities, Tastes, Potencies, and Post-digestive Transformations," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Śrī Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The forty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the specific knowledge of substances.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

In that regard, the production of a substance arises from the aggregation of earth, water, fire, air, and ether; however, its manifestation becomes distinct according to its predominance, such that one identifies it as "this is earthen," "this is watery," "this is fiery," "this is airy," or "this is ethereal."

Among these, that which is coarse, substantial, dense, slow, stable, heavy, and hard; which abounds in smell, is slightly astringent, and is generally sweet, is the earthy element. It produces stability, strength, weight, cohesion, and growth, and its specific nature is to move downward.

That which is cold, still, unctuous, slow, heavy, fluid, dense, soft, and slippery; rich in taste, slightly astringent, sour, and salty, and predominantly sweet in flavor—is of the nature of water (āpya). It produces lubrication, exhilaration, moistening, binding, and trickling.

That which is hot, sharp, subtle, dry, rough, light, and clear; which abounds in the quality of form (*rūpa*); which is slightly sour and salty, predominantly pungent in taste; and which especially has an upward-moving nature—this is the fiery (*taijasa*) element. It performs the functions of burning, cooking, cleaving, heating, illuminating, and coloring.

That which is characterized by subtlety, roughness, hardness, coldness, lightness, and clarity, which abounds in touch, is slightly bitter, and especially astringent, belongs to the air element (*vāyavīya*); it produces clarity, lightness, emaciation, dryness, and movement.
