That which is smooth, subtle, soft, pervasive, clear, distinct, possessing an unmanifest taste, abundant in sound, and belonging to the nature of space (ākāśīya), produces softness, porosity, and lightness.

By this illustration, considering that there is no substance in the world that does not become a medicine, substances endowed with their own specific potencies (*vīrya*) and qualities (*guṇa*) become effective when one observes the particular application (*yukti-viśeṣa*) and the purpose (*artha*).

When they act, that is the time; what they do is the action (*karman*); by means of what they act is the potency (*vīrya*); where they act is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*); how they act is the method (*upāya*); and what they accomplish is the fruit (*phala*).

In this regard, purgative substances abound in the qualities of earth and water; since earth and water are heavy, they move downward due to their heaviness. Therefore, by inference, purgation abounds in downward-moving qualities. Emetic substances abound in the qualities of fire and air; for fire and air are light, and due to their lightness, they rise upward. Therefore, emesis also abounds in upward-moving qualities. A substance that abounds in both sets of qualities acts as a dual-action (ubhayatobhāga) medicine. A pacifying (saṃśamana) medicine abounds in the quality of space (ākāśa). An astringent (sāṃgrāhika) medicine abounds in the quality of air, because air is of a drying nature. A digestive stimulant (dīpana) abounds in the quality of fire (due to its similarity with it). A scraping (lekhana) medicine abounds in the qualities of air and fire. A nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) medicine abounds in the qualities of earth and water. Thus, one should determine the actions of medicinal substances through inference.
And there are verses on this point:
Wind is pacified by substances derived from earth, fire, and water;
bile quickly attains relief through substances born of earth, water, and air.
In embodied beings, phlegm (śleṣman) is pacified by [excesses of] earth, fire, and wind;
whereas wind (māruta) attains increase through [excesses of] space and wind.
The bodily humor pitta is provoked by substances that are fiery in nature;
kapha increases through those born from earth and water.
Thus, having ascertained this superiority of qualities in each individual substance—
whether in pairs or even in larger groups— one should apply them with regard to the [specific] defects.

Among those qualities designated as *vīrya* (potency)—namely cold, hot, unctuous (*snigdha*), dry (*rūkṣa*), soft (*mṛdu*), sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), slimy (*picchila*), and clear (*viśada*)—the sharp and hot are fiery (*āgneya*); the cold and slimy abound in the qualities of water; unctuousness abounds in the qualities of earth and water; softness abounds in the qualities of water and space (*ākāśa*); dryness abounds in the qualities of air (*vāyu*); clarity abounds in the qualities of earth and air; and heavy and light post-digestive effects (*vipāka*) possess the qualities already mentioned. Among them, the hot and unctuous subdue Vāta; the cold, soft, and slimy subdue Pitta; the sharp, dry, and clear subdue Kapha (*śleṣman*). A heavy post-digestive effect subdues Vāta and Pitta; a light post-digestive effect subdues Kapha. Of these, softness, coldness, and heat are perceived by touch; sliminess and clarity are perceived by both sight and touch; unctuousness and dryness are perceived by sight; and sharpness is [perceived] by the production of pain in the mouth.
Heavy food causes the retention of feces and urine due to the provocation of phlegm (*kapha*), while light food causes the binding of feces and urine due to the aggravation of wind (*māruta*).

In that regard, one should observe the specific quality of taste among the elements that possess similar properties; for example, that which is sweet and heavy belongs to earth (*pārthiva*), and that which is sweet and unctuous belongs to water (*āpya*).
And there is a verse on this point: "The qualities that have been described for substances exist in the same way in bodies;
therefore, the stability, increase, and decrease of embodied beings are caused by substances."
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Specific Substances," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The forty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the specific knowledge of tastes.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
In ether, air, fire, water, and earth, there are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, increasing by one in each successive element respectively; therefore, taste belongs to water.
Due to mutual contact, mutual assistance, and mutual interpenetration, all [qualities] are present in all [elements], though they are perceived according to their predominance or subordination.
That aqueous taste, when transformed through contact with the remaining elements, is divided into six kinds, namely: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Furthermore, through mutual combination, they are divided into sixty-three types.

Among these, that which has a predominance of the qualities of earth and water is sweet; a predominance of the qualities of earth and fire is sour; a predominance of the qualities of water and fire is salty; a predominance of the qualities of air and fire is pungent; a predominance of the qualities of air and space is bitter; and a predominance of the qualities of earth and air is astringent.
Among these, sweet, sour, and salty tastes subdue Vāta; sweet, bitter, and astringent tastes subdue Pitta; and pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes subdue Śleṣman.
In that regard, wind is the self itself, bile is fiery, and phlegm is lunar.
These tastes increase their own source and pacify other sources.

Some say that because the world belongs to Agni and Soma, tastes are of two kinds: those belonging to Soma and those belonging to Agni. Among them, sweet, bitter, and astringent tastes belong to Soma; pungent, sour, and salty tastes belong to Agni. Of these, sweet, sour, and salty tastes are unctuous and heavy; pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes are dry and light. Those belonging to Soma are cold, while those belonging to Agni are hot.

In this regard, vāyu is characterized by the qualities of coldness, dryness, lightness, clarity, and obstruction; its homologous source is the astringent taste (kaṣāya-rasa), which increases its coldness through its own coldness, its dryness through its own dryness, its lightness through its own lightness, its clarity through its own clarity, and its obstructiveness through its own obstructiveness.

Pitta is characterized by the qualities of heat, sharpness, dryness, lightness, and clarity; the pungent taste (kaṭuka-rasa), which shares the same origin as it, increases its heat through its own heat, its sharpness through its own sharpness, its dryness through its own dryness, its lightness through its own lightness, and its clarity through its own clarity.

Kapha is characterized by the qualities of sweetness, unctuousness, heaviness, coldness, and sliminess; sweet taste, which shares its same origin as it, increases its sweetness through its own sweetness, its unctuousness through its own unctuousness, its heaviness through its own heaviness, its coldness through its own coldness, and its sliminess through its own sliminess.

Furthermore, its secondary taste is pungent; because it is the opposite of phlegm (*śleṣman*), its pungency overcomes sweetness, its dryness overcomes unctuousness, its lightness overcomes heaviness, its heat overcomes coldness, and its clarity overcomes sliminess.
This has been stated merely as an illustration.

Hereafter we shall describe the characteristics of the tastes (*rasa*). Among them, that which produces satisfaction, refreshes, satiates, vitalizes, produces a coating in the mouth, and increases phlegm (*śleṣman*) is sweet (*madhura*). That which produces a tingling sensation in the teeth, causes salivation in the mouth, and generates an appetite is sour (*amla*). That which produces a relish for food, causes the secretion of phlegm, and brings about softness is salty (*lavaṇa*). That which afflicts the tip of the tongue, produces agitation, seizes the head, and causes the nose to run is pungent (*kaṭuka*). That which produces a stinging sensation in the throat, creates clarity in the mouth, generates a relish for food, and brings about exhilaration is bitter (*tikta*).
That which dries up the mouth, stiffens the tongue, binds the throat, draws upon the heart, and afflicts it—that is the astringent (kaṣāya).

Hereafter we shall describe the qualities of the tastes (*rasa*). Among them, the sweet taste (*madhura-rasa*) increases the lymph-chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, *ojas*, semen, and breast milk; it is beneficial for the eyes, promotes the growth of hair, improves the complexion, bestows strength, promotes healing, clarifies the blood and lymph-chyle, is wholesome for children, the elderly, those with chest wounds, and those who are emaciated; it is most beloved by bees and ants, alleviates thirst, fainting, and burning sensations, clarifies the six senses, and produces worms and phlegm. Although it possesses such qualities, if consumed excessively and alone, it causes cough, dyspnea, intestinal stasis (*alasaka*), vomiting, sweetness in the mouth, impairment of the voice, worms, goiter, as well as tumors (*arbuda*), elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), coating of the bladder and rectum, and secretions (*abhiṣyanda*).

Sour [taste] is digestive, carminative, appetizing, a subduer of the wind (vāyu), a promoter of downward movement, a burner within the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha), cold on the outside, moistening, and generally pleasing to the heart. Yet, although it possesses such qualities, when consumed excessively and alone, it causes trembling of the teeth, closure of the eyes, horripilation, liquefaction of phlegm (kapha), and looseness of the body; furthermore, due to its fiery nature, it causes suppuration of wounds, blows, burns, bites, fractures, swellings, ulcers, dislocations, urination-related injuries, erysipelas, incisions, lacerations, piercings, and bruises, and it produces a burning sensation in the throat, chest, and heart.

Salt is purifying, digestive, disintegrating, moistening, loosening, hot, antagonistic to all tastes, a cleanser of the channels, and a softener of all parts of the body; yet, although it possesses such qualities, if consumed excessively and alone, it causes itching of the limbs, urticaria, swelling, discoloration, impairment of virility, affliction of the sense organs, burning of the mouth and eyes, and diseases such as raktapitta, vātaśoṇita, and acidity.

Pungent (kaṭuka) is digestive-stimulant, carminative, appetizing, purifying, and it pacifies obesity, lassitude, phlegm, worms, poison, leprosy, and itching; it loosens the binding of joints, causes depression, and destroys breast milk, semen, and fat. Although it possesses such qualities, if consumed excessively and alone, it produces vertigo, madness, dryness of the throat, palate, and lips, burning sensations, fever, loss of strength, trembling, pricking pain, and splitting pain, and it gives rise to Vāta-type colic in the hands, feet, sides, back, and other parts.

Bitter [taste] is astringent, appetizing, digestive, purifying, and it alleviates itching, swelling, thirst, fainting, fever, and it cleanses the breast milk; furthermore, it dries up feces, urine, moisture, fat, and pus. Although it possesses such qualities, if it is consumed excessively and alone, it produces stiffness of the neck, convulsions, facial paralysis, headache, vertigo, pricking pain, tearing sensations, cutting pains, and a bad taste in the mouth.

1.42.10. Astringent (kaṣāya) is astringent, healing, styptic, purifying, scraping, drying, compressing, and it dries up moisture; yet, although it possesses these qualities, if it is consumed in excess, it alone produces affliction of the heart, dryness of the mouth, abdominal distension, stiffness of the neck, lockjaw, trembling of the limbs, a tingling sensation, contraction, convulsions, and so forth.
Therefore, we shall describe the substances for all [of them].

For example, the sweet group (*madhura-varga*) consists, in brief, of *kākolyādi*, milk, ghee, fat, marrow, *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, barley, wheat, black gram (*māṣa*), water chestnut (*śṛṅgāṭaka*), *kaseruka*, cucumber (*trapusa*), gourd (*ervāruka*), melon (*karkāru*), bottle-gourd (*ālābu*), *kālindaka*, *takra*, *giloḍya*, *piyāla*, lotus seeds (*puṣkarabīja*), *kāśmarya*, *madhūka*, grapes (*drākṣā*), dates (*kharjūra*), *rājādana*, palm fruit (*tāla*), coconut (*nālikera*), products of sugarcane, *balā*, *atibalā*, *ātmaguptā*, *vidārī*, *payasyā*, *gokṣuraka*, *kṣīramoraṭa*, *madhūlikā*, pumpkin (*kūṣmāṇḍa*), and so forth. The sour group (*amla-varga*) consists, in brief, of pomegranate (*dāḍima*), *āmalaka*, citron (*mātuluṅga*), hog plum (*āmrātaka*), wood apple (*kapittha*), *karamarda*, *badara*, *kolla*, *prācīnāmalaka*, tamarind (*tintiḍīka*), *kośāmra*, *kāmbharya*, *pārāvata*, *vetraphala*, *lakucha*, *amlavetasa*, *dantaśaṭha*, curd (*dadhi*), buttermilk (*takra*), wine (*surā*), fermented vinegar (*śukta*), *sauvīraka*, *tuṣodaka*, fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), and so forth.

In brief, the salt group consists of *saindhava*, *sauvarcala*, *viḍa*, *pākya*, *romaka*, *sāmudra*, *paktrima*, *yavakṣāra*, *ūṣaraprasūta*, *suvarcikā*, and so forth; the pungent group generally consists of the *pippalyādi* and *surasādi* groups, as well as *śigru*, *madhuśigru*, *mūlaka*, *laśuna*, *sumukha*, *śīta*, *śītaśiva*, *kuṣṭha*, *devadāru*, *hareṇukā*, *valgujaphala*, *caṇḍā*, *guggulu*, *musta*, *lāṅgalakī*, *śukanāsā*, *pīlu*, and so forth, along with the *sālasārādi* group.

The *āragvadha* group, the *guḍūcī* group, and [the following plants]: *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *vetra-karīra*, the two types of *haridrā*, *indrayava*, *varuṇa*, *svādukaṇṭaka*, *saptaparṇa*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *śaṅkhinī*, *dravantī*, *trivṛt*, *kṛtavedhana*, *karkoṭaka*, *kāravella*, *vārtāka*, *karīra*, *karavīra*, *sumanaḥ*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *apāmārga*, *trāyamāṇā*, *aśoka*, *rohiṇī*, *vaijayantī*, *suvarcalā*, *punarnavā*, *vṛścikālī*, *jyotiṣmatī*, and so forth—these, in brief, constitute the bitter (*tikta*) group.

The Nyagrodhādi group, the Ambaṣṭhādi group, the Priyaṅgvādi group, the Rodhrādi group, Triphalā, the fruits of Śallakī, Jambu, Āmra, Bakula, and Tinduka; the fruits of the Kataka, Śāka, and Pāṣāṇabheda trees; the Sālasārādi group; and generally Kuruvaka, Kovidāra, Jīvantī, Cillī, Pālaṅkyā, Suniṣaṇṇaka, and so forth, as well as Nīvāraka and other wild grains, and pulses such as Mudga—this, in brief, is the astringent (kaṣāya) group.
In this regard, there are sixty-three combinations of these tastes.
Namely: fifteen pairs, twenty triads, fifteen tetrads, six pentads, six single tastes, and one hexad.
We shall explain their respective applications elsewhere.
And there is a verse on this point:
"The six tastes, when consumed, come under the control of whichever is strongest,
just as the humors (doṣas), when provoked, fall under the power of the most powerful one."
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Knowledge of the Specific Characteristics of Tastes," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The forty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of the various preparations of emetic substances.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Among emetic substances such as fruits and the like, the *madanaphala* (emetic nut) is the most excellent.

Now, one should administer an emetic by mixing one *prakuñca* measure of the powder of *madanapuṣpa* flowers dried in the sun with any one of the decoctions of *pratyakpuṣpā*, *asadāpuṣpī*, or *nimba*, and having combined it with honey and rock salt, one should cause the patient to vomit by giving a dose of this flower-powder.

Alternatively, one may use the powders of unripe *madana* fruits mixed with *bakula* and *ramyaka*, combined with honey and salt and heated; or a gruel made of sesame, rice, and barley prepared with the powder of unripe *madana* fruits.

Or, having taken fruits that have ripened but are not yet excessively green or pale, which have been bound with bundles of *kuśa* grass and smeared with clay and cow-dung, and which have been kept for eight nights in a heap of grains such as barley, *tuṣa*, mung beans, black gram, and rice until they are moist and split, one should extract the seeds (*phalapippalī*) and dry them in the sun. Once they are thoroughly dried and rubbed with curd, honey, and sesame paste, they should be placed inside a fine vessel. Then, while facing north, one should press them into a decoction of licorice (*yaṣṭīmadhuka*) or any other decoction such as that of *kovidāra* while it is warm, using the hollow of one's nails. After letting it stand overnight, it should be mixed with honey and rock salt, consecrated with blessings and this mantra, and administered to the patient who is facing east: [Insert Mantra]... [End of Mantra]... Thus, having consecrated it with this mantra, one should cause the patient to drink it.
May Brahmā, Dakṣa, the Aśvins, Rudra, Indra, Earth, Moon, Sun, Fire, and Wind;
the sages along with the multitude of medicinal herbs and the hosts of elemental beings, protect you.
May this medicine be for you like an elixir for the sages, like nectar for the gods,
and like fine wine for the noblest of serpents.

Specifically, in cases of fever caused by phlegm (śleṣmajvara), catarrh (pratiśyāya), or internal abscesses (antarvidradhi), or when the morbid humor (doṣa) does not flow out, one should induce vomiting repeatedly with lukewarm water mixed with husks, salt, and a paste of long pepper (pippalī), sweet flag (vacā), and white mustard (gaurasarṣapa), until the signs of proper emesis appear.

One may administer the powder of the pulp of *madanaphala*, or that same powder saturated with its own decoction, along with a decoction of *madanaphala*; or the cream (*santānikā*) of milk boiled with the pulp of *madanaphala* mixed with honey; or milk boiled with the pulp of *madanaphala*; or a gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared with milk boiled with the pulp of *madanaphala*. These are for the downward evacuation of blood and bile, and for heart-burn. Or, when the milk boiled with the pulp of *madanaphala* has turned into curd, one may give the whey (*dadhyuttara*) or the curd itself for excessive salivation, vomiting, fainting, and apoplexy. One should take the juice of the pulp of *madanaphala* like the oil of *bhallātaka*, allow it to thicken into a syrup (*phāṇita*), and have the patient lick it; or that same juice, dried in the sun, should be taken with a decoction of *jīvantī* when the pitta has reached the seat of kapha.

One may administer a decoction of the pulp of *madanaphala* with the addition (*pratīvāpa*) of *pippalī* and other drugs, or its powder mixed with either a decoction of *nimba* or *rūpikā*; this removes diseases caused by over-nutrition (*saṃtarpaṇa*) and phlegm (*kapha*). Alternatively, the powder of the pulp of *madanaphala* may be taken with a decoction of *madhuka*, *kāśmarya*, and *drākṣā*. Thus is described the procedure for *madanaphala*.

The powder of *jīmūtaka* flowers should be used with milk as previously described. When the eruptions have subsided, one should administer a milk gruel (*kṣīrayavāgū*) for those with hair on the eruptions, a cream layer (*santānikā*) for those without hair, and whey (*dadhyuttara*) for those that are greenish-pale. For those that are fully developed, one may administer curd mixed with its decoction, or wine (*surā*) processed with that decoction, in cases of phlegm disorders, anorexia, cough, dyspnea, anemia, and consumption. The application is like that of the marrow of *madana* fruit when the eruptions have reached full maturity.
In the same manner is the procedure for the *kuṭaja* fruit.
This same ritual procedure applies to the *kṛtavedhana* plants as well.
Or, the powder of Ikṣvākukusuma may be used as before; likewise, its application with milk is for cough, dyspnea, vomiting, and diseases caused by phlegm.

The use of *dhāmārgava* is like that of the marrow of *madanaphala*, particularly for tumors, abdominal enlargements, coughs, dyspnea, diseases of phlegm, and when the wind (*vāyu*) has moved into the seat of phlegm (*kapha*).

The powder of *kṛtavedhana*, *phala*, and *pippalī*, repeatedly saturated with a decoction of emetic substances, when administered or inhaled into the mouth of one who has consumed lotuses and other such items, induces vomiting; this should be employed for those whose morbid humors (*doṣas*) are not bound, as well as for those who have drunk gruel up to the throat.
Thus, these very substances serve as the most excellent agents for emesis, purgation, and head-evacuation (*śirovirecana*).
And here are the verses of Bhava: "This direction regarding the formulations of emetic substances has been fully proclaimed;
having divided it according to the disease, through the determination of time and potency."
The wise physician should prepare emetics using decoctions, fresh juices, pastes, and powders, to be administered with drinks, linctuses, and other types of food.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Knowledge of the Varieties of Emetic Substances," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The forty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of the various preparations of purgative substances.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
The root of Trivṛt, which has a reddish luster, is the best for root-purgation;
Tilvaka is preeminent among barks, and Harītakī is likewise foremost among fruits.

Among oils, castor oil is preeminent; among juices, that of kāravellikā; and among milks, that of sudhā is excellent—this is a summary of the principal [substances]. (1.44.4ef) I shall now describe their preparation correctly and in due order.
One afflicted by diseases of wind (vāta) should drink the root of the great trivṛt, which has been saturated with the juice of purgative substances and is free from impurities;
this should be powdered, enriched with rock salt and ginger, and taken with sour liquids.
In a disease caused by pitta, one should drink that [milk] with sweet preparations of sugarcane juice;
in a case born of kapha, one should drink it with guḍūcī, ariṣṭa, and the decoction of triphalā, along with trikaṭu and urine.
One should lick this powder, combined with the three spices (trivṛt, pippalī, and marica) and fresh jaggery;
having added one prastha of the juice of its root and one kuḍava of the paste of its root.
Having boiled one *karṣa* of rock salt (*saindhava-nāgara*) and then making this into a paste, one should consume it;
a portion of that paste, combined with half as much *mahauṣadha* (ginger), along with rock salt and mixed with urine, should be drunk.
Equal parts of trivṛt, nāgara, and abhayā; half a part each of well-ripened pūgaphala, the essence of viḍaṅga, marica, and dāru; this formulation, combined with rock salt and urine, [is effective].

The physician, having ground the powder derived from purgative substances with their own juices, should mix it with clarified butter prepared from those same roots; this should be consumed either as a liquid or made into pills in that very ghee.
Having placed this well-ground powder into molasses that is ready for cooking and having cooked it thoroughly,
one should then let it cool, mix it with the three aromatics (trijātaka), knead it, and administer pills according to the specific requirements of the treatment.

One part of the powder of emetic substances, prepared with four parts of decoction, should be kneaded with clarified butter cooked with that same decoction; it should then be steamed over the heat of that decoction and well-mixed.

When the molasses has reached the stage of thickening, one should carefully throw that powder into it while it is still cooking; then, having removed it from the heat once cooked, these delightful-scented *modakas* should be made when cooled—these, in brief, are the preparations for edible confections.
Having infused mung beans with their juice, a soup seasoned with rock salt and ghee is desired;
the same should be prepared with other pulses (vaidala) and likewise with emetic drugs for the purpose of purgation.
Having split a sugar-cane in two and smeared it with the pastes derived from the three *bhāṇḍī* plants, and having bound it with a rope,
one who suffers from bile diseases should eat it well-cooked by the method of *puṭapāka* once it has become thoroughly cooled.
One should lick equal parts of sugar, jasmine, cinnamon, milk-yielding plants, vidārī, and trivṛt with honey and ghee for the alleviation of thirst, burning sensations, and fever.
Combined with sugar and honey, and sprinkled with powdered *trivṛt*,
this is a purgative for those of delicate constitution, containing one part each of cinnamon, leaf-mace, and black pepper.
This cooling linctus, containing half a *kuḍava* each of sugar and honey along with *trivṛt* powder, is a purgative that destroys *pitta*.
One should take the three-fold mixture of śyāmā, alkali, ginger, and long pepper with honey;
this is the best purgative for all disorders of phlegm (kapha).
One should prepare meat juices made from *bījāḍhya*, *pathyā*, *kāśmarya*, *dhātrī*, *dāḍima*,
and *kola*, fried in oil, by adding sour fruits.
This solidified preparation, possessing a triple fragrance and combined with *trivṛt* and honey,
is a linctus used as a purgative for those who are delicate and dominated by *kapha*.

Indigo, cinnamon bark, and cardamom, along with trivṛt and sugar candy— this powder, when taken with honey and sour fruit juice, provides nourishment and cures the fever of the three humors (sannipāta).
Modakas made from equal parts of trivṛt, śyāmā, asitā, kṛṣṇā, triphalā, and honey cure sannipāta, upward-moving raktapitta, and fever.
The three parts of *trivṛt* are prescribed, and likewise, *triphalā* is equal to that;
having powdered *kṣāra*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *viḍaṅga*, [one should take them] with honey and ghee.
One should lick it with jaggery, or having made it into pills, one should consume it;
this cures abdominal tumors caused by phlegm and wind, as well as splenic enlargement and halīmaka.
This powder— consisting of śyāmā, trivṛt, nīlī, kaṭvī, mustā, and durālabhā— is a safe purgative that also eliminates other [diseases].
Cavya, indrabīja, and triphalā, when drunk with ghee, meat broth, and water, act as a purgative; indeed, this is recommended even for those who are dry of constitution.
Three parts of the cooled decoction used for purging are prescribed, along with two parts of inspissated juice (phāṇita); this mixture should then be placed again upon the fire.
Having ascertained that it has been properly prepared and cooled,
one should place it in a consecrated jar, dividing it according to the seasons into the cold and non-cold varieties.
After a month, when the essence has developed and it possesses the fragrance of honey, one may drink that excellent *āsava*;
this same procedure applies to *kṣāra-āsava* and *mūtra-āsava* as well.
One should take well-soaked mung beans and also shali rice grains, both thoroughly washed with a decoction of purgative roots, in a decoction of those same roots.
Having crushed them together into a single mass, dried them, and ground them into a fine powder,
one should prepare rice-powder moistened with the warmth of that decoction.
One should take three parts of that flour mixed with one part of fermenting agent (kiṇva), and add a decoction for the sake of the scum-water (maṇḍodaka); all of this should be combined together.
One should place that wine, having acquired its full flavor, into a jar and drink it;
this very procedure for preparing wine is also prescribed for emetic treatments.
The roots of trivṛt and others, as well as those of the first group,
the great five roots (mahat-pañcamūla), and also those of mūrvā and śārṅgaṣṭā.
Having gathered sudhā, haimavatī, triphalā, ativiṣa, and vacā,
one should prepare two parts of these [first four] and one part of these [last two].
One should prepare a decoction from one [part] and a powder from the other;
then, one should repeatedly soak crushed barley in that decoction.
Of those [medicinal substances] that are dried and gently roasted, three parts are prescribed;
having added a fourth part of powders, it is thus declared.
Immediately thereafter, having properly poured all of that into the jar,
it is well-mixed with the cool decoction of those very same [herbs].
One should prepare it as before; indeed, that is to be known as sauvīraka.
Having gathered the previously mentioned group of substances and divided them into two parts, one of these two [should be used].
Having crushed the portion and mixed it with barley, one should place it in a cooking pot;
having poured over it a decoction of *ajaśṛṅgī*, one should cook it.
Having brought these well-prepared grains down from the medicinal plants, one should separate them;
then, having properly rubbed them while still containing their husks, one should measure them as before.
Having added the powder of the previously mentioned medicinal herbs as before,
one should pour it into the jar along with that very same broth, as previously described.
Having ascertained that it has indeed acquired flavor, one should then prescribe that water of husks;
this is the procedure proclaimed for both water of husks and sauvīraka.
These two are prescribed to be drunk after six or seven nights;
this is the rule for the root of Trivṛt in all purgative treatments.
One should extract the roots of dantī and dravantī specifically from between layers of clay and kuśa grass;
having steamed them with long pepper and honey, one should remove them and dry them.
Then, one should administer it according to the Trivṛt procedure for cases of Kapha and Pitta;
with the paste and decoction of those two, one should cook Cakra oil.
Clarified butter (sarpis), when cooked [with medicinal herbs], overcomes erysipelas (vīsarpa), itching, burning sensations, and alajī;
likewise, oil overcomes urinary disorders (meha), abdominal tumors (gulma), and obstructions caused by wind (anila) and phlegm (śleṣman).
The four unctuous substances alleviate pains arising from the suppression of feces, semen, and flatus; [these are prepared] with *dantī*, *dravantī*, black pepper, *kanakāhvaya*, and *vāsaka*.
This powder of *viśvabheṣaja*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *citraka*,
processed with urine for seven days and then combined with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), should be administered as a purgative.
When digested, this nourishing honey alleviates the pain of pitta and kapha;
it destroys indigestion, pain in the flanks, anemia, splenic disorders, and abdominal enlargements.
In eight palas of jaggery, there should be twenty pathyā fruits,
one pala each of dantī and citraka, two karṣas each of pippalī and trivṛt, and ten [karṣas] of [the remaining ingredients].
Having prepared these modakas, one should eat one on every tenth day;
thereafter, one may consume them without restriction while drinking warm water.
These destroy the humors and cure malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), hemorrhoids, and skin diseases;
they consist of the three pungents (vyoṣa), the three aromatics (trijātaka), mustā, viḍaṅga, and āmalaka.
These nine ingredients, each in equal parts, are indeed eight times the quantity of *trivṛt*;
they are to be finely powdered here, along with two parts of *dantī*.
All these, having been powdered and strained here,
one should mix with six parts of sugar, along with a small amount of rock salt and honey.
Having consumed the bolus, one should then drink cold water;
this enema removes thirst, fever, vomiting, emaciation, anemia, and dizziness.
This entire group of purgatives is unrestrictive and acts as an antidote to poison;
known as the "group of eight," it is highly recommended for those suffering from bile disorders.
It may be eaten as a food item with milk as a post-digestive drink by men afflicted with disorders of bile and phlegm;
because it shares the characteristics of a solid food, it is prescribed only for those of means.
Having removed the outer bark of the *tilvaka* tree and avoiding the inner bark,
one should grind it into two parts and strain them with its decoction.
The third part has been processed;
once that part is dried, it should be administered with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) in the same manner as trivṛt.
The procedure for the eyes has been specified; now the fruits will be described.
The fruit of the *harītakī* should be freed from its stone and devoid of defects.
This should be administered according to the three-fold procedure; it destroys all diseases, acts as a supreme rejuvenative (rasāyana), promotes intelligence, and purifies malignant internal ulcers.
Harītakī, viḍaṅga, rock salt, ginger, trivṛt, and black pepper—
all these together with cow’s urine constitute a purgative.
Harītakī, bhadradāru, kuṣṭha, pūgaphala,
as well as saindhava and śṛṅgavera, constitute a purgative when taken with cow's urine.
A man should lick the powder of nīlinī fruit along with ginger and abhayā mixed with jaggery, and afterwards drink warm water.
One should drink Harītakī ground with a decoction of the Pippalyādi group and mixed with rock salt; this formulation will cause immediate purgation.
Harītakī, when eaten with ginger, or with jaggery,
or even combined with rock salt, constantly kindles the digestive fire.
Harītakī promotes the downward movement of wind, acts as an aphrodisiac, clarifies the sense organs,
and generally destroys diseases caused by over-nutrition.
Cold and dry, the āmalaka fruit removes pitta, fat, and kapha;
the bibhītaka, however, is not hot and destroys kapha and pitta.
All three [fruits] are sour and astringent, with bitter and sweet qualities; Triphalā destroys all diseases when combined with one-third part of ghee.
One who uses it continuously may also achieve the stabilization of youth;
thus one should employ the fruits according to the procedure for *harītakī*.
All purgatives, especially those derived from *caturaṅgula*,
should have their fruits harvested at the proper time and then stored in sand.
Having dried it in the heat for seven days, one should then extract the marrow;
the oil should be obtained by boiling it in water or by pressing it like sesame seeds.
Its use for children should continue for up to twelve years;
one should have them lick it with castor oil, combined with *kuṣṭha* and the three pungent spices (*trikaṭuka*).
One should drink lukewarm water; this regimen will induce purgation.
Castor oil should be taken with a threefold quantity of a decoction of triphalā.
It is appropriate when taken with milk or meat broth to induce purgation;
it is also employed for children, the elderly, those afflicted by chest wounds, the emaciated, and those of delicate constitution.
The procedure for fruits has been described; now listen, O Suśruta, to that for milks.
Among purgatives, the milk of the white-flowered leadwort (saudha) is considered the most potent.
Employed by one who lacks knowledge, that [magical power] destroys like poison due to the confusion of its application;
but when employed by one who possesses true knowledge, it can dissolve even a vast accumulation [of karma].
It quickly breaks down the humors (doṣas) and destroys even insurmountable diseases;
this applies both to the great group of five roots (mahatī pañcamūlī) and to each of the two types of *bṛhatī* individually.
Having dried it with charcoal of equal parts with decoctions,
it should be used as before with sour liquids and so forth, in a quantity the size of a jujube fruit.
A gruel made with rice and the milk of the *mahāvṛkṣa* tree, when drunk, causes quick purging; likewise, a bolus (*utkārikā*) prepared with jaggery (*guḍa*) produces the same effect.
Or a medicinal paste (leha) properly prepared with the milks of *snuhī* and cow, and clarified butter;
or long pepper (*pippalī*) soaked in *snuhī* milk and combined with salt.
Or likewise, the powder of *kāmpillaka* made into a pill and drunk with cow's urine—
[along with] *saptalā*, *śaṅkhinī*, *dantī*, *trivṛt*, and *āragvadha*.
Having soaked it for seven days in urine and thereafter in the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant,
one should sprinkle a garland or even a garment with that very powder.

By smelling or inhaling [the smoke] properly, one with a soft bowel is purged according to the prescribed methods for milk, bark, unripe fruit, and roots. Having carefully examined the disease and other factors, one should apply these treatments accordingly. (1.44.86ef)
Three *śāṇas* each of the three myrobalan barks (*triphalā*) and three *śāṇas* each of powdered *viḍaṅga*, long pepper (*pippalī*), and alkali (*kṣara*).
One should lick a bolus (modaka) with ghee and honey, or with jaggery;
one may consume it without restriction, for this is the best purgative.
This [remedy] dispels abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, cough, chlorosis, anorexia,
and other diseases caused by kapha and vata.
A person of superior intelligence should administer purgatives in ghee, oils, milks, as well as in wines, urines, and meat-broths,
and in various kinds of foods, meals, and linctuses.

Milk, juice, paste, decoction, cold infusion, and likewise hot infusion—these are indeed the six pharmaceutical preparations of medicinal substances; they are declared to be progressively lighter in their order of enumeration.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of the Formulations of Purgative Substances," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Śrī Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The forty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules for liquid substances.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Water from the atmosphere is of indescribable taste; it is nectar, life-sustaining, refreshing, supportive, and a source of consolation. It pacifies fatigue, exhaustion, thirst, intoxication, fainting, drowsiness, sleep, and burning sensations, and is exclusively the most wholesome of all things.

He perceives that very same taste, fallen upon the earth, as being distinct according to its specific location, situated in places such as rivers, streams, lakes, ponds, tanks, wells, springs, cascades, springs from the ground, scattered pools, fields, and puddles.

Regarding this, some teachers say that in regions of the earth that are red, brownish-red, pale-white, blue, yellow, and white, there arise waters that are sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent, respectively.
That, however, is not correct.

In that regard, the taste of water arises from the mutual interpenetration of earth and the other elements, according to their respective increase or decrease. Among these, in soil where the quality of earth predominates, the taste is sour and salty; where the quality of water predominates, it is sweet; where the quality of fire predominates, it is pungent and bitter; where the quality of air predominates, it is astringent; and where the quality of space predominates, the taste is unmanifest. For space is indeed unmanifest; therefore, that [water] in which space is predominant has an unmanifest taste. Consequently, when water from the atmosphere is obtained, that [unmanifest-tasting water] should be drunk.
In that regard, atmospheric water is of four kinds:
namely, *dhāra*, *kāra*, *tauṣāra*, and *haima*.
Among these, *dhāra* is the primary type because of its lightness; it, moreover, is of two kinds: that of the Gaṅgā and that of the ocean.

Among these, the water from the Gaṅgā generally rains down during the month of Āśvayuja. One should perform a test on both types [of water]: one should place a ball of unspoiled, undecomposed boiled rice (*śālyodana*) in a silver vessel and, while it is raining, take it outside. If, after remaining there for a moment, it remains exactly as it was, then it should be understood that the water is from the Gaṅgā. If its color changes or if the grains of rice become soggy, one should know it is from the ocean (*sāmudra*); that is not to be accepted. Even water from the ocean, if collected in the month of Āśvayuja, becomes like that of the Gaṅgā.
Furthermore, one should take the preeminent Ganges water during the month of Āśvayuja;

or else, that which has fallen from a portion of a clean white cloth spread out, or has dropped from the roof-terrace, or has been collected by others in pure vessels—gold, silver, or earthen—and placed it in a vessel made of gold, silver, or clay.
One should use that at all times; in its absence, [one may use] earth-born water.
And that [earth] is abundant in the quality of space.
Furthermore, it is of seven kinds, namely:
well-water, river-water, lake-water, pond-water, spring-water, water from a natural source, and water from a small pool.

In that regard, during the rainy season, one should consume water from the atmosphere or from springs because of its great excellence; in autumn, all [water] because of its clarity; in winter, water from lakes or ponds; in spring, water from wells or mountain springs; in summer, likewise; and in the monsoon, water from a stream that has not been rained upon, or indeed all [water].
Polluted by insects, urine, excrement, eggs, corpses, and putrefaction;
filled with heaps of grass and leaves; turbid and mixed with poison.
Whoever should plunge into [water] during the rainy season, or even drink fresh water,
will very quickly contract diseases both external and internal.

In that regard, one should know that water which is covered by mud, water-weeds, moss, grass, lotus leaves, and so forth; which is not reached by the rays of the moon and sun nor by the wind; and which is affected by [unwholesome] odor, color, and taste, is corrupted (*vyāpanna*).
Six defects arise in such water: those of touch, form, taste, smell, potency (*vīrya*), and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).

In that regard, roughness, sliminess, heat, and being hard on the teeth are defects of touch (*sparśadoṣa*); having many colors such as mud, sand, and moss is a defect of form (*rūpadoṣa*); having a distinct taste is a defect of taste (*rasadoṣa*); having an unpleasant odor is a defect of smell (*gandhadoṣa*); that which, when consumed, produces thirst, heaviness, colic, phlegm, and excessive salivation is a defect of potency (*vīryadoṣa*); and that which, when consumed, is digested after a long time or causes constipation is a defect of post-digestive transformation (*vipākadoṣa*).
These do not exist in the atmospheric water.

For one who has become ill, one should perform the treatment of heating with fire, exposure to the heat of the sun, or the application of cooling and soothing measures using heated iron balls, sand, or clods of earth; furthermore, one should perform consecration (adhivāsana) with flowers such as the nāga, campaka, utpala, and pāṭala.
In a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or even precious gems,
or on the ground, one should drink fragrant water containing flowers and ear-ornaments.
One should always avoid water that is putrid or out of season, for such water generates the bodily humors; one should not consume what is harmful.
He who drinks water here that is spoiled and unpurified suffers from swelling,
jaundice, skin diseases, and indigestion.
He will soon suffer from asthma, cough, catarrh, colic, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen, or from other various acute diseases.
In that regard, there are seven clarifiers for turbid water, namely:
the *kataka* nut, the *gomedaka* gem, the root of the lotus fiber (*bisagranthi*), the root of the *śaivāla* moss, cloth, pearls, and gems.
There are five types of supports:
namely, a board, a tripod, a ring of muñja grass, a water-stand, and a sling.

There are seven methods for cooling: placing [the patient] in a draft of air, sprinkling water, waving a stick, fanning with a fan, covering with a cloth, scattering sand, and suspending [the body] from a swing.
Water that is odorless, of unmanifest taste, thirst-quenching, pure, cool, clear, light, and pleasing to the heart is said to possess all excellent qualities.

Among these, rivers flowing toward the west are wholesome because their water is light; those flowing toward the east are not recommended because their water is heavy; and those flowing toward the south are not excessively harmful because they possess moderate qualities.

Among them, those originating from the Sahya mountains produce leprosy; those from the Vindhya mountains produce leprosy and jaundice; those from the Malaya mountains produce worms; those from the Mahendra mountains produce elephantiasis and abdominal enlargements; those from the Himavat mountains produce heart disease, edema, diseases of the head, elephantiasis, and goiters; those from the eastern and western regions of Avanti produce hemorrhoids; and those originating from the Pāriyātra mountains are wholesome and promote strength and health.
Rivers that flow swiftly and possess clear water are said to be light;
those that are covered with moss, turbid, and slow-moving are heavy.
Generally, rivers in desert regions are bitter and salty;
however, those created by human effort are light, sweet, and beneficial for strength.
In that regard, all terrestrial waters are to be taken at dawn, for it is then that they possess an abundance of purity and coolness, and these indeed are the supreme qualities of water.
That which is graced by the rays of the sun during the day and by the rays of the moon at night—
being neither harsh nor obstructive— is equal to the water of the sky.
Rainwater collected in a suitable vessel destroys the three humors (doṣas);
beyond that, it is strengthening, a rejuvenative (rasāyana), and promotes intelligence, depending on the nature of the container.

Water originating from the moonstone (candrakānta) is known to be a destroyer of demons, cooling, refreshing, a remover of fever, burning sensations, and poisons; it is pure and a subduer of bile (pitta).
In cases of fainting, pitta disorders, heat, burning sensations, poisoning, blood disorders, and intoxication; in those overcome by dizziness and fatigue, as well as in asthma and vomiting.
Cool water is recommended in cases of upward-moving hemorrhaging (raktapitta),
as well as in anal fissures, pain, catarrh, wind diseases, and throat obstruction.
One should avoid cold water in cases of flatulence, stiffness, a clod of earth, immediate purification,
acute fever, hiccup, and after drinking medicated fats.
Water that is not fit for drinking increases wind, is dry, stimulates digestion, is light, and is scraping;
whereas that which is obstructive to the channels is sweet, thick, heavy, and brings about phlegm.
Water from a lake destroys thirst, is strengthening, astringent, sweet, and light;
water from a pond increases wind, is sweet, astringent, and pungent in its post-digestive effect.
Water from a well (*vāpya*) removes wind and phlegm, is alkaline, pungent, and increases bile;
water from a pond (*kaupa*) is alkaline, increases bile, destroys phlegm, stimulates digestion, and is light.
The urine produced from a well is cooling, digestive, dry, sweet, and does not increase phlegm;
it destroys phlegm, stimulates the digestive fire, is beneficial for the heart, light, and easily obtained.
Udbhida salt is known to be sweet, pacifying for pitta, and non-burning;
vaikira salt is pungent, alkaline, destroys kapha, light, and stimulates digestion.
Rice grown in paddy fields is said to be sweet, heavy in digestion, and aggravating to the humors;
likewise is that grown in ponds described, though it is especially provocative of the humors.
Sea water is putrid, salty, and causes all the bodily humors (doṣas) to increase;
marshy water possesses many defects and is censured as it causes obstruction of the channels (abhiṣyandi).
Meat from the wild (jāṅgala), however, is free from these defects and is irreproachable;
it is non-burning during digestion, quenches thirst, is highly praised, and increases delight.
Water that is common to all is digestive, sweet, cooling, light, and destroys phlegm, fat, wind, and undigested matter; it stimulates digestion and cleanses the bladder.
Warm water is always wholesome for removing dyspnea, cough, and fever;
when boiled, it becomes free of agitation, devoid of foam, clear, and light.
That water is remembered as possessing all virtues when only a fourth part remains;
however, a wise person should never offer water that has stood overnight.
That which has become sour and provokes phlegm is not beneficial for one suffering from thirst,
nor for a disease arising from the drinking of alcohol or originating from bile.
In cases arising from a combination of humors (sannipāta), water that has been boiled and then cooled is recommended;
it is unctuous, sweet, cooling, pleasing to the heart, digestive, and a cleanser of the bladder.
Coconut water is aphrodisiac, heavy, and alleviates bile disorders and thirst;
it is beneficial in cases of burning sensations, diarrhea, hemorrhagic diseases, fainting, and afflictions from alcohol or poison.
Water that has been boiled and then cooled is recommended for thirst, vomiting, vertigo,
loss of appetite, coryza, excessive salivation, edema, and wasting.
In cases of weak digestive fire, abdominal disorders, skin diseases, fever, eye ailments,
as well as wounds and diabetes, one should consume water sparingly.
Thus ends the section on water. Now begins the section on milk:
that which comes from cows, goats, camels, sheep, and buffaloes.
And the milk of mares, of women, and of female elephants—
Because it is the essence of the juices of many medicinal herbs, bestows life, and is heavy,
sweet, slimy, cold, unctuous, smooth, laxative, and mild,
milk is therefore said here to be wholesome for all living beings. (1.45.48ef)

In this regard, all milk whatsoever is not prohibited for living beings due to its suitability to their species (*jāti-sātmya*); it is non-contradictory even in disorders of *vāta*, *pitta*, blood, and mental afflictions. It alleviates chronic fever, cough, dyspnea, consumption, wasting, abdominal tumors, insanity, ascites, fainting, giddiness, intoxication, burning sensations, thirst, and defects of the heart and bladder; it cures anemia, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī-doṣa*), hemorrhoids, colic, upward movement of gases (*udāvarta*), diarrhea, dysentery, vaginal diseases, uterine bleeding, and internal hemorrhaging; it removes fatigue and exhaustion. It is strengthening, aphrodisiac, virilizing, rejuvenating, intellect-promoting, a promoter of union, a stabilizer, an anti-aging agent, life-prolonging, vitalizing, nourishing, and acts as an emetic, purgative, and non-unctuous enema. Because its qualities are identical to those of *ojas*, it increases the vital essence; it is most wholesome for children, the elderly, those wounded or emaciated, and those exhausted by hunger, sexual indulgence, or physical exercise.

Cow’s milk causes little internal secretion; it is unctuous, heavy, a rejuvenative (rasāyana), cures bleeding disorders and pitta, and is cold in potency, sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect.
It is considered supreme for sustaining life and for subduing vāta and pitta;
possessing qualities equal to those of cow's milk, that of the goat is especially beneficial for those suffering from consumption.
Goat's milk is digestive, light, constipating, and it cures dyspnea, cough, and hemorrhagic disorders (asrapitta),
due to the small body size of goats and their consumption of pungent and bitter foods.
Milk cures all diseases when one avoids excessive drinking of water and physical exercise;
that of the camel is somewhat dry, hot, and salty, yet possesses a sweet taste and is light.
The meat of sheep destroys swelling, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and hemorrhoids; it removes worms, skin diseases, and poisons.
It is sweet, unctuous, heavy, and increases pitta and kapha.
Buffalo milk is wholesome in cases of pure wind disorders and cough caused by Vata;
however, it is highly obstructive, sweet, and diminishes the digestive fire.
Cow's milk induces sleep, is very cooling, more unctuous, and heavy;
the milk of one-hoofed animals is warm, strengthening, and removes wind from the limbs.
The breast milk of a woman is sweet and sour in taste, dry, with a salty aftertaste,
light, sweet, and cooling, with an astringent aftertaste.
For nasal drops and eye-drops, the *jīvana* group is wholesome—being light and digestive-stimulant;
that from the female elephant (*hastinī*) is sweet, aphrodisiac, with an astringent aftertaste, and heavy.
Generally, milk from the early morning is unctuous, stabilizing, cooling, beneficial for the eyes, and increases strength; it is heavy, causes constipation, and is cold in potency.

Furthermore, because the night possesses the qualities of the moon and lacks physical exertion, whereas for those scorched by the sun during the day, there is the service of exercise and wind; [the former is beneficial].

Milk consumed in the afternoon promotes the downward movement of wind (vāta), removes fatigue, and is beneficial for the eyes; however, raw milk is generally proclaimed to be heavy and causes secretions (abhiṣyandi).
That same [milk] is said to be lighter and non-obstructive when boiled; however, the exception is the breast milk of a woman, for that is beneficial even when raw.
Milk that is warm from the udder is beneficial; otherwise, it is the opposite.
That same milk, when boiled and cooled, is said to be heavy and nourishing.
Milk that has an unpleasant odor, is sour, discolored, or tasteless,
as well as that which is salty or clotted, should be avoided.

Thus ends the section on milk. Now begins the section on curd (*dadhi*). Curd is sweet, sour, or extremely sour; it has an astringent aftertaste (*anurasa*), is unctuous (*snigdha*), and hot (*uṣṇa*). It cures chronic catarrh (*pīnasa*), irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*), diarrhea (*atisāra*), anorexia (*arocaka*), dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*), and emaciation (*kārśya*); it is aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*), life-sustaining (*prāṇakara*), and auspicious (*maṅgalya*).
Sweet [taste] causes great secretions and increases phlegm and fat;
sour [taste] produces phlegm and bile, while excessively sour [taste] vitiates the blood.
It causes a burning sensation, promotes the discharge of feces and urine, is slow to digest, and aggravates the three *doṣas*.
It is unctuous, sweet in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), stimulates the digestive fire, and increases strength.
Cow's curd alleviates wind, is purifying, and bestows appetite;
goat's curd destroys phlegm and bile, is light, and removes the depletion of wind.
It is beneficial for dyspnea with difficult breathing and cough, stimulates the digestive fire,
is sweet in its post-digestive effect, aphrodisiac, and pacifies vāta and pitta.
Buffalo curd is unctuous and especially increases phlegm;
camel curd is pungent in its post-digestive effect, alkaline, heavy, and a purgative.
Sheep's curd aggravates phlegm and wind, and it destroys wind-disorders, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, worms, and abdominal ailments.
Vāḍava curd is sweet in taste and digestion, excessively obstructive to the channels, aggravates the humors,
stimulates the digestive fire, is harmful to the eyes, and increases vāta.
It is dry, hot, and astringent; it removes phlegm and suppresses urine.
It is unctuous, sweet in its post-digestive effect, strengthening, nourishing, and heavy.
Curd that is excellent for the eyes, foremost in its qualities, and destructive of the *doṣas* is preeminent for women;
it is light in digestion, destroys phlegm (*balāsa*), is hot in potency, and impairs the digestive fire.
Curd from cow's milk has an astringent aftertaste and increases the luster of the body;
as for the various types of curds mentioned here, such as those from cow's milk and others, each has been described separately.
Thus it should be understood that among all [animal products], that which comes from the cow is indeed superior in quality;
it subdues wind, increases phlegm, is unctuous, nourishing, and does not excessively increase bile.
One should fulfill the devotee's desire with well-strained curd;
that curd which is produced from boiled milk is remembered as being of superior quality.
The liquid part of curd (sara) is known to alleviate wind and bile, to stimulate the appetite, to increase the strength of the tissues, the digestive fire, and vitality,
and to destroy Vata.
Furthermore, [fresh] curd pacifies the digestive fire and increases phlegm and semen;
however, whey is dry, constipating, causes flatulence, and aggravates wind.
Curd is stimulating, very light, slightly astringent, and provides relish;
however, it is generally forbidden during the autumn, summer, and spring seasons.
In the winter, the cool season, and during the rains, curd is recommended;
whey removes thirst and fatigue, is light, and cleanses the channels.
It is sour, astringent, and sweet; it does not increase virility, yet it subdues phlegm and wind. It is refreshing and nourishing, and it quickly breaks up waste matter.
It quickly brings strength and creates a desire for food.

Sweet-sour, very sour, produced from thin curd, likewise produced from boiled milk, and the liquid (sara)—thus, curd is considered to be of seven kinds in this group; the qualities of whey are likewise remembered.
Thus ends the section on curd (*dadhivarga*).
Now begins the section on buttermilk (*takravarga*).

Buttermilk is sweet and sour, with an astringent aftertaste; it is hot in potency, light, and dry. It stimulates the digestive fire and removes poisons, edema, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), anemia, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, anorexia, irregular fevers, thirst, vomiting, salivation, colic, obesity, phlegm, and wind. It has a sweet post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), is beneficial for the heart, pacifies dysuria and complications arising from oleation therapy, and is non-aphrodisiac.
Buttermilk (*takra*) is that which has been churned with its fat separated, contains half water, and is neither too thick nor too liquid;
it is sweet-sour and astringent in taste. That which is churned without water and retains its fat is called *ghola*.
Buttermilk should never be taken when there is an ulcer, nor during the hot season, nor when one is weak;
it is forbidden in cases of fainting, vertigo, burning sensations, and in diseases of blood and bile.
Buttermilk is recommended during the cold season, in cases of weak digestion, in diseases arising from phlegm (kapha),
when the channels are obstructed, and when the wind (vāyu) is vitiated.
Furthermore, the sweet [taste] aggravates phlegm and pacifies bile, while the sour [taste] subdues wind and produces bile.
One should drink buttermilk that is sour and mixed with rock salt in cases of vāta; sweet and with sugar in cases of pitta;
and also combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali in cases of kapha.

Curdled buttermilk (takrakūrcikā) is constipating, increases wind, is dry, and is difficult to digest; the scum (maṇḍa) produced from buttermilk is lighter than buttermilk itself, while that produced from curdled buttermilk is lighter still.
Kilāṭa is heavy, subdues wind, and is known to bestow virility and sleep;
likewise, pīyūṣa and moraṭa are sweet, nourishing, and aphrodisiac.

Fresh butter, moreover, is light, delicate, sweet, slightly astringent, mildly sour, cooling, intellect-promoting, digestive-stimulant, cordial, constipating, pacifies pitta and vāta, is aphrodisiac, non-burning, and cures consumption, cough, ulcers, wasting, hemorrhoids, and facial paralysis; however, that which has stood for a long time is heavy, increases kapha and fat, provides strength, is nourishing, cures emaciation, and is especially recommended for children.

Butter derived from milk possesses superior unctuousness and sweetness; it is extremely cooling, promotes softness of the body, is beneficial for the eyes, astringent, cures blood-bile disorders and eye diseases, and is clarifying.

Furthermore, *santānikā* (the cream on the surface of milk) subdues wind, is nourishing, strengthening, aphrodisiac, unctuous, appetizing, sweet, and has a sweet post-digestive effect; it clarifies blood and bile, and is heavy.
This variety of curd and so forth produced from cow's milk is described as the best;
one should understand that all other remaining varieties are equal in potency to milk.

Now, regarding ghee: Ghee is sweet, mild, soft, cold in its potency, slightly obstructive to the channels, and unctuous; it pacifies upward-moving wind (udāvarta), insanity, epilepsy, colic, fever, abdominal distension, and disorders of vāta and pitta; it kindles the digestive fire; it bestows memory, intelligence, wisdom, luster, clarity of voice, delicacy, vigor, splendor, and strength; it promotes longevity, is aphrodisiac, enhances intellect, maintains youth, is heavy [to digest], beneficial for the eyes, increases phlegm (śleṣman), and pacifies sin, misfortune, and poison while destroying demons.
Cow’s ghee is excellent in its qualities: it is sweet and cooling in its post-digestive effect, it subdues wind, bile, and poison, it is foremost for the eyes, and it is strengthening.
Goat's ghee is digestive-stimulant, beneficial for the eyes, and increases strength;
it is wholesome in cases of cough, dyspnea, and consumption, and it is light in digestion.
Buffalo ghee is sweet, destroys blood-bile (raktapitta), is heavy in digestion, increases phlegm (kapha),
pacifies wind and bile (vātapitta), and is very cooling.
Camel ghee is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka); it removes swelling, worms, and poisons;
it stimulates the digestive fire, subdues kapha and vāta, and cures skin diseases (kuṣṭha), abdominal tumors (gulma), and enlargement of the abdomen (udara).
Clarified butter derived from sheep is light in digestion and does not aggravate pitta;
it is beneficial in cases of kapha, vāta, disorders of the female reproductive tract, emaciation, and tremors.
One should know that ghee from one-hoofed animals is light in digestion, hot in potency, astringent, a destroyer of phlegm, digestive, and causes the binding of urine.
Clarified butter is the foremost for the eyesight of women and is like nectar;
it promotes the growth of the body and the digestive fire, is easily digested, and destroys poison.
Ghee made from kāreṇu milk is astringent, binds the stool and urine, is bitter, stimulates the digestive fire, and is light;
it destroys kapha, skin diseases, poisons, and worms.
Furthermore, milk and ghee are astringent, pacify hemorrhagic disorders, vertigo, and fainting, and are beneficial for eye diseases.

The scum of clarified butter (sarpirmaṇḍa), however, is sweet and laxative; it destroys pain in the genitals, ears, eyes, and head, and is prescribed for enemas, nasal drops, and filling the eyes with medicine.

Old ghee (sarpiḥ) is thin, has a pungent post-digestive effect (vipāka), alleviates the three doṣas, and cures fainting, intoxication, insanity, internal hemorrhage, fever, poisoning, emaciation, epilepsy, and pain in the vagina, ears, eyes, and head; it is an appetizer and is prescribed for enemas, nasal administration, and filling the eyes.
And there is a verse on this point:
It is an ancient remedy that cures darkness of vision, dyspnea, catarrh, fever, and cough;
it destroys fainting, leprosy, poison, insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy.
Clarified butter that has been kept for one thousand one hundred years becomes "Rakṣoghna" (demon-destroying) Kumbha-sarpis; beyond that, it is called Mahāghṛta (Great Clarified Butter).

This great medicated ghee (mahāghṛta) should be drunk by those afflicted by spirits or by those with a predominance of vāta; it subdues kapha, is strengthening, purifying, and promotes intelligence, and it is especially effective in removing cataracts.
This ghee is praised as being the destroyer of all living beings.
Now, the oils.

Oil is fiery (āgneya), hot, sharp, sweet, and has a sweet post-digestive effect (vipāka). It is nourishing, pleasing, pervasive (vyavāyi), subtle, clear, heavy, laxative, expanding, aphrodisiac, a clarifier of the skin, purifying, and it promotes intelligence, softness, firmness of the flesh, complexion, and strength. It is beneficial for the eyes, binds the urine, is scraping (lekhana), has bitter and astringent secondary tastes, is digestive, reduces wind (anila) and phlegm (balāsa), destroys worms, generates internal heat (pitta) from food, alleviates pain in the female reproductive tract, head, and ears, cleanses the uterus, and is likewise recommended for affusion, massage, and immersion baths in cases of laceration, fracture, piercing, crushing, displacement, churning, injury, bruising, breaking, bursting, cauterization by alkali or fire, separation of joints, tearing, trauma, severe dislocation, or being bitten by wild animals or venomous creatures.
This should be employed for the pacification of Vata in enemas, drinks, nasal drops, filling of the ears and eyes,
and even in the preparation of food and drink.

Castor oil is sweet, hot, sharp, digestive-stimulant, pungent with an astringent aftertaste, subtle, a cleanser of the channels, beneficial for the skin, aphrodisiac, sweet in its post-digestive transformation, and youth-preserving. It purifies the female reproductive tract and semen, promotes health, intelligence, luster, memory, and strength, alleviates Vata and Kapha, and removes disorders of the lower body.

The oils extracted from the fruits of nimba, atasī, kusumbha, mūlaka, jīmūtaka, vṛkṣaka, kṛtavedhana, arka, kampillaka, hastikarṇa, pṛthvīkā, pīlu, karañja, iṅgudī, śigru, sarṣapa, suvarcalā, viḍaṅga, and jyotiṣmatī are sharp, light, hot in potency, pungent, and pungent in post-digestive effect; they are laxative and alleviate disorders of wind (vāta), phlegm (kapha), worms, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (prameha), and diseases of the head.
Among these, flax oil (kṣauma-taila) is wind-alleviating and sweet, yet it diminishes strength;
it is pungent in its post-digestive effect, harmful to the eyes, unctuous, hot, heavy, and increases pitta.
Mustard oil is anthelmintic, light, and removes itching and skin diseases (kuṣṭha);
it subdues phlegm, fat, and wind, is scarifying, pungent, and stimulates the digestive fire.
The oil of iṅgudī is slightly bitter and light;
it destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and worms, yet it impairs vision and the strength of the semen.
Safflower oil is bitter in its digestion, aggravates all the *doṣas*,
causes hemorrhaging and bile disorders, is sharp, harmful to the eyes, and causes a burning sensation.

The oils of kirātatiktaka, atimuktaka, bibhītaka, nālikera, kola, akṣoḍa, jīvantī, priyālaka, karbudāra, sūryavallī, trapusa, ervāruka, karkāru, kūṣmāṇḍa, and so forth, are sweet, have a sweet post-digestive effect (vipāka), pacify vāta and pitta, are cold in potency (vīrya), cause secretions to increase, promote the discharge of urine, and diminish the digestive fire.
The oils of madhuka, kāśmarya, and palāśa are sweet and astringent, and they pacify kapha and pitta.

Tvaraka-bhallātaka oil is hot, sweet with an astringent taste and a bitter aftertaste; it pacifies wind, phlegm, skin diseases, obesity, urinary disorders, and worms, and it removes morbid humors from both upper and lower parts of the body.

The oils extracted from *sarala*, *devadāru*, *gaṇḍīra*, *śiṃśapā*, and *aguru* are bitter, pungent, and astringent; they purify malignant ulcers and eliminate worms, phlegm, skin diseases, and disorders of wind.

The oils of *tumbī*, *kośāmra*, *dantī*, *dravantī*, *śyāmā*, *saptalā*, *nīlikā*, *kampillaka*, and *śaṅkhinī* are bitter, pungent, and astringent; they eliminate morbidities from the lower part of the body, destroy worms, phlegm, skin diseases, and Vāta, and purify malignant ulcers.
Tiktaka oil pacifies all the doṣas, is sovereignly bitter, kindles the digestive fire, is scraping, promotes intelligence, is wholesome, and acts as a rejuvenative elixir.
Ekaishika oil is sweet, extremely cooling, pacifies pitta, aggravates vata, and increases kapha.
Sahakāra oil is slightly bitter and very fragrant; it alleviates Vāta and Kapha, is parching, sweet and astringent in taste, and like its fruit, does not excessively increase Pitta.
Regarding those oils derived from fruits that have been mentioned here,
one should prescribe them after having understood their qualities and their actions, just as one would with the fruits themselves.
In brief, whatever fixed oils have been described,
all should be known to possess the qualities of oil and all to be destroyers of Vāta.
Among all oils here, sesame oil is distinguished;
because of its production and its possession of those qualities, the nature of being "oil" (taila) applies to others as well.

The fat, marrow, and bone-marrow of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals are heavy, hot, sweet, and pacify Vāta. Those of wild animals, single-hoofed animals, carnivores, and the like are light, cold, and astringent, and they pacify Raktapitta. Those of pecking birds (pratuda) and scratchers (viṣkira) pacify Kapha. Among these, ghee, oil, fat, marrow, and bone-marrow are progressively heavier in their post-digestive effect (vipāka) and are pacifiers of Vāta.

Now begins the section on honey (*madhuvarga*). Honey is sweet, with an astringent aftertaste; it is parching, cold, stimulates the digestive fire, improves the complexion, is beneficial for the voice, light, delicate, scraping, pleasing to the heart, aphrodisiac, promotes healing, cleanses, heals, is constipating, beneficial for the eyes, clarifying, and follows subtle channels. It pacifies *pitta*, *kapha*, fat, urinary disorders, hiccup, dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, vomiting, thirst, worms, and poisons; it is refreshing and pacifies all three *doṣas*. Furthermore, due to its lightness, it destroys *kapha*; and due to its sliminess, sweetness, and astringent quality, it subdues *vāta* and *pitta*.
Pauttika, bhrāmara, kṣaudra, mākṣika,
chātra, ārghya, auddālaka, and dāla— these are the eight varieties of honey.
Among these, honey from the *pauttika* bee is especially drying and hot due to its association with poison;
it cuts through wind, blood, and bile, causes a burning sensation, and produces intoxication.
Due to its sliminess, the honey known as *bhrāmara* (collected by bees) is considered heavy;
however, *kṣaudra* (the common honey) should be specifically known as cooling, light, and scraping (*lekhana*).
Therefore, honey from the Mākṣika bee is considered the most excellent because it is lighter and drier;
it is especially recommended for diseases such as asthma and others.

One should know that the *śāstra* (chickpea) is superior in its qualities: it is sweet in digestion, heavy, cooling, slimy, a conqueror of blood-bile (*raktapitta*), and a destroyer of leucoderma, urinary disorders, and worms.
Ārghya honey is highly beneficial for the eyes, an excellent remover of kapha and pitta;
it is astringent and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), strengthening, bitter, and does not increase vāta.
The *auddālaka* is palatable, beneficial for the voice, and a destroyer of skin diseases and poisons;
it is astringent, hot, and sour, increases *pitta*, and is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*).
Honey produced from flowers is parching and alleviates vomiting and urinary disorders;
fresh honey is nourishing, does not excessively remove phlegm, and is laxative.
Old [grain] removes obesity and is constipating; it is highly scraping.
When matured, it alleviates the three doshas; when raw and sour, it produces the three doshas.
Combined with various formulations, it cures many diseases;
moreover, because it consists of diverse substances, honey is the supreme vehicle for medicinal compounds.

However, because those flower juices are incompatible in terms of their various substances, tastes, qualities, potencies, and post-digestive effects, and because they may originate from poisonous bees, one should avoid consuming them when they are not warm.
Everything is counteracted by heat, for honey possesses the nature of poison;
just as poison destroys one who is afflicted by heat when administered with heat or during the heat, so too does it act upon the honey.
Moreover, due to its extreme delicacy, as well as its coolness and the presence of the juices of various medicinal herbs,
it would be especially counteracted by heat, as well as by the atmosphere and water.

Honey mixed with warm [liquids] administered for emesis does not cause a contradiction [with the preceding rules], because it has not been digested and because it does not remain [in the stomach] as before.
There is no other raw food more painful than honey;
because it is contrary to its initial preparation, it destroys everything, just like poison.

Now, the section on sugarcane: Sugarcanes are sweet, have a sweet post-digestive effect (vipāka), are heavy, cold, unctuous, strengthening, aphrodisiac, diuretic, pacify blood-bile (raktapitta), and increase worms and phlegm (kapha).
And they are of many kinds, as follows: Pauṇḍraka, Bhīruka, Vaṃśaka, Śvetaporaka,
Kāntāra, Tāpasekṣu, Kāṣṭhekṣu, and Sūcipatraka.
The Nepāla, the Dīrghapatra, the Nīlapora, and the Kośakṛt—these are the varieties [of bamboo]. Hereafter, I shall describe their qualities according to their thickness.
The Pauṇḍraka and Bhīruka varieties are very cooling, sweet, unctuous, nourishing, phlegm-increasing, laxative, non-burning, heavy, and aphrodisiac.
Vaṃśaka is considered to have qualities similar to these two, with a slight alkaline taste.
Śvetapora, however, is like vaṃśaka; it is slightly heating and subdues vāta.
The wild-sugar-cane and the ascetic-sugar-cane are considered to follow the lineage of the bamboo;
however, the wood-sugar-cane, though possessing such qualities, aggravates the wind (vāta).
The *sūcīpatra*, *nīlapora*, *naipāla*,
and *dīrghapatraka* are wind-increasing, they subdue phlegm and bile, are slightly astringent, and cause a burning sensation.
The silk-worm (*kośakāra*) is heavy, cooling, and removes blood-bile disorders and consumption;
it is exceedingly sweet in its root and likewise sweet in its middle part.
The salty taste of sugarcane is to be perceived within its foremost stalks.
The juice extracted by squeezing the teeth is non-burning, increases phlegm, alleviates wind and bile, refreshes the mouth, and is aphrodisiac.
The gur (unripe) fruit is known to be burning, constipating, and obstructive to the channels;
however, when ripe, it is heavy, laxative, unctuous, slightly sharp, and alleviates kapha and vāta.
Treacle is heavy, sweet, causes secretions to increase, is nourishing, non-aphrodisiac, and aggravates the three doṣas.

Jaggery (guḍa) is slightly alkaline and sweet, not excessively cold, unctuous, and it purifies urine and blood; it does not greatly subdue pitta, but destroys vāta, increases fat, worms, and kapha, and is strengthening and aphrodisiac.
Purified jaggery is sweet, pacifies pitta, alleviates vāta, and clarifies the blood; that which is old is considered to possess superior qualities and is regarded as most wholesome.

Matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa, and śarkarā, as they arise in this progressively refined order, are increasingly cooling, unctuous, heavy, sweeter, aphrodisiac, pacifiers of blood-bile (raktapitta), and alleviators of thirst.
To the same extent that their purity and sweetness increase,
so too do their viscosity, weight, coolness, and fluidity.

Whatever specific quality belongs to each of the varieties of sugar— whether candied sugar, granulated sugar, or refined sugar— the purgative effect of those substances is described by that very same quality.
The wise should understand that sugar is more excellent to the extent that it remains substantial, is perfectly pure, and is free from saline residue.
Honey-sugar (madhuśarkarā), moreover, cures vomiting and diarrhea; it is parching, astringent, clarifying, sweet in taste, and sweet in its post-digestive effect.
Yavāsa-śarkarā is sweet and astringent, with a bitter aftertaste; it alleviates phlegm and is laxative.
All the types of sugar mentioned are destroyers of burning sensations;
they pacify blood-bile (raktapitta) and remove vomiting, fainting, and thirst.
Phāṇita (unrefined treacle) derived from Madhūka flowers is parching, increases vāta and pitta,
destroys kapha, is sweet in its post-digestive effect, astringent, and impairs the bladder.
Now, the section on intoxicants: All intoxicants increase pitta; they are sour, appetizing, and digestive stimulants;
they are laxative, destroy kapha and vāta, are beneficial for the heart, and cleanse the bladder.
It is light in digestion, causes a burning sensation, is hot, sharp, awakens the senses, is expansive, and promotes the evacuation of feces and urine; now hear its specific qualities.
Because it is non-irritating and possesses a sweet quality,
grape wine (mārdvīka) is not strictly prohibited by the wise even in cases of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta).
It is indeed sweet yet parching, with an astringent aftertaste,
light, easily digested, laxative, and a destroyer of wasting diseases and irregular fevers.
Date wine (khārjūra) is slightly different from grape wine (mārdvīka); it aggravates wind (vāta), is clear, appetizing, subdues phlegm (kapha), is emaciating, and light.
It is astringent and sweet, pleasing to the heart, fragrant, and awakening to the senses;
it cures cough, hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract, urinary obstruction, and wind-related ailments.
Wine that is beneficial for the depletion of breast milk and blood is nourishing and digestive;
it destroys cough, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), dyspnea, and catarrh.
White wine (śvetā) increases urine, phlegm, breast milk, blood, and flesh;
it subdues vomiting, anorexia, and the piercing pain and colic in the heart, abdomen, and sides.
It is clarifying and destroys phlegm, wind, hemorrhoids, constipation, and abdominal distension.
It increases bile, has little phlegm, is dry, and aggravates wind when prepared with barley.
Surā is constipating and heavy; madhūlikā increases phlegm.
Akṣikī is known to be dry, not excessively phlegmatic, aphrodisiac, and digestive.
Kohala is provocative of the three humors (tridoṣa), a digestive stimulant, aphrodisiac, and pleasant to the palate.
Jagala is astringent, hot, a digestive aid, dry, and causes thirst, phlegm, and swelling.
The *bakva* (or *ākka*) is pleasing to the heart and removes dysentery, abdominal distension, hemorrhoids, wind-disorders, and wasting;
however, because its essence has been extracted, it causes constipation and provokes the wind (*vāta*).
Sīdhu liquor made from molasses (gauḍa) is digestive, stimulates the appetite, promotes the discharge of feces and urine,
is clear, slightly intoxicating, heavy, astringent, sweet, and acts as a digestive and appetizer.
Sugar-cane juice is sweet, appetizing, digestive, and a cleanser of the bladder;
it subdues wind, is sweet in its post-digestive effect, beneficial for the heart, and invigorates the senses.
Similarly, sidhu made from ripe juice is strengthening, improves the complexion,
is laxative, destroys swelling, stimulates digestion, is pleasing to the heart, appetizing, and beneficial for phlegm and hemorrhoids.
