It is emaciating, relishing cold, and destroys swelling and abdominal enlargement; it improves the complexion, promotes digestion, is beneficial for the voice, removes constipation, and is wholesome for hemorrhoids.
Sīdhu made from *ākṣika* (grape juice) destroys jaundice, heals wounds, is astringent, and light;
it is astringent-sweet, subdues *pitta*, and clarifies the blood.
Jāmbava is slightly astringent, causes a binding sensation, aggravates vāta, is sharp, pleasant to the heart, diuretic, and alleviates kapha and vāta.
Surāsava is sharp, pleasing to the heart, diuretic, and subdues kapha and vāta.

Madhvāsava should be known as pleasant to the palate, providing stable intoxication, and destroying disorders of Vāyu; it is light, acts as a digestive cut, and removes urinary disorders, skin diseases, and poisons.
Bitter and astringent, it destroys swelling, is sharp, sweet, and does not produce wind;
it is sharp and astringent, produces intoxication, and removes hemorrhoids, phlegm, and abdominal tumors.
Maireya liquor cures worms, fat, and wind; it is sweet, heavy, strengthening, pacifies pitta, improves the complexion, and is beneficial for the heart.
Sugarcane-juice asava is likewise sweet, heavy, strengthening, pacifies pitta, improves the complexion, and is beneficial for the heart.
Śīghru, derived from Madhūka flowers, is light, increases digestive fire and strength,
is parching, astringent, removes kapha, and aggravates vāta and pitta.
One should describe other fermented liquors made from bulbous roots, roots, and fruits according to their tastes;
fresh wine is obstructive to the channels, heavy, and provokes wind and the other humors.
That which has an unpleasant odor, a bad taste, and is unpalatable causes a burning sensation;
whereas that which is fragrant, digestive, palatable, appetizing, and destroys worms is wholesome.
Arishta causes the flow of secretions to become clear, is easily digested, and removes wind and phlegm;
it excels in its qualities due to the processing resulting from the combination of various substances.
It removes many disorders and pacifies the humors;
it is digestive, subdues phlegm and wind, is laxative, and does not aggravate bile.

It is beneficial for colic, flatulence, abdominal enlargement, splenic disorders, fever, indigestion, and hemorrhoids; the formulation beginning with *pippalī* is traditionally held to cure abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and diseases of *kapha*.
In the section on therapeutics, the various *ariṣṭas* that remove diseases will be described;
one should also prescribe the qualities and actions of *ariṣṭa*, *āsava*, and *sīdhu*.
Having observed each individual's specific condition with his intellect, the skilled physician [prescribes treatment for matter that is] thick,
burning, foul-smelling, tasteless, infested with worms, and heavy.
That which is unwholesome, fresh, sharp, hot, kept in a poor vessel,
containing few medicinal herbs, stale, perfectly clear, or slimy.
Wine should always be avoided, as should any that has only a small amount remaining;
for that which has little strength, is fresh, slimy, and heavy [is to be shunned].
That wine which aggravates phlegm (kapha) is especially difficult to digest;
that which aggravates bile (pitta) is thick, sharp, hot, and causes a burning sensation.
One should know that food which is unpalatable, insipid, putrid, infested with worms,
tasteless, and likewise stale, provokes the wind (vāta).
Though it is endowed with all defects and provokes all the bodily humors,
when it has stood for a long time and its essence has developed, it is digestive and conquers phlegm and wind.
Wine that is pleasing, clear, fragrant, intoxicating, and fit for consumption—
regarding that wine of many varieties, [one should consider] its taste and potency.
Due to its subtlety, heat, sharpness, and expansiveness, it unites with the fire;
having reached the heart, it ascends through the channels.
Agitating the senses and the mind, it intoxicates one's vigor before long.
In a man of phlegmatic constitution (*ślaiṣmika*), intoxication arises after a long time from drinking;
however, it is observed to occur before long in one of windy constitution (*vātika*), and very quickly in one of bilious constitution (*paittika*). (1.45.206ef)
In the *sāttvika* state, intoxication produces purity, dexterity, joy, a fondness for ornaments,
singing, study, good fortune, and enthusiasm for sexual union.
Intoxication in a man brings about a harsh disposition toward suffering, self-abandonment, recklessness, and persistent quarrelsomeness.
Impurity, sleep, envy, sexual misconduct, greed,
and even speaking falsehoods— these indeed constitute intoxication in the mode of darkness (tāmasa).
Shukta (fermented gruel) causes bleeding and bile, acts as a digestive solvent, and aids the digestion of food;
it cures hoarseness, promotes digestion, removes phlegm, anemia, and worms, and is light.
It is sharp, hot, diuretic, beneficial for the heart, subdues phlegm, and is pungent in its post-digestive effect; likewise, all its fermented products are similar, being especially appetizing.
Gauḍa vinegars, those fermented from juice (rasaśukta), and those fermented from honey (madhuśukta)—
as listed in order, they are increasingly heavy and cause excessive secretions.
Tuṣāmbu (fermented rice-water) stimulates digestion, is pleasing to the heart, and cures heart disease, anemia, and worms;
likewise, sauvīraka (sour gruel) destroys disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids, and acts as a purgative.
Dhānyāmla (fermented rice water), being derived from grain, is life-sustaining and a destroyer of burning sensations;
through contact or drinking, it removes wind, phlegm, and thirst, and is light [to digest].
Due to its pungency, it quickly removes phlegm when held as a gargle;
it dispels foul taste in the mouth, bad breath, impurities, dryness, and fatigue.
It is said to be illuminating, digestive, and a purgative; it is beneficial for enemas and is considered wholesome for people who dwell by the sea.
Now, regarding the urines:

the urines of the cow, buffalo, goat, sheep, elephant, horse, donkey, and camel are generally sharp, hot, pungent, bitter, with a salty after-taste, light, purifying, and they destroy phlegm, wind, worms, fat, poison, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargements, skin diseases, swellings, loss of appetite, and jaundice; they are also heart-tonic and digestive stimulants.
And on this point, [the authorities] say:
"All that [is] pungent, sharp, hot, with a secondary salty taste, light, purifying,
a destroyer of phlegm and wind, and a remover of worms, fat, and poison."

It destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargement, and tumors; it cures edema and loss of appetite; it removes anemia, acts as a purgative, is beneficial for the heart, and stimulates digestion and metabolism.
Cow’s urine is pungent, sharp, and hot; because it contains alkaline salts, it does not increase vāta.
It is light, stimulates the digestive fire, is beneficial for the intellect, increases pitta, and conquers kapha and vāta.

In cases of colic, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, flatulence, purgation, and non-unctuous enemas, as well as in conditions treatable by the administration of urine, one should employ cow's urine.
Buffalo [milk] is used for colic caused by *durnāman*, skin diseases, urinary disorders, impurities, abdominal distension,
swellings, tumors, and jaundice.
It cures cough and dyspnea, and removes edema, jaundice, and anemia;
it possesses pungent and bitter tastes, and slightly aggravates the wind humor (vāta).
Goat meat, which is alkaline, bitter, pungent, and hot, is beneficial for cough, splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, dyspnea, emaciation, and constipation; it subdues Vata.
Urine is illuminating, pungent, sharp, and hot; it cures disorders of wind and the mind, quickly removes phlegm, and is recommended for worms and skin diseases.
One should employ elephant urine— bitter, salty, purgative, subduing wind, and aggravating bile— in cases of sharp skin diseases (tīkṣṇa), scabies (kṣāra), and leucoderma (kilāsa).
Donkey urine is sharp, it destroys disorders of the mind and heart, cures diseases of the bowels,
stimulates digestion, and removes worms, wind, and phlegm.
The urine of a camel destroys swelling, leprosy, abdominal enlargement, insanity, wind-disorders, and worms;
human urine, moreover, is a destroyer of hemorrhoids and a remover of poison.
All liquid substances have thus been briefly described;
one who understands the distinctions of time and place is worthy to bestow them upon the king.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Liquid Substances," in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The forty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules for food and drink.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Having saluted Dhanvantari, Suśruta said: "It was previously stated that food is the root of living beings and the basis for strength, complexion, and vitality; furthermore, that food depends upon the six tastes (*rasas*). Tastes, in turn, reside in substances (*dravya*). The decrease and increase of the *doṣas*, as well as their equilibrium, are caused by the substance, taste, quality (*guṇa*), potency (*vīrya*), and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*). Food is the cause of the maintenance, origin, and destruction even of the world beginning with Brahmā. From food alone come growth, strength, health, and clarity of complexion and the senses. Indeed, from the improper nature of food comes ill-health. Therefore, I desire to know individually the substances, tastes, qualities, potencies, post-digestive transformations, effects, and actions of that which consists of various materials, possesses many varieties of preparation, and has manifold potencies—namely, what is eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed."

"For physicians who have not understood the true nature [of health and disease] are not capable of maintaining the state of health or suppressing disease; and since all living beings are dependent upon food, may the Blessed One instruct me in the rules for food and drink. Thus addressed, the Blessed Dhanvantari replied: "Now then, my dear Suśruta, attend closely to what is being said in accordance with your question."

Among them, the varieties of *śāli* rice include *lohitaśāli*, *kalama*, *kardamaka*, *pāṇḍuka*, *sugandhaka*, *śakunāhṛta*, *puṣpāṇḍaka*, *puṇḍarīka*, *mahāśāli*, *śītabhīruka*, *rodhrapuṣpaka*, *dīrghaśūka*, *kāñcanaka*, *mahiṣa*, *mahāśūka*, *hāyanaka*, *dūṣaka*, *mahādūṣaka*, and so forth.
They are sweet in taste, cooling in potency, light in digestion, and strength-promoting;
they subdue pitta, slightly increase vāta and kapha, are unctuous, and cause the feces to be bound and scanty.

Among them, the red variety is the best; it subdues the humors (doṣas), increases semen and urine, is beneficial for the eyes, imparts complexion and strength, is good for the voice, pleasing to the heart, and removes thirst.
It heals wounds, removes fever, and destroys all humors and poisons;
therefore, the subsequent varieties of *śāli* rice are progressively inferior, possessing qualities only slightly different from the former.
The *ṣaṣṭika* grains include the *kāṅguka*, *mukundaka*, *pītaka*, *pramodaka*, *kākalaka*, *asanapuṣpaka*, *mahāṣaṣṭika*, *cūrṇaka*, *kuravaka*, *kedāra*, and so forth.
Sweet in taste and digestion, they pacify vāta and pitta;
they are equal in qualities to śāli rice, nourishing, and increase kapha and semen.
The rain that falls during the six months beginning with Śrāvaṇa has a slightly astringent aftertaste;
it is light, mild, unctuous, pacifies the three doṣas, promotes stability, and increases strength.
Sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka) and easily digestible, it is equal to red śāli rice;
the remaining types of ṣaṣṭika rice possess qualities that differ from it only slightly, following a gradual gradation in their attributes.
Kṛṣṇavrīhi, śālāmukha, jatumukha, nandīmukha, lāvākṣaka, tvaritaka, kukkuṭāṇḍaka, pārāvataka, kapāṭaka, and so forth, are varieties of rice.

They are astringent and sweet, not sweet in their post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), and non-cold in their potency (*vīrya*). They cause little obstruction of the channels (*abhiṣyandi*) and are equal to *ṣaṣṭika* rice in binding the feces.

Among them, the *kṛṣṇavrīhi* rice is the best; it has a slightly astringent aftertaste and is light. Other varieties of *vrīhi* rice follow in succession, with qualities that differ only slightly from it.
Rice grown on land scorched by fire is light to digest,
astringent, constipating for feces and urine, parching, and it diminishes phlegm.
Terrestrial lotuses destroy phlegm and bile; they are astringent and possess a pungent aftertaste, are slightly bitter and sweet, and increase wind and fire.
Rice grown in irrigated fields is sweet, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and subdues pitta;
it is slightly astringent, produces little waste, is heavy, and increases kapha and semen.
The *ropya* and *atiropyā* varieties are light, undergo rapid digestion, and possess superior qualities;
they do not cause burning sensations, eliminate the *doṣas*, are strengthening, and increase the flow of urine.
Those *śāli* rice varieties that have regrown after being cut are dry and cause constipation;
they are bitter and astringent, subdue *pitta*, are light in digestion, and remove *kapha*.
This section on grains, including those beneficial and harmful, has been taught in detail;
likewise, the properties of inferior grains such as mudga, māṣa, and others shall now be described.
Now begins the section on inferior grains (*kudhānyavarga*).

The specific varieties of inferior grains include *koradūṣaka*, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, *śāntanu*, *varaka*, *oddālaka*, *priyaṅgu*, *madhūlikā*, *nāndīmukhī*, *kuruvinda*, *gavedhuka*, *sarabaruka*, *todaparṇī*, *mukundaka*, *veṇuyava*, and so forth.
They are hot, astringent-sweet, dry, and pungent in their post-digestive transformation;
they destroy phlegm, restrict secretions, and aggravate wind and bile.
They are known to be slightly astringent and sweet, cooling, and pacifiers of pitta. So too are kodrava, nīvāra, śyāmāka, and śāntanu.
Black, red, yellow, white, and brown varieties [of grains] are considered increasingly superior; they are dry and are known to alleviate phlegm (kapha).
Madhūlī is sweet, cooling, and unctuous, as is nandīmukhī;
among these, viśoṣī is predominantly so, as are varuka and mukundaka.
Wild bamboo seeds (veṇuyava) should be known as dry, hot in potency, pungent in post-digestive effect,
obstructing urine, alleviating phlegm, astringent, and aggravating wind.
Mudga, vanamudga, kalāya, makuṣṭha, masūra, maṅgalya, caṇaka, satīna, tripuṭaka, hareṇu, āḍhakī, and others are the split-pulse vegetables (vaidala).
They are astringent and sweet, cooling, and pungent in their post-digestive effect (vipāka); they increase vāta, bind the urine and feces, and likewise alleviate pitta and kapha.
Among those, mung beans are not excessively wind-increasing and clarify the vision;
the wild green varieties therein are considered the foremost, being equal to mung beans.
Masūra beans are said to be sweet in their post-digestive effect (vipāka) and they bind the feces; makuṣṭhaka beans produce worms, while kalāya beans increase the wind (vāta).
Āḍhakī destroys kapha and pitta and does not excessively aggravate vāta.
[Other pulses] are vāta-increasing, cold, sweet, slightly astringent, and drying.
Chickpeas destroy phlegm, blood, and bile, and they diminish virility;
yet, when combined with ghee, they are supreme pacifiers of the three doṣas.
Hareṇu and satīna beans should be known as those that bind the feces;
however, with the exception of mung and masūra, all others cause flatulence.
The black gram (māṣa) is heavy, causes loose stools and urine, is unctuous, hot, aphrodisiac, sweet, and subdues vāta.
It is nourishing, promotes the breasts, specifically bestows strength, and increases semen and kapha.
Due to its astringent nature, it does not cause the breaking up of feces, nor does it increase urine or phlegm;
it is sweet in taste and sweet upon digestion, heavy and thick, nourishing, and it promotes breast milk and relish for food.
The fruit of *ātmagupta* is said to have properties equal to those of *māṣa*, and the fruit of *kākāṇḍa* is likewise;
wild *māṣa* is prescribed as being similar in quality—dry, astringent, and non-burning.
Kulattha is hot in potency, astringent in taste, pungent in post-digestive effect, and it subdues phlegm and wind;
it destroys seminal calculi and abdominal tumors, is astringent, and cures chronic rhinitis and cough.
Wild *kulattha* is said to cure abdominal tumors, dyspepsia, piles, hiccup, and asthma; it increases blood-bile (*rakta-pitta*), destroys phlegm (*kapha*), and specifically cures eye diseases.
Slightly astringent, sweet, and bitter, sesame is constipating, increases pitta and blood, and is hot;
it is sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), highly strengthening, unctuous, and beneficial specifically as an external application for wounds.
Black sesame is beneficial for the teeth, generates fire and intellect, produces little urine, is good for the skin and hair, subdues wind, and is heavy;
among all types of sesame, the black is preeminent, the white is middling, and the others are inferior.

Barley is astringent and sweet, cold in potency, and pungent in its post-digestive effect; it removes phlegm and bile, is always wholesome for ulcers like sesame, promotes frequent urination, and increases flatus and feces.
It produces stability, digestive fire, intellect, voice, and complexion; it is slightly slimy and acts as a coarse abrasive.
It removes fat, wind, and thirst; it is extremely dry, clarifying, and beneficial for blood and bile.
Wheat (*godhūma*), which is slightly inferior to barley in these qualities but superior to all other grains,
is said to be sweet, heavy, strengthening, stabilizing, and a provider of semen and appetite.
That which is unctuous is very cold, subdues wind and bile, promotes healing, increases phlegm, and is laxative;
whereas that which is dry is astringent, causes the wasting of poison, emaciation, semen, strength, and vision, and produces a burning sensation.
The *śimba* fruit is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*) yet sweet; it obstructs the channels and increases feces, wind (*vāyu*), and bile (*pitta*).
Those various kinds of *śimba* fruits that are white, black, yellow, or red in color [share these properties].
As previously described, those [pulses] should be known as primarily pungent and hot in both taste and post-digestive effect;
likewise are the two types of *sahā*, radish sprouts, and the pods produced from the *kuśimbī* creeper.
They are known to be sweet in their post-digestive effect (vipāka) and in taste, providing strength, and subduing pitta;
yet they cause a burning sensation, are extremely dry, digest slowly by causing flatulence, and increase vāta.
All pulses (śimbā) grown from stalks (vaidalika) are considered to be palatable yet very difficult to digest;
however, the kusumbha is pungent in its post-digestive effect, pungent in taste, subdues phlegm, and is unwholesome due to its burning nature.
The *atasī* is hot, sweet in taste, subdues wind (*vāta*), increases bile (*pitta*), and is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*).
The *siddhārthaka* (white mustard) is declared to be pungent both in taste and in digestion, and it provokes blood and bile.
Likewise, the black mustard (*asita-sarṣapa*) is sharp, hot, and dry, and it destroys phlegm (*kapha*) and wind (*vāta*).
Grain that is out of season, damaged by disease, immature,
grown in unsuitable soil, or even newly harvested, is not considered to possess [auspicious] qualities.
Fresh grain is moistening; that which has been stored for a year is light. Sprouted grain causes a burning sensation, is heavy, causes constipation, and impairs vision.
The measures of time, the methods of preparation, and the proportions for all these various substances, beginning with rice and ending with mustard seeds, have been fully proclaimed.
Now, hereafter, we shall teach the groups of meats.
Namely: those dwelling in water, marsh-dwellers, domestic animals, carnivores, single-hoofed animals, and forest-dwellers—these are the six groups of meat.
Among these groups, each subsequent one is more excellent than the preceding.
Furthermore, they are of two kinds: forest-dwellers and marsh-dwellers.
In that regard, the category of wild animals (*jāṅgala*) is eightfold;

namely: those that run on their legs (*jaṅghāla*), those that scatter grain (*viṣkira*), those that peck (*pratuda*), those that dwell in caves (*guhāśaya*), those that seize by force (*prasaha*), those that are leaf-eaters (*parṇamṛga*), those that dwell in holes (*bileśaya*), and domestic animals (*grāmya*).
Among these, the runners and the scatterers are the most excellent.

The fleet-footed deer—namely the tāva, eṇa, hariṇa, ṛk� aṣka, kuraṅga, karāla, kṛtamāla, śarabha, śvadaṃṣṭra, pṛṣata, cāruṣkara, mṛgamātṛkā, and others—are astringent, sweet, light, pacifiers of vāta and pitta, sharp, pleasing to the heart, and cleansers of the bladder.

Astringent and sweet, it is pleasing to the heart and cures diseases of bile, blood, and phlegm; it is constipating, appetizing, and strengthening, and among them, the meat of the black antelope (eṇa) removes fever.
The hariṇa deer is sweet, sweet in digestion, a destroyer of the bodily humors, a stimulator of the digestive fire,
cooling, constipating for stool and urine, fragrant, and light.
Of those two, the black one is to be known as the *eṇa*, while the reddish-brown is called the *hariṇa*;
that which is neither black nor reddish-brown is designated as the *kuraṅga*.
Mṛgamātṛkā should be known as cooling and a pacifier of blood and bile;
it dispels disorders of the triple combination (sannipāta), consumption, dyspnea, cough, hiccups, and nausea.

The *viṣkira* (scattered-feed) birds that may be eaten after three days include the common quail (*lāva*), partridge (*tittiri*), grey partridge (*kapiñjala*), bustard (*vartīra*), vartika, vartaka, naptṛka, vārtīka, chakora, kalaviṅka, peacock (*mayūra*), crane (*krakara*), upacakraka, wild cock (*kukkuṭa*), sāraṅga, woodpecker (*śatapatra*), kutittiri, kuruvāhaka, yavālaka, and others.

The common quail (lāva) is light, cold, sweet, and astringent; it destroys the humors (doṣas), is constipating, digestive, and possesses an astringent-sweet taste. It has a pungent post-digestive effect (vipāka) and is highly esteemed in cases of the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (sannipāta).
The partridge is slightly heavy, warm, and sweet; it is aphrodisiac, increases intelligence and digestive fire, destroys all the *doṣas*, is constipating, and clarifies the complexion.
The francolin partridge (kapiñjala) alleviates blood-bile disorders, is cooling, and light;
it is recommended for diseases arising from phlegm and for conditions of sluggish wind.
The white partridge specifically removes hiccup, dyspnea, and wind;
it subdues wind and bile, is aphrodisiac, and increases intelligence, digestive fire, and strength.
The *laghava*, *krakara*, *hṛdya*, and *upacakraka* fish are light, astringent, sweet, and salty; they improve the skin and hair, and are beneficial for loss of appetite.
Peacock flesh strengthens the voice, intellect, digestive fire, sight, and the sense of hearing;
it is unctuous and hot, subdues wind (vāta), is aphrodisiac, and brings about perspiration, voice, and strength.
Wild chicken is nourishing; likewise is the domestic one, though that is heavy.
It destroys diseases of wind (vāta), consumption, vomiting, and intermittent fever.

The pigeons, doves, bhringarajas, cuckoos, koyaṣṭikas, kuliṅgas, gṛhakuliṅgas, gokṣveḍakas, ḍiṇḍimāṇavakas, śatapatrakas, mātṛnindakas, bhedās, parrots, mainas, valgulis, giriśas, laṭvālaṭṭūṣakas, sugṛhas, khajarīṭas, hārītas, dātyūhas, and so forth, are the birds that peck with their beaks (pratudas).
Fruits that are astringent and sweet, dry, and used as food increase wind (vāta),
alleviate bile (pitta) and phlegm (kapha), are cold in potency, and cause retention of urine with scanty feces.
The pigeon (*kāṇakapota*) causes all defects for those [who eat it]; it is a consumer of discord, defiled by impurities, and is astringent, sweet, and salty, as well as heavy.
The pigeon is known to pacify *rakta-pitta*, is clear due to its astringency,
is sweet in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and is heavy.
The common quail (kuliṅga) is sweet, unctuous, and increases phlegm and semen;
the domestic quail (veśmakuliṅga), however, cures hemorrhaging and bile disorders and is exceedingly aphrodisiac.
Lions, tigers, wolves, hyenas, bears, leopards, cats, jackals, deer, *irvāruka*, and so forth are den-dwellers.
Sweet, heavy, unctuous, strengthening, and subduers of Vāta;
being hot in potency, they are always beneficial for those suffering from disorders of the eyes and the private parts.
Crows, herons, kuraras, blue jays, vultures, hawks, owls, chillas, falcons, vultures, and so forth are the *prasahas* (birds of prey).

All these, beginning with the crow and ending with the lion, are similar in their taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation; they are especially beneficial for those suffering from consumption.
The Madgu, Mūṣika, Vṛkṣaśāyika, Avakuśa, Pūtighāsa, Vānara, and others are leaf-eating deer.
They are sweet, heavy, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and wholesome for those suffering from consumption;
they facilitate the passage of urine and feces and destroy cough, hemorrhoids, and dyspnea.
The porcupine, hedgehog, monitor lizard, rabbit, weasel, lopāka, hairy-eared animal, kadalī-mṛga, priyaka, ajagara, snake, rat, mongoose, and mahābabhru, among others, are hole-dwellers (vileśaya).
These [pulses] make the semen and urine concentrated; they are hot in potency, as previously described, and sweet in their post-digestive effect.
They subdue Vāta, increase Kapha and Pitta, are unctuous, and remove cough, dyspnea, and emaciation.
Among them, the rabbit is astringent and sweet; it pacifies pitta and kapha.
Because its potency is not excessively cold, it is considered compatible with vāta.
The iguana (godhā) is known to be sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), slightly astringent and pungent;
it pacifies wind and bile, is nourishing, and increases strength.
The *śalyaka* is sweet, destroys bile, is light, cooling, and removes poison; the *priyaka* is beneficial for wind disorders, while the *ajagara* is wholesome for hemorrhoids.
Sarpas destroy diseases such as durnāma and disorders caused by wind (vāta), as well as worms, skin afflictions, and poisons;
they are beneficial for the eyes, sweet in digestion, and increase both intelligence and digestive fire.
Among them, the *darvīkara* and *dīpaka* snakes are said to have a pungent post-digestive effect (*kaṭupākin*);
they are sweet, highly beneficial for the eyes, and promote the passage of feces, urine, and flatus.
Horses, mules, cattle, donkeys, camels, goats, rams, fat-tailed sheep, and so forth are domestic animals.
All village-grown [grains] dispel wind, are nourishing, increase phlegm and bile,
are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect, stimulate digestion, and increase strength.
The goat is known to be neither too cold, heavy, nor unctuous, and it diminishes pitta and kapha;
moreover, it is non-obstructive and destroys chronic catarrh.
Mutton is nourishing, heavy, and increases bile and phlegm;
that which originates from the fat tail is aphrodisiac and possesses qualities similar to mutton.
Cow’s milk destroys dyspnea, cough, catarrh, and irregular fever; it is beneficial for those exhausted by labor and deficient in digestive fire, and it is purifying and dispels wind.

The meat of sheep, goats, and salt-loving animals, as well as that of single-hoofed animals— this group is declared to be "jāṅgala" (wild/lean), causing little obstruction of the channels (abhiṣyandi).
Those deer and birds that dwell far from human habitation and have their range of water far away are considered to produce little internal moisture.
Those deer and birds whose dwellings are very close by and whose range is near the water are indeed highly moistening.
The group of marsh-dwellers, however, is fivefold;
namely: those that move along the banks, swimmers, shell-dwellers, legged creatures, and fish.

Among them, the elephant, gavaya, buffalo, ruru, camara, sṛmara, rohit, boar, rhinoceros, gokarṇa, kālapucchaka, kodaṅga, nyaṅku, variegated deer, wild ox, and so forth, are the animals that frequent the riverbanks.
They pacify wind and bile, are aphrodisiacs, sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect,
cooling, strengthening, unctuous, diuretic, and increase phlegm.
Among those [meats], the elephant is parching, scraping, hot in potency, and a corrupter of pitta;
it is sweet, sour, and salty, and it removes kapha and vāta.
The meat of the gavaya is indeed unctuous, sweet, and overcomes cough;
it is sweet in its post-digestive effect and promotes virility.
Buffalo meat is unctuous, hot, sweet, aphrodisiac, satiating, and heavy;
it increases sleep, virility, strength, and breast milk, and provides firmness to the flesh.
The meat of the Ruru deer is known to be sweet with an astringent aftertaste;
it pacifies Vāta and Pitta, is heavy, and increases semen.
Likewise, the meat of the yak (camara) is unctuous and sweet, it conquers cough,
is sweet in its post-digestive effect, and destroys wind and bile.
The meat of the sṛmara is known to have an astringent aftertaste;
it pacifies vāta and pitta, is heavy, and increases semen.
The meat of the boar is sudorific, nourishing, aphrodisiac, cooling, satiating, heavy, unctuous,
relieves fatigue and wind, and increases strength.
The meat of the rhinoceros destroys phlegm, is astringent, and subdues wind;
it is sacred to the ancestors, purifying, life-prolonging, constipating, and drying.
The meat of the Gokarṇa is sweet, unctuous, soft, and increases phlegm;
it is also sweet in its post-digestive effect and destroys blood-bile disorders.

The swan (*haṃsa*), crane (*sārasa*), curlew (*krauñca*), ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), osprey (*kurara*), grey goose (*kādamba*), duck (*kāraṇḍava*), pheasant (*jīvañjīvaka*), heron (*baka*), stork (*balākā*), white lotus goose (*puṇḍarīka*), water-fowl (*plava*), *śarārīmukha*, *nandīmukha*, *madgu*, *utkrośa*, *kācākṣa*, *mallikākṣa*, *śuklākṣa*, *puṣkaraśāyikā*, *konālaka*, *ambukukkuṭikā*, cloud-crying goose (*megharāva*), white vārala goose, and others such as these are the water-birds that move in flocks.
They alleviate blood-bile (raktapitta), are cooling, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and conquer wind (vāta);
they facilitate the passage of urine and feces, and are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect.
Among these, the *haṃsa* is hot, sweet, unctuous, and bestows strength upon the voice and complexion;
it is nourishing, increases semen, and alleviates disorders of wind (*vāta*).
The conch, the small conch, the pearl oyster, the snail, the bhallūka, and so forth are those that dwell within shells.
Tortoises, crocodiles, crabs, black crabs, porpoises, and so forth are the legged animals (pādinas).
Conch, tortoise, and other such [shells] have a sweet taste and post-digestive effect;
they move the wind (vāyu), are cold, unctuous, beneficial for pitta, promote feces, and increase kapha.
Among them, the black crab is strengthening when served warm,
subdues vāta, while the white crab promotes healing, increases feces and urine, and destroys vāta and pitta.
Fish, however, are of two kinds: those from rivers and those from the sea.

Among those, the river-dwelling fish—such as the *rohit*, *pāṭhīna*, *pāṭala*, *rājīva*, *varmi*, *gomatsya*, *kṛṣṇamatsya*, *vāguñjāra*, *murala*, *sahasradaṃṣṭra*, and so forth—are the river-dwellers.
Fish from rivers are sweet, heavy, and subdue the wind;
they increase blood and bile, are hot, aphrodisiac, unctuous, and cause scanty stools.
Having a slightly astringent aftertaste, these rohita fish, which feed on young grass and water-moss,
remove wind and do not excessively aggravate bile.
The *pāṭhīna* fish increases phlegm (*śleṣman*), is aphrodisiac, induces sleep, and is a flesh-eater;
it vitiates blood and bile (*rakta-pitta*) and causes the disease of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
The *murala* fish is nourishing, aphrodisiac, and likewise produces breast milk and phlegm.
Those produced in lakes and ponds are known to be glossy and of sweet taste;
those from great reservoirs are strong, while those from small amounts of water are known to be weak.
The timi, timiṅgila, kuliśapāka, matsya, nirularu, nandivāralaka, makara, gargarakā, candraka, mahāmīna, rājīva, and so forth are the marine [creatures].
Sea fish are heavy, unctuous, sweet, and not excessively heating;
they alleviate wind, are aphrodisiac, increase fecal matter, and augment phlegm.
Fish born in the sea are especially strength-promoting because they feed on flesh;
those born in rivers are superior in quality to those from the sea because they are more nourishing.
Because they are not destroyed by fire, the cauṇṭya and kaupya varieties possess superior qualities;
and because of their oiliness and sweet cooking properties, the vāpya variety possesses even greater qualities than those two.
River fish are not to be eaten when they are large, because they move about in the middle [of the water] and between the tail and the mouth;
however, among those born in lakes and ponds, the head is especially light.
Because their range is not far-reaching, they are born from springs of water;
having left behind only a small portion of their heads, those things are exceedingly heavy.
The heavy [beats] are to be known as occurring at the bottom; they are remembered as fish and lotuses.
Because of their movement across the chest, the first part of these is remembered as light.
Thus has been explained the group of meats from marshy regions that cause great secretions.

Among those, the meat of animals that are dried up, putrid, diseased, killed by venomous snakes, pierced by poisoned arrows, aged, emaciated, young, or those that do not follow a suitable regimen, are unfit for consumption; because, being devoid of essence, corrupted, destroyed, over-ripe, deficient, or incomplete in potency, they produce harmful effects. The meat of others besides these is to be accepted.
It is proclaimed to cause loss of appetite, catarrh, heaviness, and dryness;
it provokes poison, disease, death, and vomiting in children.
When increased, it causes cough and dyspnea; it is corrupted by the three doṣas and afflicted by disease;
when moistened, it produces nausea; and when emaciated, it provokes vāta.

Among quadrupeds, females are the most excellent; among birds, males; among large-bodied creatures, those with small bodies; and among small-bodied creatures, those with large bodies. Thus, among members of the same species, those with slender bodies are more excellent than those with large bodies.
We shall now explain the relative heaviness and lightness of meat according to its location and other factors.

For instance, among the tissues (dhātus) beginning with blood and ending with semen, each successive one is heavier than the preceding; likewise, [heavier parts of the body include] the thighs, shoulders, chest, head, feet, hands, waist, back, skin, the *kāleyaka* (the fleshy part between the shoulder blades), the liver, and the intestines.
One should understand that the head, shoulders, waist, back, and the two thighs on one's own sides follow the teacher in sequence, while the bodily constituents (dhātus) follow in successive order.
In the body of every living being, the middle part is declared to be heavy;
for men, the front part is heavy, while for women, it is the lower part.
The chest and neck of birds are especially considered heavy;
however, the middle part of birds is seen to be balanced by the upward-lifting of their wings.
The flesh of birds that feed on fruit is exceedingly dry,
whereas the flesh of birds that feed on other meat is highly nourishing.
Fish that feed on grain increase pitta and subdue vata;
likewise do those born in water, those from marshy lands, domestic animals, carnivores, and single-hoofed animals.
The *prasahas*, those that dwell in holes, and those known as the *jaṅghālas*, the *pratudas*, and the *viṣkiras*—these become lighter in weight in successive order;
furthermore, they cause less obstruction (*abhiṣyandi*) than the preceding ones. (1.46.136ef)
Those exceeding the standard measure, however, are of little essence within their own class, though they are large.

One should take those that are the most preeminent among all living beings in all bodies and which reside in the region of the liver; in the absence of such preeminent ones, meat from an animal of middle age, recently slaughtered, and not spoiled is to be used.
And there is a verse on this point: "In this [examination],
the movements, the limbs of the body, the natural disposition, the constituent elements (dhātus), the activities, the gender, the proportions, the refinement, and the measure are examined."
Thus ends the section on meats.
Hereafter, we shall describe the fruits.

They are as follows: pomegranate, emblic myrobalan, jujube, *kola*, *karkandhu*, *sauvīra*, *siñcitikā*, wood-apple, citron, mango, hog-plum, *karamarda*, *priyāla*, orange, lime, *lakucha*, *bhavya*, *pārāvata*, cane-fruit, *prācīnāmalaka*, *tintiḍīka*, *nīpa*, *kośāmra*, *amlīkā*, and so forth.
Amlānī fruits are heavy in taste and digestion, hot in potency,
increase Pitta, subdue Vāta, and cause the provocation of Kapha.
Among these, the pomegranate has an astringent aftertaste; it does not excessively increase bile, stimulates digestion, improves the appetite, is beneficial for the heart, and binds the feces.
That [pomegranate] should be known to be of two kinds: sweet and sour.
The sweet variety destroys the three doṣas, while the sour variety removes vāta and kapha.
The fruit of the *āmalakī* is sour, sweet, bitter, astringent, and pungent; it is laxative, beneficial for the eyes, a destroyer of all deranged humors (*doṣas*), and aphrodisiac.
It subdues wind (vāta) due to its acidity, bile (pitta) due to its sweetness and coolness, and phlegm (kapha) due to its dryness and astringency; moreover, it is superior to other fruits.
The unripe jujube (karkandhu), jujube (kola), and crab-apple (badara) increase pitta and kapha;
when ripe, they alleviate pitta and vāta, being unctuous, sweet, and laxative.
Sauvīra (fermented barley water) and badara (jujube) are ancient [remedies] that quench thirst, remove fatigue, stimulate digestion, and are light;
they are unctuous, sweet, and conquer wind and bile.
The fruit of the *śiñcitikā* is astringent, sweet, constipating, and cooling.
Raw *kapittha* is harmful to the voice, destroys *kapha*, is constipating, and increases *vāta*.
Ripe [mango] alleviates kapha and vāta; it is sweet and sour in taste, heavy, relieves dyspnea, cough, and anorexia, destroys thirst, and cleanses the throat.
Mātuluṅga is declared to be light, sour, digestive-stimulant, and beneficial for the heart;
its rind is bitter, difficult to digest, and it destroys wind, worms, and phlegm.
Meat is sweet, cold, heavy, and unctuous; it conquers wind and bile, promotes intelligence, and destroys colic, wind-disorders, vomiting, phlegm, and loss of appetite.
The filaments (kesara) stimulate digestion, are light, astringent, and destroy abdominal tumors and hemorrhoids;
they are used in cases of colic, indigestion, constipation, weak digestive fire, and disorders of phlegm and wind.
And for one suffering from a lack of relish, its juice is specifically prescribed;
it increases pitta and vāta, is beneficial for children, increases pitta, and has bound fibers.
It is pleasing to the heart, improves the complexion, is appetizing, and bestows blood, muscle, and strength;
it has an astringent aftertaste, is sweet, subdues wind (vāta), is nourishing, and heavy [to digest].
The fully ripe mango is not antagonistic to pitta;
it increases semen, is nourishing, sweet, strengthening, heavy, and digests with flatulence.
The āmrātaka fruit is aphrodisiac, unctuous, and increases phlegm;
the lakuca fruit causes the stagnation of the three doṣas and destroys semen.
The karamardaka fruit is sour, relieves thirst, stimulates the appetite, and increases pitta;
the priyāla fruit alleviates vāta and pitta, is aphrodisiac, heavy, and cooling.
It is pleasing to the heart, sweet, astringent, and sour; it is wholesome, cleanses the mouth, removes pitta and kapha, is constipating, heavy, causes flatulence, and is cooling.
Pārāvata is equally sweet, appetizing, and alleviates excessive digestive fire and wind;
likewise, nīpa and prācīnāmalaka remove the defects caused by poison.
Raw tamarind (tintiḍīka) subdues wind but produces pitta and phlegm;
when fully ripe, it is astringent, hot, digestive, appetizing, and alleviates both phlegm and wind.
Therefore, the *kośāmra* fruit is said to have qualities that differ only slightly [from the mango];
however, the ripe fruit of the *amlīkā* is similar to it, with the sole distinction that it is laxative.
The fruit of the orange is said to be sour yet sweet, pleasing to the heart, clear, and appetizing; it subdues wind, is difficult to digest, and is heavy.

The jambīra fruit alleviates thirst, colic, derangement of phlegm, vomiting, and dyspnea; it destroys obstructions caused by wind and phlegm, is heavy, and increases pitta. Airāvata and dantaśaṭha are sour and increase blood-bile (rakta-pitta).

The milky trees include the *āphala*, *jambava*, *rājādana*, *todana*, *śītaphala*, *tinduka*, *bakula*, *dhanvana*, *aśmantaka*, *aśvakarṇa*, *phalgu*, *parūṣaka*, *gāṅgerukī*, *puṣkaravarti*, *bilva*, *bimbī*, and so forth.
These fruits are cooling, they alleviate kapha and pitta,
they are astringent, dry, and sweet.
The fruit of milk-exuding trees (kṣīravṛkṣa) is heavy, constipating, and cold;
it is astringent, sweet, and slightly sour, and it does not excessively aggravate the wind (vāta).
Jambū fruit is extremely wind-increasing, constipating, and subdues phlegm and bile;
the rājādana fruit is unctuous, sweet, astringent, and heavy.
It is astringent, sweet, dry, pricking, and conquers phlegm and wind;
it is sour, hot, light, constipating, unctuous, and increases bile and digestive fire.
The *tinduka* fruit when unripe is astringent, constipating, and provocative of wind (*vāta*).
When fully ripe, it is heavy in digestion, sweet, and subdues phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*).
The fruit of the Bakula tree is said to be sweet, astringent, unctuous, constipating, firming for the teeth, and cleansing.
Sakaṣāya is astringent, cooling, sweet, digestive, and it conquers kapha and vāta;
one should know that gāṅgeruka and the fruits of aśmantaka are similar to it.
The fruit of the *phalguna* tree is constipating, sweet, unctuous, satiating, and heavy;
it is very sour, slightly sweet, has an astringent aftertaste, and is light.
One should know that the unripe *parūṣaka* subdues wind and generates bile;
that same fruit, when ripe, is sweet and destroys both wind and bile.
The lotus (pauṣkara) is sweet in its post-digestive effect, cooling, clarifying for blood and bile,
palatable, causes constipation, is strengthening, increases phlegm, and is heavy.
The young (immature) bilva fruit is described as alleviating kapha and vata, sharp, unctuous, constipating, and digestive-stimulant; it is pungent, bitter, astringent, and hot.
One should know that very same [food] when overcooked to be heavy, having a sweet after-taste,
causing a burning sensation, producing constipation, aggravating the humors, and resulting in foul-smelling flatus.
The fruit of the *bimbī* plant, along with *aśvakarṇa*, promotes breast milk and conquers *kapha* and *pitta*;
it removes thirst, burning sensations, fever, *pittāsṛj* (hemorrhagic disorders), cough, dyspnea, and consumption.
The palmyra palm, the coconut, the jackfruit, the mango, and so forth.
They say that these have sweet cooking properties and tastes, alleviate vāta and pitta,
provide strength, are unctuous, nourishing, and cooling.
The fruit of those palmyra trees has a sweet taste, is heavy, and conquers pitta;
its seed is sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), is diuretic, and conquers both vāta and pitta.
The coconut is heavy, unctuous, pacifies pitta, is sweet and cold;
it bestows strength and flesh, is beneficial for the heart, nourishing, and cleanses the bladder.
The jackfruit (panasa) is slightly astringent, unctuous, sweet in taste, and heavy.
The mango (mauca) is said to be sweet in taste, slightly astringent, and not very cold;
it cures hemorrhaging and bile, is aphrodisiac, appetizing, increases phlegm, and is heavy.
Grapes, *kāśmarya*, dates, flowers of *madhūka*, and so forth.
They say that [fruits] which cure hemorrhaging and bile are heavy and sweet;
among them, grapes are laxative, beneficial for the voice, sweet, unctuous, and cold.
It removes hemorrhaging, bile-fever, dyspnea, thirst, burning sensations, and consumption;
it is beneficial for the heart, cures urinary obstruction, and destroys pitta, blood disorders, and vāta.
The fruit of the *kāśmarya* is said to be beneficial for the hair, an elixir (*rasāyana*), and promotes intelligence;
it cures chest wounds and consumption, is pleasing to the heart, cooling, satiating, and heavy.
The *arjuna* fruit is sweet in taste and digestion and conquers *rakta-pitta*.
The flower of the *madhūka* is nourishing, heavy, and unpleasant to the heart;
its fruit is taught to pacify *vāta* and *pitta*.
Vātāma, akṣoḍa, abhiṣuka, nicula, picu, nikocaka, kaurumāṇa, and so forth.
They say that [substances] which are unctuous, hot, and heavy pacify pitta and kapha;
they are nourishing, subdue vata, are strengthening, and sweet.
The fruit of the *lavalī* is said to be astringent, subduing phlegm and bile, slightly bitter, appetizing,
pleasing to the heart, fragrant, and clear.
Vasira is cold in its post-digestive effect (śītapākyam), possesses the binding properties of *ārūṣkara*,
causes constipation, is difficult to digest, dry, cooling, and aggravates *vāta*.
It is sweet in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*) and clarifies *rakta-pitta*.
Airāvata is pungent, sour, and increases blood and *pitta*.
*Ṭaṅka* is cold, astringent, sweet, heavy, and increases *vāyu*.
The fruit of the iṅguda tree is unctuous, hot, bitter, and sweet; it destroys wind and phlegm.
The fruit of the śamī is heavy, sweet, dry, and hot; it destroys the hair.
The fruit of the śleṣmātaka is heavy, increases phlegm, is sweet, and cold.
Karīra, akṣika, and pīlu fruits, as well as the fruits of tṛṇaśūnya, are sweet, bitter, pungent, and hot; they alleviate kapha and vāta.
Among them, the *pīlu* is bitter, increases *pitta*, is laxative, and has a pungent post-digestive effect (*vipāka*);
it is sharp, hot, pungent, slightly unctuous, and overcomes *kapha* and *vāta*.

The decoction of *āruṣkara* and *tauvaraka* is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*kaṭupāki*), hot in potency, and destroys worms, fever, flatulence, urinary disorders, and upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*). It likewise cures skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), enlargement of the abdomen (*udara*), and hemorrhoids (*arśas*), being pungent in its post-digestive effect as well.
The fruit of *Aṅkola* is malodorous, heavy, alleviates *śleṣman*, and is cold;
the fruits of *Karañja*, *Kiṃśuka*, and *Ariṣṭa* destroy parasites and urinary disorders (*prameha*).
Viḍaṅga is dry, hot, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), light, and subdues vāta and kapha;
it is slightly bitter, wholesome, and destroys worms.
The fruit of the abhayā (harītakī) is healing for wounds, hot, laxative, intellect-promoting, a destroyer of the [three] doṣas, a remover of swelling and skin diseases,
astringent, digestive-stimulant, sour, and beneficial for the eyes.
It is a laxative, light, dry, and hot; it cures hoarseness, destroys worms, is beneficial for the eyes, sweet in its post-digestive taste, slightly astringent, and conquers phlegm and bile.
Betel nut removes phlegm and bile, is parching, cleanses the moisture and impurities of the mouth,
is astringent with a slight sweetness, and is slightly laxative.
Jātī-kośa, karpūra, the fruit of jātī and kaṭuka,
kakkolaka, and lavaṅga are bitter and pungent, and they remove phlegm.
Camphor is light, removes thirst, destroys moisture and foul odor in the mouth,
is slightly bitter, fragrant, cooling, light, and scarifying.
Latākastūrikā is likewise honored for thirst, dryness of the mouth, and a bad taste; it is cooling and cleanses the bladder.
The marrow of the *priyāla* is sweet, aphrodisiac, and removes pitta and vāta;
the *baibhītaka* (kernel of the *bibhītaka*) is intoxicating and destroys kapha and vāta.
The marrow of *kola* fruits is astringent and sweet; it destroys *pitta*, and likewise that of *āmalaka* destroys thirst, vomiting, and *vāyu*.
The pulp of the *bījapūraka* and the kernel of the *kośāmra* are sweet in their post-digestive effect (*vipāka*),
increase digestive fire and strength, are unctuous, and alleviate *pitta* and *vāta*.
Whatever kind of potency a particular fruit possesses here in this world,
by that very potency one should designate even its marrow.

Among fruits, that which is fully ripe is said to possess [the aforementioned] qualities; however, this should be understood to apply to fruits other than the *bilva*. Indeed, the unripe *bilva* is superior in its qualities:
it is hot, digestive-stimulant, astringent, pungent, and bitter. (1.46.209ef)
Fruit that is diseased, infested with worms, overripe, unseasonal,
or entirely immature should be avoided.
Thus ends the section on results.
Beyond this, we shall speak of vegetables (*śāka*).
Among them are the *puṣpa*, *phala*, *alābu*, *kālindaka*, and so forth.
They pacify pitta, stimulate vāta, and likewise diminish kapha;
they facilitate the passage of urine and feces, and are sweet in taste and post-digestive effect.
Among these, the immature (bāla) kūṣmāṇḍa destroys pitta; the middling (madhya) brings about kapha;
and the ripe (śukla) is light, hot, alkaline, digestive, and cleanses the bladder.
Water from the Yamunā removes all defects, is pleasing to the heart, and is wholesome for those with mental disorders;
however, it diminishes vision and semen, and increases phlegm and wind.
The *alābu* with broken seeds is dry, heavy, and extremely cold;
however, the bitter *alābu* is unpalatable, yet it subdues vomiting and the disorders of wind and bile.
Cucumber, gourd, melon, śīrṇavṛnta, and so forth.
They say that those which possess sweet and sour tastes increase phlegm and wind,
promote the evacuation of urine and feces, and alleviate blood-bile (raktapitta).
The young and deep-blue cucumber is known to remove bile;
when it is pale, it increases phlegm, and when old or sour, it removes wind and phlegm.
The fully ripe ervāruka and karkāru increase phlegm and wind;
they are alkaline, sweet, appetizing, digestive, and not excessively provocative of bile.

It is slightly alkaline and sweet; when its stalk has withered, it removes phlegm (kapha), acts as a laxative, stimulates digestion, is pleasing to the heart, cures flatulence and hardness of stool, and is light.

Long pepper, black pepper, ginger, fresh ginger, asafoetida, cumin, coriander, citron, sumukha, surasa, arjaka, bhūstṛṇa, sugandhaka, kāsamardaka, kālamāla, kuṭheraka, kṣavaka, kharapuṣpa, śigru, madhuśigru, phaṇijjñaka, mustard, rājikā, kulāhala, avaguttha, gaṇḍīra, tilaparṇikā, varṣābhū, citraka, radish, garlic, onion, kalāya, and so forth.
Pungent, hot, and appetizing substances that alleviate wind and phlegm are employed in various ways within prepared foods for the purpose of seasoning.
Among them, the fresh long pepper is heavy, sweet, cooling, and increases phlegm;
when dried, it destroys phlegm and wind, is aphrodisiac, and is not antagonistic to bile.
Fresh black pepper is sweet when cooked, heavy, and causes excessive salivation; it increases phlegm.
When dried, it is pungent, hot, light, non-aphrodisiac, and conquers phlegm and wind.
White pepper is neither too hot nor too cold in its potency;
it possesses qualities superior to those of black pepper and is especially beneficial for the eyes.
Nagara destroys phlegm and wind; it is sweet in its post-digestive effect and pungent.
It is aphrodisiac, hot, appetizing, beneficial for the heart, unctuous, light, and a digestive stimulant.
Fresh ginger is known to alleviate phlegm and wind, improve the voice, and cure constipation, flatulence, and colic;
it is pungent and hot, appetizing, beneficial for the heart, and aphrodisiac.
Asafoetida (hiṅgu) is light, hot, digestive, appetizing, and overcomes kapha and vāta;
it is pungent, unctuous, laxative, sharp, and cures colic, indigestion, and constipation.
Both types of cumin (jīraka) are sharp, hot, pungent in digestion, appetizing, and increase bile and digestive fire; they are bitter, remove phlegm and wind, and are rich in fragrance.
Kāravī and karavī are likewise to be understood as being accompanied by upakuñcikā;
they are employed in various kinds of foods, side dishes, and edibles.
Fresh cumin (kustumbarī) produces sweetness, fragrance, and agreeableness;
when dried, it is sweet in digestion, unctuous, and destroys thirst and burning sensations.
Kaṭukā destroys the humors (doṣas), is slightly bitter, and cleanses the channels.
Jambīra is digestive, sharp, and removes worms, wind, and phlegm.
It is fragrant, stimulating, appetizing, and produces clarity of the mouth;
it destroys phlegm, wind, poison, dyspnea, cough, and foul odors.
Surasa is declared to cure disorders of bile and alleviate pain in the flanks;
likewise, Sumukha should be known to have similar properties, with the specific distinction of destroying abdominal tumors.
Surasā, arjaka, and bhūstṛṇa destroy kapha, are light, dry, sharp, and hot; they increase pitta and possess pungent tastes and post-digestive effects.
Kāsamardaka is sweet, alleviates kapha and vāta, is digestive, cleanses the throat, and specifically removes pitta; it is also slightly bitter.
The common drumstick tree (śigru) is pungent, alkaline, and sweet; the bitter variety is slimy.
The honey-drumstick tree (madhuśigru) is astringent, bitter, dispels swelling, stimulates the digestive fire, and is pungent.
The mustard leaf (sārṣapa), gāṇḍīra, and veganāma are burning to the throat, obstructive to feces and urine, dry, sharp, and hot; they aggravate all three doṣas.
Citraka and tilaparṇī are light and remove phlegm and swelling;
varṣābhū destroys phlegm and wind and is beneficial for swellings, abdominal enlargements, and hemorrhoids.

The sprout of the radish is pungent and bitter in taste, pleasing to the heart, appetizing, and a stimulant of the digestive fire; it removes all the humors (doṣas), is light, and is beneficial for the throat.
Raw meat is heavy, obstructive, sharp, and causes the three doṣas;
however, that same meat, when prepared with fats, alleviates pitta and conquers kapha and vāta.
Dried potherbs pacify the three doṣas, remove the defects of poison, and are light;
however, they cause flatulence and increase wind, with the exception of dried radish.
Flower, leaf, and likewise fruit—these are prescribed as progressively more potent.
Among them, the flower destroys phlegm and bile, while the fruit subdues both phlegm and wind.

Garlic is unctuous, hot, sharp, pungent, slimy, heavy, laxative, sweet in taste, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and beneficial for the intellect, voice, complexion, and eyes; it promotes the healing of fractured bones and joints.

It destroys heart disease, chronic fever, abdominal colic, constipation, abdominal tumors, loss of appetite, cough, edema, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, weak digestion, parasites, wind disorders, asthma, and phlegm.
Onion possesses a pungent taste and a sharp quality; it is not excessively hot in potency, subdues wind, is heavy, and does not excessively increase phlegm.
It bestows strength, slightly generates bile, and further increases the digestive fire.
Unctuous, appetizing, stabilizing to the bodily tissues, strengthening, and increasing intelligence, *kapha*, and nourishment;
sweet, heavy, beneficial for blood and bile, and slimy—this is described as milk-onion (*kṣīrapalāṇḍu*).
The kalāya vegetable destroys bile and phlegm, increases wind, and is heavy;
it has an astringent aftertaste and is sweet in its post-digestive effect.
Cuccū, yūthikā, taruṇī, jīvantī, bimbītikā, nadī (or āndī), bhallātaka, chagalāntrī, vṛkṣādanī, phaṇjī, śālmalī, the fruits of the śalu and vanaspati trees, śaṇa, karbudāra, kovidāra, and so forth.
Those that are astringent, sweet, and bitter remove blood-bile (raktapitta),
destroy phlegm (kapha), increase wind (anila), are constipating, and light.
The cucu is light in digestion, kills microorganisms, is slimy, beneficial for those with wounds,
astringent-sweet, constipating, and among them, it alleviates the three doṣas.
Jīvantī is declared to be beneficial for the eyes and a destroyer of all defects;
vṛkṣādanī removes wind, while phaṇjī is considered to be of little strength.

The decoctions of the leaves of milk-exuding trees, blue lotuses, and the like, are traditionally known to be cooling and astringent; they are recommended for those suffering from hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta) and diarrhea.
Punarnavā, varuṇa, tarkārī, uruvūka, vatsādanī, bilva-śāka, and so forth.
They are hot, sweet, and bitter, and they pacify the wind (vāta);
among them, the punarnavā vegetable is especially effective for destroying swelling (śopha).
These include *taṇḍulīyaka*, *upodikā*, *aśvabalā*, *cillī*, *pālaṅkya*, *vāstūka*, and so forth.
Those who have voided urine and feces, as well as those that are alkaline and sweet,
are said to pacify wind and phlegm and cure hemorrhaging.
Sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect, it removes blood-bile and intoxication;
among these, *taṇḍulīya* is the coldest, is dry, and destroys poison.
Upodika is sweet in taste and digestion, aphrodisiac, and it pacifies vāta, pitta, and intoxication;
it is laxative, unctuous, strengthening, increases kapha, and is cooling.

Vāstūka is pungent in its post-digestive effect, destroys worms, increases intelligence, digestive fire, and strength; it is alkaline, subdues all the doṣas, is appetizing, and promotes the flow of secretions.
Pālaṅkyā should be known as similar to cillī and vāstūka, and taṇḍulīyaka;
it generates wind, binds the feces and urine, is dry, and is beneficial for pitta and kapha.
The āśvabala vegetable is dry and binds the feces, urine, and wind.

Maṇḍūkaparṇī, saptalā, suniṣaṇṇaka, survacalā, pippalī, guḍūcī, gojihvā, kākamācī, prapunnāḍa, avalguja, satīna, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā, the fruits of paṭola, vārtāku, kāravellaka, kaṭukikā, kevuka, erubūka, parpaṭaka, kirātatikta, karkoṭaka, ariṣṭa, kośātakī, vetra-sprouts, āṭarūṣaka, arkapuṣpī, and so forth.
They say these [fruits] cure blood-bile (raktapitta), are pleasing to the heart, and very light;
they also alleviate leprosy, urinary disorders, fever, asthma, cough, and loss of appetite.
Maṇḍūkaparṇī is astringent, beneficial for pitta, sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, and cold; gojihvikā is considered to have the same properties. It is also light.
Suniṣaṇṇaka is non-burning, alleviates the three doṣas, and is astringent;
avalguja is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), bitter, and removes pitta and kapha.

The potherb derived from *satiṇa* is slightly bitter, pungent, and destroys the three doṣas; it is neither too hot nor too cold and cures skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). The potherb of *kākamācī* is similar to that.
The fruits of the *bṛhatī* plants destroy skin diseases, leprosy, and worms; they alleviate *kapha* and *vāta*, and are pungent, bitter, and light.
Patola removes phlegm and bile, is beneficial for ulcers, hot in potency, bitter, and does not increase wind; it is pungent in digestion, aphrodisiac, appetizing, and digestive.

The eggplant (*vārtāka*) is said to alleviate *kapha* and *vāta*, be bitter, appetizing, pungent, light, digestive, and, when old, slightly alkaline and provocative of *pitta*. One should know that the *karkoṭaka* and the *kāravella* are likewise.
Aṭarūṣaka, vetrāgra, guḍūcī, nimba, parpaṭa,
and kirātatikta— these bitter substances remove pitta and kapha.
The leafy vegetables of the Varuṇa and Prapunāḍa plants are said to alleviate Kapha;
they are dry, light, and cold, yet they provoke Vāta and Pitta.
Black potherb (kālaśāka) is digestive, pungent, and removes the defects caused by poison;
safflower (kausumbha) is sweet, dry, hot, light, and subdues phlegm.
Nālikā-śāka is wind-increasing (vātala), it subdues pitta, and is sweet;
it cures disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) and hemorrhoids, is slightly sour, and is beneficial for vāta and kapha.
Āṅgerī is hot, astringent-sweet, and stimulates the digestive fire.
These include the *loṇikā*, *jātukā*, *triparṇikā*, *pattūra*, *jīvaka*, *suvarcalā*, *ḍuḍuraka*, *kutuṃbaka*, *kuṭhiñjara*, *kuṃtalikā*, *kuraṇṭikā*, and so forth.
They have sweet post-digestive tastes and are cold; they destroy kapha but do not excessively increase pitta.
They have a salty secondary taste, are dry, slightly alkaline, increase vata, and are laxative.

The *kuntalī* is sweet and bitter, while the *kuraṇṭikā* is astringent; both are constipating, cooling, light, and likewise dispel the bodily humors (*doṣa*). The leafy vegetable of *rājakṣavaka* and that of *śaṭī* are of the same nature.

The potherb produced from *harimanthaka* is sweet in digestion and taste, difficult to digest, laxative, sweet, dry, and excessively increases wind (*vāta*). The *kālāya* potherb is similar in these qualities.
The leaf of the *pūtikarañja* causes purgation, is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pākaja*), light, alleviates wind and phlegm, destroys swelling, and possesses a hot potency (*uṣṇavīrya*).
Betel leaf is sharp, hot, pungent, and aggravates pitta;
it is fragrant, clear, bitter, beneficial for the voice, and removes vāta and kapha.

It causes laxation, is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and is astringent; it kindles the digestive fire and purifies the mouth of itching, impurities, moisture, foul odors, and the like.
Now begins the section on flowers:

The flowers of the *kovidāra*, hemp (*śaṇa*), and the silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*) are sweet, have a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and alleviate blood-bile (*raktapitta*). The flowers of the *vṛṣa* and *agastya* are bitter, have a pungent post-digestive effect, and remove consumption and cough.
The *āgastya* [juice], being neither too cold nor too hot, is recommended for those who are blind at night.
The flowers of the Karīra and Madhuśigru have a pungent post-digestive effect (vipāka), alleviate Vāta, and promote the evacuation of urine and feces.
The flowers of the red tree, the neem, the mushka, the arka, and the asana remove phlegm and bile; the flower of the kutaja is a destroyer of skin diseases.
The lotus (*padma*) is slightly bitter, sweet, and cold; it removes *pitta* and *kapha*.
The night-lily (*kumuda*) is sweet, slimy, unctuous, refreshing, and cold.
One should know that the water-lily (*kuvalaya*) and the blue lotus (*utpala*) possess qualities that differ only slightly from these.
One should know that *sindhuvāra* is cooling and destroys *pitta*;
*mālatī* and *mallikā* are bitter and destroy *pitta* due to their fragrance.
The *vākula* and *pāṭala* flowers are fragrant, clear, and pleasing to the heart; they destroy phlegm, bile, and poison. *Nāga-keśara* and likewise saffron (*kuṅkuma*) have the same properties.
Campaka destroys red bile (raktapitta), is both cooling and heating, and subdues phlegm (kapha).
Kiṃśuka destroys phlegm and bile, and the same applies to kuraṇṭaka.
Just as one should recognize that a flower is appropriate to its tree,
so too are the shoots of the Madhuśigru plant pungent and they remove phlegm.
Kṣavaka, kulattha, caru, vaṃśa, karīra, and so forth, alleviate phlegm and promote the evacuation of urine and feces.
Among those, *kṣavaka* is worm-infested, sweet in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), and slimy;
it causes excessive secretions, increases *vāta*, and does not excessively increase *pitta* or *śleṣman*.
The shoots of the bamboo tree (veṇu) have small fruits that are sweet in taste and post-digestive effect;
they cause burning, increase wind, are slightly astringent, and are parching.
There are five types of fire originating from straw (*palāla*), sugarcane (*ikṣu*), cow-dung (*karīṣa*), bamboo (*veṇu*), and earth (*kṣiti*).

Among these, that produced from straw is sweet, has a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), is parching (*rūkṣa*), and pacifies the *doṣas*. That produced from sugarcane is sweet, with an astringent secondary taste (*anurasa*), pungent, and cold; likewise, that from cow-dung is hot, astringent, and aggravates *vāta*. That produced from bamboo is astringent and aggravates *vāta*. That produced from earth is heavy, not excessively provocative of *vāta*, and its secondary taste follows from the nature of the earth itself.
Oil-cake, sesame paste, thick gruel, and dried vegetables aggravate all the *doṣas*.
All *vaṭaka* cakes are known to cause constipation and aggravate the *vāta*.
Fresh *siṇḍākī* is *vāta*-increasing, yet it is appetizing and stimulates the digestive fire.

All sweet vegetables are generally described as breaking the wind, heavy, dry, constipating, difficult to digest, and slightly astringent. Among them, flowers, leaves, fruits, stalks, and bulbs are progressively heavier in that order.
One should avoid leafy vegetables that are coarse, over-ripe, infested with worms, grown in unsuitable places, or those that grow out of season.

Above the tubers, we shall now describe [the following]: vidārī-kanda, śatāvarī, bisa, mṛṇāla, śṛṅgāṭaka, kaśeruka, piṇḍāluka, madhvāluka, hastyāluka, kāṣṭhāluka, śaṅkhāluka, raktāluka, and the tubers of the indīvara and utpala lotuses, and so forth.
They say that [these substances] alleviate blood-bile (raktapitta), are cooling and sweet,
heavy, increase semen, and promote the growth of breast milk.
The root of the vidārī is sweet, nourishing, aphrodisiac, cooling, beneficial for the voice, and highly diuretic;
it is strengthening and alleviates pitta and vāta.
Śatāvarī removes wind and bile, is aphrodisiac, sweet and bitter;
the "great" variety (mahatī) is likewise heart-pleasing and increases intellect, digestive fire, and strength.
It cures disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids, is aphrodisiac, cooling, and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
Its sprouts are known to be bitter and to alleviate phlegm and bile.
It is said to be non-burning, a purifier of blood and bile (raktapitta),
constipating, difficult to digest, dry, tasteless, and provocative of wind (vāta).
The *śṛṅgāṭaka* and *kaśeruka* are heavy, constipating, and cold; the *piṇḍāluka* increases *kapha*, is heavy, and provokes *vāta*.
Surendrakanda destroys phlegm, is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and increases bile;
the hollow stems (karīra) of bamboo are heavy and aggravate phlegm and wind.
Roots such as the sthūla, sūraṇa, and māṇaka are slightly astringent, pungent, dry, constipating, heavy, aggravating to phlegm and wind, and they alleviate bile.
Mānaka is proclaimed to be sweet, cooling, and heavy;
Sūraṇa, with its large bulb, is not excessively hot and cures hemorrhoids.
The tubers of the kumuda, utpala, and padma are provocative of wind (vāta),
astringent, pacifiers of bile (pitta), sweet in their post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cooling.

Varāhakanda destroys phlegm (śleṣman) and is pungent in both taste and post-digestive effect (rasa-pāka); it cures urinary disorders (meha), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and worms (kṛmi), and is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
The piths from the heads of the palmyra, coconut, date-palm, and so forth.
They have sweet post-digestive tastes and potencies, they alleviate blood-bile disorders,
increase semen, subdue Vata, and also increase Kapha.
One should avoid all bulbs that are immature, out of season, decayed, diseased, infested by worms,
or those that do not grow properly.

(Now, the salts: Rock salt, sea salt, biḍa salt, sauvarcala salt, romaka salt, audbhida salt, and so forth—these salts are increasingly pungent in their potency, pacify vāta, and increase kapha and pitta; they are progressively more unctuous, sweet, and promote the easy passage of urine and feces.
Rock salt (saindhava) is beneficial for the eyes, pleasing to the heart, appetizing, light, and a stimulator of the digestive fire;
it is unctuous, sweet, aphrodisiac, cooling, and an excellent destroyer of the [three] humors.
Sea salt is sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), not excessively heating, and non-burning;
it is laxative, unctuous, slightly [sweet], a destroyer of colic, and does not excessively increase pitta.
Viḍa salt is alkaline, digestive-stimulant, subtle, and a destroyer of colic and heart disease;
it is appetizing, sharp, hot, and promotes the downward movement of wind (vāta).

Laghu-sauvarcala salt is hot in its post-digestive effect (pāka) and potency (vīrya), clear, and pungent; it destroys abdominal tumors (gulma), colic (śūla), and constipation (vibandha), is beneficial for the heart, fragrant, and improves the appetite.
Romaka salt is sharp, very hot, pervasive, and pungent in its post-digestive effect; it subdues Vata, is light, promotes secretions, is subtle, breaks up fecal matter, and increases urine.
One should know that rock salt (audbhida-lavaṇa) is light, sharp, hot, liquefying, subtle, carminative for the wind, slightly bitter, pungent, and alkaline.
The salt known as Guṭikālavaṇa removes phlegm, wind, and worms; it is scraping, aggravates bile, stimulates digestion, promotes digestion, and is a laxative.
Salt produced from saline soil, from sand, from the roots of mountains,
or from mines is pungent, cutting, and is said to be of a sharp nature.

Yavakṣāra, svarjikākṣāra, ūṣakṣāra, pākima, ṭaṅkaṇakṣāra, and others— these alkalis destroy abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids (arśas), disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa), and catarrh (pratiśyāya). All alkalis are digestive (pācana), yet they provoke blood-bile (raktapitta) and are laxative (sara).
The two alkalis derived from svarjikā and yavaśūka should be known as equal to fire;
they destroy semen disorders, phlegm, constipation, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and splenic enlargement.
The alkaline preparation (kṣāra) cooked [with medicinal herbs] is hot, subdues wind, is moistening, caustic, and diminishes strength;
it destroys fat and purifies the bladder among those [alkaline preparations].
Tīkṣṇa ṭaṅkaṇa kṣāra is said to be desiccant, wind-increasing, phlegm-destroying, and pitta-vitiating; it stimulates the digestive fire.
Gold is sweet, pleasing to the heart, nourishing, and a rejuvenative elixir;
it pacifies the three humors, is cooling, beneficial for the eyes, and destroys poison.
Silver is non-acidic, laxative, cooling, unctuous, and alleviates pitta and vāta.
Copper is astringent, sweet, scraping, cooling, and laxative.
Bell-metal is slightly bitter, scraping, beneficial for the eyes, and conquers kapha and vāta.
Iron produces vāta, is cooling, and removes thirst, pitta, and kapha.
Zinc and lead are pungent, anthelmintic, salty, and depleting; while pearl, coral, diamond, sapphire, lapis lazuli, crystal, and so forth [are cooling].
These gems are beneficial for the eyes, cooling, scraping, and destroyers of poison; they are purifying, worthy of being worn, and remove sin, misfortune, and impurity.
Regarding grains, meats, fruits, and vegetables, since they are not explicitly mentioned here due to their immeasurable variety,
one of great intelligence should prescribe them after considering their taste and their qualities as perceived by the sense organs.
Sixty-day ripening barley, wheat, red rice, mung beans,
pigeon peas, and lentils are recorded as the most excellent among grains.
In this world, among the groups of meats, the quail, the partridge, the antelope, the deer, the wild goat, the francolin, the peacock, the porcupine, and the tortoise are considered the best.
Pomegranate, emblic myrobalan, grapes, dates,
parūṣaka, rājādana, and citron are praised among the group of fruits.
Satīna, vāstuka, cuccū, cillī, mūlaka, kapotikā,
maṇḍūkaparṇī, and jīvantī are praised in the category of leafy vegetables (śāka).

Cow's milk and ghee are the best among dairy products; rock salt is the best among salts; the emblic myrobalan and pomegranate are the best among sour things; and long pepper and ginger are the best among pungent things.
Ghee is said to be best for bitter and bitter-cucumber-like vegetables, honey for sweet ones, and betel nut along with *parūṣaka* for astringent ones.
One may eat preparations of sugar and sugarcane, as well as honey and spirituous liquors;
likewise, grain that has been stored for more than a year and meat during the middle stage of life.
Food that has not stood overnight, well-prepared in the proper measure and pure;
fruit that is fully ripened, vegetables that are not dried, and fresh, young [greens].
Hereafter, I shall explain in detail the qualities of prepared food.
The scum of parched grain is wholesome for those who are pure, acting as a digestive and appetizer;
when combined with long pepper and ginger, it facilitates the downward movement of wind and is beneficial for the heart.
Peya (gruel) generates perspiration and digestive fire, is light, stimulates digestion,
cleanses the bladder, removes hunger, thirst, fatigue, and exhaustion, and facilitates the downward movement of Vata.
Vilepī is nourishing, pleasing to the heart, absorbent, and strength-increasing;
it is wholesome, sweet-tasting, light, digestive, and removes hunger and thirst.
Heart-pleasing, satiating, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and strength-increasing;
when combined with vegetables, meat, or fruits, and prepared as a sour gruel, it is difficult to digest.
Maṇḍa is devoid of grains; peyā is provided with grains;
vilepī should have many grains; and yavāgū is thin and liquid.
Rice-milk (pāyasa) is constipating, strengthening, heavy, and increases fat and phlegm;
while kṛśarā increases phlegm and bile, is strengthening, and destroys wind.
Washed rice is stainless, pure, pleasing, fragrant, and even;
when steamed, it flows well, is warm, clear, and light.
Rice that is unwashed, unstrained, unsweated, and cold is heavy;
however, rice made from fried grains should be known as light, fragrant, and a destroyer of phlegm.
Those prepared with fats, meats, fruits, tubers, and split pulses combined with sours are heavy, nourishing, and strengthening; as are those prepared with milk.
Well-cooked, dehusked, and lightly fried, a soup is light and beneficial;
likewise, boiled vegetables that have been squeezed dry and prepared with fat are wholesome.
Meat that is not cooked in fat, nor pressed, and otherwise prepared,
is by its very nature aphrodisiac, emollient, and strength-increasing.
Meat prepared with fats, dairy products, fermented grain liquids, sour fruits,
and pungent spices is beneficial, strengthening, appetizing, nourishing, and heavy.
One should know that this very same preparation of cow's milk, processed with fragrant substances,
increases pitta and kapha, and promotes strength, muscle mass, and digestive fire.
Dried meat is firm, unctuous, exhilarating, nourishing, and heavy;
it is appetizing and increases strength, intellect, digestive fire, muscle tissue, vitality, and semen.
Because it has been thoroughly ground into a paste, cooks call it *ullupta*;
being cooked over fire and endowed with the quality of complete dryness, it is therefore light.
That very same [meat], when impaled on a spit, cooked over glowing coals, and smeared with fat,
should be known as somewhat heavier due to the thorough cooking and the addition of fat.
Food that is fried, roasted, ground, heated, cooked in a clay pot (kandupācita),
dried, smeared with fat, spit-roasted, or any other of this kind;

Meat that has been prepared with oil is hot in potency, increases pitta, and is heavy; however, it is light, stimulates the digestive fire, is beneficial for the heart, appetizing, and clarifies the vision.
It is non-hot in potency, pacifies pitta, is pleasing to the mind, and is prepared with ghee;
it is nourishing, generates vitality, and removes dyspnea, cough, and consumption.

Meat broth is known to alleviate wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and fatigue; it is pleasing to the heart and is prescribed for those deficient in memory, vitality, and voice, as well as for those emaciated by fever or physical injury.
It nourishes those with broken or dislocated joints, emaciated persons, and those with diminished semen; it provides structural integrity, increases virility, and augments strength.
Combined with pomegranate, it is aphrodisiac, refined, and a destroyer of the bodily humors;
it gladdens all beings, especially those suffering from dryness of the mouth.
Sour gruel (saurava), which is sweet and cooling, is the best for removing hunger and thirst;
however, meat from which the essence has been extracted does not provide nourishment or strength.
Stagnating digestion, difficult to digest, dry, tasteless, and provocative of wind,
the *khāniṣka* is always wholesome for those with a keen digestive fire, though it is extremely heavy.
Meat, free of bone and well-cooked, should be ground again on a stone slab and combined with long pepper,
ginger, black pepper, jaggery, and clarified butter.
One should cook these together thoroughly; this is known as vesavāra.
Vesavāra is heavy, unctuous, strengthening, and a destroyer of diseases caused by wind (vāta).

Mudga soup—whether prepared or unprepared—is known to be a destroyer of phlegm, digestive, and pleasing to the heart; it is considered most wholesome for those who have undergone purification as well as for those suffering from ulcers.
That *rāgakhāḍava*, however, when combined with pomegranate and grapes,
is light to digest, does not aggravate the bodily humors (*doṣas*), and is non-contradictory to them.
A preparation made with lentils, mung beans, wheat, horse gram,
and salt does not aggravate phlegm or bile and is recommended for diseases caused by wind.
Combined with grapes and pomegranates, that [preparation] is also prescribed for those afflicted by wind (vāta);
it is taught to be appetizing, digestive, pleasing to the heart, and light in digestion.
The soups of *paṭola* and *nimba*, however, dry up phlegm and fat;
they subdue pitta, stimulate the digestive fire, are beneficial for the heart, and remove worms, skin diseases, and fever.

A soup of radish (*mūlaka*) destroys dyspnea, cough, catarrh, excessive salivation, anorexia, and fever, as well as disorders of phlegm, fat, and the throat. A soup of horse gram (*kulattha*) subdues wind (*vāta*) and cures dyspnea and chronic catarrh (*pīnasa*).
Soup made from pomegranate and āmalaka is heart-pleasing, pacifying, and light; it destroys hemorrhoids, gulma, and upward movement of wind (udāvarta), as well as tūṇī and pratūṇī.
The soup of mung beans and āmalaka generates vital breath and digestive fire, removes fainting and morbid humors, and conquers pitta and vāta;
it is constipating and beneficial for pitta and kapha.
