Soup made from barley, jujube, and horse gram is beneficial for the throat and subdues wind;
likewise, soup made from all types of grains is nourishing and increases vitality.
Khaḍaka and āmbalika are pleasing to the heart and beneficial for vāta and kapha;
pomegranate, when sour, is strengthening, destroys kapha and vāta, and stimulates the digestive fire.
Curd-sour [fermented milk] increases phlegm, is strengthening, unctuous, alleviates wind, and is heavy.
Buttermilk-sour is said to increase bile and to vitiate poison and the blood.
Khaḍa, khaḍayavāgū, ṣāḍava, pānaka,
and other such preparations are made according to the instructions of physicians.
All that is without oil and salt, and without pungent spices, should be known as "unprepared" (akṛta);
that which is combined with salt, oil, and pungent spices is "prepared" (kṛta).
Furthermore, meat broth that is combined with cow's milk products, fermented grain water (dhānyāmla), or fruit acids is beneficial;
among these, each subsequent type is lighter than the preceding one, whether it is seasoned or unseasoned.
Soup prepared with curd-whey and sour substances is known as *kāmbalika*.
A preparation of sesame and oil-cake is called *śuṣkaśāka*, as is sprouted grain (*virūḍhaka*).
Siṇḍākī is heavy and increases kapha and pitta;
likewise, they say that vaṭakas are heavy and cause a burning sensation.
Rāga-ṣāḍavas are light, nourishing, aphrodisiac, pleasing to the heart, appetizing, and digestive; they alleviate thirst, fainting, vertigo, vomiting, and fatigue.
Rasālā is nourishing, strengthening, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and appetizing;
curd combined with jaggery is emollient, pleasing to the heart, and subdues Vāta.
Barley flour mixed with clarified butter, saturated with cold water,
neither too liquid nor too thick, is designated as *mantha*.
Mantha provides immediate strength and destroys thirst and fatigue;
when prepared with sour substances, fats, and jaggery, it cures dysuria and upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
Combined with sugar, sugarcane juice, and grapes, it removes disorders of pitta;
combined with grapes and madhūka, it eradicates diseases of kapha.
A syrup made from the three groups [of fruits], which facilitates the downward movement of impurities and humors, is heavy; it may be sour or non-sour, prepared with molasses, and it is diuretic.
That same preparation, when combined with candied sugar, jaggery, and sugar-candy, and further made slightly sour, pungent, and cold, becomes a harmless refreshing drink (pānaka).
Mārdvīka juice removes fatigue and alleviates fainting, wounds, and thirst;
a beverage made from parūṣaka and kola fruits is beneficial for the heart but causes constipation.
Having understood the substances, their combinations, and the processing, as well as the dosage in all respects,
one should prescribe the heaviness or lightness of the drinks according to what is appropriate.
Thus ends the section on prepared foods.
Hereafter, I shall describe the edibles according to their taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation.
Edibles prepared with milk are strengthening, aphrodisiac, pleasing to the heart,
fragrant, non-burning, nourishing, digestive stimulants, and destroyers of pitta.
For them, *ghṛtapūra* cakes are life-sustaining, pleasing to the heart, and increase *kapha*;
they alleviate *vāta* and *pitta*, are aphrodisiac, heavy, and increase blood and muscle tissue.
Edible foods made with molasses are nourishing, heavy, and destroy Vāyu;
they do not cause burning sensations, pacify Pitta, increase semen, and augment Kapha.
Honey-topped saṃyāva cakes and those specific types of pūpa are heavy and nourishing, while modakas are indeed very difficult to digest.
Sattaka is brightening, illuminating, beneficial for the voice, a destroyer of bile, and a remover of wind; it is heavy, most delicious, and increases vitality.
It is known to be pleasing to the heart, fragrant, sweet, unctuous, productive of phlegm (kapha),
heavy, a subduer of wind (vāta), satiating, strengthening, and laxative.
Edible preparations made with meat are nourishing, subdue wind and bile, and are strengthening;
among them, those such as *phenaka* (froth-cakes) are pleasant to the heart, most wholesome, and light.
Dishes filled with mudga beans and vesavāra are considered to cause flatulence;
those filled with vesavāra and meat are heavy and nourishing.
Pāyalās increase phlegm; śaṣkulyas increase phlegm and bile.
Edible preparations made from flour are hot in potency and aggravate phlegm and bile.

Foods made from split pulses (vaidala) are generally burning, not very strengthening, and especially heavy; however, when prepared as snacks, they are light, astringent, and stimulate the wind humor (māruta).
Preparations made from mung beans (māṣa) should be known as constipating, equalizing pitta, destroying kapha, breaking up the stool, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and heavy.
Edibles made from curds (kūrcikā) are heavy and not excessively heating for the pitta humor; edibles made from sprouted grains (virūḍhaka) are heavy and increase both vāta and pitta.
Fried foods cooked in ghee cause a burning sensation and nausea, are dry, and impair the vision; yet they are pleasing to the heart, fragrant, and light to digest.

Those prepared with oil alleviate wind and bile, are strengthening, and clarify the complexion and vision; however, they cause a burning sensation, are heavy, and have a pungent post-digestive effect.
They are hot, they destroy wind and vision, increase bile, and corrupt the skin;
they are prepared with fruit, meat, sugarcane products, sesame, and black gram.
Those baked on potsherds or over charcoal embers are edible, strengthening, heavy, nourishing, and pleasing to the heart;
however, they are light and aggravate the wind (vāta).
Foods that are well-cooked and light in weight are generally considered easy to digest; however, edibles such as *kilāṭa* (coagulated milk) and similar items are heavy and increase *kapha*.
Kulmāṣas (fermented grains) increase wind, are dry, heavy, and cause loose stools;
however, vāṭya (roasted barley meal) removes upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and cures cough, chronic rhinitis, and urinary disorders.
Dhānā (fried grain) and ulumbā (dried fried grain) are light and dry up phlegm and fat.
Barley flour (śaktavaḥ) is nourishing, aphrodisiac, and removes thirst, pitta, and kapha;
when drunk, it immediately bestows strength, acts as a laxative, and subdues vāta.
A large bolus is very heavy, while that same bolus becomes light through the opposite conditions;
a linctus made of barley flour would be digested quickly due to its softness.
Parched grain (lāja) cures vomiting and diarrhea, stimulates digestion, destroys phlegm, is strengthening,
astringent-sweet in taste, light, and removes impurities from the body.
The flour of that [grain] is considered to alleviate thirst, vomiting, burning sensations, and the distress of heat;
it also removes blood-bile (raktapitta) and destroys fever accompanied by a burning sensation.
Pṛthuka grains are heavy, unctuous, nourishing, and increase phlegm;
they are strengthening, alleviate wind due to their milky nature, and act as a laxative.
Fresh rice flour (piṣṭa) made from raw rice is a healer of wounds and cures worms and urinary disorders;
it is very difficult to digest, has a sweet taste, and is nourishing.
Ancient rice flour is known to promote healing and alleviate urinary disorders.
Having carefully observed the substances, their combinations, preparations, and transformations—

whether they have been obtained according to their specific causes or even by the choice of the eaters— one should identify them according to the scriptures, since they originate from many different substances.

Therefore, we shall now describe all types of after-drinks (anupāna). Some people, having been repelled by sourness, become fond of the union with sweetness; likewise, those satiated by the union with sourness prefer sweetness. For them, we shall prescribe wholesome food according to their desire.

Whatever after-drink (anupāna) may be beneficial for one who has consumed cold water, hot water, fermented liquors (āsava), wine (madya), meat broth (yūṣa), sour fruits, sour gruel (dhānyāmla), milk, or meat juices— that should be administered here in the proper measure.
Having carefully considered the disease and the time, the wise prescribe various substances and foods;
yet among all these, they declare that pure water contained in a clean vessel is the best of all drinks.

From birth onwards, water is praised for the world, and all tastes are seen to be composed of water; this summary has been stated regarding after-drinks (anupāna), and hereafter I shall describe it in detail.
The drinking of warm water after taking fats is recommended,
with the exception of *bhallātaka* oil and *sauvarcalaka* oil.
Some say that as a post-drink (anupāna) for oil, one should take broth or sour gruel;
for honey, cold water; and for flour-based food, anything at all.
In the case of one afflicted by curd, milk-porridge, wine, or poison, as well as in similar instances,
some authorities say that lukewarm water is the appropriate after-drink for food made of flour.
Milk or meat broth is also suitable for those who eat rice, mung beans, and the like,
as well as during times of battle, travel, heat-induced exhaustion, and in cases of illness from irregular wine.
As a post-digestive drink for black gram and similar foods, fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) or the whey of curd is recommended;
however, for those accustomed to alcohol, wine is esteemed as a post-digestive drink with all types of meat.
For those who do not drink liquor, water or sour fruit juice is recommended;
for those exhausted by heat, travel, speaking, or women, milk is like nectar.
For those who are emaciated or corpulent, honey-water is prescribed as a post-prandial drink;
however, for those free from disease, it is proclaimed that various [medicinal drinks] should be taken during the meal.
Unctuous and warm food is wholesome for wind (vāta); for phlegm (kapha), dry and warm is desired;
and for bile (pitta), a sweet and cool after-drink is beneficial.
Milk and sugarcane juice are beneficial for those suffering from blood-bile disorders; likewise, fermented liquors (āsava) made from Arka, Shelu, and Śirīṣa are for those afflicted by poison.
Henceforth, I shall describe in due order the specific after-drinks (anupāna) for each group [of drugs]; listen to all of them from me.

Among these, for the various species of grain, sour jujube (*badarāmla*) is prescribed; for split pulses (*vaidala*), fermented rice water (*dhānyāmla*); for the *jaṅghāla* (swift-running) and *dhanvaja* (desert-dwelling) animals, a *pippalyāsava* (fermented liquor of long pepper); for the *viṣkira* (scattered-feeders), a *kolabadarāsava* (fermented liquor of jujube and wild jujube); for the *pratuda* (pecking birds), a *kṣīravṛkṣāsava* (fermented liquor of milk-exuding trees); for the *guhāśaya* (cave-dwellers), a *kharjūranālikerāsava* (fermented liquor of dates and coconut); for the *prasaha* (force-feeding birds), an *aśvagandhāsava* (fermented liquor of ashwagandha); for the *parṇamṛga* (leaf-eating deer), a *kṛṣṇagandhāsava* (fermented liquor of black fragrant grass); for the *bileśaya* (hole-dwellers), a *phalasārāsava* (fermented liquor of fruit-pith); for the single-hoofed animals, a *triphalāsava* (fermented liquor of the three myrobalans); for the multi-hoofed animals, a *khadirāsava* (fermented liquor of khadira); for the *kūlacara* (bank-dwellers), a *śṛṅgāṭakakaśerukāsava* (fermented liquor of water chestnut and lotus root); for the *kośavāsin* (shell-dwellers) and *pādina* (footless aquatic creatures), that same [liquor] is used; for the *plava* (floaters), a *ikṣurasāsava* (fermented liquor of sugarcane juice); for the fish of rivers, a *mṛṇālāsava* (fermented liquor of lotus stalks); for the marine fish, a *mātuluṅgāsava* (fermented liquor of citron); and for sour fruits, a *padmotpalakandāsava* (fermented liquor of the roots of the lotus and water lily).

For astringent substances, there is an *āsava* of pomegranate and cane; for sweet substances, a *khaṇḍāsava* (molasses-based *āsava*) combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*); for palm fruits and the like, *dhanyāmla*; for pungent substances, an *āsava* of *dūrvā*, *nalaveṭra*, and cane; for *pippalī* and the like, an *āsava* of *śvadaṃṣṭrā* and *avasukā*; for *kūṣmāṇḍa* and the like, an *āsava* of *dārvī* and *karīra*; for *cuccū* and the like, an *āsava* of *lodhra*; for *jīvantī* and the like, an *āsava* of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*); for the *kusumbha* vegetable, that same [preparation]; for *maṇḍūkaparṇī* and the like, an *āsava* of the great five roots (*mahāpañcamūla*); for the top of the palm tree and the like, an *āsava* of sour fruits; for *saindhava* salt and the like, a *surāsava* or *āranāla*; and water may be used for all [substances].
And there are verses on this subject:
Of all post-prandial drinks, rainwater is the best;
or whatever water is wholesome for a person, that is said to be beneficial for him.
In cases of wind (vāta) or phlegm (kapha), water should be warm; in cases of bile (pitta) or blood (rakta), it should be cold.
Likewise, food that is heavy due to defects or consumed in excessive quantity [should be treated similarly].
With the aforementioned after-drink (anupāna), food is easily digested;
it is appetizing, nourishing, aphrodisiac, and a breaker-up of the accumulation of the humors (doṣas).
Satiating drinks produce softness, remove fatigue and exhaustion, are pleasant, stimulate digestion,
pacify the humors, and are supreme for quenching thirst.

A proper after-drink (anupāna) is always said to be strengthening and complexion-promoting; when drunk at the beginning [of a meal], it causes emaciation, but when consumed in the middle, it stabilizes the body.
Drunk later, it causes nourishment; therefore, one should administer it after careful consideration.
For those who drink non-liquid substances, food that has reached a state of stability and is not moistened [by liquids] [is digested properly].
Therefore, one should drink a post-drink (anupāna) that produces no affliction;
however, one suffering from dyspnea or cough, or afflicted by diseases of the supraclavicular region, should not drink it.
One whose chest is injured, who suffers from excessive salivation, or whose voice is impaired, should not practice drinking, traveling, speaking, studying, singing, sleeping, or eating.
For that [vitiated wind], having corrupted the stomach (āmāśaya) and remaining in his throat and chest,
produces many diseases such as excessive salivation, loss of digestive fire, and vomiting.
This consideration of relative weight does not transcend inherent nature,
nor does it deviate from the sequence of successive refinements, measures, and times.
This reflection is indeed proclaimed for those beings who are of slow action, lacking digestive fire, unhealthy, delicate, and accustomed to comfort.
For those who are strong, those whose food is coarse, those men whose digestive fire is blazing,
and those who are constant in their ritual duties— for them, [the recitation] is not strictly required.
Thus ends the section on all types of post-prandial drinks (anupāna).
Now, my child, listen in detail to the entire procedure for food (āhāra-vidhi).
The kitchen should be constructed so as to be free from bones, unconfused [in its layout], and pure.

In that regard, the physician should cause food that is endowed with excellence, well-prepared, and fit for consumption to be presented in a clean place and properly protected by trustworthy attendants.
One should offer food that has been rendered free of poison by being touched with anti-venomous medicines, sprinkled with water from fans,
and neutralized by efficacious mantras.
Henceforth, I shall describe in its entirety the preparation of food:
ghee should be served in a vessel of black iron, while gruel should be served in a silver one.
One should indeed offer fruits and all kinds of edible foods upon the leaves;
those that are dried or smeared with ghee should be placed upon golden vessels.
One should offer liquids and juices upon silver vessels;
one should cause all curds and *khaḍa* preparations to be placed upon stone vessels.
One should offer very cold or well-boiled milk in a vessel made of copper;
one should cause water, syrups, and wine to be given in earthen vessels.
One should serve the *rāga-ṣāḍava* and *saṭṭaka* dishes in cool, beautiful vessels made of glass or crystal, or in vessels variegated with lapis lazuli.
In front, in a clean, very spacious, and beautiful vessel,
the cook should serve rice with soup and well-prepared condiments.
One should place fruits, all kinds of edible foods, and whatever is dried up on the right side for the one who is eating.
One should cause to be served on the left side curd-liquors, juices, water, syrups, milk, buttermilk, soups, and drinks.
A wise person should place all varieties of molasses preparations— rāgas, ṣāḍavas, and saṭṭakas— in front, and also in the middle of the two [other groups].
Having understood this regarding the preparation of food,
the wise man [should serve] the eater in a secluded, delightful, auspicious, and pure place, free from the bustle of others.
Then, on a level ground strewn with fragrant flowers, one should feed [the guests] with excellent,
well-prepared food that is wholesome, desirable, and possesses the desired tastes and other qualities.
Food that is pleasing, pure, not too hot, and freshly prepared is beneficial.
One should eat what is sweet first, followed by sour and salty flavors in the middle.
Afterwards, the physician should administer the remaining tastes in the meals;
at the beginning, the wise man should eat fruits such as pomegranate and others.
After that, one should eat thin gruels, then soft foods, and after that various kinds of solid foods; some say that one should first eat the thick food and then the others in reverse order.
At the beginning, at the end, and in the middle of a meal, the āmalaka fruit is praised for men; it is harmless and removes all defects.
The physician should administer lotus stalks, lotus fibers, lotus roots, tubers, sugarcane, and the like before a meal, but never after one has eaten.
Seated comfortably and upright, with the body balanced and not intent on food,
one should at the proper time consume that which is wholesome, light, unctuous, quickly digested, warm, and predominantly liquid.
One who has mastered the traditional scriptures, being hungry, should eat food in moderation;
food eaten at the proper time brings satisfaction, and wholesome food does not cause distress.
Light food digests quickly; unctuous and hot food bestows strength and stimulates the digestive fire.
Food that is eaten rapidly, balanced, free from defects, and predominantly liquid, undergoes digestion evenly and swiftly.
One digests food comfortably when taken in moderation, and it maintains the equilibrium of the bodily constituents;
this is prescribed for those seasons in which the nights are known to be exceedingly long.
On those days, however, when the days are very long, one should eat only in the morning, taking food that is rich in substances antagonistic to those [faults].
Among those, that which is prescribed for that specific time is praised in the afternoon;
this applies also to those nights and days which are remembered as being equal in duration.
Having made day and night equal, one should take food at those [meals]; nor should one eat before the time has arrived, after the time has passed, or in quantities that are deficient or excessive.
For a man who eats at an improper time while his body is still heavy,
he contracts various diseases or meets with death.
When one eats at the wrong time, the fire of digestion is impaired by the wind;
consequently, what has been eaten is digested with great difficulty, and one has no desire for a second meal.
It produces a sense of dissatisfaction even with what is meager, causes a loss of strength, and excessively engenders laziness, arrogance, hypocrisy, and despondency.
Therefore, one should consume food that is well-prepared by proper means, free from these defects,
and endowed with the qualities as previously described.
Having analyzed the defects, the time, and other factors during both periods,
one should discard what is impure, corrupted, or cast off, like stones, grass, or clods of earth.
One should avoid food that is disliked, stale, tasteless, or putrid;
as well as food that has been prepared long ago, kept for a long time, or made cold and then reheated.
That which is unrefined and scorched does not appear sweet;
whatever is sweeter, one should provide that in increasing degrees.
One should rinse the mouth with water repeatedly while eating;
when the tongue is thus purified, food will taste as fresh and delicious to him as it did before.
His tongue, having been thoroughly satiated by that first delicious [taste], would not find other things so sweet; therefore, it must be rinsed in between.
Wholesome food generates cheerfulness, strength, nourishment, enthusiasm, joy, and happiness; unwholesome food produces the opposite.
Even after eating, one should desire more of that delicious food;
having eaten, one should drink water according to reason, and while eating, one should drink in between.
One should slowly remove food stuck between the teeth with a tooth-cleansing stick;
for if it is not extracted, it will cause an unpleasant odor in the mouth.

When food is digested, Vāyu increases; when it is improperly digested (vidagdha), Pitta indeed increases; and immediately after eating, Kapha also increases. Therefore, Kapha is said to be provoked by eating.
One should clear away [the odor] with incense, or with pleasant astringent, pungent, and bitter substances,
such as betel nut, *kaṅkola*, camphor, clove, and jasmine flowers.
The wise man [should cleanse his mouth] with fruits that are pungent or astringent, which produce clarity in the mouth,
or with fragrant betel leaves.
Having eaten, one should sit like a king until the fatigue from the food has passed;
then, having walked a hundred paces, one should lie down on the left side.
One should enjoy sounds, forms, tastes, smells, and touches that are pleasing to the mind;
by doing so, food remains properly digested.
One should vomit up sounds, forms, tastes, touches, and even odors that are loathsome,
as well as impure food that has been eaten and excessive laughter.
He should desire neither a bed nor a seat, nor even excessive softness;
neither fire nor sun, nor swimming, nor a carriage, nor even a mount.
One should never be addicted to the consumption of a single taste; one should not habitually consume food that consists mostly of vegetables or inferior grains, nor that which is sour.
One should never consume flavors either individually or all at once;
moreover, one should not take a second meal until the digestive fire has been cleared by the previous one.
One who eats while the previously consumed food is still undigested destroys the digestive fire;
therefore, one should avoid food that is heavy by its quantity as well as by its substance.
One should not eat flour-based foods at all, or if hungry, only in small measure;
one should drink twice as much water so that food is properly and easily digested.
Among drinks, linctuses, and other edibles, each subsequent category should be known as heavier than the preceding.
For heavy foods, half-satiation is desired; for light foods, full satiation is intended.
Furthermore, food that is predominantly liquid or entirely liquid is not considered heavy by measure.
Even food rich in liquids becomes properly digested if it is dry;
however, food that is excessively dry does not undergo digestion well.
The food becomes compacted and undissolved, leading to a burning sensation,
in one whose bile resides in the food-carrying channel or in the digestive fire.
Any other food that causes a burning sensation during digestion will likewise cause a burning sensation for him;
moreover, dry, incompatible, or constipating food brings about a disorder of the digestive fire.

Some authorities maintain that indigestion (ajīrṇa) consists of three types—undigested (āma), improperly digested (vidagdha), and obstructed (viṣṭabdha)—caused respectively by phlegm (kapha), bile (pitta), and wind (anila); they also recognize a fourth type arising from the persistence of undigested chyle (rasaśeṣa).
Due to excessive drinking of water, irregular eating, suppression of natural urges, and the reversal of sleep patterns,
even food that is wholesome and light, when consumed at the proper time, does not undergo digestion in a person.
Food consumed by one who is afflicted by envy, fear, or anger; who is greedy; who is oppressed by disease or dejection; or who is possessed by hatred, does not undergo proper digestion.
Food that has reached the state of *āmā* (undigested) becomes sweet; that which has reached the state of *vidagdha* (partially digested) becomes sour.
That which is somewhat cooked (*vipakva*) yet causes intense piercing pain and colic is called *viṣṭabdha*; it is characterized by flatulence and the obstruction of opposing bodily winds (*vāta*).
When there is purity of eructation yet no desire for food arises and there is heaviness in the heart,
this is called the fourth type of indigestion (ajīrṇa), characterized by regurgitation due to the presence of residual rasa.
Fainting, delirium, vomiting, excessive salivation, lassitude, and vertigo—
these complications arise from indigestion, as does even death itself.
In that regard, fasting (laṅghana) should be performed for undigested food; emesis (vamana) is beneficial for partially digested food;
sudation (svedana) is wholesome for obstructed food; and one should lie down to rest when only the essence of the food remains.
Therefore, one should quickly induce vomiting with warm salt water;
and fasting should be observed until the patient returns to his natural state.
Therefore, one should treat this patient with jumping exercises once the body has become light,
until he returns to his natural state in terms of both the humors and the vital strength.

Food that is joined with what is wholesome and unwholesome is known as "equal eating" (samaśana). Eating too much, too little, or at the wrong time should be understood as "unequal eating" (viṣamāśana).
That which is eaten while the previous meal is undigested is called *adhyashana* (overeating);
this triad quickly destroys [the digestive fire] or produces many diseases.
For food that has become indigestible in a person quickly reaches full digestion through cold water;
for it subdues the pitta by its coolness and, due to its moist nature, leads it downward.
But for one whose food, as soon as it is eaten, causes a burning sensation, and for whom the heart, stomach, and throat burn,
he shall obtain relief by licking grapes combined with *abhayā* and honey, or simply by licking *abhayā*.
If a person who is unctuous and strong should have a doubt regarding indigestion at the time of eating,
he who seeks his own welfare, being free from apprehension, should consume a beneficial food in the morning after first chewing a wholesome dose of *abhayā* with ginger.

When even a very small amount of food, obstructed by the humors (*doṣa*), remains latent and does not cover the path of the digestive fire, hunger arises even though there is indigestion; that hunger destroys one of dull intellect like poison.
Henceforth, I shall explain in detail the functions of the qualities;
for the qualities, which reside in various substances, are inferred by their actions.
The cold [substance] is refreshing, astringent, and overcomes fainting, thirst, perspiration, and burning sensations; the hot [substance] is the opposite of that and is especially digestive.
That which is unctuous, soft, and thoroughly oily produces strength and complexion;
the dry is the opposite of that, being especially astringent and rough.
Picchila (slimy) is strengthening, healing, increases phlegm, and is heavy;
viśada (clear) is the opposite of this, and it dries, absorbs, and heals.
The sharp [taste] causes burning and digestion, promotes secretion, and is mild; otherwise, it is the opposite.
The heavy [taste] produces chronic conditions and coatings, provides strength, and acts as a nourishing and bulk-promoting agent.
The *laghu* (light) type is the opposite of that; likewise, there are the *lekhana* (scraping) and *ropaṇa* (healing) types.
These ten and others are described according to their functions, through the specific actions of each.
I shall now declare ten other qualities, beginning with fluidity; learn them from me.
Fluidity (drava) is moistening; density (sāndra) is thick and acts as a binder.
Smoothness (ślakṣṇa) should be known as being like sliminess (picchila), while roughness (karkaśa) is like clarity (viśada). 1.46.519ef.
A pleasant odor is associated with happiness; it is subtle, fragrant, appetizing, and mild.
An unpleasant odor is the opposite of this; it causes nausea and loss of appetite.
The *sara* taste is said to be *anulomana* (downward-moving), while the *manda* taste is remembered as promoting travel (*yātrākara*).
The *vyavāyin* taste, having pervaded the entire body, conduces to digestion (*pāka*).
Expanding and thus blossoming, it releases the bonds of the elements;
acting swiftly, it likewise flows rapidly through the water like oil.
The subtle [wind], due to its subtlety, is known as that which follows the subtle channels;
thus, the twenty qualities have been duly proclaimed.
Henceforth, I shall fully explain the determination of the course of food:
for in the body composed of the five elements, food itself consists of the five elements;
once properly digested, it increases its own respective qualities in five ways.
Undigested food increases phlegm, while that which is over-digested increases bile;
however, food that is properly digested and devoid of residue promotes nourishment.

Feces, urine, and the impurities of food are the waste products; the essence previously described is the *rasa*. Distributed by the *vyāna* breath, it nourishes all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*).
Phlegm, bile, excrement in the orifices, sweat, nails and hair,
eye-secretion, feces, and oiliness on the skin are, respectively, the impurities of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
When the heart has awakened during the day, as it does for one who is awake like a lotus,
food is beneficial even at night, provided the bodily constituents have not become moistened by undigested matter.
Especially for one who is fast asleep at night with the heart closed [in sleep],
daytime [exposure] is not beneficial when there is indigestion, due to the moist and relaxed state of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Whoever diligently recites this procedure, which is approved by the Great Sage and the preeminent royal seer,
that best of scholars is indeed worthy to prescribe medicine for kings and for great-souled beings.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, composed by the great sage Suśruta, the disciple of the Blessed Lord Śrī Dhanvantari; and with this,
the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā is completed.
The First Chapter of the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna).
Now, therefore, we shall expound the etiology of wind-diseases (vātavyādhi).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Having clasped the feet of Dhanvantari— the best among the upholders of dharma and born from the nectar— Suśruta questioned him.
O best among speakers, tell me of the wind in its natural state and when it is deranged by provocative factors— its locations, its functions, and the diseases it causes.
To him that best of physicians spoke those words:
"This is the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, who is designated as Vāyu."
Because of his sovereignty, because he is eternal, and likewise because he is all-pervading,
he is the self of all and is saluted by all the worlds.
This is the cause of the maintenance, origination, and destruction of all beings;
it is unmanifest, yet its effects are manifest; it is dry, cold, light, and rough.
Moving horizontally, doubling in strength, and abounding in dust,
he is of inconceivable power, the leader of all defects, and the sovereign of the multitude of diseases.
It acts swiftly and moves repeatedly, residing in the receptacle of digested food and the anus;
learn from me the symptoms of it as it roams within the body.

When undisturbed, the vital air (vāyu) maintains the equilibrium of the humors (doṣas), the bodily constituents (dhātus), and the digestive fire (agni); it ensures the proper engagement with sense objects and facilitates the smooth performance of all physiological functions.

When undisturbed, Vāyu brings about the proper functioning of the sense organs and their objects, the absence of disorder in the humors (doṣas), the elements (dhātus), and the digestive fire (agni), as well as the smooth performance of all bodily functions. Just as fire is divided fivefold according to its names, locations, actions, and constituent forms;
For that single wind remains divided by means of names, locations, and functions.
Prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna, and apāna—
these five vital airs, abiding in their respective locations, sustain the embodied being.
That wind which moves through the mouth is called prāṇa;
it sustains the body, causes food to enter within, and also supports the vital breaths.
The corrupted [wind] generally produces diseases such as hiccup, dyspnea, and others.
That which moves upward is called udāna, the foremost of the vital airs.
By that [wind], the specific qualities of speech, song, and so forth are set in motion;
furthermore, it especially produces diseases located above the clavicle.
The Samāna [vāyu], which moves through the stomach and the intestines and is conjoined with the digestive fire,
digests the food and indeed differentiates its various constituent parts.

Moving throughout the entire body and intent on circulating the nutrient fluid (rasa), the Vyāna wind produces diseases such as abdominal tumors (gulma), loss of digestive fire (agnisāda), and diarrhea (atīsāra).
When provoked, it causes sweating and the discharge of blood, performs five types of bodily movements, and generally produces diseases that pervade the entire body.
The apāna wind, whose abode is the receptacle of digested food, draws downward at the proper time the feces,
urine, semen, embryo, and menses.
When provoked, it causes terrible diseases localized in the bladder and rectum;
whereas disorders of the semen and urinary disorders (prameha) arise from the provocation of the Vyāna and Apāna breaths.
When provoked simultaneously, they would undoubtedly shatter the body.
Hereafter, I shall explain [the symptoms] as they reside in various different locations.
Indeed, when the wind (vāyu) is excessively provoked, it produces various disorders;
when the wind is enraged in the stomach (āmāśaya), it causes diseases such as vomiting and others.
Located in the colon (pakvāśaya), it causes delusion, fainting, thirst, a gripping sensation in the heart,
pain in the sides, rumbling in the intestines, and colic in the navel.
When provoked, the wind (vāyu) may cause difficulty in passing urine and feces, abdominal distension, pain in the three regions [of the body],
and the impairment of the sense organs, such as the ears.
Residing in the skin, [the Vāyu] causes discoloration, throbbing, roughness, numbness,
a tingling sensation, pricking pain, tearing of the skin, and cracking.
Located in the blood, it causes ulcers; located in the flesh, it causes painful nodules (granthi);
likewise, located in the fat, it produces painless nodules with little discomfort.
When it has reached the vessels, it causes pain, contraction, and distension of the vessels;
when it has reached the tendons, it causes stiffness, tremors, pain, and convulsions.
When it has entered the joints, it destroys the joints and causes pain and swelling;
when it resides there, it produces the wasting of the bones, their splitting, and intense pain.
Likewise, when the wind is located in the marrow, pain never subsides;
whether there is a lack of discharge or an abnormal discharge, this occurs when the wind is associated with semen.
The wind of men, being omnipresent, moves sequentially through the elements of the hands, feet, and head,
or pervades the entire body.
The "all-pervading" (sarvaga) type causes stiffness, displacement, numbness, swelling, and pain;
when combined with the aforementioned locations, it produces mixed pains.
When the wind has reached the bodily constituents, it produces these aforementioned diseases;
when the wind is associated with bile, there may be burning sensations, feverish heat, and fainting.
When that very [vāta] is occluded by kapha, there is coldness, swelling, and heaviness;
there is a pricking pain as if from needles, aversion to touch, and numbness.
The remaining disorders of pitta occur when it is combined with vāta and blood;
when pitta envelops the prāṇa breath, vomiting and a burning sensation arise.
When Udāna is enveloped by Kapha, there is weakness, exhaustion, drowsiness, and discoloration;
when it is combined with Pitta, there is fainting, burning sensations, vertigo, and fatigue.
In the case of obstruction by kapha, there is absence of perspiration and exhilaration, weak digestion, and coldness with stiffness;
when combined with pitta in the samāna vāyu, there is perspiration, burning sensations, heat, and fainting.
When the apāna vāyu is enveloped by kapha, there is an increase in phlegm (kapha) in the feces and urine, along with horripilation;
when it is associated with pitta, there is burning, heat, and menorrhagia.
When that very same vyāna is enveloped by kapha, there is heaviness in the lower body;
when it is enveloped by pitta, there is a burning sensation, tossing of the limbs, and exhaustion.
When Vyāna is enveloped by Kapha, the symptoms are heaviness of all the limbs, stiffness of the bones and joints, as well as a general paralysis of movement.
Generally, this occurs in those who are delicate, who engage in improper diet and lifestyle,
and who are excessively afflicted by disease, travel, sexual indulgence, intoxicants, and physical exertion.

Vātarakta becomes aggravated due to the reversal of seasonal suitability, the improper administration of oleation and other therapies, lack of sexual intercourse, or in those who are corpulent. Furthermore,
the Vāyu becomes provoked in one who travels by means of elephants, horses, camels, or other such vehicles, when their respective causes are indulged in.
By consuming foods that are sharp, hot, sour, alkaline, leafy vegetables, and the like, and by frequently indulging in heat and similar afflictions.
The blood quickly becomes vitiated, and having moved swiftly, it obstructs the path of the wind.
Due to that obstruction of its path, the wind becomes excessively provoked and rapidly vitiates the blood to an extreme degree.
That [wind], when combined with vitiated blood due to its predominance, is called vātarakta;
likewise, pitta combined with vitiated blood, and kapha, being itself vitiated, combined with vitiated blood.

In Vatarakta (gout), the feet are afflicted by touch, characterized by pricking pain, piercing sensations, dryness, and numbness; in Pitta-Asṛkja (blood-bile type), they become intensely burning, extremely hot, red, swollen, and soft.
When the blood is vitiated by phlegm (śleṣman), the feet are itchy, white, cold, swollen, thickened, and stiff;
when the blood is vitiated by all [three] doshas, the doshas manifest their respective symptoms on the feet.

In the premonitory stage (prāgrūpa), the [limbs] are flaccid, perspiring, and cold, or the opposite; they are accompanied by discoloration, pricking pain, numbness of the skin, heaviness, and swelling.
Taking its stand at the base of the feet, and sometimes even on the hands or the throat,
it creeps up that body like angry poison.
That which is split open at the knees, that which is cracked and oozing, and that which is afflicted by calamities such as the wasting away of vital breath and flesh; |||
That hemorrhage would be incurable, yet manageable if it has arisen for a year;
however, when the provoked wind (māruta) enters all the vessels (dhamanīs), [it becomes incurable].
It repeatedly and swiftly agitates the body;
because it moves about and repeatedly causes that agitation, it is known as the "Agitator" (Ākṣepaka).
If the wind, accompanied by phlegm, remains in those very same locations and causes [the phlegm] to fall repeatedly at intervals, that is known as apatānaka.
That [wind], like a staff, causes stiffness; it is the difficult-to-cure Daṇḍāpatānaka.
Then, lockjaw (Hanugraha) occurs excessively and is attended with great difficulty.
He who bends his body like a bow is known as Dhanuḥstambha;
he is characterized by [contractions] located in the fingers, the ankles, the abdomen, the hollows of the armpits, the chest, and the throat.
When the forceful wind (vāyu) violently agitates the network of tendons,
the patient has fixed eyes, a stiff jaw, and broken sides, and vomits phlegm (kapha).
When a person bends inward like a bow,
then the powerful wind produces an internal extension within him.
When it is located in the external network of tendons and causes external extension,
the wise declare it incurable, as it results in the breaking of the chest, hips, and thighs.
Vāyu combined with kapha and pitta, as well as vāyu alone, may cause ākṣepaka; the fourth type is born from injury (abhighātaja).
Apataṅka does not succeed [in being cured] when it is caused by miscarriage, excessive hemorrhaging,
or physical trauma.
When the vital air (mātariśvā), excessively provoked, enters the vessels that course downward, obliquely, or upward through the body;
Then, loosening the ligaments of one side of the body, it destroys that side;
indeed, the best of physicians call this Pakṣāghāta (hemiplegia).
He whose entire half-body becomes unresponsive and unconscious either falls from there or, oppressed by the vital winds, gives up his life-breaths.
A hemiplegia caused by pure vāta is known to be most difficult to cure;
that associated with another [dosha] is curable, while that caused by wasting (kṣaya) is incurable.
When the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated, it departs from its place and ascends; it afflicts the heart, the head, and the temples, and it causes the limbs to convulse and bend.
With eyes closed, motionless, or even with eyes fixed, he groans;
or else, breathless or breathing with great difficulty, his consciousness is lost.
When the heart is unobstructed, one becomes healthy; but when it is obstructed, one becomes deluded. This condition, caused by vāta combined with kapha, should be known as apatantraka.
Covered by phlegm, that very [wind], through daytime sleep, sitting in one place, and looking at open roads, produces stiffness of the neck.

The Vāyu (wind), having afflicted the joints of the head, nose, lips, chin, forehead, and eyes, produces Ardita (facial paralysis) by distorting the face.
The half of the face becomes distorted, the neck is twisted,
the head shakes, there is a blockage of speech, and there is a deformity of the eyes and other organs.
In that [side], there is pain in the neck, chin, and teeth;
for one in whom horripilation, trembling, and turbid vision appear first.
When the wind moves upward, causing numbness in the skin, pricking pain, and stiffness of the neck and jaw,
those expert in diseases call that affliction *ardita*.
For one who is emaciated, whose eyes do not blink, who speaks incessantly and with attachment,
and for one who is afflicted and trembling, even a treatment lasting three years will certainly not succeed.
When the tendons (kaṇḍarā) of the heels and the toes are afflicted by Vāyu, they seize the movement of the thighs; this condition is indeed known as Gṛdhrasī.
The tendon (kaṇḍarā) that runs from the back of the arms to the fingers of the hands is known as Viśvācī; it causes the loss of function in both arms.
A swelling arising from vāta and blood, located in the middle of the knee and accompanied by great pain, is called Śiraḥ;
it is preceded by Kroṣṭuka and is thick like the head of a jackal.
When the Vāyu situated in the waist seizes the tendons (kaṇḍarā) of the thigh,
the person becomes a Svañja;
he becomes a Paṅgu (lame) due to the destruction of both thighs.
One who trembles while walking and moves as if stumbling should be known as a *kalāyasvañja*, whose joints and ligaments have become loose.
When the foot is placed unevenly, the wind (vāyu) causes pain;
this condition, localized in the *khaḍulaka* [ankle], is to be known as *vātakaṇṭaka*.
Vāyu, combined with pitta and blood, causes a burning sensation in the feet;
one should designate that condition as pādadāha (burning of the feet), especially when it occurs from walking.
When one's feet experience a tingling sensation as if they were falling asleep,
that should be recognized as *pādaharṣa* (numbness of the feet), arising from the provocation of *kapha* and *vāta*.
The wind situated in the region of the shoulder,
having dried up the ligaments and contracted the vessels located there, produces avabāhuka (wrist-drop).
When the wind,
either pure or mixed with phlegm, obstructs the channel that carries sound, deafness is produced thereby.
When the wind, as if piercing the jaw, temples, head, and neck,
causes pain in the ears, that is called karṇaśūla (earache).
Vata, accompanied by kapha, obstructing the sound-carrying vessels (dhamanīs),
renders men incapacitated, mute, nasal-voiced, or stammering.
That sensation which moves downward, arising from the receptacles of feces and urine,
and as if piercing the anus and the generative organ, is designated as *tūnī*.
That same [disease], arising in the rectum and genitals and spreading in the reverse direction, reaches the colon through its impulses; it is known as Pratitūnī.
One should recognize as *ādhmāna*— a terrible condition born from the obstruction of wind— an abdomen that is distended, excessively painful, and greatly swollen with a sense of fullness.
One should recognize that very condition— arising from the stomach (āmāśaya), with the sides and heart released,
and characterized by flatulence— as *pratyādhmāna*, caused by wind (vāyu) agitated by phlegm (kapha).
One should recognize Vātāṣṭhīlā as a hard, elongated, and elevated knot, like a stone,
which obstructs the external passage.
One should call that very same condition *pratyaṣṭhīlā* when it arises obliquely within the abdomen, accompanied by pain and obstructing flatus, feces, and urine.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Vata Diseases," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of hemorrhoids (arśas).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
There are six types of hemorrhoids: those caused by wind, bile, phlegm, blood, and their combination, as well as those that are congenital.

In that regard, in those who lack self-control, the *doṣas*—provoked by the aforementioned aggravating factors, as well as specific conditions such as eating incompatible foods, overeating, excessive sexual indulgence, sitting on hard seats, riding on uneven vehicles, and the suppression of natural urges—become aggravated either individually, in pairs, or collectively, or together with the blood. As previously described, they spread through the principal vessels (*dhamanīs*), descend, reach the anus, and having corrupted the folds of the rectum (*gudavalīs*), they produce fleshy growths (*māṃsaprarohas*). This occurs especially in those with weak digestion.
Furthermore, these growths (*kandās*) attain further development through contact with grass, wood, stones, clods of earth, clothing, and the like, or through contact with cold water.
These are called hemorrhoids.
In that regard, they say the anus is attached to the large intestine and measures four and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas).

Within it, there are three folds (valayas) arising at intervals of one and a quarter finger-breadths, namely the *pravāhaṇī*, the *visarjanī*, and the *saṃvaraṇī*; each is four finger-breadths in length, and all are one finger-breadth in height across their width.
They are also described as resembling the spiral of a conch shell, situated one above the other,
and in color, they are said to resemble the palate of an elephant.
The lip of the anus is declared to be one and a half barley-corns in length from the tips of the hairs.
The first [vein], however, is located at a distance of one finger-breadth from the anus and the lips.

The premonitory symptoms of those [diseases] that are yet to arise are: lack of faith in food, difficult digestion, acid eructation, burning sensation, flatulence, thirst, weakness in the thighs, abdominal distension, emaciation, excessive belching, swelling of the eyes, rumbling in the intestines, cutting pain in the anus, apprehension of anemia, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī-doṣa), and consumption (śoṣa), as well as cough, dyspnea, loss of strength, fainting, drowsiness, sleepiness, and weakness of the sense organs.
Once they have been born, these very characteristics become even more clearly manifest.

In that condition, due to the action of Vāta, the stools become parched, reddish-brown, discolored, and irregular in their center; they take on the shapes of Kadamba flowers, Tuṇḍikerī fruits, tubular stalks, buds, or needle-points. Afflicted by these, the patient voids feces accompanied by pain in a compact mass. Furthermore, he experiences pain in the regions of the waist, back, flanks, penis, anus, and the lower abdomen.
Moreover, abdominal tumors (gulma), prostate enlargement (aṣṭhīlā), splenic disorders (plīhodara), and ascites (udara) may arise in him as a direct consequence of this same cause.
The person becomes one whose skin, nails, eyes, teeth, face, urine, and excrement are black.

The [stools] caused by pitta have blue tips, are thin, spreading, yellowish in appearance, resembling the color of liver, shaped like a parrot’s tongue, having a central ridge like a barley grain, similar to the mouth of a leech, and are moist. Afflicted by these, a person suffers from diarrhea accompanied by burning sensations and blood.
Fever, burning heat, thirst, and fainting also become its complications.
Furthermore, the person's skin, nails, eyes, teeth, face, urine, and feces become yellow.
Those born of *kapha* (ślaiṣmika) are white, deep-rooted, firm, round, glossy, and pale; they have the shape of a *karīra* fruit, a jackfruit stone, or a cow’s udder.

They do not burst nor do they discharge pus, and they are characterized by excessive itching. One afflicted by them suffers from diarrhea that is associated with *kapha*, copious in quantity, and resembling the wash-water of meat. Furthermore, swelling, cold fever, anorexia, indigestion, and heaviness of the head arise in him as direct consequences of those [tumors].
The person becomes one with white skin, limbs, nails, eyes, teeth, face, urine, and excrement.
Those born from blood resemble the sprouts of the *nyagrodha* tree, coral, or the fruit of the *kākaṇantikā*; they possess the characteristics of bile (*pitta*).
When they are compressed by deeply impacted feces, they suddenly discharge a large amount of excessively vitiated blood.
And when that [blood] flows excessively, complications arising from the over-abundance of blood occur.
Those born from the combination of the three humors possess the characteristics of all the humors.
The innate [impurities] have their characteristics in corrupted blood and semen.
Their purification must be accomplished through the removal of those very defects.

In particular, these are difficult to see, harsh, dusty, dreadful, and directed inward; one afflicted by them becomes emaciated, eats little, has limbs covered with visible veins, has few offspring, diminished semen, a weak voice, is irritable, has low digestive fire and vitality, and is extremely lethargic.

Likewise, one suffers from diseases of the nose, head, eyes, nostrils, and ears; and is constantly afflicted by rumbling in the stomach, flatulence, a coating in the heart, loss of appetite, and so forth.
And there is a verse on this point:
"The best of physicians should treat those [hemorrhoids] situated in the external, middle, and internal folds;
however, for those arising from the innermost fold, he should perform treatment only after declaring them incurable."
The aggravated *doṣas*, having reached the penis (*meḍhra*), vitiate the flesh and blood and produce itching.
From that scratching, an ulceration arises.
In that ulceration, fleshy excrescences (*praroha*) born of vitiated flesh arise, which are bristly and discharge slimy blood from the inside or from the surface.

These [worms], however, destroy the penis and impair virility; having entered the vagina, they produce tender, foul-smelling, slimy, blood-discharging, umbrella-shaped growths called *karīra*. They also damage the vagina and the menstrual flow (*ārtava*). Having reached the umbilical region, they produce tender, foul-smelling, slimy growths resembling the mouths of earthworms. When these have moved upward, they cause hemorrhoids (*arśas*) in the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth. Among those located in the ears, there occurs deafness, pain, and putridity of the ear canal.
In those [diseases] arising in the eyes, there is obstruction of the eyelids, pain, discharge, and loss of vision.

In those arising in the nose, there is excessive catarrh, frequent sneezing, difficulty in breathing, foul-smelling nasal discharge, nasal speech, and headache. In those arising in the mouth, there occurs hoarseness of voice due to any one of the throat, lips, or palate being affected by them, as well as loss of the sense of taste and various diseases of the mouth.
The *vyāna* wind, when aggravated, takes hold of the *śleṣman* (phlegm) and produces stable polyp-like growths on the exterior;
these are called *carma-kīla* or hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi*).
And there are verses on this point:
In those "stake-like" swellings (kīla), a pricking pain arises due to Vāta;
however, one should indicate that they have the same color as the skin and a nodular (granthi) consistency due to Kapha.
Dryness, blackness, smoothness, as well as an elevated roughness— these are the characteristics of a carmakīla (skin-tag) born from pitta and blood.
The general characteristics of hemorrhoids have been described in detail;
however, the best of physicians should treat all of them according to what was previously specified.
When the symptoms of two doṣas are observed together in cases of hemorrhoids (arśas), one should recognize that as a combination (saṃsarga); and that combination is of six types.
One should designate those diseases caused by the three doṣas as palliable when their symptoms are mild;
likewise, those born from two doṣas (dvandvaja) and those which have taken refuge in the second layer of skin (vali).

They say those [diseases] arising from the three humors (sannipāta) and those that are congenital (sahaja), even if they have persisted for more than a year, are difficult to cure; however, one should avoid treating them altogether.
Those whose limbs are all afflicted by diseases such as piles have their downward wind obstructed;
thus the apāna wind is turned back.
Then, having united with the vyāna breath, it consumes the light of embodied beings.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Hemorrhoids," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||2||
The Third Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of urinary calculi (aśmarī).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
There are four types of urinary calculi; they are based on phlegm, namely: those caused by phlegm, by wind, and by bile.
And if by Śukra.

In that case, the aggravated *śleṣman* (phlegm) of one who does not habitually undergo purification and who indulges in unwholesome things, having entered the bladder mixed with urine, produces a calculus (*aśmarī*).

Their premonitory symptoms are fever, pain in the bladder, anorexia, dysuria, and pain in the bladder, head, scrotum, and penis; furthermore, there is difficulty in urination, exhaustion, and a fishy odor to the urine.
In the premonitory stage of a stone, a person voids urine that is painful according to the specific sensation, foul-smelling, thick, and turbid, with great difficulty.

Then, once [the stones] have formed, there occurs pain in any one of the umbilicus, the bladder, the perineal raphe, or the urethra during urination; obstruction of the urinary stream, the presence of blood in the urine, spraying of the urine, and the discharge of urine that is as turbid as cow’s urine, resembling *gomedaka* gemstones, and mixed with gravel; furthermore, he experiences pain from running, leaping, swimming, riding on the back of an animal, traveling on hot roads, or walking long distances.

Among these, phlegmatic calculus (śleṣmāśmarī) occurs when one excessively consumes phlegm-provoking food, which becomes excessively accumulated and, having increased, takes hold of the opening of the bladder and obstructs the channel. Due to this obstruction of urine, the bladder feels as if it is being torn, split, or pricked; it becomes heavy and cold. Furthermore, the stone here is white, unctuous, large, resembling a hen’s egg, or the color of a Madhūka flower. One should recognize this as the phlegmatic type.
When phlegm (śleṣmā) combined with bile (pitta) reaches a state of accumulation, attains the aforementioned growth, and takes hold of the opening of the bladder, it obstructs the channel.

Due to this obstruction of urine, the bladder becomes irritated, sucked, burnt, and as if cooked; there is also a hot wind (feeling). In this case, the stone (aśmarī) is reddish, yellowish, black, resembling the stone of the Bhallātaka fruit, or honey-colored.
One should recognize this as the bilious (paittikī) type.
When phlegm, combined with wind, reaches a state of condensation and attains the aforementioned increase, it occupies the opening of the bladder and obstructs the channel.
Due to that obstruction of urine, intense pain arises;
then, being excessively tormented, the patient gnashes his teeth.
He presses upon the navel;
he rubs the penis;
he touches the anus.

He suffers from flatulence and burning sensations; his urine, feces, and flatus are expelled with difficulty during urination; and in this condition, the stone (aśmarī) becomes dark-brown, rough, uneven, hard, and covered with thorns like the flowers of the Kadamba tree.
One should know that to be the vātikī [type].

Generally, these three types of stones occur especially among children due to their fondness for daytime sleep, eating at improper times, overeating, and foods that are cold, unctuous, heavy, and sweet; because of their small bladder capacity and lack of developed musculature, these stones are easily grasped and extracted from the bladder. However, in adults, the seminal stone (śukrāśmarī) occurs as a result of semen.

Due to the obstruction of sexual intercourse or from excessive sexual indulgence, the semen becomes agitated but fails to be discharged. Because it follows an aberrant path, the *vāyu* (wind) seizes it from all sides between the penis and the scrotum and draws it inward. Having drawn it in, it dries it up;
that [dried substance] then obstructs the urinary passage, causing painful urination (*mūtrakṛcchra*), pain in the bladder, and swelling of the testicles.
As soon as it is pressed, it dissolves right at that entrance; one should know that to be *śukrāśmarī* (semen-stone).
And there are verses on this point:

gravel (śarkarā), sand (sikatā), urinary disorder (meha), that called ash (bhasman), and the deformity of stones (aśmarī-vaikṛta). Gravel should be known as being similar to the stone (aśmarī) in its characteristics and pain.
When the wind is favorable, she issues forth especially in small quantities;
being divided in form by the wind, she is called "sugar" (śarkarā).
Pain in the heart, weakness in the thighs, colic in the abdomen, and trembling;
thirst, upward-moving wind (flatus), blackish discoloration, debility, and pallor of the limbs.
Anorexia and indigestion occur when it is afflicted by gravel;
when it has entered the urinary tract, that obstructed [stone] may produce complications.
Weakness, exhaustion, emaciation, pain in the abdomen,
loss of appetite, pallor, hot wind (uṣṇavāta), thirst, cardiac distress, and vomiting [arise].
The bladder, covered with thin skin, is situated in the middle of the navel, back, waist, scrotum, anus, groins, and penis; it faces downward and has a single opening.
The bladder, the head of the bladder, the penis, the testicles,
and the anus— these are interconnected, for they are all situated within the cavity of the pelvic bones.
In appearance like a gourd, it is composed of veins and sinews;
it is the receptacle for urine, the reservoir of waste, and the supreme abode of the vital breaths.
The urinary channels located there in the receptacle of digested food constantly nourish the urine,
just as rivers fill the ocean.
Because of their subtlety, their thousands of openings are not perceived,
even though urine is led from the interior of the stomach by means of these channels.
Whether waking or sleeping, it is filled by that very outflow;
like a new vessel placed in water, it is filled from all sides up to its brim.
Just as a jar is filled with water, so too is the bladder filled with urine;
in the same way, it is filled by the entry of vāta, pitta, or even kapha.
Combined with the urine, it enters [the bladder] due to moisture and forms a stone,
just as when clear water is poured into a new jar.
In the course of time, it becomes mud, and from that arises the formation of stones;
just as the wind and the lightning-fire consume the celestial waters.
In the same way, heat accompanied by vāyu destroys the phlegm (balāsa) located in the bladder;
when the vāyu in the bladder is in its natural state, urine flows properly,
whereas various disorders indeed arise when it is contrary to its natural course.
Obstructions of urine, urinary disorders (prameha), as well as defects of semen,
and whatever urinary defects there may be, indeed occur in the bladder itself.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Urinary Calculi," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of fistula-in-ano.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

There are five types of fistula-in-ano (bhagandara), caused respectively by vāta, pitta, śleṣman, sannipāta, and exogenous factors (āgantu); they are named śataponaka, uṣṭragrīva, parisrāvin, śambūkāvarta, and unmārgin. They are called bhagandaras because they cause tearing (dāraṇa) in the regions of the vulva, anus, and bladder;
when unruptured, they are called piḍakās, but once ruptured, they are termed bhagandaras.

In that case, the wind (vāyu) of those who consume unwholesome food becomes aggravated; having receded and become stagnant, it corrupts the flesh and blood within one or two finger-breadths around the anus and produces a reddish-colored pustule.
This produces specific sensations such as piercing pain (toda) and so forth.
If left untreated, it undergoes suppuration.
Furthermore, because it is situated near the bladder, the ulcer becomes moistened and is filled with minute openings like those of a *śataponaka* (a type of leech);
these openings continuously discharge an excessive, clear, and frothy secretion.
Moreover, the ulcer is beaten, split, cut, and as if pricked by needles.
The anus also becomes fissured;
and when neglected, there occurs the discharge of flatus, urine, feces, and semen through those very same openings. This condition is called *śataponaka* (hundred-streamed fistula-in-ano).

Pitta, however, when aggravated and driven downward by Vata, remains as before and produces a thin, elevated pustule shaped like a camel's neck (*uṣṭragrīvākārā*); it causes specific pains such as sucking sensations (*coṣa*) and the like. If not treated, it undergoes suppuration, and the ulcer feels as if it were being burned by fire or alkali. It discharges a foul-smelling, hot secretion.
If neglected, it emits flatus, urine, feces, and semen; this is called *bhagaṃdara-uṣṭragrīva*.
When phlegm (śleṣman) is aggravated and driven downward by the wind (samīraṇa), it remains as before and produces a pustule that is white in appearance, stable, and itchy;
this [pustule] produces specific sensations for him, such as itching and so forth.
And if it is not treated, it undergoes suppuration.
The ulcer is hard, inflamed, and characterized by excessive itching; it constantly discharges a slimy secretion.
If neglected, it emits flatus, urine, feces, and semen; this type of fistula-in-ano is called *parisrāvin* (the discharging type).

The aggravated *vāyu*, having seized the aggravated *pitta* and *śleṣman*, moves downward and, remaining as before, produces a pustule (*piḍakā*) the size of the tip of a big toe, exhibiting all [the symptoms of] its signs.
It produces specific types of pain for him, such as piercing, burning, itching, and so forth.
And if it is not treated, it undergoes suppuration.
The ulcer discharges a secretion of various colors, and specific types of pain arise therein like whirlpools in a full river; this fistula-in-ano is called *śambūkāvarta*.

When a bone-thorn, swallowed by a foolish person greedy for meat along with food, becomes mixed with deep-seated feces and is driven downward by the downward wind (apāna), it fails to pass properly and erodes the rectum. Then, a putrefaction caused by the wound arises.
And within that wound, where there is a putrefying mass of flesh smeared with pus and blood—like ground saturated with water—worms are born.
Devouring the rectum, they tear it apart in many ways from the sides.
Through those channels created by the worms, wind, urine, feces, and semen emerge; this condition is called unmārgin bhagaṇḍara (fistula-in-ano with displaced tracts).
And there are verses on this point:
A small, painful swelling that arises and is quickly pacified in the region of the anus should be known as *piḍakā*, distinct from *bhagaṇḍara*.

When a carbuncle (piḍakā) occurs at a distance of two finger-breadths from the anus, with its roots deeply embedded and accompanied by pain and fever, it should be known as bhagaṃdarī; the opposite of this is [the other type].
Due to the discharge of feces while riding various vehicles, the anus becomes afflicted with itching, pain, burning, and swelling;
pain in the waist is also present—these are the premonitory symptoms of fistula-in-ano (bhagandara).
All types of fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) are indeed terrible and difficult to cure;
among them, those arising from the three doshas and that caused by injury (kṣataja) are incurable.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Fistula-in-Anus," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

In one who follows a wrong diet and lifestyle—specifically one who eats food that is heavy, antagonistic, unwholesome, or undigested; or who, after drinking oleaginous substances or undergoing emesis, engages in physical exercise or sexual intercourse; or who frequently eats the meat of domestic, marshy, or aquatic animals with milk; or who, having been heated by external warmth, sinks into water or suddenly suppresses an urge to vomit—the wind (vāyu), becoming aggravated, seizes the deranged bile (pitta) and phlegm (śleṣman). Having entered the transverse-moving vessels (sirās), it agitates them and scatters [the humors] everywhere toward the external pathways.

And wherever the humors (doṣas) are dispersed and emerge, there mandalas appear. Thus, when the humor has arisen in the skin and, having increased in those various places, is not counteracted, it enters the interior, corrupting the constituent elements (dhātus).

Its premonitory symptoms are roughness of the skin, sudden horripilation, itching, excessive perspiration or lack thereof, numbness of various parts of the body, spreading of wounds, and blackness of the blood.
In that regard, there are seven major types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and eleven minor types of leprosy;
thus, there are eighteen types of leprosy in total.
In that regard, the major leprosy (mahākuṣṭha) types are: aruṇa, udumbara, ṛṣyajihva, kapālaka, kākaṇaka, puṇḍarīka, and dadru-kuṣṭha.
The minor leprosy (kṣudrakuṣṭha) types are also: sthūlāruṣka, mahākuṣṭha, ekakuṣṭha, carmadala, visarpa, parisarpa, sidhma, vicarcikā, kiṭibha, pāmā, and carkarī.
All types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) are accompanied by vāta, pitta, śleṣman, and worms;
however, the specific mention of a particular doṣa is due to its predominance.
Among these, *aruṇa* is caused by wind (*vāta*);
*udumbara*, *ṛkṣajihva*, *kapālaka*, and *kākaṇaka* are caused by bile (*pitta*);
and *puṇḍarīka* and *dadru-kuṣṭha* are caused by phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Their significance consists of their increasing gravity through action, their progressive penetration into the bodily constituents (dhātus), and their incurability.
In that regard:
those caused by Vāta are reddish, thin, spreading, and associated with pricking, piercing, and numbness;
those caused by Pitta have the shape and color of a ripe Udumbara fruit and are called Audumbara.
Those resembling the tongue of a deer (or bear) are the *ṛṣyajihva* types, which are rough. Those resembling black potsherds are the *kapālakuṣṭha* types.

Those resembling the fruit of the *kākaṇantikā* plant, being exceedingly red-black, are the *kākaṇaka* types. For all four of these, the common symptoms are burning, pricking pain, inflammation, and a sensation of fuming, along with rapid onset, suppuration, bursting, and the appearance of worms.
Due to phlegm (śleṣman), the puṇḍarīka type of kuṣṭha resembles the petals of a white lotus;

the pauṇḍarīka type has the color of linseed flowers or is coppery, characterized by spreading, pustules, and the presence of ringworm-like lesions (dadru). The common features of both these types are elevation, circular shape, itching, and chronic onset.
Hereafter we shall describe the minor types of leprosy (kṣudrakuṣṭha):
in the Mahat-pūrvaka type of leprosy, there occur large, very painful, hard eruptions at the joints; the skin becomes contracted, cracked, and numb, and there is a sense of exhaustion in the limbs.
That leprosy by which the body becomes blackish-red is called Ekakuṣṭha;
that by which itching, pain, burning, and heat occur on the palms and soles is called Carmadala.
That disorder which spreads rapidly in all directions like erysipelas (visarpa), overwhelming the skin, blood, and flesh,
and causing fainting, burning, intense pricking pain, and suppuration, is known as visarpa.
When small pustules slowly spread over the body and exude fluid, they call that *parisarpa*.
One should recognize *sidhma* as being accompanied by itching, white, and without discharge; it is thin and generally occurs on the upper part of the body.
In *vicarcikā*, there is excessive itching, pain, and roughness on the limbs;
when this same condition occurs in the feet, it is called *vipādikā*, characterized by itching and accompanied by burning sensations and pain.
That which is exuding, circular, dense, and intensely itchy, and is glossy and black, they call *kiṭibha*.
*Pāmā* is characterized by small pustules that are accompanied by discharge, itching, and burning.
That very same condition, characterized by eruptions accompanied by burning sensations arising on the buttocks, hands, and feet, is designated as *kacchū* (scabies).
A pustule on the body that is attended by itching and is devoid of discharge is called *rakasā*.
Aruḥ, sasidhma, rakasā, and that which is mahat-ekakuṣṭha—these arise from kapha;
one type, parisarpa, arises from the provocation of vāyu; one should know the remaining types to be born from pitta.
Kilāsa is also merely a variety of kuṣṭha; it is of three types: caused by vāta, by pitta, and by śleṣman.

The distinction between *kuṣṭha* (leprosy) and *kilāsa* (vitiligo) is that *kilāsa* is confined to the skin alone and does not discharge [fluid]. That which is caused by *vāta* is circular, reddish, rough, and prone to flaking;
that caused by *pitta* resembles the petal of a lotus and is accompanied by a burning sensation.
Due to phlegm (śleṣman), it is white, unctuous, thick, and itchy;
among these, a circular patch that is raised at the edges, has reddish hair, and has been cauterized by fire is incurable.
In cases of *kuṣṭha* (skin diseases), however, contraction of the skin, numbness, perspiration, swelling, cracking, deformity of the limbs, and impairment of the voice result from *vāta*;
suppuration, bursting, falling off of the fingers, breaking of the ears and nose, redness of the eyes, and the growth of parasites result from *pitta*;
and itching, discoloration, swelling, discharge, and heaviness result from *śleṣman*.
Among those, the Pauṇḍarīka and Kākaṇa types that have been active from the very beginning are incurable.
And there are verses on this point:
Just as a tree that has grown, having reached a great length of time,
penetrates deep into the earth with its roots nourished by rain.
In this way, leprosy (kuṣṭha), having arisen in the skin over the course of time,
gradually pervades the bodily constituents (dhātus) of a man who fails to provide a remedy.
When the skin is afflicted by kuṣṭha, there occurs a loss of tactile sensation, perspiration, slight itching,
discoloration, and a rough texture.
Numbness of the skin, horripilation, excessive perspiration,
itching, and suppuration occur when kuṣṭha is located in the blood.
Excessive thickness, dryness of the mouth, roughness, the eruption of pustules,
pricking pain, cracking, and hardness occur when Kuṣṭha has taken hold of the muscle tissue (māṃsa).
Foul odor, exudation, pus, as well as worms,
and even the cracking of the limbs occur when the kuṣṭha is located in the fat (medas).
When [the vital essence] has taken refuge in the bones and marrow, there occurs the collapse of the nose, redness of the eyes, the appearance of worms in wounds,
and indeed the impairment of the voice.
When [the vāyu] has reached the seat of semen (śukrasthāna), the symptoms are lameness, loss of mobility, wasting of the limbs, discharge from the wounds,
and likewise those previously mentioned.
When the blood and semen of a man and woman are corrupted by the defect of leprosy (kuṣṭha),
any offspring born of them should be known as likewise afflicted with leprosy.
Kuṣṭha localized in the skin, blood, and flesh is curable for one who possesses self-control; when it reaches the fat, it becomes palliable; beyond that, it is incurable.
They say that leprosy (kuṣṭha), a disease of sin, arises from such actions as killing a Brahmin, a woman, or a virtuous person, or seizing the property of others.
If one dies from leprosy, the disease returns even upon rebirth;
it is proclaimed that leprosy is a disease characterized by painful afflictions throughout the body.
By adhering to the great practice prescribed for diet and conduct,
through the use of distinguished medicinal herbs and the cultivation of austerity,
the living being who is liberated by that means shall attain a meritorious state.
Through incidental contact with the body, through breath, through eating together,
through sharing a bed or a seat, and even through [the use of] clothing, garlands, and ointments.
Leprosy, fever, consumption, and ophthalmia,
as well as other infectious diseases, are transmitted from person to person.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Kuṣṭha," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Sixth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of urinary disorders (prameha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

One should recognize that a person who is addicted to sleeping during the day, lack of exercise, and laziness, and who consumes cold, unctuous, sweet, fatty, and liquid foods and drinks, will become afflicted with prameha.

When, for one who has thus engaged [in the disease], the undigested wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman) reach a state of unity with the fat (medas), follow the urine-carrying channels, descend, and reaching the opening of the bladder, burst it open, they then produce urinary disorders (prameha).

Their premonitory symptoms, however, are burning sensations in the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, unctuousness, sliminess, and heaviness of the limbs, sweetness and whiteness of the urine, drowsiness, lassitude, thirst, foul odor, labored breathing, the formation of impurities on the palate, throat, tongue, and teeth, matting of the hair, and excessive growth of the nails.
In that regard, all types of prameha are characterized by turbid and abundant urine.
All [these] indeed arise from all the [three] humors, together with pustules.
In that regard:

1. From *kapha*, there are ten curable types—*udakameha*, *ikṣuvālikāmeha*, *surāmeha*, *sikatāmeha*, *śanairmeha*, *lavaṇameha*, *piṣṭameha*, *sāndrameha*, *śukrameha*, and *phenameha*—because the *doṣas* and the *dūṣyas* (the tissues affected) require similar treatments. From *pitta*, six palliable types arise—*nīlameha*, *haridrāmeha*, *amlameha*, *kṣārāmeha*, *mañjiṣṭhāmeha*, and *śoṇitameha*.

Because the humors (doṣas) and the affected tissues (dūṣyas) act discordantly; and because among those caused by Vāta, the four types—ghee-meha, fat-meha, honey-meha, and elephant-meha—are the most incurable due to their extreme gravity.
Therein, *śleṣman* (phlegm) combined with *vāta*, *pitta*, and fat (*medas*) produces the *śleṣma-pramehas*;
*pitta* combined with *vāta*, *kapha*, blood (*śoṇita*), and fat produces the *pitta-pramehas*;
and *vāyu* combined with *kapha*, *pitta*, muscle-fat (*vasā*), marrow (*majjā*), and fat produces the *vāta-pramehas*.

In that regard: one who passes urine resembling water but without its sensation is a *udakamehin*; one who passes urine equal to sugarcane juice is an *ikṣuvālikāmehin*; one who passes urine equal to wine is a *surāmehin*; one who passes urine accompanied by pain and mixed with sand is a *sikatāmehin*; one who passes urine slowly, along with phlegm and in a slimy manner, is a *śanairmehin*; one who passes clear urine equal to salt is a *lavaṇamehin*; one whose body hair stands on end and who passes urine equal to flour-water is a *piṣṭamehin*; one who passes turbid and thick urine is a *sāndramehin*; one who passes urine equal to semen is a *śukramehin*; and one who passes urine drop by drop, frothy and transparent, is a *phenamehin*.

Hereafter, we shall describe those caused by pitta: one who has *nīlameha* passes urine that is frothy, clear, and blue; one who has *haridrāmeha* passes urine with a burning sensation that resembles the color of turmeric; one who has *amlameha* passes urine with the taste and smell of sour liquid; one who has *kṣārameha* passes urine resembling flowing alkaline water; one who has *mañjiṣṭhāmeha* passes urine with the appearance of mañjiṣṭhā-water; and one who has *śoṇitameha* passes urine with the appearance of blood.
