Hereafter, we shall describe those caused by Vāta: one suffering from *sarpirmeha* passes urine resembling clarified butter; one suffering from *vasāmeha* passes urine resembling muscle fat (*vasā*); one suffering from *kṣaudrameha* passes urine with the color of honey; and one suffering from *hastimeha* passes urine continuously, like an intoxicated elephant.

The complications arising from Kapha are: the crawling of flies over the body, laziness, increase of muscle mass, catarrh, flaccidity, anorexia, indigestion, excessive salivation, vomiting, sleepiness, cough, and dyspnea. Those arising from Pitta are: tearing of the testicles, a sensation of bladder rupture, pricking pain in the penis, cardiac pain, acid reflux, fever, diarrhea, anorexia, nausea, a sensation of being smoked over, burning, fainting, thirst, loss of sleep, anemia, and yellowness of the feces, urine, and eyes. Those arising from Vata are: gripping pain in the heart, restlessness, insomnia, stiffness, tremors, colic, and constipation.
Thus, these twenty types of prameha, along with their complications, have been explained.
In that condition, ten types of carbuncles arise in the pramehin whose body is permeated by fat and marrow and whose bodily constituents (dhātus) are affected by the three doshas.
They are as follows: śarāvikā and sarṣapikā.
Kacchapikā, Jālinī, and Vinatā.
One who has borne children; a type of smallpox; a skin eruption resembling a scarlet fever rash.
Vidārikā and vidradhikā.
A boil the size of a shallow bowl (śarāva), having that same appearance and with a depression in its center, is called śarāvikā;
one shaped like a white mustard seed and of that same dimension is called sārṣapī.
Kūrmasaṃsthānā, characterized by constant burning, should be known by the wise as Kacchapikā; Jālinī, however, is marked by intense burning and is covered with a network of flesh.
A large blue carbuncle is known as Vinatā;
that carbuncle which is large and covered with small ones is to be known as Putriṇī.
That which is shaped like a lentil (masūra) should be known as masūrikā;
whereas alajī is red or white, covered with eruptions, and is extremely painful.
Round and hard like the root-tuber of the vidārī plant,
and possessing the characteristics of an abscess (vidradhi), it should be known by the wise as vidradhikā.

One should avoid treating carbuncles that have arisen in the anus, heart, head, shoulders, back, or vital organs (marmans), especially when accompanied by complications or occurring in those with weak digestive fire.
Compressing the entire body and joined with fat, marrow, and muscle-fat, the Vayu moves downward; therefore, diseases born of Vayu are indeed incurable.
Where the appearance of the premonitory symptoms of prameha is observed,
and where the urine is even slightly increased in quantity, one should designate that person as a pramehin (a patient with urinary disorder).
One should designate that person as suffering from *prameha* (urinary disorder) in whom all or half of the premonitory symptoms have appeared, and who passes urine excessively.
One afflicted with carbuncles, severely oppressed by complications,
is declared to be a case of madhumeha (diabetes mellitus), and that is proclaimed as incurable.
And he desires standing from walking, sitting from standing;
from sitting he chooses lying down, and from lying down he desires sleep.

Just as, indeed, from the specific combinations of the five primary colors—produced by their respective intensification or diminution—there arises the production of many other colors such as variegated, tawny, reddish-brown, pigeon-grey, and black;

even so, through the specific combinations of humors (doṣas), tissues (dhātus), wastes (malas), and dietary factors—produced by their respective intensification or diminution—the various classifications of urinary disorders (pramehas) come into being.
And there is a verse on this point:
"Indeed, all types of prameha, if left untreated over time, turn into madhumeha; at that stage, they truly become incurable."
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Prameha," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||6||
The Seventh Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of abdominal enlargements (udara).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Dhanvantari, the most excellent among the upholders of dharma, who was a royal sage equal to Indra,
instructed his auspicious disciple Suśruta— the son of a Brahman-sage and endowed with humility.

They say that these [types of abdominal enlargement] are: those caused by individual or combined doshas, as well as plīhodara (enlarged spleen), baddhaguda (intestinal obstruction), the seventh which is āgantuka (exogenous), and the eighth which is dakodara (ascites).
In a person with extremely weak digestive fire who consumes unwholesome food, or due to the consumption of dried and putrid food,
or from the improper administration of oleation and other therapies, [the humors] increase and enter the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha).
The doshas produce terrible abdominal enlargements characterized by the appearance of a tumor;
the vitiated essence of food, like oil from the digestive tract, flows out and is driven by the force of the wind.
Slowly lifting the skin all around, it expands and creates the abdomen;
that is its premonitory sign, for in the abdomen there are indeed lines, as well as the loss of strength, complexion, and desire.
Pain in the bladder characterized by wasting, lack of digestion, and a burning sensation, along with swelling in the feet;
that which, having seized the sides, abdomen, back, and navel, increases and is covered with black veins.
That which is characterized by colic, flatulence, and a violent sound, accompanied by piercing pain and splitting sensations, is of the nature of wind (vāta).
That which is associated with burning heat, thirst, fever, and inflammation, where the veins appear yellow, is [of the nature of bile].
Pittodara is characterized by yellow eyes, feces, urine, nails, and face, with a slow increase in size;
it is cold to the touch, covered with white veins, heavy, and stable, accompanied by whiteness of the nails and face.
Kaphaja Udara is unctuous, accompanied by great swelling and lassitude, and increases slowly over time;
it occurs in women of immoral conduct who consume food and drink mixed with nails, hair, urine, feces, or menstrual blood.
To whomsoever enemies administer emetics, or who consumes tainted water or poisonous substances,
his blood is quickly provoked by the aggravated humors (doṣas), which produce the terrible abdominal disease (jaṭhara) characterized by three symptoms.
In particular, he becomes irritable and suffers from a burning sensation; being afflicted, he faints repeatedly, and becoming pale and emaciated, he withers away from thirst.
The terrible *dūṣyodara* has been described; now listen as I describe *plīhodara*.
In a person who consumes burning and obstructing foods, the blood and phlegm become excessively vitiated.
The constant enlargement of the spleen is called *plīhodara* by those who know it;
it increases specifically on the left side, and in this condition, the patient suffers from exhaustion.

When the liver on the side opposite to the spleen is vitiated, the patient suffers from mild fever, diminished digestive fire, complications characterized by symptoms of Kapha and Pitta, loss of strength, and extreme paleness;
this condition is to be known as Yakṛddālyudara.
In whose intestines waste matter, along with food that is prone to adhere, or combined with or separate from small stones,
accumulates there as impurity accompanied by the humors (doṣas), just like a mixture gradually [building up] in a pipe.
His feces are obstructed in the rectum and emerge only with great difficulty, in very small quantities;
meanwhile, his abdomen, which has increased in size between the heart and the navel, becomes foul-smelling like excrement.
One who suffers from obstructed feces (baddhaguda) should be diagnosed by inducing vomiting; thereafter, learn of the "parisrāvi" type of abdominal enlargement:
when a foreign body (śalya) consisting of food enters the intestine, it pierces that bowel, whether it has arrived there naturally or otherwise.

Therefore, a watery discharge flows from the anus, appearing like water; furthermore, it flows profusely from the rectum. Below the navel, the abdomen becomes distended, and it is excessively pricked with needle-like pains and feels as if it is burning.
This is declared to be *parisrāvyudara*; now learn from me as I describe *dakodara* (ascites):
one who, though having drunk unctuous substances, or been given an oil enema, or even vomited, purged, or treated with a non-unctuous enema [remains afflicted].
If one drinks cold water immediately, the channels that carry it become impaired;
or, when those channels are smeared with oily substances, dakodara (water-belly) arises as before.
That which is smooth, large, with a deeply sunken navel, and excessively elevated as if filled with water—
like a leather bag that becomes agitated, trembles, and even makes a sound— that is *dakodara* (ascites).
Distension, inability to walk, debility, weak digestion,
swelling, exhaustion of the limbs, obstruction of flatus and feces,
burning sensation, and thirst indeed occur in all types of abdominal enlargements.
For indeed, all bellies eventually return to the state of water through digestion; therefore, one should avoid them [at that time].
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Abdominal Enlargement," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of obstructed labor (mūḍhagarbha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

The fetus is released from its attachments due to specific factors such as sexual intercourse, riding in vehicles or on mounts, traveling on roads, stumbling, falling, injury, running, trauma, sleeping or sitting on uneven ground, suppression of natural urges, the consumption of excessively dry, pungent, or bitter foods, grief, excessive use of alkaline substances, diarrhea, emesis, purgation, swinging, indigestion, miscarriage, and so forth.

It is like a fruit released from its attachment to the stalk by various forms of impact. Once its attachments are loosened, it moves beyond the uterus and, slipping through the openings of the liver, spleen, and intestines, causes agitation within the abdominal cavity.

Due to the agitation of her womb, the apāna vāyu becomes obstructed and, having produced one or another of the following—pain in the flanks, bladder, head, or abdomen, distension, or retention of urine—it causes the expulsion of the fetus when it is still young by means of a discharge of blood. Sometimes, that very same fetus, when fully developed, having arrived improperly at the birth canal but not being expelled, and being confounded by the vitiated apāna vāyu, is called a *mūḍhagarbha* (an obstructed or malpresented fetus).
Then there are the *kīla*, *pratikhura*, *bījaka*, and *parigha*.

Among these, that which emerges with arms, head, and feet upward, obstructing the opening of the birth canal like a stake, is the *kīla*; that which has its hands, feet, and head protruded but remains attached to the body is the *pratikhura*; that which emerges with only one head and one arm is the *bījaka*; and that which stands obstructing the opening of the birth canal like a crossbar (*parigha*) is the *parigha*. Some say that thus it is of four kinds, but that is not correct. Why? Because when it is afflicted by vitiated winds and enters the birth canal in various ways, then the count is exceeded.

In that regard, some enter the vaginal opening with both thighs; some with one thigh flexed; some with the body and thighs flexed, having arrived obliquely on the buttocks; some remain obstructing the vaginal door with the chest, side, or back; some have the head turned toward the inner side of the flank and enter with one arm; some have the head flexed and enter with both arms; some have the middle part of the body flexed and enter with hands, feet, and head; and some enter the vaginal opening with one thigh and the anus with the other—thus, in brief, the eight types of presentation of the malpresented fetus (mūḍhagarbha) have been described.
Among these, the two final types of obstructed labor (mūḍhagarbha) are incurable.

Furthermore, one should avoid treating those afflicted by the remaining conditions, such as those suffering from the impairment of the senses and their objects, displacement of the birth canal, constriction, indigestion, dyspnea, cough, or vertigo.
And there are verses on this point:
By the transformation of time, just as a fruit is released from its stalk,
it inevitably falls by its own nature and not otherwise.
Thus, through the passage of time, the fetus residing in the womb, once released from its binding within the channels,
proceeds toward birth.
Just as that very fruit, when afflicted by worms or a blow from the wind,
falls even out of season, so too may there be a miscarriage of the fetus.
Up until the fourth month from that point, there is a discharge of the embryo;
thereafter, in the fifth or sixth months, there is a fall of the fetus with a stable body.
But she who, cold-limbed and shameless, causes her head to throb,
and whose blue veins stand out prominently— she destroys the fetus, and he likewise destroys her.
When the fetus has died within, there is a lack of fetal movement, the disappearance of the signs of pregnancy, a dark-yellowish pallor,
foulness of breath, and internal pain.
Afflicted by mental and external distresses of the mother,
and further tormented by diseases, the fetus perishes within the womb.
If the womb of a woman who has died from a snakebite throbs,
the physician should immediately open her at the time of birth and extract the child.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Malpresented Fetus," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||8||
The Ninth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the diagnosis of abscesses (vidradhi).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari said.
The illustrious teacher of all the immortals, the lord of the earth who abides beyond all signs,
spoke this entire definition of the piercing of the vital channels to his disciple.
The humors (doṣas), having vitiated the skin, blood, flesh, and fat, and taking refuge in the bones,
gradually produce a severe swelling that rises very high.
The wise call that which has large roots, is painful, and is either circular or elongated, a *vidradhi* (abscess); it should be known to be of six types.
The symptoms of these six types— arising from the humors individually, from all of them combined, as well as from injury and blood— will now be fully described.
A Vata-born abscess is black or reddish-brown, rough, extremely painful, characterized by various stages of onset and suppuration, and is very intense in its sensation.
A pitta-originated abscess (vidradhi) resembles a ripe udumbara fruit or is dark-brown, accompanied by fever and a burning sensation;
it arises rapidly and suppurates quickly.
Arising from Kapha, the ulcer is pale like an arrow, cold, stiff, with little pain,
slow to develop, slow to suppurate, and accompanied by itching.
Their discharges are known to be thin, yellow, and white respectively;
whereas that of the ghāṭāla type is multicolored, painful, and a thick, copious discharge.
Furthermore, a Sannipatika abscess (vidradhi) ripens irregularly when it occurs in one afflicted by various factors or wounded,
or in a person who indulges in unwholesome practices.
The heat of the wound, fanned by the wind, impels the blood along with pitta;
consequently, fever, thirst, and a burning sensation arise in that embodied being.
This is an exogenous abscess (vidradhi) characterized by the symptoms of a pitta-type abscess;
it is covered with black vesicles, is dark-brown in color, and is accompanied by intense burning, pain, and fever.
A blood abscess (raktavidradhi) is said to possess the symptoms of a bile abscess (pittavidradhi).
These abscesses have indeed been described; among them, however, that which arises from all three doshas (sarvaja) is incurable.
Those internal abscesses are described as occurring above [the navel] due to the consumption of heavy,
unwholesome, incompatible, dry, or mixed foods.
The doshas, provoked either individually or collectively by excessive sexual indulgence, physical exertion, suppression of natural urges, and burning foods, manifest in the form of a gulma.
Like an anthill, they cause an internal abscess to swell up at the anus,
the opening of the bladder, the navel, the abdomen, or likewise in the groins.
One should recognize the symptoms [of abscesses] in the kidneys, liver, spleen, heart, or pleura by means of the characteristics of external abscesses.
One should distinguish between the undigested and the digested from the chapter on the examination of the undigested and the digested;
now hear specifically the symptoms according to the particular location [of the disease].
In the rectum, there is obstruction of flatus; in the bladder, difficulty and scanty urination;
in the umbilical region, hiccups as well as flatulence; and in the abdomen, provocation of the wind (vāta).
In a suppurative abscess (vidradhi) arising in the groins, there is severe gripping pain in the waist and back;
in those of the kidneys, there is contraction of the sides; and in that of the spleen, there is obstruction of respiration.
There is intense stiffness of all the limbs and a severe, piercing pain in the heart;
there is labored breathing and thirst, with excessive parching when the disease arises from the *kloman*.
Whether it be unripe or ripe, large or otherwise,
every abscess arising from a vital spot (marman) is said to be difficult to treat.
Those [wounds] above the navel that have ripened go upward, while others go downward;
one lives if they discharge downward, but does not live if they discharge upward.
If those [vessels] other than the heart, the navel, and the bladder are pierced from the outside, a man might perhaps survive; but in the case of the others, he never survives.
In women who have given birth to stillborn children or those who have given birth with difficulty,
a terrible blood-abscess arises due to unwholesome factors, causing a burning fever.
Even in those who have delivered properly, if blood has not been discharged from the body,
it may cause a blood-born abscess (vidradhi) in the abdomen known as makkalla.
If it is not pacified after seven days, then it becomes fully suppurated;
now I shall clearly explain the specific differences between abscesses (vidradhi) and tumors (gulma).
Since both gulma and vidradhi arise from the same defects (doṣas),
why does gulma not suppurate while vidradhi undergoes suppuration?
There is no fixed location for internal swellings (gulma), whereas an abscess (vidradhi) has a specific site;
the humors themselves take the form of a swelling, while an abscess occurs in the flesh and blood.
A tumor (gulma) that moves through the hollows of the body, like a bubble upon the water,
does not undergo suppuration because it is of such a nature.
Due to the abundance of flesh and blood, an abscess undergoes suppuration;
due to the deficiency of flesh and blood, a tumor does not undergo suppuration.
A gulma remains within its own respective dosha, whereas an abscess (vidradhi) resides in the flesh and blood;
therefore, an abscess suppurates, but a gulma does not suppurate.
That which arises in the heart, the navel, or the bladder, when suppurated, as well as that born from the three doṣas, should be rejected;
then the terrible suppuration of the marrow (majjaparīpāka) arises.
When he finds no opening because his bones and flesh have been destroyed,
he is then consumed by that disease as if by a blazing fire.
By that heat of the marrow within the bones, it is shattered as if being burned;
this transformation, having become like a thorn, causes the afflicted one long-lasting suffering.
Then, when the disease gains access through his karma,
it becomes oily, white, cold, and heavy, with an abundance of fat.
When the bone is broken and pus flows out, those skilled in the scriptures know this to be an abscess (vidradhi) located within the bone,
which brings about pain from all the humors (doṣas).
Thus ends the ninth chapter, named "The Diagnosis of Abscesses," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Tenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of erysipelas, sinus ulcers, and diseases of the breast.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
When the aggravated doshas, having reached the skin, flesh, and blood, produce a swelling that spreads through all the limbs,
remains flat rather than elevated, and manifests its own specific symptoms here quickly, they call it *visarpa* because of its spreading in every direction.
The wind-natured [gaṇḍa] is blackish, soft, rough, and accompanied by symptoms of body-ache, piercing pain, pricking, and wind-fever;
however, when it is covered with uneven swellings due to extreme corruption, that very same condition is indeed declared to be avoidable.
When it is of the nature of bile (pitta), moving rapidly, characterized by fever, burning, suppuration, and an abundance of eruptions and fissures, and resembling the color of blood;
and when the flesh and vessels have been destroyed by the increase of the humors (doṣas), appearing like mud from a stream—that ulcer cannot be cured.
That which is of the nature of phlegm (kapha) spreads slowly, does not suppurate quickly, is unctuous, white, swollen, and characterized by mild pain, constriction, and itching.
That which possesses the nature of all three humors has a threefold color and pain, is deep-seated, and, once suppurated, does not heal due to the destruction of the flesh and vessels.
Upon reaching a fresh wound on a person of aggravated humors,
the pitta and blood cause a swelling that is dusky or reddish, accompanied by excessive fever, burning, and suppuration, and covered with black pustules resembling horse-gram.
Visarpas caused by vāta, kapha, and pitta are curable, as is that which arises from all three combined; however, that caused by injury (kṣata) does not attain success.
Furthermore, those types previously shown to have symptoms of both pitta and vāta, as well as all those occurring in the vital spots (marmas), are indeed difficult to cure.
He who, because a swelling is not yet ripe, neglects it when it has ripened, or he who, being of wicked conduct, neglects a wound filled with abundant pus—
having burst open his previously mentioned internal locations, that pus then enters within.
Because it moves excessively, it is called *gati*; and because it flows like a channel (*nāḍī*), it is considered a *nāḍī*.
It arises from the three *doṣas* either individually, combined, or due to a foreign body (*śalya*).
Among these, due to wind (vāta), the discharge is rough and fine-mouthed, accompanied by pain, and flows excessively mixed with foam at night;
it causes thirst, burning sensations, piercing pain, lassitude, fever, and breaking pain, and due to bile (pitta), it flows excessively yellow and hot during the day.

One should know that the *rātrisruti* (nocturnal discharge) arises from *kapha*, characterized by copious, thick, white, and slimy discharge, occurring at night, with a sense of stiffness, pain, hardness, and itching.
One should recognize the three types arising from the combination of [two] doshas by observing the symptoms described for those two doshas.

One should designate that [fever] as the "Night of Death," which arises from the provocation of wind, bile, and phlegm, and is like a terrible night that brings about destruction; in it, burning fever, labored breathing, fainting, and dryness of the mouth occur, along with the aforementioned symptoms.
Once lost, the foreign body (śalya) moves with difficulty through the aforementioned locations;
it quickly causes a flow of frothy, churned, clear blood mixed with heat, accompanied by constant and sudden pain.
Indeed, as many destinations as there are, and by whatever causes they arise,
so many breast diseases may occur in women through those very same causes.
The vessels of young girls, which rest upon the breasts, have their openings closed;
because of this non-discharge of impurities, no diseases of the breasts occur.
Furthermore, for those very women who have given birth or are pregnant, these [channels] become naturally dilated;
they arise from this very source.
The clarity of the rasa, which is sweet and produced by the consumption of digested food,
reaches the breasts from the entire body and is designated as "stanya" (breast milk).
Even when the limbs have been dissected, semen is not seen;
nevertheless, because it is supported by the entire body, it is described as having the characteristic of pervading the whole body.
That very [desire] arises from seeing a woman in motion, from remembering her,
from hearing her voice, from touching her, and from sexual arousal.
A mind that is perfectly serene is said to be the cause of joy;
likewise, a woman’s breast milk is so because it originates from the essence of food.
That very [semen] flows forth like semen due to contact with offspring, or even from seeing, remembering,
or grasping the body.
There, continuous unctuousness is said to be the cause of discharge;
that [semen] becomes turbid due to vāta and floats upon the water when cast therein.
From bile (pitta), it is sour and pungent, with yellow streaks and a yellow tint in water;
from phlegm (kapha), it is thick, slimy, and sinks in water;
when all [humors] are vitiated, it possesses all the symptoms; and it also becomes corrupted by injury (abhighāta).
One should designate that milk as pure which, when thrown into water, becomes one with it, being white, sweet, unaltered in color, and clear.
Whether containing milk or even devoid of milk, once the humors (doṣas) reach a woman's breasts,
they vitiate the blood and flesh, leading to the development of breast diseases.
Of these five types, however, with the exception of the blood-born abscess (śoṇita-vidradhi),
their symptoms are identical to the symptoms of external abscesses.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Visarpa, Nāḍī, and Diseases of the Breast," in the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna) of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The eleventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of glandular swellings, tumors, and goiters.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
When the Vāta and other [doshas] are vitiated, they corrupt the flesh and blood, as well as the fat permeated by Kapha;
they produce a swelling that is circular, elevated, and knotted, and for this reason it is designated as a Granthi (glandular swelling).
It stretches, throbs, and experiences a piercing pain; it is pushed back and torn apart.
Dark, hard, and distended like a bladder, it bursts and discharges clear blood born of wind (vāta).
It is burned, fumes, is sucked dry, is cooked, and even seems to blaze up;
reddish or yellowish due to bile, it bursts open and discharges extremely hot blood.
Cold, discolored, with little pain and excessive itching, it is characterized by a firm consistency like a stone;
it grows slowly due to the provocation of phlegm (kapha), and when it bursts, it discharges thick, white pus.

The swelling caused by fat (medas) increases and decreases along with the growth and wasting of the body; it is unctuous, large, slightly painful, and intensely itchy. When incised, the fat that issues forth resembles oil-cake or clarified butter.
Indeed, the Vāyu, having displaced the network of vessels (sirā-pratāna) through various efforts arising from exertion in one who is weak,
compresses, contracts, and dries it up, quickly forming a raised, circular knot (granthi).
That knot (granthi) is formed by the veins (sirāja); it is difficult to cure if it is painful and mobile.
However, one that is painless, immobile, large, or arising from a vital spot (marma) should be rejected as incurable.
Fat accumulated in the jawbones, armpits, axillae, upper arms, neck,
and throat causes Kapha to produce a firm, round, or elongated nodule that is unctuous and associated with little pain.
When that [swelling] is covered with nodules the size of *āmalaka* seeds, resembling a net of fish eggs,
and likewise by other growths of the same color, they call it *apacī* due to its excellence of accumulation.
Accompanied by itching and slight pain, these ulcers burst and discharge; some perish while others arise.
Indeed, this disease, caused by fat and phlegm, is very difficult to cure and persists for many years.
In some part of the body, the humors (doṣas), having become concentrated and corrupted the flesh,
produce a growth that is round, firm, slightly painful, large, deeply rooted, slow to increase, and non-suppurating.
Those learned in the scriptures declare that swelling which produces an accumulation of flesh is called arbuda;
it arises from vāta, pitta, kapha, blood, muscle, and fat.
That which arises from it always possesses characteristics identical to those of the [original] pustule;
the vitiated dosha, having afflicted the blood and constricted the vessels, remains without suppuration.
It swells with secretions, a mass of flesh covered with fleshy sprouts that grows rapidly;
it constantly discharges foul blood and is incurable, being of the nature of blood.
Due to being afflicted by complications arising from the depletion of blood, one becomes pale;
moreover, when tormented by an arbuda (tumor), the vitiated flesh produces a swelling in a limb that has been injured by blows with the fist or similar trauma.
Painless, glossy, uniform in color, uncooked, stone-like, and immovable—
this [growth] occurs intensely in a man whose flesh is corrupted and who is excessively devoted to meat.
This fleshy tumor (māṃsārbuda), however, is declared incurable; even among those that are curable, one should avoid these:
one that has exuded, one born upon a vital organ (marman), one located in the channels (srotas), or one that is immovable.
Indeed, when another [tumor] arises upon one already born, that should be known as an arbuda by those who know arbudas;
and that which is born as a pair, whether simultaneously or sequentially, is called a dvirarbuda, and that is incurable.
Due to the predominance of phlegm (kapha) and especially because of the abundance of fat (medas), all tumors (arbuda) by their very nature do not undergo suppuration;
this is because of the stability of the humors (doṣa) and their tendency toward hardening.
Vata and Kapha, having increased in the throat and likewise combined with fat (medas), produce a swelling (gaṇḍa) characterized by their respective symptoms;
this they call Galagaṇḍa.
That which is accompanied by throbbing, covered with black veins, and is either black or reddish-brown, is of the nature of wind (vāta).
That which is accompanied by fat, thickened over time, and becomes exceedingly glossy, is painless.

One who is habituated to harsh speech undergoes a long period of ripening [of karma], and only by chance might it ever reach fruition; meanwhile, that person experiences a bitter taste in the mouth as well as a parching of the palate and throat.

The Kapha-type [abscess] is firm, similar in color to the skin, with little pain and intense itching; it is cold and large, grows slowly over a long period, takes a long time to suppurate, and is sometimes characterized by mild pain.
The mouth of that person becomes sweet, and there is a coating on the palate and throat;
it is oily, soft, pale, and without unpleasant odor. This condition, caused by fat (medas), is free from disease yet accompanied by excessive itching.
It hangs down like a gourd, having a small base and subject to decrease and increase in accordance with the body;
the person's mouth becomes oily, and it constantly makes a gurgling sound in the throat.
A physician should avoid treating one who has a goiter if he breathes with difficulty, whose entire body is flaccid, who has been ill for over a year,
who suffers from anorexia, who is emaciated, and whose voice is broken.
If a swelling is fixed and hangs from the neck like a scrotum—
whether it be large or small— one should designate that as galagaṇḍa.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Galagaṇḍa, Gaṇḍamālā, Apaci, and Arbuda," in the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna) of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Twelfth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of elephantiasis (vṛddhi), venereal sores (upadaṃśa), and filariasis (ślīpada).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
There are seven types of hernias (vṛddhi), caused by wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (śleṣman), blood (śoṇita), fat (medas), urine (mūtra), and the intestines (antra).
Among these, in the two hernias caused by urine and the intestines, the cause of their origin is exclusively one of those arising from wind.

Indeed, when any one of the humors (doṣas) becomes aggravated in the lower part of the body and enters the vessels (dhamanīs) that carry [blood] to the scrotum, it produces an enlargement of the scrotum; this condition is called vṛddhi.
The premonitory symptoms of those [women] who are to give birth are pain in the bladder, waist, scrotum, and penis, suppression of flatus, and swelling of the scrotum.

In that regard, they describe an increase of *vāta* as being like a bladder distended with air—stretched, rough, and characterized by pain from wind without any visible cause; an increase of *pitta* as resembling a ripe *udumbara* fruit, accompanied by fever, burning heat, and steam, and characterized by rapid onset and suppuration; an increase of *śleṣman* as hard, with little pain, cold, and itchy; and an increase of blood (*rakta*) as covered with black vesicles, possessing the symptoms of an increase of *pitta*.
An increase of fat (*medas*) is soft, unctuous, itchy, with little pain, and resembles the fruit of the palmyra palm; an increase of urine occurs in one who habitually suppresses the urge to urinate.
As it moves, it becomes agitated like a water-filled leather bag, causing pain during urination and swelling of the testicles and the scrotum.

One should recognize this as *mūtravṛddhi*. Due to specific types of exertion—such as carrying heavy loads, wrestling with strong opponents, or falling from trees—the *vāyu* (vital air) increases and becomes provoked; seizing a portion of either the large intestine or the other [small intestine] in a disordered state, it descends, reaches the inguinal joint, and remains there in the form of a knot. If not treated, over time it enters the scrotum and causes swelling of the testes.
That swelling becomes distended like an inflated bladder, elongated,
and it moves upward with a sound when pressed;
once released, it becomes distended again.
They declare that increase of mantras to be unattainable.

In that regard, due to excessive sexual intercourse or excessive celibacy, or likewise by excessively indulging in a woman who is an extreme practitioner of celibacy, or one who has long been abandoned, or who is menstruating, or has long hair, coarse hair, matted hair, or hidden hair; one with a narrow opening or a wide opening; one who is disliked, or lacks desire; whose vulva has been washed with unclean water, or not washed at all; one afflicted by a vaginal disease, or naturally having a defective vulva, or a non-vulva—by such means, the aggravated *doṣas* reach the penis and produce swelling (*śvayathu*) in the presence or absence of a wound. This occurs through the application of nails, teeth, poison, or thorns; through binding, striking with the hands, or cohabiting with quadrupeds; through washing with unclean water, or through compression, or through the suppression of the urge of semen, or through failure to wash after intercourse, and so forth.
They call that an "upadaṃśa" (side-dish).
It is of five kinds, [arising] from the three defects individually or collectively, and from blood.

Among these, the vātika type is characterized by roughness, cracking of the skin, stiffness of the penis, a rough swelling, and various types of vāta-related pain. The paittika type involves fever, swelling resembling a ripe udumbara fruit, intense burning, rapid suppuration, and pittaja pains. The ślaiṣmika type features a swelling that is itchy, hard, and oily, along with kaphaja pains. The raktaja type is marked by the appearance of black vesicles, excessive bleeding, the signs of pitta, and an extreme degree of fever, burning, and emaciation.
It may sometimes be palliable; however, in the case of the "all-originated" type, there is the appearance of all symptoms, tearing of the penis, the emergence of worms, and death.
When the aggravated humors—vāta, pitta, and kapha—descend downwards and settle in the groins, thighs, knees, and calves, they eventually take hold of the foot and gradually produce swelling.
This is called *ślīpada* (elephantiasis).
It is of three types, caused respectively by vāta, pitta, and kapha.

Among these, the type born of Vāta is rough, black, and harsh, characterized by pain from wind without apparent cause, and it frequently cracks open. The type born of Pitta has a yellowish appearance, is somewhat soft, and is mostly associated with fever and a burning sensation. The type born of Śleṣman (Kapha), however, is white, glossy in appearance, mildly painful, heavy, marked by large nodules, and covered with thorns.
In that regard, those places where an anthill has spread over a very large area and has existed for more than a year are to be avoided.
And there are verses on this point:
one should know that all three of these types of elephantiasis arise from an excess of phlegm (kapha),
because both heaviness and enlargement do not exist without phlegm.
In those regions where there is an abundance of stagnant water and which remain cool throughout all seasons, elephantiasis (ślīpada) occurs especially frequently.
Elephantiasis (ślīpada) arises in the feet as well as in the hands of men;
some experts in the subject maintain that it also occurs in the ears, eyes, nose, and lips.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Vṛddhi, Upadaṃśa, and Ślīpada," in the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna) of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||12||
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of minor diseases (kṣudraroga).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
In brief, there are forty-four minor diseases.

They are as follows: ajagallikā, yavaprakhyā, andhālajī, vivṛtā, kacchapikā, valmīka, indravṛddhā, panasikā, pāṣāṇagardabha, jālagardabha, kakṣā, visphoṭaka, agnirohiṇī, cippa, kunakha, anuśayī, vidārikā, śarkarārbuda, pāmā, vicarcikā, rakasā, pādadārikā, kadara, alasa, indralupta, dāruṇaka, aruṃṣikā, palita, masūrikā, yauvanapiḍakā, padminīkaṇṭaka, jatumaṇi, maśaka, carmakīla, tilakālaka, nyaccha, vyaṅga, parivartikā, avapāṭikā, niruddhaprakaśa, saṃniruddhaguda, ahipūtana, vṛṣaṇakacchū, and gudabhraṃśa.
Smooth, matching the color of the skin, knotted, painless, and resembling a seal-ring impression—
this is known as Ajagallikā, arising from Kapha and Vāta, occurring in children.
A boil shaped like a barley grain, very hard, knotted, and embedded in the flesh,
caused by phlegm and wind, is called Yavaprakhya.
One should recognize that as *andhālajī*, which is thick, mouthless, elevated, circular,
and contains little pus, arising from kapha and vāta.
One should recognize that as "vivṛtā," which has an open mouth, causes great burning, resembles a ripe udumbara fruit,
is circular, and arises from pitta.
When five or six hard pustules, elevated like a tortoise shell,
are clustered together due to the aggravation of Kapha and Vāta, they are known by the wise as Kacchapikā.
A knot that gradually accumulates like an anthill on the palms, the soles of the feet, the joints, the neck, or above the clavicle;
Surrounded by openings characterized by swelling, moisture, burning, and itching,
this disease called valmīka arises from the combined action of kapha, pitta, and vāyu.
The physician should recognize Indravṛddhā as a swelling arising from vāta and pitta, which is covered with pustules in the center like a lotus flower.

One should recognize that circular, elevated, blood-stained eruption covered with pustules and causing pain as Gadūrbhikā, born from Vāta and Pitta. Or, there may be a pustule of intense pain all around the ears or on the back.
One should know that the *panasikā* arising from phlegm and wind is like a lotus root (*śālūka*).
One should recognize as *pāṣāṇagardabha* a firm swelling arising at the joint of the jaw, characterized by little pain and caused by phlegm and wind.
A swelling caused by pitta that spreads like erysipelas (visarpa),
is thin, produces burning fever, and does not suppurate, should be known as jālagardabha.
One should recognize as irivellikā a circular swelling located on the head, accompanied by severe pain and fever,
possessing all [the qualities] and exhibiting all the symptoms.
One should designate as *kakṣā* those black, painful eruptions occurring on the arms, sides, shoulders, and armpits, which arise from the provocation of *pitta*.
Having seen such a single swelling on the skin, resembling a pustule,
caused by the provocation of bile, they call it by the name Gandha.
Eruptions resembling burnt flesh, accompanied by fever, arising from pitta and blood,
occurring either in some parts or throughout the body, are known as visphoṭaka.
Those boils that arise on the sides of the armpits, which are hard as flesh, cause internal burning and fever, and resemble a blazing fire; [these are known as kakṣā].
Within seven days, ten days, or a fortnight, they kill the man;
one should know that as Agni-rohiṇī, which is incurable due to the derangement of the humors (sannipāta).
When bile and wind, taking hold of the flesh of the nail, produce pain, burning, and suppuration,
one should designate that disease as *cippa*.
That very condition is called *akṣataroga*, and it is also known as *upanakha*;
it occurs when the nail is vitiated by trauma, becoming rough, black, and harsh.
One should know that such a mark as this indicates a person of noble birth;
it is deep-seated, with little inflammation, matching the color of the skin, and situated upon the surface.
The physician should recognize that as *anuśayī*, which, due to phlegm (*kapha*), undergoes internal suppuration;
it is round like the tuber of a *vidārī* plant and occurs at the armpits and the joints of the groins.
One should recognize the red Vidārikā as being born from all [doshas] and possessing all their characteristics;
it occurs when Kapha, fat, and Vāyu reach the flesh, vessels, and ligaments.
They form a knot; once it is pierced, this [fluid]—honey, ghee, or fat—flows out excessively as a discharge, and therein the Vāyu has increased.
Having dried up the flesh, it produces knotted gravel (śarkarā) again;
thereafter, the vessels (sirāḥ) become foul-smelling, excessively moist, and multicolored.
One should recognize that as *śarkarārbuda* when blood flows out suddenly;
*pāmā*, *vicarcī*, and *rakasā* are declared among the *kuṣṭha* diseases.
In one who habitually walks about, the wind,
having taken refuge in the soles of the feet which have become excessively dry, produces a painful fissure.
In humans, this occurs when the foot is crushed by gravel or wounded by thorns and the like,
or when the humors (doṣas), following the fat and blood, become deranged.
A hard, knotted growth, either depressed in the center or elevated,
the size of a *kola* fruit, painful, and discharging, is called *kadara*.
One should diagnose that as Alasa, characterized by the fingers and the spaces between them being moist,
accompanied by itching, burning sensations, and pain, resulting from contact with foul mud.
The bile, following the paths of the hair follicles and combined with the wind, causes the hairs to fall out;
thereafter, the phlegm along with blood [is discharged].
It obstructs the hair follicles, whereby the growth of other hairs becomes impossible;
that is known as indralupta, khālitya, and rujyā.
When the scalp becomes harsh, itchy, rough,
and cracked due to the provocation of kapha and vāta, one should recognize that condition as dāruṇaka.
One should recognize *aruṃṣikā* as the presence of multiple eruptions on the head that have many openings and excessive discharge,
caused by the provocation of phlegm, blood, and parasites.
The bodily heat produced by anger, grief, and fatigue, when it reaches the head, cooks the bile;
by that, gray hair is produced.
Pustules that are copper-colored or yellowish, accompanied by burning fever and pain,
appearing on the limbs, the face, and within the body, should be known as *masūrikā*.
Pustules resembling the thorns of the Śālmalī tree, produced by phlegm, wind, and blood, arise on the faces of young people; these are known as Mukhadūṣikā.
Covered with thorns, circular, itchy, and pale in its patches—
this condition, known by that name, arises from kapha and vāta, resembling the thorns of a lotus plant.
A painless, even, elevated circular patch arising from phlegm and blood is known as *sahaja* (congenital); a slightly red and smooth [spot] is known as *jatumaṇi*.
If a mole is seen on the body that is painless and stable,
black like a bean, and raised, one should call it a *maṣaka* caused by wind (*anila*).
One should recognize as *tilakālaka* those black spots, the size of sesame seeds, which are painless and even,
resulting from the drying up of wind, bile, and phlegm.
Whether large or small, or even white,
a natural, painless mark on the body is designated as *nyaccha*.
The Carma-kila (skin-nail) is proclaimed to have its origin and cause in these two:
the Vayu, provoked by anger and exertion, becomes conjoined with Pitta.
Because it suddenly appears on the face and then spreads into a circular patch,
one should designate that as a *vyaṅga* (freckle) on the face— painless, thin, and dark-brown.

They know that when the wind, which moves everywhere, excessively affects the skin of the penis through rubbing, pressing, or likewise through injury, it results in a dark discoloration on the body or face known as *nīlikā*.
Then the skin, afflicted by wind, retracts;
and beneath the jewel, the sheath hangs down in the form of a knot.
Accompanied by pain and a burning sensation, and sometimes undergoing suppuration,
one should recognize that as *pravr̥ttikā*, arising from both wind (*māruta*) and exogenous factors (*āgantu*).
That same [discharge], when it is itchy and hard, is produced from phlegm (śleṣman).
When a man approaches a young woman who has little desire due to sexual excitement, [the discharge becomes] itchy and hard.
Or from striking with the hand, or from the forceful upward turning of the skin,
or even from rubbing or pressing, through the obstruction of the flow of semen;
One should know that condition in which the skin is torn open as avapāṭikā;
thus, when afflicted by Vāta, the skin retracts toward the glans penis.
But when the stone is bound by the skin, it obstructs the urinary stream;
when that passage is blocked, there is a scanty flow and absence of pain.
If urine flows from a person but the glans penis does not burst,
one should know that the avapāṭikā ulcer is poorly healed and has its opening obstructed.
Due to the suppression of natural urges, the wind becomes obstructed and, taking refuge in the rectum,
blocks the great channel and makes its opening narrow.
Due to the subtlety of the path, his feces pass with great difficulty;
one should recognize this disease as sanniruddhaguda, which is very hard to overcome.
In a child whose anus has not been washed while filled with feces and urine, there may arise,
upon sweating but not being bathed, an itching sensation born of blood and phlegm.
From scratching that [eruption], pustules and discharge quickly arise;
when these have coalesced into a terrible ulcer, one should know it as *ahipūtana*.
When the filth residing in the penis of one who has neglected bathing and grooming becomes moistened by sweat,
it then produces itching.
In that condition, from scratching, pustules and discharge quickly arise;
they call this vṛṣaṇakacchū, which is born from the provocation of phlegm and blood.
When the rectum protrudes outward due to straining or diarrhea in a person whose body is dry and weak, one should diagnose that as *gudabhraṃśa* (prolapse of the rectum).
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Minor Diseases," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||13||
The fourteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of the defects of the *śūka*.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
In those who desire the enlargement of the penis and engage in it without due order, eighteen diseases caused by the defects of the seminal hair (śūkadoṣa) arise.

They are as follows: sarṣapikā, aṣṭhīlikā, granthi, kumbhīkā, alajī, mṛdita, saṃmūḍhapiḍakā, avamantha, puṣkarikā, sparśahāni, uttamā, śataponaka, tvakpāka, śoṇitārbuda, māṃsārbuda, māṃsapāka, vidradhi, and tilakālaka.
A pustule caused by the breaking of a grain of Śūka,
resembling a white mustard seed (gaurasarṣapa) and arising from Kapha and blood, should be known by the wise as Sarṣapikā.
Due to the provocation of the wind (vāta) by irregular internal factors, a hard, painful swelling arises with bristling hairs that are distorted by poison; this is called *piḍakā-aṣṭhīlikā*.
That which is constantly filled with bristling hairs and knotted together is produced from phlegm (kapha).
Kumbhīkā, arising from blood and bile (rakta-pitta), is inauspicious and resembles the bone of a jambu fruit.
One should consider that which is characterized by the symptoms of alajī to be alajī;
however, that which is crushed, pressed, or inflamed due to the provocation of vāyu is [mṛditaka].
When the hands are severely macerated,
there occurs "saṃmūḍhapiḍakā," characterized by many long pustules that burst in the middle.
That avamantha causes pain and horripilation due to the presence of kapha and blood;
it is covered with pustules (piḍakā) produced by pitta and blood.
That which has the appearance of a lotus bud should be known as *puṣkarikā*;
it causes a loss of sensation and blood tainted by *śūkadhūpita*.
A red pustule resembling a mung bean or a black gram, born of blood and bile, is known as the best [type of carbuncle]; however, it may also be caused by hair or indigestion.
When a body is covered on all sides with minute openings,
it should be known as the disease called Śataponaka, which arises from wind and blood.
Skin inflammation accompanied by fever and a burning sensation, caused by bile and blood,
and afflicted with black, reddish eruptions and pustules,
wherein the underlying tissue experiences intense pain— this should be known as *śoṇitār-buda* (a blood tumor).
One should recognize a fleshy tumor arising from flesh by the defects of the flesh;
in this condition, the muscles waste away and all kinds of pains are present.

The physician should recognize that swelling as a "meat-cooking" (māṃsapāka) caused by all the doṣas; one should diagnose it as an abscess (vidradhi) produced by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), as previously described.
Black, variegated, or even poisonous thorns,
when cast upon it, quickly burn the penis away without leaving a trace.
One should recognize as a tilakālaka that which arises from a derangement of the humors (sannipāta), wherein the flesh of the embodied being turns black and then sloughs off.
Among those, the fleshy tumor (māṃsārbuda), that which is known as the inflammation of flesh (māṃsapāka),
the abscess (vidradhi), and those that are black moles (tilakālaka) do not succeed in being cured.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Śūkadoṣa," in the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna) of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of fractures.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

They teach that there are many kinds of fractures of the bones caused by various types of trauma, such as falling, being crushed, blows, being thrown, or being bitten by predatory beasts and wild animals.

In that regard, the various types of fractures, when examined, are found to be of two kinds: those involving the displacement of joints (sandhivimukta) and those involving the shaft of the bone (kāṇḍabhagna).
Among these, there are six types of joint-displaced fractures and twelve types of shaft fractures.
In that regard, dislocation is of six types: the locked, the crushed, the separated, the rotated, the depressed, and the hyperextended, as well as the laterally displaced.

In that regard, the general characteristics of a dislocation (sandhimukta) are said to be the loss of power for extension, contraction, rotation, and throwing [of the limb], as well as severe pain and intolerance to touch.

In the case of *vaiśeṣika* (dislocation), when the joint is crushed, there is swelling on both sides and the onset of pain, with various types of pain appearing especially at night; when the joint is separated, there is slight swelling, constant pain, and deformity of the joint; when the joint is twisted, there is irregularity of the limb due to the displacement of the joint's sides and pain; when the joint is depressed, there is loosening of the joint and intense pain; when it is excessively displaced, there is the over-extension of the two bones of the joint and pain; and when it is displaced obliquely, there is the displacement of one bone from its side and extreme pain.

Hereafter, we shall describe the twelve types of shaft-fractures (kāṇḍabhagna): the crab-like fracture (karkaṭaka), the horse-ear fracture (aśvakarṇa), the pulverized fracture (cūrṇita), the crushed fracture (piccita), the bone-stripped fracture (asthicchallita), the shaft-fracture (kāṇḍabhagna), the marrow-penetrating fracture (majjānugata), the excessively displaced fracture (atipātita), the curved fracture (vakra), the severed fracture (chinna), the split fracture (pāṭita), and the burst fracture (sphuṭita).

Excessive swelling, throbbing, shifting, intolerance to touch, a sound upon pressure, drooping of the limbs, the manifestation of various types of pain, and a lack of relief in all conditions—this, in brief, is the description of the symptoms of a compound fracture (kāṇḍabhagna).

The specific distinctions are as follows: when it is crushed on both sides, the bone is broken in the middle and protrudes like a knot; when it is [broken] like an *aśvakarṇa*, it rises up like an *aśvakarṇa* (horse-ear) leaf.
When touched, one should understand that it is shattered and emits a sound. When it is pressed, it becomes broad and develops considerable swelling.
In the flanks, the bone is sunken and protruding; the bone is displaced;
it quivers, being violently trembling; it is broken like a reed;
and the bone-fragment, having entered into the marrow within the bone, causes the marrow to swell—thus it is "reaching to the marrow."
A bone that has been completely severed and brought down is "cut through.
One that is bent but not yet separated from the bone is "crooked. One that remains on one side is "partially severed."
It is torn, split open in many ways, and characterized by intense pain;
it is distended as if filled with awns, vast, and burst open—thus it is called "sphuṭita."

Among these, those in which the bone is crushed, split, or completely shattered, and where the marrow is reached, are difficult to cure; as are fractures in the emaciated, the elderly, and children, as well as those in patients suffering from chest wounds, wasting diseases, leprosy, or asthma, and those located at the joints.
And in this regard, there are verses:
"The physician should avoid treating a case where the pelvic bone is fractured, or where it is dislocated at the sacroiliac joint, or displaced, or crushed against the pubic region."
One should avoid a skull that is not joined together, one that is crushed on the forehead,
or one that is broken at the breast, the temples, the back, or the head.
Furthermore, any bone that was poorly formed from the beginning, or even a joint,
or a bone that was properly aligned yet became misaligned due to improper placement or faulty binding;
One should also avoid that which undergoes transformation due to agitation;
furthermore, there are three stages of middle age that have been proclaimed.
In that state, a person who has been treated by a knowledgeable physician should remain steady;
for while the young bones may bend, the cartilages (nalaka) break.
The skulls split apart and the necklaces burst asunder.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, named "The Diagnosis of Fractures," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The sixteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of diseases of the mouth.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
There are sixty-five diseases of the mouth occurring in seven locations.
Among them, the locations are the two lips and the roots of the teeth.
The teeth; the tongue; the palate.
The throat; and "all" [refers to the following].
Among those, eight are in the lips.
Fifteen are in the roots of the teeth;
eight are in the teeth;
five are in the tongue.
Nine in the palate;
seventeen in the throat;
three in all the sense-bases.
Among those, the disorders of the lips are caused by vāta, pitta, śleṣman, sannipāta, blood, muscle, fat, or injury.
When the lips become rough, harsh, stiff, black, and afflicted with intense pain,
they are indeed split and cracked due to the provocation of the wind (vāta).
Covered extensively with vesicles shaped like mustard seeds, accompanied by burning, suppuration, and discharge, and appearing blue or yellow due to pitta; this is the pittaja type.
They are covered with painless pustules of the same color as the skin;
due to kapha, they are itchy, swollen, slimy, cold, and heavy.
Those which are sometimes black, sometimes yellow, and likewise sometimes white,
and are characterized by a combination of humors (sannipāta), should be known as being covered with many pustules.
Covered with pustules the color of dates,
afflicted by blood, they flow with blood and possess the luster of blood.
When the two lips are diseased, swollen, thick, and protruding like lumps of flesh,
living beings become entrapped there from both sides of the mouth.
Due to fat, they resemble the surface of ghee, being itchy, firm, yet soft.
They discharged a clear, crystal-like secretion that flowed copiously.
The two lips become blood-red, they crack and are torn due to injury; furthermore, they are described as being knotted together and accompanied by itching.
Those located at the roots of the teeth are: śītāda,
dantapuppuṭaka,
and dantaveṣṭaka.
Śauṣira, Mahāśauṣira, Paridara.
Upakuśa, Dantavaidarbha, and Vardhana.
The flesh and the five channels.
If blood suddenly flows from the gums,
and they become foul-smelling, blackish, moist, and soft;
The gums decay and eat away at one another;
that disease, arising from phlegm and blood, is called śītāda.
When there is a large, painful swelling on three of the teeth,
it should be known as Dantapuppuṭaka, caused by phlegm and blood.
When pus and blood flow and the teeth become loose,
that condition is to be known as *dantaveṣṭa*, arising from vitiated blood.
Swelling at the roots of the teeth accompanied by pain, arising from phlegm and blood,
characterized by salivation and itching— this disease is known as Śauṣira.
The teeth waver from their sockets and the palate is torn asunder;
the gums fester and the mouth is tormented with pain.
In that [disease], which is known as mahāśauṣira, all the teeth become afflicted;
the gums wither away, and the patient spits out blood.
That disease arising from pitta, blood, and kapha is indeed to be known as Paridara; there is burning and suppuration in the gums, and because of these, the teeth become loose.
When struck, they bleed with little pain;
once the blood has flowed, they swell and a foul odor arises from the mouth.
That disease in which Upakuśa occurs is caused by pitta and blood;
when the roots of the teeth are rubbed, a great swelling arises.
The teeth also become loose; this is Vaidarbha, born from injury. Due to the wind (māruta), an excessive tooth grows, accompanied by intense pain.
That disease is considered Vardhana; once it has arisen, the pain subsides.
In the case of the posterior lower tooth, there is a large swelling accompanied by great pain.
That which causes salivation and is produced by kapha should be known as adhimāṃsaka;
the five types of sinus tracts (nāḍīs) located at the roots of the teeth are to be understood as previously described.
Those affecting the teeth are: dālana,
krimidantaka,
and dantaharṣa.
Bhañjanaka; dantaśarkarā; kapālikā.
Śyāvadantaka and Hanumokṣa.
When the teeth are split in many ways and accompanied by intense pain,
that condition should be known as *dālana*, which arises from the movement of the *sadāgati* wind.
Black, fissured, unstable, discharging, accompanied by swelling and great pain,
and characterized by pain without apparent cause— this dental disease arising from Vata should be known as Kṛmidantaka.
One should recognize that disease as *dantaharṣa* (tooth-aversion), caused by the wind (*samīraṇa*), in which the teeth endure both cold and heat, yet do not tolerate touch.
When the face becomes crooked and there is breaking of the teeth along with intense pain,
that disease caused by kapha and vāta is known as bhañjanaka.
That which is like sugar-candy (śarkarā), hardened into a deposit upon the teeth, and which destroys the qualities of the teeth, is to be known as *danta-śarkarā* (calculus).
When the enamel of the teeth breaks apart along with the tartar,
that very condition should be known as *kapālikā*, which destroys the teeth.
He whose teeth have been completely scorched by bile mixed with blood,
and have consequently become either dark-brown or blue, is called Śyāvadantaka.
When the jaw-joint is displaced by various factors due to vāta,
it should be known as the disease hanumokṣa, characterized by symptoms similar to those of ardita.
The thorns located on the tongue are of three kinds, corresponding to the three humors (doṣas): alāsa,
upajihvikā, and [the third].
The tongue, when afflicted by Vāta, becomes cracked and numb, appearing like the leaves of a vegetable;
by Pitta, it becomes yellow and is intensely burned, covered with reddish thorns;
by Kapha, it becomes heavy and thick, covered with fleshy excrescences resembling the thorns of the Śālmali tree.
A severe swelling on the surface of the tongue, caused by phlegm and blood, is known as Alāsa;
when it has increased, it stiffens the tongue, and the root of the tongue undergoes intense suppuration.
A swelling in the form of a protrusion at the tip of the tongue, arising from an elevation of the tongue and originating from phlegm and blood,
accompanied by salivation, itching, and burning, is called *upajihvikā*.
Those located in the palate are: galaśuṇḍikā,
tuṇḍikerī, and adhruṣaḥ.
The tortoise;
the arbuda;
a mass of flesh.
Tālupuppuṭa, tāluśoṣa, and tālupāka.
A long swelling, resembling an inflated bladder, which arises from the root of the palate due to phlegm and blood,
and causes thirst, cough, and dyspnea, is designated by physicians as the disease known by the name Kaṇṭhaśuṇḍī.
A swelling that is stiff and red in the region of the palate should be known as *raktaja* (blood-born); it is called *adhruṣa*, and is characterized by intense pain and fever.
One should know that a tortoise-shaped swelling caused by phlegm (kapha) is elevated like a tortoise, painless, slow to arise, and not red;
however, a swelling in the center of the palate shaped like a lotus, arising from blood, should be known as an arbuda, possessing the symptoms previously described.
They call a painless mass of flesh located within the palate "duṣṭamāṃsa" (vitiated flesh) caused by phlegm.
A painless, stable growth the size of a jujube fruit, arising from phlegm mixed with fat at the site of the palate, is called "puppuṭa."
In *tāluśoṣa* (palate dryness), the palate becomes excessively parched; it arises from Vāta when accompanied by Śvāsa, and from Pitta.
Pitta causes a most terrible suppuration in the palate; this condition they call *tālupāka* (suppuration of the palate).
There are five types of *rohiṇī* located in the throat:
*kaṇṭhaśālūka*,
*adhijihva*, and so forth.
Balaya, Balāsa, Ekavṛnda.
Vṛnda;
Śataghnī; Gilāyu.
Throat abscess;
throat swelling;
loss of voice.
Māṃsatāna and Vidārī.

When wind, bile, and phlegm—either individually, combined, or all together—are aggravated and likewise affect the blood, they corrupt the flesh and produce sprouts that obstruct the throat; this disease is indeed Rohiṇī, which takes away life.

Those fleshy sprouts that arise all over the tongue and cause intense pain by obstructing the throat— those they call Rohiṇī, produced by Vāta and characterized by severe complications arising from the nature of Vāta.
That which arises from the cause of pitta is characterized by rapid onset, rapid burning, and rapid suppuration, and it causes intense fever;
whereas that which originates from kapha obstructs the channels, has slow suppuration, and is heavy and stable.
Deep-seated in its maturation, with irresistible vigor, manifesting the symptoms of the three doṣas and arising from their triad,
covered with eruptions and possessing signs identical to those of pitta— this type, characterized by blood, is declared incurable.
A hard, firm swelling arising from phlegm (kapha) in the throat, the size of a jujube stone, which acts like a thorn or a bristle and is curable only by the application of a surgical instrument,
is called *kaṇṭhaśālūka*.

A swelling in the form of a tip on the tongue, arising from phlegm mixed with blood above the attachment of the tongue, is indeed to be known as the disease Adhijihva; one should avoid this when suppuration has set in.
Balāsa alone, obstructing the passage of food, causes a swelling that is elongated and elevated;
they call that condition "valaya," which must be avoided as its power is entirely irresistible.
When Kapha and Vata are aggravated, they produce swelling in the throat accompanied by the affliction of dyspnea;
the experts call this difficult-to-cure disorder, which cuts into the vital organs (marman), by the name Balāsa.

That swelling which is rounded and elevated, accompanied by burning, itching, and is slow to suppurate, soft, and heavy, is proclaimed by its name as *ekavṛnda*; this disease is produced from both *balāsa* (phlegm) and *kṣataja* (blood).
They describe *vṛnda* as a swelling that is elevated, circular, intensely burning, and characterized by acute fever;
one should know that it arises from the provocation of *pitta* and blood, while *vṛndaka* is accompanied by a pricking pain and results from the provocation of wind and blood.

A thick, circular swelling that obstructs the throat, covered excessively with fleshy growths, causing the increase of various diseases and arising from the three *doṣas*, is known as *śataghnī*; it is incurable like a [lethal] *śataghnī* weapon.

A hard, slightly painful knot the size of an *āmalaka* seed, located in the throat and composed of phlegm and blood, which makes food appear as if stuck there, is known as *gilāyu*; it is curable by surgical means.
That swelling which arises pervading the entire throat and in which all types of pain are present is a "throat abscess" (galavidradhi) caused by all three doṣas;
it is indeed identical to the abscess born of all [the doṣas].
A great swelling that obstructs food and water, accompanied by a severe fever and the cessation of the movement of wind,
which arises from phlegm mixed with blood in the throat— this is proclaimed as *galauṣa*.
When one, being extremely exhausted, breathes incessantly with a broken voice and a parched, loosened throat,
due to the channels of wind being smeared with phlegm— that disease should be known as *svaraghna* (voice-destroying) caused by labored breathing.

That swelling which is extensive, extremely painful, and gradually causes obstruction of the throat is called *māṃsatāna*; it is a hanging growth that destroys life, a disorder produced by all [three] humors.

One should recognize Vidārī in the mouth as a swelling accompanied by constant burning and piercing pain, reddish in color, with putrid and sloughing flesh, caused by Pitta; it is specifically located on the side toward which the patient lies.
All swellings, however, are caused by wind, bile, phlegm, and blood.
He whose face is covered all over with eruptions accompanied by pricking pain from a morbid wind (vāta) is called Sarvasara;
and he whose face is covered with thin, reddish-yellow eruptions accompanied by burning is likewise [Sarvasara] due to the provocation of bile (pitta).
That which is covered with [eruptions] accompanied by itching and slight pain, and is characterized by swelling, is indeed caused by phlegm (kapha).
That which arises from bile (pitta) and is caused solely by blood is designated by some as "mouth-inflammation" (mukhapāka).
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Diseases of the Mouth," in the Section on Diagnosis of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
Suśruta Saṃhitā. Now begins the Section on Anatomy (Śārīrasthāna).
Chapter One.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the section on the contemplation of all beings with respect to the body.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

The cause of all beings, itself without a cause, characterized by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, consisting of eight forms, and the source of the origin of the entire world—this is that which is called the Unmanifest (avyakta).
That one [principle] is the substratum for the many knowers of the field (kṣetrajña), just as the ocean is for aquatic creatures.

From that unmanifest (avyakta), the Great One (mahat) arises, possessing its very characteristics; and from that Great One, characterized as such, the ego (ahaṅkāra) arises, possessing its own characteristics.

That [ego] is threefold: the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi*. Among these, from the *vaikārika* ego, aided by the *taijasa*, there arise eleven organs possessing those same characteristics.
They are as follows: the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, genitals, anus, feet, and the mind.
Among these, the first five are the faculties of cognition (buddhīndriya);
the other five are the faculties of action (karmendriya);

and the mind (manas) partakes of the nature of both. Furthermore, from the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) when assisted by the fiery element (taijasa), the five subtle elements (tanmātra) arise, possessing the same characteristics as that [ego-principle].
Namely: the subtle element of sound,
the subtle element of touch,
and the subtle element of form.

The subtle element of taste, the subtle element of smell—these are their specific manifestations, namely sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; from these arise the gross elements: ether, air, fire, water, and earth. Thus has this twenty-fourfold enumeration of principles been explained.
In that regard:
the objects of the sense organs of cognition are sound and the rest; those of the organs of action are, respectively, speaking, grasping, sexual pleasure, excretion, and locomotion.

The unmanifest, the Great One (mahat), the ego (ahaṅkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātras)—these eight are the primal natures (prakṛtis); the remaining sixteen are the transformations (vikāras).
Their respective domains are their *adhibhūta*; they themselves are the *adhyātma*. As for the *adhidaivata*: for the intellect (*buddhi*) it is Brahmā;
for the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) it is Īśvara;
for the mind (*manas*) it is the Moon.
The quarters are [the essence] of the ear;
the wind is [the essence] of the skin;
the sun is [the essence] of the eye.
Water is the [subtle essence] of the tongue;
earth is that of the nose;
fire is that of speech.
Indra is in the two hands;
Viṣṇu is in the two feet;
Mitra is in the anus.
"Prajāpati [is the deity] of the lap."
In this regard, this entire group [of principles] is indeed insentient.
The twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, when conjoined with cause and effect, becomes the sentient knower.
Although the Pradhāna is devoid of sentience, they teach that it engages in activity for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa, and they cite milk and other such examples as the reasons for this.
Henceforth, we shall explain the similarities and differences between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).
They are as follows: both are indeed beginningless;
both are indeed endless.
Both are without gender;
both are eternal;
both are not posterior (or, according to another reading, both are posterior).

And both are all-pervading. However, Nature (prakṛti) is one, insentient, composed of the three qualities (triguṇa), possessing the nature of a seed, possessing the nature of productivity, and possessing the nature of neutrality.

The Spirits (puruṣas), on the other hand, are many, sentient, devoid of qualities, not possessing the nature of a seed, not possessing the nature of productivity, and possessing the nature of neutrality.

In this regard, since the effect conforms to its cause, all these particularities consist of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; because they are colored by those [qualities] and because they are composed of them, some teachers declare that persons (*puruṣas*) themselves possess those very qualities.
In medical science, however:
"Nature, God, time, chance, and likewise destiny..."
And those of broad vision consider transformation to be the primordial nature.
One should designate the elements as being composed of that very [consciousness] and possessing its qualities alone.
And by them, the entire collection of beings, characterized by those [elements], was manifested.
Its application in relation to medical treatment has been described at all times.
For in the practice of medicine, there is no concern higher than that for living beings.

For it has been stated: "The collection of substances from which [the body] arises is called the primary elements (bhūta) and so forth; and in Āyurveda, the sense organs are described as being composed of these elements (bhautika), as are the objects of the senses."
And there is a verse on this point:
"By means of a sense faculty, a human being perceives its own respective sense object."
It is certain that because they share a common origin, one does not arise from another; such is the established rule.

Furthermore, in the treatises of Āyurveda, the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) are not taught to be omnipresent or eternal; rather, they cite reasons that demonstrate the knower of the field to be a non-omnipresent, eternal person. According to the established doctrines of the Āyurvedic sciences, the knowers of the field are non-omnipresent and eternal; they migrate through the animal, human, and divine realms due to the causes of merit and demerit. These [knowers] are to be grasped by inference, are supremely subtle, possess consciousness, and are eternal; they become manifest at the union of blood and semen.

Since it has been stated that "the person (puruṣa) is the aggregate of the five great elements and the embodied being," this very same person, as the agent of action (karmapuruṣa), is the subject of medical treatment.

Its qualities are pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, effort, inhalation and exhalation, opening and closing of the eyes, intellect, mind, volition, deliberation, memory, discernment, determination, and the perception of objects.

The *sāttvika* qualities, however, are: benevolence, a taste for sharing, forbearance, truthfulness, righteousness, faith, knowledge, intellect, wisdom, memory, fortitude, and freedom from attachment. The *rājasa* qualities, however, are: an abundance of suffering, a habit of wandering about, lack of fortitude, egoism, untruthfulness, lack of compassion, hypocrisy, pride, exhilaration, and anger. The *tāmasa* qualities, however, are: despondency, atheism, a disposition toward unrighteousness, dullness of intellect, ignorance, poor judgment, a habit of inaction, and excessive sleepiness.

The aerial [qualities] are: sound, the sense of hearing, the collection of all cavities, and distinctness. The windy [qualities] are: touch, the sense of touch, the collection of all movements, the vibration of the entire body, lightness, and buoyancy. The fiery [qualities] are: form, the sense of sight, color, heat, brilliance, digestion, impatience, sharpness, and valor. The watery [qualities] are: taste, the sense of taste, the collection of all fluids, heaviness, coldness, unctuousness, and semen. The earthy [qualities] are: smell, the sense of smell, the collection of all solid forms, and heaviness.
In that regard, space abounds in *sattva*; wind abounds in *rajas*;
and fire abounds in both *sattva* and *rajas*.
Water abounds in *sattva* and *tamas*; earth abounds in *tamas*.
And there are two verses on this point:
"One should point out that all these are mutually interpenetrated."
However, the manifest characteristic of all [categories] is held to reside in their respective substances.
Eight are declared to be the primary natures (prakṛtis), while the modifications (vikāras) are exactly sixteen.

And the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is, in brief, [the distinction] between that which is independent and that which is dependent. (*Note: The reading "asvatantraparatantrataḥ" is found in some manuscripts.*)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Contemplation of All Beings," in the Section on Anatomy (Śārīrasthāna) of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||1||
The Second Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the section on the body entitled "The Purification of Semen and Menstrual Blood."
As the Blessed One Dhanvantari has said.
Due to wind, bile, phlegm, blood, a corpse-like odor, sinews, putrefaction, pus, depletion, urine, feces, and semen, they are incapable of procreating offspring.
Among these, there is the color and sensation of wind due to wind;
the color and sensation of bile due to bile;
and the color and sensation of phlegm due to phlegm.
It has the color and sensation of blood, is abundant with a cadaverous odor,
and is formed into a mass by phlegm and wind;
it resembles putrid pus due to bile and phlegm.

The previously mentioned depletion caused by pitta and vāta is characterized by the odor of urine and feces, while that caused by sannipāta has the odor of a corpse, knots, putrefaction, pus, and depleted semen; among these, those with the odors of a corpse, knots, putrefaction, pus, and depleted semen are difficult to cure.
However, those involving urine, feces, or semen are incurable; other [cases] are curable. (*This reading is not found in the manuscript copy.*)

Menstrual blood (ārtaava) also becomes non-seed (abīja) when afflicted by the three doshas with blood as the fourth, either individually, in pairs, or all together. That too is to be recognized by its specific dosha-related color, pain, and other characteristics.
Among these, that which resembles a corpse, a knot, putrid matter, pus, or is diminished, or resembles urine and feces, is incurable; the rest is curable.
And there are verses on this point:
