Among those, one should conquer the first three defects of semen by means of oleation, sudation, and other such therapies.
The wise physician [should treat it] with specific therapeutic procedures as well as with urethral enemas (uttara-vasti).
The physician should have the man drink ghee when his semen has become putrid.
It is prepared with *dhātakī* flowers, *khadira*, pomegranate, and *arjuna*.
Or else, one should administer clarified butter prepared with the śālasāra and other [medicinal] drugs.
Or [it may be prepared] in ashes produced from *śaṭī* or from *pālāśa* wood, which have become like a knot.
And it has been established [that the sense-organ] is like pus in the case of the parūṣaka fruit, the vaṭa tree, and so forth.
That which was previously mentioned and that which will be stated hereafter is the duty for one whose vital seed has been exhausted.
In the case of vitprabha, one should administer the prepared [mixture] with citraka, uśīra, and hiṅgu.
[In some versions, the following additional reading is found: "An intelligent person should perform the sequence beginning with oleation for these six [patients] in this order.
One who has been oleated, emetic, purged, treated with a non-unctuous enema, and then given an unctuous enema;
One should properly treat a patient afflicted by seminal disorders with an uttarabasti (urethral/vaginal enema).
It has the luster of crystal, is liquid, unctuous, sweet, and possesses the fragrance of honey.
Some, however, desire semen that resembles oil or honey.
One should perform the procedure ending with the uttarabasti for the purification of the menstrual flow.
For women who possess affection and other such qualities, there are four conditions regarding the menstrual flow.
One should prepare medicinal pastes, boluses, wholesome foods, and mouth-rinses.
When the knot has formed, one should drink pāṭhā, tryūṣaṇa, and vṛkṣakāṇi.
In the menses, which resemble foul-smelling pus and are like excrement; |||
One should drink the decoction of *bhadraśrī* and likewise the decoction of sandalwood— [the latter being] foul-smelling and resembling pus.
And the administration of remedies that remove defects of the semen, according to their respective requirements.
This purification of the humors (*yoga*) is beneficial even during the remaining stages of menstruation; likewise, rice, barley, wine, and meat that increases *pitta* are wholesome.
That which resembles rabbit's blood, or that which is like the juice of lac;
They praise that menstrual blood which does not stain one's garment.
That very [practice] has been carried to excess, being performed even during the improper season.
One should recognize as *asṛgdara* (menorrhagia) that which differs from other characteristics of blood [reading: "one should recognize it as characterized by the stated symptoms"].
Every case of menorrhagia is accompanied by body aches and pain.
Upon its excessive increase, there occurs weakness, giddiness, fainting, darkness of vision, and thirst.
Burning sensation, delirium, pallor, lassitude, and diseases born of wind (vāta).
The physician [should treat] that minor affliction of a young woman who is devoted to wholesome practices.
One should treat it properly according to the prescribed method for *raktapitta*.
Due to the channels being obstructed by the humors (doṣas), the menstrual blood of a woman perishes.
In that condition, fish, horse gram, sour substances, sesame, black gram, and liquor are beneficial.
In drinking, urine and buttermilk; and in food, curd and fermented gruel.
The previously described hemorrhage (rakta), along with its symptoms and treatment, has been explained.
Nevertheless, in this case, a remedy must be applied, just as one would treat a loss of blood.
Thus, [he is] one whose semen is not vitiated, and she is one whose menstrual flow is pure.

From the first day of the fertile period onwards, she should observe celibacy and avoid sleeping during the day, applying collyrium, shedding tears, bathing, anointing with unguents, oil-massage, cutting the nails, running, laughing, talking excessively, listening to loud noises, scratching herself, and exertion from the wind.
What is the reason? One who sleeps during the day will have a child who is habitually sleepy; one who applies collyrium will have a child who is blind.
From weeping, one's vision is impaired;
from bathing and anointing, one becomes habitually miserable;
and from anointing with oil, one becomes afflicted with leprosy.
From cutting one's nails, one becomes a person with deformed nails; from running about, one becomes fickle;
from laughing, one’s teeth, lips, palate, and tongue become dark;
and from excessive talking, one becomes a chatterer.
From hearing excessively loud sounds, a child becomes deaf;
from scratching [the womb], it becomes bald;
and from exposure to wind and physical exertion, the fetus becomes insane—one should therefore avoid these things.
She should lie upon a bed of darbha grass, subsisting on whatever food she can take with her palms, a shallow bowl, or leaves;
for three days she must protect her husband.

Then, on the fourth day, having bathed for purification, wearing unwashed garments and being fully adorned, he should present her—after the recitation of auspicious benedictions has been performed—to her husband.
For what reason?
A woman who has bathed after her menses should first look upon whatever kind of man she sees.
Therefore, she should give birth to such a son and present him as her husband.
Then the preceptor should perform this rite for the fulfillment of the purpose.
And at the conclusion of his work, the discerning man should indeed undertake this sequence.

Then, in the afternoon, a man who has observed celibacy for a month, being lubricated with ghee, should eat *śāli* rice with ghee and milk; he should approach a woman who has likewise observed celibacy for a month, who is lubricated with oil and whose diet consists primarily of oil and beans, at night, having won her confidence through conciliation and other means. One desiring a son should approach her on the fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, or twelfth day, alternating in this manner.
Among these, one should know that each subsequent one possesses greater longevity and health.
Indeed, on these days, there is prosperity for progeny, sovereignty, and strength.
From this point forward, one who desires a female child should perform [the rite] on the fifth, seventh, ninth, and eleventh lunar days; the thirteenth and subsequent days are censured.

In this regard, sexual intercourse on the first day after a woman has reached her season is detrimental to the longevity of men. Furthermore, the embryo conceived then is released from its life-breaths at birth (variant reading: "is not released from its life-breaths"). It is likewise on the second day, or in the lying-in chamber. On the third day as well, the child will have incomplete limbs or be short-lived. However, on the fourth day, the child will have complete limbs and be long-lived. Moreover, seed that enters while the menstrual blood is still flowing does not produce any beneficial result.
Just as an object cast against the current in a river turns back and does not go upstream, so too should this be regarded.
Therefore, one should avoid her for three nights according to the rule;
after that, one may approach her once a month.

And during these days after she has conceived, one should press either Lakṣmaṇā, Avaṭaśuṅgā, Sahadevā, or Viśvadevā with milk and give three or four drops into the right nostril for her who desires a son; [in some books, the phrase "for her who desires a daughter" is read additionally before "into the left"] and she should not spit them out.
Surely, through the presence of these four factors, a conception shall occur according to the prescribed rule.
Just as a sprout arises from the conjunction of the season, the field, water, and seed.
Thus born, they are handsome, possessed of strength, long-lived, and great beings (*mahāsattva*).
Virtuous sons become the liberators from debt and are beneficial to those who have sons.

In that regard, the fire element (tejodhātu) is the source of all complexions. When it is predominant over the water element (apdhātu) at the time of emerging from the womb, it makes the fetus fair-complexioned; when predominant over the earth element (pṛthivīdhātu), it makes it dark.
One in whom the earth and space elements predominate is dark-complexioned;
one in whom the water and space elements predominate is fair-complexioned.
Some say that whatever the color of the food a pregnant woman consumes, her offspring will be of that same color.
In that regard, the fire element that has not entered into the range of vision causes blindness from birth;
that same element, when accompanied by phlegm (rakta), results in red eyes,
and when accompanied by bile (pitta), results in yellowish-brown eyes.
That which is accompanied by phlegm results in white eyes;
that which is accompanied by wind results in deformed eyes.
And there are verses on this point:
Just as a lump of ghee, having come into contact with fire, melts away;
The menstrual flow of a woman flows forth likewise upon union with a man.
When the two living beings have entered the womb within the seed by means of the internal wind.
Those two who are preceded by dharma and its opposite are called the Yamas.
Due to the extremely small amount of seed from his parents, a man may become an āsekya (one who must be sprinkled).
Having consumed that semen, he undoubtedly attains the erection of his banner.
He who would be born from a foul womb is designated as Saugandhika.
Having smelled the scent of the vulva and the penis, he gains strength.
He who, through lack of celibacy and so forth, behaves toward his own wife as he would toward other women, acts like a man [toward himself].
He is to be known as a *kumbhīka*;
now hear further about the *īrṣyaka*.
Having seen the sexual union of others, he who engages in sexual union [himself].
He should be known as envious; now hear about the fifth, the eunuch.
He who, out of delusion, approaches his wife during her fertile period as if she were a mere courtesan.
From that, one who possesses the appearance and behavior of a woman is born, designated as a *ṣaṇḍha*.
Or, during her fertile season, if the woman should act like a man, [the child will be male].
In that case, if she should be a maiden, she would possess the conduct of a man.
The āsekya, the sugandhī, the kumbhīka, and likewise the īrṣyaka.
These should be known as those who do not emit semen; one who lacks semen is designated as a *ṣaṇḍha* (eunuch).
But by this affliction, their veins carrying semen [become obstructed].
Through joy they attain expansion, and from that, the raising of the banner occurs.
Endowed with such modes of diet, conduct, and activity as these, they [should remain].
A man and a woman would come together, and their son would be just like them.
When two women, desiring a man, should somehow approach one another;
Discharging semen into one another, they are born there boneless.
If a woman who has bathed after her menses should engage in sexual intercourse during a dream, [she becomes pregnant].
For the wind, having taken up the menstrual blood, indeed forms the embryo within the womb.
Month by month, the signs of pregnancy increase in the pregnant woman.
The kalala is produced from her, devoid of paternal qualities.
And those who have the distorted forms of snakes, scorpions, and gourd-creepers.
These wombs of women should be known as belonging to those who have committed great sins.
The fetus may be destroyed by the provocation of wind (vāta) or by the neglect of the mother's pregnancy-longings (dauhṛda).
One might become hunchbacked, withered, lame, mute, or even speech-impaired.
But due to the lack of faith and the inauspicious deeds committed in the past by one's mother and father, [the child may suffer].
And through the provocation of the wind and other humors, the embryo may undergo deformity.
Due to the smallness of the impurity and the lack of connection between the wind and the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya).
For one situated in the womb does not indeed discharge wind, urine, or feces.
With the mouth covered by the placenta and the throat constricted by the umbilical cord.
And because the passage of the wind is obstructed, the one dwelling in the womb does not cry out.
The embryo experiences the agitation of inhalation and exhalation, as well as dreams.
Arising from the agitation caused by the mother’s sighs, gasps, and dreams.
The formation of bodies, and the falling out and regrowth of teeth.
And that there is an impossibility of hairs [growing] on these [palms and soles] is due to their very nature.
In their previous bodies, they constantly cultivated an intellect devoted to the scriptures.
There are men who are preponderantly composed of living beings and who remember their previous births.
Impelled by which karma, one attains rebirth.
One resorts to those very same qualities that were practiced in a previous body.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Purification of Semen and Menstrual Blood," in the Section on Anatomy (Śārīrasthāna) of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Third Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical section on the descent of the embryo.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

The semen is of the nature of Soma (lunar), while the menstrual blood is of the nature of Agni (fiery); furthermore, there is the presence of other elements here as well, in subtle and specific proportions, due to mutual assistance, mutual favor, and mutual interpenetration.
In that regard, when a woman and a man unite, the vital air (vāyu) impels the fiery element (tejas) out from the body;
then, through the conjunction of fire and wind, the semen is discharged, enters the womb, and mingles with the menstrual blood (ārtava).

Then, through the union of Agni and Soma, the embryo—being joined—is received into the womb. It is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the feeler, the toucher, the smeller, the seer, the hearer, the taster, the Person (*puruṣa*), the creator, the goer, the witness, the sustainer, and the speaker; it is designated by such synonymous names as "Who is this? and so forth. Through its connection with the day-and-night cycle (*dina*), it is imperishable and inconceivable. Being impelled by the wind, together with the elemental self (*bhūtātman*) and the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, as well as with the celestial, demonic, and other dispositions, it enters and remains within the womb.
In that regard, due to the predominance of semen, there is a male; due to the predominance of the menstrual blood (ārtava), there is a female;
and due to the equality of both, there is a neuter.
The fertile period (*ṛtu*) lasts for twelve nights once menstruation has been observed; some, however, say that it exists even when menstruation has not yet been observed.
And there are verses on this point:
[One should recognize a woman] whose face is full and serene, and whose mouth and teeth are moist.
She spoke words pleasing to those in hell, her belly, eyes, and hair hanging down.
With her arms, breasts, hips, navel, thighs, loins, and buttocks quivering.
And one should know that she who is overcome by joy and longing is in her season.
Just as a lotus inevitably closes when the day has passed.
When the fertile season has passed, the womb of a woman likewise becomes closed.
Accumulated over a month, that menstrual blood then flows from the two vessels at the proper time.
The wind should lead [the embryo] to the opening of the birth canal, which is slightly dark and foul-smelling.
Then, after twelve years had passed, blood began to flow once again.
For those whose bodies have been ripened by old age, it reaches its end at fifty years.
In even days, a male is said to be conceived; on other [odd] days, a female.
Therefore, being pure during the period favorable for conception, one who desires offspring should approach his wife.
In that regard, the signs of one who has just conceived a fetus are: fatigue, exhaustion, thirst, weakness in the thighs, the retention of semen and blood, and throbbing in the vagina.
The darkening of the nipples on the breasts and likewise the emergence of the line of body hair.
And even her eyelashes close together especially tightly.
He vomits involuntarily and recoils from pleasant fragrances.
Excessive salivation and lassitude are also said to be the symptoms of a pregnant woman.

From that time forward, one should strictly avoid sexual intercourse, physical exercise, over-satiation, excessive emaciation, sleeping during the day, staying awake at night, grief, riding in vehicles, fear, sitting in a squatting posture, the application of oleation and other such treatments, bloodletting at improper times, and the suppression of natural urges.
Whichever part of the fetus is oppressed by the afflictions of the humors (doṣas) in a pregnant woman, [that part will be impaired].
That very portion of that child, while still dwelling in the womb, is being tormented.

In that regard, in the first month, the *kalala* is produced. In the second month, as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are being matured by cold, heat, and wind, a solid mass (*ghana*) arises if it is to be a male; if a female, a fleshy lump (*peśī*); if a neuter, a bubble-like mass (*arbuda*). In the third month, the five protuberances of the hands, feet, and head are formed, and the differentiation of the limbs and sub-limbs becomes subtle. In the fourth month, the differentiation of all the limbs and sub-limbs becomes distinct.
Due to the manifestation of the heart within the embryo, the element of consciousness becomes manifest.

Why? Because that is its location; therefore, in the fourth month, the embryo forms an intention regarding the objects of the senses. And they call a woman whose heart is doubled "dauhṛdinī" (one possessing pregnancy-longings).
From the neglect of her pregnancy-longings (*dauhṛda*), a woman gives birth to a son who is humpbacked, with withered arms, lame, dull-witted, dwarfed, with deformed eyes, or even sightless.
Therefore, whatever she may desire, that one should cause to be given to her;
for when her longings are fulfilled, she gives birth to a son who is heroic and long-lived.
And there is a verse on this point:
Whatever objects of the senses that pregnant woman desires to enjoy, the physician, having procured them, should cause her to receive them for fear of injury to the fetus.
Having attained her pregnancy-longings, she shall give birth to a son endowed with excellent qualities.
If her pregnancy-longing is not fulfilled, she may experience danger either to the fetus or to herself.
In whatever sensory objects there may be a disregard for one's pregnancy-longing (dauhṛda), [misfortune follows].
Suffering would arise for the son in each and every sense organ accordingly.
If a woman experiences a longing during her pregnancy for the sight of a king, [she should fulfill it].
She gives birth to a son who is meaningful and highly fortunate.
Due to a pregnancy-longing for items such as fine linen, silk, and ornaments.
She gives birth to a graceful son who seeks ornaments.
In the hermitage, she gives birth to one who is self-restrained and virtuous in character.
But from an image of a deity, he gives birth to one who resembles a retainer.
Indeed, upon seeing species of predatory beasts, one gives birth to a violent disposition.
By eating the flesh of a monitor lizard, one gives birth to a son who is characterized by steadfastness [or, according to another reading, "endurance"];
but by eating the flesh of cows, one gives birth to a strong son who likewise endures all hardships.

From the longing of a buffalo for its mate, a hero is born who has red eyes and is covered in hair; [this is because, due to the absence of transformation, the state of the original nature is not lost].
From the meat of a boar, one shall beget a son who is a brave dreamer.
A son who always roams the forest, possessing shanks as powerful as those of a deer leaping along the path.
From the *sṛmara* [deer] comes one with an agitated mind, and from the *taittira* [partridge], one who is constantly afraid.
Therefore, whatever woman conceives a longing for things not mentioned here, [it should be granted].
She will give birth to one who is equal to her in bodily conduct and character.
Impelled by karma, the rebirth of a living being must necessarily come to pass.
In whatever way, through the conjunction of fate, she may conceive a longing in her heart.
In the fifth [week], the mind becomes more awakened;
in the sixth, the intellect;
and in the seventh, the differentiation of all the major and minor limbs becomes more distinct.

In the eighth [month], the vital energy (*ojas*) becomes unstable. One born therein would not live, due to the lack of vital energy and because he belongs to the portion of Nirṛti. Therefore, one should cause an offering (*bali*) of meat-rice to be given to him. He is born in one of the ninth, tenth, eleventh, or twelfth [months].
Otherwise, it becomes subject to modification.
Indeed, the umbilical cord of the embryo is attached to the mother’s nutrient-carrying vessel;
it conveys to him the essence, potency, and vigor of the mother’s food. By means of that nourishment, his growth occurs.

From the moment of conception (*niṣeka*) until the differentiation of the major and minor limbs has occurred, it is the moistening by the obliquely coursing vessels (*dhamanī*) that carry rasa and pervade all parts of the body which sustains life.

Regarding the formation of the embryo, Śaunaka says that the head is formed first, because it is the root of the primary sense organs (or, according to another reading, "the body and sense organs"). Kṛtavīrya says it is the heart, because it is the locus of the intellect and the mind. Pārāśarya says it is the navel.

"For from that, the body of the embodied being grows; [it is] 'the hands and feet,' so says Mārkaṇḍeya, because movement of the embryo has its root there. "The middle part of the body," says Subhūti Gautama, because the development of all the limbs is dependent upon it. But that is not correct.
Dhanvantari states that all the major and minor limbs arise simultaneously;

however, because of the embryo's subtlety, they are not perceived, just like the fibers within a bamboo sprout or the components within a mango fruit. For example, when a mango fruit is fully ripe, its fibers, flesh, seeds, and pulp are seen separately due to the passage of time; yet those very same parts are not perceived when the fruit is young.

Because of their subtlety; time brings about the manifestation of those subtle things, such as hair and so forth. By this very principle, the bamboo sprout is also explained. Thus, although all the major and minor limbs exist in the fetus during its youth, they are not perceived due to their subtlety; it is only through the passage of time that they become manifest.
In this regard, we shall explain the bodily characteristics of the embryo that are derived from the father, the mother, aging, the self, living beings, and suitability. Of the embryo:
hair of the head, beard, body hair, bones, nails, teeth, veins, ligaments, arteries, semen, and other such firm structures are derived from the father.
Flesh, blood, fat, marrow, heart, navel, liver, spleen, intestines, anus, and so forth are the soft parts derived from the mother.
The growth of the body, strength, complexion, stability, and decline are born of the *rasa* (nutritive essence).
The sense organs, cognition, discernment, lifespan, pleasure, pain, and so on are derived from the self (*ātman*).
We shall explain those born of the *sattva* later on;
vigor, health, strength, complexion, and intelligence are born of suitability (*sātmyaja*).

In that regard, one should know that she whose breast on the right side first shows signs of milk, whose right eye becomes large, who first stretches out her right thigh, who has a longing (*daurhṛda*) for substances with masculine names, who perceives in her dreams lotuses, blue lotuses, white lotuses, mangoes, and the like—all of which have masculine names—and whose facial complexion is bright, will give birth to a son. In the opposite case, she will give birth to a girl.
One should know that she whose two sides are elevated and whose abdomen protrudes in front, possessing the characteristics previously described, will give birth to a neuter child.
She whose abdomen is sunken in the middle, like a trough, will give birth to twins.
And there are those here who are devoted to deities and Brahmins, yet remain intent on impurity and improper conduct.
Those who possess [right] qualities produce great virtues, whereas those who are the opposite produce a lack of virtue.
The formation of the major and minor limbs arises from its own inherent nature alone.
Whatever merits and defects arise in the formation of the major and minor limbs;
These various states of the embryo are to be understood as arising from the causes of dharma and adharma.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Descent of the Embryo," in the Section on Anatomy (Śārīrasthāna) of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||3||
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical section entitled "The Description of the Embryo."
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
Fire, moon, wind, goodness, passion, darkness, the five senses, and the elemental self—these are the vital breaths.
For him who has thus proceeded, as the semen and blood are being transformed, seven layers of skin (*tvac*) arise, like the curdled film on the surface of milk.
Of these, the first is named *Avabhāsinī*;
it illuminates all colors and manifests the fivefold shadow.
It is eighteen parts of a grain of rice in measure and is presided over by Siddha, Padma, and Kaṇṭaka; the second is named Lohitā,
sixteen parts of a grain of rice in measure.

The third is named Śvetā, measuring twelve parts of a grain of rice (*vrīhi*); it is the seat for skin eruptions (*carmadala*), ringworm (*ajagallī*), and lice (*maśaka*). The fourth is named Tāmrā, measuring eight parts of a grain of rice;
it is the seat for various types of leucoderma (*kilāsa*) and leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). The fifth is named Vedinī.
The sixth is named Rohiṇī; it is five parts of a grain of rice in size, has leprosy and erysipelas as its primary sites,
and is equal in measure to a grain of rice.

The seventh layer, named *māṃsadharā*, measures two grains of rice in thickness; it is the site of glandular swellings (*granthi*), abscesses (*apaci*), tumors (*arbuda*), elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), and goiters (*galagaṇḍa*),
as well as fistulas (*bhagandara*), ulcers (*vidradhi*), and hemorrhoids (*arśas*).

This measurement which has been specified applies to fleshy areas, but not to the forehead or delicate parts such as the fingers; for he will state regarding the abdomen: "one should pierce it to a depth equal to the belly of a thumb using the tip of a grain of rice."
[In the body there are six layers of skin; ... (Ca.Sū.Śā.A.7.Sū.5).
"The sixth, however, sustains life"—this is the reading in the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha.
As for the "layers of skin" (tvacaḥ): they are the earth-like element that serves as the covering of the entire body, [the site] of the sense organ of touch, and of the channels that carry sweat.]
[This applies] even to the hairs, including all the hair-pores.
From a gross perspective, these [layers] are divided into two strata: the outer cuticle and the inner cuticle.
Among them, the outer cuticle is extremely thin, the substrate for colors such as black and fair, and it manifests as burns and blisters upon contact with fire.
The skin is internal; it is thick, the protector of the body, and the drawer of moisture and other fluids.
It is the primary seat of the element of touch and the channels for the flow of sweat (Pratyakṣaśārīra, Prabhā, pp. 5–6).
Furthermore, there are indeed seven layers (*kalās*) that exist as the boundaries between the tissues (*dhātus*) and the visceral cavities (*āśayas*).
And there are these verses on this point: "Just as the heartwood is seen within logs when they are being split apart..."
For in this way, the element is indeed seen within the flesh as it is being cut.
They are covered with sinews and enveloped by the fetal membrane.
And they know those portions of the constituent parts (*kalā*) to be enveloped by phlegm (*śleṣman*).

[In some books, the following is read additionally: "In front of this, that moisture of food which resides within the internal receptacles of the elements (*dhātu-āśaya*), once digested by the heat of the body, is called *kalā*.

Among them, the first is named the *māṃsa-dhārā* (flesh-bearing layer); in it, the expansions of the veins (*sirā*), ligaments (*snāyu*), arteries (*dhamanī*), and channels (*srotas*) exist within the flesh.

[The reading preferred by Hārāṇacandra is "māṃsagatānām"; the reading preferred by Vaiśampāyana Hariprapanna is "māṃsa-sirā-snāyu-dhamanī-srotasām". For a detailed explanation, see pages 164–165 of the introduction to the *Rasayogasāgara*.]
And there is a verse on this point: Just as lotus stalks and fibers grow forth in every direction, so it is here.
Just as mud and water exist upon the earth, so do the veins and other [channels] exist within the flesh.
The second layer is named Raktadhara (blood-bearing), situated within the flesh;

in it, blood is found especially in the vessels, the liver, and the spleen. Regarding this, there is a verse: Just as milk flows from a milky tree when it is struck, [so does blood flow from the body].
From the wound in the flesh, blood is thus quickly shed in abundance.
The third is named Medodharā; for fat (medas) exists in all beings within the abdomen, in the small bones, and in the large [bones] it becomes marrow (majjā).

[And that very thing, covered by the skull on the head, is called the brain and the marrow. This is an additional reading in the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*. "Fat (medas)—it is a fatty tissue of the body equal to thickened ghee;
its location is within the abdomen."

And below the skin is *vasā*, which is a fatty substance (*sneha*) that has entered between the muscles; its entry into the fat (*medas*) is due to their having a common material cause (*tulyopādānatva*).
That which is called *majjā* (marrow) is the fatty substance located within the bone.
It is of two kinds: yellow and red.
Therein, the yellow is within the bones of the marrow-cavities;
the red is in the other bones.

And in the extremities of the long bones (nalakāsthi), this [bone marrow], although not distinct from fat (medas) in its gross form, is indeed a separate constituent (dhātu) due to its specific functional difference. (Pratyakṣa-śārīra, Prabhā commentary, p. 10).
And there is a verse on this point:
Marrow is specifically situated within the large bones, residing in their interior.
In all other cases, however, it is said that the fat is accompanied by blood.
The oily essence of pure flesh is designated as fat (vasā).
The fourth is named Śleṣmadharā; it exists in all the joints of living beings.
And there is a verse on this point:
"Just as a wheel turns smoothly when the axle is lubricated with oil."
The joints function properly and remain well-knit by means of phlegm.
The fifth is named Purīṣadhara; it is situated in the receptacle for digested food (pakvāśaya) and separates the waste matter within the abdominal cavity.
And there is a verse on this point:
The liver is situated all around the abdominal cavity as well as the intestines.
The impurity-sustaining power (kalā) divides the waste situated in the unduka.

The sixth is named *pittadhārā*; it maintains the four kinds of food and drink that have been consumed, once they have moved from the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and reached the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*).
The sixth [channel] is named Pittadhara; it is situated between the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and the small intestine (*pakvāśaya*).

Because it serves as the seat of the internal fire, it forcibly holds back the food directed from the stomach toward the small intestine, dries it with the heat of bile (*pitta*), digests it, and releases what has been digested.
However, when it is afflicted by the *doṣas*, due to weakness, it releases even undigested matter.

Therefore, because it receives food, it is further designated as the *grahaṇī* (the receptor). Its strength is indeed bile (*pitta*), which is synonymous with fire (*agni*); thus, supported, nourished, and sharing a single destiny with fire, it sustains the body. Regarding this, there is a verse: [From the *Śārīrasthāna* of the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha*] And here [is the verse]: The *grahaṇī* is the seat of the digestive fire; it is the receptacle of food and drink. It is the root of the body, and it is said to be the very life-force itself. When it is impaired by wind, bile, or phlegm, or by all three combined, it causes various diseases in the body. When it is in its natural state, it maintains health. Therefore, one should always protect the *grahaṇī*. It is like a king who protects his kingdom through his ministers. Thus has been explained the *grahaṇī*. One should know that the entire body depends upon it. Just as a tree perishes when its roots are cut, so does the body perish when the *grahaṇī* is destroyed. Therefore, one should preserve the *grahaṇī* with great care. It is the foundation of all bodily functions. Thus ends the section on the *grahaṇī*. May there be well-being.
The food that has been eaten, chewed, and drunk, once it has entered the stomach of men—
That [food] is digested at the proper time, having been dried by the heat of the bile.
The seventh is named Śukradhārā; it pervades the entire body of all living beings.
And there are verses on this point:
Just as butter exists in milk, and as sweetness exists hidden in sugarcane juice.
Likewise, the best of physicians should know that semen exists within the bodies of men.
Two finger-breadths on the right side, and also below the opening of the bladder.
The semen of a man flows out through the path of the urinary tract.
Regarding the statement, "Two finger-breadths on the right side and below the opening of the bladder,
the semen of a man issues forth through the path of the urinary tract," the reading "two finger-breadths on the left" (*dvyaṅgule vāme*) is more appropriate;
otherwise, it would contradict both direct observation and one's own experience.
For it is stated in the Suśruta [Saṃhitā] itself (Pratyakṣaśarīra, Upodghāta): "Indeed, two [channels] carry semen for the manifestation of semen, and two for the emission of semen."
Likewise, the semen residing throughout the entire body of one whose mind is serene— (page 72).]
And for one who exerts himself among women, that [semen] flows forth from joy.
In women who have conceived, the pathways of the channels that carry the menstrual flow (ārtava) are obstructed by the embryo.

In that case, one lives with the arrow [embedded] within, either because it has fallen out through suppuration or because it has not been extracted; [the vessel] situated between the eyebrows is named Sthapanī.

In that regard, it is like Utkṣepa; five joints are distributed on the head, known as the Sīmanta [sutures]. In that regard, death occurs through insanity, fear, or mental anguish; [there are] the confluences of vessels (*sirāsannipāta*) in the midst of the vessels that nourish the nose, ears, eyes, and tongue—[these are] the fourfold structures known as *śṛṅgāṭaka*.
Regarding the phrase "tatrāpi":
those are the four vital points (*marmāṇi*). Therein also occurs immediate death. Above the interior of the head, at the junction where the vessels converge, is the hair-whorl known as *adhipati*.
In that case as well, death occurs immediately [the reading 'asadyomaraṇam' is noted as an alternative].
Thus, these thirty-seven vital points (marmans) located above the clavicle have been explained.
And there are verses on this point:
"The upward-tending vessels are at the head, at the shoulder-joint, and at the sides of the armpits; each is measured by one finger-breadth from the root of the breast."
The wrist and the ankle measure two finger-breadths; the knee, along with the elbow, measures exactly three.
They say there are four [marmas] in the heart, the bladder, the tongue-tip, and the anus; five in the navel; ten in the head; and two in the throat.
Know that those [measures] are equal to the span of one's own palm when the fingers are curled; the remaining ones, in their full extent, are half a finger-breadth less.
Having observed this authoritative standard, those who know the truth declare that the work should be accomplished by avoiding the use of weapons.
Even when struck from the side, it destroys the vital point (marman) here; therefore, one must avoid the seat of the vital points.
When the hands and feet of men are severed, the vessels contract; therefore, only a small amount of blood flows out.
Having encountered this terrible and immeasurable calamity, men do not go to their destruction like trees whose branches have been completely severed.
When those swift, deep-seated vessels are injured, blood flows excessively and the wind (vāyu) causes intense pain.
Thus they indeed meet their destruction there, like trees whose roots have been severed by the falling of weapons.
Therefore, the hands and feet of one who strikes them must be swiftly severed at the wrists and the ankles.
They declare that the vital points (marmas) constitute half the scope of the subject of arrows, because those struck in the vital points do not die instantly.
If some should survive there by virtue of a physician's skill, they will undoubtedly suffer from infirmity.
With their chests and skulls shattered and mangled, they remain alive despite their bodies being struck down by weapons.
And their thighs, arms, feet, and hands were all severed, and various blows had been struck at their vital organs.
The splendors of Soma and the Maruts, as well as the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas.
The elemental self (bhūtātman) generally resides in the vital points (marmas) of men.
Therefore, embodied beings do not survive when struck in their vital points (marmans).
The non-attainment of the objects of the senses, and the perversion of the mind and intellect.
And various intense pains arise when the āśuhara [wind] is struck.
But when the hatred persists for a long time, there is certainly a depletion of the bodily constituents in men.
Then, due to the exhaustion of the elements and because of the sensations, the living being perishes.
In the case of producing a deficiency [of a sense organ], it occurs solely through the skill of the physician.
The body, when joined with activity, may fall into a state of impairment.
In the case of those [plants] that destroy arrows (viśalyaghna), one should understand the previously mentioned reason as well.
The vital points (marmas) cause pain when injured, resulting in various types of affliction.
And if one falls under the power of a quack physician, they bring about a deficiency at the end.
From cutting, splitting, striking, burning, and even tearing asunder.
One should recognize that injury to the vital points (marmans) possesses characteristics identical to those [of the aforementioned injuries].
But there is indeed some injury to the vital points which results either in slight harm or even in no harm at all.
Generally, those struck in their vital spots either fall into a state of deformity or die.
For those various disorders that arise in the bodies of men do so by taking hold of the vital points (marmas).
Generally, these become most difficult for a man, even when being accomplished through great efforts.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Individual Vital Points," in the Section on Anatomy of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Seventh Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical treatise (śārīra) named "The Classification of the Colors of the Veins" (*sirāvarṇavibhakti*).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

There are seven hundred vessels (sirā); by means of these, this body is moistened and sustained—like a garden by water-carrying channels or like a field by irrigation ditches—and is provided with specific functions such as contraction and extension. Their extensions are like the veins of a tree leaf, and their root is the navel;
from there they spread upwards, downwards, and across.
And you should know that, within the body of embodied beings, however many veins there may be that arise therein.
All of them are fixed at the navel and extend outward in every direction.
The vital breaths of living beings reside in the navel, and the navel is supported by the vital breaths.
The navel is surrounded by vessels, like the hub of a wheel by its spokes.
Of these, there are forty root vessels; of these, ten carry wind, ten carry bile,
and ten carry phlegm.
There are ten blood-carrying channels.
Of those wind-carrying channels located in the regions of wind, there are one hundred and seventy-five;
an equal number of bile-carrying channels are located in the region of bile.
Those carrying kapha are located in the seat of kapha; those carrying blood are located in the liver and spleen. Thus, these constitute seven hundred vessels.
Among those, there are twenty-five vāta-carrying vessels (sirā) in one leg;
by this, the other leg and both arms are explained.
Specifically, however, there are thirty-four in the trunk (koṣṭha); of these, eight are located in the pelvis (śroṇī), resting upon the anus and the penis.
Two on each side,
six on the back,
and just as many on the belly.
There are ten in the chest;
forty-one above the collarbone;
and of those, fourteen are in the neck.
Four in the ears;
nine in the tongue;
six in the nose.
There are eight in the eyes.
Thus, these one hundred and seventy-five vessels that carry wind (*vātavahā*) have been explained.
This same division applies to the remaining [vessels] as well.
Specifically, there are ten veins in the eyes that carry bile (*pitta*), and two in the ears; likewise, there are those that carry blood and those that carry phlegm (*kapha*).
Thus, these seven hundred veins have been explained with their respective divisions.
And there are verses on this point:
[It is characterized by] the non-obstruction of actions and the absence of delusion regarding cognition and deeds.
The wind, moving through the channels (sirās), also produces other qualities.
But when the provoked wind enters its own channels, [it causes disease].
Then, various diseases arising from wind (vāta) are produced in him.
Radiance, appetite for food, digestive fire, and freedom from disease.
Pitta, spreading through its own channels, produces these [symptoms] as well as other qualities.
When the naturally situated bile courses through its own channels, [it remains in its normal state].
Then various diseases arising from bile (pitta) are produced in him.
Oiliness in the limbs provides stability, strength, and vigor to the joints.
Furthermore, the phlegm (balāsa), moving through its own channels, also produces other qualities.
But when the provoked phlegm enters its own channels, [it causes the following symptoms].
Then various diseases arising from phlegm (śleṣman) are produced in him.
The filling of the elements is undoubtedly the knowledge of touch.
It causes one's own veins to flow with blood and produces other beneficial qualities as well.
But when the provoked blood courses through its own carrying vessels (sirās), [it produces the following symptoms].
Then, various diseases arising from the blood are produced in him.
For there are no channels that carry only wind, nor likewise those that carry only bile.
Or they carry phlegm; therefore, these are known as the "all-carrying" vessels.
For when the vices are corrupted, elevated, intensified, and rushing forward—
Therefore, they are traditionally known as "carrying all," because they certainly lead one away from the right path.
There, the blood-red vessels carrying the wind are filled with air.
From pitta, they are hot and blue;
from kapha, they are cold, white, and stable.
The Rohiṇī vessels, however, carry blood; they are neither excessively hot nor excessively cold.
Henceforth I shall declare those veins which the physician must not pierce.
He brought about their emaciation and even death; indeed, it would become like a disease for them.
A wise person should know that there are four hundred vessels in the branches.
And one hundred and thirty-six in the chest, and sixty-four in the head.
There are sixteen vessels in the limbs and exactly thirty-two in the trunk.
Fifty [veins] above the collarbone are proclaimed to be non-piercable.
In that regard, there are one hundred vessels (*sirā*) in each leg; of these, one is called *jāladharā*,
and three are internal— among them, two are designated as *urvī* and one is designated as *lohitākṣā*.
These, however, are not to be incised. By this, the other thigh and the two arms are explained. Thus, there are sixteen [muscles] in the limbs that are not to be operated upon with a knife.
There are thirty-two in the pelvis;
of these, eight are not to be operated upon—two in each of the "vitapas" (buttock regions).
And there are two at the hips and the sacrum; eight on each side.
One should avoid piercing each of these as it extends upward.
There are also two located at the side-joints; and twenty-four on the back, situated on both sides of the spinal column. (*The word "pṛṣṭhe" is not read in some manuscripts.)

Of those [veins], one should avoid two pairs of the *bṛhatī* vessels that course upward; the same number [two pairs] are in the abdomen. Of those, one should avoid two pairs on each side of the line of hair above the penis. There are forty [veins] in the chest.
Of those, fourteen are not to be treated with the knife—two in the heart.
There are two at each root of the breasts;
thus, there are eight on both sides in the regions of the nipples, the armpits, and the shoulders. In this way, there are thirty-two surgical sites (शल्यकृत्य) on the back, abdomen, and chest.
Six hundred and forty vessels (sirā) are located above the collarbone (jatru); among them, fifty-six are in the neck (śirodharā). [Note: Some versions read "fifty-eight" here.]
Among those, one should avoid the eight and four known as vital points (*marmans*):
two in the nape of the neck (*kṛkāṭika*) and two in the temples (*vidhura*).
Thus, there are sixteen non-puncturable vessels in the neck; eight on each side of the jaws.
Of these, one should avoid the two junctional vessels (sandhi-dhamanī) on each side. There are thirty-six [vessels] in the tongue;
of these, sixteen below are not to be operated upon with a blade.
There are two channels carrying taste and two carrying speech; there are twenty-four in the nose.
Among these, one should avoid the four that are situated near the nose.
And among those very [channels], one should avoid one at the soft region of the palate; thirty-eight in both eyes (or, according to another reading, thirty-six in both eyes);
one of them should be avoided at the outer corners of the eyes; ten in the ears;
from among those, one should avoid each of the sound-carrying channels; and sixty in the forehead for those that go to the nose and eyes.
One should avoid four [lines] following the ends of their hair;
one each at the two whorls;
and one at the *sthapanī*.
One should avoid ten [veins] in the two temples (*śaṅkha*);
among those, one should avoid each single vein located at the junction of the temples. (Thus, these veins located in the nose and eyes are to be understood. There are twelve [veins] in the head;
among those, one should avoid two located in the *utkṣepa* [sinuses].
"One at each of the hair-parting lines, and one on the crown";
thus, there are fifty [vital points] above the collarbone that are not to be pierced by weapons.
And there is a verse on this point:
"The vessels (sirās) that have spread out from the navel pervade the body on all sides."
Just as the tendrils of lotus roots, stalks, and the like depend upon water, so it is with this.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Classification of Veins," in the Section on Anatomy of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||7||
The eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical treatise on the procedure for venesection.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

One should not venesection the veins of children, the elderly, those who are rough, those suffering from chest wounds or emaciation, the timid, the exhausted, those debilitated by alcohol, travel, or women, those who have undergone emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), or unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), those who are awake at night, the impotent, the thin, pregnant women, and those afflicted by cough, dyspnea, wasting, aggravated fever, convulsions, hemiplegia, fasting, thirst, or fainting. Furthermore, one should not venesection those veins that are prohibited from being pierced, nor those that are indicated for venesection but remain unobserved.
And they are seen to be unrestrained,
and restrained yet not having arisen.

Regarding those disorders previously mentioned that are curable by bloodletting, as well as others not mentioned here, one should perform venesection according to one's practice and according to the proper method, provided they have not yet reached a state of suppuration.
Furthermore, even for those [procedures] that are prohibited, venesection is not prohibited in cases of poisoning, afflictions, or life-threatening emergencies.

There, having prepared the patient—who has been lubricated and fomented, who has eaten food consisting mostly of liquids (or gruel) that is contrary to the specific doshas, or who has drunk gruel—at the appropriate time, one should have him sit or stand; then, without endangering his vital breaths, having secured the area of the body with a cloth, bandage, leather, inner bark, or creeper—neither too tightly nor too loosely—and having taken up the surgical instrument as prescribed, one should pierce the vein.
Neither in extreme cold, nor in excessive heat, nor in a strong wind, nor in a place without shelter.
The venesection of veins should never be performed on one who is free from disease.

In that procedure, having seated the patient afflicted with *vyādhyasira* facing the sun on a seat one *aratni* high, and having placed his two elbows upon his two contracted thighs—with his hands resting on top of the two joints, their thumbs tucked inside and formed into fists—the physician should wrap a binding cloth over the neck and the fists. Then, having had another person standing behind him grasp both ends of the cloth with the left hand turned upward, the physician should say: "Press the instrument against the middle of the back for the purpose of raising the vein."

And one should place a "manikin" (karmapuruṣa) with its mouth filled with air [the variant reading says: "one should fill the mouth of the manikin with air"]; this is the method of restraint for the application of instruments upon the vessels located in the head, excluding those that enter the interior of the mouth.

In that case, having raised the slightly contracted foot high and wrapped it below the knee-joint with a cloth, one should press the ankle with both hands; then, having bound it four finger-breadths above the site to be pierced with a tourniquet made of any material such as a hempen cloth, one should pierce the vein of the foot.

Alternatively, having placed the hands above with the fists formed by concealing the thumbs properly upon the seat, and having bound the tourniquet as before for the patient seated comfortably, one should pierce the vein of the hand.

For those suffering from *gṛdhrasī* or *viśvācī*, one should pierce [the vein] while the patient is seated with his knees and elbows drawn in, his back arched toward the hips, back, and shoulders, his head hanging down, and his back trembling. For ailments of the abdomen or chest, one should pierce while the patient extends his chest, raises his head, and trembles his entire body.
When the body is supported by the two arms, [the vein] at the sides;
when the penis is lowered, [the vein] at the penis;
when the tip of the tongue is raised and bitten, [the vein] below the tongue.
One should apply [the instrument] to the palate of one whose mouth is excessively opened, or to the roots of the teeth;
having thus examined with the intellect other mechanical means and methods for elevating the veins, one should employ them according to the condition of the body and the nature of the disease.
In fleshy areas, one should insert the instrument to the depth of a barley-corn (*yava*);
in other [areas], to half a barley-corn, or to the depth of a grain of rice (*vrīhi*) using a rice-mouthed instrument (*vrīhimukha*).
Over bones, one should pierce to the depth of half a barley-corn with a small axe-shaped instrument (*kuṭhārikā*).
And there are verses on this point:
"One should pierce [the vein] during the rains when the sky is cloudless, or during the summer season when it is cool."
In the winter season, at midday—these three are remembered as the times for using weapons.
By the proper application of the surgical instrument, blood flows in a continuous stream.
One should remain blocked for a moment and then designate that [vein] as well-pierced.
Just as yellow dye first flows forth from safflower blossoms.
Likewise, when the veins have been pierced, the vitiated blood flows out first.
For one who is fainted, excessively terrified, exhausted, or thirsty.
Veins that have been pierced do not flow [properly] if they have not been raised and secured with a bandage.
Of one whose [strength] is exhausted, whose many humors are aggravated, and who is struck down by fainting (or, according to another reading, "overwhelmed").
Having caused her to rest further in the afternoon, she [should be made to rest] on the following day, or even after three days, or on the day after that.
However, even a wise physician may leave some blood remaining along with the residual humors.
One should not cause it to flow excessively; the remainder should be overcome with pacifying treatments.
For an embodied being who is strong, possessed of many humors, and in the prime of youth.
They maintain that one prastha is the maximum measure for the extraction of blood.

In cases such as *pādadāha* (burning of the feet), *pādaharṣa* (numbness of the feet), *avabāhuka* (sciatica), *cipya*, *visarpa*, *vātaśoṇita*, *vātakaṇṭaka*, *vicarcikā* (eczema), *pādadārī* (cracking of the feet), and so forth, one should pierce the vein with a *vrīhimukha* instrument two finger-breadths above the *kṣipra* marman. [Regarding this, Hārāṇacandra notes that some include *avabāhuka* here; he states that this is correct because it is intended to be treated by venesection in the prescribed therapeutic procedure. Furthermore, the term *cipya* is not mentioned in some recensions.]
In the case of elephantiasis (ślīpada), one should follow the treatment as it will be described later.
For the conditions known as kroṣṭukaśiras, lameness (khañja), club-foot (paṅgu), and Vāta-pain, the site is four finger-breadths above the ankle on the calf.
For scrofula (apacī), the site is two finger-breadths below the indrabasti.
In cases of *gṛdhrasī*, the vein is located four finger-breadths above or below the knee joint;
in cases of goiter (*galagaṇḍa*), it is situated at the root of the thigh.

By this, the other leg and both arms are explained; however, specifically for the left arm, it is found either internally at the elbow joint, in the middle of the arm, or between the little finger and the ring finger, corresponding to the spleen.
Likewise, on the right arm—in the region called the liver (*yakṛt*) and in the phlegm-belly (*kaphodara*)—they prescribe this very same [vein] for cough and asthma as well. (Note:
Hārāṇacandra states that the reading "in the liver-mouth and the phlegm-belly" found here is not based on an authoritative source, because venesection is of no use for the phlegm-belly.)
In cases of *viśvācī*, it is like [the point for] a vulture's nest;
for *pravāhikā* and *śūlinī*, it is two finger-breadths all around the hip;
and for disorders of *parivartikā*, *upadaṃśa*, *śūka*, and defects of the semen, it is in the middle of the penis.
In cases of urinary distension (*mūtravṛddhi*), [the incision is made] on the side of the testicles;
in cases of ascites (*dakodara*), it is four finger-breadths below the navel on the left side of the midline.

[*"Aha! There is some teacher who has neither heard nor properly studied [the scriptures], for when it is intended to perform venesection for the purpose of draining the morbid humors (doṣa) and fluid in cases of urinary distension (mūtravṛddhi) and ascites (dakodara), he considers only the venesection itself and declares—contrary to what was never heard before and being inconsistent—the following: 'in urinary distension, on the side of the scrotum,' and 'in ascites, four finger-breadths from the navel on the left side of the raphe. By doing so, he proclaims his own lack of learning, his lack of practical experience, and his status as one who previously pierced veins in the wrong place," says Hārāṇacandra. For internal abscess (antarvidradhi) and pain in the sides (pārśvaśūla), [on the left side, between the armpit and the breast]; [after this, the phrase "this very [vein] in phlegmatic ascites (kaphodara) on the left side" is read additionally in some manuscripts].
Some say it is located between the shoulders in cases of *bāhuśoṣa* and *avabāhuka*;
in *tṛtīyaka* fever, it is situated in the middle of the *trika* joint;
and in *caturthaka* fever, it is located at the lower shoulder joint and situated on one side of the body.
In cases of epilepsy, [one should apply it] to the middle of the jaw-joint;
in cases of insanity, to the junction of the temple and the hairline, and to the chest, the outer corners of the eyes, and the forehead;
and for diseases of the tongue and dental ailments, to the lower lip.
On the palate for diseases of the palate; above both ears for earache and its related ailments;
and at the tip of the nose for the loss of the sense of smell and diseases of the nasal passages.
In eye diseases such as *timira* (blindness) and *akṣipāka* (inflammation of the eyes), one should apply [the enema] through the nose, or through the *lālāṭī* or *apāṅgī* vessels.
And these same [vessels] are used for diseases of the head such as *adhimantha* (ophthalmia) and others.

Hereafter, we shall explain the improper methods of venesection (duṣṭavyadhana). In this regard, there are twenty types of faulty punctures: the poorly pierced (durviddhā), the excessively pierced (atividdhā), the curved (kuñcitā), the pressed (piccitā), the bruised (kuṭṭitā), the non-exuding (aprasrutā), the over-excited (atyudīrṇā), the struck at the end (ante'bhihatā), the dried up (pariśuṣkā), the constricted (kūṇitā), the trembling (avepitā), the pierced without elevation (anutthitaviddhā), the wounded by the instrument (śastrahatā), the obliquely pierced (tiryagviddhā), the missed (apaviddhā), the unpierceable (avyadhyā), the run-away (vidrutā), the milch-cow-like (dhenukā), the repeatedly pierced (punaḥpunarviddhā), and those pierced in the flesh, veins, ligaments, bones, joints, or vital spots (marmas). These are the twenty faulty punctures.

Among these, that which is pierced by a minute instrument, from which blood flows imperceptibly, and which is accompanied by pain and swelling, is called "badly pierced" (durviddhā). When pierced with an instrument exceeding the proper measure, blood enters deep within or there is excessive hemorrhage; this is called "over-pierced" (atividdhā).
The same applies to a curved incision.
It was crushed by blunt weapons, swollen, and pounded;
it had not been reached [in its entirety], yet it was repeatedly struck by weapons at both ends and hacked many times;
with blood not flowing due to cold, fear, and fainting, it was "unstreaming" (aprasrutā).
Pierced by a sharp, large-mouthed instrument, it is excessively aggravated;
pierced at the edge, it bleeds little blood at first but is struck at the end, becoming dry as the blood is depleted and filled with wind;
when struck in four parts, it has slightly discharged blood and becomes constricted.
For one trembling due to being bound in an improper position, there occurs a confusion of the blood; she is called "trembling" (vepitā).
The same applies to one who has been pierced but has not yet risen.
One whose blood flows excessively because it has been severed is "struck by the blade" (śastrahatā), as it causes obstruction to medical treatment.
A wound made by a weapon applied obliquely is "obliquely pierced" when only a small portion remains [unpierced].
It is "lacerated" when wounded in many places due to the application of an inferior weapon.
It is "incapable of being pierced" when it has not been treated with a weapon.
*Anavasthitavidvā* is one that has been pierced and then fled.
*Ārohadvyadhā* is so called because it is repeatedly struck in the same region, resulting in frequent bleeding.
*Dhenukā* is—su- [the rest of the definition follows].
Repeatedly pierced by the striking of earth and weapons— [reading "abhinnā" as "avicchinnā" in another version]—
and pierced again and again in the flesh, sinews, bones, vessels, joints, and vital points (marmans), it produces pain, swelling, deformity, and death.
And there are verses on this point:
"There is no one truly skilled in the veins, for they are unstable by their very nature."
They revolve like fish; therefore, one should strike them with great effort.
But when a weapon is grasped unknowingly and brought down upon the body, [there is no fault].
These misfortunes arise, as do many other calamities.
Neither by applications of unguents and the like, nor even by medicinal plasters, is it [healed] in such a manner.
Diseases quickly attain pacification, just as they do from a properly performed venesection.
Venesection is proclaimed in the Śalyatantra to be half of medical treatment.
Just as a properly administered enema is for the treatment of the body, so too is [this] when rightly applied.

In this regard, those who have undergone oleation (snigdha), sudation (svinna), emesis (vānta), purgation (virikta), non-unctuous enema (āsthāpita), unctuous enema (anuvāsita), or venesection (sirāviddha) must avoid the following until they regain their strength: anger, exertion, sexual intercourse, daytime sleep, excessive speech, physical exercise, fasting, standing, sitting, walking about, cold, wind, heat, incompatible foods, unwholesome food, and indigestion.
Some authorities maintain that this period lasts for one month.
We shall explain these matters in detail further below.
And in this matter,
you [should act] with leeches, horns, gourds, as well as with suckers and feet.
One should extract the vitiated blood that has become deeply embedded, just as one did previously.
When the blood has flowed deeply, leeches should be applied; when it has become thickened, scarification is beneficial.
When blood pervades the limbs, one should use a horn; when it resides in the skin, one should use a gourd.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Procedure for Venesection," in the Section on Anatomy of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Ninth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical treatise on the description of the vessels.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

Twenty-four vessels (dhamanī) originating from the navel have been described. Regarding this, some say that there is no distinction between the veins (sirā), the vessels (dhamanī), and the channels (srotas); for they maintain that the vessels and the channels are merely modifications of the veins.

But that is not correct. For the *dhamanīs* and the *srotas* are indeed distinct from the *sirās*. Why? Because of the difference in their characteristics (*vyañjana*), because of the restriction regarding their origins (*mūla-sanniyama*), because of the distinction in their functions (*karma-vaiśeṣya*), and because of scriptural authority (*āgama*). However, due to their mutual proximity, their having similar origins and functions, and their subtlety (*saukṣmya*), there appears to be a non-distinction in their functions even though they are actually distinct.
Of those vessels indeed originating from the navel, ten course upwards, ten course downwards,
and four course transversely.

The upward-moving channels sustain the body by conveying specific modifications such as sound, touch, form, taste, smell, exhalation, inhalation, yawning, hunger, laughter, speaking, weeping, and so forth. Having reached the heart, they become threefold;
these are thirty in number.
Among them, ten carry pairs of wind, bile, phlegm, blood, and nutrient essence respectively.
One perceives sounds, forms, tastes, and odors with eight [faculties];
one speaks with two;
and one produces vocal sound with two.
By two [channels] one sleeps;
by two one awakens;
and there are two that carry tears.
Two [channels] carry breast milk in women, residing in the breasts;
those same two carry semen in men through the breasts.
Thus, these thirty channels, along with their divisions, have been explained.
By these [vessels], the abdomen, sides, back, chest, shoulders, neck, and arms are supported and maintained above the navel.
And there is a verse on this point:
"Those who are destined for the higher realms perform all these actions in every respect."
I shall now describe, according to their respective natures, the actions of those [karmas] that lead downward.
The downward-moving [channels], however, carry down wind, urine, feces, semen, menstrual blood, and so forth.
Having reached the seat of bile (*pittāśaya*), they separate the digested essence of food and drink situated therein by means of heat;
carrying it upward, they satisfy the body and supply it to the upward-moving and lateral-moving [channels].
They fill the seat of the rasa (nutritive fluid) and separate the urine, feces, and sweat; they arise in three types within the space between the stomach and the large intestine.
These are thirty in number; of these, ten carry each two [channels] for vāta, pitta, kapha, blood, and rasa.
Two [channels] carrying food are supported by the intestines;
two carry water;
and two carry urine, having reached the urinary bladder.
Two [channels] carry semen for its manifestation;

two are for emission. These very same ones also carry the blood known as the menses (ārtava) of women, [and they also emit it]. (*Note: Some manuscripts do not contain the word "visṛjataḥ" [they emit].*)
Two are the excrement-carrying channels (varconirasanyau), connected to the large intestine (sthūlāntra).
Eight others, which course transversely, convey sweat to the vessels (dhamanī). Thus, these thirty [channels] have been explained with their divisions.
By means of these downward-flowing channels, the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), the waist, urine, feces, the anus, the bladder, the penis, and the thighs are supported and maintained.
And there is a verse on this point:
"But those who go downwards perform all these actions in every respect."
I shall now fully describe those who go among the animals, and their respective karmas as they truly are.
Of the four vessels that course horizontally, each is divided further and further into a hundred and a thousand branches;
they are indeed innumerable.
By means of these, this body is latticed, bound together, and stretched out.
Their openings are connected to the hair follicles;
through these, they carry away sweat and nourish the internal fluids both internally and externally.
By those very same channels, the potencies of massage, affusion, immersion, and ointments reach the interior of the body, having been processed within the skin.

And by means of these very [channels], one perceives touch as either pleasant or unpleasant; thus, these four vessels (dhamanīs), which extend throughout all the limbs, have been explained with their respective divisions.
And as it is said here:
"Just as cavities exist naturally within lotus stalks and fibers."
Likewise, the vessels (dhamanīs) have their own channels through which the nutrient essence (rasa) is accumulated.
Then, having become the five masters, they cultivate the five faculties five times over the five [objects].
Having cultivated the five faculties with respect to the five [objects], they return to a state of fivefold dissolution at the time of destruction.
Hereafter, we shall explain the characteristics of the vessels (srotas) when their roots are pierced.
These [vessels] carry breath, food, water, plasma, blood, flesh, fat, urine, feces, semen, and menstrual blood.
When they are unimpaired, there is health; some of them have many branches, and these possess numerous specific varieties.
Therein, there are two [channels] carrying the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Their root is the heart, as are the vessels (*dhamanī*) carrying the nutrient fluid (*rasa*)—[the reading "carrying the vital breath" (*prāṇavāhinī*) is also found]. If one pierces these, there occurs shouting, bending, delusion, whirling, trembling, or death. There are also two [channels] carrying food.
The root of those two is the stomach and the food-carrying vessels (dhamanīs).
One pierced there suffers from flatulence, colic, aversion to food, vomiting, thirst, blindness, and death. There are two water-carrying [vessels];
their roots are the palate and the kloman.

In that case, for one who is pierced [in the *rasa*-carrying vessels], there is thirst, incurability, and a dark discoloration of the limbs, as well as immediate death. There are two *rasa*-carrying [vessels];
their root is the heart and the *rasa*-carrying arteries (*dhamanī*).

For one pierced therein, there is emaciation, and death occurs as in the case of a piercing of the life-carrying [vessels], along with its characteristic signs. There are two blood-carrying [vessels].
The roots of these two are the liver, the spleen, and the blood-carrying vessels.
One pierced there experiences a dark discoloration of the limbs, fever, burning sensations, pallor, excessive loss of blood, and redness of the eyes. There are two [vessels] carrying muscle tissue.
Their roots are the tendons, the skin, and the blood-carrying vessels.
In that case, for one who is pierced [in these vessels], there occurs swelling, wasting of the flesh, enlargement of the veins, and death. There are two vessels carrying fat (*medas*);

their roots are the waist and the kidneys. In one pierced there, there is the appearance of sweat, unctuousness of the limbs, dryness of the palate, massive swelling, and thirst. There are two vessels carrying urine (*mūtra*).

The root of those two is the bladder and the penis. When pierced there, the symptoms are a non-distended bladder, suppression of urine, and stiffness of the penis. There are two vessels carrying feces;
their roots are the large intestine and the anus.
In that [latter case], for one who is pierced, there is non-healing, foul odor, and knotted intestines. There are two channels carrying semen; their roots are the breasts and the testicles.

In that [case], for one who is pierced, there is impotence, delayed ejaculation, and blood in the semen (or, according to another reading, "lack of ejaculation"). There are two channels carrying the menstrual flow (*ārtava*).
The roots of these two [the uterus and the vagina] are the uterus (garbhāśaya) and the vessels carrying the menstrual flow (ārtavavāhinī dhamanī).

If one of these is pierced, it results in sterility, intolerance of sexual intercourse, and loss of menstruation; from the cutting of the perineal raphe (sevanī), the appearance of pain occurs; and the symptoms of piercing the bladder or rectum have been stated previously.
However, in the case of a wound to a channel (srotas), one should treat the patient after first declaring the prognosis.
Once the splinter has been extracted, however, one should treat the wound according to the prescribed rules for wounds.
And there is a verse on this point:
"That which extends from the root within the body is the pervasive channel."
That should be known as the *srota* (channel), excluding the *sirā* (veins) and *dhamanī* (arteries).
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Arteries," in the Section on Anatomy of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Tenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the section on the body concerning the description of the pregnant woman.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

From the first day of conception, the pregnant woman should remain constantly joyful, pure, well-adorned, dressed in white garments, and devoted to peace, auspicious rites, the deities, Brahmins, and her elders.
She should not touch those who are dirty, disfigured, or have impaired limbs;
she should avoid foul odors and unsightly things.
One should avoid conversations that cause agitation;
one should not consume food that is dry, stale, putrid, or damp.

One should avoid going outside, as well as empty houses, shrines, cemeteries, and taking shelter under trees. One should shun states of being such as anger and fear (or, according to an alternative reading, "anger and disgrace"), as well as speaking loudly and other such acts, and those things which destroy the fetus.
One should not habitually indulge in oil massages, rubbing the body, and similar treatments;
nor should one exhaust the body,
and one should avoid those things previously mentioned.
One should provide a bed and seat with a soft mattress, neither too high nor lacking a headrest, and free from crowding.
One should feed her food that is pleasing to the heart, predominantly sweet, unctuous, and prepared with digestive stimulants; this regimen should remain general until the birth.
In particular, during the first, second, and third months of pregnancy, the pregnant woman should consume a diet consisting primarily of sweet, cold, and liquid substances.

Specifically, some authorities maintain that in the third month she should be fed *ṣaṣṭika* rice with milk; in the fourth, with curd; in the fifth, with milk; and in the sixth, with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).
Alternatively, in the fourth month, one should provide food mixed with milk and fresh butter, along with the meat of wild animals, which is pleasing to the heart.
In the fifth [month], she should be given milk mixed with ghee (or, according to another reading, "to one who is weak, [milk] for the weak").
In the sixth, one should have her drink a dose of ghee prepared with *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, or a gruel (*yavāgū*).
In the seventh, [she should drink] ghee prepared with the *pṛthakparṇī* group of drugs.

In this manner the fetus grows. In the eighth month, for the purpose of clearing old feces and for the downward movement of the wind (*vāyu*), one should administer an enema (*āsthāpana*) using jujube-water mixed with the paste of *balā*, *atibalā*, and *śatapuṣpā*, along with milk, curd-whey, oil, salt, *madanaphala*, honey, and ghee.
Thereafter, one should perform an oil-enema (*anuvāsana*) using oil prepared with milk and sweet or astringent decoctions.
For when the wind moves downward, delivery occurs easily and the woman remains free from complications.

From this point forward, until the time of delivery, one should treat her with unctuous barley gruels and the meat-broths of wild animals; thus treated, a woman who is unctuous and strong delivers easily and without complications.

In the ninth month, on an auspicious lunar day and so forth, one should cause her to enter the lying-in chamber (*sūtikāgāra*). Therein, for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, the birth-chamber (*ariṣṭa*)—constructed from *bilva*, *nyagrodha*, *tinduka*, and *bhallātaka* wood—should be built upon ground that is white, red, yellow, and black respectively.

Two alternative readings, *sarvāṅgāram* and *sarvāgāram*, are also found. The entire chamber should be constructed with a couch made of the same material [as the deity], its walls plastered, its furnishings well-arranged, and having either an eastern or southern entrance; it should be eight cubits long and four cubits wide, and provided with protective and auspicious rites.
For when the womb has become slack and the bond of the heart is released, [the fetus departs].
When there is pain in the hips along with vaginal discharge, she should be known as one who is about to give birth.

In that state, for one whose delivery is imminent, there is constant pain throughout the waist and back, frequent discharge of feces, urination, and the secretion of mucus from the opening of the vagina.

When she is about to give birth, having had auspicious rites and the recitation of benedictions performed for her, surrounded by young women, holding in her hand a fruit with a masculine name, well-anointed and sprinkled with warm water, one should have her drink this prepared gruel mixed with ghee up to the throat. Then, she should be placed on a wide, soft bed provided with a pillow, lying on her back with her thighs not bent; four women of mature age, skilled in midwifery, with trimmed nails and deemed trustworthy, should attend to her.
Then, having anointed her perineum (*viśikhāntara*) with oil in the direction of the hair and facing the opening, one should address her thus: "O fortunate lady, push forth!
She must not push until [the signs] have arrived.

Then, when the connection of the umbilical cord has been released and there is pain in the hips, the groin, and the head of the bladder, she should push very gently. (The word *pūrvaṃ*—found in some manuscripts—is not present here.)
From that point, upon the emergence of the fetus, it is intense;

then, as the fetus enters the opening of the birth canal, it becomes even more severe due to the state of being pierced by the [birth] pains. From premature delivery, it gives birth to one who is deaf, mute, hunchbacked, with a distorted jaw, or one whose head strikes upward, or one afflicted by cough, asthma, and consumption, or one who is deformed.
In that regard, one should bring the reverse order into conformity with the direct order.
In the case of obstruction of the fetus, one should fumigate the birth canal with the slough of a black cobra or with *piṇḍītaka*.
One should bind the root of *hiraṇyapuṣpī* to the hands and feet,
or one should wear *suvarcalā* or *viśalyā*.
Then, having removed the fetal membrane (*ulba*) from the newborn— and [according to another reading] having cleared both the mouth and the face with rock-salt ghee (*saindhava-sarpiṣ*)—

one should apply a cotton swab (*picu*) soaked in ghee to the head. Thereafter, having extended the umbilical cord (*nābhi-vardhī*) for eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*), tied it with a thread, one should cut it.
And one should properly tie a portion of that thread around the neck of the boy.

Then, having comforted the boy with cool water and performed the birth-rites (*jātakarman*), one should have him lick honey, clarified butter, and *anantā* powder with the ring finger. Thereafter, having anointed him with *balā*-oil, one should bathe him with a decoction of milk-trees, or with water infused with all fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*), or with water heated by red-hot silver or gold, or with a lukewarm decoction of *kapittha* leaves—according to the season, according to the bodily humor (*doṣa*), and according to one's means.
