Immediately after that, because the vessels situated in the heart have become dilated.
The breast milk of women begins to flow after four nights or three nights.
Therefore, on the first day, one should have the child drink honey and ghee mixed with *anantā* (atīsa), purified by mantras, three times a day. On the second day, ghee prepared with *lakṣmaṇā*;
and on the third day as well. Thereafter, until the breast milk has been withheld, one should have him drink honey and ghee in a quantity equal to the palm of one's own hand, twice a day.
Then, one should treat the woman who has recently given birth by anointing her with balā oil and administering a decoction of vāta-alleviating herbs.

If, however, there is residual morbidity (doṣa), on that same day one should have her drink a powder of pippalī, pippalīmūla, hastipippalī, citraka, and śṛṅgavera mixed with warm jaggery-water—or, according to some versions, mixed with fat—or simply with warm water.
One should continue this for two or three nights, or until the menstrual blood (śoṇita) becomes pure.
Once she has become pure, one should then have her drink for three nights either a medicated oil-gruel (*snehayavāgū*) prepared with *vidārigandhā* and other herbs, or a milk-gruel (*kṣīrayavāgū*).
Thereafter, considering her strength and the power of her digestive fire, one should feed her boiled *śāli* rice prepared with barley, jujube fruits, and horse-gram (*kulattha*).

By this regimen, after being treated for a month and a half, she shall be released from her dietary and behavioral restrictions and may be designated as having recovered from childbed (*vigatasūtikā*).
Some say it is from the reappearance of the menstrual flow.
One should have the woman who has recently given birth, if she is of a dry constitution, drink a dose of either ghee or oil with a decoction of the *pippalyādi* group as a follow-up.
She should maintain a regimen of oleation for three or five nights. If she is weak, one should have her drink barley gruel (*yavāgū*) for three or five nights.
After this period, one should treat her with unctuous food.
One should generally sprinkle her with a copious amount of warm water and avoid anger, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and the like.
And on this point, you two [should know]: whatever disease arises in a woman after childbirth from improper conduct, [that is the result].
It may become difficult to cure or even incurable due to excessive depletion.
Therefore, one should consider that [treatment], as well as the place and time, in accordance with the disease, suitability, and the therapeutic action.

One should always treat her after careful examination; in this way, she will not meet with misfortune. [Alternative reading: "One should indeed treat her after careful examination; thus she will not meet with misfortune.
Furthermore, another [remedy] causes flatulence and distension as she falls;
therefore, one should wipe her throat with a finger wrapped in hair.
Or one should fumigate the opening of her womb with bitter gourd, kṛtavedhana, mustard seeds, and snake slough, mixed with pungent oil;
or one should smear the palms of her hands and the soles of her feet with a paste of lāṅgalī root;
or one should pour the milky sap of the mahāvṛkṣa over her head.
One should administer a paste of *kuṣṭha* and *lāṅgalī* with either wine or urine;
or a paste of *śāla* root (or *śāli* root, according to another reading) or the *pippalyādi* group with wine.
Or one should administer an enema (*āsthāpana*) using the scum of *surā* liquor mixed with the milky sap of *siddhārthaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *lāṅgalī*, and *mahāvṛkṣa*.
With these same ingredients, one who has achieved mastery should administer a urethral enema using oil prepared with white mustard seeds;
or, with a hand that is lubricated and has trimmed nails, one should extract [the foreign body].

In a woman who has recently given birth and whose body is emaciated, blood that has not been properly purified or drained may be excessively obstructed by the local Vāyu. This causes a mass (granthi) to form below the navel, in the flanks, in the bladder, or at the neck of the bladder. Consequently, there arise pains in the navel, bladder, and abdomen. The colon feels as if it is being pierced by needles, split, or torn apart.
There is distension throughout the abdomen and retention of urine; these are the symptoms of Makkalla.

In that case, one should have him drink water prepared with the *vīrataru* group of drugs, mixed with ghee (*sarpiṣ*) and lukewarm water—or according to another reading, salted water—along with the powder of salt and the addition (*pratīvāpa*) of *uṣaka* and other substances;
or the powder of *yavakṣāra* with a decoction of the *pippalyādi* group;
or the powder of the *pippalyādi* group with the scum of wine (*surāmaṇḍa*).
One should drink either a decoction of *varuṇa* and other drugs with the addition of *pañcakola* and *elā*,
or a decoction of the *pṛthakparṇī* group mixed with *bhadradāru* and black pepper;
or one should eat old jaggery combined with *trikaṭu*, *caturjātaka*, and *kustumburu*.
Or one may drink clear *ariṣṭa*.
Then, one should lay the infant, wrapped in linen, upon a bed covered with linen cloth;
one should fan him with branches of the *pīlu*, *badarī*, *nimba*, and *parūṣaka* trees,
and one should apply a small amount of oil to his head every day.
One should fumigate him with incenses that destroy demons (*rakṣas*),
and one should scatter those demon-destroying substances upon his hands, feet, head, and neck.
Furthermore, one should scatter here grains of sesame, linseed, mustard, and chaff.
One should kindle a fire at the site of the affliction and attend to the treatment of the ulcerated wound.

Then, on the tenth day, the mother and father, having performed auspicious rites and ceremonies and having recited prayers for well-being, should bestow a name as they desire, or a name based on the lunar mansion [nakṣatra].

Then, one should approach a nurse (*dhātrī*) who matches the child's complexion, who is of medium stature and middle age, free from disease, virtuous, steady, not greedy, neither too thin nor too fat, whose milk is clear, whose lips are not pendulous, whose breasts hang down and project, who is free from physical defects, free from vices, whose calf is living, who is a good milker, affectionate toward her child, not given to mean acts, born of a noble family, and endowed with most of these qualities; she should be dark-complexioned for the sake of increasing the child's health and strength. Among them, one with projecting breasts would cause deformity, while one with pendulous breasts, by covering the nose and mouth, would bring about death.

Then, on an auspicious lunar day, having seated the child facing north—his head bathed and wearing new garments—and having seated the nurse facing east, he should cause the child to drink from her right breast, which has been washed, slightly massaged, and consecrated with this mantra.
"O fortunate lady, may the four oceans, flowing with milk from your breasts,
be ever present for the strength and growth of this child."
"O lady of auspicious countenance, having drunk this milk which has the essence of nectar,
may your son attain a long life, just as the gods did after consuming the amṛta. Otherwise, from the consumption of various types of breast milk that are unsuitable, the arising of disease occurs.

Even when the milk has not been drained, if an infant drinks from breasts that are extremely rigid and filled with milk, the flow becomes obstructed; this leads to the onset of cough, dyspnea, and vomiting.
Therefore, one should not give breast milk of such a kind to infants.
The loss of breast milk in a woman occurs due to anger, grief, lack of affection, and other such factors.

Therefore, for the purpose of generating her milk, one should produce a state of mental well-being in her and administer barley, wheat, śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, meat broth, surā liquor, sauvīraka, oil-cakes, garlic, fish, kaśeruka, śṛṅgāṭaka, lotus root, vidārī-kanda, madhuka, śatāvarī, nalikā, lābu, kāla-śāka, and similar substances.
Then one should examine her breast milk in water.

If it is cold, pure, thin, and has the luster of a conch shell; if, when placed in water, it becomes one with it, is without froth, without fibers, and neither floats nor sinks, one should know that it is pure.
By means of that, the child’s health, bodily growth, and increase in strength will occur.

One should not give breast milk to a woman who is hungry, afflicted by grief, exhausted, has vitiated bodily constituents (*dhātu*), is pregnant, feverish, excessively emaciated, excessively obese, has indigestion (*vidagdhabhakta*), or has consumed incompatible food (*viruddhāhāra*). Nor should one give it to one who has been overfed. Furthermore, one should not give the child medicine while the previous medicine is undigested, for fear of generating a violent onset of the humors (*doṣa*), the medicine, and the waste products (*mala*). *Note: Regarding the variant readings, "vidagdhabhakṣya" is found in some manuscripts, and "doṣauṣadhāśanānām" is also encountered in certain texts, though this latter reading is not available in all copies.*
And there are verses on this subject:
"The nurse, however, by means of heavy foods, poisons, or those that aggravate the humors..."
The humors (doṣas) become aggravated in the body, and consequently, the breast milk becomes vitiated.
The humors of a woman—vata and the others—become corrupted when she indulges in improper food and conduct.
By that [fault], they corrupt the milk, and consequently, physical diseases afflict the infant.
These [factors] become wholesome, and the physician should correctly discern them.
Wherever pain arises in his limbs or minor members, [he should apply the remedy].
She touches him again and again, and when being touched, she weeps.
One with closed eyes should not maintain the gaze when there is pain in the head located at the crown.
When it is located in the bladder, the patient suffers from urinary obstruction, pain, thirst, and fainting.
Accompanied by retention of feces and urine, discoloration, vomiting, abdominal distension, and rumbling in the intestines.
One should recognize the humors (doṣas) in the abdominal cavity and those located throughout the entire body by means of [the child's] cries.
And for those [stages], one should administer the aforementioned mild, excising medicine in the proper dosage with milk and ghee prepared from milk to the mother and the wet-nurse;
to the child who consumes milk and rice, it should be given to himself and the wet-nurse;
and for the child who consumes solid food, the decoctions and other remedies should be administered to himself alone, not to the wet-nurse.
In that case, after one month, for those who drink milk, one should administer a dose of medicine equal to the amount grasped by two finger-joints;
for those who eat milk-rice, a paste-dose equal to a jujube seed (kola);
and for those who eat solid food, a dose equal to a jujube fruit.
Those formulations of medicines which shall be proclaimed as healers for those diseases—
Having smeared those two breasts with that paste, one should let the infant suckle them.
In cases of fever caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha, [one should fast] for one, two, and three days respectively.
Ghee is beneficial for those who drink breast milk; for the other two [types], it is beneficial according to their respective needs.
And out of fear of thirst, one should not let the infant suckle at the breasts here.
One should administer purgation enemas and emetics only in cases of emergency, and not otherwise.
3.10.42 | If, due to the depletion of the brain matter (mastuluṅga) and other factors, the wind (vāyu) causes the palate bone to bend;
For him who is afflicted by the wretchedness of thirst, [the water] boiled with ghee and sweet substances [is prescribed].
It should be applied as a drink or an ointment, and likewise used for sprinkling with cold water.
The navel, distended by wind and accompanied by pain, is designated as tuṇḍī.
One should pacify it with wind-alleviating treatments, such as oleation, sudation, and poultices.
But when there is suppuration of the rectum, one should administer a Pitta-subduing treatment for children.
Rasāñjana is especially beneficial when used both for drinking and as an external application.

For one whose diet consists of milk, one should administer ghee prepared with white mustard, *vaca*, *māṃsī*, *payasyā*, *apāmārga*, *śatāvarī*, *sārivā*, *brāhmī*, long pepper, turmeric, costus, and rock salt.
For one who eats rice with milk, [ghee] prepared with licorice, *vaca*, long pepper, leadwort, and the three myrobalans is recommended.

For one who eats solid food, [ghee] prepared with the two groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*), milk, *tagara*, *bhadradāru*, black pepper, licorice, *viḍaṅga*, grapes, and twice the amount of *brāhmī* is prescribed; by this, the child attains health, strength, intelligence, and longevity.
Furthermore, one should take care of the child’s physical comfort; one should not threaten him,
nor should one wake him suddenly out of fear of causing him alarm.
One should not suddenly pull it out or throw it up, for fear of injury from wind and other humors;
nor should one cause it to sit down, for fear of causing a hunchbacked deformity.

One should always attend to it with hundreds of pleasing things, without any desire to harm it. Thus, with an unassailed mind, it grows; indeed, with an unassailed mind, it flourishes. Constantly endowed with exalted vitality, it becomes free from disease and possesses a very serene mind.
One should protect the child from wind, heat, lightning, light, trees, creepers, empty houses, low-lying places, and the shadows of buildings, as well as from difficult-to-grasp calamities.
One should not release a child onto something impure, nor into the open air, nor onto uneven ground.
Nor [should one study] during heat, wind, or rain, nor when there is dust, smoke, or water.
Because of his habitual suitability for milk, he [drank] goat's milk, or even cow's milk.
One should give it to children in the proper measure, observing their needs until the breast milk is sufficient.
And for six months, one should feed him light and wholesome food.

He should always remain devoted to his inner apartments, having provided protection against the fear of calamities; for children must be guarded with great effort from the afflictions caused by the planets.

Now, if the child trembles, is terrified, weeps, loses consciousness, strikes the nurse or himself with his nails and teeth, gnashes his teeth, moans, yawns, twitches his eyebrows, stares upward, spits foam, bites his lips, becomes violent, has broken or undigested stools, cries out with a piteous and distressed voice, stays awake at night, becomes weak, has withered limbs, smells like fish, a cat, a muskrat, or a bedbug, and no longer desires the nurse’s breast-milk as he did before—these, in general, are the signs of being afflicted by a graha.
We shall explain this in detail later.
And having recognized him as capable, one should cause him to receive the knowledge according to his caste.

Then, for him who has reached twenty-five years of age, one should bring home a twelve-year-old wife, thinking, "He shall obtain the ancestral duties, wealth, pleasure, and progeny. [Note: While some versions read "one should take a wife," Vāgbhaṭa reads, "A woman of full sixteen years united with a man of full twenty," and Vṛddhavārabhaṭa states, "A man of twenty-one years should marry a girl about twelve years old; when she is sixteen, the twenty-five-year-old man should strive for the sake of offspring."]
For it is recited: "Then indeed, having attained virility, those two procreated offspring endowed with vigor.
[Regarding the phrase "in one less than sixteen years," the reading "in one less than twelve years" is found in the manuscripts. [He reached twenty-five.]
Whatever offspring she conceives, it perishes while remaining within her womb.
Or, even if born, he would not live long; or, if he should live, his faculties would be weak.
Therefore, one should not cause conception to take place when the woman is extremely young.
One should never perform the rite of impregnation when the woman is excessively old, suffering from a chronic disease, or afflicted by some other disorder;
for a man who is likewise in such a condition, those same defects arise.
In that case, due to the factors previously mentioned, the fetus may fall, accompanied by pain in the uterus, waist, groins, and bladder, as well as the appearance of blood.

There, one should treat the condition with cold affusions, immersions, ointments, and the like, and with the drinking of milk boiled with the drugs of the jīvanīya group. When there is throbbing in the fetus, one should repeatedly administer milk processed with utpala and other such drugs for the purpose of stabilizing it. When the fetus is descending, there occurs burning sensation, pain in the flanks and back, menorrhagia, distension of the abdomen, and retention of urine. Furthermore, as the fetus moves from place to place, there is congestion within the abdominal cavity.

In that condition, unctuous and cold treatments should be employed. If there is pain, one should administer milk boiled with *mahāsahā*, *kṣudrasahā*, *madhuka*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *kaṇṭakārī*, mixed with sugar and honey. If there is retention of urine, [milk] boiled with *darbha* and other [diuretic herbs] should be given. If there is constipation (*ānāha*), [milk] boiled with *hiṅgu*, *sauvarcala*, garlic, and *vacā* should be given. If blood flows excessively, one should lick a powder of *koṣṭhāgārikā*, house-soot, *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī* flowers, *navamālikā*, red ochre (*gairika*), resin (*sarjarasa*), and *rasāñjana*, mixed with honey. Alternatively, according to availability, one should drink a paste of the bark and young shoots of the *nyagrodha* group of trees with milk.
Or one should apply a paste of blue lotus (*utpala*) and so forth, or a paste of *kaśeru*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and *śālūka*, with boiled milk;
or rice flour mixed with sugar, honey, and sweetness, with a decoction of the fruit of the *udumbara* tree and its aquatic tubers;
or one should place a piece of cloth soaked in the fresh juice of the *nyagrodha* group of trees within the vagina.
Now, if blood is not seen [in the discharge], one should have her drink milk prepared with madhuka, devadāru, mañjiṣṭhā, and payasyā;
or that same milk prepared with aśmantaka, śatāvarī, and payasyā; or prepared with the vidārigandhādi group;
or prepared with the two types of bṛhatī, utpala, śatāvarī, sārivā, payasyā, and madhuka.

Thus, for one who has miscarried quickly, the pains subside and the fetus is nourished. Once the fetus is stabilized, she should be fed milk prepared with the tender fruits of the *udumbara* tree. When the [period of] gestation has passed, she should be treated for as many days as there were months of pregnancy with gruels (*yavāgū*) that exclude salt and fats, and are prepared with digestive (*pācanīya*) herbs such as *uddālaka*. In cases of pain in the bladder or abdomen, one should administer old jaggery combined with digestive stimulants, or an *ariṣṭa* (fermented medicinal liquor). Because the channels have been seized by complications of Vāta, the fetus becomes sluggish.
Remaining [in that state] for too long, he perishes;
one should treat him with a mild regimen beginning with oleation (sneha) and so forth.
One should have him drink gruel (yavāgū) prepared with the juice of *utkrośa* and containing a generous amount of fat.

Or one should eat boiled *kulmāṣa* (half-cooked grains) prepared with black gram (*māṣa*), sesame (*tila*), and young *bilva* fruits, and drink honey-wine (*madhumādhvīka*) for seven nights. In the case of a fetus that has become stagnant due to the passage of time, one should especially strike the mortar containing grain with a pestle, or resort to uneven vehicles and seats. The fetus, being afflicted by *vāta*, indeed withers away;
it does not fill the mother's womb and moves feebly.
One should treat it with nourishing milks and meat broths. [The embryo] consists of semen and blood, entered by *vāyu* and endowed with the life-force (*jīva*).
It fills the stomach.
Sometimes, when it has subsided spontaneously, people say it was "carried off by Naigameṣa.
Sometimes, when that very same [wind] has dissolved away, they call it "Nāgodara"; in that case as well, the remedy is like that for one who has dissolved [into the body].
Henceforth, we shall explain the monthly ritual.
Madhuka, śākabīja, payasyā, and suradāru.
Aśmantaka, black sesame seeds, tāmravallī, and śatāvarī.
Vṛkṣādanī, payasyā, and the utpala-sārivā creeper;
Anantā, sārivā, rāsnā, padmā, and likewise madhuka.
Bṛhatī, kāśmarī, the sprouts of milk-exuding trees, bark, and ghee;
Pṛśniparṇī, balā, śigru, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and madhuparṇikā.
Śṛṅgāṭaka, lotus stalk, grapes, kaśeru, madhuka, and sugar.
My dear child, these seven yogas are completed by half-verses.
These should be administered in their respective order, combined with milk, in cases of miscarriage.
Kapittha, bṛhatī, bilva, paṭola, ikṣu, and digdhikā—
On the eighth day, the physician should have her drink the roots boiled in milk.
In the ninth month, one should drink madhuka, anantā, payasyā, and sārivā.
Milk prepared with ginger and payasyā is beneficial when administered on the tenth day.
Or ginger with milk is beneficial, as are licorice and deodar.
In this way, the fetus is nourished and intense pain is pacified.
Furthermore, for a woman whose menses have ceased but who conceives again after six years, the son born will be short-lived.

Now, when a disease arises in a pregnant woman at an improper time, one should induce emesis with food prepared with sweet and sour substances and then restore the downward movement of the humors (anulomana).
One should prescribe mild palliative measures for her food and drink,
and she herself should eat food that is predominantly sweet and not harmful to the fetus.
And one should administer mild treatments as appropriate, provided they are not contraindicated for the fetus.
And there are these verses on the subject: Gold, well-prepared powder, kuṣṭha, honey, ghee, and vacā.
Matsyākṣaka, śaṅkhapuṣpī, honey, clarified butter, and gold.
Arkapuṣpī, honey, ghee, powdered gold, and vacā.
Gold dust, kaiḍarya, white dūrvā grass, ghee, and honey.
Four excellent qualities have been declared in all four half-verses.
They increase the physical form, intelligence, strength, and wisdom of princes.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Pregnant Woman," in the Section on Anatomy of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
Thus ends the third section, the Śārīrasthāna, in the Suśruta-saṃhitā composed by the great sage Suśruta, the disciple of the Blessed Lord Śrī Dhanvantari, as instructed by him. 3.
The Suśruta Saṃhitā. Now begins the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsā-sthāna). Chapter One.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment concerning the two types of ulcers.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

There are two types of wounds: endogenous (śārīra) and exogenous (āgantu). Of these, the endogenous is caused by the derangement of wind (pavana), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), blood (śoṇita), or their combination (sannipāta); the exogenous is caused by falling from a height, being crushed, or being struck by men, animals, birds, predatory beasts, or reptiles, or by fire, caustic alkali, poison, sharp medicinal applications, splinters, potsherds, horns, wheels, arrows, axes, spears, lances, and other such weapons.
In this regard, although the general nature of a wound is the same, it is called "the chapter on the two types of wounds" because of its capacity to address the purpose of arising from two causes.

In every case of a traumatic wound, the specific procedure for applying cooling measures—just like those used for pitta—is intended to pacify the spreading heat of the injury at that very moment; furthermore, the application of honey and ghee is for the purpose of healing. Thus, these two reasons constitute the purpose for their administration. However, at a later stage, treatment should be conducted according to the specific affliction of the *doṣas*, just as in the case of endogenous diseases.
Furthermore, the specific afflictions caused by the *doṣas* are, in brief, of fifteen types,
due to their capacity for spreading,
as stated in the section on the inquiry into ulcers (*vraṇapraśna*); some say they are of sixteen types because of their purity (*śuddhatva*).
Its characteristic is twofold: general and specific.
Among these, the general is pain.
*Vraṇa* refers to the powdering of the limbs; it is called *vraṇa* because it causes a wound (*vraṇayati*).
Furthermore, its specific characteristic consists of the particular symptoms of wind (*vāta*) and the other [humors].

Among these, that caused by *vāta* is dark reddish-brown, thin, cold, slimy, with little discharge, dry, prone to crackling sounds, abundant in throbbing, stretching, piercing, and tearing pains, and devoid of flesh.

That caused by *pitta* arises quickly, has a yellowish-blue appearance, resembles the water of the *kiṃśuka* flower, is hot, discharging, and produces burning, suppuration, redness, and other disorders; it is afflicted with yellow pustules. That caused by *kapha* is characterized by constant and intense itching, has thick margins, is covered with a network of stiff veins and ligaments, is hard, pale in appearance, with mild pain, and discharges a white, cold, thick, and slimy fluid; it is heavy.

That which has the luster of a mass of young sprout leaves, is covered with a network of black pustules and boils, smells like a stable, is painful, tends to fume, discharges blood, and exhibits the symptoms of *pitta*—this is caused by blood (*rakta*).

That which is characterized primarily by pricking pain, burning, and fuming, has a yellowish-red appearance, and discharges a secretion of that same color—this is caused by wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*).

That which tends to itch, is accompanied by pricking pain, is dry, heavy, harsh, and repeatedly discharges a small amount of cold, slimy secretion—this is caused by wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*).
The teacher always says: [the ulcer] is hot, yellowish-white, and exuding [discharge] due to pitta and kapha;
it is dry, thin, characterized by much pricking pain, feels as if numb, has a reddish-brown appearance, and exudes discharge of that same color due to vāta and blood;
and it resembles the surface of clarified butter, smells like the water used for washing fish, is soft, spreading, hot, black, and exuding [discharge] due to pitta and blood.
[An ulcer] that is red, heavy, unctuous, slimy, predominantly itchy, stable, and discharging blood-stained pale fluid arises from phlegm (kapha) and blood (rakta).
One that is characterized by throbbing, pricking, burning, and a sensation of fuming, and discharges yellowish or reddish fluid, arises from wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and blood.
One that is characterized by itching, throbbing, and a tingling sensation, and discharges pale, thick, and bloody fluid, arises from wind, phlegm, and blood.
That which is characterized primarily by burning, suppuration, redness, and itching, and which discharges pale, thick, and bloody secretions, arises from *pitta*, *śleṣman*, and blood.
That which is endowed with the specific characteristics of three types of color, pain, and discharge, arises from *vāyu*, *pitta*, and *kapha*.

That which abounds in intense burning, churning, throbbing, piercing pain, heat, suppuration, redness, itching, and numbness, and is endowed with various colors, pains, and specific discharges, arises from *vāyu*, *pitta*, *kapha*, and blood.
A pure wound is one that has the appearance of the surface of the tongue, being soft, glossy, smooth, free from pain, well-positioned, and without discharge.
There are sixty therapeutic measures for that ulcer.

Namely: fasting, application of ointments, affusion, massage, fomentation, protection, poulticing, ripening, drainage, oleation, emesis, purgation, excision, incision, splitting, scraping, probing, extraction, puncturing, suturing, joining, compression, restoration of blood, cooling measures, poultices (*utkārikā*), decoctions (*kaṣāya*), wicks (*varti*), pastes (*kalka*), clarified butter (*sarpis*), oil, medicinal extracts (*rasakriyā*), dusting with powder, fumigation of wounds, rubbing up, rubbing down, mild procedures, harsh procedures, caustic treatment (*kṣārakarman*), thermal cautery (*agnikarman*), blackening, whitening, rubbing with drugs, hair growth, hair removal, enema therapy (*bastikarman*), urethral/vaginal enema (*uttarabastikarman*), bandaging, insertion of leaves, anthelmintic treatment, nourishing therapy, antidotes for poison, head-purgation (*śirovirecana*), nasal medication (*nasya*), gargling, medicated smoking (*dhūma*), honey, clarified butter, mechanical appliances (*yantra*), diet, and protective rites.
Among these, decoction, wick, paste, medicated ghee, oil, resinous extract, and powdering are the agents for purification and healing. Among them, eight surgical procedures have been described:
blood-stasis, alkali therapy, cauterization, mechanical instruments, major surgery, protective measures, and the application of bandages.

We shall describe elsewhere the procedures for oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, enemas (basti), urethral/vaginal enemas (uttara-basti), head-purgation, nasal medication, medicinal smoking, and gargling.
Whatever other remaining categories of therapeutic measures exist, those will be discussed here.

Swelling (śopha) has been previously taught as being of six types. Its eleven treatments begin with depletion (apatarpaṇa) and end with purgation (virecana); these are especially applicable for the counteracting of swelling.

Furthermore, they are not contraindicated when the swelling has reached the state of an ulcer (vraṇa); however, the remaining [treatments] are generally intended solely as causes for the counteracting of ulcers.
Depletion is the first therapeutic measure; it is the general and most important treatment for all types of swelling.
And in this regard,
for the purpose of pacifying the increase of the humors (doṣas) in an embodied being whose body is bound by those humors,
non-nutritive therapy (apatarpaṇa) should be administered after considering both the humor and the vital breath (prāṇa).
This should not be performed by those afflicted with upward-moving wind, thirst, hunger, dryness of the mouth, or fatigue,
nor by pregnant women, the elderly, children, the weak, or the timid.
In cases of swellings that have just arisen and wounds with severe pain,
one should apply a medicinal paste using the appropriate drugs for each specific condition.
Just as pouring water upon a house set ablaze quickly extinguishes the fire,
so does an ointment alleviate pain.
For soothing, purification, as well as for the removal of swelling,
and for excision and healing, an ointment (lepa) shall serve those purposes.

In the case of swelling caused by Vāta, one should perform affusions with warm ghee, oil, fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), meat broth, and decoctions of Vāta-alleviating herbs, for the purpose of pacifying the pain.

In cases caused by Pitta, blood, trauma, or poison, one should perform affusions with non-warm milk, ghee, honey, sugar-water, sugarcane juice, and decoctions of sweet herbs and milky trees. In the case of swelling caused by Kapha, however, one should perform affusions with non-warm oil, urine, alkaline water, wine, vinegar, and decoctions of Kapha-alleviating herbs.
Just as fire, when drenched with water, attains tranquility,
so too the fire of the afflictions is suddenly extinguished by such sprinkling.
An oil massage, when applied after observing the state of the humors (doṣas), brings about the pacification of those humors and produces softness.
He is prescribed first for procedures such as sudation and massage,
and subsequently he is enjoined for treatments such as bloodletting.
Fomentation should be applied to swellings that are painful, severe, and hard,
as well as to ulcers of a similar nature.
For firm and painful swellings, a mild softening treatment should be performed;
having first applied oil and then fomented with a bladder-tube, one should proceed slowly thereafter.
The wise physician should massage [the area] with the palm or the thumb;
furthermore, he should apply a poultice (upanāha) to both types of swellings, whether they are immature (āma) or inflamed (vidagdha).
An undigested swelling subsides with pacifying measures, while a digested one undergoes suppuration;
however, that swelling which does not recede despite treatments ending in purgation [should be treated differently].
One should effect its ripening by collecting medicinal herbs combined with curd,
buttermilk, wine, vinegar, and fermented grain-liquids.
Having made them unctuous and salted, one should cook a wholesome *utkārikā*;
with that warm preparation containing *airaṇḍa* leaves, one should cause the swelling to subside.
If one intends to cook wholesome food for the sake of allaying sensations and likewise for the sake of bringing the cooking process to completion;
When swelling has recently arisen, one should perform bloodletting;
likewise when it is swollen, hard, dark-colored, reddish, and accompanied by pain.
Bloodletting is beneficial for wounds that are inflamed or uneven,
and especially so for those containing poison, whether by means of leeches or with the feet [of birds].
For the purpose of pacifying pain and likewise for the non-attainment of suppuration,
[this is indicated] for those with complications, those who are dry, those who are emaciated, and those suffering from the wasting of ulcers.
The drinking of medicated fats (sneha-pāna), prepared with appropriate drugs,
is prescribed, especially for swelling accompanied by an excess of flesh and afflicted by phlegm (kapha).
Emetic therapy is beneficial for a wound that is heavily contaminated with dark blood,
as well as for those wounds afflicted by vitiated wind and bile that persist for a long duration.
Those skilled in the treatment of wounds praise purgation for wounds that are non-suppurating, hard,
and stable.
Likewise, excision is prescribed for sinews, abscesses, and the like;
as well as for those with internal pus, those lacking an opening, and those that are elevated like a mound.
In cases where diseases are mobile, surgical incision is prescribed;
this applies to children, the elderly, the infirm, the emaciated, the timid, and even to women.
When diseases have arisen upon vital points (marmas), incision is prescribed;
likewise, when a swelling is fully ripened, consolidated, and pressed by compressions.
When the humors have been brought to a state of ripening, that [treatment] should be performed by one who understands it,
using well-ground drugs that cause splitting, or alternatively, with alkali.
The physician should treat those with hard, thick-lipped ulcers that repeatedly crack and have elevated,
hardened margins by means of cauterization.
One should draw it evenly and well-drawn, leaving nothing out;
one should scrape it level with a sharp instrument according to the measurement of the paths.
One should cause linen, cloth, cotton, foam, barley-alkali, rock salt,
and rough leaves to be provided for the purpose of scraping.
The physician should gently probe fistulas, those containing foreign bodies, those with displaced channels,
and those with sinus tracts, using blades of grass, hair, fingers, or a probe.
The channels of the eyes, the urinary passage, and the anus are mouthless and filled with blood;
one should probe them with smooth probes made from the shoots of the cucu-podaka plant.
Whether the wounds are covered or uncovered, the wise physician should extract the foreign body as soon as it has reached the point of extraction, in accordance with the prescribed method.
In a disease that is treatable by incision, one should apply the surgical instrument according to the specified location and measurement,
and drain the morbid humor (doṣa) as previously described.
In those cases where wounds are afflicted by suppuration, where flesh has been removed, or where the wound is gaping,
suturing and the joining of the parts must be performed as previously described.
One should thoroughly compress from all sides with the prescribed compressing substances even those ulcers located in vital spots (marmans) that have pus within and narrow openings.
One should overlook the plaster as it dries during the process of compression;
nor should one apply it directly against the face, for in that way the morbid humor (doṣa) is discharged.
When blood has flowed profusely in many ways due to those various signs,
the stabilization of the blood (śoṇitāsthāpana) should be performed as prescribed by the physician.
For wounds characterized by burning, suppuration, and fever due to the provocation of pitta,
and for those overwhelmed by blood, the treatment should be cooling.
One should apply thick plasters made of the aforementioned cooling substances ground with milk and saturated with ghee,
and one should also administer very cold affusions.
In cases where ulcers have diminished flesh, secrete only a thin discharge, do not suppurate, and are characterized by pricking pain, hardness, roughness, aching, and trembling; |||
One should cook an auspicious *utkārikā* in the group of wind-alleviating [substances], in the group of sour [substances], likewise in the *kākolyādi* group, and in oleaginous seeds.
And for those that are stable,
painful, foul-smelling, moist, and especially slimy, fomentation (svedana) should be performed.
Purification should be performed using the purifying decoctions previously mentioned;
for wounds that contain internal foreign bodies, have narrow openings, are deep, or are situated within the flesh,
one should apply wicks (varti) prepared with purifying substances in the proper sequence.
One should purify those who are covered with putrid flesh and those who possess great faults.
With the previously mentioned substances for making wicks, prepared as a paste according to availability,
[one should treat] those deep-seated ulcers vitiated by pitta, which are afflicted with burning and suppuration.
One should conquer ulcers that have protruding flesh, are dry, and discharge profusely by using clarified butter for purification mixed with cotton-seed fruit.
The wise physician should cleanse [the wound] with oil mixed with mustard oil;
for those cases not purified by oil, one should employ a purifying medicinal extract (rasakriyā).
For ulcers with firm flesh,
one should prepare a decoction according to the prescribed method using the aforementioned substances, and then place it over the fire once more.
The wise physician should give surāṣṭrajā together with kāsīsa and manaḥśilā, and then he should apply haritāla to that [wound].
Having applied this, which is mixed with the juice of mātuluṅga, combined with honey, and well-massaged, to the wounds,
one should remain [with the bandage] for three days at a time, and then again for another three days.
The wise physician should treat deep-seated wounds filled with fat and foul-smelling with smooth cleansing plugs made from medicinal powders.
For those wounds characterized by purity, a healing decoction is beneficial;
in that case, it should be prepared by the knowledgeable physician using the substances as specified.
For those who are painless, pure, and likewise profound,
there are healing wicks made from the ingredients of healing wicks for the purpose of implantation.
For those ulcers from which putrid flesh has been removed, where the site for new flesh has not yet grown,
a healing paste made from sesame seeds mixed with honey should be applied.
Due to its sweetness, heat, and unctuousness, it destroys wind (vāta);
due to its astringency, sweetness, and bitterness, it also removes bile (pitta).
Due to its heat, astringency, and bitterness, it is beneficial for kapha;
when combined with purifying and healing agents, it both purifies and heals.
Combined with nimba leaves and honey, it is known as a purifying (saṃśodhana) application;
combined with the two aforementioned substances and clarified butter, it is also a healing (uparopaṇa) application.
Some wise men say that a paste made from sesame and barley should be applied;
it pacifies what is undigested and even promotes the digestion of what is already digested.
It breaks open a suppurated wound and cleanses one that has been opened; likewise, it promotes healing in wounds caused by bile, blood, poison, or external trauma, even those that are deep-seated.
A wise physician should heal wounds overcome by phlegm and wind with healing ointments prepared from ghee processed with milk.
One should cause an ointment oil (ropaṇa-taila) to be prepared with the medicinal substances as previously described,
for those wounds that are not sterile, unstable, purified, or severely corrupted.
The physician should prepare a medicinal paste (rasakriyā) containing two parts of turmeric for the purpose of healing;
this promotes the healing of wounds located in the skin where the flesh is firm and even.
The wise physician should apply the powder according to the procedure previously stated for its respective location;
this is the method proclaimed for both purification and healing.
This [treatment] has been stated generally for all wounds because there is no distinction among the doshas;
it is established by traditional scripture and likewise observed through its results.
It should be employed like a mantra and must never be subjected to critical analysis;
one may, however, divide it according to one's own intellect into the seven categories beginning with decoctions (kaṣāya).
The medicinal drugs that were previously mentioned by me according to their application— namely,
the two initial groups of five roots (pañcamūla) and the group that subdues wind (vāta)— [should be used].
This [group] should be administered when wind is vitiated, in the seven categories beginning with decoctions;
it consists of the Nyagrodhādi group and that which is known as the Kākolyādi group.
These two [decoctions] should be administered when pitta is vitiated, within the seven categories beginning with decoctions;
as well as the group beginning with āragvadha, which is proclaimed to be hot (uṣṇa).

These two [medicines] should be given when there is vitiation of phlegm (kapha); however, when the humors are combined, the groups of drugs should be administered in a balanced manner for wounds characterized by diseases following the nature of wind (vāta), as well as those accompanied by discharge.
One should fumigate [the wounds] with linen, barley, clarified butter, and other substances used for fumigation,
as well as for those that are dried up, have little flesh, or are deep-seated.
A man should apply emollient medicated ghees and ointments,
and he should consume the meat of carnivorous animals according to the prescribed rules.
The flesh of one whose mind is pure increases with flesh;
it brings about the healing of wounds whose soft flesh has been destroyed.
One should prepare it with the aforementioned powdered substances mixed with honey;
this is the opinion of Matariśvana for the treatment of hard, malignant ulcers.
A mild procedure should be administered and blood should also be let;
one should apply oleation and affusions combined with Vata-alleviating medicinal herbs.
Indeed, a firm binding produces softness and rapid healing;
it is beneficial for making tender flesh firm when applied to the skin of dhava,
priyaṅgu, aśoka, and rohiṇī trees.
Having made equal parts of triphalā, dhātakī flowers, rodhra,
and sarjarasa into fine powders, one should dust the ulcer with them.
One should treat with alkaline therapy those ulcers that have lost their flesh, are hard, itchy, long-standing,
and likewise difficult to cleanse.
One should treat with cauterization those wounds from which urine flows from stone-like growths, as well as others that discharge blood,
and those whose joints have been completely severed.
However, for those who have become excessively habituated to white (purgatives), black therapy is beneficial.
One should soak bhallātaka fruits that have been previously saturated with urine in milk;
then, having cut them in two, one should place them in an iron vessel.
Then, having buried another jar, one should join that [first] jar to it;
having joined mouth to mouth, one should then burn them with cow-dung.
The physician should gradually cause that fat which flows out to be collected;
having burnt the flesh of domestic, marshy, and cloven-hoofed animals, he should reduce them to a fine powder.
One should apply this white substance mixed with oil to the wound;
furthermore, one should prepare the various animal fats (sārasneha) according to the procedure prescribed for bhallātaka.
And whatever oils for fruits there may be, their application is as previously described;
however, because black hair is difficult to grow, the treatment for whitening (pāṇḍukarma) is beneficial.

The fruit of the *rohiṇī* plant, having been kept for seven nights in goat's milk, should be ground with that same milk into a very fine paste; this is beneficial for restoring one's natural complexion.
One should apply a plaster consisting of fresh powdered kapālikā, vaidūrya,
sarja, kāsīsa, and madhuka, mixed with honey.
When the flesh has been removed from a wood-apple (kapittha), one should fill it with goat urine,
along with ferrous sulfate (kāsīsa), yellow pigment (rocanā), blue vitriol (tuttha), yellow orpiment (haritāla), and realgar (manaḥśilā).
One should also place bamboo scrapings, prapunnāḍa,
and rasāñjana beneath an arjuna tree, causing them to remain in the ground for a month.
After one month, he should then apply a black ointment to the wound,
consisting of equal parts of hen’s eggshells, kataka, and madhuka.
Likewise, one should cause sea-urchin and powdered gems to be administered;
these pills, ground with urine, serve as a rubbing agent for wounds.
Having prepared ink from elephant tusks along with the finest *rasāñjana*,
hair grows even on the palms of the hands through the application of this ointment.
By means of the skin, hair, hooves, horns, bones, and ashes of quadrupeds,
the ground smeared with oil and sprinkled with their powder shall become covered in hair once again.
One should collect green vitriol and the tender leaves of the Naktamāla tree; ground with the juice of Kapittha, this is a supreme means for the growth of body hair.
If a wound covered with hair does not heal properly,
one should remove the hair from it using razors, knives, or forceps.
Two parts of conch powder and one part of yellow orpiment,
ground together with fermented gruel (śukta), is an excellent means for removing body hair.
Furthermore, there is oil from the *bhallātaka* fruit as well as the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant.
The wise man, having gathered together the finest hair-removing powder in one place.
One should perform hair removal by grinding together the long stalks of the plantain tree, ash, salt, and *śamī* seeds with cold water.
Having burnt the tail of a house lizard, a plantain stalk, amla fruit, and ingudi seeds, one should cook that ash with oil and water over the sun; this destroys the hair.
In the case of a wound vitiated by Vāta, which is dry and excessively painful—
especially if located in the lower part of the body— an enema (basti) is prescribed.
In cases of urinary obstruction, disorders of urine, disorders of semen, stone-related wounds,
and likewise disorders of the menstrual flow, the urethral enema (uttara-basti) is also beneficial.
Since a wound is cleansed by bandaging, becomes supple,
and even heals without fear, therefore bandaging is prescribed.
For trees that are stable but have little flesh (sapwood) and do not grow back due to dryness,
the application of leaf-fertilizer should be performed according to the specific disorder and the season.
In cases of Vata-born [hemorrhoids], one should use the leaves of eraṇḍa, bhūrja, pūtīka, and haridrā,
as well as āśvabala and kāśmarī leaves.
A wise physician should apply the leaves of milk-exuding trees as well as aquatic plants to a wound vitiated by blood and bile (raktapitta).
One should apply the leaves of pāṭhā, mūrvā, guḍūcī, kākamācī,
haridrā, and śukanāsā in a wound caused by kapha.
A leaf that is not harsh, not torn, not withered, delicate,
not eaten by insects, and soft is said to be possessed of merit.
The medicinal essence is oil, and the cloth is placed between layers of leaf;
since it absorbs [the moisture], one should apply a leaf on top of the plaster.
For the purpose of producing coldness or heat, and for the sake of cohesion through unctuousness,
a knowledgeable physician should prescribe a medicinal leaf along with the administered drugs.
When flies come to the wound and deposit worms,
a most dreadful swelling arises from where they have been consumed.
Severe and varied pains arise, as well as a discharge of blood;
in such cases, the Surasādi group is beneficial for both washing and filling the cavity.
The barks of *saptaparṇa*, *karañja*, *arka*, *nimba*, and *rājādana*, ground with cow’s urine, are beneficial; alternatively, a sprinkling with alkaline water is also recommended.
Or, having covered it with a piece of flesh, one should extract the worms from the ulcer;
I shall describe the twenty species of worms in detail in the subsequent section.
For those who have been ill for a long time, who are emaciated, and whose wounds are drying up,
every nourishing regimen should be employed while carefully protecting the digestive fire of the body.
I shall describe, according to their respective divisions in these ritual manuals (kalpas), the recognition of one afflicted by poison, the determination of that poison, and its medical treatment.
A skilled physician should administer head-purgation (śirovirecana) for those ulcers that are itchy, accompanied by swelling, and located above the clavicles.
For those wounds that are painful, afflicted by wind (vāta), dry, or located above the clavicle,
the knowledgeable physician should administer nasal medication (nasya).
For the purpose of expelling the humors, for the destruction of pain and burning sensations,
and for the removal of impurities arising from the tongue and teeth.
For a mouth ulcer, a gargle— whether warm or cold— is prescribed for both cleansing and healing the wound.
One should treat diseases located above the clavicle, as well as ulcers arising from phlegm and wind that are accompanied by swelling,
discharge, and pain, by means of medicinal smoking.
For the purpose of suppressing the heat of the wound and likewise for the sake of healing,
honey and clarified butter are prescribed for fresh, extensive wounds.
For those wounds that are deep-seated, narrow-mouthed, afflicted by a foreign object (śalya),
and from which manual extraction is impossible, the application of an instrument (yantra) is prescribed.
Light in measure, light in quality, unctuous, warm, and a stimulator of the digestive fire—
such food should always be given by the wise to those suffering from all types of wounds.
One who is afflicted by a wound must always be protected from nocturnal wanderers through the prescribed methods of protection,
as well as by restraints and observances.
The ulcer has six roots, eight types of management, and is characterized by five features;
it is established through sixty procedures and four methods of treatment.
In this formulation prepared with few medicinal substances, which I have [presented] out of fear of excessive prolixity,
there is no fault in adding other substances that are equivalent to those already mentioned.
Or, in cases where a disease is mentioned incidentally or possesses many rare remedies,
medical treatment must nevertheless be carried out according to the circumstances as they arise.
Even if a substance mentioned by name is unsuitable for a particular disease, one should remove it; however, one may add a suitable substance even if it has not been explicitly mentioned.
The complications of both the ulcer and the patient are manifold;
among them, five—beginning with odor—are recognized as the complications of the ulcer.
Fever, diarrhea, fainting, hiccup, vomiting, anorexia,
dyspnea, cough, indigestion, and thirst— these afflict the one who has been wounded.
Although these procedures for wound management have been described by Vyāsa in such detail,
I shall further explain the treatment specifically for fresh wounds below.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Two Types of Wounds," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||1||
The second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of acute wounds (sadyovraṇa).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
Dhanvantari, the most excellent among the upholders of dharma and skilled in speech,
instructed his disciple Suśruta, the son of Viśvāmitra, in the science of surgery.
I shall now describe the characteristics of those wounds of various forms that are caused by weapons with diverse bases and edges, struck upon various parts of the body.
They were elongated, square, triangular, and circular;
likewise, they resembled half-moons, were vast, and were curved.
Wounds that are new (āgantuka) may have a middle resembling the concavity of a shallow bowl, or they may have a middle like a barley grain; such are the various shapes wounds can take.
Ulcers born of the humors (doṣas) may burst spontaneously, but not those caused by medical intervention;
for a physician who understands the morphology of ulcers does not fall into confusion.
Even among wounds that are extremely difficult to see and deformed,
that ancient physician [Dhanvantari] appears with an infinite form as an adventitious being.
In brief, according to its characteristics, it is proclaimed to be of six kinds:
severed, split, pierced, wounded, and crushed.
They say that the sixth type is the "rubbed" (ghṛṣṭa); I shall now describe its characteristics:
it is a wound that is either transverse or straight, and is elongated.
The falling of a limb is also taught to be "cut" (chinna);
likewise, when the internal cavity [of the body] is struck by spears, javelins, double-edged swords, sword-blades, horns, and so forth.
If even a small amount flows from a wound, it is indeed called "pierced" (bhinna);
the locations for the stomach (āmāśaya), the digestive fire (agni), the intestines (pakvāśaya), urine, and blood are as follows.
The heart, the duṇḍuka, and the lungs are designated as the "visceral cavity" (koṣṭha).
When that is pierced and filled with blood, fever and a burning sensation arise.
Blood issues from the urinary tract, the anus, the mouth, and the nose;
there is fainting, labored breathing, thirst, abdominal distension, and a lack of desire for food.
There is obstruction of feces, urine, and flatus; discharge of sweat, redness of the eyes, a metallic taste in the mouth, and foul odor of the body.
There is pain in the heart and also in the sides; hear from me the specific symptoms here:
when the blood is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), one vomits blood again and again.
When it has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), there is excessive distension, extremely severe colic, pain,
and a sense of heaviness.
There is also coldness below the navel and the emergence of blood from the orifices;
even when the receptacle is not perforated, the intestines are filled through their minute openings.
Just as the weight of water is perceived in a jar with its mouth covered,
so too is the weight of a limb perceived when it is struck by a fine-pointed arrow, even in the absence of an internal receptacle.
One should designate that as "pierced" which is protruding or has come out;
it is neither excessively cut nor excessively split, but possesses the characteristics of both.
One should designate as a "wound" (kṣata) any uneven lesion on the body; however, that part of the body which has become swollen due to a blow or pressure is termed a "bruise" (vraṇa).
One should know that limb to be crushed when it is covered with marrow and blood, its skin gone,
whether due to friction or otherwise.
That which is accompanied by the discharge of pus and blood is taught as "rubbed" (ghṛṣṭa).
When [the wound] is cut, pierced, perforated, or lacerated, blood flows excessively.
Due to the depletion of blood, the wind (vāyu) causes intense pain there;
in that condition, the drinking of unctuous substances (sneha) is beneficial, as is its application by sprinkling (sekana).

One should apply poultices (upanāhana) consisting of seasoned meat (veśavāra), rice mixed with sesame (kṛśara), and well-oiled substances; one should also employ fomentation with grains (dhānyasveda) and unctuous ointments (ālepana).
An enema prepared with unctuous substances processed with wind-alleviating herbs is prescribed;
moreover, in cases of being pricked or rubbed, blood does not flow excessively.
When that [dosha] moves excessively, burning and suppuration arise;
therefore, for the purpose of suppressing the heat as well as the burning and suppuration, [one should act].
Cool ointments should be applied and cool affusions administered;
this is the summary for these six aforementioned conditions, beginning with the severed wound.
All that is to be known regarding the treatment of fresh wounds has been presented;
hereafter, I shall explain the treatment for those who have suffered severed limbs.
Any wounds that are gaping and located on the head or the sides of the body should be sutured according to the prescribed method and bound firmly.
Having restored the ear, which had been displaced from its position, to its natural state,
one should suture it as prescribed and saturate the canal with oil.
When the nape of the neck has been severed and even the wind (vital breath) is departing,
one should properly position it, bind it, and suture it continuously.
In this manner, one should perform a sprinkling with clarified butter and goat's milk;
lying on his back, he should eat food and remain well-restrained.
One should quickly and properly suture the widely gaping wounds caused by oblique blows falling upon the limbs,
having first correctly repositioned the joints and bones in their proper sequence.
Having quickly bound it with a twisted bandage, one should then sprinkle it with oil;
a gophaṇā-bandage should be applied with leather, or whatever else is beneficial.
If there is a wound on the back, one should have the person lie on their back;
otherwise, if the wound is on the chest, one should have the person lie on their stomach.
Having completely cut off the branch and burnt it with oil,
the wise man should bind it with a sheath-fastening and perform the necessary healing.
Sandalwood, padmaka, rodhra, blue lotuses, priyaṅgu,
turmeric, madhuka, and milk shall be the eighth ingredient here.
Oil cooked with these is an excellent healer of wounds:
sandalwood, karkaṭāhvā, the two sahe, māṃsī, and amṛtā.
Hareṇu, lotus stalk, triphalā, padmaka, and utpala—
this thirteen-ingredient trivṛt, or this same formula combined with milk, [is used for purgation].
Oil prepared by decoction is beneficial for the purpose of pouring over the wound and for its healing;
hereafter, I shall describe the treatment for those who have suffered a perforation.
If the eye is ruptured and non-functional, but that which is unruptured hangs down,
one should slowly reposition it to its proper place, ensuring the vessels are not distorted.
One should properly press [the area] with the hand using the inner surface of a lotus petal;
thereafter, an emollient treatment (tarpaṇa) and nasal therapy (nasya) should be administered with this clarified butter.
Having ground together goat's ghee, a vessel of milk, madhuka, blue lotuses,
and both jīvaka and ṛṣabhaka, one should cook the clarified butter.
This ghee is recommended for injury to all the eyes;
it is also for that embodied being from whose abdomen a wick-like growth has emerged from the fat.
Having bound it with a thread by one who is skilled in suturing, and having sprinkled it with decoction, ashes, and earth,
the physician should cut it with a blade heated over fire while it is combined with honey.
Once the wound has been bandaged and the food is well digested, the drinking of clarified butter is prescribed;
even in the absence of drinking medicated fats, the drinking of milk is ordained.
Combined with sugar, liquorice, lac, or śvadaṃṣṭrā,
and also with citrā, this destroys pain and burning sensations.
There may be flatulence, death, or piercing pain caused by the incision;
however, one should apply the oil that will be described for the fatty gland (medogranthi).

A foreign body (śalya) that has reached the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha), either by passing through the skin, piercing the vessels and other structures, or bypassing them, produces the aforementioned complications.
In that case, one should avoid a patient who has internal redness, a pale complexion, cold feet, hands, and face, cold breath, bloodshot eyes, and a distended abdomen.
When blood is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), emesis is said to be the beneficial treatment;
when it is located in the large intestine (pakvāśaya), purgation should undoubtedly be administered.
A non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) should be administered with warm purifying decoctions and with the unctuous-free broth of barley,
jujube, and horse gram.
One who has lost excessive blood, or whose abdominal cavity is ruptured, should eat food or drink gruel mixed with rock salt;
or, he should drink blood.
But that man who has established his own natural course of excrement, urine, and wind lives even when the abdominal cavity is perforated, provided he is free from other complications.
A mantra that has emerged unbroken should be re-entered; it must not be otherwise.
However, some say that even such a mantra is rendered defective if its head is seized by an ant.
Having washed the wound smeared with grass, blood, and dust,
one who has trimmed his nails should slowly insert it, lubricated with ghee.
One should cause dry food soaked in milk and saturated with ghee to enter [the mouth];
one should touch the throat with a finger and even cause agitation with water.
Seizing them by their hands and feet, those of great strength raised them up and shook them as they would shake [something] while thrusting them inside.
Likewise, the intestines enter within and press upon their own constituent parts;
whether due to the smallness or the largeness of the wound, that which is difficult to penetrate may occur.
Then, having measured it with that same standard, the physician should insert the instrument into the wound;
once it is positioned in its proper place, he should diligently suture the wound.
One should extract it from its location, whether it is easily accessible or well-protected;
then, having bound it with a cloth bandage, one should cause an application of clarified butter to be given.
One should drink lukewarm ghee mixed with *citrā* oil for the purpose of softening the stool and for the downward movement of the flatus.
Then the physician should prepare this oil for the purpose of filling [the wound],
using the barks of aśvakarṇa, dhava, mocakī, and meṣaśṛṅgī.
One should also take the roots of śallakī, arjuna, vidārī, and the milk-exuding trees (kṣīrin),
as well as the root of balā, and cook oil with these.
He should heal the wound with that [mixture] and strive [in this way] for the duration of one year;
having sprinkled the feet of one whose testicles have been removed with water, he should likewise sprinkle his eyes.
Having inserted the testicles through the perineal incision, one should then suture them;
thereafter, a gophaṇikā-bandha (a "turban" or "loop" bandage) should be applied by securing the instrument at the waist.
One should not apply an oil enema, for by that the wound becomes moistened;
[one should instead use] kālānusārya, aguru, elā, jātī, candana, and padmaka.
One should prepare a healing oil from stone, wood, honey, and tuttha;
when the foreign body has been removed from the head, one should insert a cotton wick.
If the wick is not inserted, the brain matter will ooze from the wound;
then the wind (vāyu) will destroy him, therefore one should treat it in this manner.
As the wound heals, one should gradually remove the plug bit by bit;
when it has been removed from one part of the body, one should insert a lubricated wick into another part.
Once the bleeding has ceased, the procedure beneficial for fresh wounds (sadyaḥkṣata) should be applied;
even those wounds that are deep-seated or narrow should be rendered free of blood.
Having prepared [the medicine] with a fine nozzle, one should irrigate [the eye] with oil processed with *cakrā*,
*samaṅgā*, *rajanī*, *padmā*, the "trivarga," and *tuttha*.
Having collected viḍaṅga, kaṭukā, pathyā, guḍūcī, and karañjikā, one should cook oil at the proper time; this is an excellent healing remedy.
With tālīśa, padmaka, māṃsī, hareṇu, aguru, candana,
the two types of haridrā, lotus seeds, uśīra, and madhuka— by means of these [one should prepare the remedy].
The oil described for treating fresh wounds is excellent for healing those that have matured.
In the case of a laceration, the procedure for lacerations should be performed; in the case of a contusion, the procedure for fractures should be followed.
In cases of abrasion, one should quickly suppress the pain and treat the wound with medicinal powders;
this applies likewise to those whose bodies are torn apart, who have fallen, who are crushed, or even those who are struck down.
One who eats meat broth should be made to stay in a vat filled with oil;
this same procedure should be performed for one who is emaciated or whose vital organs have been struck.
For the dressing, irrigation, and drinking of those with wounds,
oil or clarified butter should always be administered after duly considering the nature of the body and the season.

The medicated ghees that I shall describe with diligence for the treatment of pitta-type abscesses (pittavidradhi) should be administered by a knowledgeable physician in cases of fresh wounds (sadyovraṇa).
The physician should immediately irrigate a fresh wound accompanied by pain with ghee that is not too cold,
or alternatively, with Bala oil.
Samaṅgā, rajanī, padmā, pathyā, tuttha, suvarcalā,
padmaka, rodhra, madhuka, viḍaṅga, and hareṇukā.
Tālīśa leaves, nalada, sandalwood, lotus filaments,
mañjiṣṭhā, uśīra, lac, and also the sprouts of milk-exuding trees.
Having collected priyāla seeds and young fruits of the tinduka tree as they are available,
one should cook oil with these.
For all fresh wounds that are not vitiated by morbid humors,
one should employ healing treatments that are astringent, sweet, cooling, and unctuous.
For fresh wounds, one should follow the previously mentioned regimen for seven days;
in the case of malignant ulcers, purification should be performed both upwards and downwards.
Likewise, drying [the body], dietary regulation, and the letting out of blood;
decoctions from the group beginning with *rājavṛkṣa* and washing with those beginning with *surasā*.
Oil prepared with the decoction of those very same [drugs] is desired for purification;
or oil processed with alkaline substances according to the procedure for alkalis (kṣārakalpa) is used.
Dravanti, cirabilva, dantī, and likewise citraka;
pṛthvīkā, nimba leaves, kāsīsa, and tuttha as well.
Trivṛt, tejovatī, nīlī, the two types of haridrā, rock salt, sesame seeds,
bhūmikadamba, suvahā, śukākhyā, and lāṅgalāhvayā.
Naipālī, jālinī, madayantī,
mṛgādanī, sudhā, mūrvā, arka, kīṭāri, haritāla, and karañjikā.
One should perform purification using these oils according to what is appropriate;
likewise, ghee or whatever is available, as well as medicinal pastes (kalkas), should be used for purification.
In the case of Vata-type [fever], a paste of Saindhava salt, Trivṛt, and Eranda leaves should be used;
in the Pitta-type, a paste of Trivṛt, Haridrā, and Madhuka mixed with sesame seeds is prescribed.
In cases of wounds born of phlegm (kapha), one should employ sesame oil, tejohvā, dantī, svarjika, and citraka;
the procedure for treating malignant ulcers should also be applied to the ulcers caused by urinary disorders (prameha) and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
The sixfold determination of traumatic wounds (sadyovraṇa) which was previously taught cannot be further elaborated upon even by those who speak with certainty.
But some who consider themselves learned, being arrogant with pride, speak in many ways by joining that [Veda] with prefixes and particles.
Whatever has been spoken by them in great variety remains contained within these six alone;
just as particulars reside in the universal, the state of being six is considered supreme.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Immediate Fractures," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||2||
The third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of fractures.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
In a person who eats little, lacks self-control, has a predominance of wind (vāta),
and is afflicted by complications, a fracture heals with great difficulty.
One who has suffered a fracture should avoid salt, pungent substances, alkaline matter, sourness, sexual intercourse, exposure to the sun, physical exercise, and even dry food.
Shali rice, meat broth, milk, ghee, and soup made from satīna beans—
such nourishing food and drink should be given by one who understands to the person with a fracture.
One should collect the bark of the Madhūka, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Palāśa, and Kakubha trees, as well as that of the Vaṃśa, Sarja, and Vaṭa trees, for the purpose of the Kuśa grass.
For the purpose of anointment, one should collect mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, red sandalwood,
and powdered śāli rice, mixed with clarified butter that has been washed a hundred times.
In the cool seasons, imprisonment shall take place every seven days;
in the intermediate seasons, it should be carried out every fifth day.

In the case of fractures involving the bones of the trunk (āgneya), one should apply the bandage after three days, or according to the severity of the injury; for if it is bound too loosely, stability of the joint will not be achieved.
Even with a tight bandage, swelling, pain, and suppuration may occur in the skin and other tissues;
therefore, those who know the truth recommend a moderate (sādhāraṇa) bandage for a fracture.
A decoction of the Nyagrodha group, well-cooled, should be used for sprinkling;
however, in cases of pain, one should apply milk boiled with the Pañcamūla.
Or, having determined the appropriate time and the specific humor (doṣa), the wise physician should apply lukewarm *cakrataila* combined with drugs that subdue that particular humor.
One should administer cooling affusions and cooling plasters,
as well as the milk of a cow that has recently calved, mixed with ghee and prepared with sweet medicinal herbs.
A person with a fracture should drink cool milk mixed with lac in the morning;
however, for one with a fracture accompanied by a wound, the wound should be treated with ghee and honey in abundance.
Having removed [the fragments] with decoctions, one should treat the remainder as in the case of a fracture;
indeed, a fracture occurring in the first stage of life is thus easily managed.
For a person of little affliction, during the cold season and while still in the first stage of life,
the joint will become firm within one month in this manner.
In the middle [case], it is prescribed after double the time; in the upper [case], after triple the time.
One should raise what is depressed and press down what is elevated.
One should stretch what is excessively contracted, draw it upward from what has gone downward,
and likewise treat it with stretching, pressing, contractions, and bandaging.
The wise physician should stabilize all the joints in the body— whether they are mobile or immobile— by means of these methods of stabilization.
Furthermore, the physician should not attempt to mobilize a joint that is crushed or dislocated;
instead, he should apply cold affusions and medicinal plasters to it.
Once the injury has been removed, the joint returns again to its natural state,
provided it is wrapped according to the prescribed method with a bandage smeared with clarified butter.
Having placed kusha grass upon a cloth, one should perform the binding according to the rules;
hereafter, the procedure for a fracture of the individual parts shall be explained.
Having crushed the nail-joint with an awl so that blood follows it,
and having massaged it until the blood flows out, one should apply a plaster of ground śāli rice.
Having set the finger— whether it is fractured or dislocated—
so that it is straight, one should wrap it with a thin cloth bandage and apply a pouring of ghee.
Having anointed the foot with ghee when the sole is fractured,
one should bind it with a cloth bandage upon a bed of kusha grass and must not engage in physical exertion.
Having thoroughly anointed the calves and thighs with oil,
one who is well-composed should apply cool tree bark and wrap them with a cloth bandage.
The wise physician should indeed excise the protruding thigh bone using the wheel-technique; whether it is cracked or crushed, he should then bandage it as previously described.
One should pull up or down a person whose waist is broken;
then, once the joint is restored to its place, one should treat it with enemas (basti).
Then, while the patient stands smeared with ghee,
the binding ligatures should be adjusted along the broken ribs, whether on the right or the left sides.
Then, having applied a medicinal pad, one who is well-composed should wrap it;
he should then lay the man either in a cauldron filled with oil or in a wooden trough.
When the joint of the armpit and shoulder is dislocated, the wise physician should lift it with a mace and, once it is restored to its place, should bind it with a cross-brace (svastika-bandha).
Likewise, one should rub the elbow joint with the thumb;
having rubbed the joint, one should then press it once it has been displaced from the elbow.
One should extend and then flex it, and apply an infusion of oil;
one should perform this likewise for the knee, the ankle, and the wrist.
Having made both surfaces level for the embodied being whose surface has been crushed,
one should apply a bandage with oil and cause a pouring of water over it.
First one should hold a lump of clay, and after that salt;
once strength has been produced in the hand, one should practice holding a stone.
One should raise the swollen eye that has been fomented with a pestle;
likewise, one should press down the elevated part and bind it firmly.
The treatment for a fractured arm should be performed in the same manner as that for the thigh;
however, when the neck is twisted or has slipped downward, [the procedure is different].
Then, having grasped the hollows of the jaw and raised the person upward,
one should place kusha grass evenly [between the teeth] and wrap it with a cloth bandage.
One should keep him lying on his back for seven nights without weariness,
having brought together the two jawbones when the joint of the jaw has become dislocated.
Once the patient has been properly fomented and stabilized, the physician should administer the five-fold oil treatment (pañcāṅgī),
and ghee prepared with Vāta-alleviating and sweet drugs is highly recommended for use as a nasal medication (nasya).
One should not squeeze teeth that are unbroken, loose, or bleeding;
for a young person, one should apply cooling ointments externally.
Then, having sprinkled him with cool, healing waters, one should treat him;
and the drinking of milk through the stalk of a blue lotus is prescribed.
In the case of an elderly person, however, one should avoid extracting loose teeth;
rather, having straightened the nose—whether it be sunken or twisted—with a probe, [one should proceed].
One should insert two double-mouthed tubes separately into each nostril;
then, having wrapped [the area] with a cloth bandage, one should apply an irrigation of ghee.
One should bind a broken ear after aligning it evenly and saturating it with clarified butter;
thereafter, one should perform the treatment prescribed for fresh wounds.
When the skull is fractured, excluding the brain, one should apply honey and clarified butter, then bandage it; furthermore, one should drink clarified butter for seven days.
If a limb becomes swollen from a fall or a blow but remains uninjured,
the physician should apply cold plasters, affusions, and sprinklings.
Now, for those whose shanks or thighs are broken, a bed made of door-panels is beneficial;
furthermore, five pegs should be employed by the wise physician for the purpose of binding them.
Just as no movement is possible for that which is broken,
so too two pegs are placed on each side of the joint and one peg at the base.
One should apply this procedure in cases of fractures or dislocations of the hips, the spinal column, the chest, or the collarbones.
Once the joints have been long liberated, lubricated, fomented, and softened,
one should properly restore them to their natural state through the prescribed methods and with intelligent application.
When a fracture has healed crookedly or with an uneven union,
one should break it open and realign the fracture, and thereafter treat it as a fresh fracture.
With a concentrated mind, one should imagine a dry bone protruding at the edge of the wound;
or, at the junction of the joints, one should perform the treatment as for a fracture with an open wound.
For those with fractures in the upper part of the body, brain-paste and ear-filling are beneficial;
the drinking of ghee and nasal medication (nasya) are recommended, while oil enemas (anuvāsana) are indicated for fractures in the extremities.
Hereafter, I shall describe the oil that heals fractures:
one should soak black sesame seeds in fresh water every night.
Having dried it day after day, one should saturate it with cow's milk;
for the third week, however, one should saturate it with water infused with madhuka.
Then, once they have been thoroughly dried after being soaked again in milk,
the physician should powder them along with the Kākolyādi group, yaṣṭyāhva, mañjiṣṭhā, and sārivā.
Having powdered kuṣṭha, sarjarasa, māṃsī, suradāru,
candana, and śatapuṣpā, one should mix them with sesame powder.
For the purpose of alleviation, milk boiled with all types of fragrant substances should be prepared;
the physician should then cook that oil with four times the amount of this milk.
Cardamom, aṃśumatī, patra, jīvaka, tagara,
as well as rodhra, prapauṇḍarīka, and kālānusārivā;
Having ground together saireyaka, kṣīraśuklā, anantā, madhūlikā,
śṛṅgāṭaka, and the previously mentioned medicinal herbs.
One who is learned in the scriptures should cook this oil with these ingredients over a gentle fire;
this oil is always beneficial for those with fractures in all medical procedures.
In cases of facial paralysis, hemiplegia, dryness of the palate,
as well as facial palsy, stiffness of the neck, diseases of the head, earache, and lockjaw;
It is beneficial for deafness, for blindness, and for those who have suffered loss through women;
likewise, it is wholesome when used as a drink, an unguent, a nasal drop, an enema, or in food.
