By this very [practice], the growth of the neck, shoulders, and chest is produced,
as well as a face resembling a lotus accompanied by fragrant breath.
This scented oil, known by this name, removes all disorders of wind;
it is worthy of kings and should be prepared only for kings by those who are skilled.
One should cook the oils of cucumber, Akṣa, and Priyāla together with sweet substances,
adding muscle fat as available, and boil them in ten times the amount of milk.
This supreme oil quickly effects the healing of fractures when used for drinking,
massage, nasal administration, enema therapy, and irrigation.
The physician should strive to ensure that the fracture does not undergo suppuration;
for when the flesh, vessels, and ligaments have suppurated, the condition is cured only with great difficulty.
One should declare a fracture to be properly set when the joint is reunited, not displaced, with no loss of limbs, no protrusion, and when movement and activity are comfortable.
Thus ends the third chapter, named "The Treatment of Fractures," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||3||
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diseases caused by Vāta.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
When the Vāta is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), after inducing emesis in the proper sequence,
the Ṣaḍdharaṇa formulation should be administered for seven nights with lukewarm water.
Citraka, indrayava, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, ativiṣā, and abhayā:
this formulation known as Ṣaḍdharaṇa is remembered as a pacifier of diseases caused by vāta.
When [the disease] has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), unctuous purgatives (snehavirecana) should be administered,
as well as cleansing enemas (basti) and medicinal boluses (prāśa) with a high proportion of salt.
When [the vāyu] has reached the bladder, the procedure for purifying the enema should be performed;
and when it is provoked in the ears and other [senses], the therapeutic sequence that subdues vāyu should be applied.
One should employ oleation, massage, poultices, rubbing, and plasters;
and when the disease has reached the skin, flesh, blood, and vessels, one should perform bloodletting.
When Vāyu has reached the tendons, joints, and bones, one should, without weariness, apply oleation, poultices, cauterization,
bandaging, and massage.
When the wind has ceased or when the bone has been split by manual friction,
the physician, being strong, should insert a tube into the bone and suck out the air.
When the Vata has reached the semen, the treatment for seminal disorders should be administered through immersion baths,
the kuṭī- and karṣū-saṃsvedas, bed-sweating, massage, and enemas.
The wise physician should conquer vāta affecting all the limbs by means of venesection,
and the intelligent one should conquer that which is localized in a single limb or situated in the joints by using horn-bleedings (śṛṅga).
When [the condition] is associated with phlegm, bile, and blood that are not mutually antagonistic,
the physician should perform bloodletting repeatedly in cases of numbness caused by wind (supti-vāta).
One should also apply a plaster consisting of the smoke from a salt-house mixed with oil;
likewise, milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī) and the juice of sour fruits [are beneficial].
A very unctuous barley broth is beneficial for those with disorders of Vāta;
likewise, the Kākolyādi group, combined with all sour substances, subdues Vāta.
Sālvana is declared to be meat from marshy regions along with water, combined with all types of fats,
pleasantly warm, and distinctly salted.
Therefore, one should always apply oleation therapy for those suffering from wind disorders (vāta),
whether a limb is being bent with pain, or it is afflicted by pain, or even if it is stiff.
One should bind it firmly with bands made of linen, cotton, or wool,
or within a skin-sack belonging to a cat, a mongoose, a lion, or a deer.
Or one should cause the patient to enter [the chamber] well-anointed and treated with a poultice (sālvaṇa),
when the Vāyu has reached the shoulders, chest, or the sacrum (trika), as well as the neck (manyā).
Emesis and nasal medication (nasya), when administered by a skilled practitioner, destroy [the disease];
likewise, a head-pouch (śirovasti) or bloodletting destroys that which has reached the head.
One should skillfully retain the oil for a thousand measures therein,
whether the vital air (samīraṇa) pervades the entire body or is localized in a single limb.
The enema alone restrains [the disease] as a mountain restrains the force of the wind;
likewise, oleation, sudation, massage, enema, and unctuous purgation [are effective].
Head-poultice (śirobasti), head-oleation, medicated smoking, and likewise unctuous smoking; lukewarm oil-gargles and likewise unctuous nasal drops (nasya).
Flavors, milks, meats, fats, and whatever is oily;
foods that are sour with fruits, as well as those that are unctuous and salty.
There were lukewarm sprinklings of water as well as massages,
along with saffron, aguru, patra, kuṣṭha, elā, and tagara.
Silken, woolen, and fine-linen garments, as well as heavy cotton cloths,
and inner chambers protected from wind and sun;
A soft bed, exposure to fire, and likewise the practice of celibacy—
in brief, such measures as these should be applied for those suffering from wind-diseases (vāta).
One akṣa each of trivṛt, dantī, suvarṇakṣīrī, saptalā, śaṅkhinī, triphalā, and viḍaṅga;
a paste (kalka) of the size of a bilva fruit of tilvaka root and kampillaka;
and two pātras each of the juice of triphalā and curd.
One vessel of ghee should be prepared by mixing all these ingredients together and cooking them. This Tilvaka-sarpis is prescribed as an unctuous purgative for those suffering from diseases of Vata.
The same procedure as that for Tilvaka is to be observed for Aśoka and Ramyaka as well.

Having gathered the wood used for oil-pressing sesame seeds, one should cut them into small pieces, crush them into fragments, and boil them in a large cauldron after submerging them in water for a considerable time.

Then, taking the oil that rises from the surface of the water with either a ladle or the hand, one should cook it according to the procedure for preparing medicated oils, adding medicinal herbs that counteract wind (vāta).
This is taught as *aṇutaila* for those suffering from wind diseases; it is called *aṇutaila* because it is produced from minute (*aṇu*) oil-bearing substances.

Then, having thoroughly burned a plot of ground with many logs of the five great roots (*mahāpañcamūla*) until it is blackened and consumed, and after the fire has been extinguished for one night, one should remove the ashes. Once the ground has cooled, one should drench it with a hundred jars of oil prepared with the *vidārigandhādi* group of herbs mixed with an equal amount of milk, and let it stand for one night. Then, taking as much of the soil as has become oily, one should pour hot water over it in a large cauldron.

In that process, whatever oil rises to the surface, one should collect it with both hands and store it in a well-protected place. Then, one should cook that oil for a thousand-fold distillation (*sahasrapāka*) with a thousand parts each of decoctions of wind-alleviating herbs, meat broth, milk, and sour liquids, for as long as it takes to complete the cooking. Once it has been properly prepared and completed, one should place it well-protected in a vessel made of gold, silver, or clay.
This is the oil fit for a king, possessing irresistible potency after being cooked a thousand times; likewise, that which is cooked a hundred times is called *śatapāka*.

One should grind fresh leaves of *gandharvahasta*, *muṣkaka*, *naktamāla*, *āṭarūṣaka*, *pūtīka*, *āragvadha*, *citraka*, and others together with salt in a mortar, place them in a jar containing oil, seal it, and burn it with cow-dung cakes; this is taught as *patralavaṇa* for the treatment of wind diseases (*vātaroga*).

Likewise, having crushed the stems of *snuhī*, *vārtāka*, and *śigru* along with salt, one should fill a jar with it, add clarified butter, oil, fat, and marrow, seal it, and burn it with cow-dung cakes; this is taught as *snehalavaṇa* for diseases of wind (*vāta*). (Thus ends *kāṇḍalavaṇa*.)

Having collected fresh Gaṇḍīra, Palāśa, Kuṭaja, Bilva, Arka, Snuhī, Apāmārga, Pāṭalā, Pāribhadraka, Nādeyī, Kṛṣṇagandhā, Nīpa, Nimba, Nirdahanī, Aṭarūṣaka, Naktamāla, Kapūtika, Bṛhatī, Kaṇṭakārikā, Bhallātaka, Iṅgudī, Vaijayantī, Kadalī, the two types of Bāṣpa, Ikṣuraka, Indravāruṇī, Śveta-mokṣaka, and Aśoka—this group along with their roots, leaves, and branches—one should mix them with salt, burn them as previously described, strain the liquid according to the procedure for alkali (kṣārakalpa), and cook it down.
As an after-throw (prativāpa) here, one may add the Hiṅgvādi group or the Pippalyādi group.

This auspicious salt compound is prescribed for those suffering from wind disorders, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, loss of digestive fire, indigestion, hemorrhoids, and anorexia, as well as for those afflicted by coughs and other ailments caused by parasites; it is to be administered both with drinks and with food.
And there is a verse on this point:
"Because it causes the discharge [of toxins], because it possesses a heating nature, because it ripens the humors (doṣas),
and because it ripens the bodily constituents (saṃskāra), this is recommended for diseases of Vāta."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vata-diseases," in the Section on Therapeutics of the venerable Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||4||
The Fifth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of the great wind-diseases (mahāvātavyādhi).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Some say that vātaśoṇita is of two kinds, superficial (uttāna) and deep-seated (avagāḍha); however, that is not correct.
For it first becomes superficial like kuṣṭha and later, over time, becomes deep-seated.
Therefore, it is not of two kinds.

In this regard, when the wind (*vāyu*) is provoked by factors such as violent conflict and the like, and in a person habituated to consuming heavy, hot, or excessive food, the vitiated blood (*śoṇita*) obstructs its own path and unites with that wind; thus, simultaneously producing pain caused by both wind and blood, it is called *vātarakta*.
That [disease], having first established itself in the hands and feet, subsequently pervades the entire body.

Its premonitory symptoms are piercing pain, burning, itching, swelling, stiffness, roughness of the skin, throbbing of the veins, ligaments, and arteries, weakness in the thighs, and the sudden appearance of dark-red patches on the palms, soles, fingers, ankles, wrists, and other parts.
In one who fails to treat it or behaves improperly, the disease becomes more manifest.
Its specific characteristics have been described; in such a case, for one who does not counteract it, deformity occurs.
And in this regard,
it is generally said that vātarakta becomes aggravated in those who are delicate, those who indulge in improper diet and lifestyle, and also in those who are corpulent and habituated to comfort.

In that regard, one should undertake treatment for a patient who is not afflicted by the loss of vital breath, flesh, or strength; thirst; fever; fainting; labored breathing; cough; stiffness; anorexia; indigestion; spreading of the disease; or contraction of the limbs; who is strong, self-possessed, and provided with the necessary means.

In that case, at the very outset—provided the patient does not have many wind disorders, dryness, or emaciated limbs—one should repeatedly administer small quantities of blood-letting, avoiding the obstruction of the channels for fear of aggravating the wind.

Then, having prepared the patient with treatments such as emesis and so forth, and once he has consumed his meal and the wind is predominant, one should have him drink old ghee mixed with honey and *akṣaya*.
Alternatively, one may give goat’s milk mixed with half its volume of oil and combined with *madhuka* and *akṣaya*.
Or [a gruel] prepared with *śṛgālavinnā*, sweetened with sugar and honey;
or prepared with *śuṇṭhī*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and *kaśeruka*;
or prepared with *śyāmā*, *rāsnā*, *suṣavī*, *śṛgālavinnā*, *pīlu*, *śatāvarī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and the two groups of five roots (*pañcamūlī*).

One should prepare oil by boiling it with milk that has been cooked eight times with a decoction of the two *pañcamūla* groups; this oil should be processed with an addition (*pratīvāpa*) of the pastes of *madhuka*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *sarala*, *bhadradāru*, *vacā*, and *surabhi*. This oil should be used for drinking and other purposes. Alternatively, one may use oil prepared with a decoction of *śatāvarī*, *mayūraka*, *kiṇihī*, *ajamodā*, *madhuka*, *kṣīravidārī*, *balā*, *atibalā*, and the *tṛṇapañcamūla*, with an addition of the *kākolyādi* group.
Or, one may use *balā-taila* processed a hundred times (*śatapāka*).

One should perform affusion with milk boiled with roots that alleviate Vāta, or with sour liquids. Alternatively, a poultice (pradeha) should be prepared from barley, Madhuka, Eraṇḍa, sesame, and Varṣābhū. In this regard, five types of milk-porridges (pāyasa) for the purpose of poultices are described: these are prepared by cooking ghee, oil, muscle fat, marrow, and milk with powdered barley, wheat, sesame, mung beans, and black gram, each mixed individually with the paste of Kākolī, Kṣīrakākolī, Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, Bala, Atibalā, lotus root, lotus stalk, Śṛgālavinnā, Meṣaśṛṅgī, Priyāla, sugar, Kaśeruka, Surabhi, and Vacā.

Or a poultice (utkārikā) made from the fruit-pulp (*phalasāra*) of *snaihika* trees; or a minced meat preparation (*veśavāra*) of fish and meat mixed with powdered barley, wheat, sesame, mung beans, and black gram;

or a compress (*upanāha*) consisting of the pulp of *balvaja*, *tagara*, *devadāru*, *sarala*, *rāsnā*, *hareṇu*, *kuṣṭha*, *śatapuṣpā*, and *elā*, combined with wine (*surā*) and the whey of curd (*dadhimastu*).
In cases where Vata is predominant, an application of Madhuśigru root mixed with Mātuluṅga, sour substances, Saindhava salt, and ghee, or a paste of sesame, should be used.
When pitta is predominant, one should administer a decoction of *drākṣā*, *revata*, *kaṭphala*, *payasyā*, *madhuka*, *candana*, and *kāśmarya*, sweetened with sugar and honey;
or a decoction of *śatāvarī*, *madhuka*, *paṭola*, *triphalā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*;
or a decoction of *guḍūcī*.
Alternatively, one may use a decoction of sandalwood and other such drugs to alleviate fever caused by *pitta*, sweetened with sugar and honey;
or ghee prepared with sweet, bitter, and astringent herbs; or a sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) with a decoction of lotus stalks, *mṛṇāla*, *bhadraśrī*, and *padmaka* mixed with half as much milk;

or with milk, sugarcane juice, or rice-water mixed with *madhuka* and sugar; or with grape and sugarcane decoctions mixed with whey, wine, or fermented grain-liquor (*dhānyāmla*); or an anointing (*abhyaṅga*) with ghee processed with the *jīvanīya* group of herbs.

Or one may use clarified butter purified a hundred times (*śatadhauta-ghṛta*), or ghee cooked with a paste and decoction of the *kākolyādi* group. A poultice (*pradeha*) made from *śāli*, *ṣaṣṭika*, *nala*, *vañjula*, *tālīsa*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *galodya*, *gaurī*, *gairika*, *śaivala*, *padmaka*, lotus leaves, and so forth, ground with fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*) and mixed with ghee, should be applied.
Even when wind (*vāta*) is predominant, this poultice should be applied lukewarm.
The same applies when blood is excessively abundant;
one should repeatedly let the blood flow and apply very cold poultices.

In cases where phlegm (śleṣman) is predominant, one should administer a decoction of *āmalaka* and *haridrā* sweetened with honey, or a decoction of *triphalā*; or a paste of *madhuka*, *śṛṅgavera*, *harītakī*, and *tiktarohiṇī* mixed with honey. Alternatively, one should eat *guḍaharītakī* with either cow’s urine or water. Furthermore, a sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) should be performed using oil, urine, alkaline water, wine, fermented gruel (*śukta*), or decoctions of drugs that subdue phlegm.

An ointment (abhyaṅga) should consist of hot decoctions of the *āragvadha* group, or ghee prepared with whey, urine, wine (*surā*), fermented gruel (*śukta*), madhuka, sārivā, and padmaka. A poultice (*pradeha*) should consist of the powders of sesame, mustard, and linseed mixed with *śleṣmātaka*, *kapittha*, *mudga*, and *śigru*, ground with alkali and urine; or a paste of white mustard; or a paste of sesame and *aśvagandhā*;
or a paste of *priyāla*, *selu*, and *kapittha*.
The paste of Madhuśigru and Punarnavā;
the paste of Vyosha, Tikta, Prithakparni, and Bṛhatī—these five applications (pradehas), ground with alkaline water and made lukewarm, [are used].
Alternatively, Śāliparṇī, Pṛśniparṇī, and the two types of Bṛhatī, ground with milk and mixed with Tarpaṇa [oil], [are used].
In cases of combined or simultaneous involvement (saṃsarga and sannipāta), one should apply a mixed course of treatment.

In all cases, one should consume jaggery and harītakī; or one should drink long pepper (pippalī) ground with milk or ground with water, increasing the dose by five or ten fruits respectively for ten nights while subsisting on a diet of milk-rice, and thereafter gradually decrease the dose.

In this manner, up to five or ten [pippalīs]; this is the *pippalī-vardhamānaka* (the increasing dose of long pepper), which cures disorders of wind and blood (*vāta-śoṇita*), irregular fevers (*viṣama-jvara*), anorexia, jaundice (*pāṇḍu-roga*), splenic enlargement (*plīhodara*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), cough, dyspnea, edema, emaciation, loss of digestive fire (*agni-sāda*), heart disease, and abdominal dropsy. One should cook ghee with milk, adding a paste of life-promoting (*jīvanīya*) drugs as an additive, and apply it as an ointment. A poultice made of *saha*, *sahadevā*, sandalwood, *mūrvā*, *mustā*, *priyāla*, *śatāvarī*, *kaśeru*, *padmaka*, *madhuka*, *śatapuṣpā*, and *vidārī*, ground with milk and mixed with the scum of ghee (*ghṛta-maṇḍa*), should also be applied.
Alternatively, a paste of *saireyaka*, *kaṭarūṣaka*, *balā*, *atibalā*, *jīvantī*, and *suṣavī* ground with goat’s milk;

or a paste of *kāśmarya*, *madhuka*, and *tarpaṇa* ground with cow’s milk may be used. For massage, there should be "lump-oil" (*piṇḍataila*) prepared from beeswax, *mañjiṣṭhā*, resin (*sarjarasa*), and *sārivā*, boiled with milk. For drinking, aged ghee or ghee cooked with the juice of *āmalaka* should be used in all cases; for sprinkling (*pariṣeka*), oil processed with the *jīvanīya* group of drugs should be used, or oil prepared with a decoction and paste of the *kākolyādi* group, or oil prepared with a decoction and paste of *suṣavī*.
Or one may use oil prepared with only a decoction of *kāravellaka*; or *balā-taila* for sprinkling, immersion baths, enemas, and food.

One should eat fresh rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, barley, or wheat, along with milk, the meat-broth of wild animals, or mung-bean soup, provided it is not sour. One should also perform bloodletting frequently. And when the humors have increased excessively, the procedures of emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*), and unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) should be administered.

(4.5.13) Having drunk a decoction prepared from paṭola, triphalā, bhīru, guḍūcī, and kaṭukā, one quickly conquers the pain born of vāta-śoṇita. There are also verses on this subject: [Additional verses follow]
Through such practices of *kriyā-yoga*,
a wind-blood disorder (*vātāsṛj*) that has recently arisen is cured by physicians, whereas one that has been present for a long time is merely palliated.
Poultices, fomentations, ointments, and massages,
as well as spacious, pleasant, and wind-protected shelters.
Soft pillows for the cheeks and comfortable beds,
as well as gentle massages, are recommended in cases of vātarakta (rheumatism).
One should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, anger, the consumption of hot, sour, and salty foods,
sleeping during the day, and heavy, obstructive food.

One should treat a patient who does not suffer from convulsions (apatānaka), whose eyes are not sunken, whose eyebrows are not distorted, whose penis is not paralyzed, and who is free from perspiration, trembling, delirium, falling from his bed, or excessive extension of the limbs.

In that case, one should first apply oleation and sudation to the body, and then treat him with a sharp nasal drop (avapīḍana) for the purpose of purifying the head. Immediately thereafter, one should have him drink clear ghee cooked with a decoction of the vidārigandhādi group, along with meat broth, milk, and curd.

For indeed, the wind does not flow excessively; therefore, having gathered the group of wind-alleviating drugs such as *bhadradāru* and others, along with barley, jujube, and horse-gram, and the flesh of marshy and aquatic animals—these five groups combined—one should boil them together. Taking that decoction, one should cook it with sour milk and curd-whey, along with ghee, oil, fat, and marrow, adding a paste of the sweet-tasting drugs (*madhuraka*) as an after-throw. This *trivṛta*-based preparation should be administered to those suffering from *apatānaka* for sprinkling, immersion baths, massage, drinking, food, non-unctuous enemas, and nasal drops. Furthermore, one should apply fomentation according to the prescribed methods of sudation.
Or, one should place [the victim] in a well filled with a strong wind and warm chaff, husks, and dried cow dung, up to the mouth of the well;
or one should have him lie upon a heated blacksmith’s hearth, or upon a heated stone sprinkled with liquor and covered with *palāśa* leaves;
or one should cause him to sweat by means of *kṛśara*, *āveśavāra*, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Oil prepared with the fresh juices of *mūlaka*, *kora*, *būṣphūrja*, *arjaka*, *arka*, *saptalā*, and *śaṅkhinī* should be employed for affusion and other treatments in cases of apatānaka.
Sour curd mixed with black pepper and *vacā*, when drunk by one who has not eaten, destroys apatānaka; alternatively, oil, ghee, fat, and honey may be used.
This is the procedure prescribed for apatānaka caused by pure vāta.
When [the condition] is combined with other doshas, a combined treatment should be administered.

During intervals between bouts of pain, one should apply pressure-massage (avapīḍa); and one should consume the fats of the red rooster, the crab, the black fish, the porpoise, and the boar, or milk processed with vāta-alleviating drugs.

Or one may prepare a gruel (yavāgū) cooked with barley, jujube, horse-gram, radish, curd, ghee, and oil; once his impulse has been removed for ten nights by means of oleation, purgation, non-unctuous enema, and unctuous enema, one should treat him; one should also observe the therapeutic measures prescribed for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) and perform protective rites.
One should treat a self-controlled patient who possesses the necessary resources and is afflicted by hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta), whose limbs are not yet withered, and who suffers from pain.

In that case, having first prepared the patient with oleation and sudation, one should purify him with a mild purification therapy, administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) and a decoction enema (āsthāpana), and then treat him according to the protocol for ākṣepaka at the appropriate time; furthermore, a specific cranial enema (mastiska-śirovasti) is indicated here, and Aṇu-taila should be used for massage.
Sālvaṇa should be used for the purpose of poultices, and Balātibalā for the purpose of oil enemas; thus, remaining vigilant, one should follow this course of treatment for three or four months.
In cases of stiffness of the neck as well, this same procedure is prescribed;
specifically, one should treat it with nasal medications that alleviate Vāta and Kapha, and with dry sudation.
One should not cause a person suffering from apatantraka to fast. One should not employ emesis, oil enemas, or non-unctuous enemas.
If the breath is obstructed by vāta and śleṣman, one should release it with strong medicinal insufflations.
One should administer Tumburu, Puṣkaramūla, Hiṅgu, Amlavetasa, Pathyā, and the three salts to be drunk with a decoction of barley.

Furthermore, one should prepare a Prastha of ghee by cooking it with fifty Pathyās, two Palas of Sauvarcala salt, and four times as much milk; this should be used to perform treatments that alleviate Vāta and Kapha.

One should treat a patient who is afflicted, suffering, strong, self-controlled, and provided with the necessary means according to the procedures for Vata-disorders. This should be done with specific treatments such as cranial enemas (*mastishka-śirobasti*), nasal drops (*nasya*), medicinal smoke (*dhūma*), poultices (*upanāha*), oleation (*snehana*), and tubular fomentation (*nāḍī-sveda*). Then, having collected *mahāpañcamūla* along with its grass, the *kākolyādi* group, the *vidārigandhādi* group, the meat of aquatic and marshy animals, and likewise aquatic tubers, one should boil them in two parts water and one *droṇa* of milk until only the milk remains. Having removed it from the heat, strained it, and mixed it with one *prastha* of oil, one should place it back on the fire.

Then, having removed the oil that has mixed with the milk and allowed it to cool, one should churn it. From that, one should take the oil that rises to the surface and cook it again with sweet medicinal herbs, sesamum, and milk.

This milk-oil (kṣīratela) should be employed for drinking, massage, and other treatments for those suffering from facial paralysis; or, if devoid of oil, it may be used as milk-ghee (kṣīrasarpiḥ) for nourishment and protection.

In cases of *ghṛdhrasī*, *viśvācī*, *kroṣṭukaśiras*, lameness (*khañja*), club-foot (*paṅgula*), *vātakaṇṭāka*, burning of the feet (*pādahar�a*), tingling of the feet (*pādaharṣa*), *avabāhuka*, deafness (*bādhirya*), and diseases of the wind located in the vessels (*dhamanīgatavātaroga*), one should perform venesection (*sirāvyadha*) according to what has been stated and according to the specific location;
however, this excludes *avabāhuka*, for which one should instead observe the treatment prescribed for wind-diseases (*vātavyādhi*).
In the case of earache (*karṇaśūla*), one should instill into the ear ginger juice mixed with oil, honey, and rock salt, made lukewarm;
or goat’s urine, honey, and oil;
or oil prepared with the fresh juices of *mātuluṅga*, pomegranate, and *tintiḍīka*, along with urine.
Or one may apply a poultice prepared with vinegar, wine, fermented gruel, urine, and salt; furthermore, one should administer fomentation by means of tube-fomentations (nāḍīsveda).
One should also observe the treatment for diseases caused by Vāta; we shall explain this further in the subsequent section.
One should administer *tūnī* and *pratūnī* with oil, salt, and warm water;
or a powder of *pippalī* and other such drugs; or ghee strongly seasoned with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*).
And one should treat him with enemas.

In the case of flatulence (ādhmāna), one should treat it with fasting, warming the palms, digestive powders, medicinal fruit-suppositories (phalavarti), digestive (pācanīya) and appetizing (dīpanīya) enemas; and after fasting, at the time of eating, foods prepared with digestive stimulants such as coriander and cumin.
In the case of recurrent flatulence (pratyādhmāna), one should administer emetics, fasting, and digestive stimulants.
Regarding the *aṣṭhīlā* and *praty-aṣṭhīlā* swellings, the classification of treatment is like that for abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and internal abscesses (*vidradhi*).

Having powdered asafoetida, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, long pepper), *vacā*, *ajamodā*, coriander, *ajagandhā*, pomegranate, tamarind, *pāṭhā*, *citraka*, alkali of barley, rock salt, *viḍa* salt, *sauvarcala* salt, *svarjikā* salt, root of long pepper, *amlavetasa*, *śaṭī*, root of *puṣkara*, *hapuṣā*, *cavya*, cumin, and *pathyā*, one should repeatedly saturate them with the juice of *mātuluṅga* and form pills the size of an *akṣa* seed. Then, a person suffering from disorders of Vāta should consume one pill every morning.

This formulation cures cough, dyspnea, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, anorexia, heart disease, flatulence, pain in the flanks, abdomen, and bladder, as well as constipation, difficulty in urination, splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, *tūnī*, and *pratūnī*.
And there are verses on this point:
Vata may be present alone, or associated with the doshas, or occluded by the dhatus;
it should be recognized through signs and inference, and treated without contradiction.
When Vayu, combined with fat (medas), produces a swelling that is painful, dense, and cold,
the physician should treat that patient in the same manner as one with ordinary swelling.
When the Vāyu, enveloped by Kapha and fat, reaches the thighs,
then there occurs body ache, a sense of stiffness, horripilation, pain, and fever.
Afflicted by sleep, his thighs become stiff, cold, and devoid of sensation; they feel heavy and unstable, as if they were no longer his own.
They call this ūrustambha, while others call it āḍhyavāta;
in that condition, a person should drink the ṣaḍdharaṇa powder, excluding the use of fats.
Likewise, one should take a beneficial preparation made with hot water and the group of drugs beginning with pippalī;
or, one should lick the powder of triphalā mixed with honey and kaṭukā.
Or one should drink excellent guggulu with urine, or even śilājatu;
thereby it destroys the wind (vāyu) that is overcome by phlegm (kapha) and accompanied by fat.
Heart disease, loss of appetite, abdominal tumors, as well as internal abscesses,
alkaline urine, sweating, dryness, and emollient massages;
One should apply an ointment made of Karañja fruit and mustard seeds mixed with abundant urine;
as for food, one should eat old Śyāmāka, Kodrava, Uddālaka, and Śāli rice.
With a broth of dried radish or the juice of *paṭola*,
with the meat of wild animals prepared without ghee, and with wholesome vegetables that are unsalted.
When the phlegm and the fat have been largely diminished,
then one should again administer treatments such as oleation (sneha) and so forth.
Guggulu is fragrant, light, subtle, pungent, and hot; it is bitter in taste, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), laxative, pleasing to the heart, unctuous, and slimy.
Fresh [grain] is nourishing and aphrodisiac, whereas old grain is depleting;
due to its sharpness and heat, it destroys kapha and vāta, and because of its mobility, it removes impurities and pitta.
Due to its fragrance, it destroys foul-smelling cavities, and due to its subtlety, it stimulates the digestive fire.
It should be taken in the morning with water decocted from triphalā, dārvī, paṭola, and kuśa.
Having obtained it, one should drink it with urine, alkalis, or warm water;
when it is digested, one should eat with vegetable soups, meat broths, or milk, and thus, within a month, one destroys [the disease].
It cures abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), abdominal enlargements along with fistula-in-ano,
worms, itching, loss of appetite, vitiligo, tumors, and even glandular swellings.
It destroys swellings caused by wind aggravated in the channels, as well as leprosy and malignant ulcers;
it subdues the wind located in the viscera, the joints, and the bones, just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Major Vata Diseases," in the Section on Therapeutics of the venerable Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||5||
The Sixth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of hemorrhoids.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
There are four types of therapeutic methods for hemorrhoids (arśas), namely: medicine, caustic alkali, fire (cauterization), and the surgical instrument.
Among these, those that have arisen recently and are characterized by mild doshas, signs, and complications are curable by medicine.
Those that are soft, spreading, deep-seated, and elevated should be treated with alkaline substances;
those that are rough, stable, broad, and hard should be treated with fire;
and those that have thin roots, are elevated, and are moist should be treated with surgical instruments.
In that regard, there is a medicinal treatment for hemorrhoids that are curable by medicine and those that are not visible;
however, listen to the procedure being described for those that are to be treated with alkali, fire, or surgery.

In that case, having seated a strong patient who is afflicted by *arśas* (hemorrhoids), has been lubricated and fomented, and has eaten a small amount of unctuous, warm food consisting mostly of liquids for the purpose of pacifying the increase of Vāyu-pain; and having placed him on a clean, level board or bed in a sheltered place during moderate weather with the clouds dispersed, with his buttocks facing the sun, his upper body resting on another person's lap, lying supine with his hips slightly raised and covered with a cloth or blanket, his neck and thighs bound with a restraining cloth, and his body held firmly by attendants so that it is motionless—then, for him whose anus has been smeared with ghee, one should slowly insert the ghee-smeared instrument, which is straight and has an opening at the tip, into the rectum as he strains.
Having observed the hemorrhoid once it has been introduced,
one should press it with a probe and wipe it clean with either a cotton swab or a cloth.
One should apply the alkali; having applied it, one should close the opening of the instrument with the hand and wait for about a hundred breaths.
Then, after wiping it off and having considered both the strength of the alkali and the strength of the disease, one should apply it again.
Then, observing that the hemorrhoid resembles a ripe *jambava* fruit, is sunken, and slightly bent, one should withdraw [the instrument].
One should wash away the caustic with fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), or with curd-whey (*dadhimastu*), vinegar (*śukta*), or fruit-acid.
Then, having extinguished [the heat] with ghee mixed with *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, one should remove the instrument, raise the patient, and sprinkle him with warm water while he is seated in warm water;
some say with cold water.

Then, having brought him into a windless room, one should give the instructions for the regimen; if there is a remainder, one should burn it again. In this manner, one should proceed with each treatment every seven nights. Among those many [treatments], one should first treat the right side, then the left from the right, and then the back from the left.
Then [he recites] "the eldest."
Among those, conditions caused by vāta and śleṣman should be treated with fire-cauterization (agni) and alkali (kṣāra);
those caused by pitta and rakta should be treated with mild alkali alone.

In that regard, the signs of a properly cauterized [rectum] are: downward movement of the wind (vāta), relish for food, stimulation of the digestive fire (agni), lightness, the emergence of strength and complexion, and satisfaction of the mind.

However, in the case of excessive cauterization (atidagdha), there occurs tearing of the anus, burning sensation, fainting, fever, thirst, excessive discharge of blood, and complications arising from those causes.

In the case of insufficient cauterization (hīnadagdha), there is a dark discoloration, small ulcers, itching, derangement of the wind (anila), lack of clarity in the sense organs, and non-subsidience of the disorder.
One should cut and burn large [fleshy growths] while they are still vital.

Those that have protruded excessively and are filled with morbid humors should be treated without the use of mechanical instruments by means of fomentation, massage, oleation, immersion, poultices, bloodletting, medicinal pastes, alkali, fire, or surgery.
Those from which blood is flowing should be treated according to the procedures for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders).

Those with loose stools should be treated according to the procedure for diarrhea; those with constipated feces should be treated according to the procedure for the internal administration of fats or the procedure for upward-moving wind (udāvarta). This is the method for cauterization of hemorrhoids located in all sites.
Having reached [the site], one should apply the alkali using one of the following: a ladle, a brush, or a probe.
In the case of prolapsed rectum (bhraṣṭaguda), however, one should perform the application of alkali and other treatments without the use of an instrument.
In all cases, one should consume food consisting of śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, barley, or wheat, made unctuous with ghee, along with milk or with soup made from nimba or paṭola.
One should consume vegetables according to one's specific dosha, such as vāstūka, taṇḍulīyaka, jīvantī, upodikā, aśvabalā, balā, mūlaka, pālaṅkyasa, naṭa, cillī, cuccū, kalāya, vallī, or others;
and whatever else is unctuous, kindles the digestive fire, destroys hemorrhoids, and promotes the passage of urine and feces, that too should be used.

Once the hemorrhoids have been cauterized, the patient should be anointed with unctuous substances and generally follow a therapeutic regimen of oleation and other measures for the purpose of kindling the digestive fire and guarding against the provocation of *vāyu*.

Specifically, in cases of *vāta*-type hemorrhoids, one should drink clarified butter prepared with *vāta*-subduing and digestive-stimulating drugs, mixed with powders such as those beginning with *hiṅgu*.
In cases of *pitta*-type hemorrhoids, one should take clarified butter with a decoction of the *pr̥thakparṇī* group of herbs, to which digestive-stimulating drugs have been added as an adjunct.
In cases of bleeding hemorrhoids (rakta-arśas), one should cook [the oil] in a decoction of sumañjiṣṭhā, muruṅgī, and other such drugs;
in cases of kapha-type hemorrhoids, in a decoction of the surasādi group.
One should also treat the complications according to their respective natures.
Furthermore, one should apply alkali, fire, or surgical instruments to the anus only after exerting the utmost effort;
for through their misapplication, impotence, swelling, burning, intoxication, fainting, flatulence, distension, diarrhea, straining, or even death may occur.

Hereafter, we shall explain the dimensions of the instrument (*yantra*). In that regard, the instrument may be made of iron, ivory, horn, or wood; it should be shaped like a cow’s teat. For men, it is four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length and five finger-breadths in circumference;

for women, it is six finger-breadths in circumference and one palm-span (*tala*) in length. It should have two openings for the purpose of inspection, but only one opening for the surgical procedure; for when there is only a single entrance, the instruments, caustic alkali (*kṣāra*), and cautery (*agni*) do not pass through excessively. As for the measurement of the opening, it should be three finger-breadths in length and the thickness of the belly of a thumb in circumference.
When one finger-breadth remains, below that by half a finger-breadth, there is a circular pericarp (karṇikā) rising half a finger-breadth high; this is the summary of the form of the yantra.
Hereafter, we shall describe the medicinal pastes for hemorrhoids (arśas). First: a paste of turmeric powder mixed with the milky sap of *snuhī*.
Second: a paste of the powder of cock’s dung, *guñjā*, turmeric, and long pepper, ground with cow’s urine and bile.
Third: a paste of *dantī*, *citraka*, *suvarcikā*, and *lāṅgalī*, ground with cow’s bile.
The fourth [preparation] is a paste of long pepper, rock salt, costus, and the fruit of *śirīṣa*, ground with the milky sap of *snuhī* or the milky sap of *arka*.

Oil cooked with *kāsīsa*, yellow orpiment, rock salt, *aśvamāraka*, *viḍaṅga*, *pūtīka*, *kṛtavedhana*, *jambu*, *arka*, *uttamāraṇī*, *dantī*, *citraka*, *alarka*, and the milky sap of *snuhī*, when used as an ointment, causes hemorrhoids to fall away.
Hereafter, we shall describe formulations for the management of invisible hemorrhoids that are curable by medicine. In the morning, one should consume *guḍaharītakī*.
Or, practicing celibacy (*brahmacārī*), one should take a hundred *harītakī* fruits processed with a *droṇa* of cow’s urine, mixed with honey, every morning according to one's strength.
Alternatively, one may take the root of *apāmārga* with rice-water and honey every day.
One may consume the paste of *śatāvarī* root with milk;

or *sīdhu* liquor mixed with *citraka* powder, or the finest *sīdhu* mixed with *bhallātaka* powder; or a churned drink of roasted barley flour (*saktumantha*) without salt, taken with buttermilk (*takra*).
Alternatively, one may use buttermilk—whether sour or non-sour—that has been poured into a jar whose interior has been smeared with the paste of *citraka* root, for use with drinks and foods.
This same preparation with buttermilk (*takrakalpa*) may also be made with *bhārgī*, *āsphotā*, *yavānī*, *āmalaka*, and *guḍūcī*.

Alternatively, one who abstains from food may consume buttermilk daily for a month with *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, *cavya*, *citraka*, *viḍaṅga*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *harītakī*, following the previous method.
Or, one may take milk boiled with a decoction of *śṛṅgavera*, *punarnavā*, and *citraka*.
One should consume the bark of *kṛtavedhana* mixed with treacle and a paste of *pippalī* and other spices, along with honey;
or one should take the powder of *hiṅgu* and other ingredients prescribed for major diseases of the wind (*mahāvātavyādhi*), while subsisting on buttermilk or milk.
Alternatively, one may take milk prepared with alkaline salts and the root-ash of *citraka*, or milk prepared with the ash of the *palāśa* tree.
Or boiled sour gruel prepared with the alkali of *palāśa* wood;
or the strained alkaline water of *pāṭalā*, *apāmārga*, *bṛhatī*, and *palāśa*, mixed daily with clarified butter;
or a paste of the roots of *kuṭaja* and *bandāka* taken with buttermilk.

One should consume either a paste of *citraka*, *pūtīka*, and *nāgara* with *pūtīka* alkali, or ghee prepared with alkaline water and the addition of *pippalī* and other spices; or one should regularly take a handful (*prasṛta*) or a small measure (*prakuñca*) of black sesame seeds every morning, followed by cold water as an after-drink. By these means, the digestive fire increases and the hemorrhoids are pacified.
One should take one *tulā* each of the two *pañcamūla*s (the minor and major), *dantī*, *citraka*, and *pathyā*, and boil them in four *droṇas* of water.

Then, having taken the decoction reduced to one-fourth, when it has become well-cooled, one should mix it with one *tulā* of jaggery (*guḍa*), place it in a vessel of ghee, and leave it for a month in a heap of barley.
Thereafter, one should have the patient drink a dose every morning.
By this, hemorrhoids, disorders of the grahaṇī, anemia, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and loss of appetite do not occur, and the digestive fire becomes kindled.
Two palas each of pippalī, marica, viḍaṅga, elavāluka, and lodhra;
five palas of indravāruṇī;
and ten palas of the pulp of kapittha.
Half a *prastha* of *pathyā* fruits and one *prastha* of *dhātrī* fruits—
having boiled these together in four *droṇas* of water.
Having strained it until only a quarter remains,
and having mixed it with two *tulās* of well-cooled jaggery,
one should place it in a vessel of clarified butter.
One should let it dry for a fortnight in a heap of barley; then, every morning, one should consume it according to one's strength.

Indeed, this *ariṣṭa* destroys splenic disorders, loss of digestive fire, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), heart disease, anemia, edema, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargements, and worms, while promoting strength and complexion.
In those cases where vāta predominates, oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enema, and unctuous enema are not prohibited.
In those born of pitta, purgation is indicated;
likewise, in those born of blood, palliative treatment is indicated.
In cases arising from kapha, there should be the use of ginger and horse-gram (kulattha).

In cases arising from all three doṣas, one should employ the treatments as previously described for each respective doṣa. Furthermore, milk processed with the appropriate medicinal herbs should be used in all cases.

Hereafter, we shall explain the procedure for *bhallātaka*. Having collected ripe, undamaged *bhallātaka* fruits, one should take a single fruit and cut it into two, three, or four pieces; having boiled them according to the method for preparing a decoction (*kaṣāya*), one should consume a *śukti* measure of that decoction every morning while it is still lukewarm, having smeared the palate, tongue, and lips with ghee.
Then, in the afternoon, the diet should consist of milk, ghee, and rice. In this manner, one should increase the dose by one each time until it reaches five.
Thereafter, one should increase it by five each time until it reaches seventy.
Having reached seventy, one should further reduce it by five each time until it reaches five;
then, from five, one should reduce it by one each time until it reaches one.
By thus consuming a thousand bhallātaka fruits, one becomes free from all skin diseases and hemorrhoids, strong, healthy, and lives for a hundred years.

Having extracted the oil from *bhallātaka* seeds according to the procedure described in the chapter on the two types of ulcers (*dvivraṇīya*), one should consume it every morning in a dose of one *śukti*.
When it has been digested, the diet and the excellence of the results are as previously stated.

Alternatively, having extracted the oil from the kernels of *bhallātaka*, one who has eliminated the bodily impurities (*doṣas*) and whose digestion is well-stimulated should enter a windless chamber and consume either one *prasṛti* or one *prakuñca* according to one's strength.
When that has been digested, the diet consists of milk, ghee, and boiled rice.

Having used [the preparation] in this manner for one month, one should protect oneself by following the prescribed diet for three months; thereafter, having removed all afflictions, one becomes endowed with a fine complexion, strength, and the powers of hearing, comprehension, and retention, and attains a lifespan of a hundred years.
Furthermore, by using it month after month, there is an increase in lifespan of one hundred years for every hundred years.
Having used it in this manner for ten months, one becomes a thousand-year-old.
And there are verses on this point:
"Just as all types of leprosy are destroyed when the seeds of the saptaparna tree are consumed, so too are all hemorrhoids destroyed when the seeds of the vṛkṣaka and āruṣkara trees are consumed."
Just as the sixteen types of urinary disorders (prameha) do not escape the application of turmeric,
so too the visible growths arising from the rectum do not withstand alkaline caustic or fire.
Clarified butters that kindle the digestive fire, electuaries, iron preparations, wines,
and fermented liquors should be administered after considering the predominance of the humors.

In cases of hemorrhoids, one should strictly avoid suppressing natural urges, riding on the back of a woman, traveling in vehicles, sitting in a squatting posture, and foods that aggravate the respective humors.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Hemorrhoids," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Seventh Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of urinary calculi (aśmarī).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Stone (aśmarī) is considered a dreadful disease, resembling Death itself;
when young, it is curable by medicines, but when fully developed, it requires surgical excision.
In its initial stages, a sequence beginning with affection [for the body] is observed;
by that means, the roots of the disease go to their complete diminution.
Pāṣāṇabheda, vasuka, vaśira, aśmantaka,
as well as śatāvarī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā.
Kapotavaṅkā, ārtagala, kaccaka, uśīra, and kubjaka.
Vṛkṣādanī, bhallūka, and varuṇa are fruits produced from plants.

Ghee prepared with a decoction of barley, horse gram (kulattha), jujube fruits (kola), and the seeds of the clearing nut tree (kataka), along with the addition of ūṣaka and other such ingredients; |||
It quickly breaks up stones (aśmarī) produced by wind;
[it consists of] alkaline preparations, gruels, meat soups, decoctions, and milks.
And one should prepare foodstuffs from this group which destroys wind (vāta):
kuśa, kāśa, sara, gundrā, itkaṭa, moraṭa, and aśmabhit.
Varī, vidārī, vārāhī, śālimūla,
trikaṇṭaka, bhallūka, pāṭalā, pāṭhā, pattūra, and then kuruṣṭikā.
Ghee prepared with punarnavā and śirīṣa boiled together,
along with śilājatu, madhuka seeds, and indīvara, [is effective].
A paste made from the seeds of trapusa, ervāruka, and other such plants, when applied auspiciously,
quickly breaks up urinary calculi (aśmarī) born of pitta.
In this group of pitta-alleviating substances, one should prepare alkaline preparations, gruels, soups, decoctions, milks, and various foods.
The group beginning with Varuṇaka consists of guggulu, elā, hareṇu,
kuṣṭha, bhadrādi, marica, citraka, and surāhvaya.
Cooked with these, as well as with goat's ghee and the Ūṣakādigaṇa group,
it quickly breaks up a stone (aśmarī) produced from phlegm (kapha).
In this group that destroys phlegm, one should prepare alkaline preparations, gruels, soups, decoctions, milks, and various foods.
One should drink water mixed with jaggery and the powdered fruits of *picuka*, *aṅkola*, *kataka*, *śāka*, and *indīvara* to alleviate gravel (*śarkarā*).
The bones of a curlew, a camel, and a donkey; *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *tālamūlikā*, *ajamodā*, the root of the *kadambara* tree, and *nāgara*.
Yellow [powders] mixed with sugar,
or the powder of Trikaṇṭaka seeds combined with honey, should be taken with wine or warm water to break up gravel.
For seven days,
one should drink the alkali of those substances mentioned for use with ghee, strained through sheep's urine and mixed with sheep's milk, to break up urinary calculi.
Combined with the alkaline ashes of the dung of domestic animals and processed slowly,
an addition of *uṣaka* and other ingredients, along with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), should be made therein.
This alkaline preparation,
derived from the paste of sesame, apāmārga, kadala, palāśa, and barley, breaks up even urinary calculi, abdominal tumors, and gravel.
Alkali should be drunk with goat's urine; it is the supreme destroyer of urinary gravel.
One should likewise prepare the alkali of *pāṭalā* and *karavīra* in this same manner.
One should drink a paste of śvadaṃṣṭrā, yaṣṭikā, and brahmī, each equal to one akṣa;
or alternatively, one may drink śobhāñjanaka and mārkava together with the substance known as eḍaka.
Or, one afflicted by pain should drink the root of *kapotavaṅkā* with sour liquids such as wine,
or drink milk prepared with that same root.
The group of drugs beginning with vīratara should be employed in every way, whether prepared with harītakī and others, or indeed prepared with varṣābhū.
If it does not subside through the application of medicated ghees, alkalis, decoctions, milks, and urethral enemas (uttara-basti),
then the subsequent procedure is excision.
Since even for a skilled physician success in this world is uncertain,
this procedure is therefore proclaimed to be the last resort.
Inaction leads to certain death, while action brings uncertainty;
therefore, a doer of good deeds should act only after consulting the Lord.

Then, having comforted the patient—who is afflicted by disease, has been lubricated with oleation, has had his bowels cleared, has been slightly emaciated, whose body has been anointed and fomented, who has eaten, for whom the rites of *bali*, *maṅgala*, and *svastivācana* have been performed, and for whom the necessary materials have been prepared according to the procedure described in the "Section on Preliminary Preparations" (*Agropaharaṇīya*)—the physician should then take hold of that strong and undaunted man. He should place him on a plank level with the knees, with his upper body resting in the lap of another person seated in front; he should lie supine with his waist elevated, supported by a cloth, with his knees and elbows drawn in and bound together by a cord or strips of cloth.
Then, having massaged the left side of the patient whose navel region has been well-anointed with oil, one should press down with the fist from below the navel until the stone has descended.

Then, having anointed the index and middle fingers of the left hand with oil and trimmed their nails, one should insert them into the anus; having reached the perineal raphe (*anusevanī*), one should bring the fingers between the anus and the penis by means of effort and strength.
Having positioned the enema bag so that it is free of air, not too long, and not uneven—
One should press it firmly with the two fingers so that the foreign body becomes elevated like a knot.
If, once the arrowhead has been extracted, he has eyes that are wide open, is unconscious, with his head hanging down like a corpse, and remains motionless as if dead; |||
One should not extract the arrow from him; rather, he would die if it were extracted.
However, in the absence of these symptoms, one should indeed strive to extract it.
Then, having spared the raphe on the left side by the measure of a barley grain, one should apply the instrument to the extent of the stone's size;
some say it may be done on the right side for the sake of ease of procedure.
One should strive so that the stone is neither split nor pulverized.
For even a small amount of powder, once applied, increases further;
therefore, one should apply it with the entire edge of the instrument. However, in women, the uterus is situated close to the side of the bladder;
therefore, one should apply the instrument to them like a scoop.
Otherwise, these [symptoms] would instead result in a wound that discharges urine.

Or, in a man, there may be the discharge of urine due to the injury of the urethral opening; however, apart from a wound caused by a urinary stone (*aśmarī*), a ruptured bladder does not occur in a single way. A ruptured bladder in two places caused by a stone is not curable.
A patient with a bladder split in one place due to a stone-induced ulcer may survive because of the repeated application of treatment,
the incision performed according to the scriptures, and the swelling of the foreign body (śalya) due to the discharge [of urine].
Once the foreign body has been extracted, the patient should be immersed in a tub of warm water and subjected to sudation (sveda).
For thus the bladder is not filled with blood; or, when it is full, one should introduce a decoction of milk-tree (kṣīravṛkṣa) through the flower-tube.
And there is a verse on this point:
A decoction of milk-exuding trees (kṣīravṛkṣa), when administered through a flower-catheter (puṣpanetra),
quickly expels urinary calculi as well as any blood located in the bladder.

For the purpose of purifying the urinary tract, one should give him a full measure of jaggery (*guḍa*). Then, having drawn out [the stone], one should anoint the wound with honey and ghee and have him drink, twice daily for three nights, warm gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared with urine-purifying substances and mixed with ghee. After three nights, for ten nights, one should feed him a small amount of soft rice with milk thickened with jaggery (for the purpose of purifying the urine and blood, and for moistening the wound).

After ten nights, one should treat him with sour fruits and the meat-broth of wild animals (*jāṅgala*). Then, for another ten nights, one should diligently apply fomentation (*sveda*) to him using either unctuous substances or liquid fomentation. One should wash his wound with a decoction of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) and apply a paste of *rodhra*, *madhuka*, *mañjiṣ�ṭhā*, and *prapauṇḍarīka* to the wound. Oil or ghee cooked with these same ingredients plus *haridrā* should be used as an ointment for the wound. Furthermore, one should treat the stagnant blood with urethral enemas (*uttarabasti*). If after seven nights the urine does not return to its natural passage, one should cauterize the wound with fire according to the prescribed method.

And for one who has entered his own urinary passage, one should treat him with urethral enemas (uttarabasti), non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) using sweet and astringent decoctions. Alternatively, if a seminal stone (śukrāśmarī) or gravel (śarkarā) has entered the urinary tract by chance and become lodged within it, one should remove it through the channel. If this is impossible, one should incise the passage with a surgical instrument and extract it with a hook (baḍiśa).
Once the wound has healed, the patient should not mount a woman, a horse, a mountain, an elephant, a chariot, or a tree for one year.
One should not float in water,
nor should one eat while the teacher is present.

One should avoid injuring eight [structures]: the urine-carrying channel, the semen-carrying channel, the scrotal ducts, the urethra, the perineal raphe (sevanī), the vagina, the anus, and the bladder.
Among these, injury to the urine-carrying channels results in death due to the bladder being filled with urine;
injury to the semen-carrying channels results in death or impotence.
From injury to the scrotum and the urinary channels, impotence occurs;
from injury to the urethral orifice, involuntary discharge of urine occurs; and from injury to the perineal raphe or the vagina, the onset of pain occurs.
The symptoms of a perforation of the bladder and rectum have been described previously.
And there is a verse on this point:
A physician unskilled in surgical procedures may destroy many mortals by failing to recognize the eight vital points (*marmans*) from which the channels of living beings arise.
The perineal raphe, the two semen-carrying channels at the testicles,
the anus, the urethral opening, the urine-carrying channel, the vagina, and the bladder as the eighth.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Calculi," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of fistula-in-ano.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Five types of fistula-in-ano have been described.
Among them, the *śambūkāvarta* (conch-shaped) and that caused by a foreign body (*śalyanimitta*) are incurable; the remaining types are difficult to cure.

In that regard, one should treat a patient afflicted by a fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara) with the eleven-fold therapeutic measures beginning with fasting and ending with purgation, provided the abscess has not yet suppurated. Once the abscesses have suppurated, the patient should be lubricated, immersed in a bath, and fomented; then, having placed him on a bed and secured him with a splint as in the case of hemorrhoids, one should examine the fistula to determine whether it is directed upward or downward.

Then, having inserted the probe, one should raise it with care and extract [the fistula] with a surgical instrument; likewise, when the mouth is internal, having properly inserted the instrument and applied the probe so that it reaches the opening of the fistula while the patient is straining, one should apply the instrument; or, having reached it, one may apply fire or caustic—this is the general procedure for all cases.
Specifically, however,
the physician should create incisions within the channels in a case of *śataponaka*; then,
once those have healed, he should treat the remaining channels.
The pathways are interconnected with one another, and the external ones are to be severed in many ways;
the physician who severs the channels that are not interconnected does so in a single manner.
He would cause the wound of the creature's anus to gape open;
his excrement and urine then follow that opened passage.
The wind (vāyu) causes flatulence and severe pain in the rectum;
even a physician who has mastered the medical treatises would undoubtedly conceal this [diagnosis].
Therefore, a wound in the case of the disease śataponaka, which has many openings, should not be opened by a wise physician.
The *ardhalāṅgalaka* cut should be made, or the *lāṅgalaka*;
or the *sarvatobhadraka* should be made, or even the *gotīrthaka*.
The physician should then cauterize all the sinus tracts with fire;
for a delicate and timid person, the treatment of *śataponaka* is indeed difficult.
In that condition, one should quickly apply fomentation (sveda) to remove pain and stiffness,
using the prescribed fomentation substances such as kṛśara, apāyasa, and others.
One should [offer] the meat of domestic, marshy, or aquatic animals, or even of birds such as the quail that scratch for food;
likewise, the vṛkṣādanī, castor-oil plant (eraṇḍa), the bilva group, and so forth.
Having prepared a well-made decoction, one should pour it into a vessel of oil;
with that, the physician should apply fomentation to the ulcer by means of a tube.
One should cook sesame, castor seeds, linseed, mung beans, barley, wheat,
mustard seeds, salts, and the group of sour substances in a single cooking pot.
One should cause the patient to sweat with that [mixture], for it succeeds thus while being administered;
once sweated, one should have him drink this [decoction] along with kuṣṭha and salts.
Vacā, hiṅgu, and ajamodā in equal parts [should be taken] with ghee,
or with mārdvīka wine, or with sour gruel, or with surā or sauvīraka.
Then the physician should sprinkle his wound with honey-processed oil,
and he should also irrigate the anus with oils that alleviate disorders of Vāta.
By this procedure, one's own feces and urine return to their proper channels;
other severe complications also succeed here, without a doubt.
The disease known as Śataponaka occurs on the neck of a camel; hear now the treatment for it.
Having identified it as being on the camel's neck, one should excise it and apply caustic.
Fire is not honored here for the purpose of removing the flesh of satisfaction;
rather, one should cause it to be sprinkled with sesame seeds mixed with ghee and ground flour.
Thereafter, one should apply a bandage and perform an irrigation with clarified butter;
on the third day, having removed it, the physician should cleanse the wound according to its specific requirements.

Then, having ascertained that it is clean, the wise physician should apply [the treatment] in the proper sequence; in the case of a discharging ulcer, he should first excise the channels of the discharge.
One should cauterize the path of the discharge with either an alkaline solution or fire;
then, one should sprinkle the anal region with lukewarm *aṇutaila*.
Poultices and plasters combined with urine and alkali should be prepared,
as well as affusions with emetic drugs in the proper measure.
Knowing it to have become soft and accompanied by slight discharge and pain,
one should seek out its path and excise it with a blade shaped like a jujube leaf.
Having cut off the crescent moon, the full moon-circle, and the needle-mouth [folds] with their openings facing downward,
one should thoroughly cauterize them with fire or, alternatively, with alkali.
Then, one should purify the child using mild cleansing procedures first,
whether the fistula-in-ano is external, internal, or opening toward the mouth.
For her, one should administer purgatives, fire-treatment, surgery, and alkaline applications;
whatever is mild or sharp, that indeed one should apply to her.
A powder of āragvadha, niśā, and kālā, saturated with honey and ghee and applied as a wick at the opening of the wound,
is beneficial for purifying ulcers.
This yoga quickly destroys [the disease], just as the wind disperses a cloud;
for a physician, when the disease is of exogenous origin, should carefully excise the vessel with a surgical instrument.
With a Jambū-wooden instrument, or with a red-hot probe,
the wise physician, being well-composed, should cauterize that ulcer as prescribed.
One should perform the procedure for killing worms as well as the extraction of foreign bodies;
however, this [condition] arising from the three doṣas should be rejected at the outset, undertaken [only with caution], or even avoided altogether.
This karma has been fully explained for all of them in due order;
now, however, listen to where the pain arises from the falling of weapons upon them.
In that case, sprinkling with warm oil of Aṇu is recommended;
one should use a vessel filled with Vāta-alleviating herbs and provided with small holes like a sieve.
Having smeared the anus with oil, one should sit upon a heated vessel that is emitting steam;
or, while lying down, one should draw out the sweat through a tube to alleviate the pain;
or, by immersing oneself in warm water, the pain is likewise pacified.
A wise physician should cause bandages and poultices such as *sālvaṇa* to be prepared using plantain, deer-skin, jackal-skin, priyaka-wood, and antelope-skin.

One should cause [the patient] to drink the three pungents (kaṭutrika), vacā, asafoetida (hiṅgu), salts, and dīpyaka, along with sour liquids, horse-gram decoction, wine, fermented gruel (sauvīraka), and so forth.
Jyotiṣmatī, lāṅgalakī, śyāmā, dantī, trivṛt, tilā,
kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, golomī, tilvaka, and girikarṇikā.
Kāsīsa, kāñcana, and kṣīrī constitute the group of purifying agents; likewise, trivṛt, tilā, nāgadantī, mañjiṣṭhā, and payas are considered purifiers.
This scraping treatment should be performed with rasāñjana combined with rock salt and honey,
along with the two types of haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, and nimba leaves.
A paste of trivṛt, tejovatī, and dantī removes sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa).
Kuṣṭha, trivṛt, sesame, dantī, māgadhī, rock salt, and honey [are used for this purpose].
Rajanī, triphalā, and tuttha are beneficial for the purification of wounds.
So too are māgadhī, madhuka, rodhra, kuṣṭha, elā, and hareṇu.
Samaṅgā, dhātakī, sārivā, the two types of rañjanī,
priyaṅgu, sarjarasa, padmaka, and padmakesara.
Having gathered these ingredients— lime, vacā, lāṅgalakī, beeswax, and rock salt—
the wise man should cook them with oil.
This oil is indeed beneficial for the purpose of healing glandular swellings (gaṇḍamālā), skin eruptions (maṇḍala), and carbuncles (mehi), as well as for destroying fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara).
The Nyagrodhādi group of drugs is beneficial for both cleansing and healing;
oil or clarified butter cooked with this group destroys fistula-in-ano.
Trivṛt, dantī, haridrā, the root of arka, loha, aśvamāraka,
the essence of viḍaṅga, triphalā, the milks of snuhī and arka, and honey.
One should cook this oil with beeswax;
it should be applied specifically for the purpose of destroying fistula-in-ano.
Citraka, kārkī, trivṛt, pāṭhā, malapū,
hayamāraka, sudhā, vacā, lāṅgalakī, saptaparṇa, and suvarcikā.
A wise physician, having prepared Jyotiṣmatī oil, should cook it;
for this Syandana oil should be administered copiously in cases of fistula-in-ano.
The wise physician should consider the two types of wound treatment— purification and healing— as well as the process of desiccation, according to the specific stages of the wound.
The expert in surgical instruments should remove the lip of the hemorrhoid instrument above the opening;
then, in the case of fistula-in-ano, one should apply this [instrument], which resembles a half-moon.
A man whose wound has healed should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, anger, riding on the back of animals, and heavy objects for one year.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fistula-in-ano," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Ninth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

Skin diseases arise from incompatible eating, overeating, unwholesome habits, the suppression of natural urges, improper administration of oleation and other therapies, sinful actions, and the influence of past karma.

In that regard, one suffering from skin diseases (tvagdoṣa) should avoid meat, fat, milk, curd, oil, horse gram (kulattha), black gram (māṣa), flat beans (niṣpāva), sugarcane products, flour-based preparations, sour substances, incompatible foods, overeating, indigestion, burning foods, obstructive foods, daytime sleep, and sexual intercourse.

Thereafter, one should eat fresh rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, barley, wheat, *koradūṣa*, *śyāmāka*, *oddālaka*, and so forth, with the broth or soup of either green gram (*mudga*) or pigeon pea (*āḍhakī*), mixed with neem leaves (*nimba-patra*) and *aruṣkara*.
Or, one may take [these grains] prepared with ghee or mustard oil, using the flowers of *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *avalguja*, and *āṭarūpikā*.

Or one may provide what has been prescribed in the group of bitter substances (tiktavarga); or, for those accustomed to meat, one should offer the flesh of wild animals (jāṅgala) devoid of fat; oil of the Vajraka type for the purpose of massage (abhyaṅga); a decoction (kaṣāya) of the Āragvadhādi group for rubbing the body (utsādana); and a decoction of Khadira for drinking, sprinkling (pariṣeka), immersion baths (avagāha), and so forth. This is the classification of diet and conduct.
In that regard, during the premonitory stages, one should employ purification from both ends.
When [the disease] has reached the skin, purificatory measures and ointments are indicated.
When it has reached the blood, purificatory measures, ointments, decoction-drinks, and blood-letting are indicated.

When meat has appeared [in the ulcer], there should be cleansing, ointments, decoction-drinks, blood-letting, and the administration of *ariṣṭa*, *mantha*, and *prāśa*. A case that has reached the stage where the four therapeutic measures have been applied is considered palliable (*yāpya*) for a self-controlled patient who follows the prescribed regimen.

In such a case, after purification and blood-letting, one should employ the administration of *bhallātaka*, *śilājatu*, mineral exudates, *mākṣika* honey, *guggulu*, *aguru*, *tuvaraka*, *khadira*, *āsana*, and iron preparations; however, one should never undertake the fifth measure [excision].
In that regard, one should first treat the leper according to the procedure for drinking oleaginous substances (*sneha*).

One should prescribe oil or ghee prepared with *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *guḍūcī*, and the two groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*) for those suffering from *vāta-kuṣṭha*, to be used for drinking and massage.
Ghee prepared with *dhava*, *aśvakarṇa*, *kakubha*, *palāśa*, *picumarda*, *parpaṭaka*, *madhuka*, *rodhra*, and *samaṅgā* should be administered to those suffering from *pitta-kuṣṭha*.

For those suffering from *kaphaja* leprosy, [oil] prepared with *priyāla*, *śāla*, *āragvadha*, *nimba*, *saptaparṇa*, *citraka*, black pepper, *vacā*, and *kuṣṭha*, or [oil] prepared with *bhallātaka*, *abhayā*, and *viḍaṅga* is recommended;
for all types of leprosy, however, *tuvaraka* oil or *bhallātaka* oil is indicated.

Equal parts of *saptaparṇa*, *āragvadha*, *ativiṣā*, *ikṣuraka*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *amṛtā*, *triphalā*, *paṭola*, *picumarda*, *parpaṭaka*, *durālabhā*, *trāyamāṇā*, *mustā*, *candana*, *padmaka*, *haridrā*, *upakulyā*, *viśālā*, *mūrvā*, *śatāvarī*, *sārivā*, *indrayava*, *āṭarūṣaka*, *ṣaṭgranthā*, *madhuka*, *bhūnimba*, and *gṛṣṭikā* should be made into a paste (*kalka*).
To this paste, one should add ghee four times its quantity, twice as much juice of *dhātrī* fruit, and four times as much water; having mixed these together thoroughly, one should cook them.

This medicated ghee, known as Mahātiktaka, pacifies leprosy, toxic fevers, hemorrhaging, heart disease, insanity, epilepsy, abdominal tumors, abscesses, cough, menorrhagia, goiter, cervical lymphadenitis, elephantiasis, anemia, erysipelas, hemorrhoids, impotence, itching, scabies, and similar ailments.

Take two-pala portions each of triphalā, paṭola, picumanda, āṭarūṣaka, kaṭurohiṇī, durālabhā, trāyamāṇā, and parpaṭaka; having added these to one droṇa of water, take the decoction remaining after one-fourth has evaporated. Then, having added one prastha of ghee along with half-pala portions each of these drugs to be ground into a paste—namely trāyamāṇā, musta, indrayava, candana, kirātatikta, and pippalī—one should cook it.

This ghee, known as Tiktaka, alleviates skin diseases, toxic fevers, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract, edema, anemia, erysipelas, and impotence; it also destroys diseases located above the clavicle.

Therefore, after the patient has been lubricated and fomented with any one of these [oils] and ghees, one should pierce one, two, three, four, or five veins. One should repeatedly scarify the elevated circular patches (maṇḍalas), or perform scarification (pracchana). Alternatively, after rubbing them with sea-foam, śāka, gojī, or the leaves of kākodumbarikā, one should apply an ointment made from the pastes of lac, resin (sarjarasa), rasāñjana, prapunnāḍa, avalguja, tejovatī, aśvamāraka, arka, kuṭaja, and revata roots, ground either in urine or in bile.
Alternatively, one may apply a paste made of *svarjikā*, *tutthaka*, *kāsīsa*, *viḍaṅga*, *agāradhūma*, *citraka*, *kaṭuka*, *sudhā*, *haridrā*, and *saindhava*.

Or, having added these same substances to the alkaline solution prepared according to the method for alkalis, once the *pālāśa* alkali has been strained, one should cook it until it becomes thick like molasses (*phāṇita*), then remove it from the heat and apply it as a plaster.
Alternatively, one may use a paste of *jyotiṣka* fruit, lac, black pepper, *ppilī*, and jasmine leaves.
Alternatively, with a paste of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *arka* latex, sesame, *śigru*, and black pepper;
or with a paste of natron (*svarjikā*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), blue vitriol (*tuttha*), *kuṭaja*, *citraka*, *viḍaṅga*, black pepper, *rodhra*, and realgar;
or with a paste of *harītakī*, *karañjikā*, *viḍaṅga*, white mustard (*siddhārthaka*), salt, *rocanā*, *valguja*, and turmeric.
These seven proven ointments for curing all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) have been proclaimed; hereafter, listen to me regarding the specific treatments for ringworm (dadrū) and vitiligo (śvitra).
Lac, kuṣṭha, mustard seeds, tagara, turmeric, and the seeds of *cakramarda*,
combined together and ground with buttermilk— this ointment, mixed with the seeds of radish, is prescribed for ringworm.

This formulation— a paste ground with the juice of wood-apple (kapittha)— consisting of *cakramarda* seed produced from the Indus region, *keśara* produced from sugarcane, and *tārkṣyaśaila*, quickly destroys ringworm (*dadrū*).
Hemakṣīrī, vyādhighāta, śirīṣa, nimba, sarja, vatsaka, and sājakarṇa—
when employed for bathing, smearing, and rubbing, these quickly destroy severe cases of ringworm (dadrū) in this world.

Having given the root of *bhadrāsajñā* equal to that of the *udumbara* root, and having crushed the root of *malapvā*, one should drink the prepared water while it is warm or pleasantly lukewarm; this will cure eruptions (*sphoṭa*), vitiligo (*śvitra*), and *puṇḍarīka*.
An ointment made from burnt elephant hide or the skin of a dvīpin, mixed with oil, is applied when the pustules have burst;
furthermore, a single application of a worm (*pūtikīṭa*) soaked in the alkaline solution (*kṣāra*) derived from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree destroys vitiligo.
The soot of a black snake and, secondly, oil from the bibhītaka tree—
when all of this is ground together and applied as an ointment, it quickly destroys all cases of vitiligo.
Oil boiled seven times with one and a half parts of water and an equal part of the alkaline solution prepared according to the prescribed method,
using four times as much oil, is the foremost remedy for leucoderma when used as an ointment.
Having ground prapunnāḍa seeds, kuṣṭha, and yaṣṭīmadhuka mixed with ghee,
one should give it to a white domestic cock that has fasted for three meals and is hungry.
Having collected that excrement of his and having cooked it thoroughly, one should scrape it from all sides;
by applying this practice for a month, one destroys even leucoderma.
When the alkali has been well-burnt and the water-plant (jalagaṇḍaja) has been thoroughly infused in elephant urine,
one should add ten parts of avalguja seed and boil it in a measure of one droṇa.

When this [mixture] attains a sticky consistency, one should then form it into a whole pill. Having rubbed [the skin] with it, one should apply it to the vitiligo; thus it will quickly return to its natural color.
Having well-prepared a decoction from the bark of mango and harītakī fruits,
and having soaked a wick in the milky sap of the banyan tree, the wise man should place it into that [decoction] within a copper lamp.
Having ignited it and taken the soot produced therefrom, and having likewise dissolved it in the juice of *pathyā*,
that leprosy (kilāsa), when thoroughly rubbed [into the skin] and sprinkled with oil mixed with pungent substances, departs.
The seeds of *āvalguja* are foremost, along with those from the river, *kākāhvā*, and *udumbarī*, as well as lac;
iron powder, *māgadhī*, and *tārkṣyaśaila* should be made in equal parts, together with black sesame seeds.
Having made a wick from that [substance] ground with the bile of cows, an ointment should be applied by those afflicted with vitiligo; it removes the white spots.
By this application, the bile of a peacock removes vitiligo, or alternatively, hrivera burnt and combined with this [same bile] does so.
Tuttha, ālaka, kaṭuka, vyōṣa, siṃha, arka, hayamāraka,
kuṣṭha, avalguja, bhallātaka, kṣīriṇī, sarṣapa, and sr̥hī.
The leaves of *tilvaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *pīlu*, and *āragvadha*;
the seeds of *viḍaṅga* and *aśvahantrī*; and the two types of *haridrā* and *bṛhatī*.
By these two formulations, white leucoderma (śvitra) is destroyed entirely through external application;
having taken one hundred fruits each of vāyasī, phalgu, and tiktā separately.
One should boil two *prasthas* of iron filings, three *āḍhakas* of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
and [the mixture] in three *droṇas* of water until two parts remain from the original quantity.
When it has thickened, one should cook it further with these pastes finely ground:
indrayava, vyosha, tvak, daru, and caturaṅgula.
One should administer ghee cooked with pārāvatapadī, dantī, bākucī, keśara, and kaṇṭakārī to those suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
By drinking it, [it overcomes] that which resides in the humors and tissues; likewise, by massage, it overcomes that which resides in the skin.
Even the incurable Nīla leprosy of men it subdues.
One should take one *tulā* each of the bark of *triphalā*, *trikaṭuka*, *surasā*, *madayantīkā*, *vāyasī*, and *āragvadha*.
Likewise, ten palas each of kākamācī, arka, varuṇa, dantī, kuṭaja, citraka, dārvī, and nidigdhikā [should be taken] separately.
One should cook [the ingredients] in three droṇas of water until six prasthas remain;
[one should also add] one āḍhaka each of dung-juice, curd, milk, and urine separately.
In the same way, ghee prepared with bhūnimba,
