vyoṣa, citraka, karañja fruit, nīlikā, śyāmā, valguja, and pīlu accomplishes that [therapeutic goal].

Ghee prepared with Nīlinī and Nimba flowers cures leprosy (kuṣṭha). When applied as an ointment, it produces uniform coloration of the limbs for those afflicted with vitiligo (śvitra). Furthermore, Mahānīla ghee subdues fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara), worms, and hemorrhoids (arśas).
Cow’s urine mixed with citraka, trikaṭu, and honey should be placed in a jar of clarified butter;
after a fortnight, those suffering from vitiligo (śvitrin) should drink this, and for this condition, one should also follow the regimen prescribed for skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
The leaves of *pūtīka*, *arka*, *sruva*, *narendradruma*, and *saumanasa*, ground with [animal] urine and applied as a plaster,
destroy vitiligo, ringworm, ulcers, malignant hemorrhoids, and sinus ulcers.
After this, once the vitiated blood has flowed out, one should lubricate the patient with ghee once his vitality has returned;
then, having induced vomiting with strong formulations, one should vigilantly eliminate the morbid humors (doṣas) thoroughly, first and then subsequently.

Whether one has vomited poorly or even purged poorly, a leper whose body is pervaded by aggravated humors will undoubtedly and quickly reach a state of incurability; therefore, one should eliminate all of his humors completely.
One should undergo emetics every fortnight, and a purgative should also be administered every month;
for blood should indeed be let twice a year in small quantities, and nasal medication should be given every three nights.
Having licked a paste of harītakī, trikaṭu, and sugar-cane products mixed with oil, one is quickly freed from the disease of leprosy (kuṣṭha).
Alternatively, one should lick together āmalakī, harītakī, vibhītaka, pippalī, and viḍaṅga, combined with honey and clarified butter.
Having drunk haridrā (turmeric) in the measure of one pala with urine for a month, one shall reach the end of chronic disease.
Likewise, citraka (plumbago), finely ground, or pippalī (long pepper) mixed with urine as previously described, should be drunk.
In the same manner, one should drink Tārkṣya for a month and constantly smear the body with it;
likewise, equal parts of Āriṣṭī bark, Sāptaparṇī, Lākṣā, Musta, the two Pañcamūlas, and the two Haridrās [should be used].
Having combined equal parts of mañjiṣṭhā, akṣa, vāsaka, devadāru, pathyā, agni, vyoṣa, dhātrī, and viḍaṅga,
and having made them into a powder, one should consume it in a measure of one pala along with viḍaṅgas.
A person is freed from leprosy by using either Traiphala ghee or a droṇa of ghee combined with Vyōṣa;
furthermore, ghee prepared in a decoction of Akṣapīḍa, which has been cooked in a droṇa each of cow’s urine and water, also destroys leprosy.
Ghee that has been aged in *āragvadha*, *saptaparṇa*, *paṭola*, *vṛkṣaka*, *naktamāla*, *nimba*, and *muṣkaka*, along with the two types of *haridrā*, destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
Rodhra, ariṣṭa, padmaka, raktasāra, saptāhva, akṣa, vṛkṣaka, and bījaka should be used for the bath of a person who is burning with fever; or alternatively, tribhaṇḍī mixed with honey may be drunk.
A leper should eat old mung beans, prepared with neem-water and oil, whenever meat falls from his teeth;
or, having regained his strength, he should drink a decoction of neem, or a decoction of arka, alarka, and saptacchada.
When the limbs of the horse-eating demon have been consumed, an ointment consisting of the root of *viḍaṅga* mixed with urine should be applied;
one should also sprinkle him with urine and feed him all kinds of food prepared with *viḍaṅga*.

Oil of *kārañja* or mustard, or that of *śigru* and *kośāmra*, should be applied to the wounds; or oil cooked with all pungent and hot substances along with rock salt. For the remaining treatment, it should be managed like a case of *duṣṭavraṇa* (malignant ulcer).
The roots of Saptaparṇa, Karañja, Arka, Mālatī, and Karavīra,
as well as those of Snuhī, Śirīṣa, Citraka, and Āsphota.
Viṣa, lāṅgala, vajra, kāsīsa, āla, manaḥśilā, karañja seeds, trikaṭu, triphalā, and the two types of rajanī.
One should collect white mustard seeds, viḍaṅga, and prapunnāḍa;
with these ground in urine, one should cook oil that destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
This vajraka ointment, when applied as an unguent, removes disorders of the channels (nāḍī) and malignant ulcers;
it consists of siddhārthaka, the two types of karañja, the two types of haridrā, and rasāñjana.
Kuṭaja, prapunnāḍa, saptaparṇa,
mṛgādanī, lākṣā, sarjarasa, arka, asphota, āragvadha, and snuhī.
Śirīṣa, tuvara, kuṭaja, aruṣkara,
vacā, kuṣṭha, kṛmighna, mañjiṣṭhā, lāṅgalī, and likewise citraka.
Mālatī, kaṭutumbī, gandhāhvā, and likewise mūlaka;
saindhava, karavīra, gṛhadhūma, and likewise poison.
One should cause kampillaka, sindūra, tejohvā, and tutthaka—
each in equal parts— to be ground into a paste.
One should provide double the amount of cow urine and four times the amount of sesame oil;
[the oil] may be either the highly potent karañja or the highly efficacious mustard oil.
Through massage, it destroys all types of leprosy, scrofula, fistula-in-ano, sinus tracts, and dreadful malignant ulcers; of this there is no doubt.
This oil, possessing great qualities, is known by the name Mahāvajraka;
it is prepared from lac and other ingredients ground with bile and urine.
The physician should place it in a bitter gourd for seven days;
then, after the man has drunk the proper dose and been anointed with that [ointment], [he should proceed].
One should cause it to lie in the sun; thus its impurities depart in every way.
Having raised up the one whose impurities have been drained and who has bathed with Khadira water, [one should proceed].
One should have him drink gruel prepared with Khadira water;
likewise, [one should administer it] with the drugs belonging to the group of purifiers and those that destroy leprosy.
One should prepare oils, clarified butters, plasters, and rubs;
and every morning one should employ auspicious purgative formulations—
five, six, seven, or eight of them— by which one does not lose one's natural vigor.
Or one may drink the urine of a young camel; when it has been digested, one should eat a diet of milk.
This cures even deep-seated skin diseases (kuṣṭha) within six months.
One afflicted by leprosy, desiring to reach the end of the disease,
should employ khadira in every way— through bathing, drinking, eating, and so forth.
Just as leprosy destroys a patient through its own excessive strength,
so too does the khadira tree destroy leprosy when it is applied with vigor.
One who keeps the hair and nails short, remains free from fatigue, eats wholesome food, is devoted to medicinal herbs,
and avoids women, meat, and wine— a leper such as this dispels his leprosy.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Kuṣṭha," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||9||
The Tenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of major skin diseases (mahākuṣṭha).
As the Blessed One Dhanvantari has said.
In cases of skin diseases, urinary disorders, ailments of phlegm, and severe swellings of the entire body,
as well as for those who are obese and desire leanness, one of supreme intelligence should prescribe these formulations.
One should dry crushed and winnowed barley that has been soaked overnight in cow urine upon a large mat of *kiliñja* grass.
In this manner, one should steep and dry it for seven nights.
Then, having caused those grains to be parched in a skull, one should reduce them to flour.

Every morning, one should have the patient suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha) or urinary disorders (prameha) drink [the powder] mixed with a fourth part of the powder of bhallātaka, prapunnāṭa, avalguja, arka, citraka, and viḍaṅga, along with musta, using a decoction of the sālasārādi group or a decoction of thorny trees (kaṇṭakivṛkṣa). In the same manner, having prepared groats (saktu) from barley that has been soaked in a decoction of the sālasārādi group, or a decoction of the āragvadhādi group, or in cow and horse dung, one should add the powders of bhallātaka and the other drugs and administer them with a decoction of any one of the following—khadira, aśana, nimba, rājavṛkṣa, rohitaka, or guḍūcī—which is sweetened with sugar and honey, combined with grapes, and made sour with pomegranate, āmalaka, or vetasa, and seasoned with rock salt (saindhava). This is the procedure for all types of medicinal gruels (mantha).

One should consume barley-based foods such as parched grains, roasted grains, boiled barley, cakes, stuffed pastry-cases, fritters, pancakes, and *kuṇāvī*; and one should utilize wheat, bamboo-seeds, and wild barley according to the same methods prescribed for barley.

Now we shall describe the *ariṣṭas*. Take six *pala*s each of *pūtīka*, *cavya*, *citraka*, *suradāru*, *sārivā*, *dantī*, *trivṛt*, and *trikaṭu*; one *kuḍava* of *badara* and one *kuḍava* of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). These should be reduced to powder. Then, having first prepared a vessel by smearing its interior with honey and ghee, and having performed the preliminary purification, one should add seven *kuḍavas* of water, half a *kuḍava* of this powder, and half a *tulā* of jaggery (*guḍa*), along with the aforementioned powders. Having kept it well-protected, one should let it ferment for seven nights in a heap of barley.
Thereafter, one should consume it according to one's strength.

This *ariṣṭa* destroys leprosy, urinary disorders, obesity, anemia, and edema. In this same manner, one should prepare *ariṣṭas* from the *śālasāra* group, the *nyagrodha* group, and the *āragvadha* group.

We shall now describe the fermented liquors (*āsava*). One should prepare three parts of warm water that has been strained through *palāśa* ash and cooled, together with two parts of molasses (*phāṇita*), according to the procedure for *ariṣṭa*.

In this same manner, one should prepare fermented liquors from the alkalis of sesame and other plants; likewise, one should prepare them from the groups beginning with *śālasāra*, *vaṭa*, and *āragvadha*, as well as from various urines.

Now we shall describe the preparation of *surā* (fermented liquor). Having taken the heartwood of *śiṃśapā* and *khadira*, and having uprooted the *uttamāraṇī*, *brāhmī*, and *kośavatī* plants, one should boil all of these together according to the procedure for decoctions and take the liquid for the sake of the *maṇḍodaka*.
One should then press the fermenting agent (*kiṇva*) and flour as prescribed.
In this manner, one should prepare *surā* from the heartwood of *śāla* and so forth, from *nyagrodha* and so forth, and from *āragvadha* and so forth.
Having added these, one should cook it.

Then, having removed it from the fire when it is neither too liquid nor too thick, one who has not yet eaten his morning meal should lick a palmful of it mixed with honey. In this same manner, one should prepare electuaries (lehas) from the groups beginning with Śālasāra, Nyagrodha, and Āragvadha.

Therefore, we shall describe the preparation of powders. Having taken one *prastha* of the powder of the heartwood of the *śālasāra* group, it should be soaked many times with a decoction of the *āragvadha* group and then administered with a decoction of the *śālasāra* group itself. The same procedure applies to the fruits of the *nyagrodha* group.
One should likewise prepare a powder from the flowers of the *āragvadha* group.

Hereafter, we shall describe the iron preparations (*ayaskṛti*). Thin leaves of sharp iron, smeared with the group of salts (*lavaṇavarga*), heated over a fire of cow-dung cakes, should be quenched sixteen times in a decoction of *triphalā* and the heartwood of *śāla* and other trees.
Then, they should be heated over charcoal of *khadira* wood until the heat has subsided, reduced to a fine powder, and strained through a thick cloth.
Thereafter, one should consume an appropriate dose according to one's strength, mixed with ghee and honey.
When it has been digested, one should take food that is not sour or salty according to the specific disease.
By using [this medicine] in this manner for one *tulā*, one destroys leprosy, obesity, edema, anemia, insanity, and epilepsy, and lives for a hundred years.
For every additional *tulā*, there is an increase of a hundred years [of life].
By this, the iron preparations for all metallic substances are explained.

Having taken the fresh juice of *trivṛt*, *śyāmā*, *agnimantha*, *saptalā*, *kevuka*, *śaṅkhinī*, *tilvaka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *palāśa*, and *śiṃśapā*, and having poured it into a trough made of *palāśa* wood, one should quench an iron ball heated by *khadira* charcoal twenty-one times. Having taken that [iron ball], one should pour the juice back into it and cook it in a pot over a fire of cow-dung. Then, having removed it when only a fourth part remains, and having strained it, one should again throw in iron plates heated by fire.
While this is being prepared, one should add a portion of the powder of the *pippalyādi* group, two parts of honey, and an equal amount of clarified butter.
Then, once it has cooled, one should place it well-protected in an iron vessel.
Thereafter, one should consume it according to the requirements, either as a *śukti* or a *prakuñca*.
When it has been digested, one should follow a diet appropriate for the specific disease.
This medicinal preparation of iron cures even incurable skin diseases (kuṣṭha) or urinary disorders (prameha);
it reduces obesity and destroys swelling (śopha).
It rescues one who has sunk [into distress] and is specifically prescribed for those afflicted by consumption (rājayakṣman). By means of this, a person attains a lifespan of a hundred years.

One should pour a decoction of *śālasāra* and other woods into a palāśa wooden vat, quench heated iron bars [in it], and then pour the liquid into a consecrated jar. Having added a portion of the powder of *pippalī* and others, along with honey and jaggery, one should store it well-protected.

One should consume this *mahauṣadhāyaskṛti* after it has stood for a month or half a month, according to one's strength. In the same manner, one should prepare it using the *nyagrodha* group and the *ārevata* group as well.

Therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the *khadira* wood: having dug around a *khadira* tree that is grown in a commendable location, undamaged, and of middle age, one should cut its central root and place an iron vessel inside it so that it is capable of receiving the resin. Then, having smeared it with cow-dung and clay and scattered it with fuel mixed with cow-dung, one should set fire to it so that as it burns, the resin flows down into it. Thereafter, one should consume an appropriate dose after mixing it with the juice of *āmalaka*, honey, and ghee.
Once digested, the diet and regimen should be followed according to the procedure prescribed for *bhallātaka*.
When one *prastha* has been consumed, there is an increase in the lifespan by a hundred years.
One should boil a *tulā* of the heartwood of *khadira* in a *droṇa* of water, remove it when reduced to a sixteenth part, and store it in a protected place.
Having mixed that with the juice of *āmalaka*, honey, and ghee, one should consume it.
This same procedure applies to all the heartwoods of trees.
One should consume daily in the morning either a *tulā* (100 palas) of the powder of the heartwood of *khadira*, or the appropriate dose of a decoction of the heartwood of *khadira*,
or sheep's ghee prepared with a decoction of the heartwood of *khadira*.

One should consume the fresh juice or the decoction of *amṛtavallī* every morning, or ghee prepared with it. In the afternoon, one should eat boiled rice with ghee along with *āmalaka* soup. By using this for a month, one is liberated from all types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
One *droṇa* each of black sesame, *bhallātaka* oil, *āmalaka* juice, clarified butter, and the decoction of the *śālasāra* group [of drugs], along with one *pala* each of the following:

the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), the pulp of *kaparūṣa* fruit, *viḍaṅga* seeds, the heartwood of *citrā*, *arka*, *avalguja*, the two types of *haridrā*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *dravantī*, *indrayava*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, *ativiṣā*, *rasāñjana*, and *priyaṅgu*. One should cook these together according to the procedure for preparing medicated fats (*sneha*). Once it is properly cooked, one should remove it from the fire, strain it, and store it in a well-protected place.
Then, having prepared his body, he should rise every morning, mix a quantity of the powder equal to a hollowed palm (śukti) with honey, and consume it.

Once it has been digested, he should eat soft rice cooked in water infused with *khadira* wood, accompanied by ghee and unsalted soup of mung beans and *āmalaka* fruits, while continuing to drink *khadira* water.
By using one *droṇa* of this preparation in this manner, he becomes free from all skin diseases, possesses a purified body, is endowed with memory, and lives for a hundred years free from disease.
And on this subject,
a wise person may prepare thousands of varieties of spirits, fermented liquors, decoctions, electuaries, powders, and iron-preparations, using this as the seed.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Major Kuṣṭha," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The eleventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of prameha (urinary disorders).
As the Blessed One Dhanvantari has said.

There are two types of prameha: the congenital and that caused by unwholesome factors. Among these, the congenital is produced by defects in the seeds of the mother and father; that caused by unwholesome factors arises from the consumption of harmful diet.

Of these two, one afflicted by the former becomes emaciated, rough, eats little, is intensely thirsty, and has a habit of wandering about; the one afflicted by the latter generally becomes stout, eats much, is unctuous, and is prone to lying on beds, sitting, and sleeping.
In that regard, one should treat the emaciated with procedures refined by food and drink,
and the obese with those involving depleting therapies.

And they shall all avoid sauvīraka, tuṣodaka, śukta, maireya, surā, āsava, water, milk, oil, ghee, products of sugarcane, curd, flour-based foods, sour gruels, and the flesh of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals.
Thereafter, he should eat rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, barley, wheat, *kodrava*, and wild *uddālaka* grain, optionally combined with chickpeas, pigeon peas, horse gram, or mung beans;
and these should be accompanied by bitter and astringent vegetable preparations prepared with the oils of *nikumbha*, *iṅgudī*, mustard, or linseed;
or else with the meat of wild animals that has been cleared of its fat, is not soured, and is not cooked in ghee.

In that case, from the very beginning, one should cause the patient suffering from prameha to undergo oleation with any of the oils or with ghee prepared with the *priyaṅgvādi* group of drugs; then, one should induce strong emesis and administer a strong purgation.

Immediately after the purgation, one should perform a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) using a decoction of the *surasādi* group, mixed with honey and rock salt, and containing an addition (*vāpa*) of *mahauṣadha*, *bhadradāru*, and *mustā*.
If there is a burning sensation, one should use a decoction of the *nyagrodhādi* group, free of oil.
Then, once the body is purified, one should have the patient drink turmeric mixed with honey and the juice of *āmalaka*;
or a decoction of *triphalā*, *viśālā*, *devadāru*, and *mustaka*;
or a paste of *śāla*, *kampillaka*, and *muṣkaka* measuring one *akṣa*, sweetened with honey and combined with turmeric and the juice of *āmalaka*.

Alternatively, one may use the paste of the flowers of *kuṭaja*, *kapittha*, *rohitaka*, *bibhītaka*, and *saptaparṇa*; or the decoctions of the bark, leaves, roots, fruits, and flowers of *nimba*, *āragvadha*, *saptaparṇa*, *mūrvā*, *kuṭaja*, *somavṛkṣa*, and *palāśa*.
These five formulations are explained as destroyers of all types of urinary disorders (*meha*).
Furthermore, beyond this, one should administer the following specific treatments: for one suffering from *udakameha*, one should have them drink a decoction of *pārijātaka*;
for one suffering from *ikṣumeha*, a decoction of *citraka*;
and for one suffering from *śanairmeha*, a decoction of *khadira*.
For one suffering from *lavaṇameha*, a decoction of *pāṭhā*, *aguru*, and *haridrā*;
for one with *piṣṭameha*, a decoction of *haridrā* and *dāruharidrā*;
for one with *sāndrameha*, a decoction of *saptaparṇa*.
For one suffering from *śukrameha* (semenuria), one should administer a decoction of *dūrvā*, *śaivala*, *plava*, *haṭha*, *karañja*, and *kaseruka*, or a decoction of *kakubha* and *candana*.

For one suffering from *phenameha* (frothy urine), one should give a decoction of *triphalā*, *āragvadha*, and *mṛdvīkā*; this is sweet like honey. Among the *paittika* (bile-related) types, for one suffering from *nīlameha* (blue-colored urine), one should cause them to drink a decoction of the *śālasārādi* group or a decoction of *aśvattha*.
For one with haridrāmeha, a decoction of rājavṛkṣa; for one with amlameha, a decoction of the nyagrodhādi group;
for one with kṣārameha, a decoction of triphalā.
For one suffering from *mañjiṣṭhāmeha*, a decoction of *mañjiṣṭhā* and sandalwood should be administered.

For one suffering from *śoṇitameha*, a decoction of *guḍūcī*, the stones of *tinduka*, *kāśmarya*, and dates (*kharjūra*) mixed with honey should be given. Hereafter, we shall describe formulations for palliative purposes even in cases that are incurable.

For instance, for one suffering from *sarpirmeha*, one should have them drink a paste of *kuṣṭha*, *kuṭaja*, *pāṭhā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and *kaṭurohiṇī* with a decoction of *guḍūcī* and *citraka*.
For one suffering from *vasāmeha*, one should administer a decoction of *agnimantha* or a decoction of *śiṃśapā*.
For one suffering from *kṣaudrameha*, a decoction of *kadara* and *kramuka*.

For one suffering from *hastimeha*, a preparation of the ashes of *tinduka*, *kapittha*, *śirīṣa*, *palāśa*, *pāṭhā*, *mūrvā*, and *duḥsthi*. Furthermore, for one suffering from *dahyamāna*, one should have them drink a gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared with a decoction of aquatic tubers, sweetened with milk, sugarcane juice, and honey.

Thereafter, one should prepare fermented liquors (ariṣṭas), metallic preparations (ayas-kṛtis), electuaries (lehas), and spirituous drinks (āsavas) from priyaṅgu, anantā, yūthikā, padmā, trāyantikā, lohitikā, ambaṣṭhā, the bark of pomegranate, śālaparṇī, padma, tuṅga, keśara, dhātakī, vakula, śālmalī, śrīveṣṭaka, and mocarasa; or alternatively, from śṛṅgāṭaka, giloḍya, bisa, mṛṇāla, kāśa, kaseruka, madhuka, āmra, jambu, asana, tiniśa, kakubha, kaṭvaṅga, rodhra, bhallātaka, palāśa, carmavṛkṣa, girikarṇikā, śītaśiva, nicula, dāḍima, ajakarṇa, harivṛkṣa, rājādana, gopaghoṇṭā, and vikaṅkata. One should also consume various preparations of barley and rice, and should be given gruel (yavāgū) prepared with the aforementioned decoctions.
Or to drink astringent decoctions.

One should cause the lord—who is honored for his great wealth and who detests food and medicine—to drink any one of the following fermented liquors (*āsava*) in no small quantity: those strongly infused with *pāṭhā*, *abhayā*, and *citraka*, or honey; or he should frequently drink *mādhvīka* wine accompanied by roasted meat on a spit as a side dish. Furthermore, one should serve him drinks and foods seasoned with honey, *kapittha* fruit, and black pepper.

One should give him the powders of the dung of camels, mules, and donkeys as food; one should feed him with soups mixed with asafoetida and rock salt, and with mustard-based condiments. One should provide him with drinks and foods that are not incompatible [with his condition] and possess flavor and fragrance. Furthermore, those suffering from advanced urinary disorders (prameha) should practice physical exercise, wrestling, games, and the maneuvers of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, or they should train in the use of weapons and missiles.

Whether he be without wealth or without kinsmen, devoid of shoes and an umbrella, subsisting on alms, staying for only one night in a village, with his self restrained like a sage, he may travel a hundred *yojanas* or even more.
Or, though possessing great wealth, he may live with deer, subsisting on *śyāmāka* and *nīvāra* grains, or feeding on *āmalaka*, *kapittha*, *tinduka*, and *aśmantaka* fruits;
or, consuming their urine and dung, he may constantly follow the cows.
Or, adopting the livelihood of a Brahmin who gathers grains by gleaning, he should pull out the chariot of Brahman;
otherwise, he should constantly till the soil or dig a well,
and he must always protect himself from weakness.
And there is a verse on this point:
A poor man who acts thus without indolence, solely by the physician's instruction,
is liberated from prameha within a year or even sooner.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Prameha," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||11||
The Twelfth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of carbuncles (piḍakā) arising from urinary disorders (prameha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

The nine types of pustules beginning with śarāvikā have been described previously; when they occur in a person with vitality, are small, located in the skin and flesh, soft, slightly painful, and suppurate and burst quickly, they are curable.
One should treat the patient suffering from *prameha* who is afflicted by these [symptoms].

In the stage of premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), one should prescribe fasting, decoctions of trees (*vanaspati*), and goat's urine. If one does not act thus, the urine, sweat, and phlegm (*śleṣman*) of that person—who consumes sweet food—become sweet, and *prameha* becomes manifest.

In that case, one should employ purification (*saṃśodhana*) for both [upper and lower tracts]. If one does not act thus, the aggravated *doṣas*, having vitiated the muscle tissue (*māṃsa*) and blood (*śoṇita*), produce swelling or various complications.

In that case, the remedy has been stated as venesection; if one does not act thus, the swelling increases excessively and undergoes suppuration with intense pain. For that, the application of the surgical instrument and the treatment of the ulcer have been prescribed; if one does not act thus, the pus, having burst internally and created a large cavity within the hollow, becomes incurable due to its growth. Therefore, one should treat the patient suffering from prameha from the very beginning.

Take ten *pala*s each of *bhallātaka*, *bilva*, *ambu*, *pippalīmūla*, *udakīryā*, *varṣābhū*, *punarnavā*, *citraka*, *śaṭī*, *snuhī*, *varuṇaka*, *puṣkara*, *dantī*, and *pathyā*; and one *prastha* each of *yava*, *kola*, and *kulattha*. Boil these in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-fourth, then remove from the heat. Add half a *pala* each of *vacā*, *trivṛt*, *kampillaka*, *bhārgī*, *nicula*, *śuṇṭhī*, *gajapippalī*, *viḍaṅga*, *rodhra*, and *śirīṣa*, along with one *prastha* of ghee, and cook it thoroughly. This preparation, known as Dhānvantara, destroys urinary disorders (*meha*), edema (*śvayathu*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), abdominal enlargements (*udara*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), splenic disorders (*plīha*), abscesses (*vidradhi*), and carbuncles (*piḍakā*).
Indeed, those suffering from *madhumeha* (diabetes mellitus) are difficult to purge because their bodies are pervaded by fat (*medas*).
Therefore, one should administer a sharp purification (*śodhana*) for them.

All types of *prameha*, when afflicted by carbuncles (*piḍakā*) and accompanied by complications (*upadrava*), receive the technical designation *madhumeha* due to the commonality of sweetness and honey-like odor in the urine and other secretions.
And one should not cause them to sweat by any means whatsoever;
for due to their abundance of fat, their bodies would dissolve from sweating.
Furthermore, due to the weakness of the *rasāyanī* channels, the morbid humors (*doṣas*) of those suffering from urinary disorders (*pramehin*) do not ascend;
consequently, carbuncles (*piḍakās*) manifest in the lower part of the body of those with honey-like diabetes (*madhumehin*).
For unripened abscesses, the treatment is like that for swellings;
for those that have ripened, it is like that for ulcers. One should first apply an ulcer-healing oil, and use a decoction of the *āragvadhādi* group for the purpose of rubbing the area (*utsādana*).
A decoction of *śālasāra* and related drugs should be used for sprinkling;
a decoction of *pippalī* and related drugs for drinking and in food.
One should consume the powders of the roots of *pāṭhā*, *citraka*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *kṣudrā*, *bṛhatī*, *sārivā*, *somavalka*, *saptaparṇa*, *āragvadha*, and *kuṭaja*, mixed with honey and molasses.
Having boiled the decoction of the *śālasāra* group [of drugs] until one-fourth remains, one should remove it from the heat, strain it, and then bring it back to the fire to re-cook it.
While it is being cooked, one should add powdered *āmalaka*, *rodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, *dantī*, black iron powder, and copper powder.
When this has thickened into a consistency like molasses (*lehībhūta*) without burning, one should remove it from the fire and store it in a well-protected place.
Then one should employ it as appropriate;
this electuary is the destroyer of all types of urinary disorders (meha).

Take nine parts each of triphalā, citraka, trikaṭuka, viḍaṅga, and mustā, and an equal amount of powdered black iron (kṛṣṇāyaś-cūrṇa). Having combined all these together, one should consume an appropriate dose mixed with ghee and honey. This is Navāyasa; by its use, indigestion (jāḍarya) does not occur.
The digestive fire is nourished;
and diseases such as durnāman, swelling, anemia, skin disorders, indigestion, cough, asthma, and urinary disorders do not occur.
When the decoction of śālasāra and other ingredients has been reduced to one-fourth its original volume and strained,
one should then add honey when it has cooled.
Molasses that has reached a thickened consistency, purified jaggery,
and the finely ground powders of the pippalyādi group of drugs.
One should pour [the ingredients] together into a single jar that has been purified, smeared with ghee,
coated internally with long pepper powder and honey, and is clean, firm, and well-sealed.
There, the wise man should repeatedly apply thin leaves of sharp iron that have been heated in the charcoal of khadira wood.
Having sealed it well,
one should place it in a pit of barley for three or four months, or until the metal has completely dissolved.
Then, having produced that juice, one should consume it every morning according to one's strength and as is appropriate,
and one should arrange his diet accordingly.
This [preparation] produces leanness in those who are strong, promotes the digestion of fire when it has subsided,
removes swelling, cures abdominal tumors, and destroys skin diseases, urinary disorders, and jaundice.
Lohāriṣṭa is highly efficacious; it quickly cures enlargement of the spleen, destroys intermittent fevers, and removes obstructions caused by excessive secretions.
When the urine of a patient suffering from prameha is no longer slimy and turbid, but becomes clear,
bitter, and pungent, then it is declared that health has been restored.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Prameha-piḍakās," in the Cikitsā-sthāna of the Śrī Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||12||
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of madhumeha (diabetes mellitus).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
A wise physician should treat a patient suffering from prameha who has developed honey-like urine and has been abandoned by other doctors, using this yoga.
In the month of Śuci, when the moon is in the constellation Śukra, the mountains, heated by the rays of the sun,
indeed exude from their rocks a natural resin with the appearance of lac.
Known as śilājatu, it destroys all diseases and is derived from one or another of the six metals, such as tin and the rest.
It should be known that, according to its own scent, this mineral known on earth as having six origins arises from metal; it is called śilājatu because it has the luster of lac (jatuprabha).
That [mercury] possesses both the potency and the essence of that iron;
among tin, lead, iron, and so forth, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
Even when applied in the most excellent manner, [these substances] are traditionally held to possess excellent qualities;
yet they are all bitter, pungent, with an aftertaste of astringent, and laxative.
It is pungent in digestion, hot in potency, drying, and likewise incising;
among those [grains], that which is black, light, unctuous, and free from grit is best.
That which has the scent of cow’s urine is declared to be the most excellent;
having been infused with the collection of essences and freed from defects at the break of dawn, it is so prepared.
One should drink it, finely ground, with the decoction of heartwood according to one's strength;
once that has been digested, one should eat food with the meat broth of wild animals.
Having thus utilized the *tulā* measure of this nectar-like substance from the Daughter of the Mountain,
one becomes endowed with a beautiful complexion and strength, and is freed from diabetes mellitus (*madhumeha*).
He shall live for a full hundred years, free from old age and like unto an immortal; for every hundred palas [of merit], he lives a hundred years, and for every thousand palas, a thousand years.

The regimen for avoidance is prescribed according to the procedure for *bhallātaka*: it cures urinary disorders (*meha*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), epilepsy (*apasmāra*), insanity (*unmāda*), elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), and artificial poisons (*gara*).
Shilājatu, when consumed for a period of time, quickly dispels consumption, swelling, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, jaundice, and irregular fever.
There is no disease which bitumen cannot destroy;
it likewise breaks up long-accumulated gravel as well as urinary stones.
And when this [mercury] is to be stirred with beneficial medicinal substances,
one should likewise [stir] the honey-like mineral born of the Tāpī river, which is like nectar.
Drinking [mercury] that is sweet and has the luster of gold, or sour and has the brilliance of silver,
destroys old age, leprosy, urinary disorders, anemia, and consumption.
One who has been purified by that [practice], who possesses faith, and who desires to live, should avoid pigeons and horse-gram (kulattha),
provided he has transcended the requirements of the five purificatory rites (pañcakarma).
By this method, a wise person may even cure leprosy;
for there are *tuvaraka* trees that grow in the lands of the western ocean.
When the clouds arrive, one should gather their well-ripened fruits, whose shoots are shaken by the wind and tossed by the movement of ripples and waves.
Having extracted the marrow even from those [bones], having dried it and ground it into powder,
one should press it in a wooden vat like sesame seeds, or cause it to flow out like safflower.

That oil, having been collected again, should be cooked until the water is completely evaporated; then, having removed it from the heat, one should store it in a pit of dried cow-dung for exactly one fortnight.
Having been anointed with oil, sweated, and cleansed of impurities, the diligent practitioner,
after an interval of one fortnight, should, on an auspicious day at the beginning of the bright fortnight, observe a fast for four meals.
One should drink a dose of oil purified by mantras according to one's strength;
I shall now declare the mantra with which this is consecrated.
O essence of marrow, O you of great heroism, purify all the elements!
Acyuta, whose hands hold the conch, the discus, and the mace, commands you.
Therefore, by that means, his humors (doṣas) move repeatedly both upward and downward;
consequently, he should drink a cold gruel (yavāgū) in the evening, prepared without fat or salt.
A man should drink oil for five days according to this procedure,
and for a fortnight he should avoid [other food], subsisting instead on rice with mung bean soup.
In this way, within just five days, one is liberated from all types of leprosy;
that same [preparation] is properly prepared by boiling it well in three times the amount of khadira decoction.
As before, one should drink it for a month from a fortnight [of the lunar cycle], remaining vigilant;
having anointed one's body with that, one should take the prescribed food.
By this application, one may quickly cure a man afflicted with leprosy who has a broken voice, bloodshot eyes, and a body that is shattered and consumed by worms.
That same [milk], when drunk with ghee and honey along with Khadira water and a diet of bird meat broth,
makes one live for two hundred years.
That very [substance], when employed as nasal medication for fifty days,
makes one handsome, endowed with a retentive memory, and grants a lifespan of three hundred years.
When drunk in the proper measure, its marrow purifies a person;
moreover, mahāvīryastuvaraka is supreme in removing leprosy and urinary disorders.

Its marrow, burnt with smoke inside and cast into oil along with rock salt and collyrium, destroys pterygium, ama, night-blindness, and cataracts; by means of this collyrium, it also cures the disease of *nīlī* and blurred vision (*taimira*).
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Madhumeha," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The fourteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of abdominal enlargements (udarāṇi).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Eight types of abdominal enlargements (udara) have been previously mentioned.

Among them, those caused by intestinal obstruction (baddhaguda) and intestinal perforation (parisrāvin) are incurable; the remaining ones are difficult to cure (kṛcchrasādhya). One should undertake treatment for all of them only after informing the patient of the prognosis. Of these, the first group of four is curable by means of medicine.
The upper [type] is treatable by surgery;
however, due to the prolongation of time, all [types] that are treatable by surgery should either be avoided or [treated with extreme caution].

A woman suffering from abdominal enlargement (udarī) should avoid heavy, obstructive, dry, burning, unctuous, and meat-based foods, as well as affusion and immersion baths; she should always eat śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, barley, wheat, and nīvāra grain.

In that regard, for one suffering from abdominal distension caused by Vāta (vātodari), one should first administer oleation with ghee prepared with the Vidārigandhādi group of drugs; then, having induced downward movement of the bowels with ghee cooked with Tilvaka,
one should perform both non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) and unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using a decoction of the Vidārigandhādi group enriched with oil extracted from Citrā fruits.
One should apply a poultice made with *sālvaṇa* to the abdomen;
one should feed the patient milk prepared with the *vidārigandhādi* group of drugs and the meat-broth of wild animals;
and one should foment the area repeatedly.

In the case of one suffering from *pittodara*, having first administered oleation with ghee processed with the sweet group of drugs, and having induced downward movement of the bowels (*anulomana*) with ghee processed with *śyāmā*, *triphalā*, and *trivṛt*,
one should administer non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) and unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) using a decoction of the *nyagrodhādi* group, enriched with sugar, honey, and ghee.
One should apply a poultice of milk-porridge (pāyasa) to the abdomen and feed the patient milk prepared with the vidārigandhādi group of drugs.

In a patient suffering from abdominal enlargement caused by *śleṣman* (phlegm), one should first apply oleation with ghee prepared with a decoction of the *pippalyādi* group. Then, having induced downward movement of the bowels with ghee cooked with the latex of *snuhī*,
one should administer both non-unctuous (*āsthāpana*) and unctuous (*anuvāsana*) enemas using a decoction of the *muṣkakādi* group, enriched with *trikaṭu*, urine, alkali, and oil.
One should apply a poultice (upanāha) to the abdomen using a paste made of hemp, linseed, dhātakī, fermenting agent (kiṇva), mustard seeds, and radish seeds.

One should feed the patient either with a soup of horse gram (kulattha) heavily seasoned with the three pungents (trikaṭuka) or with milk-rice (pāyasa). Furthermore, one should foment the patient repeatedly.

Having rejected the treatment for a woman with a poisoned womb (*dūṣyodarinī*), one should treat her for a month or half a month with ghee prepared with the expressed juices of *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī*;

or alternatively, with ghee prepared with the milk of the *mahāvṛkṣa*, wine, and cow’s urine. Once her bowels are purified, one should have her drink with wine a paste made from the roots of *aśvamāraka*, *guñjā*, and *kākādanī*. Or, having had black snakes bite the stalks of sugarcanes, she should eat them; or she may eat the fruits of creepers. Alternatively, she should consume poison derived from roots or tubers.
Therefore, he becomes non-existent or attains another state of being.
And in this regard,
because it is rooted in provoked wind (vāyu) and because of the accumulation of impurities (mala),
they frequently recommend downward purgation (anulomana) for all types of abdominal enlargements (udara).
Hereafter, we shall describe the general applications.
For example: one should consume castor oil every day for a month, or for two months, either alone, combined with urine, or combined with milk, while abstaining from water.
Alternatively, one may consume buffalo urine with milk for seven nights while remaining without solid food.
Or, for a fortnight, one should subsist on camel’s milk while abstaining from solid food and water;
or, for a month, one should consume long pepper (*pippalī*) according to the previously mentioned procedure; or, one may take *nikumbha* oil combined with rock salt (*saindhava*) and *ajamodā*.
Alternatively, for wind-pain (*vāta-śūla*), one should administer [a preparation] prepared with a hundred pots of fresh ginger juice;
or one should consume milk cooked with ginger juice;
or a paste of *cavya* and ginger with milk; or likewise [a paste of] *sarala*, *devadāru*, and *citraka* with milk.
One should drink either a paste of *muraṅgī*, *śālaparṇī*, *śyāmā*, and *punarnavā*; or *jyotiṣka* fruit oil mixed with milk, *svarjikā*, and asafoetida;
or one should eat a *harītakī* accompanied by jaggery.

Alternatively, one may administer a thousand *pippalī* fruits that have been soaked for a period of time in the milky sap of the *sruti* plant; or, having prepared a poultice (*utkārikā*) from the powder of *pathyā* and *kṛṣṇā* soaked in the milky sap of *snuhī*, one should cook it and give it to the patient. Or, one should add one *prastha* of *harītakī* powder to an *āḍhaka* of clarified butter, melt it over charcoal embers, stir it with a churning-stick, and keep it well-protected for half a month in a heap of barley straw.
Then, having removed it and strained it, one should add the decoction of *harītakī*, sour gruel, and curd, and cook it again.
One should administer it for a month or half a month according to the requirements.
Having infused the milk of the *mahāvṛkṣa* into cow's milk, one should cook it.
Once cooked, having removed it from the heat and allowed it to cool, one should churn it with a churning stick, take the butter, and cook it once again with the milk of the *mahāvṛkṣa* itself.

One should administer this for a month or half a month, according to what is appropriate. Take half a *karṣa* each of the following: *cavya*, *citraka*, *dantī*, *ativiṣā*, *kuṣṭha*, *sārivā*, *triphalā*, *ajamoda*, *haridrā*, *śaṅkhinī*, *trivṛt*, and *trikaṭuka*. Add eight *karṣas* of the pulp of *rājavṛkṣa* fruit and two *palas* of the milky sap of *mahāvṛkṣa*.

Take eight *palas* each of cow’s milk and urine. Having added all of this to one *prastha* of ghee, one should cook it. One should administer this, as appropriate, for a month or half a month. These four types of ghee, beginning with *tilvaka-ghṛta*, are to be employed for the purpose of purgation in cases of abdominal enlargement (*udara*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), abscesses (*vidradhi*), inguinal hernia (*aṣṭhīlā*), flatulence (*ānāha*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), insanity (*unmāda*), and epilepsy (*apasmāra*). Furthermore, one should frequently consume fermented urine, *ārishta*, *ariṣṭa*, and wine, prepared with the abundant milky sap of the *mahāvṛkṣa*; or else, a decoction of purgative substances heavily supplemented with ginger (*śṛṅgavera*) and *devadāru*.

One should take one-pala portions of the substances used for emesis, purgation, and head-evacuation, as well as the substances enumerated in the *pippalyādi* and *vacādiharidrādi* groups, and the aforementioned salts—all finely ground. Having added all these to the group of urines (*mūtragaṇa*) and one *prastha* of the milky sap of the *mahāvṛkṣa*, one should cook them over a mild fire, stirring constantly, until the paste is not burnt. Once it is properly cooked, it should be removed from the heat; when cooled, one should form pills (*guṭikā*) of the size of an *akṣa*. One, two, or three of these pills should be consumed according to one's strength for three or four months.

This procedure of *ānāhavartikriyā* is especially employed for major diseases; it specifically destroys worms residing in the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*) and cures cough, dyspnea, worms, skin diseases, catarrh, anorexia, indigestion, and upward movement of gases (*udāvarta*).

Having ground together the pulp of *madana* fruit, *kuṭaja*, *jīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *dhāmārgava*, *trivṛt*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), and mustard seeds with salt, and mixing them with either the milky sap of the *mahāvṛkṣa* or urine, one should form a suppository the size of a thumb. For a patient suffering from abdominal enlargement (*udara*) and intestinal obstruction (*ānāha*), after the anus has been lubricated with oil and salt, one, two, or three of these should be inserted into the rectum.

This procedure of the "obstruction-suppository" (*ānāhavarti*) is to be employed in cases of obstruction of flatus, urine, or feces, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), flatulence, and intestinal obstruction.

In a patient suffering from splenic enlargement (plīhodara), who has been treated with oleation and sudation and has eaten curd, one should pierce the vein on the inner side of the elbow of the left arm.

One should then massage the spleen with the hand to cause the blood to flow out. Thereafter, once the body has been purified, one should have the patient drink the alkali of oyster shells with milk, or alternatively, asafoetida and sauvarcali salt with milk.
Or barley-alkali with Palāśa-alkali that has been strained;
or barley-alkali with the water of Kiṃśuka-alkali that has been strained many times;
or the alkali of Pārijātaka, Ikṣuraka, and Apāmārga.
A soup of *śobhāñjana* mixed with oil, combined with long pepper (*pippalī*), rock salt (*saindhava*), and leadwort (*citraka*);
or else the alkaline water of the *pūtikarañja*, strained with sour liquids and heavily seasoned with black salt (*viḍlavaṇa*) and long pepper.

Take one *pala* each of long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), chaba pepper (*cavya*), leadwort (*citraka*), fresh ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), and rock salt (*saindhava*).
To these, add one *prastha* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and an equal amount of milk; boil them together until cooked.

This is the medicated ghee known as *Ṣaṭpalaka*. It cures splenic disorders, loss of digestive fire, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), edema, anemia, cough, dyspnea, catarrh, upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvavāta*), and irregular fevers.
Or indeed, one with weak digestive fire should consume the powder beginning with hiṅgu (asafoetida).
This same procedure for the division of the action applies even when the liver is being incised;
however, the specific distinction is that the venesection is performed on the right arm.
Having bent the wrist once and directed [the vein] with the left thumb,
the physician should quickly cauterize the vein with an arrow for the pacification of the spleen disease.

In cases of *baddhaguda* (intestinal obstruction) and *parisrāvin* (intestinal fistula), the patient should first be treated with oleation (*snigdha*) and sudation (*svinna*), and then anointed (*abhyakta*). Leaving four finger-breadths below the navel and to the left of the line of hair (*romarājī*), the abdomen should be incised. Having extracted the intestines to a length of four finger-breadths and examined them, one should remove any stone or hair that is causing the intestinal obstruction in the case of *baddhaguda*, or any accumulation of impurities. Then, having anointed the intestines with honey and ghee, they should be restored to their proper place, and the external abdominal wound should be sutured. In the case of *parisrāvin* as well, the procedure is exactly the same, except that after extracting the foreign body, the intestinal discharges must be thoroughly cleansed.
Having inserted that intestinal tube into the opening, one should have it bitten by black ants;
once they have bitten, one should remove their bodies but not their heads,
and then one should suture it as before.
One should effect the rejoining as previously described;
having coated it with black earth mixed with licorice (*yaṣṭīmadhuka*), one should treat it with a bandage.
Then, having brought it into a windless room, one should prescribe the regimen of conduct.
And one should cause him to dwell in a vat of oil or a vat of clarified butter, subsisting on milk.

For one suffering from *dakodara* (ascites), after being anointed with oil that alleviates *vāta* and fomented with hot water, and while being firmly supported by attendants and wrapped from the armpits downwards, one should pierce a depth of the size of a thumb’s belly using a *vrīhimukha* instrument, four finger-breadths below the navel and to the left of the line of hair (*romarājī*).
There, having attached a tube made of tin or another metal—either with two openings or as a side-tube—one should drain the morbid fluid (*doṣodaka*).
Then, having removed the tube and anointed the wound with oil and salt, one should treat it with a bandage.
One should not remove all the morbid water (doṣodaka) on a single day;

for if it is removed too suddenly, thirst, fever, body aches, diarrhea, dyspnea, cough, and burning of the feet may arise, or the abdomen may become excessively distended in one whose vital strength has not yet been restored. Therefore, one should drain the morbid water very gradually, allowing an interval of three, four, five, six, eight, ten, twelve, or sixteen nights between sessions. Once the morbid matter has been discharged, the abdomen should be wrapped very tightly with a woolen cloth, silk, or leather.
Likewise, the wind does not cause flatulence; for six months one should feed [the patient] with milk or the meat-juice of wild animals (*jāṅgala*).
Then, for three months, one should feed him with half-milk mixed with fruit-acid or with the meat-juice of wild animals.
For the remaining three months, he should consume light and wholesome food.
In this way, one becomes free from disease within a year.
And in this regard,

for those suffering from all types of abdominal enlargements, milk boiled [with medicinal herbs] or the meat-juice of wild animals should be administered by the skilled physician during the administration of enemas, purgatives, drinks, and likewise during the procedures for the rules of diet.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Abdominal Enlargement," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of obstructed labor (mūḍhagarbha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
There is nothing more difficult than the extraction of a dead fetus; for in this case, one must perform the procedure by touch amidst the vagina, liver, spleen, intestinal cavities, and uterus.
One must perform drawing out, pushing down, turning, excising, tearing, cutting, pressing, straightening, and splitting with a single hand, without harming either the fetus or the pregnant woman.
Therefore, having consulted the ruler and exerting the greatest effort, one should proceed.
In this regard, eight types of fetal malpositions have been briefly described; furthermore, there are three natural obstructions caused by defects of the head, the shoulders, or the buttocks.

If the fetus is alive, one should strive to extract it from the womb of the woman who has given birth. If it cannot be extracted, one should cause her to hear the mantras for inducing delivery; these we shall now declare.
O beautiful lady, may Amṛta, Soma, and Citrabhānu,
as well as the horse Uccaiḥśravas, dwell in your palace.
This nectar has indeed been drawn from the waters; may it cause this embryo of yours to be released easily, O woman.
May Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Vāsava, together with the salt oceans and the clouds, grant you peace.
The fetters of the animal are released; the rays are released by the sun.
Released from all fear, O embryo, come, come, you who are free from distress!
And one should administer the medicinal remedies as prescribed.

When the woman has died, she should be placed supine with her thighs flexed and her waist raised by a support of cloth; having smeared [her] with dhanvana, nagavṛttikā, śālmalī, clay, and ghee, one should insert the hand into the birth canal and extract the fetus.
In that case, if it has come out with the legs first, one should pull it out in the natural direction.
If the fetus has entered with one thigh, one should draw it out by extending the other thigh.
If it has arrived on its buttocks, one should press the buttocks, lift it upward, extend both thighs, and draw it out.
If it has come across like a transverse bar, one should lift the posterior half upward, bring the anterior half straight toward the birth canal, and draw it out.
If the head is turned to the side, one should press the shoulder, lift the head upward, bring it to the birth canal, and extract it.
If the fetus has taken hold with both arms, one should press the shoulders upward, bring the head in the natural direction, and extract it.
The last two types of obstructed births (*mūḍhagarbha*) are incurable.
Thus, when [the patient] is incapable [of recovery], one should apply the surgical instrument.
One should never, under any circumstances, cut open a living being with a weapon;
for if it is cut open, it will surely cause the destruction of both its mother and itself.
But when the disorder becomes unbearable, it is better to induce the miscarriage;
there should be no reversal of this for a pregnant woman. Therefore, one should not let an opportunity that has arisen go to waste.
Then, having comforted the woman, he should split open her head with a circular blade or a finger-sword;
having extracted the cranial plates and grasped them with a pin, he should remove them from the chest or the armpit; or [he may do so] from the unbroken head at the temple or the cheek.
Having severed the arms at the shoulder region of one whose [limbs] are stuck to the shoulders;
or, having torn open like a distended leather bag the abdomen filled with wind, he should extract the entrails once they have become flaccid;
or, in the case of one stuck to the hips, [he should extract] the hip-bones.
In short, whatever part of the fetus becomes stuck,
the physician should properly extract it by cutting, while protecting the woman with great effort.
The various movements of the fetus arise from the provocation of the wind (vāyu);
in that regard, a physician of no small intelligence should act according to the prescribed rules.
A wise man should not neglect a dead fetus even for a moment;
for it quickly kills the mother, like an animal deprived of breath.
One who understands the internal [anatomy] should perform the excision with the edge of the mandala instrument;
for a sharp-pointed vṛddhipatra might otherwise injure the woman.
Then, the physician should cause another [fetus] that is falling to descend as before;
or he may remove it by hand, or by pressing upon both sides.
The wise physician should repeatedly shake the woman or press upon her shoulder-blades;
thus, for one whose birth canal has been lubricated with oil, he should cause the fetus to descend.
When the fetus has been thus extracted, one should sprinkle her with warm water;
then, once her body has been anointed, one should apply oil into her womb.
In this way, the birth canal becomes softened and that pain is pacified.
[One should also use] black pepper, its root, ginger, cardamom, asafoetida, bhārgī, and dīpyaka.
One should administer vacā, ativiṣā, rāsnā, and cavya, having powdered them together with a fatty medium (sneha),
for the purpose of liquefying the morbid humors (doṣas) and for the alleviation of pain.
One should likewise administer their decoction, paste, or powder, excluding any fatty medium;
[and also] śāka-bark, hiṅgu, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Likewise, the physician should also have her drink Tejovatī as before for three nights, or five or seven days; thereafter, she should drink unctuous substances again.
One should cause him to drink fermented liquor (āsava) at night, or well-prepared ariṣṭa;
and water from śirīṣa and kakubha is beneficial for rinsing the mouth.
Any other complications that may arise should be treated according to their respective natures;
she should remain entirely purified and eat only unctuous, wholesome, and small quantities of food.
She should constantly devote herself to sudation and oil massage, remain free from anger,
and for ten days it is beneficial to consume milk prepared with vata-alleviating herbs in her diet.
One should administer the liquid for ten days, or treat her as appropriate during the remainder;
then, having recognized that the woman of excellent complexion is free from complications and has been properly purified.
After four months have passed, one may gradually resume [the use of] vaginal nourishment,
massage, drinking, enemas, and food.
One should also give this Balā oil to her, which wards off wind disorders,
along with a decoction of Balā roots and one boiled with Daśamūlī.
Take eight auspicious parts each of a decoction of barley, jujube, and horse gram, as well as eight parts of milk, and one part of oil; then combine them together.
Having ground together a sweet powder mixed with rock salt,
as well as aguru, resin of the sarja tree, sarala, and devadāru;
Mañjiṣṭhā, candana, kuṣṭha, elā, kālānusārivā,
māṃsī, śaileyaka, patra, tagara, sārivā, and vacā.
Śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā—
this [mixture], when properly prepared in a vessel made of gold, silver, or even clay, [is beneficial].
Having added these properly, one should place them well-secured in a jar;
this is known as Balā-taila, which cures all disorders of Vāta.
Therefore, one should cause the woman who has recently given birth to take the proper dose according to her strength;
as should a woman desiring conception and a man whose semen is depleted.
It is to be employed in every way for those whose bodily humors are depleted by wind (vāta), who have been struck in their vital points (marman), who are reeling, who have been beaten,
as well as for those with fractures and those overcome by exhaustion.
This indeed cures ākṣepaka and other wind-related diseases,
as well as hiccups, cough, eye disorders, abdominal tumors, and difficult-to-cure dyspnea.
By using this for six months, one eliminates intestinal hernia;
the person’s bodily constituents become fresh, and he attains stable youth.
For this must indeed be done by kings, as well as by those men who hold royal rank,
and by those men who are happy, delicate, and wealthy.
Having extracted oil many times from sesame seeds that have been soaked in a decoction of *balā*,
one should prepare that auspicious oil by subjecting it to a hundredfold cooking (*śatapāka*) with that same decoction.
One should administer [the medicine] according to one's strength in a sheltered room free from drafts;
once it has been digested, one should eat unctuous sixty-day rice with milk.
Having consumed a droṇa of this according to the prescribed method, one should eat food for twice that duration; thereafter, one becomes endowed with strength and a healthy complexion.
A person shall become liberated from all sins and attain a lifespan of a hundred years;
likewise, for every *droṇa* [of the substance], an increase of one hundred [years] is proclaimed.
In the chapter on *balā* preparations, [the procedure applies] to *atibalā*, *guḍūcī*, *ādityaparṇī*,
*saireyaka*, *vīrataru*, *śatāvarī*, and *trikaṇṭaka*.
A wise person should prepare oils from madhuka and prasāriṇī;
one should also boil blue lotus and the root of varī in cow's milk.
Then the physician should cook sesame oil a hundred times with that [milk];
he should add well-ground pastes of the ingredients for Bala-taila into it.
The physician should understand the application of all these [medicines],
as well as their specific qualities, particularly like those of Bala oil.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Malpresented Fetus," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||15||
The sixteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of abscesses (vidradhi).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Six types of abscesses (vidradhi) have been described; among them, the one caused by all three humors (sarvaja) is incurable.
In the remaining types, while they are still in the stage of inflammation (āma), treatment should be performed quickly as in the case of swelling (śopha).
In the case of a Vāta-vidradhi (abscess caused by Vāta), a thick, lukewarm paste made from the roots of Vāta-subduing plants, combined with ghee, oil, and muscle fat, should be applied.
Meat from marshy regions and aquatic animals, prepared with the Kākolyādi group, along with saturating agents,
fats, acids, and salts, should be employed for poultices (upanāhana).
One should constantly cause [the patient] to sweat with meat preparations mixed with sesame, milk, and milk-rice,
and likewise one should also let the blood flow out.
If it has been treated in this manner and is ready for cooking,
one should cook it, then incise it with a surgical instrument, and once incised, cleanse it.
Having washed it with a decoction of the five roots,
one should fill it with oils containing a high proportion of salt, combined with the Bhadradaru group of drugs and licorice.
Having purified [the patient] with Traivṛta oil combined with purgative drugs,
one should heal the wound with Traivṛta oil prepared with the Pṛthakparṇī and other herbs.
In the case of a Pitta-type [abscess], one should apply a plaster made of sugar, parched grain, madhuka, and sārivā ground with milk;
or alternatively, a plaster of payasyā, uśīra, and candana ground with milk.
One should sprinkle [the area] with decoctions that have been boiled and then cooled, or with milk, or likewise with sugarcane juice,
or even with life-promoting (jīvanīya) medicated ghees mixed with sugar.

The wise man should lick the powder of triple-dried *harītakī* with honey as a liquid, and he should extract the blood with leeches once it has become suppurated, considering the unwholesome nature of the condition.
Having washed [the wound] with a decoction of milk-yielding trees or with water,
one should apply [medicinal paste] made of sesame seeds, yaṣṭīmadhuka, and honey, combined with clarified butter.
Having applied an ointment, one should wrap the wound with a thin cloth using prapauṇḍarīka,
mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, uśīra, and padmaka.
Ghee prepared with turmeric and milk promotes the healing of wounds,
as do [preparations] with kṣīraśuklā, pṛthakparṇī, samaṅgā, rodhra, and candana.
It may be prepared from the tender sprouts or the bark of the Nyagrodha and other such trees,
or from the fresh leaves and fruits of the Naktamāla.
The leaves of *sumanā*, as well as those of *paṭola* and *ariṣṭa*;
the two types of *haridrā*, beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), *madhuka*, and *tiktarohiṇī*.
Priyaṅgu, the root of kuśa grass, the bark of nicula,
mañjiṣṭhā, sandalwood, uśīra, utpala, sārivā, and trivṛt.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with the medicinal parts of these [drugs] in their respective proportions;
this pacifies malignant ulcers and purifies sinus ulcers.
This auspicious preparation beginning with *karañja* is for fresh wounds;
it also treats all types of malignant ulcers and those for which the prescribed treatment has been abandoned.
The deep-seated channels (nāḍīs) that have been recently severed,
as well as even those dreadful ulcers caused by fire or caustic alkali (kṣāra).
They are undoubtedly pacified by an oblation consisting of karañja and other such substances,
as well as by bricks, sand, clods of earth, cow dung, husks, and dust.
One should constantly foment a phlegmatic abscess with warm urines,
as well as with decoction-drinks, emetics, medicinal pastes, and poultices.
One should repeatedly remove the blood with a gourd, and likewise with a decoction of *āragvadha*;
having incised it, one should wash it with a decoction of *āragvadha*.
Having filled the ulcer with turmeric, trivṛt, śaktu, and sesame seeds mixed with honey,
one should bandage it properly as prescribed.
Then, one should prepare an oil from kulatthikā, dantī, trivṛt, śyāmā, arka, and tilvaka, along with cow's urine and rock salt; this is beneficial in that condition.

An expert physician should perform all the therapeutic measures for both types of abscesses— those caused by blood and those caused by external factors— without exception, just as one would for a Pitta-type abscess.
When an internal abscess has arisen while still unripe, a person should drink a decoction of the Varuṇādi group with the addition of the Uṣakādi group as a medicinal paste; this is soothing.
The ghee prepared from these two groups of drugs,
when used for purgation and consumed every morning, destroys an abscess before long.
With these same groups of drugs, well-prepared and combined with oil,
one should quickly administer both the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) and likewise the unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
Or even the Madhuśigru tree, when its seeds are sown in drinks, ointments, or food,
destroys an unripened abscess according to the specific dosha involved.

Shilājatu may be drunk with sour gruel, fermented grain-water, urine, or even with wines and other spirits; or one may drink it with decoctions prepared from groups of drugs according to the specific doshas involved.
One should also apply guggulu as the primary substance, along with ginger and deodar; one should perform oleation and poultices, and always ensure the downward movement of the humors.
The physician should puncture the vein as specified for an abscess caused by phlegm (kapha);
however, some authorities state that in cases arising from blood, bile, or wind (vāta), the procedure should be performed on the arm.
Or, having incised a suppurated swelling that has bulged outward, one should treat it like a wound;
once the discharge has flowed out, whether upward or downward, [one should apply] maireya, sour liquids, surā, or āsava.

One should drink a decoction of *varuṇaka* and other such herbs, or even the tree *madhuśigru*; likewise, one may eat boiled rice prepared with white mustard seeds in water boiled with the roots of *śigru*.
A person should eat with soups made from barley, jujube, and horse-gram,
and every morning he should consume a measured dose of oil-cake ghee.
Or, for the sake of pacification, one may use a decoction prepared from the *trivṛt* group of drugs;
the physician should strive in such a way that it does not reach the stage of suppuration.
When an abscess has fully developed, success is not considered certain;
however, one should proceed with treatment after declaring the prognosis hopeless in the case of an abscess arising from the marrow.
For those who have been treated with oleation and sudation, one should perform bloodletting;
one should apply the treatment prescribed for abscesses, or once it has suppurated, one should incise the bone.
Then, having ascertained that the arrowhead has been removed, the cleansing of the wound must be performed;
one should wash it with a bitter decoction, and likewise, bitter ghee is beneficial.
If the discharge of marrow does not cease in an embodied being,
the wise physician should administer purificatory measures such as decoctions (kaṣāya) and others.
Oil should be cooked with priyaṅgu, dhātakī, rodhra, kaṭphala, tiniśa, and saindhava; this serves to heal abscesses and wounds.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Abscesses," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The seventeenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of erysipelas, sinus ulcers, and diseases of the breast.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
Of the three types of visarpa that occur at the outset, those not caused by sannipāta or injury are curable.
For these curable cases, one should administer medicated ghees, affusions, and likewise topical pastes prepared with groups of drugs appropriate for that condition.
Mustā, śatāhvā, suradāru, kuṣṭha, vārāhī, kustumburu, kṛṣṇagandhā,
and other drugs belonging to the uṣṇa (hot) group that subdue vāta should be employed in affusions, ointments, and likewise in decoctions.
Indeed, that which is known as the five roots— both the small and the large varieties of the thorny type, as well as those derived from creepers—
should be employed by the physician in decoctions, for sprinkling, in clarified butter, and likewise in oil.
Kaseru, śṛṅgāṭaka, padma, gundrā, along with śaivala and the mud of utpala,
mixed with clarified butter and applied as a very cold paste between layers of cloth, should be used as a plaster for a pitta-type visarpa.
Hrīvera, lāmajjaka, sandalwood, srotoñjana, pearls, gems, and red ochre— these,
ground with milk, mixed with ghee, and made into very cool, thin ointments, should be applied for comfort.
Prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, payasyā, mañjiṣṭhikā, padmaka, candana,
and sugandhikā— this fragrant plaster should be applied by the physician for the relief of pitta-type visarpa.
One should perform sprinkling with groups of Nyagrodha plants and prepare ghee from their expressed juice;
furthermore, one should administer sprinklings with cold milks, honey-water, sugar-water, and sugarcane juices.
[The application] of ghee [is indicated] for gaurī, madhuka, aravinda, rodhra, ambu, rājādana, and gairika;
likewise for ṛṣabha, padmaka, sārivā, kākolī, medā, kumuda, and utpala.
Having added water to a paste made of sandalwood, honey-sugar, grapes, śrīparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, and śatāvarī, as well as from the nyagrodha group and the sthirā group;
Four times the quantity of milk, along with one part of the *gaṇa* of the five roots beginning with *bilva*, should likewise be boiled down to one *prastha*;
when used for irrigation, it destroys bile-born erysipelas (*visarpa*) and sinus tracts (*nāḍī*).
This ghee, beginning with that of Gaurī, when drunk, destroys eruptions, malignant ulcers, diseases of the head, and inflammation of the mouth;
it is indeed recommended for children afflicted by planetary spirits or suffering from consumption.
A plaster composed of aja, aśvagandhā, saralā, kālā, saikaiṣikā, or ajaśṛṅgī,
ground with cow's urine and applied as an ointment, quickly destroys erysipelas (visarpa) born of kapha.
Kālānusārya, aguru, coca, guñjā, rāsnā, vacā, śītaśiva,
eranda-parṇī, pālindī, muñjāta, and mahīkadamba are beneficial for types of visarpa caused by kapha.
The Varuṇa-gaṇa should be employed by the wise in all therapeutic procedures;
for purification and bloodletting are indeed the best treatments for erysipelas (visarpa).
Having thoroughly purified all [types of sinus] that have reached suppuration, the wise physician should treat them according to the prescribed procedure for ulcers.
A sinus arising from the three doṣas is incurable; indeed, the remaining four types are curable with effort.
In that case, having first treated an ulcer caused by Vāta with poultices and then completely incising the sinus tract containing pus,
one should apply a bandage here using sesame seeds and Apāmārga fruits ground together with rock salt (saindhava).
And for the constant cleansing of the vagina, one should employ the great *pañcamūla*,
as well as *hiṃsrā*, turmeric, *kaṭukā*, *balā*, *gojihvikā*, and the root of the *bilva* tree.
Having removed the oil, the wise physician should cook it for the purpose of purifying, filling, and healing the ulcer;
first, however, he should apply poultices (utkārikā) containing milk and ghee to a wound of a Pitta-nature.
Having removed the foreign body, one should fill the wound with a paste of sesame, *nāgadantī*, and *yaṣṭyāhva*;
furthermore, for its constant cleansing, a skilled practitioner should always employ *niśā* (turmeric) along with *soma* and *nimba*.
Ghee prepared with *śyāmā*, *atribhaṇḍī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the two types of *haridrā*,
*rodhra*, and *vṛkṣaka*, along with milk, cures the spreading of the disease even when it has reached the internal cavities (*koṣṭha*) by means of nourishing the ulcerated area.
Having properly applied a poultice to a sinus caused by phlegm using horse gram (kulattha), white mustard (siddhārthaka), alkali (śaktu), and fermenting grain-scum (kiṇva), and having softened it,
one who acts decisively should probe for the track and, once identified, excise it completely with a surgical instrument.
One should apply neem, sesame, danti, and rock salt combined with saindhava salt to the ulcer.
For washing, one should employ the fresh juices of karañja, neem, jātī, akṣa, and pīlu.

For the benefit [of the patient], one should prepare a beneficial oil from *suvarcikā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *citraka*, *nikumbha*, *tālī*, *tala*, and *rūpikā*, as well as from the fruits of *apāmārga*, together with urine.
Having incised the sinus originating from the foreign body, extracted the foreign body, and thoroughly cleansed the passage,
one should purify it with sesame seeds mixed abundantly with honey and ghee, and thereafter quickly effect healing.
Having prepared a decoction from the unripe fruits (śalāṭu) of the kumbhīka, kharjūra, kapittha, bilva, and other forest trees,
one should cook oil therein, adding mustā, saralā, and priyaṅgu.
One should apply *sugandhikā*, *mocarasa*, *ahi-puṣpa*, *rodhra*, and *dhātakī*;
by this, a sinus tract arising from a splinter or a wound shall heal quickly and with ease.
In the case of those who are emaciated, weak, or timid, and for a vein that is situated near a vital organ (marman),
a wise physician should cut it with an alkaline thread rather than with a surgical instrument.
Having sought the path with the probe, following the direction of the arrow-thread, one should insert the needle at the end of the track; then, quickly withdrawing it, one should raise it up.
Having brought the thread to the end, one should apply a firm tie;
then, having observed the strength of the caustic, one should insert another thread.
The wise physician should apply caustic until the track is cut;
this same procedure should be performed by a knowledgeable physician even in the case of fistula-in-ano.

Or, having covered [the wound] on all sides with needles having barley-shaped points, one should tie it at the base with a thread; and once the [flesh] has been cut away, one should bandage the wound.
The physician should apply those wicks (varti) described in the chapter on the treatment of two types of wounds to all sinus tracts;
these consist of the bark of the ghoṇṭā fruit, salts, lac, betel nut, and leaves with salt.
This paste, made into a wick with the milky sap of *Sruhi* and *Arka*, destroys sinus tracts (*nāḍī*) before long;
likewise, a wick composed of *Bibhītaka*, mango stone, *Vaṭa* sprouts, *Hareṇukā*, and the seeds of *Śaṅkhinī* [achieves the same].
And likewise, the Vārāhikanda root should be applied to the channels after mixing it with oil.

The seed of *dhattūra*, the seed of *madana* and *kodrava*, *kośātakī*, *śukanasā*, and *mṛgabhojinī*, as well as the seed and flower of *aṅkoṭa*, should be used in the various applications; having been ground into powder and extracted with lac-water, it is to be applied to those [substances] whose impurities have been removed.
Likewise, for the benefit of one suffering from abdominal enlargement, they carefully prescribe beef,
cow-dung ash, or the best salt (saindhava) combined with honey and administered through a tube.
The physician should apply that oil which is prescribed for malignant ulcers to all types of sinus tracts;
moreover, oil mixed with these very same ingredients in powdered form, when administered, destroys the path [of the disease] without delay.
Oil prepared with these very same ingredients together with urine, when administered, removes [the condition] from its course within seven nights;
likewise, oil prepared with the roots and bulbous fragments of *piṇḍītaka* soaked in the juice of *varāha* and *sauvīra*.
This oil, prepared with the tubers known as *amaravarāyudha*,
along with *bhallātaka*, *arka*, black pepper, the best salt (*saindhava*), *viḍaṅga*, the two types of *rajanī*, and *citraka*, quickly removes the disease of *gati*.
Oil prepared with the juice of *mārkava* destroys sinus tracts caused by kapha and vāta, as well as scrofula (*apacī*) and ulcers.
When the breast milk has become morbid, the physician should, on the day the milk has been digested, cause the wet-nurse who has drunk the oil to undergo emesis.
On the day following the vomiting, she should consume neem water mixed with honey and māgadhikā, and subsist on a diet of mudga-gram soup.
In this manner, she should vomit for three, four, or six days, or she may drink clarified butter combined with triphalā.
One should drink a decoction of Bhārgī with honey, or the best decoction from the Āragvadhādi group, for the purpose of purifying the milk.
This general instruction has been taught; therefore, based on the specific defects that have descended into the milk, the physician should pacify them according to their respective natures.
Having examined the disease arising from the breast, he should apply whatever treatment has been frequently prescribed for an abscess (vidradhi).
Even when it has begun to suppurate, one should indeed endeavor to ripen it by means of poultices and the application of medicinal foods;
for if the breast is bound up too quickly due to its soft flesh, it will undergo total putrefaction and burst open.
When the breasts have matured, one should avoid the milk-carrying channels (nāḍīs) and apply the instrument to the dark areola;
