likewise, when they are unripe, inflamed, or have reached suppuration, one should constantly express the milk from the nurse's breasts.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Visarpa, Nāḍī, and Diseases of the Breast," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The eighteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of glandular swellings (granthi), scrofula (apaci), tumors (arbuda), and goiter (galagaṇḍa).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Then, the physician who knows the detailed procedure should apply the treatment for swelling to these hard knots;
he must also constantly preserve the patient's strength, for when that strength is protected, it destroys the power of the disease.
The physician should administer oil, ghee, or both; or, having added muscle fat, he should prescribe Trivṛt;
or he may give the four-fold unctuous substance (catuḥsneha) or two of them, prepared with Apehivātā and Daśamūla.
Hiṃsrā, rohiṇī, amṛtā, bhargī, śyonāka, bilva, aguru, kṛṣṇagandhā, and gojī,
ground together with tālapatrī, should be applied as a plaster upon a knot (granthi) caused by vāta.
One should apply various types of fomentation and poultices, as well as other well-known medicinal pastes;
or, having incised the suppurated area and removed the pus, one should wash it with the decoctions of bilva, arka, and narendratoya.
One should cleanse the ulcer with sesame seeds mixed with the five-finger (pañcāṅgula) leaves and combined with rock salt;
once purified, one should heal the ulcer with an oil prepared with rāsnā and sarala.
Alternatively, leeches are beneficial for a condition caused by pitta when they have been prepared with a decoction of viḍaṅga, yaṣṭīmadhuka, and amṛtā combined with milk;
furthermore, sprinkling with milk and water is recommended.
One should drink cooling decoctions of the kākoli group mixed with sugar;
or one may drink the powder of harītakī with grape juice or even with sugarcane juice.
One should apply plasters made from the barks of Madhūka, Jambu, Arjuna, and Vetasa;
or one should repeatedly apply plasters made from the bulbs of Tṛṇaśūnya mixed with sugar, or those derived from Muculunda.
Having incised the suppurated area and removed the pus, one should wash it with a decoction of the "lords of the forest" (trees).
After cleansing it with sesame seeds and *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, ghee cooked with drugs of the sweet group should be applied.
When the humors have been removed in the proper sequence, the physician should, in the case of a tumor arising from phlegm (kapha),
perform a softening massage on the patient after fomentation, using the thumb, a metal instrument, a stone, or a bamboo staff.

The wise physician should apply an ointment made from the roots of *vikaṅkata*, *āragvadha*, *kākaṇantī*, *kākādanī*, and *tāpasavṛkṣa*, as well as from *piṇḍaphala*, *arka*, *bhārgī*, *karañja*, *kālā*, and *madana*.
One should extract an immature swelling that has not reached suppuration and does not subside, having incised it;
once the blood has been removed, the surgeon who has accomplished the task should cauterize it and apply the procedure prescribed for fresh wounds.
This procedure should be applied by those skilled in the rules to those fleshy growths that are hard and large;
or, having incised them with a blade once they have quickly ripened, one should wash them with the most wholesome decoctions.
One should purify that [wound] with cleansing agents, primarily alkaline ones mixed with abundant honey and jaggery;
once it is purified, an oil cooked with viḍaṅga, pāṭhā, and turmeric should be applied.
In a case arising from fat (medas), the wise physician, for the patient's benefit, should apply a paste of sesame seeds, place a double layer of cloth over it,
and repeatedly rub it with a heated metal instrument that has been tempered in fire, taking care not to cause burns.
Having smeared a wooden probe with lac or heated resin, one should apply fomentation to it;
or, having applied the instrument and removed the fat, one should cauterize it, or else, once it is well-matured, one should incise it.
Having washed it with urine and well-ground sesame seeds mixed with suvarcikā and other ingredients, combined with haritāla, rock salt (saindhava),
honey, and clarified butter, and enriched with alkali, one should thoroughly cleanse this [wound].
One should prepare an oil cooked with two parts each of karañja, guñjā, vaṃśāvalekhā, and iṅguda, along with urine,
as well as with jīmūtaka, kośavatī fruits, and dantī, dravantī, and trivṛt.
Clarified butter prepared with these ingredients destroys even advanced apacī;
its potency is doubled when combined with nirguṇḍī, jātī, bārhiṣṭha, jīmūtaka, honey, and rock salt.
For severe and aggravated cases of duṣṭāpacī, they prescribe strong emesis as the best treatment;
furthermore, oil prepared with kaiḍarya, bimbī, and karavīra is beneficial, as is head-purgation (mūrdhavirecana).
Oil prepared with the natural juice of śāsvoṭaka is beneficial for nasal purgation (nasyavirecana);
likewise, the essence of madhūka is beneficial for pressing out (avapīḍa), as are the fruits of śigru or kharamañjarī.
Having extracted the unripened tumors arising from the vital points (marmans), one should subsequently apply fire;
or else, having scarified them with a surgical instrument according to the instructions, one should rub them with caustic (kṣāra).
Having measured twelve finger-breadths from the heel toward the indrabasti, the wise physician should avoid that area,
make an incision, extract the net-like structures resembling fish-eggs, and then apply fire.
Having divided the well-measured body of the creature from the ankle to the ear into eight parts, one should divide the portion below the knee;
others say that the straight penetration of the nose should be made by leaving a space of one eye-measure from the testicles of the "King of the Gods" (the horse).
Or, for the complete removal of apacī swellings, the physician should properly make three lines above the wrist,
separated by the distance of one finger's breadth.
At the time of administering the powder, one should add soot produced from the fat of a lizard, a crow, a monitor lizard,
a snake, and a tortoise, along with Ingudi oil— the same oil that will be prescribed for those suffering from elephantiasis (ślīpada).
One should employ purgative fumigation and should always subsist on a diet of barley and mung beans,
using the powders of the five seeds of *karkāru*, *kairava*, *nārikela*, *priyāla*, and *pañcāṅgula*.
One should apply poultices (upanāha) for a vātārbuda with warm, oil-infused applications prepared with milk, ghee, and water;
one should also employ the primary types of poultices made with prepared meats or vesavāra.
The skilled physician should apply sudation and repeatedly extract blood by means of a tube or a horn;
or he should drink the medicine known as Śatāhvā, Trivṛt, or that prepared with decoctions of Vāta-subduing drugs, milk, and sour liquids.
In the case of a pitta-arbuda, mild fomentation and poultices should be applied, as well as purgation of the body;
furthermore, after rubbing the growth with the leaves of udumbara, śāka, and gojī, one should smear it profusely with honey.

Having caused the discharge [of the humors], a skillful practitioner should apply a paste composed of finely ground sarjarasa, priyaṅgu, pattaṅga, rodhra, añjana, yaṣṭikāhva, āragvadha, goji, soma, and śyāmā.
A person suffering from a pitta-tumor or its resulting abdominal disease should drink ghee prepared with *klītaka*, along with the juices of *śyāmā*, *giri*, *añjanakī*, grapes, and *saptalī*.
In the case of a tumor (arbuda) arising from phlegm in a person who has been purified, once the blood has been drained,
one should apply a plaster made from medicinal substances that remove the humors (doṣas) from both above and below, prepared as a paste.
One should apply a plaster made of the droppings of pigeons and doves mixed with bell-metal and indigo, along with the substances known as *śuka* and *lāṅgala*,
combined with the urine of a crow and *adana* roots, or else one should apply a plaster smeared with alkali.
One should apply a plaster made from the paste of flat beans, oil-cake, and horse gram, enriched with meat and mixed with curd-whey,
so that worms may swarm there and flies may leave them behind.
When only a small portion remains and it has been eaten away by worms, one should then scrape it and subsequently apply fire;
or, that which has a small base should be wrapped with sheets of tin, copper, or lead, or with iron.
A vigilant physician, without harming the vital breaths, should repeatedly apply caustics, fire, and surgical instruments;
for the purpose of purifying the wound, a decoction made from the leaves of *āsphota*, jasmine (*jātī*), and *karavīra* is desired.

Once the ulcer is purified, one should apply oil cooked with bhārgī, viḍaṅga, pāṭhā, and triphalā. An expert in the procedure should treat ulcers that have spontaneously reached suppuration according to the prescribed regimen for maturation.
Then, having fomented the arbuda of the thigh, incised it, and purified it, one should quickly suture it once the blood has ceased.
Then, [one should apply] powders of haridrā, gṛhadhūma, rodhra, and pataṅga, together with manaḥśilā and añjana.
Having treated the ulcer with honey-thickened applications, one should apply Karañja oil once it has been purified;
for those who treat tumors while leaving a residue of the morbid humors, they quickly recur.
Therefore, one should extract them entirely, for if they remain with a residue, they will cause harm just as fire does;
first, one should foment the swelling caused by wind with a tube using the crushed leaves of wind-alleviating herbs.

The wise and diligent physician, having first applied fomentation, should drain the ulcer using various sour substances, urine, warm milks, oils, and meats; once it is purified, he should apply a poultice.
With sesame seeds combined with hemp, *atasī*, radish, drumstick tree (*śigru*), fermenting grain (*kiṇva*), and the marrow of *priyāla*;
and with black pepper (*kālā*), *amṛtā*, drumstick tree, *punarnavā*, arka, *gajapippalī*, *karahāṭa*, and *kuṣṭha*...
One should repeatedly apply a plaster made from ekaiṣikā, vṛkṣaka, and tilvaka, ground with wine and sour gruel.
One should drink oil prepared with amṛtavallī, nimba, haṃsāhvaya, vṛkṣaka, and pippalī, along with the two types of balā and devadāru; this is always beneficial for the disease of galagaṇḍa.
In the case of a disorder arising from phlegm (kapha), one should first apply fomentation and poultices, then perform bloodletting;
thereafter, [one should treat it] with ajagandhā, ativiṣā, viśalyā, viṣāṇikā, kuṣṭha, and śukāhvayā.
One should apply a plaster made of well-ripened *suguñjā* seeds ground with water and the ashes of *palāśa* wood, while not being cold;
one should also drink oil prepared with the five salts and *māgadhikā* (long pepper).
Inducing vomiting, head-purgation (errhines), and purgative fumigation are beneficial;
or else, the physician should always somehow apply the procedure for inducing suppuration in those two conditions that have reached a state of suppuration.
Barley-based foods and mung bean soups mixed with the three pungents (kaṭutrika), honey, and urine, along with ginger,
paṭola, and nimba, should be administered for the benefit of those suffering from goiter (galagaṇḍa).
In the case of a disorder arising from fat (medas), one should venesect the patient after he has been oleated, following the prescribed instructions;
furthermore, an external application (pradeha) made with śyāmā, sudhā, iron filings, purīṣa-dantī, and rasāñjana is beneficial.
For one's benefit, one should drink the pith of *sāla* trees in the morning,
either stirred with urine or having cut and split it open with a blade, extracted its marrow, and then sewn it up for the sake of healing.
One should burn it with marrow, clarified butter, fat, and honey; once burnt, one should apply more clarified butter and honey.
Then, blue vitriol and alum, powdered and combined with yellow pigment (rocanā), should be added to it.
For its benefit, one should apply oil and give ash produced from heartwood or from cow dung;
the decoction of triphalā is always beneficial, as is firm bandaging and a diet of barley.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Granthi, Apaci, Arbuda, and Galaganda," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The nineteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of scrotal enlargement (vṛddhi), venereal diseases (upadaṃśa), and elephantiasis (ślīpada).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Excluding intestinal hernia, there are six types of abdominal enlargement;
among these, one should avoid riding on horses and other vehicles, physical exercise, sexual intercourse, and the suppression of natural urges.

In that case, when there is an increase of Vata from the outset, one should have the patient— who has been lubricated with the three-fold fat (traivṛta)— undergo sitting on a high seat, walking, fasting, and [administering] heavy [medicines].
Once he has been fomented according to the prescribed method, one should administer a purgative to the man,
or else give him the oils of *kośāmra*, *tilvaka*, and castor seeds (*eraṇḍa*).
Or, for a month, one should drink castor oil mixed with milk;
thereafter, at the appropriate time, the wise person [should administer it] with decoctions and pastes of drugs that subdue Vāta.
One should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) to one who has already undergone the procedure and has eaten rice with meat broth;
thereafter, one should treat him with oil prepared with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka).
One should apply oleation and poultices, as well as applications that alleviate Vāta;
or, once the abscess has suppurated, one may open it while carefully avoiding the perineal suture.
Then, once it has burst, one should follow the prescribed procedure;
in the case of an unripened abscess born of pitta, the treatment for a pitta-granthi is beneficial.
Or, once it has ripened, one should cause it to burst; once burst, one should cleanse it with honey and ghee.
When it is purified, the physician should apply healing oil and medicinal paste.
In cases arising from blood, the physician should extract the blood using leeches,
or he may administer a purgative mixed with sugar and honey.
One should always apply the procedure for a bile-based glandular swelling (pittagranthi), whether it is in the stage of undigested matter (āma) or fully ripened (pakva).
For a swelling caused by phlegm (kapha), one should apply a plaster made of [medicinal herbs] ground with urine and heated.
One should drink a decoction of yellow wood (pītadāru) combined with urine;
or even apart from the procedure for softening (vimlāpana), the regimen prescribed for phlegmatic glandular swellings (śleṣmagranthi) is beneficial.
When it has ripened and burst open, a purifying oil is desired,
prepared from *sumanā*, *aruṣkara*, *aṅkoṭha*, and *saptaparṇa*.
In the case of an abscess arising from fat (medas), one should apply fomentation and then plaster it with the drugs of the surasādi group,
or with head-purgative (śirovirecana) substances mixed with urine and made lukewarm.
Having wrapped the swollen area with a cloth and comforted the person,
one should protect the scrotum and the perineal raphe while making an incision with a curved blade.
Then, having extracted the fat, one should apply it with green vitriol (kāsīsa) and rock salt;
once it has been purified as prescribed, one should cause oil to be applied.
Having prepared [the paste] with realgar, clay, salt, and *āruṣkara*,
and having applied it to the fistula caused by urine, one should wrap it with a cloth bandage.
One should pierce below the side of the suture with a vrīhimukha instrument;
then, having inserted a double-mouthed tube there, the physician should drain it.
Having extracted the urine from the channel, one should apply a bandage with a cloth-pouch;
once it is purified, one should apply healing ointment, while avoiding any measures that might cause injury to the intestines.
When the swelling has not yet reached the scrotum, the procedure for increasing the wind (vāta) is beneficial;
in that case, one should cauterize the part located at the groin with three [applications] in the shape of a crescent moon.
One should avoid [the vein] that has reached the sheath for the sake of obstructing the correct path;
rather, having pierced the skin at the middle of the thumb, one should cauterize it, reversing the limbs.

By this very same procedure, one who is self-restrained should cauterize swellings caused by Vāta and Kapha; however, in those two cases, there is an additional requirement for the excision of tendons.
Having carefully avoided the *sevanī* at the edge of the ear above the conch-shell [of the neck],
one should pierce the vein either normally or by inversion for the cure of intestinal hernia (*antravṛddhi*).
When the upadaṃśas (venereal sores) are curable,
one should venesect the vein in the middle of the penis after the patient has been treated with oleation and sudation, or one should apply leeches.
It removes excessively elevated doshas from both sides;
for one whose doshas have been immediately extracted, pain and swelling subside.
Alternatively, if the patient is weak or if a purgative has not been administered,
one should remove the excessively aggravated doshas with a non-unctuous enema (nirūha).
One should apply a plaster for vāta-type [skin diseases] using prapauṇḍarīka, yaṣṭyāhva, varṣābhū, kuṣṭha, dāru, sarala, aguru, and rāsnā.
One should apply a warm, unctuous plaster made from the seeds of *nicula* and castor, along with barley, wheat, and parched grain flour, for conditions arising from Vāta.
An irrigation with substances beginning with *prapauṇḍarīka*,
along with *gaurī*, *añjana*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *ariva*, *uśīra*, and *padmaka*, is recommended.
One should thoroughly apply a cooling plaster for the Pitta-type fever using smooth sandalwood and blue lotuses,
as well as with lotus, water-lily, lotus-stalks, sarja, arjuna, and vetasa.
One should apply a plaster composed of substances unctuous with ghee and madhuka for the pitta-type [wound],
and one should sprinkle it with ghee, milk, sugar, sugarcane juice, and water boiled with udumbara.

Alternatively, that which arises from phlegm (kapha) should be treated with a very cold decoction of the banyan tree (*vaṭa*) and others, or with the bark of the *sāla*, *aśvakarṇa*, *ajakarṇa*, and *dhava* trees.
One should apply a warm plaster made of *rajanī*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *surā*,
*suradāru*, and flour mixed with oil.
Alternatively, one should apply a plaster made of saptaparṇa, pāṭhā,
and apāmārga, and sprinkle [the area] with the decoctions of surasā and āragvadha.
Thus, one should treat the condition with cleansing, ointments, affusions, and bloodletting,
as well as with beneficial therapeutic applications previously described in the Section on General Principles.
The physician should strive so that it does not undergo putrefaction;
for if the veins, ligaments, skin, and flesh are scorched, the penis is destroyed.
Furthermore, once suppuration has set in, one should indeed treat it quickly with a surgical instrument;
then, having removed [the pus], one should apply a plaster of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and honey.
The leaves of the karavīra, as well as those of the jātī, āragvadha,
vaijayantī, and arka, should be employed for washing.
Saurāṣṭrī, red ochre, tuttha, puṣpakāsīsa, rock salt, rodhra,
rasāñjana, dārvī, orpiment, and realgar.
One should likewise prepare fine powders of hareṇukā and elā;
that powder, combined with honey, is highly esteemed for the treatment of upadaṃśa (venereal sores).
The shoots of the Jambu, Amra, Sumanā, Nimba, and Śvetakāmboji; the bark of the Śallakī, Badarī, Bilva, Palāśa, and Tiniśa.
The barks of milky trees should be used together with triphalā in a decoction;
with that decoction, the physician should certainly wash the ulcer.
In this very decoction, the wise physician should cook oil,
combined with gojihvā, viḍaṅga, yaṣṭīmadhu, and all the fragrant substances (sarvagandha).
This is considered the best healing agent among all adjuncts:
svarjika salt, tuttha, kāsīsa, śaileya, and rasāñjana.

A powder made from substances equal in measure to realgar (manaḥśilā) destroys wounds and erysipelas (visarpa). Ashes produced by burning guṇḍrā grass, along with yellow orpiment (haritāla) and realgar, [likewise act as a remedy].
This is the supreme pacifier for *upadaṃśa* and *visarpa*:
*mārkava*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *dantī*, copper powder, and iron filings.
This destroys the secondary disease (upadaṃśa) just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree;
even when there are two secondary diseases, one should perform the treatment after having rejected this [specific remedy].
Having observed the strength and weakness of the doshas, one should apply that which is appropriate for those two;
listen further specifically regarding the complications (upadamsha) arising from all three doshas.
One should apply the treatment for malignant ulcers;
if the penis is putrefied, it should be excised, and thereafter the physician should cauterize the remaining part with a Jambū-leaf heated to the color of fire.
Having ascertained that it has been properly cauterized, one should apply honey and ghee;
once the wound is clean, one should apply a healing paste, oil, or whatever else is beneficial.
When elephantiasis caused by Vāta has been treated with oleation and sudation,
the physician should perform venesection four finger-breadths above the ankle joint.
Once the body has been nourished by enemas (basti),
one should treat the patient by drinking castor oil mixed with urine for one month.
One should eat milk-rice with ginger boiled in water, and one should consume it mixed with ghee;
likewise, cauterization with fire is recommended.
In cases of ślīpada caused by pitta, one should pierce the vein below the ankle and perform treatments that alleviate jaundice,
as prescribed for pitta-type arbuda and visarpa.
The physician should pierce a well-identified vein at the thumb in the case of a kapha disorder;
furthermore, the person should frequently drink astringent decoctions mixed with honey.
Or one may drink the paste of abhayā with any one of the urines,
along with kaṭukā, amṛtā, śuṇṭhī, viḍaṅga, dāru, and citraka.
Alternatively, for a daily medicinal plaster, bhadradāru and citraka are beneficial,
or else viḍaṅga, marica, arka, nāgara, and citraka.
One should drink oil cooked with bhadradāru, elūka, and all types of salts; furthermore, a diet of barley-gruel is always beneficial.
One should drink either mustard oil or the juice of *pūtīkarañja* leaves according to one's strength for the cure of elephantiasis (*ślīpada*).
By this very same procedure, a wise physician who understands the distinctions of time and suitability should administer the juice derived from Putrañjīvaka.
Having added the resin of *kevuka* and *kandana*, salt,
and the aforementioned juice that has been cooked, this potion, which is a victory for physicians, should be drunk.
Kākādanī, kākajaṅghā, bṛhatī,
kaṇṭakārikā, kadambapuṣpī, mandārī, lambā, and likewise śukanasā;
Having burnt it with urine, one should strain that ash according to the procedure for alkaline preparations;
therein, one should add the juice of *kākodumbarikā* as a counter-incorporation (*pratīvāpa*).
A decoction from the fruit of Madana, as well as the fresh juice of Śukākhyā—
this alkali, when consumed as a drink, destroys elephantiasis (ślīpada).
It destroys scrofula, goiters, disorders of the digestive tract,
loss of appetite, and all types of poisons.
Oil prepared with these very [substances] is highly esteemed for use as nasal drops and for massage;
it destroys these same diseases, as well as those malignant ulcers which afflict men.
Having burnt Dravanti, Trivṛtā, Dantī, Nīlī, Śyāmā,
as well as Saptalā and Śaṅkhinī, one should strain them with urine.
One should also administer a decoction of triphalā; this alkali, when prepared and drunk, moves downward, and its blessings are equal to those of the ancient sages.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vṛddhi, Upadaṃśa, and Ślīpada," in the Cikitsitasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twentieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of minor diseases (kṣudraroga).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
In that regard, one should treat ajagallikā and māṃsā with leeches;
the physician should also apply a paste of pearl, śrughnī, and yavakṣāra.
Alternatively, the wise physician should treat a suppurated [abscess] with the paste of śyāmā, aṅkola, and pāṭhā,
according to the prescribed procedure for ulcers.
One should first treat andhālajī, yavaprakhyā, panasī, kacchapī,
and pāṣāṇagardabha with sudation (sveda).
One should apply a paste of realgar, yellow orpiment, kuṣṭha, and devadāru;
once they have reached suppuration, one should incise them and treat them like ulcers.
Vivṛtā, indravṛddhā, gardabhī, jālagardabha,
irivellī, gandhanāmī, kakṣā, and likewise visphoṭaka;
The physician should treat pitta-born visarpa with medical measures;
once it has suppurated, he should heal it with ghee prepared with sweet medicinal herbs.
The physician should sprinkle the *cipya* with warm water, incise it, and drain it;
then, having anointed it with *cakrataila*, he should dust it with the powder of *sarja*.
One should treat this with bandaging, or if it is impossible, burn it with fire;
thereafter, one should heal it with oil processed with sweet medicinal herbs.
This same procedure should indeed be performed by the physician for an ingrown nail (kunakha);
furthermore, the physician should treat a sinus tract (anuśayī) like a phlegmatic abscess (śleṣmavidradhi).
Having thoroughly massaged a vidārikā tumor and applied fomentation, one should soften it and then apply a plaster made from well-ground nagavṛttika,
varṣābhū, and bilva roots.
Or, once the state of ulceration has been reached, having performed the procedure of purification,
an oil boiled with astringent and sweet decoctions is beneficial for the purpose of healing.
An unripe vidārikā tumor should be drained by means of hidden leeches;
one should then apply a plaster made from the paste of ajakarṇa roots along with those of pālāśa.
Having incised the suppurated area with a surgical instrument,
one should apply a paste made from paṭola and picumarda, mixed with sesame and clarified butter.
Having increased [the size of] the wound with decoctions of milk-yielding trees and of Khadira,
one should wash it clean and then cause that purified [wound] to heal again.
One should treat a carbuncle caused by phlegm (śarkarārbuda) according to the procedure for a carbuncle caused by fat;
one should treat scabies, eczema, and ringworm in the same manner as leprosy.
An ointment made of beeswax, śatāhvā, and white mustard seeds is recommended;
or else, oil extracted from vacā, dārvī, and mustard seeds, or oil derived from naktamāla.
One should apply oil extracted from heartwood, boiled with pungent substances, for massage;
in cases of cracking of the feet (pādadāryā), one should perform venesection and employ fomentation and massage.
An application to the feet made of beeswax, fat, marrow, resin powder, and ghee,
mixed with *yavāhvā* and *gerika*, is highly recommended.
Having washed the feet with sour gruel (āranāla),
an ointment made from the paste of nimba, sesame, kāsīsa, and āla, along with rock salt, is beneficial for those suffering from alasa.
Lac juice or abhayā should be used, or bloodletting should be performed;
likewise, oil prepared with the decoction of kaṇṭakārī or mustard oil is beneficial.
Or one may apply a medicinal paste made from the powders of kāsīsa, rocanā, and śilā;
having excised and cauterized [the area], one should conquer the disease known as kadarasa with fatty oil.
In cases of Indralupta (alopecia), one should release a vein on the head after the patient has been treated with oleation and sudation;
then, one should apply a paste of realgar, green vitriol, and blue vitriol along with black pepper.
Alternatively, an application of the paste of *kaṭannaṭa* wood is recommended;
or, after making a deep incision, one should repeatedly apply the paste of *guñjā*.
For the sake of pacification, one should apply an ointment or prepare an elixir (rasāyana) cooked with mālatī,
karavīra, agni, and naktamāla.
Oil is recommended for massage as a supreme remedy for the eradication of indralupta (alopecia);
in cases of arūṃṣikā (scald-head), after bloodletting, one should sprinkle the area with water infused with nimba.
One should apply an ointment consisting of the juice of horse dung mixed with rock salt,
or a paste made from yellow orpiment, turmeric, nimba, and paṭola.
One should apply a paste made of yaṣṭī, nīlotpala, eraṇḍa, and mārkava;
oil used for massage is also praised as a remedy that removes indralupta (alopecia).
In cases of dāruṇaka, one should perform venesection on the head after the patient has been treated with oleation and sudation.
One should apply nasal drops (avapīḍa), head-poultices (śirobasti), and massage;
for cleansing, water prepared with the alkaline ash of kodrava and grass is recommended.
I shall describe hereafter the procedure for the destruction of premature graying (palita).
In cases of smallpox (masūrikā), applications such as ointments that destroy skin diseases (kuṣṭha) are beneficial.
The treatment prescribed for Pitta- and Kapha-type Visarpa is also recommended;
having excised the Jatumani, one should likewise treat the Masaka, Tilaka, and Alaka.
One should cauterize with alkali or with fire slowly and gradually according to the proper method;
venesection is recommended for depressed moles (nyaccha), freckles (vyaṅga), and blue-black spots (nīlikā).
According to the proper method and according to the practice, one should perform venesection on the veins of the forehead and other locations;
having rubbed the skin, one should apply a paste made by grinding the milky sap of milk-exuding trees mixed with milk.
Alternatively, an ointment consisting of balā, atibalā, yaṣṭyāhva, and haridrā may be applied;
or an ointment of payasyā, aguru, kālīya, and gairika may be used.
One should smear it with the tusk of a boar combined with honey and clarified butter;
alternatively, a paste of *kapittha* and *rājādana* is said to be beneficial.
In youth, during the appearance of pimples, emesis is especially beneficial;
likewise, an external application of vacā, rodhra, saindhava, and mustard seeds is recommended.
An ointment consisting of kustumburu, vacā, lodhra, and kuṣṭha is beneficial for the disease known as padminī-kaṇṭaka;
one should induce emesis with nimba-water.
One should administer the drinking of ghee prepared with that very [substance] along with honey;
a paste of nimba and āragvadha is beneficial for use as a rubbing powder.
One should apply a poultice (upanāha) made from a skin that has been well-steamed and anointed with ghee;
then, having lubricated it, one should gradually draw the skin over [the swelling] and press upon the stone.
Once the jewel has been inserted,
one should foment the skin with poultices (upanāhana) made of Vāta-alleviating substances such as Sālvaṇa and others, for either three nights or five nights.
The physician should administer enemas that alleviate Vata and feed the patient with unctuous foods;
in this manner, one should conquer Vapāṭikā according to the specific Dosha involved.
When the light has been extinguished, one should insert a tube— either made of iron, wood, or fashioned from lac— into both openings, having smeared it with clarified butter.
For the purpose of sprinkling, the fat and marrow of a porpoise and a boar,
along with wheel-oil (cakrataila) combined with Vāta-alleviating substances, should be employed.
Every three days, one should properly insert a progressively thicker cannula;
thus, one should gradually enlarge the channel and feed the patient unctuous food.
Having incised or opened the perineum, one should treat it like a fresh wound;
this applies to the diseases of obstructed anus (sanniruddha-guda), valmīka, and vahnirohiṇī.
Having rejected [other treatments] as appropriate, one should then perform medical treatment; one should cure Agnirōhiṇī according to the procedure described for Visarpa.
In the case of a constricted anus, the treatment for obstructed fecal matter should be applied;
having excised the growth with a surgical instrument, one should treat it with alkali or fire.
Having purified it according to the procedure prescribed for arbuda, one should apply healing measures;
this applies to a case of valmīka that is not excessively advanced and does not arise in a vital spot (marman).
Having performed purification there, the physician should let out the blood using the roots of kulatthikā,
along with guḍūcī and salt.
One should apply a plaster made from the roots of ārevata, likewise the roots of dantī,
and the roots of śyāmā, mixed with meat broth and parched grain flour.
The physician should apply a poultice (upanāha) that is very unctuous and pleasantly warm;
he should recognize it as being ripe when all the stages have occurred in their proper sequence.
Having recognized this and then excised it, the wise physician should cauterize it;
having cleared away the corrupted flesh, he should rub the area with an alkaline solution.
Having recognized that the wound is purified, the wise physician should apply healing remedies:
*sumana* flowers, *granthi*, *bhallātaka*, and *manaḥśilā*.
Nimba oil prepared with kālānusārī, sūkṣmailā, sandalwood,
and agallochum is beneficial for healing an anthill wound.
Furthermore, a swelling over the hands or feet that is covered with many holes like an anthill should be rejected by the wise man.
After purifying the breast milk of the nurse, the child's *ahipūtanā* should be treated with a decoction prepared from *paṭola* leaves,
the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *rasāñjana*.
Drinking ghee destroys even severe ahipūtana;
a decoction of triphalā, kola, and khadira promotes the healing of wounds.
An ointment made of kāsīsa, gorocanā, tuttha, haritāla, and rasāñjana ground with sour gruel; or else, the bark of badarī ground with rock salt [is applied].
One should employ the powder produced from *kapāla* and *tuttha* at the time of powdering;
one should treat *muṣkakacchū*, as well as *ahipūtana* and *pāmā*, in this manner.
In the case of a prolapse of the rectum (gudabhraṃśa), one should foment the rectum, anoint it with unctuous substances, and reinsert it;
then, one should apply a "cow-horn" bandage (gophaṇābandha) using a piece of leather with a central opening.
For the purpose of expelling the wind,
one should repeatedly apply fomentation using the great five roots (mahat-pañcamūla) in milk, along with a mouse deprived of its entrails.
Having cooked oil in that [decoction] together with Vata-subduing herbs,
one should cure this difficult prolapse of the anus through drinking and massage.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Minor Diseases," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||20||
The twenty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of the disorder caused by the *śūka* (the bristle-like hair of insects).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Having properly incised a sarṣapī abscess, one should dust it with astringent powders;
one should also prepare an astringent oil for the healing of the wound.
One should repeatedly apply leeches to the *aṣṭhīlikā* (stone-like tumor),
and if it still does not subside, one should extract it like a *kapha*-granulation.
The wise physician should constantly apply fomentation with tubular instruments (nāḍī-sveda) to a knotted swelling,
and should apply very unctuous poultices that are pleasantly warm.
One should incise a kumbhīkā ulcer that has reached suppuration and, once purified,
treat it with oil prepared from triphalā, lodhra, tinduka, and āmrātaka.
Having caused the blood to be drawn by leeches, one should then sprinkle the alaji with decoctions;
oil prepared with those same decoctions is desired for healing.
One should sprinkle the area after it has been massaged with lukewarm Balā oil,
and apply a poultice that is unctuous with ghee, sweet in taste, and comfortably warm.
One should quickly treat a deeply congested carbuncle with leeches;
once it has ripened, one should incise it and apply a plaster of honey and clarified butter.
When the Avamantha has reached maturity and burst open, oil is prescribed,
prepared from Dhava, Aśvakarṇa, Pattaṅga, Sallakī, and Tindukī.
One should apply all cooling measures to the *puṣkarikā* swelling;
one should extract the blood with leeches and sprinkle it with clarified butter.
In the event of loss of sensation, one should extract blood and apply sweet medicinal pastes;
one should also irrigate the area with very cold milk, sugarcane juice, and clarified butter.
The physician should extract the boil known as uttamā with a hook;
having extracted it, he should dust it with decoctions mixed with honey.
The Rasakriyā preparation should be administered when the Śataponaka ulcer has been scarified;
immediately thereafter, oil prepared with Pṛthakparṇī and other drugs should be applied.
A wise physician should treat a skin-inflammation (tvakpāka) like erysipelas (visarpa),
and for a blood-born tumor (śoṇitaja arbuda), the treatment should be like that for a blood-born abscess (raktavidradhi).
Having carefully examined each case, one should administer decoctions, pastes, medicated ghees, oils, powders, and medicinal extracts, as well as procedures for purification and healing.
The drinking of ghee is beneficial, as is a purgative that is wholesome;
the letting of blood is beneficial, as is a light diet.
Having rejected cases of arbuda, māṃsapāka, vidradhi, and tilakālaka,
the physician should properly administer treatment.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Śūkadoṣa," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diseases of the mouth.
As the Blessed One Dhanvantari has said:
In cases of Vata-type [diseases], the wise physician should administer anointment with the four kinds of fats combined with beeswax, as well as tubular fomentation (nāḍī-sveda).
In cases of lip-spasms (oṣṭhakopa), one should apply sālvana poultice and fomentation;
furthermore, oil that alleviates vāta is beneficial for use as a nasal medication (nasya) and for the brain (mastiṣka).
One should apply as a rubbing paste (pratisāraṇa) śrīveṣṭaka, sarjarasa, suradāru, guggulu, and the powder of yaṣṭīmadhuka.
One should treat an abscess arising from the provocation of pitta and blood by means of leeches,
and one should perform the entire therapeutic procedure exactly as prescribed for a pitta-type abscess (pittavidradhi).
Head-purgation, medicated smoking, fomentation,
and gargling should be employed once the blood has been removed in cases of oedema of the lips caused by kapha.
Trikaṭu, svarjikākṣāra, yavakṣāra, and likewise viḍa salt,
combined with honey, should be applied as a rubbing paste (pratisāraṇa).
When the abscess has been fomented, incised, and purified of fat, the application of fire (cauterization) is beneficial;
a rubbing with a paste of priyaṅgu, triphalā, and lodhra mixed with honey is also recommended.
The treatment for those diseases of the lips that are curable has been proclaimed;
now the treatment for diseases located in the roots of the teeth shall be described.
When the blood has been removed from a cold abscess (śītāda), one should boil ginger and mustard seeds in water;
then, a gargle consisting of triphalā, musta, and rasāñjana should be applied.
A plaster composed of priyaṅgu, musta, and triphalā;
and nasal drops prepared with triphalā, madhuka, utpala, and padmaka.
In the case of a tender swelling of the gums (dantapuppuṭaka), bloodletting should be performed;
then, an alkaline preparation containing the five salts and honey should be used as a rubbing agent (pratisāraṇa).
Head-purgation (śirovireka), nasal medication (nasya), and unctuous food are beneficial;
once the gums have been drained, one should rub the wounds with medicinal pastes.
Powders of rodhra, pattaṅga, yaṣṭyāhva, and lakṣā, combined with honey, should be used as a gargle;
likewise, milky trees (kṣīrin) should be employed together with honey, ghee, and sugar.
In cases of śauṣira, after blood has been removed, one should administer ghee prepared with the drugs of the kākolyādi group and ten parts of milk as a nasal medication (nasya),
along with a paste of rodhra, musta, and rasāñjana.
An application with honey is recommended; for gargling, the milky trees (kṣīrin) are beneficial, as are sārivā, utpala, yaṣṭyāhva, sāvararā, aguru, and candana.
Ghee prepared with ten parts of milk is highly esteemed for use as a nasal drop (nasya). In cases of Paridara, the wise physician should perform the treatment prescribed for Śītāka.
In cases of upakuśa, one should first cleanse both sides and the head,
and then drain the blood using the leaves of kākodumbarikā and gojī.
One should rub [the area] with salts mixed with honey and the three pungents (vyoṣa),
along with long pepper (pippalī), white mustard, ginger, and the fruit of the naicula tree.
One should mix it with lukewarm water and hold it as a gargle;
likewise, ghee prepared with the drugs of the sweet group is beneficial for both gargling and nasal medication.
In the case of Dantavaidarbha, one should cleanse the roots of the teeth with a surgical instrument;
thereafter, one should apply alkali and employ all cooling treatments.
Having extracted the supernumerary tooth, one should then apply fire;
furthermore, the wise physician should perform the procedure in the same manner as for caries of the teeth.
Having excised the excess flesh, one should treat the wound with these powders mixed with honey:
vacā, tejovatī, pāṭhā, svarjikā, and yavaśūka.
Pippalī with honey is prescribed here as a gargle;
a decoction of paṭola, triphalā, and nimba is beneficial for rinsing the mouth;
and head-purgation (śirovireka) as well as purgative fumigation (dhūma) are also recommended.
Listen to me regarding the general treatment of sinus tracts and their specific varieties here:
one should perform the procedure for removing sinus sores on the teeth.
If a tooth should erupt in such a way that it pierces the dental nerve,
one should extract that tooth after cutting through the gums with a blade, provided it is not an upper tooth.
After purifying it, one should cauterize it with alkali or fire;
for if it is neglected, the disease certainly spreads to the jawbone, splitting the tooth.
Therefore, one should extract a broken and unstable tooth along with its root;
but when the upper tooth has been extracted, it should be one that is rooted and firmly bound.
Indeed, from an excessive administration of blood-letting, the aforementioned terrible diseases arise;
the person becomes one-eyed, and facial paralysis (ardita) occurs in him.
Therefore, the physician should not extract even a loose upper tooth;
for cleansing [the mouth], one should use the Jāti, Madana, Svādukaṇṭaka, or Khadira trees.
The decoction is prepared from *jāti*, *madanaka*, and pungent, sweet *kaṇṭaka* plants,
as well as from *yaṣṭyāhva*, *rodhra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *khadira*.
Oil is a purifying agent, for it destroys the disease located in the roots of the teeth;
the treatment for the roots of the teeth has been described, and now the treatment for the teeth themselves will be explained.
Warm gargles of unctuous substances, such as ghee or the three sweet substances (traivṛta),
as well as decoctions of wind-alleviating herbs, destroy the condition of sensitive or painful teeth.
Unctuous medicated smoke is beneficial, as are unctuous nasal drops, food, meat broth,
rice gruel, milk, cream, and clarified butter.
Head-poultices (śirobasti) are beneficial, as is the therapeutic regimen that subdues Vāta;
the physician, without injuring the roots of the teeth, should extract the tartar (śarkarā).
Then one should rub those [teeth] with lac powder mixed with honey;
furthermore, one should perform the entire therapeutic procedure for sensitive teeth (dantaharṣa) without omission.
The kapālikā type is the most difficult to treat; even in that case, this procedure is beneficial.
One should conquer caries with drainage after having applied fomentation, once the tooth has become immobile.
Likewise, [it is treated] with head-poultices that subdue Vata, by holding oil-filled gargles,
with ointments of Bhadradārvādi and Varṣābhū, and with unctuous foods.
Having extracted the foreign body, one should treat the site and the cavity;
then, with vidārī, yaṣṭyāhva, śṛṅgāṭaka, and kaseruka, [one should apply a paste].
Oil prepared with ten times its quantity of milk is beneficial when used as a nasal drop (nasya).
In cases of lockjaw (hanumokṣa), one should perform the treatment prescribed for facial paralysis (ardita).
One suffering from dental disease should avoid sour fruits, cold water, dry food, tooth-cleansing sticks,
as well as excessively hard foods.
The treatment for curable diseases of the teeth has been declared;
I shall now describe the procedure for the successful management of curable diseases of the tongue.
Whatever treatment was previously prescribed for wind-born inflammation of the lips (oṣṭhaprakopa),
that should be administered by the physician for thorns (kaṇṭaka) arising from wind.
In cases of wounds caused by pitta where vitiated blood has been expelled,
the application of sweet medicinal pastes as a rub (pratisāraṇa), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), and nasal drops (nasya) are beneficial.
When the thorns arising from phlegm have been scraped away and the blood has diminished,
a paste of the Pippalyādi group mixed with honey should be applied as a rubbing agent.
One should also take morsels of food with white mustard and rock salt,
and one should feed the patient with soups made from patola, nimba, vārtāku, and alkaline preparations.
Having scraped the upajihvā, one should rub it with an alkaline substance;
furthermore, one should treat it with head-purgatives (śirovireka), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), and medicinal smokes (dhūma).
The ritual for those [mantras] belonging to the tongue has been declared; now that for those of the palate will be explained:
having drawn up the uvula with the pinchers formed by the thumb and finger, [one should perform the rite].
The physician should cut [the tongue] with a circular blade while it is positioned upon the palate; he should cut it to one-third [of its length], neither too long nor too short.
From excessive excision, blood may flow profusely and the patient may die because of it;
from insufficient excision, there occurs swelling, salivation, drowsiness, vertigo, and darkness of vision.
Therefore, a physician who is experienced and skilled in observed practice should carefully excise the uvula and then follow this prescribed procedure.
Then, one should rub that [wound] with long pepper (marica), ativiṣā, pāṭhā, vacā, kuṣṭha, and kuṭannaṭa,
combined with honey and salt.
Having decocted vacha, ativisha, patha, rasna, katukarohini,
and nimba, one should apply that as a gargle (kavala).
One should prepare an auspicious, highly fragrant wick from the five parts of *iṅgudī*, *kiṇihī*, *dantī*, *saralā*, and *suradāru*, ground together.
Then the patient should drink the smoke twice a day to destroy the phlegm;
furthermore, a soup made from mung beans prepared with alkali is beneficial for food.
In cases of Tuṇḍikerī, Dhruṣa, Kūrma, Saṅghāta, and Tālupuppuṭa, this same procedure should be followed; the distinction lies only in the surgical operation.
In the case of inflammation of the palate (tālupāka), a procedure that destroys pitta should be performed;
in the case of dryness of the palate (tāluśoṣa), oleation and sudation, as well as measures that destroy vāta, are prescribed.

The treatment for those born from the palate has been proclaimed; now the procedure for those born in the throat will be described. For those born under Sādhya and Rohiṇī, the letting of blood is beneficial.
Emetics, inhalation of medicated smoke, gargling, and nasal therapy should be employed;
furthermore, once the blood has been removed, one should rub the area affected by Vata with salts.
One should also frequently hold lukewarm oleaginous gargles;
for the Pitta-type [disease], one should rub it with Pataṅga, sugar, and honey.
A decoction of grapes (drākṣā) and *parūṣaka* is beneficial for gargling;
one should treat the phlegmatic type (*ślaiṣmikī*) by rubbing it with house-soot (*agāradhūma*) and pungent substances.
Oil prepared with white *viḍaṅga*, *dantī*,
and rock salt (*saindhava*) should be employed for nasal administration (*nasya-karman*) as well as for holding in the mouth (*kavala-dhāraṇa*).
The physician should treat Rohiṇī arising from blood in the same manner as Pitta disorders;
having drained Kaṇṭhaśālūka, one should treat it like Tuṇḍikerī.

One should eat barley-food once a day, in small quantities and with unctuous substances; and one should treat the disease of the uvula (adhijihvikā) in the same manner as the disease of the epiglottis (upajihvikā).
Having drained a single mass, one should perform the purificatory procedure;
furthermore, that disease known as gilāyu should be treated with a surgical instrument.
One should incise a galavidradhi that is located away from vital spots (marmas) and is fully suppurated;
if it arises from Vāta and spreads everywhere, one should rub it with powders of salts.
Oil prepared with Vata-alleviating drugs is beneficial for gargling and nasal administration;
thereafter, the wise physician should give him this unctuous medicinal smoke (dhūma).
One should procure the piths of the śāla, rājādana, eraṇḍa, sāra, iṅguda, and madhūka; as well as guggulu, dhyāmamāṃsī, kālānusārivā, śrī, sarjarasa, śaileya, and beeswax (madhūcchiṣṭa).
Having thoroughly mixed all those medicinal powders with an oil according to the proper method,
the wise physician should apply that preparation, along with honey, as an ointment using the stalk of a *ṭiṇḍūka* fruit.
This medicated smoke, prepared with all the ingredients, is considered excellent for oleation;
it destroys phlegm, subdues wind, and cures diseases of the mouth.
In the case of a person whose entire system is vitiated by pitta, once the body has been purified,
every treatment that alleviates pitta— sweet and cooling— should be administered.
In the case of a sarva-sara (generalized) disease caused by kapha, one should employ gargles, medicinal washes, medicated smoking, and purificatory therapies that alleviate kapha.
One should drink ativiṣā, pāṭhā, musta, and suradāru,
along with rohiṇī, kaṭukā, and the fruits of kuṭaja.
A person, using cow urine in portions equal to the number of fingers [on one's hand],
removes all diseases caused by phlegm through this formulation.
One should administer gargles with milk, sugarcane juice, cow urine, curd-whey, sour gruel,
and also with oils and clarified butter, after having observed the specific humor involved.
The treatment for those diseases arising from the mouth that are curable has been proclaimed;
now those diseases which are incurable, as they have been described therein, will also be explained.
In cases of lip inflammation (oṣṭhaprakopa), those arising from muscle, blood, or the three doṣas should be avoided;
in the roots of the teeth, however, the conditions characterized by the three signs (triliṅga) and sinus formation (sauṣira) are contraindicated.
In the teeth, decay, blackening, and breaking do not succeed;
in the tongue, indolence occurs, and likewise, a tumor arises in the palate.
Svaraghna, Valaya, Vrnda,
Vidāryālasya, Galauṣṭha, Māṃsatāna, Śataghnī, and Rohiṇī.
Indeed, these nineteen diseases are declared to be incurable;
even for them, the physician should proceed with treatment only after having formally renounced it.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Mouth," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||22||
The twenty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of swellings (śopha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

The sixfold swelling arising from the [individual] constituent parts has been described according to its characteristics and its treatment; however, that which spreads everywhere (sarvasara) is fivefold, namely:
caused by vāta, pitta, śleṣman, sannipāta, and poison.

In that regard, in one who has not been satiated, or who travels on foot excessively, or who consumes food in excess, or who eats flour-based foods, green vegetables, potherbs, and salts; or in one who is emaciated and consumes excessively sour substances; or in one who consumes clay, baked earth, potsherds, gravel, or the meat of marshy aquatic animals; or in one suffering from indigestion due to sexual indulgence, or from the consumption of incompatible foods; or in one exhausted by the jolting of elephants, horses, camels, chariots, or infantry—these factors, having vitiated the humors (doṣas) and the tissues (dhātus), produce swelling throughout the entire body.

Among these, swelling caused by Vāta is reddish or black, soft, and characterized by unstable, piercing, and other such specific types of pain; swelling caused by Pitta is yellowish or reddish, soft, spreading rapidly, and characterized by burning sensations and other such specific types of pain; swelling caused by Śleṣman is pale or white, unctuous, hard, cold, and slow-spreading.

In this context, the *kaṇḍvādayaḥ* (itching and so forth) are specific types of sensations. *Sannipāta-śvayathu* (inflammatory swelling due to the derangement of all three humors) possesses all colors and sensations. That caused by poison (*viṣanimitta*), however, arises from the administration of poison (*gara*), the consumption of contaminated water, immersion in putrid water, or being dusted with powder smeared by poisonous creatures; or it results from contact with grass, wood, and the like that have been touched by poisonous urine, feces, or semen. It is mild, quickly appearing, hanging down, and either mobile or immobile, and it is characterized primarily by burning, suppuration, and redness.
And there are defects in this regard: for those located in the stomach (āmāśaya) cause swelling in the upper part;
those in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) cause it in the middle; and those situated in the seat of feces cause it below.
When they have reached the entire body, they cause a generalized swelling;
that swelling which occurs in the middle part of the body is difficult to cure, as is that which is pervasive throughout the whole body.
That which creeps upward, becoming an omen of death in half the body,
along with dyspnea, thirst, debility, fever, vomiting, and loss of appetite;
Hiccups, diarrhea, and coughs indeed cause swelling;
I shall describe their remedies both in general and in detail.
All those suffering from swelling should avoid sour substances, salt, curd, jaggery, muscle fat, milk, oil, ghee, flour-based foods, and heavy items.
In that regard, for swelling caused by Vāta, one should administer Traivṛta or castor oil (eraṇḍa-taila) for a month or half a month.
For swelling caused by Pitta, one should administer ghee prepared with a decoction of the Nyagrodhādi group.
For swelling caused by Śleṣman, one should administer ghee prepared with the Āragvadhādi group.

In cases of swelling caused by the combination of humors (sannipāta), one should mix one vessel of snuhī milk with twelve vessels of sour liquids, add dantī and dravantī as a paste, cook it with ghee, and have the patient drink it;
this is the remedy for conditions caused by poison.
Hereafter, we shall teach the general treatment: by employing any one of the four *tilvaka* ghees mentioned in the section on abdominal enlargements (*udara*), one overcomes swelling (*śvayathu*);
or one may practice the application of urine-based suppositories (*mūtravarti*);
or one may take *navāyasa* daily with honey.
Or one may take a powder of viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, kuṭaja fruit, bhadradāru, nāgara, and marica with warm water;
or powders of the three pungents (trikaṭu), alkali, and iron with a decoction of triphalā;
or urine mixed with an equal amount of milk.
One should consume either *harītakī* with an equal amount of jaggery,
or *devadāru* and *śuṇṭhī*,
or *guggulu* with urine, followed by a decoction of *varṣabhū* as an after-drink.
Or [one may take] equal parts of jaggery with urine, followed by a decoction of *varṣābhū* as an after-drink;
or equal parts of ginger (*śṛṅgavera*) with jaggery;
or a decoction of *varṣābhū* with a paste of radish and ginger, followed daily for a month by milk as an after-drink.
Or one should eat *mudga* bean balls prepared with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) boiled in a decoction of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) and *varṣābhū*.
Or one should drink milk boiled with long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), *cavya*, *citraka*, *mayūraka*, and *varṣābhū*; or milk boiled with *sahā* and the root of *uraṅgī*.
Or [one may take] oil prepared with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), castor root, and the root of *śyāmā*;
or [oil] prepared with *varṣābhū*, ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), *sahā*, and *devadāru*.

Likewise, one should eat barley food or wheat food with rice-water mixed with the paste of *alābu* and *bibhītaka* fruits, along with a salt-free and slightly oily mung-bean soup prepared with milk, long pepper (*pippalī*), black pepper (*marica*), and ginger.

One should perform affusion with decoctions of *vṛkṣaka*, *arka*, *naktamāla*, *nimba*, and *varṣābhū*; an external application (*pradeha*) should be made with *sarṣapa*, *suvarcalā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *śārṅgeṣṭā*. One should constantly employ sharp emetics, purgatives, and non-unctuous enemas according to the specific humor involved, as well as oleation, sudation, and poultices.
Furthermore, one should frequently venesect to let out blood, except in cases where swelling is a complication.
And in this regard, there is a verse:
one who desires to destroy swelling should avoid flour-based foods, sour things, salts, wine, clay, sleeping during the day,
meat from non-forest animals, women, ghee, oil, milk, and heavy substances.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, named "The Treatment of Swelling," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||23||
The twenty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the prevention of future ailments.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
That which must constantly be performed by a wise person who is healthy and desires well-being— rising up again and again— I shall now fully declare.
Therein, first, the tooth-stick should be twelve finger-breadths in length,
as thick as the little finger, straight, without knots, and free from blemishes.
One should employ that which has an odd number of joints, is fresh, grown in a commendable soil,
and is appropriate after considering the season, the bodily humor (doṣa), the taste, and the potency.
Having risen in the morning, one should consume that which is astringent, sweet, bitter, or pungent;
among the bitter, the neem (nimba) is best, and likewise, the catechu (khadira) is best among the astringent.
Madhūka is the best among sweet substances, and Karañja likewise among pungent ones;
[this formulation] is prepared with honey, the three pungents (vyoṣa), the three groups of drugs (trivarga), oil, and rock salt (saindhava).
One should daily cleanse the teeth with the powder of *tejovatī*,
rubbing each tooth individually with a soft brush.
Using tooth-powder while not injuring the gums removes foul odors and the coating of the mouth,
as well as phlegm.
It produces clarity, a relish for food, and cheerfulness;
however, one should not consume it when diseases of the throat, palate, lips, or tongue have arisen.
Furthermore, in cases of indigestion, dyspnea, cough, hiccups, and vomiting;
in those who are weak, suffering from indigestion, afflicted by fainting, or intoxicated by liquor; [these should not be administered].
A person afflicted by headache, one who is thirsty, one who is exhausted, one overcome by fatigue from drinking,
one suffering from facial paralysis, one with earache, and one with dental disease;
A tongue-scraper made of silver, gold, or even wood is recommended; it should remove the impurities of the tongue, be soft, smooth, and ten finger-breadths in length.
Holding oil in the mouth as a gargle (snehagaṇḍūṣa) is pleasant; it removes bad taste, foul odor, swelling, and numbness of the mouth, strengthens the teeth, and promotes appetite.
Or with decoctions of milk-trees mixed with milk,
or likewise with a decoction of bhillotaka, or of āmalaka.
One who is healthy may wash the face and eyes with cold water;
however, [this practice] causes darkening of the face, dryness of the mouth, pustules, and even freckles.
It destroys diseases caused by blood and bile (raktapitta) instantly;
it provides comfort, is light [to digest], and one sees firmly with the eyes.
Srotoñjana originating from the Sindhu region is considered the best; it is pure, removes burning, itching, and impurities, and cures moisture and pain of the eyes.
It brings forth a radiant form and endures both wind and heat;
eye diseases do not arise from it; therefore, one should apply collyrium.
One who has eaten, one who has bathed with the head, one exhausted by vomiting or riding in a vehicle,
one who has stayed awake at night, and one who is afflicted with fever should not apply collyrium.
Auspicious betel leaves, combined with camphor, nutmeg, kakkola, cloves, and katuka,
along with powdered areca nut.
It produces clarity, fragrance, luster, and excellence of the face;
it purifies the jaw, teeth, voice, impurities, tongue, and the sense organs.
It pacifies excessive salivation, is pleasing to the heart, destroys diseases of the throat,
and is wholesome for a person who has just awakened from sleep, after eating, after bathing, or after vomiting.
It is not beneficial for those afflicted by hemorrhaging, pitta-disorders, wasting from injury, thirst, or fainting; nor for those who are dry, weak, or suffering from emaciation of the face.
Likewise, head-massage removes diseases located in the head;
it brings about softness, length, abundance, and glossy blackness of the hair.
It brings satisfaction to the head, makes the face well-skinny,
provides nourishment to the sense organs, and fills the head completely.
One should collect equal parts of madhuka, kṣīraśuklā, sarala, devadāru, and kṣudraka— these five substances known by those names.
One should cook Cakrataila with the paste (kalka) and decoction (kaṣāya) of those [drugs];
one should always apply this oil to the head of the patient while it is still cool.
A hair-comb cleanses the hair and removes dust, insects, and impurities;
filling the ears with oil destroys pain in the jaw, neck, head, and ears.
Anointing the body produces softness, restrains kapha and vāta,
generates nourishment for the bodily constituents (dhātus), and bestows cleanliness, complexion, and strength.
Sprinkling (sekah) removes fatigue, alleviates wind (anilah), restores broken joints,
and pacifies the pain of wounds, burns by fire, blows, and abrasions.
Just as the sprouts of a tree flourish when its root is moistened with water,
so indeed does the growth of the elements occur when they are nourished by affection.

Oil applied in a bath, when properly administered, nourishes the body by satisfying it through the openings of the vessels, the pores of the skin, and the arteries, thereby bestowing strength upon the physique.
In that regard, the wise physician, knowing the constitution, suitability, season, location, doshas, and morbidities, should employ either oil or ghee for massage and affusion.
One should never, under any circumstances, apply [these treatments] when there is a defect in the digestive fire (sāma-doṣa);
likewise, those suffering from acute fever and those whose food is undigested should by no means be anointed with oil.
Likewise, for a man who has undergone purgation, emesis, or a non-unctuous enema,
there may be difficulty in treating the disease from the two preceding procedures, or even its incurability.
On that day, diseases such as sluggish digestion (agnimāndya) and others are said to afflict those remaining;
one should never administer [emesis] for diseases arising from over-nutrition (santarpaṇa).
Action that produces physical exertion is designated as *vyāyāma*;
having performed that, one should thoroughly massage the body for its comfort.
The growth of the body, radiance, well-proportioned limbs,
a stimulated digestive fire, freedom from laziness, stability, lightness, and cleanliness.
Endurance of fatigue, exhaustion, thirst, heat, cold, and so forth,
as well as supreme health, arises from physical exercise.
There is nothing equal to it for the reduction of corpulence;
nor do enemies forcibly overwhelm a mortal who exerts himself through physical training.
Old age does not suddenly assail him and take hold;
moreover, the flesh of one who delights in physical exercise becomes firm.
Diseases do not approach one whose limbs have been perspired through exercise and who has massaged his feet with oil,
just as small animals do not approach a lion.
Even food that is deficient in age, form,
or quality may be made wholesome for one who constantly engages in physical exercise, despite its being otherwise incompatible.
Whether it is well-digested or undigested, food is digested without harm;
for physical exercise is always beneficial for those who are strong and eat unctuous food.
And that [milk] is considered most wholesome for them during the cold and spring seasons;
yet it should be consumed daily by men seeking their own welfare in all seasons.
One should engage in physical exercise with only half of one's strength; otherwise, it destroys [the vital force].
When the wind situated in its own place within the heart enters the mouth, [it is time for exercise].
For a person performing physical exercise, the characteristic of half that strength depends upon age,
power, the body, as well as place, time, and diet.
One should engage in exercise after due consideration; otherwise, one may incur disease, such as wasting, thirst, loss of appetite, vomiting, hemorrhaging, vertigo, and exhaustion.
Cough, wasting, fever, and dyspnea arise from excessive physical exertion;
likewise, one suffering from internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), one who is emaciated, one with wasting disease (śoṣa), and one afflicted by asthma or cough due to chest injury.
One who has eaten, one who is exhausted by sexual indulgence, and one afflicted by thirst or vertigo should avoid it.
Rubbing with unguents (udvartana) alleviates Vata and dissolves Kapha and fat.
It stabilizes the limbs, is the supreme means for removing toxins from the skin,
clarifies the openings of the channels (sirās), and kindles the fire residing in the skin.
Through rubbing and massaging, these two [qualities] will undoubtedly arise;
from massaging, the bodies of women especially become radiant with beauty.
Udgharṣaṇa (rubbing with fragrant powders), which possesses qualities such as exhilaration, auspiciousness, cleanliness, and lightness,
should be known to remove itching, skin eruptions, and disorders of Vāta.
The *phenaka* posture quickly produces steadiness and agility in the thighs;
it also removes itching, urticaria, wind-related stiffness, impurities, and diseases.
Tejana is the application of fire to the skin; vivecanam is the opening of the openings of the vessels (veins);
and udgharṣaṇa is rubbing with a rough brush for the destruction of itching and urticaria.
It removes sleepiness, burning sensations, and fatigue; it dispels perspiration, itching, and thirst;
it is pleasing to the heart, purifies the impurities, is excellent, and awakens all the sense organs.
Bathing pacifies lethargy and sin, bestows contentment, increases virility,
purifies the blood, and also stimulates the digestive fire.
Bathing the head with warm water is always detrimental to the eyes;
one should declare that bathing the head with cold water is beneficial for the eyes.
When there is an aggravation of phlegm and wind, having ascertained the relative strength and weakness of the disease,
one may at will perform a head-bath with warm water for the purpose of medicine.
Excessively cold water aggravates phlegm and wind during the cold season,
while excessively hot water aggravates bile and blood during the hot season.
And that [ghee] is forbidden in cases of diarrhea, fever, earache, and afflictions from wind (vāta),
as well as for those suffering from flatulence, anorexia, indigestion, or who have just eaten.
This unguent bestows good fortune, improves the complexion, increases affection, vigor, and strength,
and removes perspiration, foul odors, discoloration, and fatigue.
Even for those for whom bathing is forbidden, this unguent is prescribed;
it is a destroyer of demons, bestows vigor, and is supremely conducive to good fortune.
The wearing of jasmine, saffron, and gems increases delight; from the application of facial ointments, the eyes become firm and the face possesses full cheeks.
It is free from defects and pimples, lovely, resembling a lotus,
with thick lashes, clear, beautiful, and possessing a pure, radiant orb.
Through the application of collyrium to the eyes, the pupils become clear;
it brings fame, leads to heaven, promotes longevity, and increases wealth and grain.
The worship of the deities, guests, and Brahmins increases one's lineage;
food provides immediate gratification, bestows strength, and sustains the body.
Washing the feet increases life-span, vitality, enthusiasm, mindfulness, vigor, and digestive fire; it removes dirt from the feet, as well as disease and fatigue.
It clarifies the eyes, is aphrodisiac, destroys demons,
increases affection, induces sleep, brings comfort to the body, is beneficial for vision, and removes fatigue and numbness.
Anointing the feet with oil is always beneficial, as it makes the skin of the feet soft;
it cures diseases of the feet, is aphrodisiac, destroys demons, and increases affection.
Wearing footwear is always conducive to ease of movement and vigor;
however, it is detrimental to health, shortens life, and causes injury to the eyes.
For human beings, constant walking on foot without footwear always pacifies sins and cleanses the hair of the head, the nails, and the body hair.
It produces joy, lightness, and good fortune; it increases enthusiasm;
it wards off arrows; and it enhances cleanliness, complexion, luster, and strength.
The turban, adorned with hair-ornaments, is purifying; it wards off wind, heat, and dust, and protects against rain, wind, dust, heat, cold, and other such elements.
Holding a parasol brings luster, clarity of vision, vigor, and auspiciousness;
it dispels fear from dogs, reptiles, serpents, and horned beasts.
It destroys the faults of fatigue and stumbling, and is highly praised for the elderly;
it increases one's essence, enthusiasm, strength, stability, fortitude, and valor.
Holding a staff provides support and destroys fear;
sitting comfortably produces complexion, phlegm, stoutness, and delicacy.
Walking a moderate distance destroys complexion, phlegm, corpulence, and delicacy;
walking too much has the opposite effect and causes old age and weakness.
Furthermore, that walking which does not cause excessive strain to the body bestows longevity,
strength, intelligence, and digestive fire, and awakens the senses.
A comfortable bed and seat alleviate fatigue and wind, are aphrodisiac, and bestow nourishment, sleep, and fortitude; an uncomfortable one is considered to possess the opposite qualities.
The peacock-feather fan provides vigor and drives away flies and other insects;
the breeze from a fan destroys thirst, burning sensations, fatigue, perspiration, and fainting.
It induces pleasure and sleep, is aphrodisiac, removes phlegm, wind, and fatigue;
it is soothing, and brings clarity to the flesh, blood, and skin, providing comfort.

An airy place causes dryness, discoloration, and stiffness, while removing burning sensations and promoting digestion; it also cures perspiration, fainting, and thirst. An airy-free place has the opposite effect.
In summer and autumn, a person should enjoy pleasant breezes;
however, for the sake of longevity and health, one should always stay in a windless place.
Sunlight causes bile, thirst, digestive fire, perspiration, fainting, vertigo, and loss of blood;
it also produces burning sensations and discoloration, whereas shade counteracts these effects.
Agni (pungent substances) destroys the obstruction caused by vāta and kapha, as well as coldness and shivering;
however, it vitiates undigested matter (āma), secretions (abhiṣyanda), old age, and blood-bile (raktapitta).

Sleep, when indulged in at the proper time, produces nourishment, complexion, strength, enthusiasm, a bright digestion, and freedom from lethargy, as well as the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus).

In that regard, from the very beginning, one should indeed attend upon [the teacher] with short nails and hair, being pure, dressed in white garments, wearing a light turban, an umbrella, and sandals, holding a staff in hand; speaking at the proper time with words that are beneficial, measured, and preceded by sweetness; being like a kinsman to all beings, acting with the approval of elders and teachers, having good assistants, and with an undistracted mind.
Furthermore, this should not be done at night;
nor on places where there are hair, bones, thorns, stones, husks, ashes, heaps of refuse, skulls, embers, impurities, bathing grounds, or sites for ritual offerings.
Nor [should one discharge it] over uneven ground, an Indra-pillar, a crossroads, or a chasm.
One should not speak words that are hostile to the king, harsh, malicious, or false;
nor should one utter slanders against the gods, Brahmins, or ancestors; nor should one associate with those who are hated by the king, the insane, the outcaste, the mean, or the base.
One should avoid climbing trees, mountains, precipices, uneven ground, anthills, or mounting upon wicked horses, elephants, and the like;
as well as descending into full rivers, oceans, unknown ponds, chasms, or wells;
and one should avoid dwelling in ruined or empty houses, cremation grounds, or desolate forests, as well as exposure to fire, panic, or associating with predatory beasts, serpents, and insects.
And [avoid] proximity to village raids, quarrels, the clash of weapons, venomous snakes, reptiles, and horned animals.
One should not pass between fire, a cow, a teacher, a Brāhmaṇa, a swing, or a married couple.
One should not follow after a corpse.
And one should not step upon the shadow of a deity, a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, a sacred tree (caitya), a banner, a sick person, an outcaste, or an evildoer.
One should not look at the sun as it sets or rises; nor should one report to anyone a cow suckling her calf, one sucking milk, or one grazing in another's field;
nor should one report the falling of meteors, portents, or rainbows.
One should not blow on fire with one's mouth;
nor should one strike water or the earth with one’s hands or feet.
One should not suppress the urges of wind, urine, feces, and so forth.

One should not discharge these urges outside in the vicinity of a village, a city, a temple, a cremation ground, a crossroads, a body of water, or on a path; nor should one do so openly, nor facing the wind, fire, water, the moon, the sun, a cow, or a teacher.

One should not scratch the ground. One should not, with the mouth uncovered, emit yawning, eructation, coughing, sighing, or sneezing in an assembly. One should not, in the presence of a teacher, lean back in a chair or stretch out one's legs.
One should not probe the openings of the ears, nose, teeth, or eyes with a finger.
One should not fan one's hair, face, nails, clothes, or limbs.
One should not make music with one's limbs, nails, or mouth.
One should not strike, cut, or break pieces of wood, clods of earth, grass, or similar objects.

One should not expose oneself to headwinds or the heat of the sun. One should not sit near a fire immediately after eating. One should not sit on a seat that is too high or one made of insufficient wood.
One should not hold the neck unevenly;
one should not perform any activity or eat with the body held unevenly;
nor should one gaze fixedly at anything, especially at light, the sun, or subtle, moving, or flickering objects.
One should not carry a burden upon the head.

Nor should one excessively indulge—even if accustomed—in sleep, wakefulness, lying down, sitting, standing, walking, traveling by carriage, riding on vehicles, running, jumping, leaping, swimming, crossing over, laughing, talking, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, and so forth.
One should gradually withdraw even from a habitual practice if it is harmful;
one should gradually engage even in what is beneficial if it has not been practiced before;
but one should never do so with that which is entirely deficient.
One should not sleep with one's head downward; one should not eat from a broken vessel,
nor without a vessel.
One should not drink water with cupped hands.
At the proper time, one should eat food that is wholesome, moderate, unctuous, and predominantly sweet, having been supervised by a physician.
One should avoid the food of village communities, groups, courtesans, shopkeepers, enemies, those who give feasts for profit, rogues, and outcasts.
The remaining [objects]— those with undesirable forms, tastes, smells, touches, sounds, or mental objects—
as well as others of such qualities given in haste,
and those even [rendered unwholesome] by being touched by flies or hair.

One should not eat without having washed one's feet; nor when oppressed by the urge to urinate or defecate; nor during the two twilights; nor without being supported; nor at a time that has passed; nor in deficient or excessive quantities; nor [should one eat food] from which the oil has been extracted.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor milk that is spoiled or stale;
one should not eat curd at night, nor that which is devoid of ghee and sugar.
It should not be taken without meat broth, nor without honey, nor hot, nor without āmalaka;
otherwise, it would produce many diseases such as leprosy and erysipelas.
One should not look at one's own reflection in water, nor enter the water naked.

One should not indulge in gambling, excessive consumption of intoxicants, acting as a guarantor, serving as a witness, challenging others to a match, attending social gatherings, or playing musical instruments.
One should not wear garlands, umbrellas, shoes, gold, or fine garments that have been worn by others. While impure from eating, one must not touch a Brāhmaṇa, a fire, or a cow.
And there are verses on this subject:
"In whichever season whichever humors become aggravated in embodied beings,
those specific tastes should be administered by the wise in those very seasons."
One should not drink water during the rainy season; one should drink it in measured quantity during autumn.
During the four months of the rainy season, one should drink water with moderation.
