In autumn and spring, a person may drink [the liquor] warm at will; however, in summer it should be cold.
In winter and spring, one should drink sidhu and arishta.
In summer one should drink milk that has been boiled and cooled; in the rainy season, one should drink meat broth; during the downpour, one should drink vegetable soup;
and at its conclusion, one should drink water that is naturally cool.

One who is healthy should take [the medicine] in this manner; however, another person, following the nature of their humors and diet, should take it with oil mixed with powdered rock salt and long pepper.
One should drink it for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire and must not suppress natural urges;
it kindles the internal fire in men and serves to pacify diseases.
One should properly administer oleation and other therapies during the rainy season, autumn, and spring;
emesis is indicated for kapha, purgation for pitta, and enemas for vata.
Physical exercise is always praised in all three [seasons] as it destroys the humors;
even food that is incompatible when eaten does not cause harm through exercise.
One should be focused on the purification of excretion, sexual intercourse, and food;
however, a wise person should not desire the accumulation of faults or physical and mental suffering.
Furthermore, a self-possessed man should protect himself from excessive sexual union with women;
[for it causes] ailments such as piercing pain, cough, fever, asthma, emaciation, jaundice, and consumption.
From excessive sexual intercourse, diseases such as convulsions (akṣepaka) and others arise;
[those who practice moderation] are long-lived, have slow aging, and are endowed with a beautiful body, complexion, and strength.
They possess firm and well-developed muscles and are self-restrained with women;
a man should approach a woman only every third day.
In all seasons, during the heat, the wise man should approach his wife once every fortnight. He should likewise avoid her when she is menstruating, unwilling, unclean, or displeasing.
One who is advanced in caste, advanced in age, or likewise afflicted by disease;
one with missing limbs, one who is pregnant, one who is disliked, or one possessed of defects of the womb.
A man should not approach a woman who is of the same lineage, the wife of his guru, one who has renounced the world, or one who is forbidden during the twilight hours or on sacred festival days.
At the time of dawn, at midnight, and likewise at midday;
in a place that causes shame, in an exposed spot, or in an impure place.
A person who is hungry, diseased, or agitated in mind;
one who has the urge to pass wind, feces, or urine; and one who is weak from thirst or sexual passion [should not study].
One should avoid retaining semen when it has been emitted into the womb of an animal or a non-woman,
and even if one is strong, one should avoid its discharge into a defiled womb.
Excessive emission of semen and covering the head while standing or lying on one's back are especially censured.
Even in play, a wise man seeking his own welfare should avoid a woman who has reached her menses,
for such a man is of undisciplined self.
From that, there would be a loss of vision, lifespan, and luster, as well as unrighteousness;
[this applies to approaching] a woman wearing ascetic marks, the wife of a guru, one of the same lineage, or during the sacred festival days (parvan).
If one approaches an elderly woman or during the two twilights, there will be a loss of life;
if she is pregnant, there will be injury to the fetus; if she is diseased, there will be a loss of strength.
If the woman has missing limbs, is defiled, is loathed, is barren,
or is in an uncovered place or an impure location, there will be a loss of semen and of mental vigor.
Hungry, agitated in mind, thirsty at midday, and weak while standing,
one suffers the loss of semen and the provocation of wind.
From excessive indulgence, emaciation occurs, leading to the depletion of semen;
for one who is diseased, pain arises in the spleen, and death as well as fainting ensue.
At dawn and at midnight, the wind and bile become aggravated;
likewise in animals, in women, and in those with diseased wombs.
Likewise, dysentery, the provocation of wind (vāyu), and the depletion of semen result from the suppression of the urge to defecate,
urinate, or discharge semen.
Furthermore, semen-stone (śukrāśmarī) arises quickly when [the organ] is turned upward;
therefore, one should avoid all such things, for they are harmful in both worlds.
When semen has been aroused through delusion, it must not be retained under any circumstances;
[one should instead approach] a woman endowed with youth, beauty, and virtue, who is of similar character and noble birth.
Desirous, he should, being joyful and strengthened by aphrodisiacs, judiciously enjoy a woman who is likewise desirous, joyful, and adorned.
Edible foods with sugar, milk with sugar, meat broth,
bathing with a fan, and sleep are beneficial at the conclusion of sexual intercourse.
This has been stated in brief as the mere essence of good conduct:
health, long life, wealth, or even heaven are attained by men who practice it.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Future Diseases," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||24||
The twenty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of miscellaneous diseases (Miśrakacikitsita).
As the Blessed One Dhanvantari has said.
It has been stated previously that swellings of the palate (pālyāmaya) must be drained; now understand them:
Paripoṭa, as well as Utpāta, Unmantha, and Duḥkhavardhana.
The fifth is the *parilehī*; these are known as the diseases of the ear-lobe (*karṇapālī*).
Due to excessive delicacy, or when [the lobe] has been released for a long time and suddenly begins to grow again, [these diseases arise].
A painful swelling of the earlobe that is cracked,
resembling black or reddish-brown in color, and rigid, is known as Paripoṭaka caused by Vāta.
Due to contact with heavy ornaments, or even from being struck or rubbed,
a dark swelling may occur at the earlobe, accompanied by burning, suppuration, and pain.
That disorder is considered to arise from blood or from blood-bile;
furthermore, when one forcibly stretches the ear, the Vayu becomes aggravated in the earlobe.
Having seized the phlegm, it produces a swelling with the color and pain characteristic of that [phlegm];
this disorder, characterized by itching, is called Unmanthaka and is born from phlegm and wind.
When an itching, burning, and painful swelling occurs on the ear, accompanied by suppuration and located in the skin, it is known as Vardhamāna; this condition increases one's suffering.
Kapha, blood, and parasites produce eruptive pustules on the margin resembling mustard seeds,
which are characterized by discharge and accompanied by itching, burning, and pain.
Arising from phlegm, blood, and parasites, it spreads here and there;
as it licks the earlobe along with the ear-canal, it is known as Parilehī.
For these terrible diseases of the palate afflict a man who fails to take remedial action;
indeed, if neglected, they destroy the palate of one who indulges in improper diet and lifestyle.
Therefore, the physician should quickly apply the sequence beginning with oleation (sneha) to those [conditions],
as well as massage, affusion, plasters, and bloodletting.
I shall describe the massage both in general and in detail,
using kharapuṣpā, yaṣṭimadhu, rock salt, and devadāru.
One should cook ghee, oil, fat, marrow, and beeswax with well-ground roots of *aśvagandhā*, radish, and *avalguja*, along with their fruits.
Then, in the case of *paripoṭaka*, one should smear the edges with these [drugs] mixed with milk:
*mañjiṣṭhā*, sesame seeds, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *sārivā*, blue lotus, and *padmaka*.
Oil prepared with sarodhra, kadamba, bala, jambu, and mango sprouts,
combined with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), is a destroyer of utpāta (sudden, violent onset).
Oil cooked with tālapatrī, aśvagandhā, arka, the fruit of bākucī, rock salt (saindhava),
and the fat of a crab and a monitor lizard [is effective].
An enema made from *sarala* and *lāṅgalī* is beneficial for destroying *unmantha*;
likewise, one should perform irrigation with a decoction of *aśmantaka*, *jambu*, and *āmrā* leaves.
One should dust the earlobe, which has been anointed with oil, with powders of prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, and the two types of rajanī, used as an unguent.
One should cook oil with a paste of lac and viḍaṅga and apply it;
for parilehikā, one should apply a fomentation with a ball of cow dung and then rub the area.
Alternatively, [one may use] ground viḍaṅga combined with trivṛt, śyāmā, and arka;
or seeds of karañja and iṅgudi combined with kuṭaja and āragvadha.
Alternatively, mustard oil prepared with all [the aforementioned drugs], combined with black pepper,
nimba leaves, and beeswax, is beneficial for massage.
When the limbs are afflicted by disease, or are emaciated and rigid,
one should apply this unguent for the sake of nourishment and softness.
One should cook the marrow of animals from arid and marshy lands, along with muscle fat, oil, and fresh ghee,
adding ten times the amount of milk and the group of sweet (madhura) drugs.
One should likewise take apāmārga, aśvagandhā, and auspicious lac-resin;
once these have been processed and thoroughly strained, one should store them in a well-protected place.
One should always anoint the hair-follicles after they have been well-steamed and massaged;
by this means, the follicles grow healthy, free from disease, and free from affliction.

[The teeth] become soft, well-nourished, even, glossy, and fit for ornamentation. Having powdered together indigo leaves, bee-pollen, arjuna bark, piṇḍītaka, black iron filings, sahacara flower produced from seed, and harītakī, vibhītaka, and āmalakī; |||
Having measured all this together as being equal to mud from a lotus-pond,
and having joined one side and placed it inside an iron jar with a lid in a chamber;

One should cook this oil mixed with the juice derived from *bhṛṅga* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). When the cooking is nearly complete, one should drop a leaf of the crane (*balākā*) into it for the purpose of testing.
When it becomes as dark blue as a female bee, then,
having placed that well-matured substance in a vessel of black iron and kept it for a month, its application through massage destroys gray hair.

Having ground together the three fruits, iron filings, collyrium, liquorice, and the two types of sārivā,
all with the juice of the heartwood of the bījaka tree mixed with modayantī;
Afterwards, having thoroughly stirred one *prastha* each of the seven liquids containing the essence, one should keep it protected for ten days;
then, placing that oil extracted from *akṣa* seeds in a fine iron vessel, one should cook it with great care.
Once cooked, one should place it in a new iron vessel and administer it as a nasal drop (nasya) after the body has been thoroughly purified.
While being treated with these oil massages (abhyaṅga), the patient should eat black gram (māṣa) or rice-and-pulse porridge (kṛsarā).
After a month, his hair becomes thick and curled at the tips, with the luster of bees or collyrium;
likewise, other hairs grow upon his bald spot, and old age does not suddenly come upon him.
Supreme strength shall arise in one's senses, and the face shall become free from wrinkles;
this oil must not be given to one who lacks desire, nor to one who does not seek it, nor to one who has not performed service, nor indeed to an enemy.
Lac, the two types of *rodhra*, the two types of *haridrā*, realgar, orpiment, *kuṣṭha*, *nāga*, red ochre, and pigments;
likewise, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *ugrā*, that which originates from *surāṣṭra*, *pattaṅga*, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and collyrium.
The bark of the golden-angled (hemāṅga) tree, the pale leaves of the banyan (vaṭa), kālīya, padmaka (the heartwood of the lotus),
the center of the lotus, red and white sandalwood, mercury, and the group of drugs beginning with kākoli— all these should be ground with milk.
Fat, marrow, beeswax, cow's ghee, milk, and a decoction of milky trees—
all these, when cooked together, constitute the preeminent ghee for anointing the face.
This destroys vitiligo and excessively advanced melasma, as well as certain pustules that have appeared on the face;
it makes the face lotus-like, free of wrinkles, full-cheeked, and beautiful.
A physician should always administer this foremost anti-leprotic ghee to kings, their wives, and men of equal status,
as well as to those who suffer from elephantiasis (vaipādika) in their feet.
One should apply a paste of powdered harītakī, leaves of ariṣṭa, mango bark, the stalk of a pomegranate flower, and the leaf of madayantikā; this cosmetic unguent for the limbs is worthy of a king.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, named "The Treatment of Miscellaneous Diseases," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||25||
The twenty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa) for those whose strength has diminished.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
For one who is healthy, of vigorous youth, and practices aphrodisiacs,
sexual intercourse every day during all seasons is not prohibited.
For those elders who desire sport, for those who wish to be beloved by women,
for those diminished by attachment to women, for the impotent, and for those of scanty semen.
For men who are pleasure-seekers, wealthy, endowed with beauty and youth,
and who have many wives, aphrodisiac formulations are beneficial.
When, through proper application,
a man with excessive vigor satisfies women, it is for this reason that it is called *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac).
There were various kinds of foods and diverse drinks;
likewise, there were voices that were pleasing to the ear and touches that were pleasant to the skin.
The night adorned with the moon, a passionate woman in the bloom of youth,
song that captivates the ear, betel, wine, and flower garlands.
Pleasant fragrances, variegated forms, delightful groves,
and the absence of mental resistance—
these things act as aphrodisiacs for a man when his mind is wounded by the desire for pleasure through various unappealing circumstances.
Impotence resulting from sexual union with a woman who is disliked is known as mental impotence;
it is also caused by the excessive consumption of pungent, sour, hot, and salty substances.
The depletion of the somatic elements (saumyadhātu) is observed as one form of impotence;
another is known to be that of one who is habitually addicted to excessive sexual intercourse and does not engage in aphrodisiac practices (vājīkaraṇa).
He suffers the collapse of his virility caused by the depletion of semen,
or again, through a severe disease of the penis or even the cutting of a vital organ.
This fourth type of impotence in men arises from the impairment of virility;
that which is impotent from birth is known as innate impotence.

The sixth type of impotence is considered to arise from the suppression of the vital energy of a strong man whose mind is agitated, due to the practice of celibacy; it is caused by the resulting hardness of the semen.
Congenital impotence and that which arises from the cutting of vital points (marmans) are incurable;
however, for the other curable types, one should apply the opposite of the causative factors.
Hereafter, I shall describe the aphrodisiac regimen:
either a powder of sesame, mung beans, vidārī, and śāli rice; or else—
One should cook an *utkārikā* (a medicinal bolus) moistened with the sugarcane juice of the Pauṇḍraka variety, rubbed together with rock salt (*saindhava*),
and combined with boar fat and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Having consumed that, a man may approach a hundred women;
[likewise, one who consumes] sesame seeds repeatedly saturated in milk prepared with goat testicles.
A man who eats *śaṣkulī* cakes prepared with the fat of a porpoise and cooked in sesame oil may approach a hundred women as if they were virgins.
One who eats two testicles of a goat, prepared in milk and ghee along with long pepper and salt,
may approach a hundred women.
One should cook cakes (pūpalikā) in clarified butter using equal parts of the powders of long pepper (pippalī), black gram (māṣa), śāli rice, barley (yava), and wheat (godhūma).
Having consumed that and drunk milk sweetened with sugar,
a man may proceed like a sparrow for ten times in uninterrupted succession.
Having licked well-prepared powder of vidārī,
processed with its own juice and combined with ghee and honey, one approaches ten women.
In this manner, having licked the powder of āmalaka impregnated with its own juice and combined with sugar,
honey, and ghee, one should drink milk.
By this means, even an eighty-year-old man rejoices like a youth when goat testicles,
seasoned with long pepper and salt and prepared in ghee, are consumed.
Or one may eat the flesh of the porpoise; these are indeed highly aphrodisiac. Likewise, one should eat the eggs of the crab, the tortoise, and the crocodile.
Or a man should drink the semen of a buffalo, a bull, or a goat;
or a man may drink milk prepared with the fruit, root-bark, and sprouts of the Aśvattha tree.
Having drunk the paste of Vidāri roots with boiled milk, along with sugar and honey, a man rejoices like a sparrow.
Having drunk [a decoction] equal in measure to an udumbara fruit, even an old man becomes like a youth;
this is done with one pala of black gram (māṣa) combined with honey and clarified butter.
Having licked this and drunk milk, a man becomes as strong as a horse;
likewise, wheat cooked in milk together with the fruits of *ātmaguptā* [should be consumed].
One should eat these cooled and mixed with ghee, and afterwards drink milk;
this is the ghee prepared from the eggs of the monitor lizard, the rat, the frog, and the sparrow.
By massaging the feet, one gains strength; however, one should not let the foot touch the ground.
As long as it does not touch the earth, one should move continuously.
A man who drinks the powder of the fruits of *svayamguptā* and *ikṣuraka* mixed with sugar and warm milk will not suffer from sexual debility.
One seeking strength should drink the powder of uccaṭā in this manner;
a man should likewise drink bean soup combined with the fruits of svayaṃguptā.
Having boiled the fruit of *guptā*, the seeds of *gokṣuraka*, and likewise *uccaṭā* with cow's milk,
a man who drinks it after stirring it with a ladle and mixing it with sugar remains exhilarated throughout the entire night.
Having drunk a preparation of black gram, vidārī, and uccaṭā combined with cow’s milk, honey, and ghee,
and well-conjoined with sugar, a man becomes as sexually vigorous as a sparrow throughout the entire night.
The milk of cows that have calved for the first time, whose calves are grown, and which are fed with masha leaves,
is praised for living beings who desire strength.
All groups of milky plants and meats, as well as the Kākolyādi group, are highly esteemed;
therefore, one should employ them for the purpose of aphrodisiac therapy (vājīkaraṇa).
These aphrodisiac formulations bestow pleasure, progeny, and strength;
they should be employed by those with purified and well-nourished bodies, taking into account the season and other relevant factors.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment for Aphrodisiacs for Those with Diminished Strength," in the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The twenty-seventh chapter:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the elixir (rasāyana) that pacifies all injuries.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
In the early or middle stage of life, a wise physician should always administer rasāyana to a person whose body has been prepared through oleation and purification.
The practice of alchemy is not appropriate for one whose body is impure;
it does not shine upon a soiled garment, like a dye applied to it.
I shall describe the prevention of those injuries to the body arising from the humors as well as those of mental origin, which have been taught in various sections.
Cold water, milk, honey, and clarified butter— each taken singly,
two at a time, three together, or all combined— if drunk beforehand, will stabilize one's vital age.

In that regard, one should take the powder of *viḍaṅga* seeds mixed with *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and honey, and consume it with cold water according to one's strength; one should likewise drink cold water after it. This should be done every day for a month. Alternatively, that same powder may be taken with honey and a decoction of *bhallātaka*, or with honey and a decoction of grapes.
Or with honey and the juice of *āmalaka*;
or with a decoction of *guḍūcī*.

Thus, there are these five applications. When [the medicine] has been digested, one should eat boiled rice mixed with ghee along with unsalted, slightly oily soup of green gram (*mudga*) and *āmalaka*. These [applications] destroy even severe hemorrhoids.
They destroy worms and generate the power of comprehension and retention. Furthermore, with use month after month, there is an increase in lifespan of one hundred years for each hundred-year period.

One *droṇa* of *viḍaṅga* seeds should be steamed like flour on a griddle until they are softened and their astringency is removed; having taken them down while still moist, one should grind them on a stone and place the paste in a sturdy iron jar filled with honey-water. During the rainy season, it should be buried within a heap of ash inside the house for four months.
At the end of the rains, having extracted it and purified the body, one should perform a thousand oblations (*sahasrasaṃpāta*) and consume it every morning according to one's strength.
When it has been digested, one should eat rice with ghee along with unsalted broth made from green gram and *āmalaka*.
He should sleep on a bed of dust.
After one month, worms emerge from all his limbs;
these he should remove with a bamboo splinter after having anointed himself with *aṇu* oil.
In the second [month], ants; in the third, lice—one should likewise remove them.
In the fourth, teeth, nails, and hair fall out; in the fifth, auspicious qualities and marks arise. And he attains a superhuman body that possesses the brilliance of the sun.
He becomes capable of hearing from afar and seeing from afar. Having cast aside passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), he abides in goodness (*sattva*).

Producing unprecedented knowledge through what has been heard and studied, possessing the strength of an elephant and the speed of a horse, youthful again, he attains a lifespan of eight hundred years; for him, *aṇu* oil is intended for anointing the body.
Sandalwood is for the purpose of anointment;
his diet and regimen are according to the procedure prescribed for *bhallātaka*.
This same procedure applies to *kāśmarya* fruits that have been de-seeded, with the exception of sleeping on the ground and eating [only] there; for in this case, one should eat with boiled milk.
The rest is the same as before, including the blessings.
These are to be used in disorders caused by blood and bile (*rakta-pitta*).

As it has been said: having entered one's dwelling, one should drink half a *pala* or one *pala* of *balā* root mixed with milk. Once digested, the diet should consist of milk, ghee, and rice. By using this for twelve nights, one’s youth remains for twelve years; by using it for a hundred days, one’s youth remains for a hundred years.
In the same way, there is the use of atibalā, nāgabalā, vidārī,
and śatāvarī; specifically, however, one should take atibalā with water and nāgabalā powder with honey.
The powder of vidārī with milk;
likewise for śatāvarī. The rest is the same as before, and the blessings are identical.

These medicinal herbs are prescribed for those desiring strength, for those suffering from emaciation, for those afflicted by internal hemorrhaging (rakta-pitta), for those vomiting blood, and for those undergoing purgation.
Having prepared a powder from the root of *vārāhī* in equal parts with *tulā*, one should drink a dose mixed with honey, stirred into milk.
Once digested, the diet should consist of milk, ghee, and rice.
The prohibitions here are as before. By employing this practice, one attains a lifespan of a hundred years and inexhaustible potency with women.

Having sprinkled milk with this very powder, one should churn it once it has been boiled and cooled, produce clarified butter (*ājya*), and consume it mixed with honey either twice daily—at dawn and dusk—or at a single time.
When it is digested, the diet should consist of milk, ghee, and rice.
By using it in this manner for a month, one attains a lifespan of a hundred years.

One who desires eyesight or vital breath should boil the roots of *bījakasāra* and *agnimantha*, and prepare a *prastha* measure of *māṣa* beans in that decoction. While it is being cooked, one should add a paste (*kalka*) of *citraka* roots the size of an *akṣa* nut and a fourth part of *āmalaka* juice.

Then, having removed it from the heat once it has been cooked, one should perform the *sahasrasampāta* oblation over it; when it has cooled, one should mix it with honey and ghee and consume it according to one's strength.
One should eat salt sparingly according to what is suitable for one's constitution.

When the previous meal is digested, one should eat rice with ghee along with unsalted soup of mung beans and āmalaka, or with milk, for three months. By these two applications, the eyes become like those of Suparṇa, one gains no small strength, becomes inexhaustible in sexual vigor with women, and attains a lifespan of a hundred years.
And there is this verse on the subject:
"The man who eats the seeds of the *śaṇa* plant prepared with milk,
along with milk, his youth does not decay."
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Rejuvenation for Alleviating All Afflictions," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The twenty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of rejuvenation (rasāyana) for those desiring intelligence and longevity.
As the Blessed One Dhanvantari has said.

One desiring intelligence and longevity should take the fruits of white *avalguja* that have been dried in the sun, grind them into a fine powder, and mix it with jaggery. Having stirred this, one should place it in an oil-jar for seven nights within a heap of grain.
After seven nights, having extracted it, one should administer a bolus according to one's strength before sunrise to a person whose bodily humors (*doṣas*) have been eliminated.
One should drink warm water afterwards; and the procedure for entering the house is the same as that prescribed for *bhallātaka*.

Having digested the medicine, one should, in the afternoon, sprinkle one’s body with cold water and eat a meal of *śāli* or *ṣaṣṭika* rice mixed with milk sweetened by sugar. By using this for six months, one becomes free from sin, endowed with strength and complexion, eloquent in learning, possessed of memory, free from disease, and attains a lifespan of a hundred years. For one suffering from skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), jaundice (*pāṇḍu*), or abdominal dropsy (*udara*), one should stir half a *palā* measure of the powder with the urine of a black cow and administer it as a bolus when the sun has lost its redness.
In the afternoon, one should eat rice with clarified butter along with unsalted *āmalaka* soup.

By using it in this manner for one month, one becomes possessed of mindfulness, free from disease, and attains a lifespan of a hundred years. This same method of application applies to the roots of *citraka* and to *rajanī*; however, regarding the root of *citraka*, two palas as a lump is the maximum dosage.
The rest is as previously described.

One whose humors have been eliminated and who has consumed the mixed food should enter his dwelling in the prescribed order, take the fresh juice of *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, offer it into the fire with a thousand oblations (*sahasrasaṃpāta*), and drink it mixed with milk according to his strength, followed by milk as an after-drink (*anupāna*).
When that [juice] is digested, he should consume barley-food with milk; or he may eat it together with sesame seeds for three months, with milk as an after-drink.

Once it is digested, his diet should consist of milk, ghee, and rice. By using it in this manner, one becomes endowed with Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasī*) and becomes a reciter of the sacred scriptures; he attains a lifespan of one hundred years.
Having fasted for three nights, one should consume this [mixture] for three nights.
After the three nights have passed, one should take milk and clarified butter;
or else, one should drink a bolus the size of a *bilva* fruit, having stirred it into milk.
Having used it in this manner for twelve nights, a wise person becomes one with a lifespan of a hundred years.

Having had his impurities removed and having entered the house, he should take a meal that is not mixed with other foods; then, taking the fresh juice of *brāhmī*, he should perform a sacrifice with a thousand oblations and consume it according to his strength.
When the medicine has been digested, he should drink unsalted barley gruel in the afternoon, or, if he is accustomed to milk, he should eat with milk.
Having used it in this manner for seven nights, one becomes endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*) and becomes wise.
Having used it for a second seven-night period, one produces whatever text one desires, and what has been lost becomes manifest to him.
Having used it for a third seven-night period, one retains even a hundred [verses] after they have been recited only twice.
By using it in this manner for twenty-one nights, misfortune departs; the goddess of speech enters him in bodily form;
all the Vedas attend upon him;
he becomes a possessor of sacred learning and lives for five hundred years.

In two *prasthas* of *brāhmīsvara-sa* (juice of *Brāhmī*), one should add one *prastha* of ghee, one *kuḍava* of *viḍaṅga* seeds, two *palas* each of *vacā* and *amṛtā*, and twelve each of *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, and *bibhītaka*. Having ground these finely and mixed them together, one should cook them and store the preparation in a well-protected place.
Then, according to the previous procedure, one should consume the appropriate dose according to one's strength. Once digested, the diet should consist of milk, ghee, and boiled rice.
And here the resolution is as before.
By this, worms emerge from above, below, and across;
misfortune departs.

One who has a lotus-like complexion, stable youth, and a retentive memory for what is heard attains a lifespan of three hundred years; indeed, they prescribe this very [procedure] as a purification therapy for leprosy, chronic fevers, epilepsy, insanity, poisons, possession by spirits, and other major diseases.
Having entered the house only after his impurities have been removed, he should drink a bolus of Himalayan *vacā* the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, consecrated with mantras and stirred with milk.
When that has been digested, his diet should consist of milk, ghee, and boiled rice.
He should employ this regimen for twelve nights.
Then his ear is opened;
from a second repetition he becomes possessed of memory;
from a third repetition he grasps what has been heard.
Having used it for four times twelve nights, one overcomes all sin;
the vision of Tārkṣya arises,
and one becomes a hundred years old.
Having boiled two palas each of the other two types of *vacā* in milk, one should drink it;
the diet is the same,
and the blessings are the same as before.
By consuming a droṇa of clarified butter processed a hundred times with vacā, one attains a lifespan of five hundred years;
it also cures goiter, scrofula, elephantiasis, and hoarseness of voice.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the elixir for those desiring long life,
which, when combined with mantras and medicinal herbs, yields its fruit within a year.
If a man offers the powder of bilva fruit by the thousands of times under the Puṣya asterism,
reciting the Śrīsūkta at dawn day after day, he shall obtain gold along with prosperity.
One should lick [this] mixed with ghee and honey, which is the supreme destroyer of misfortune;
likewise, one should drink the decoction of the root of the bilva tree, excluding its bark, day after day.
Having bathed and offered oblations with a concentrated mind, one should consume it together with milk;
this is remembered as bestowing a lifespan of ten thousand years and becoming possessed of a well-yoked chariot.
Having offered a hundred thousand oblations of a decoction of lotus stalks mixed with honey and parched grain,
it is known as the Amogha, joined with the Yuktaratha.
Gold, lotus seeds, honey, parched grain, and priyaṅgu—
when drunk with cow's milk, this destroys misfortune.
A decoction of blue lotus petals boiled with cow's milk,
together with gold and sesame seeds, is traditionally held to be the destroyer of misfortune (Alakṣmī).
Cow’s milk, gold, and beeswax— these,
when drunk after a hundred thousand oblations have been offered, are known as the "Yuktaratha" (the chariot-yoking) mixture.
The triad consisting of vacā-ghṛta (Vaca-ghee), gold, and bilva-powder increases intellect,
longevity, health, nourishment, and good fortune.

Having prepared oil by adding it to a decoction of one *tulā* of *vāsā* root, and having offered a thousand oblations [into the fire], one should consume it; this is said to be purifying and conducive to longevity.
One should eat barley-grains mixed with long pepper and honey, overcoming even other barley; thus one's training shall be like that of a well-disciplined foot-soldier.
By consuming this triad of honey, powdered āmalaka, and gold,
even one seized by an evil spirit is released from the danger to life.
Śatāvarī ghee, properly consumed day after day along with honey and gold, shall bring even a king under one's control.
Gośīrṣa sandalwood, mohanikā, madhuka, honey,
and gold— this combination should be drunk by one desiring good fortune.
One should always drink cow's ghee prepared with a decoction of red and blue lotuses combined with liquorice, along with gold.
And one should drink milk prepared with those same [herbs] when they arise;
it destroys misfortune, is always life-prolonging, and leads to sovereignty and good fortune.
Wherever a mantra is not specifically enjoined for these yogic practices and means of accomplishment,
the three-footed Gāyatrī should be recited there in every instance.
These herbs destroy evil, bestow prosperity,
and even grant a man the strength of a serpent and a likeness unto the immortals.
Constant study, debate, examination of other systems,
and service to teachers learned in those sciences— this is the collection of qualities that produce intelligence and memory.
Food that promotes longevity when digested, the non-suppression of natural urges,
celibacy, non-violence, and the avoidance of rash acts.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Elixir for Those Desiring Intelligence and Longevity," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||28||
The twenty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the elixir (rasāyana) for the prevention of diseases arising from one's own nature.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
In the beginning, Brahmā and the other gods created the nectar known as Soma;
the ritual procedure for its use, which destroys old age and death, shall now be described.
Indeed, the Blessed One Soma, though being truly one, is divided into twenty-four forms by distinctions of place, name, shape, and potency.
Aṃśumān, Muñjavān, Candramas who has the luster of silver,
Dūrvāsoma, the youngest, and Śvetākṣa who has the brilliance of gold.
Pratānavant, Tālavṛnta, Karavīra, Aṃśavant,
Svayaṃprabha, Mahāsoma, and he who was carried off by Garuḍa.
The Gāyatra, the Traiṣṭubha, the Pāṅkta, the Jāgata, the Śākvara,
as well as the Agniṣṭoma and the Raivata, are designated according to their descriptions.
He who is joined with the three-footed Gāyatrī and is called the Lord of the Stars—
these are declared to be the Somas by the auspicious names mentioned in the Vedas.
For all of these, there is a single rule for worship;
they all possess equal qualities, and their ritual procedure shall now be described.

Therefore, one desiring to consume any one of these *soma* juices, having prepared all the necessary implements and attendants, should have a three-walled pavilion constructed in an auspicious location. Having removed his bodily impurities and restricted his diet, he should, during an auspicious lunar day, *karana*, *muhūrta*, and asterism, take the radiant stalk (*aṃśumat*) that has been brought according to the ritual of the *adhvara* sacrifice, pressed, and offered into the fire. Inside the pavilion, having performed the auspicious rites and recitations for well-being, he should pierce the *soma* bulb with a golden needle and extract the milk into a golden or silver vessel in a measure of one *añjali*.
Then, without tasting it, he should consume it all at once.

Then, having sipped water and placed the remainder in the waters, having composed his self through restraint and discipline, remaining silent, he should dwell within while being attended by his friends.
Having drunk the elixir (rasāyana), one should remain focused on it, pure, and stay in a windless place;
one may sit, stand, or walk, but under no circumstances should one lie down.
Having eaten in the evening and performed the *upaśruta* rite for peace, he should lie down on a bed of *kuśa* grass covered with a black antelope skin while being attended by his friends.

Or, if thirsty, he may drink a small measure of cold water; or, if hungry, milk. Then, having risen in the morning, performed the *upaśruta* rite for peace, and performed the auspicious ceremonies (*kṛtamaṅgala*), he should touch a cow and sit right there.
When the *soma* has been digested, vomiting arises in him.

Then, after he has vomited [the substance] smeared with blood and mixed with worms, one should give him milk that has been boiled and cooled in the evening. Then, on the third day, he passes down worms mixed with the stool.
Freed from those specific impurities such as the acceptance of undesirable gifts and the eating of forbidden food, his body becomes pure.
Then, after he has bathed in the evening, one should give him milk just as before.
One should lay him upon a bed spread with linen cloth; then, on the fourth day, swelling arises in him.
Thereafter, worms emerge from all his limbs.
On that day, he should lie upon the bed while being strewn with dust.

Then, in the evening, he should offer milk as before; in this manner he should proceed on the fifth and sixth days. Only this difference is that he should offer him milk at both times. Then, on the seventh day, having become fleshless and reduced to skin and bone, he breathes only through the intake of Soma.
On that day, having sprinkled him with pleasantly warm milk and having anointed his body with sesame, Madhuka, and sandalwood, one should have him drink milk.

Then, on the eighth day at dawn, having sprinkled him with milk, anointed his limbs with sandalwood paste, and given him milk to drink, one should have him leave his bed of dust and lie upon a bed spread with linen cloth;
thereby his flesh is nourished and his skin is no longer cracked.

His teeth, nails, and body hair fall out. From the ninth day onward, he should be anointed with *aṇu* oil and sprinkled with a decoction of *somavalka*. Then, on the tenth day, one should administer this very same treatment. Thereby his skin attains firmness. One should proceed in this manner during the eleventh and twelfth days. Then, from the thirteenth day onward, there should be sprinkling with a decoction of *somavalka*. One should continue thus until the sixteenth day. Then, on the seventeenth and eighteenth days, his teeth emerge—towering, glossy, with the luster of diamond, beryl, and crystal, even, firm, and enduring.

From that time forward, he should consume milk-gruel made with non-glutinous *śāli* rice until [the number of days] reaches twenty-five; then, one should give him soft *śāli* rice with milk at both meal times.
Thereupon, his nails grow, shining like coral, the *indragopaka* insect, or the rising sun;
they become firm, glossy, endowed with auspicious marks, and his hair likewise grows fine.

The skin shall have the luster of a blue lotus, flax flower, or beryl. After one month, he should have his hair shaved. Having shaved it, he should smear his head with a paste of *uśīra*, sandalwood, and black sesame, or bathe it with milk. Immediately thereafter, after seven nights, hair grows that resembles bees or collyrium—curled, firm, and glossy. Then, after three nights, having gone out from the vicinity of the first dwelling, he should stay for a moment and then re-enter.
Then, for him, oil of *bala* should be applied for the purpose of massage;
barley flour for the purpose of rubbing the body;
and pleasantly warm milk for the purpose of pouring over the body.
A decoction of *ajakarṇa* is for the purpose of rubbing the body;
well-water with *uśīra* is for the purpose of bathing;
and sandalwood is for the purpose of anointment.
His soups and broth preparations should be mixed with the juice of *āmalaka*.
For the purpose of consuming [the medicine], he should take black sesame seeds prepared with milk and *madhuka*.
Thus for ten nights; then, for another ten nights, he should remain in the second stage (*parisara*); thereafter, in the third stage, he should remain for another ten nights, stabilizing himself.
He may occasionally resort to sunlight or fresh air, and then re-enter his dwelling.
He should not look at himself in a mirror or in water because he possesses a handsome form; thereafter, for another ten nights, he should avoid anger and other such passions.
Thus is the classification of their application for all [castes].
Specifically, however, the *soma* plants such as creepers, climbing vines, and shrubs should be consumed by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Their quantity, moreover, is four half-handfuls (*muṣṭi*).

One should press the *aṃśumat* [Soma] in a golden vessel and the *candramas* in a silver one; by consuming those two, one attains eightfold sovereignty and enters the god Īśāna. As for the remaining [Somas], they may be pressed in vessels made of copper, clay, or on a spread red hide; the Soma juices are to be consumed by the three social classes, excluding the Śūdra.
Then, on the full moon day of the fourth month, having honored the Brahmins in a pure place and performed auspicious rites, he should go forth as prescribed.
Having consumed Soma, the lord of herbs,
the discerning man maintains his body in its youthful state for ten thousand years.
Neither fire, nor water, nor poison, nor weapons,
nor even missiles are capable of bringing about the end of his life.
He acquires the strength of a thousand noble elephants that have reached sixty years of age and have flowed [with rut] in many ways.
Whether he wishes to go to the Ocean of Milk, the abode of Śakra, or even to the Northern Kurus,
his movement is unimpeded wherever he desires to go.
Like Kandarpa in beauty and like another moon in splendor,
that one of great luster gladdens the minds of all living beings.
He truly masters all the Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs;
with his resolve unfailing, he moves through the entire world like a god.
All Soma plants indeed have fifteen leaves;
they grow during the bright fortnight and fall away during the dark fortnight.
Then, one leaf of the Soma plant is produced day by day;
on the full moon of the bright fortnight, it possesses fifteen leaves.
Day after day, one leaf withers away;
and at the end of the dark fortnight, the creeper remains entirely alone.
Aṃśumān has the scent of clarified butter; Kandavān has the luster of silver;
Muñjavān has a bulb shaped like a plantain tree and leaves like those of garlic.
Candramas, who has the luster of gold, always moves upon the water;
and there are also Garuḍāhṛtanāman, Śvetākṣa, and Pāṇḍura.
Those two, hanging from the treetops like the sloughed skins of snakes, shone thus;
others likewise appeared as if variegated with diverse circular patterns.
All these Soma plants, however, should be known as having fifteen petals;
they are recorded as possessing milky stalks and various kinds of leaves.
On Himavat, Arbuda, Sahya, Mahendra, and likewise Malaya;
on Śrīparvata, Devagiri, and likewise on Devasaha mountain.
On Mount Pāriyātra and on Vindhya, as well as at Lake Devasunda,
there are great mountains that rise up to the north of the Vitastā.
There, the moon, the best of the Somas, floats as if with joy;
and in its regions, even the sun shines like the Muñjava mountain.
In its vicinity there is also Mount Muñjavat and Mount Aṃśumat;
furthermore, in Kaśmīra, there is a divine lake named Kṣudrakamānasa.
There are the Gāyatra, the Traiṣṭubha, the Pāṅkta, the Jāgata, and the Śākvara;
here there are also other Somas, possessing splendor equal to that of Soma.
Those unfortunate ones who have insulted physicians here—
those most unrighteous men, as well as those who are ungrateful,
those who hate medicine, and likewise those who hate Brahmins— do not see them [the physicians].

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Rejuvenation (Rasāyana) for the Prevention of Diseases by Their Own Nature," in the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsā-sthāna) of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirtieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the elixir (rasāyana) known as Nivṛttasantāpīya.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Just as the deities rejoice in heaven, their afflictions having ceased,
so too do human beings on earth rejoice upon obtaining these medicinal herbs.

Now, indeed, there are seven types of persons who do not employ elixirs (*rasāyana*): namely, one who lacks self-control, the indolent, the poor, the negligent, the addicted, the evildoer, and the one who disregards medicine.
For seven reasons they do not succeed: namely, through ignorance, lack of undertaking, instability of mind, poverty, lack of self-reliance, unrighteousness, and the non-availability of medicine.
Now we shall explain the medicinal herbs: therein are ajagari,
śvetakāpotī, and kṛṣṇakāpotī.
Gonāsī,
Vārāhī, Kanyā.
*chatrā*, *aticchatrā*,
*kareṇuḥ*.
Ajā, cakrakā, and ādityaparṇī.
Brahmasuvarcalā,
Śrāvaṇī, Mahāśrāvaṇī.
Golomī, Ajalomī, Mahāvegavatī.
Thus, eighteen great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadhi) of equal potency to Soma have been explained.
Their therapeutic actions, blessings, and praises are declared in the scripture to be identical to those of Soma.
Of these, when offered into the fire-chamber, one should consume a kuḍava measure of the milk of those that yield milk, all at once.
Of those [plants] that are root-bearing but do not yield milk, three stalks measuring the length of the forefinger are the proper measure for use.
The *śvetakāpotī* should be eaten together with its roots and leaves.

Having cut the *gonasī*, *ajagarī*, and *kṛṣṇakāpotī* into pieces including their nails, one should boil them in milk, strain the liquid, and after it has been sprinkled with clarified butter and offered in sacrifice, consume it all at once.
The *cakraka* plants [should be taken] with milk only once.
*Brahmasuvarcalā* should be consumed for seven nights according to the method for solid foods.
Of the remaining [plants], five *palas* each, boiled in one *āḍhaka* of milk, should be removed when one *prastha* remains, strained, and consumed only once.
The rules for food and conduct have been explained as being like those for *soma*;
the only difference is that fresh butter (*navanīta*) is used for the purpose of anointing. The rest remains the same until the conclusion of the ritual.
And there are verses on this point:

these [practices], when performed in due order, make a man youthful, possessing the prowess of a lion, handsome, eloquent in speech according to the scriptures, and grant him a lifespan of two thousand years.
Wearing armlets, earrings, and a crown, adorned with divine garlands, sandalwood paste, and garments,
he whose resolve is unfailing moves through the sky, which is difficult to traverse due to the clouds.
Wherein birds fly and water-bearing clouds move, there is the movement of one perfected by medicinal herbs; but the movement in the realm of Soma-perfection is supreme.
Now I shall describe the characteristics of the medicinal herbs individually:
that which has variegated brown circles, resembles a serpent, and possesses five leaves.
The Ajagarī should be known by the wise as measuring five aratnis;
it is leafless, has a golden luster, and is two finger-breadths thick at its base.
The Śvetakāpotī is said to be serpent-shaped with red edges;
it has two leaves, grows from a root, is reddish-brown, and has black spots.
One should know the *gonasī* plant to be two *aratnis* in length, shaped like a cow;
it yields milk, is hairy, soft, and its juice is like sugarcane juice.
One should likewise designate the black and pigeon-colored varieties;
the Vārāhī, produced from the bulbous root, possesses the very form of a black serpent.
One should know that Ekapatrā, Mahāvīryā, and Bhinnāñjanasamaprabhā are the two spells,
Chatrā and Aticchatrakā, which destroy Rākṣasas and arise from the root-mantras.
They ward off old age and death, are white and pigeon-colored in appearance,
and possess twelve beautiful petals resembling the feathers of a peacock.
The great medicinal herb named Kanyā is born from a bulb and possesses golden latex;
it is called Kareṇu, and by means of its elephant-like bulb, it yields abundant milk.
The Dviparṇinī has leaves resembling those of the Hastikarṇapalāśa;
its bulb is like a goat's udder, it contains milk, and it has the appearance of a tear.
The great medicinal plant *ajā* is to be known as white, pale like a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon;
it is a small shrub with variegated flowers resembling the *kākādanī*.
One should know the Cakrakāma herb as the warder-off of old age and death;
it possesses a root and five leaves, as tender as fine red silk.
It should be known as Ādityaparṇinī, for it always follows the sun;
shining like gold, it creeps everywhere along the edges of the water.
The goddess Brahmasuvarcalā resembles a lotus pond filled with milk;
its shoots are a cubit in length and its leaves measure two finger-breadths.
With flowers shaped like blue lotuses and fruits resembling collyrium,
the great Śrāvaṇī cow is to be known as golden-hued and full of milk.
Śrāvaṇī is pale in appearance and possesses the characteristics of the great śrāvaṇī;
golomī and ajalomī grow from hairy tubers.
It resembles the haṃsapādī with its detached leaves arising from the root,
or it is identical in all respects to the śaṅkhapuṣpī.
Possessed by a great fever and resembling the sloughed skin of a serpent,
she is born at the end of the rainy season under the name Vegavatī.
The extraction of those medicinal herbs which were proclaimed at the beginning as being seven and serpent-like in form must always be performed with this mantra.
For the sake of auspiciousness, may you indeed be pacified through penance or through spiritual power, for the sake of Mahendra, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, the Brāhmaṇas, and even the cows.
With this mantra, the wise man should consecrate all [the offerings],
excluding those who are faithless, indolent, ungrateful, and performers of evil deeds.
Neither the Soma juices nor those equal to Soma can be obtained;
likewise, the nectar remaining after being drunk by the gods, headed by Brahmā, cannot be found.
It was deposited in the waters possessing the potency of Soma, in Soma himself, the lord of herbs,
as well as in the excellent lake Devasunda and in the great river Sindhu.
Furthermore, the pure Brahmasuvarcalā is seen at the edges of the waters;
likewise, Ādityaparṇinī is to be known [as appearing] when the snow has melted.
The Ajagarī and the Gonasī are always seen there;
and in Kaśmīra is a divine lake named Kṣudrakamānasa.
The Kareṇu, the Kanyā, the Chatrā and Aticchatrakā,
as well as the Golomī, the Ajalomī, and the great Śrāvaṇī.
In the spring, the Kṛṣṇasarpa and the Gonasī are seen after crossing the river Kauśikī to the east of the Sañjayantī.
A region of the earth covered with anthills for three yojanas should be known as *kāpotī*; there, white [spots] on the tops of the anthills are to be recognized.
On Mount Malaya and at Nala-setu, the Vegavatī herb is always present;
one should consume it on the full moon day of Kārtika while fasting.
One should behave here as one would toward Soma; such is the fruit proclaimed.
All medicinal herbs and Soma plants are to be sought on Mount Arbuda.
It was covered with peaks frequented by the gods that pierce the masses of clouds,
and with famous sacred fords (tīrthas) resorted to by perfected seers and deities.
It was adorned everywhere with caves of terrifying form, whose interiors resounded with the roars of lions,
and with various minerals of diverse colors.
In rivers, on mountains, in lakes, as well as in sacred forests and hermitages—
everywhere all [the treasures] must be searched for, for everywhere the earth holds riches.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Elixir for the Cessation of Fever," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The thirty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the medical treatment concerning the administration of oleation (sneha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
This person has unctuousness as his essence;
the vital breaths (prāṇas) consist largely of unctuousness and are maintained by unctuousness.
Indeed, unctuousness is to be employed in drinks, oil enemas, brain-massage, head-enemas, urethral enemas, nasal drops, ear-filling, body massage, and in food.

In that regard, unctuousness (sneha) has been described as having two origins and four varieties, along with the qualities of unctuousness. Among these, cow-derived ghee is the foremost among mobile beings,
while sesame oil is the foremost among immobile beings.

Hereafter, we shall describe the oils of immobile plants according to their specific purposes and their primary effects. Among them, the oils of *tilvaka*, *eraṇḍa*, *kośāmra*, *dantī*, *dravantī*, *saptalā*, *śaṅkhinī*, *palāśa*, *viṣāṇikā*, *gavākṣī*, *kampillaka*, *śampāka*, and *nīlinī* act as purgatives. The oils of *jīmūtaka*, *kuṭaja*, *kṛtavedhana*, *ikṣvāku*, *dhāmārgava*, and *madana* induce emesis.
The oils of *viḍaṅga*, *kharamañjarī*, *madhuśigru*, *sūryavallī*, *pīlu*, *siddhārthaka*, and *jyotiṣmatī* purge the head.
Oils of *karañja*, *pūtīka*, *kṛtamāla*, *mātuluṅga*, *iṅgudī*, and *kirātatiktaka* are employed for malignant ulcers (*duṣṭavraṇa*).
Oils of *tuvaraka*, *kapittha*, *kampillaka*, *bhallātaka*, and *paṭola* are used for major diseases (*mahāvyādhi*).
Oils of *trapusa*, *ervāruka*, *karkāruka*, *tumbī*, and *kūṣmāṇḍa* are used for urinary obstructions (*mūtrasaṅga*).
The oils of *kapotavaṅkā*, *avalguja*, and *harītakī* are for urinary calculi (*aśmarī*) associated with sugar;
the oils of *kusumbha*, mustard, *atasī*, *picumarda*, *atimuktaka*, *bhāṇḍī*, bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*), and *kaṭabhī* are for urinary disorders (*prameha*).
The oils of the fruits of *tāla*, coconut, *panasa*, *moca*, *priyāla*, *bilva*, *madhūka*, *śleṣmātaka*, and *āmra* are for wind (*vāyu*) associated with bile (*pitta*).
The oils of *bibhītaka*, *bhallātaka*, and *piṇḍītaka* are for blackening;
the oils of *śravaṇaka*, *kaṅguka*, and *kaṭuṇṭuka* are for whitening;
and the oils of the heartwood of *sarala*, *pītadāru*, *śiṃśapā*, and *aguru* are for ringworm, leprosy, and skin eruptions.
All oils indeed pacify Vāta;
thus have the qualities of oil been explained in brief.
Henceforth, we shall explain the procedure for the cooking of decoctions (kaṣāya) and medicated fats (sneha).

Regarding this, some say: "One part of bark, leaf, fruit, root, and so forth, with four times that amount of water, boiled down until one-fourth remains—this is the method for preparing a decoction; and having added four times the liquid to six prasṛtas of fat, along with four medicinal boluses each the size of an akṣa—this is the method for cooking a medicated fat. However, this is not correct, because it is not established by authoritative tradition (āgama).
We shall now explain the measurement of the *pala*, *kuḍava*, and so forth. In this system, twelve medium-sized grains of rice (*dhānyamāṣa*) constitute one gold *māṣaka* (*suvarṇamāṣaka*).

Sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*; alternatively, nineteen medium-sized *niṣpāva* beans constitute a *dharaṇa*. Two and a half of those [gold *māṣakas*] make one *karṣa*. From that point upward, increasing by four times each step, the measures of *pala*, *kuḍava*, *prastha*, *āḍhaka*, and *droṇa* are produced.
Furthermore, one *tulā* is one hundred *palas*; twenty of those make one *bhāra*. This is the measure for dry substances; for moist or liquid substances, it is double that amount.

In that regard, having cut into pieces those items such as bark, leaves, fruits, and roots—which are measured in any appropriate quantity and dried in the sun—by cutting them into fragments where they are to be cut, and by breaking them into fine particles where they are to be broken; then, having sprinkled them with eight or sixteen times their weight of water and boiled them in a vessel until one-fourth remains, one should remove [the liquid]. This is the procedure for preparing a decoction (*kaṣāya*).
Having boiled [the herbs] in oil until one-fourth remains, one should remove it; this is the procedure for cooking a decoction in oil. The liquid [used] should be four times the amount of the oil.

The medicinal paste (kalka) should consist of one-fourth the quantity of the oil (sneha). Having combined these together, one should cook them; this is the method for cooking medicated oils (snehapākakalpa).

Alternatively, having added one *tulā* of bark, leaf, fruit, root, and so forth, to one *droṇa* of water, one should boil it down until one-fourth remains and then remove it; this is the method for preparing a decoction (kaṣāyapākakalpa). Then, having added one *pala* of ground medicinal herbs as a paste to one *kuḍava* of oil, along with four times that amount of liquid, one should cook it; this is the method for cooking medicated oils (snehapākakalpa).
And in this matter, where the quantity of oil, medicinal drugs, or water has not been specified by you,
this rule should be adopted; however, where it has been specifically indicated, one should follow that very same measure.
When no liquid is specified for a preparation requiring a liquid, water is understood to be used in all cases;
when neither a paste (kalka) nor a decoction (kvātha) is specifically indicated, one should employ them from that same group (gaṇa).
Hereafter, we shall explain the procedure for the cooking of medicated fats (sneha).
That [cooking] is of three kinds: namely, mild (mṛdu), medium (madhyama), and [intense].

Regarding "sharp" (*khara*): therein, that medicine which consists merely of the separation of oil and medicinal herbs is called "mild" (*mṛdu*). That medicine which is clear and non-sticky, like beeswax, is called "medium" (*madhyama*).
When the medicinal substance is black, slightly faded, clear, and glossy, it is called *khara* (rough); beyond this point, the fat becomes burnt (*dagdhasneha*).
That [burnt fat] should be processed again properly.
In that regard, the *mṛdu* (soft) state is for drinking and food intake.
The medium [dose] is for nasal medication and massage;
however, the coarse [dose] is for enema and ear-filling.
And in this regard, when the sound has ceased and the foam has likewise subsided,
one should declare success upon the attainment of the proper fragrance, color, taste, and other qualities.
In this manner, a skilled physician should recognize [the state of] clarified butter when it has been cooked;
if there is an excessive amount of froth from the oil, one should indicate that the remainder is like clarified butter.

Hereafter, we shall explain the procedure for the internal administration of oleaginous substances (sneha-pāna). Now, for a patient with a light digestive tract who has performed auspicious rites and recitations for well-being, one should administer a dose of either oil or ghee according to his strength to drink at sunrise, when the sun is situated on the peak of the eastern mountain, glowing yellow-red like a mass of molten gold. Immediately after drinking it, he should rinse his mouth with warm water and, wearing sandals, may move about as he pleases.

The drinking of ghee is recommended for those afflicted by dryness, wounds, or poison; for those suffering from disorders of wind (vāta) and bile (pitta); and for those with deficient intelligence, memory, or mindfulness.
Those afflicted by intestinal worms or wind-disorders, those with increased phlegm and fat,
those accustomed to oil, and those desiring firmness of the body should drink oil.
Men who are emaciated by physical exertion, whose semen and blood are depleted,
who suffer from great pain, and whose digestive fire, wind, and vital breaths are powerful, are considered fit for the consumption of muscle fat (vasā).
Those of cruel intent, who endure afflictions, are afflicted by wind, and possess blazing fires—
all of them shall obtain marrow, or clarified butter combined with their own specific medicines.
Ghee alone should be given in the case of Pitta disorders; in Vata disorders, it should be combined with salt;
and in cases of excessive Kapha, it should be combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali.
Having carefully observed the relative proportions of the humors (doṣas) and their combinations,
one should administer treatments through the sixty-three varieties of tastes (rasas), both in their combined and individual forms.
One who is habituated to fats, capable of enduring hardship, and who drinks the fat at a time that is neither too hot nor too cold, should drink it clear;
for drinking it clear is indeed praised.
One should drink oil during the daytime in the cold season and at night in the hot season;
one with a predominance of vāta and pitta should drink it at night, while one with a predominance of vāta and kapha should drink it during the day.
In hot weather, it causes fainting, delirium, and insanity in one with a predominance of wind and bile;
in cold weather, it produces heaviness, loss of appetite, and colic in one afflicted by wind and phlegm.
If thirst should arise in a person who has drunk medicated oil, he should drink warm water;
if it is not thus alleviated, he should vomit the oil using warm water.
One should apply cool ointments to the head and immerse it in cold water;
this should be done at a dosage that can be digested when one-fourth of the day has passed.
That measure, when honored, kindles the digestive fire even when the humors are slight;
it is the measure that would be fully digested by the time half a day has passed.
That [diet] which is aphrodisiac and nourishing is recommended when the humors are moderate;
the dose should be such that it is fully digested when one-fourth of the meal remains.
That dose which is emollient and is honored when the humors are abundant,
should be digested during the latter part of the day.
Having abandoned languor, fainting, and intoxication, that measure should be considered honored;
it is the measure which, being undisturbed, is fully digested within a day and night.
It destroys skin diseases, burning sensations, insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy;
the wise physician should administer the first dose according to the patient's digestive fire.
Indeed, an excessive amount of oil drunk may cause a threat to life;
this occurs for one whose oil does not digest due to improper conduct or because of its great quantity.
If it becomes obstructed and is not digested, one should induce vomiting with warm water;
thereafter, one should administer the unctuous substance again to the person whose digestive tract has become light.
When there is doubt as to whether the unctuous substance has been digested or not, one should drink warm water.
By that, the belching becomes pure and there is an appetite for food;
however, while it is being digested, thirst, burning sensations, giddiness, exhaustion, aversion, and fatigue may arise.
Then, having sprinkled that man whose oil has been digested with warm water,
one should have him drink warm gruel at will, prepared with slightly soaked rice.
Either a broth or a soup, fragrant and devoid of fat,
or one prepared with very little ghee, or a thick gruel (vilepī) is prescribed.
One should drink it for three days, four days, five days, or likewise six days;
after seven nights, the oleaginous substance, when used regularly, becomes habituated to the body.

One should administer [the medicine] along with food to those who are delicate, emaciated, aged, or very young, as well as to those who dislike fats, those afflicted by thirst, and during the hot season.
Pippalī, salt, the four types of fats, and the whey of curd— when these are drunk together, this is indeed called "instant oleation."
A gruel prepared as a soup, fried in meat broth and made unctuous,
when drunk in small quantities, is said to cause immediate oleation.
A gruel prepared with milk and ghee, containing very few grains of rice and served warm while still containing its own fat,
is said to provide immediate oleation when consumed.
Long pepper, salt, ghee, sesame paste, and hog's fat,
when drunk together in a single dose, are said to produce instantaneous oleation.

Having milked a cow into clarified butter mixed with powdered sugar that is contained in a milking vessel, one who is dry (devoid of oiliness) should drink the milk; this is called "immediate oleation" (sadyah-snehana).
A decoction of barley, jujube, and horse-gram combined with long pepper,
along with milk, curd, wine, and ghee as the eighth ingredient— this is the preparation.
This ghee, proven effective when drunk, is the best for providing immediate oleation;
this supreme ghee should be given to a king or those equal to a king.
Those formulations which have been correctly described should be administered to those who are weak, the elderly, those with weak digestion, women, the afflicted, and those with minor ailments.
One suffering from indigestion,
acute fever, weakness, anorexia, obesity, fainting, or intoxication should avoid the drinking of unctuous substances (sneha).
A man who has been afflicted by vomiting, one suffering from thirst, one who is exhausted, one overcome by the fatigue of travel,
one who has been administered an enema, one who has undergone purgation, and one who has vomited— these should not eat.
A man should not drink oil at an improper time or on a cloudy day;
likewise, a woman who has recently given birth should avoid drinking oil at an improper time.
From the drinking of unctuous substances, various diseases arise in these men;
or the diseases reach a state of difficulty, or else they do not succeed at all.
If there remain blood, moisture, and impurities in the uterus,
one should then abandon unctuousness and employ digestive and drying treatments.
After ten nights, one should properly administer unctuous therapy;
[otherwise] the feces will be knotted and dry, and food will be digested only with great difficulty.
The wind causes a burning sensation in the chest and rushes upward from the abdomen;
the person becomes discolored, weak, and parched.

Excessive unctuousness, looseness of the skin and feces, a stimulated digestive fire, softness of the limbs, exhaustion, lightness of the body parts, the perception of oiliness at the lower part of the body,
and likewise a sense of aversion toward further oleation— these are the signs of one who has been properly oleated.
Aversion to food, salivation, burning in the rectum, dysentery,
and excessive discharge of feces are the signs of one who has been excessively oleated.
One should apply oleation to the dry with unctuous substances, and desiccation to the excessively unctuous with śyāmāka grain, koradūṣa grain, food, buttermilk, oil-cake, and parched grain flour.

A person who habitually consumes fats (sneha) becomes one whose internal fire is kindled, whose digestive tract is purified, whose bodily constituents are fresh, and who is endowed with strength and complexion; he possesses firm sense organs, is slow to age, and lives for a hundred years.
For one afflicted by disease, unctuousness is beneficial for kindling the weakened digestive fire;
however, when those two [the fire and the food] are endowed with strength, they cannot be suddenly overcome by the various defects arising from food.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment Concerning the Use of Oleation," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||31||
The thirty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the therapeutic treatment concerning the application of sudation (sveda).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
There are four kinds of sudation, namely: sudation by heat, sudation by steam,
and sudation by poultice.
Regarding the term "liquid sudation" (dravasveda), it includes all varieties of sudation.
In that regard, the heat of an ascetic is produced by means of the palms of the hands, a bronze ball, a skull-bowl, sand, or a cloth;
and for one who is lying down, the heating of the limbs is performed repeatedly with charcoal from the *khadira* tree.
Regarding steam-sudation (*ūṣmasveda*): one should sprinkle with water or acidic substances skull-bones, stones, bricks, or iron balls that have been heated to the color of fire.
With these wrapped in moist lac, one should apply sudation to the affected part of the body.

Alternatively, one should take the steam from a heated jar filled with meat broth, milk, curd, fats, fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), or decoctions of leaves and twigs that alleviate *vāta*, after covering oneself with it.

Alternatively, having joined her mouth to a jar with its opening facing downwards through a side hole, and having inserted a tube shaped like an elephant's trunk into that hole, one should apply fomentation to her.

One should apply sudation to a patient suffering from vāta disorders while he is comfortably seated, well-anointed, and covered with a heavy garment, using a tube shaped like an elephant's trunk; for this method reaches all parts of the body easily and does not distress the person.
A tube three elbows long, bent at three points,
shaped like an elephant’s trunk, made of *kailiñja* reeds, and measuring half a fathom in length, is beneficial for the purpose of inducing perspiration.
Having dug a pit in the ground measuring one man's height,
having burned it with wood from the Khadira tree, and likewise sprinkled it with milk, grain-water, and sour gruel;
Having covered [the patient] with leaf-cuttings while they lie down, one should then apply sudation;
or, as before, one should apply sudation after burning the stone or removing its ash.
As before, having constructed a hut with four doors and sat within it, one should heat him by placing glowing embers at the four internal doors and causing him to sweat.

Alternatively, having properly steamed grains or cooked rice, one should spread them out on a mat of reeds or something similar and, covering a person lying down with them, apply heat; in this manner, one should apply heat using the warmth of dust, cow dung, husks, chaff, or straw.

For *upanāha-sveda*, one should apply a plaster made from the roots of wind-alleviating (*vāta-hara*) plants ground with sour liquids, heavily seasoned with salt, and well-oleated; then, while it is comfortably warm, one should foment the area.

Similarly, one should foment using the pastes of the *kākolyādi* group, the *elādi* group, or the *surasādi* group; or with pastes of sesame, linseed, and mustard; or with *kṛśara*, *pāyasa*, or *utkārikā*; or with *vaiśavāra* or *sālvaṇa* preparations, all wrapped in thin cloth.

As for liquid fomentation (*dravasveda*), one should cause the patient to undergo fomentation by immersing them in a lukewarm cauldron or a wooden tub filled with a decoction of Vāta-alleviating substances.

Likewise, one may immerse them in milk, meat broth, vegetable soup, oil, fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), ghee, muscle fat (*vasā*), or urine. Furthermore, one should sprinkle the patient with these same substances when they are pleasantly warm, as well as with medicinal decoctions (*kaṣāya*).
Among these, dry heat and steam are specifically destroyers of phlegm;
poultice-sudation is a destroyer of wind;
and when either of these is combined with bile, it is liquid sudation.

When the Vāyu is associated with Kapha and Medas, one should induce perspiration by staying in a windless place, exposure to the sun, wearing heavy garments, wrestling, walking on foot, physical exercise, carrying loads, and through anger.
And there are verses on this point:
The fourfold sudation that has been described is applied in two ways—
either over the entire body or on a specific part of the body.
For those embodied beings for whom nasal medication (nasya) and enema (basti) are to be administered,
and for any others who require purification (śodhana), it is held that they should first be subjected to sudation (sveda).
After the foreign body has been extracted, a woman with retained placenta who is free from complications should be fomented;
likewise, a woman who has delivered properly at the right time should be fomented by one who knows [the procedure].
A patient suffering from fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, or urinary calculi should first and then later undergo sudation;
we shall describe the remaining cases in the treatise.
Sudation should not be applied by those skilled in sudation under any circumstances to one who has not been anointed with oil, nor to one whose body is not unctuous;
for it is observed in the world that dry wood, when subjected to the application of heat, quickly goes to pieces.
The doshas, moistened by unctuous substances, situated within the tissues, remaining in their own locations, or lingering in the channels—
when properly treated with sudation, they attain a state of liquefaction and are expelled entirely from the visceral cavity by purificatory therapies.
Properly applied, sudation produces brilliance of the digestive fire, softness of the skin, clarity of the complexion, faith in food, and purity of the bodily channels;
it destroys sleep accompanied by drowsiness and quickly mobilizes stiffened joints.

The excretion of sweat, the alleviation of disease, lightness, a desire for cold, and softness of the patient—these they declare to be the signs of proper sudation; in the case of improper sudation, these very same signs are reversed.
If there is excessive sweating, it causes pain in the joints, a burning sensation, the eruption of blisters, and the provocation of pitta and blood;
it also brings about fainting, giddiness, feverish heat, thirst, and exhaustion. In such a case, one should immediately apply cooling measures.
One suffering from anemia, urinary disorders, hemorrhaging, consumption, emaciation, indigestion, abdominal disease, or poisoning;
one afflicted by thirst or vomiting; a pregnant woman; one who has consumed alcohol; and a person with diarrhea—these individuals should not be subjected to sudation.
Through excessive sweating, their bodies would meet destruction, and their ailments would become incurable.
A weak person and one with indigestion are candidates for sudation if they are both fit for it;
in these cases, the wise physician should employ mild sudations for those diseases treatable by sudation,
as well as when the heart, scrotum, or eyes are involved.
One should administer all types of sudation to a person who has digested his food, in a windless place,
after anointing the body with oil and covering the eyes with cold objects.
And while it is being fomented, one should repeatedly touch the heart with cool substances;
once it has been properly sweated and massaged, the patient should bathe slowly in warm water.
One should feed him when he is well-anointed, his limbs covered, and situated in a sheltered place free from drafts;
the food should be non-obstructive to the channels, and one should instruct him in all the proper rules of conduct.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment Concerning the Application of Fomentation," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of complications resulting from emesis and purgation.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Defects that have diminished should be nourished;
those that are aggravated should be pacified;
and those that have increased should be eliminated.
The established conclusion is that the years must be preserved as equal.
Emesis and purgation are primarily employed for the elimination of the humors (doṣas);
therefore, attend to the procedure for these two as it is being described.

Then, having observed that the patient has been oleated and sweated, that his doshas are no longer obstructed by foods that cause secretions, and thinking, "I shall administer emesis tomorrow," he should feed one who possesses a sharp digestive fire, is strong, has abundant doshas, is afflicted by a major disease, and is accustomed to emetic therapy.
And there is a verse on this point:
"By means of various wholesome foods, the humors of embodied beings are agitated;
then, when the patient has been lubricated and fomented, emesis administered results in proper action."

Then, on the following day, during the morning at the common time, one should administer a dose of any one of the emetic substances—decoction, paste, powder, or oil—and induce vomiting according to the requirements, having observed the specific nature of the patient's digestive tract (*koṣṭha*). One should prescribe emetics that are unwholesome, loathsome, foul-smelling, or unsightly. Emetics with qualities opposite to these are for purgation. In that regard, for those suffering from diseases treatable by emesis who are delicate, emaciated, young, old, or timid, one should have them drink milk, curd, buttermilk, or barley gruel up to the throat.

One should wait for a moment while the patient who has drunk the medicine is being warmed with hands heated by fire; then, one should recognize that the medicine has become loosened by the emergence of perspiration, has moved from its own places, and has entered the stomach.

Then, knowing that nausea has set in, the patient—seated on a stool knee-high and well-supported on the forehead, back, sides, and neck by trusted attendants—should be made to vomit by touching his throat with either a finger, *gandharvahasta* root, or a lotus stalk, until the signs of proper vomiting appear.
And in this regard, the teachers say that excessive salivation, impurity of the heart, and itching are the signs of difficult vomiting;
while an excess of pitta, loss of consciousness, and pain in the heart and throat are the signs of excessive vomiting.
When the pitta has moved forward easily following the kapha, when the heart, throat, and head are purified,
when the body feels light, and when the discharge of kapha has ceased, one should determine that the person has vomited well.
