Having observed that he has properly vomited, one should have him drink whichever of the unctuous, purgative, or soothing medicated smokes is appropriate according to his capacity, and then prescribe the proper regimen of conduct.
And on this point there are verses:
Then, in the afternoon, having sprinkled his body with pure, clean water and warm water,
one should feed him with soups or broths made from horse-gram, mung beans, āḍhakī, or the meat of wild animals.
Cough, throat inflammation, hoarseness of voice, drowsiness, lethargy, foul breath,
afflictions by poison, excessive salivation of phlegm, and disorders of the digestive tract— these never occur for a person who vomits [the phlegm].
Just as flowers, fruits, and sprouts on a tree perish instantly when the tree is cut down,
so too, when phlegm is removed by purification, the disorders born from it come to an end.
One should not administer emesis to those suffering from cataracts, upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), abdominal tumors (gulma), enlargement of the spleen (udaraplīha), worms, or exhaustion;
nor to those who are obese, those with chest wounds, the emaciated, the extremely thin, those afflicted by urinary disorders, or those with purely Vata-related diseases.
One should not administer [emetics] to those suffering from impairment of the voice, those addicted to Vedic study, those afflicted by difficult vomiting,
poor digestion, or thirst, nor to children, those with upward-moving blood (ūrdhvāsrapitta), the hungry, the excessively dry, pregnant women, or those suffering from udāvarta or recent fever.
Through disrespect and contempt, diseases of embodied beings become difficult to cure or even incurable; therefore, these are known as "non-subject-to-treatment" (avāmya).
These individuals— those afflicted by indigestion, those who require emesis, those suffering from poisoning,
and those with excessively aggravated phlegm— should also be treated with water infused with madhuka.

Women, however, [should avoid it] if they suffer from poisoning, emaciation, defects of breast milk, weak digestion, insanity, epilepsy, elephantiasis, tumors, scrotal enlargement, urinary disorders, fever, anorexia, indigestion, diarrhea, heart disease, mental confusion, erysipelas, abscesses, indigestion, salivation, nausea, dyspnea, cough, chronic rhinitis, fetid nose, inflammation of the throat, lips, or mouth, ear discharge, epiglottis, ranula, goiter, or downward hemorrhaging; as well as those afflicted by diseases arising in the seats of *kapha* and other disorders dominated by *kapha*.

Purgation should also be administered to one who has been oleated, sudated, and vomited; for if purgation is given to one who has not vomited, even if the purging is otherwise correct, the phlegm (śleṣman) displaced downward covers the duodenum (grahaṇī),
causing heaviness or producing dysentery (pravāhikā).

Then, thinking "I shall administer a purgative to the patient tomorrow," one should feed him a light meal in the forenoon and have him drink sour fruits with warm water. Then, on the following day, having observed that the patient's phlegm (śleṣman) has subsided and having examined him according to the *Āturopakramaṇīya* chapter, one should give him the appropriate dose of medicine to drink.
In that regard, the digestive tract (koṣṭha) is of three types: mild, cruel, and moderate.
Among these, one with a predominance of bile (pitta) is soft;
he is purged even by milk. One with a predominance of wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman) is hard; he is difficult to purge. One with balanced humors (doṣas) is moderate.
That is common.
In that regard, the measure is mild for a mild [person],
and sharp for a cruel one.
A moderate dose should be administered;
having drunk the medicine and being focused on it, one should be purged while lying near the bed.
Having drunk a purgative, a wise person should not suppress the urges;
he should sleep in a windless place, avoid contact with cold water, and should not strain himself.
And just as in emesis, the expectorated matter, the medicine, phlegm, bile, and wind pass out in succession,
so too in purgation do urine, feces, bile, the medicine, and phlegm pass out.
In this regard, there are the following verses:
When the heart, stomach, and rectum are not purified, and there is burning, itching, and retention of feces and urine, the purgation is not proper.
Fainting, prolapse of the rectum, excessive discharge of phlegm, and the onset of colic are the signs of excessive purgation.
When the morbid humors associated with phlegm have been expelled, when there is lightness at the navel and satisfaction of the mind,
and when the vital air (vāyu) has returned to its natural downward course, one should determine that the person has been properly purged.
One should not administer the thin gruel (peyā) on that day to a patient with weak digestion, one who is not emaciated, or one who has undergone an inadequate purgation;
however, one should give it to a patient who is emaciated, afflicted by thirst, or well-purged—thin, pleasantly warm, and light.
When properly administered, purgation produces clarity of intellect, strength of the sense organs, stability of the bodily constituents, vigor, a bright digestion, and the gradual maturation of age.
Just as for aquatic creatures there occurs destruction when the water is removed,
so too, when pitta is extracted, there occurs the destruction of those afflictions that are of the nature of pitta.

Those with weak digestion, those who have been excessively oleated, children, the elderly, and the obese; those suffering from chest wounds, emaciation, fear, or affliction; the exhausted, the thirsty, those with undigested food, pregnant women, and those whose blood flows downward—[these should not undergo purgation].
Those who have recently consumed alcohol, those suffering from alcoholism, women who have recently given birth,
those who have recently miscarried, those afflicted by foreign bodies, and those who have not been prepared with oleation and other therapies are not fit for purgation.
Men who are unfit for purgation meet their destruction when administered purgatives by the ignorant.

Those who should be purged are those suffering from fever, artificial poison (garā), anorexia, hemorrhoids, tumors, abdominal enlargement, glandular swellings, abscesses, anemia, epilepsy, heart disease, gout (vātarakta), fistula-in-ano, vomiting, diseases of the female genital tract, erysipelas, abdominal tumors, pain in the colon, constipation, choleraic disorders, intestinal torpor (alasaka), urinary retention, leprosy, eruptive skin eruptions, urinary disorders, flatulence, splenic disorders, edema, scrotal enlargement, injuries from weapons, wounds from alkali or fire, malignant ulcers, ophthalmia, cataracts, partial blindness, excessive lacrimation, burning sensations in the head, ears, eyes, nose, mouth, anus, or penis, upward movement of blood (raktapitta), intestinal worms, and those afflicted by other Pitta-originated disorders as well as other diseases characterized by a predominance of Pitta.
Purgation [removes] the morbid humors by means of their liquidity, subtlety, sharpness, heat, and expansiveness;
emesis, however, removes the humor according to its natural tendency, otherwise it would not do so.
A purgative, being digested, goes downward taking the morbid humor (doṣa) with it;
conversely, an emetic, being undigested, moves upward due to the excellence of its qualities.
In one with a soft bowel and a stimulated digestive fire,
an excessively sharp purgative will not properly eliminate the morbid humors (doṣas), as they have been driven out with excessive force.
That medicine which, when drunk in the morning at the time when the previous meal has been digested,
undergoes digestion itself and eliminates the humors (doṣas), is highly praised.

In one who is weak, one should repeatedly eliminate the unstable humors when they are small in quantity; however, when they are abundant, one should pacify them even if they have already been displaced.
One should eliminate the mobile doshas when they have matured, whether the patient is strong or weak;
for mobile doshas, if neglected, will cause a person suffering for a long time.
One should administer purgatives to a patient with weak digestion and a hard bowel, after having kindled the digestive fire with ghee containing alkali and salt,
and rendered the patient unctuous and sudated.
In one who has been lubricated and fomented, the morbid humor (doṣa), forcibly provoked by medicinal drugs,
does not remain hidden within the channels, just as water does not cling to a greased vessel.
One who has already drunk an excessive amount of unctuous substances should not take an unctuous purgative;
for the humors, though displaced from their seats, will again become adherent in the channels.
Those suffering from poisoning, trauma, pustules, swelling, anemia, or erysipelas,
as well as those with skin diseases (kuṣṭha) or urinary disorders (prameha), should be purified without being excessively oleated.
Having first rendered the patient dry, one who is habituated to oleation should again be oleated and then purified;
by this means, the humors removed from him become strength-promoters.
One should first administer a mild medicine to a person who has not previously undergone purification, after which the patient's digestive tract (koṣṭha) has been ascertained;
thereafter, a full purificatory treatment (saṃśodhana) should be performed.
A king should drink medicine that is pleasant, provides visible results, is agreeable to the heart, requires only a small dose, possesses great efficacy, and involves little harm or risk.
He who drinks a purificatory medicine without having practiced oleation and sudation will find his body shattered like dry wood in a fire.

The doshas of a person, having been mobilized by oleation and sudation and induced by unctuous tastes, reside in the gastrointestinal tract (kostha) and can be easily removed by purificatory therapies.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Complications Managed by Emetics and Purgatives," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of complications arising from emesis and purgation.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Emesis and purgation, when administered for the sake of a physician or a patient, may result in fifteen types of complications.
Among these, the downward movement of emetics and the upward movement of purgatives are distinct; common to both, however, are the conditions of residual medicine and the digestion of the medicine.
The state of being free from minor defects;
wind-pain;
lack of application.
Excessive application;
the taking of life; flatulence.
Parikartikā (cutting pain),
parisrāva (diarrhea with mucus), and pravāhikā (tenesmus).
The drawing toward the heart,
the obstruction,
and the seizing of the limbs.

In that case, for one afflicted by hunger, possessing an excessively sharp digestive fire (*atitīkṣṇāgni*), and having a soft bowel (*mṛdukoṣṭha*), the emetic substance remains stagnant or moves downward due to the similarity of its qualities (*guṇasāmānyabhāvāt*). This results in the failure to achieve the desired effect and the provocation of the *doṣas*. One should quickly lubricate such a person with unctuous substances and then induce vomiting again with even stronger emetics.

In one whose stomach (āmāśaya) is impure, whose phlegm (śleṣman) is agitated, or who has undigested food remaining, a purgative that is unpalatable or excessive, when drunk, moves upward. In that case, there is a failure to achieve the desired result and an aggravation of the humors (doṣas). There, having quickly induced vomiting in one whose stomach is impure and whose phlegm is predominant, one should again administer a stronger purgative. However, if the condition is associated with undigested matter (āma), the treatment should be like that for āma itself.
If the medicine is unpalatable, excessively large in dose, or neither palatable nor measured correctly, it will rise upward; in such a case, one should not administer a third dose of the medicine.
Instead, one should purge the patient with linctuses mixed with honey, ghee, and molasses.
A small dose of medicine that is poorly prepared and remains localized—whether intended for the upper or lower route—does not expel the *doṣas*.

In such cases, there occurs thirst, pain in the flanks, vomiting, fainting, breaking pain in the joints, nausea, restlessness, and impurity of eructations. In the case of an upper-route purgative, one should quickly induce vomiting with warm water.

In the case of a lower-route purgative as well, if the medicine has been left residual, the *doṣas* have rushed out excessively, or if the patient is very strong and exhibits signs of inadequate purging, one should likewise induce vomiting.
In one with a cruel digestive tract and an excessively sharp fire, a medicine that is small in dose or deficient in quality undergoes digestion like food.
Consequently, the aggravated doshas, not being expelled at their proper time, cause a confusion of diseases and a loss of strength.
Therefore, one should administer a medicine that is neither small nor mild in dose.

Medicine that is ununctuous, insufficiently processed, or used in small quantity destroys only minor morbid humors (doṣas). In the case of emesis, the residual doṣa causes heaviness, nausea, impurity of the heart, and an increase in the disease. In that situation, one should have the patient drink medicine appropriately and induce a more thorough emesis. In the case of purgation, however, it causes cutting pain in the anus, flatulence, heaviness of the head, non-expulsion of the doṣa, or an increase in the disease. One should treat that patient with oleation and sudation again and induce a more thorough purgation.
If it is firm or characterized by many shifting defects, or if it possesses little quality on the third day.
If a dry medicine is administered by one who has not undergone oleation and sudation, or by one who does not observe celibacy, it provokes the *vāyu*.
Therein, the provoked *vāyu* causes pain in the sides, back, hips, neck, and vital organs (*marman*), as well as fainting, giddiness, intoxication, and loss of consciousness.

This is called *vāta-śūla*. One should treat this by massaging with oil, applying sudation through washing and fomentation, and then administering an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) prepared with *yaṣṭīmadhuka*.

If a person whose body has not been prepared by oleation and sudation drinks medicine that is either too small in quantity or deficient in its qualities, it does not reach [the site of action] above or below; instead, having merely agitated the *doṣas*, it causes a loss of strength along with them.
In that case, flatulence, cardiac oppression, thirst, fainting, and a burning sensation occur.
This is called "insufficiency" (*ayoga*); one should quickly induce emesis with water containing *madana* fruit and salt, or administer purgation with very strong decoctions.
In one who has vomited poorly, the aggravated humors (doṣas), having pervaded the body, produce itching, swelling, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), pustules, fever, aching of the limbs, and pricking pains;
therefore, one should eliminate them entirely with emetic medicine.

In one who has not been lubricated or fomented and has undergone poor purgation, there occurs stiffness and distension of the abdomen below the navel, colic, obstruction of flatus and feces, or the appearance of itching and circular patches (maṇḍala).

Having established him [in the procedure] and re-humidified him, one should purge him with a sharp [purgative]. If the purgation does not proceed sufficiently or if the impure matter remains, one should have him drink warm water to stimulate it and apply fomentation to the sides and abdomen with the heat of the palms.
From that, the morbid humors (doṣas) are set in motion.

When the minor morbid humor has been mobilized and the medicine has been digested, one should further purify the patient—who has many remaining morbid humors, whose body has been prepared by oleation and sudation, and who has been fasting for ten nights or more—on the remainder of the day.
One who is difficult to purge should first be treated with a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana), then oleated again, and subsequently purged.
Women who serve near kings, merchants, and Vedic scholars generally possess a constitution characterized by the suppression of natural urges due to shame, fear, and greed.

Therefore, these individuals are difficult to purge because of their high wind (vāta) content; for this very reason, one should purify them after they have been well-oleated and treated with sudation.
If medicine that is excessively sharp or administered in excess is given to one who is very thirsty and perspiring, or whose digestive tract is extremely soft, it may cause over-action (*atiyoga*).
In the case of excessive emesis (*vamana*), there occurs an excessive discharge of *pitta*, loss of strength, and a powerful aggravation of *vāta*.

One should treat this by anointing the patient with ghee, immersing him in cold water, and administering linctuses mixed with sugar and honey according to the specific requirements. In the case of excessive purgation (*virecana*), there is an excessive discharge of *kapha*, followed later by a discharge containing blood.
In that condition as well, there is a loss of strength and a powerful aggravation of Vāta.

One should sprinkle him with very cold water or have him bathe in it; then, one should induce vomiting with cold rice-water mixed with honey. Furthermore, one should administer a picchā-basti (mucilaginous enema) to him.
One should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) to him with milk and ghee;
one should give him the Priyaṅgvādi group of drugs to drink with rice-water,
and one should feed him either milk or meat broth.
When that very excessive emesis becomes aggravated, one spits or vomits blood.

In that condition, complications such as protrusion of the tongue, retraction of the eyes, twisting of the jaw, thirst, hiccup, fever, and loss of consciousness arise. For this patient, one should administer a churned drink (*mantha*) made with the powder of goat’s blood, sandalwood, *uśīra*, and collyrium, mixed with sugar-water.

Alternatively, one may give a gruel prepared with fruit juices containing ghee, honey, and sugar; or a gruel prepared with the leaf-buds (*śuṅgā*) of the *vaṭa* and other trees, mixed with honey; or a gruel prepared with drugs that bind the stool.
One should feed [the patient] with milk or the broth of wild animals.

One should treat him according to the procedures for excessive hemorrhage (*atisruta-śoṇita*). If the tongue protrudes excessively, one should rub it with a powder of pungent and salty substances, or smear it with sesame and grapes, and then press it back inside.
If it has entered deep within, others should eat sour food in front of him. Once it has retracted, one should press the eyes, which have been anointed with ghee.
One should treat thirst and other such conditions according to their respective remedies;
in the case of one who has lost consciousness, one should cause the sounds of flutes, lutes, and singing to be heard.
In the case of excessive purgation (*virecanātiyoga*), water mixed with froth flows downward, followed by a discharge resembling the wash-water of meat and vital blood (*jīvaśoṇita*).

Thereafter, prolapse of the rectum (*gudaniḥsaraṇa*), tremors, and complications from excessive emesis occur. One should treat that patient according to the protocol for the loss of blood. For one whose rectum has prolapsed, one should anoint the rectum, apply fomentation, and push it back inside, or consult the treatment for minor diseases (*kṣudraroga*).
In the event of trembling, one should perform the treatment prescribed for wind-disease (vātavyādhi).
For protrusion of the tongue and similar conditions, the remedy has already been stated.

Or, if the vital blood flows excessively, one should administer an enema with very cold milk boiled with the fruits of *kāśmarī*, *badarī*, and *dūrvā*, along with *uśīra*, mixed with the scum of ghee (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*) and collyrium (*añjana*).

One should treat him with enemas (basti) prepared from a decoction of the *nyagrodha* group of drugs mixed with sugarcane juice, ghee, and blood. In cases of spitting blood, one should apply the therapeutic measures prescribed for *raktapitta* and bloody diarrhea. Furthermore, one should administer the *nyagrodha* group of drugs in his drinks and food.
To determine whether it is vital blood (*jīva-śoṇita*) or bile-blood (*rakta-pitta*), one should throw a cotton wick or a cloth into it.

If the cloth retains its color even after being washed with warm water, it should be understood as vital blood; furthermore, one should give it to a dog mixed with cooked rice or with parched grain flour (*saktu*).
If the dog consumes it, it should be understood as vital blood; otherwise, it is bile-blood.

If a medicine that is not warm or ununctuous is drunk by one who has residual food, who possesses many doshas, whose digestive tract is dry, and whose constitution is dominated by vāta, it causes flatulence (ādhmāna).

In that condition, there occurs the retention of flatus, urine, and feces, distension of the abdomen, breaking pain in the sides, pricking pain in the anus and bladder, and an aversion to food. This is called ādhmāna; it should be treated with fomentation, non-obstructive enemas, digestive stimulants, and medicinal enemas.

In a person who is emaciated, has an extremely soft bowel, weak digestive fire, or is dry, if an excessively sharp, hot, salty, or very dry medicine is drunk, it vitiates the *pitta* and *vāyu*, resulting in cutting pain (*parikartikā*). In that condition, there occurs a cutting sensation with burning in the anus, navel, penis, and the head of the bladder, along with obstruction of flatus, distension by wind, and aversion to food; for this, a slimy enema (*picchābasti*) prepared with *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, black sesame paste, honey, and ghee is indicated.

Once he has been sprinkled with cold water and has eaten his meal with milk, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using either the scum of ghee or oil prepared with licorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka).
In a person with a cruel digestive tract (*krūrakoṣṭha*) and excessively abundant *doṣas*, mild medicine administered causes the *doṣas* to become agitated but does not eliminate them completely.
Consequently, those *doṣas* produce a morbid discharge (*parisrāva*). In that condition, there occur weakness, abdominal distension, loss of appetite, and lassitude of the limbs.
In this condition, bile and phlegm, accompanied by pain, flow out from the ears;
this is called *parisrāva*. One should administer an enema (*āsthāpana*) using decoctions of *ajakarṇa*, *dhava*, *tiniśa*, *palāśa*, and *balā*, mixed with honey.
Once the morbid humors have subsided and the patient is lubricated, one should perform purification again.
When medicine is administered to one who is either excessively dry or excessively unctuous, it fails to reach its destination and excites the flatus and feces due to the suppression of natural urges.

In that case, dysentery (pravāhikā) occurs; there, the patient frequently strains and passes stool that is accompanied by wind, burning, and pain, and is heavy, slimy, white, black, or blood-stained, along with phlegm. This condition should be treated according to the procedure for excessive discharge (parisrāva).
If one, out of ignorance, suppresses the force of a medicine that has already begun to act by moving upward or downward, the humors (doṣas) cause it to settle in the heart.

There, being excessively tormented by pains due to the affliction of the primary vital points (marmans), the patient grinds his teeth, rolls his eyes upward, licks his tongue, faints, and becomes unconscious.
Fools abandon such a case; however, one should massage him and apply a fomentation using steamed grain.
One should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) with oil prepared from *yaṣṭimadhuka*.
One should also prescribe a sharp head-purgative (*śirovirecana*) for him.
Then, one should induce emesis with rice-water mixed with *yaṣṭimadhuka*.
And one should treat him with enemas (basti) according to the increase of the specific dosha.

However, if one whose humors have become aggravated moves upward or downward and resorts to a cool room, water, wind, or other such things, his humors—becoming obstructed in the channels and reaching a state of stagnation—cause the retention of flatus, urine, and feces, and thus become bound up. In that case, flatulence, burning sensations, fever, and intense pains arise; having quickly induced vomiting for him, one should perform the appropriate treatment at the right time. In the case of downward movement, however, one should administer a purgative consisting of substances that eliminate humors from the lower part of the body, mixed with rock salt, sour liquids, and urine.

One should administer non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) according to the specific dosha involved, as well as the dietary regimen according to the dosha; however, in cases of double-sided hemorrhage (ubhayatobhāga), one should treat the specific complications according to their respective natures.
Whatever cutting pain occurs in the rectum during purgation corresponds to the irritation of the throat during emesis;
whatever downward discharge occurs corresponds to the excessive secretion of phlegm in the upper part of the body; and whatever dysentery occurs below corresponds to dry eructations above.
And there is a verse on this point:
"These fifteen complications that have been described according to their true nature are known to arise from excessive,
improper, or deficient administration of purgation."
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Complications Arising from Emetics and Purgatives," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||34||
The thirty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment concerning the dimensions and classifications of the enema nozzle (netra) and the enema bag (basti).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Regarding that, the teachers state that among the therapeutic actions such as oleation (sneha) and others, the enema therapy (basti-karma) is the most preeminent.
Why? Because the enema performs many functions; indeed, through the combination of various substances, the enema here effects the purification, pacification, and binding of the doshas.
It also acts as an aphrodisiac for one whose semen is diminished.
It nourishes the emaciated;
it reduces the corpulent;
it delights the eyes.
It removes wrinkles and graying hair;
it stabilizes youth.
When properly administered, enema therapy brings about the nourishment of the body, improvement of complexion, strength, health, and an increase in lifespan.

Likewise, it is employed for the purpose of [treating] fever, diarrhea, darkness of vision, catarrh, diseases of the head, adhimantha, facial paralysis, convulsions, hemiplegia, diseases of single or all limbs, flatulence, abdominal diseases, vaginal pain, gravel-like colic, scrotal enlargement, venereal sores, constipation, dysuria, abdominal tumors, gout, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and the loss of semen, menses, or breast milk, as well as conditions such as stiffness of the heart, jaw, or neck, urinary stones, obstructed labor, and so forth.
And there is a verse on this point:
Enema is recommended for vāta, pitta, kapha, and rakta;
in cases of dual or triple humoral combination (saṃsarga and sannipāta), enema alone is always beneficial.

In that regard, one should prepare enema-nozzles (*netra*) for those aged one year, eight years, and sixteen years, measuring six, eight, and ten finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) respectively; their circumferences should match those of the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger; they should have a *karṇikā* (a ridge or stopper) placed at the tip at one and a half, two, and two and a half finger-breadths respectively; their openings should be like the tubes of the wings of a heron, a hawk, and a peacock, with channels the size of a green gram, a black gram, and a pea respectively.
Into these nozzles, the quantity of the enema substance (*āsthāpanadravya*) should be administered in two, four, and eight *prasṛta* measures, measured by the patient's own hand.
In the intervals between the rainy seasons, one should indeed increase the dosage for the eyes and the bladder,
having carefully considered the age, strength, and physical constitution [of the patient].
Beyond twenty-five [finger-breadths], it is twelve finger-breadths long; at the base, its circumference is that of the belly of a thumb,
and at the tip, its circumference is that of the belly of a little finger.
At the front, it has a pericarp situated three finger-breadths [in from the edge],
with an opening equal in width to the channel of a vulture's wing-feather,
and a cavity the size of a jujube stone.
Some say the opening should be the size of a moist *kalāya* (pea); all [nostrils] at the base have two flanges (*karṇikā*) for the purpose of securing the enema bag.
The prescribed quantity of the non-unctuous enema substance (*āsthāpanadravya*) is twelve *prasṛta*s.
For those over seventy years of age, the length of the nozzle (*netra*) is the same as this.
But the measure of the substance is like that of one sixteen years of age.
A mild enema should be administered, especially for children and the elderly;
for if a sharp enema is administered to them, it may indeed destroy their strength and life.

The nozzle for an ulcer should be eight finger-breadths long, with a channel capable of admitting a mung bean; having examined the ulcer, one should apply appropriate oleaginous substances and decoctions.

In that regard, the nozzles may be made of gold, silver, copper, iron, bronze, ivory, horn, gem, or the heartwood of trees; they should be smooth, firm, shaped like a cow's tail, straight, and provided with a globular tip.
And the enemas should be made from the intestines of cows, buffaloes, boars, goats, or sheep; they should be unscarred, soft, not too thick, firm, and of the proper dimensions.
In the absence of a tube, a catheter made of reed, bamboo, or bone is beneficial;
in the absence of a bladder, a thin skin or a thick woven cloth is suitable.
The enema bag, however, should be free from any coating, clean, well-wiped,
neither too soft nor too rigid nor too thin, and repeatedly rubbed with oil.
Having fixed it at the base of the eye with its opening turned downward,
and having bound it with heated iron, one should cauterize it at the edge of the cornea.
Then, having turned the bladder inside out and tied it securely, one should store it away;
and with that [bladder], one should administer both the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) and the oil according to the prescribed rules.
In that regard, enema (basti) is of two types: the purgative (nairūhika) and the oleaginous (snaihika). [The former is] the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana).
*Nirūha* is synonymous with *basti*; its variant form is *mādhutailika*; its synonym is *yāpana*;
its other names are *yuktaratha* and *siddhabasti*.
It is called *nirūha* because it eliminates morbid humors (*doṣa*) or because it dries up the body's secretions;
it is called *āsthāpana* because it stabilizes youth or because it stabilizes the lifespan.
Furthermore, we shall explain the procedure for *mādhutailika* in the section on the treatment of the therapeutic application of *nirūha*.
The classification of the unctuous enema (*snehabasti*) prescribed according to its specific measures and qualities is the *anuvāsana*.
It is called *anuvāsana* because, even when administered daily, it does not cause harm, or because it is given every day.
Its further classification includes the *mātrābasti*, which is reduced by half or half again of the standard dose and is not subject to the usual dietary restrictions (*aparihārya*).
Nirūha is considered to be purificatory, scarifying, oleaginous, and nourishing. Once the channels have been properly purified by nirūha, the unctuous substance (sneha) flows through them,
just as water flows through channels from which all impurities have been removed.
It removes all defects and sustains the life of the body;
therefore, an oil enema is prescribed for one whose body has been purified.

In this regard, those afflicted by insanity, fear, grief, thirst, anorexia, indigestion, hemorrhoids, anemia, vertigo, intoxication, fainting, vomiting, leprosy, urinary disorders, abdominal enlargement, obesity, dyspnea, cough, dryness of the throat, or swelling; as well as those suffering from chest wounds, those who are emaciated, women pregnant for three or four months, the weak, those with weak digestion, those unable to endure [the procedure], and children or the elderly—provided they do not suffer from wind-diseases (vātaroga)—should not be given an unctuous enema (anuvāsya) nor should they be administered a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpayitavya).

A person suffering from abdominal enlargement, urinary disorders, skin diseases, or obesity must certainly be treated with non-unctuous enemas (sthāpana); they should by no means be given unctuous enemas (anuvāsana).
From the administration of these enemas, there may arise incurability of the disorders;
even when incurable, there would generally be a sinking or exhaustion of the limbs.
When properly administered, the enema remains in these locations: in the colon, the pelvis, and everywhere below the navel.
The potency of the enema follows the body through the channels from the colon,
just as the potency of water poured at the root of a tree ascends to the tree itself.
And that enema, whether administered alone or containing waste matter, quickly returns;
however, its potency is led away by the downward-moving vital airs (apāna) and the others.
By means of its potency, the enema draws out the humors from the feet to the head,
just as the sun, situated in the sky above the earth, draws up the juices from the ground while remaining in the digestive tract.
Having stirred up the accumulations situated in the waist, back, and belly with vigor, he—
when properly applied— extracts the humors (doṣas) by pulling them out from their roots.
Since Vāyu is the master over the provocation of the three doṣas,
therefore, when it is excessively increased, it strikes down the body.
No treatment other than enema can withstand the force of the wind,
just as the shore withstands the force of the ocean whose waters are lashed by the wind.
A enema, when properly administered, brings about the nourishment of the body, improvement of complexion, strength, health, and an increase in lifespan.
Hereafter we shall describe complications. Among them, the eye may be displaced or turned away.
Pressed against the side; excessively raised;
drooping.
"Thrown askance"— these are the six faults of the formal vow (*praṇidhāna*): it is too thick, it is coarse,
it is bent.
Subtly divided;
having a pericarp both near and far;
with extremely fine apertures.
Excessively long,
excessively short,
and having uneven edges— these are the eleven defects of the eyelids; [the twelfth is] excessive thickness.
Smallness; having holes;
being spread out.
"Improper binding" refers to the five defects of enema administration: excessive pressure,
insufficient pressure,
repeated pressing, [delayed withdrawal], and [premature withdrawal].
"Transgression of time" refers to four faults of affliction: immaturity,
deficiency,
and excess.
Excessive coldness;
excessive heat; excessive sharpness.
Excessive softness;
excessive oiliness; excessive dryness.

Excessive thickness, excessive liquidity—these are the eleven defects of the substance (dravya); administering [the medicine] while the patient is with head down, head up, face downward, face upward, body contracted, or lying on the right side—these are the seven defects of the bed (śayyā). Thus, these forty-four complications are caused by the physician.
The fifteen signs of a patient will be described in the chapter on the treatment of complications in the patient; however,
oleation (sneha), when obstructed by eight causes, does not return [from its site], including obstruction by the three doṣas or being overcome by food.
Mixed with impurities;
deeply penetrated;
of that which has not been steamed.
It is not hot;
it occurs in one who has eaten little;
and "little" refers to the causes pertaining to the physician and the patient.
But there is non-application of both;
flatulence;
and cutting pain.
Diarrhea;
dysentery;
cardiac displacement.
Seizing the limbs, excessive application,
and taking life— these are the nine complications caused by physicians.
And here it is said: "In brief, seventy-six complications have been proclaimed;
I shall describe their diagnosis and their successful treatment immediately thereafter."
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Measurement and Classification of the Netra and Basti," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||35||
The thirty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of complications arising from the application of enemas and the nozzle.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
If the eyes are moved or likewise rolled back, there may be a wound or pain in the rectum; in that case, the treatments for fresh wounds should be applied.
If the eyes are raised too high or droop down, there will be pain in the anus;
in this case as well, a Pitta-subduing procedure should be performed, along with irrigation using oleaginous substances.
If the nozzle is directed obliquely or pressed against the sides,
the enema does not enter properly due to the obstruction of the mouth; therefore,
one who understands correctly should ensure the nozzle is held straight.
If the nozzle is too thick or rough, it may cause abrasion and pain in the anus due to friction;
its treatment is as previously described.
If the nozzle is too close to the neck of the bladder, or if the eyes are split, or if it is of minute size, the enema will be ineffective;
therefore, one should avoid these defects.
When the rectum is reddened and protrudes due to the pressure on the vital point (marman) of the anus, blood flows;
in this case as well, the treatment consists of pitta-alleviating measures and slimy enemas (picchila-basti).
In the case of a short or minute nozzle, there is distress and the enema fails as before;
returning from that state, it may cause diseases born of the obstruction of the enema.
In the case of a long and large stream, it should be understood as being like an excessive compression;
likewise, when the bladder is distended and thick, it is like the defect of a poorly tied [vesica].
When the leather is small, the quantity [of contents] is small, or the qualities of the substance are considered few;
likewise, when it is poorly bound or split by insects, it should be understood as being like a "split eye" (bhinnanetra).
If the enema is administered with excessive force, it enters the stomach;
driven by the vital wind (vāyu), it then emerges through the nostrils or the mouth.
In that case, one should quickly apply pressure to the throat and shaking [of the head],
as well as strong head-purgatives and body-purgatives, and cold affusions.
If the enema is pressed too slowly, it reaches the colon (pakvādhāna) but does not achieve its purpose; therefore, one should press it with proper force.
Through excessive compression, the internal air becomes further oppressed;
by that, flatulence and severe pains arise, for which appropriate enemas (basti) should be administered.
Due to the lapse of time, affliction and disease increase;
in that case, one should further administer an enema that destroys the strength of the disease.
Indeed, unprocessed oleation causes swelling of the penis and scrotum;
in that case, a purificatory enema and purgation are beneficial.
Both enemas that are deficient in dose are considered ineffective;
likewise, those that are excessive in dose cause abdominal distension, exhaustion, and diarrhea.
The two [types of] excessively hot and sharp [purgatives] cause fainting, burning sensations, diarrhea, and pitta;
both the mild and the cold [types] cause the obstruction of wind (vāta) and flatulence.
In those cases involving debilitated patients and others, the therapeutic procedure should be antagonistic [to the disease];
however, one should administer a thick non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) along with an application of paste to the anus and the bladder.
Alternatively, it may cause dysentery;
therefore, one should administer a thin enema when the disease is thick and a thick enema when the disease is thin.
An excessively unctuous enema is said to cause extreme dullness, while a dry one causes stiffness and flatulence;
therefore, one should administer a dry enema when there is excessive unctuousness, and an unctuous one when there is dryness.
Know that the defects are similar to those of excessive compression;
furthermore, in the case of an upward-turned head (ucchīrṣaka), the enema causes swelling and difficulty in urination.
In that case, an uttara-basti (urethral/vaginal enema) administered after proper sudation is beneficial and brings comfort;
however, if administered to one lying prone, the enema follows a wrong path and does not reach the colon.
In this condition, the vāyu afflicts the heart, the rectum, and the abdominal cavity;
furthermore, when the passage is obstructed in one lying supine, the enema does not reach the interior.
The wind within becomes agitated due to the agitation and confusion of the eyes;
likewise, when the body is contracted, it is likewise applied to both thighs.
If a person is afflicted by wind (vāta), the enema does not return properly to the body;
however, when administered to one who is standing, the enema quickly returns downward.
Furthermore, it does not satisfy the internal disposition; therefore, it is indeed not beneficial.
Moreover, an enema administered [in this manner] does not reach the entire colon.
Since the [tube] follows the left side of the patient who is reclining on his right side,
the administration of enemas in the inverted (nyubja) and other such postures is not at all recommended.
Subsequently, one should treat any agitation of the wind (vāyu) there according to its specific requirements;
the complications arising from the oil enema (snehabasti), however, will be described in the section on their treatment.
Now I shall describe the complications arising from improper application, along with their treatments:
a non-warm, under-medicinal, or deficient enema, when administered, does not reach its destination.
They declare that state, characterized by obstruction, flatulence, and colic, to be "ayoga" (insufficiency of administration);
in that case, a sharp enema and a sharp purgative are beneficial.
Furthermore, an enema that is administered when food has not been fully digested, or when there is an excess of morbid humors (doṣas),
or when it is excessively large for one who has overeaten, or when it is only lukewarm, is ineffective.
Indeed, food that is not hot, salty, or unctuous, or if it is taken in excessive measure,
as well as food containing too much fecal matter, will quickly cause flatulence in a person.
In cases where there is extremely severe pain in the heart, waist, sides, and back,
a very sharp enema (basti) is beneficial, as is an oil enema (anuvāsana).
An enema that is excessively sharp, overly salty, or dry, when administered,
provokes the Vayu along with Pitta and causes cutting pain (parikartikā).
In that condition, one should not cut the region of the navel, bladder, or anus;
for such a person, a slimy enema (picchābasti) and an unctuous enema prepared with sweet drugs are beneficial.
Excessively sour, salty, or pungent food leads to diarrhea;
in such a case, weakness and exhaustion of the limbs arise in the embodied being.
From that, pitta may flow out and produce a burning sensation in the rectum;
in such a case, a picchā-basti (mucilaginous enema) and an enema with milk and ghee are beneficial.
From a sharp nirūha enema followed by an anuvāsana enema, there may arise pravāhikā (diarrhea),
accompanied by burning and colic, wherein phlegm and blood are passed with great difficulty.
In that condition, a feather-cleansing enema (picchābasti) is beneficial, as is a meal with milk;
likewise, an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with oil prepared with ghee and drugs of the sweet group is recommended.

An excessively sharp Nirūha enema, or an Anuvāsana enema administered during the presence of Vāta, causes the [enema fluid] to flow upward toward the heart; likewise, an Anuvāsana enema given when Vāta is predominant may cause it to do so.
There, various pains arise from the humors (doṣas), along with intoxication, fainting, and heaviness of the limbs;
in such a case, one should administer a purifying enema (basti) that removes all the humors.
In one who is rough, has an excess of vāta, or has slept in an improper position,
an enema that is too dry, mild, or contains insufficient medicinal ingredients will cause stiffness of the limbs.
In that [condition], lassitude of the limbs, stiffness, yawning, cramps, tremors, and pain in the joints are observed;
for it, sudation, oleation, and enemas are prescribed.
An enema that is too hot, too sharp, or given in too large a quantity, or one administered to someone who has sweated excessively,
or to someone with very few morbid humors (doṣas), leads to over-action (atiyoga).
The symptoms of excessive purgation (virecanātiyoga) are the same as those [of excessive enema];
in that case, the application of a cold picchā-basti is beneficial.
Where, due to excessive administration, there is a loss of vital essence (jīva) like that of one who has been purged,
a beneficial slimy enema (picchābasti) containing blood should be administered into the water.
Those nine complications which have been described in relation to the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) should also be recognized here by the skilled as occurring in unctuous enemas (snehabasti).
Thus have all the complications been described, along with their symptoms and treatments;
the physician must act in such a way that these indeed do not occur.

After vomiting, purgation occurs after one fortnight; thereafter, a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) should be administered. One who has received a non-unctuous enema may receive an unctuous enema (anuvāsya) immediately, whereas one who has been purged should wait seven nights.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Complications Arising from the Application of the Netra-basti," in the Cikitsā-sthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the medical treatment of oil enemas (anuvāsana) and urethral/vaginal enemas (uttara-basti).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
When seven nights have passed since the purgation, once the patient has regained strength,
has been provided with food, and has received an unctuous enema (anuvāsana), a second unctuous enema should be properly administered.
The dosages for non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) that have been prescribed according to age should be reduced by one-quarter when administered as unctuous enemas (snehabasti) for embodied beings.
One should administer an enema to a man who has already voided flatus, feces, and urine; for if the oil is administered while these are obstructed, it will not enter within.
An unctuous enema (snehavasti) should be administered only to a person whose body is purified;
for only then does it bestow the potency of the unctuous substance and permeate the entire body.
Henceforth, I shall describe in due order the oils used for internal drinking,
oil enemas, and nasal administration, which destroy many diseases.
With śaṭī, puṣkara, kṛṣṇāhvā, madana, and amaradāru;
with śatāhvā, kuṣṭha, yaṣṭyāhvā, vacā, bilva, and hutāśana.
Having cooked oil with twice the amount of well-ground [medicinal paste], four times the amount of water, and twice the amount of milk,
it should be administered as an enema to facilitate the downward movement of obstructed flatus.
It destroys hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract, flatulence, and irregular fever,
as well as Vata diseases located in the waist, thighs, back, and abdomen.
With vacā, puṣkara, kuṣṭha, elā, madana, amaradāru, and saindhava; with the two types of kākolī, yaṣṭimadhu, the two types of medā, and narendrā;
With pāṭhā, ajīvajīvaka, bhārgī, candana, kaṭophala, saralā, aguru,
bilva, ambu, vājigandhā, agni, and vṛddhi;
One should cook oil with vidanga, āragvadha, śyāmā, trivṛt, māgadhikā, and ṛddhi, ground together, along with milk and the decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla).
It is prescribed and recommended for those suffering from abdominal tumors, constipation, loss of digestive fire, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, urinary retention,
and wind-related diseases, when administered according to the procedure for anuvasana enema.
With citraka, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, dantī, bilva, vacā, and miṣa; with saralā, aṃśumatī, rāsnā, nīlinī, and caturaṅgula.
With cavya, ajamoda, kākolī, the two types of medā, suradruma, jīvaka, ṛṣabha, varṣābhū, vaśagandhā, and śatāhvā;
One should cook oil with milk along with reṇukā, aśvagandhā, mañjiṣṭhā, śaṭī, puṣkara, and taskara; this destroys diseases caused by vāta.

When administered quickly into the bladder, it is recommended for those suffering from sciatica, lameness, spinal deformity, urinary obstruction, and upward movement of urine, as well as for those with diminished strength and digestive fire.
With bhūtīka, eraṇḍa, varṣābhū, rāsnā, vṛṣaka,
rohiṣa, daśamūla, sahā, bhārgī, ṣaḍgranthā, and amaradāru;
With balā, nāgabalā, mūrvā, vājigandhā, the two types of amṛtā,
sahācara, varī, viśvā, kākanāsā, and vidārī;
Oil boiled with a decoction of barley, black gram, linseed, *kola*, and horse gram,
with the addition of the *jīvanīya* group of drugs, and four times the quantity of milk,
cures disorders located in the calves, thighs, sacrum, sides, shoulders, arms, neck, and head.
When practiced through the application of enemas, it destroys disorders of vāta.
One lives [long] by means of atibalā, medā, the two types of kākolī,
jīvaka, ṛṣabha, ativiṣā, kṛṣṇā, kākanāsā, vacā, and amarī.
With rāsnā, madana, yaṣṭyāhva, saralā, bhīru, candana, svayaṅguptā, śaṭī, śṛṅgī, kalasī, and the two types of sārivā;
Oil cooked with flour and eight times its quantity of milk should be administered as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana);
it increases semen, digestive fire, and strength.
It is nourishing, subdues Vata and Pitta, and is supreme in removing abdominal tumors (gulma) and distension;
when administered as a nasal drop or a drink, it cures diseases of the regions above the clavicle.
With madhuka, uśīra, kāśmarya, kaṭukā, utpala, and candana;
with śyāmā, padmaka, jīmūta, indrayava, ativiṣā, and ambu.
One should cook clarified butter with one-fourth part oil and eight parts milk, combined with a decoction of the Nyagrodhādi group; when administered as an enema, it is highly beneficial.
It destroys burning sensations, menorrhagia, erysipelas, vātaśoṇita, abscesses, and diseases such as pitta-rakta fever; it overcomes all ailments produced by pitta.
With lotus stalks, blue lotuses, lotus roots, the two types of sārivā, keśara, the two types of sandalwood, bhūnimba, lotus seeds, and kaseruka;
Oil and ghee cooked with *paṭola*, *kaṭukā*, *raktā*, *gundrā*, *parpaṭa*, and *vāsaka*, ground together with the juice of *tṛṇamūla*, [are used for anointment].
Combined with double the amount of milk and employed for enema therapy,
or used as nasal drops, massage oil, or a drink, it destroys many diseases caused by pitta.
With triphalā, ativiṣā, mūrvā, trivṛt, citraka,
vāsaka, nimba, āragvadha, ṣaṭgranthā, saptaparṇa, and the two types of niśā;
Oil cooked with equal parts of guḍūcī, indrasurā, kṛṣṇā, kuṣṭha, sarṣapa, and nāgara, and saturated with the juice of the surasādi group [of herbs], [is beneficial].
When administered as a drink, anointment, gargle, nasal drop, or enema,
it overcomes diseases caused by kapha, such as obesity, lassitude, and itching.
With pāṭhā, ajamodā, śārṅgeṣṭā, the two types of pippalī,
nāgara, sarala, aguru, kālīya, bhārgī, cavya, and amaradruma;
Castor oil, or sesame oil cooked with these— namely, long pepper, cardamom, yellow myrobalan, katukarohiṇī, śaṭī, pippalīmūla, and kaṭphala— is likewise effective.
Administered as an enema with a double portion of decoction made from the roots of *vallī* and *kaṇṭaka*,
it destroys all diseases caused by *kapha*.
With viḍaṅga, uśīra, saindhava salt, śaṭī, puṣkaramūla,
citraka, kaṭphala, ativiṣā, bhārgī, vacā, kuṣṭha, and surāhva;
With medā, madana, yaṣṭyāhva, śyāmā, nicula, and nāgara; with śatāhvā, nīlinī, rāsnā, kalasī, and vṛṣareṇu.
One should prepare oil— either castor oil or the oil of *muṣkaka* and other such plants— saturated with the juices of *bilva*, *ajamoda*, *kṛṣṇāhvā*, *dantī*, *cavya*, and *narādhipa*.

Through the administration of unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), it quickly destroys splenic enlargement, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), blood disorders, abdominal tumors (gulma), flatulence (ānāha), diseases caused by kapha,
urinary disorders (prameha), gravel (śarkarā), and hemorrhoids (arśas).
Even if it is impure, if it is excessively afflicted by wind alone,
one should administer an enema at all times of day and night.

For one who is dry and has an excess of Vāta, after administering two or even three unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) and knowing that the body has become lubricated, one should subsequently administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha).
Even if it is not ununctuous, if it is excessively afflicted by wind alone, the wise physician should treat it with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) that are highly enriched with fats.
Then, once it has been properly established, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) for disorders of Vāta and the other humors using oils of Bilva, Yaṣṭīmadhu, and Madanaphala, respectively.

One should not administer an enema at night, for the aggravation of the humors (doṣas) occurs during the night; moreover, the oil-enema, being endowed with its potency, may cause flatulence, heaviness, and fever.
When the humors are situated in their respective locations during the day, when the digestive fire is endowed with the essence of food,
and when the channels of the body have their openings clearly open, the unctuousness and vital energy (ojas) circulate throughout.
An oil enema (anuvāsana) should be administered at night and during warm weather to a man who has an excess of pitta, diminished kapha, dryness, or is afflicted by diseases of vāta.
Since diseases such as burning sensations and others may arise during the day due to heat or an excess of bile (pitta), the physician should administer [the treatment] at dusk.
In winter and spring, during the day in summer, and at the end of the rainy season and autumn,
one desiring to eliminate the doshas mentioned as being aggravated by drinking should administer oleation at the close of day.
At any time of day or night,
when there is severe pain and the food has been digested, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) to a patient with a predominance of Vāta.
One should never administer an unctuous substance to one who has not eaten;
because of the emptiness of the stomach due to its purity, the oil would rise upward.
One should always administer an oil enema after the patient has been fed while their hands are still moist;
for if unctuous therapy is applied when food is improperly digested, it will cause fever.
One should not administer an oil enema after feeding a patient very unctuous food;
for fat applied in two ways may produce intoxication or fainting.
For food that is dry causes one who has eaten it to lose strength and complexion;
therefore, after feeding a person with food mixed with oil, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
Therefore, having observed the specific disease, one should feed the patient a diet consisting of broth, milk, or meat-juice—
reduced by one-quarter from the standard amount— and then administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
Then, having been well-anointed with oil, gently fomented with warm water,
fed according to the scriptures, and made to walk about, the patient should be prepared for the non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
After discharging feces and urine, one should administer an unctuous enema (sneha-basti);
however, the procedure for the application of a decoction enema (nirūha) will be explained hereafter.
Then, with affection directed [toward the object], lying on one's back, there may be a hundred utterances;
likewise, with all limbs extended, the vital energy (vīrya) flows forth.
One should strike him gently on the palms three times each;
then one should strike him on the buttocks, and thereafter lift him from the bed three times.
Having thus prepared the enema, one who is free from excessive exertion and moderate in speech should lie down at will on a well-spread bed, devoted to his prescribed regimen.
Combined with powdered rock salt and *śatāhvā*, it should be administered lukewarm; thus it comes out quickly and easily.
If an oil enema (anuvāsana) administered once returns immediately,
it is due to excessive heat, excessive sharpness, or being oppressed by the vital wind (vāyu).
If a dose is too large, or if it is heavy due to containing medicinal substances, another smaller dose should be administered; for [the medicine] does not adhere or remain if it is excessively oily.
An enema deficient in oil causes the retention of flatus, feces, and urine;
whereas an excessive enema causes burning, exhaustion, tenesmus, and pain.
He whose oil, along with flatus and feces,
returns quickly without burning or heat, has been properly administered an unctuous enema.
Then, in the evening, once the food has been digested and the unctuous substance has returned [to its natural state],
one should feed light food at will, provided the person's digestive fire is kindled.
In the morning, warm water prepared with coriander and ginger should be given;
by that, his digestive fire is kindled and a desire for food arises.
In the procedures for oil enemas (snehabasti), the wise have prescribed this method;
by this method, one should administer six, seven, eight, or even nine applications.
Enema treatments should be administered to them, with a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) given in between;
however, once the first enema has been administered, it lubricates the bladder and the groin.
The second [type], when correctly administered, conquers the wind located in the head;
the third, when employed, generates strength and a healthy complexion.
The fourth [unctuous substance] should lubricate the lymph-chyle (rasa), while the fifth lubricates the blood;
likewise, the sixth should lubricate the flesh (māṃsa), and the seventh the fat (medas).
The eighth and ninth [days] are for the bone and marrow respectively;
thus, one should properly treat the defects residing in the semen by doubling the duration.
He who administers eighteen sets of eighteen enemas according to the prescribed method and the rules for the period of post-treatment recovery;
Possessing the strength of an elephant and equal to the speed of a horse, with the splendor of an immortal,
free from sin, a retainer of sacred learning, such a man shall live for a thousand years.
One should not habitually employ either the unctuous enema (snehabasti) or the decoction enema (nirūha) exclusively;
for from the unctuous enema arise the destruction of the digestive fire and the aggravation of humors, while from the decoction enema arises the danger of wind (pavana).
Therefore, one who has undergone purgation should receive an oil enema, and one who has received an oil enema should undergo purgation;
in this way, there will be no provocation of pitta or kapha, nor any danger from vāta.
For one who is dry and has an excess of wind, the physician should administer an unctuous enema day after day;
for others, however, he should do so every third day, out of fear of injury to the digestive fire.
For those who are dry, a small amount of unctuousness administered over a long period is not harmful;
likewise, for those who are already unctuous, a small dose of a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) is recommended.
Hereafter, I shall describe the complications arising from oil enemas (snehabasti).
When the powerful doshas, such as vata and the others, are present in the digestive tract (kostha), [the following occur].
Then, that weak potency, having overcome the various types of oleaginous substances, produces complications; and yet, that oleation does not cease.
In that case, when the unctuous substance is overcome by vāta, there occurs astringency of the mouth,
yawning, various pains of vāta, tremors, and irregular fever.
When the unctuous substance (sneha) is overcome by pitta, there occurs a pungent taste in the mouth,
along with burning sensation, thirst, fever, perspiration, and yellowness of the eyes, urine, and limbs.
When the unctuous substance is overcome by phlegm (kapha), there occurs excessive salivation,
a sweet taste in the mouth, heaviness, vomiting, labored breathing, cold fever, and loss of appetite.
In that case, if the unctuous substance (sneha) is overcome by the doshas, one should administer an enema (basti) and employ those remedies which pacify the respective doshas.
When, due to overeating, the unctuousness does not reach [the lower parts] because it is overwhelmed by food, then the stomach becomes heavy, there is colic, and there is no movement of the wind.
Heartache, a bad taste in the mouth, labored breathing, fainting, vertigo, and loss of appetite [occur];
in that condition, at the conclusion of fasting therapy, a digestive-stimulant regimen is prescribed.
When the unrefined oil, mixed with impurities, no longer moves [through the channels],
then bodily exhaustion, flatulence, dyspnea, and colic arise.
In the case of heaviness of the colon (pakvāśaya), one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) prepared with sharp drugs,
as well as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) likewise processed with sharp medicinal agents.
In one who is pure, there is the appearance of oiliness when oiliness has long since vanished;
there is a coating upon the limbs and a sinking of all the sense faculties.
The mouth has a greasy odor, and there is cough, dyspnea, and anorexia;
in such cases, where the patient feels as if excessively oppressed, the successful treatment consists of non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana).
If unrefined and impure oil is administered in a small quantity that is cold and mild, it does not reach its destination; consequently, the patient passes stool only slowly.
When there is obstruction, heaviness, flatulence, and colic localized in the colon (pakvāśaya),
an asthāpana enema, followed by an anuvāsana enema, should be administered immediately.
For one who has eaten little, the oil given will be small in quantity and weak in quality;
it does not reach [the joints], yet it causes exhaustion, nausea, and intense distaste.
In that case as well, an āsthāpana enema with a purifying (śodhanīya) formulation should be administered; likewise, an anvāsana enema with a purifying unctuous (sneha) substance is recommended.
Even if the oil returns after a day and night, it does not cause harm;
moreover, it produces the benefits of an enema, though once digested, its efficacy becomes slight.
If an oil enema (snehabasti) that has not been expelled causes no distress—
whether it is entirely retained, insufficient, or obstructed by dryness— it should be overlooked by the wise physician.
If the oil does not return within a day and night, one should eliminate it with purificatory therapies;
if the oil from an unctuous enema does not return, no further oil should be administered.
Thus have all the complications of the urethral enema (uttara-basti), along with their symptoms and treatments, been described. Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the uttara-basti.
The nozzle should be fourteen finger-breadths long, measured by the patient's own fingers;
its tip should be like the stalk-end of a mālatī flower, with an opening large enough for a mustard seed to pass through.
The maximum dose of medicated oil is declared here to be one *prakuñca*;
for those below twenty-five years of age, one should administer a dose determined by one's own discretion.
It has a well-settled pericarp in the center of women's [vagina], measuring four finger-breadths in width;
it is ten finger-breadths long and shaped like a mudga bean, with an opening for the passage of urine.
Those who truly know it maintain that [the length] should indeed be equal to the span of the penis;
one should insert [the instrument] four finger-breadths into their birth canal.
In the urinary tract of girls, however, it should be two finger-breadths long, while for others it should be one finger-breadth;
the procedure for these shall be explained according to the rule as follows.
In this case, one *prasṛta* of oil—measured by the hollow of one's own fingers—should be administered as the maximum dose; any amount less than that is determined according to one's discretion.
The bladder of a sheep, a pig, or even that of a goat is highly recommended;
in their absence, one should employ the throat-skin of birds.
In its absence, a foot of leather from a water-skin, or even softer than that, [should be used].
Then, having lubricated the patient with oil, fomented him, and loosened his bowels—
Having drunk barley-gruel mixed with ghee and milk according to his strength,
he sat down evenly upon a cushioned seat that reached up to his knees.
Then, having placed the man with his head and bladder-base well-anointed with warm oil in an even position, one should stimulate his penis.
Having first searched with a probe, one should then very gradually insert the eye-spoon,
lubricated with ghee, to a depth of six finger-breadths.
Some desire the application of the enema to be equal in length to the distance from the penis to the navel;
then one should slowly press the bladder and gradually withdraw the nozzle.
Then, in the afternoon, once the patient's appetite has returned,
the wise physician should feed them a measured portion with milk, or with vegetable soup, or with meat broth.
By this procedure, one should administer three or even four enemas;
for a woman, the wise physician should administer them while she lies on her back with her knees raised.
One should press the vagina correctly and apply it with gentle pressure;
one should insert it toward the opening of the vagina using a nozzle with three ridges.
For the purpose of purifying the uterus, the quantity of the decoction should be double that of the unctuous substance;
for a woman, it should be one prasṛta, while for a man it should be two prasṛtas.
In the case of a woman other than a maiden, the physician should likewise apply the measure of the bladder to the enema known as the *uttara-basti* (urethral/vaginal douche) until it returns.
One should further administer an enema combined with purifying groups of drugs,
or one should insert into the rectum a suppository composed of purifying substances.
Or the wise physician should insert the probe into the opening of the enema tube,
or he should press below the navel with an upward-directed fist using force.
One should prepare suppositories with the leaves of *āragvadha* and the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍī*,
ground with cow's urine and mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*).
Having divided mung beans, cardamom, and mustard seeds according to the patient's age,
one should insert them with a probe into the bladder for the purpose of inducing its emptying.
Or it may be prepared with house-soot, bṛhatī, pippalī fruits, and rock salt,
ground together with sour gruel, cow’s urine, wine, and dry ginger.
Having observed the successful completion of the unctuous enema (anuvāsana),
one should administer the procedure with cold water of licorice (madhuka) mixed with sugar and honey.
When the bladder is thus being burned, the wise physician should administer an enema with a decoction of milk-tree barks and with cold milk.
It treats vitiated semen and blood in women,
the excessive flow of menses and its suppression, severe urinary obstructions and increased urinary disorders, as well as gynecological diseases and their complications.
The superior enema (uttara-vasti) destroys seminal discharge, gravel, urinary stones, and pain in the bladder, groin, and penis;
it also cures other dreadful diseases arising from the bladder, as well as various types of urinary disorders (meha).
The signs of correct administration, complications,
and the procedure for the enema known as *uttara-basti* are the same as those for the oil enema (*sneha-basti*).
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Anuvasana and Uttara Basti," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the medical treatment regarding the procedure for non-unctuous enemas (nirūha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

Then, once the patient has undergone the preparatory oil enema (*anuvasana*), one should administer the non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*). Having ensured that the patient’s body is well-anointed and fomented, and that the urges to evacuate have been released, one should have him lie on his left side at midday in a clean room sheltered from the wind, upon a long bed with a firm base, with the pelvic region elevated and without a pillow. He should lie with his right thigh flexed and the other extended, being cheerful, having digested his food, restrained in speech, and with his body well-positioned. Then, placing the nozzle over his left foot, one should press the bulbous part (*karṇikā*) upward with the thumb and toes of the other (right) foot.
Having contracted half the opening of the bladder with the little finger and the ring finger of the left hand,
and having opened the other half by means of the middle finger, the index finger, and the thumb,
one should pour the medicinal substance into the bladder.

Having grasped the medicinal substance with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger of the right hand— ensuring it is not poured over, not stretched out, not bubbly, not constricted, not blown upon, and is adjacent to the medicine—
one should then hold it from above with the other [hand] and pour [the liquid] down with the right hand.
Then, having wrapped it with thread around the edge of the medicine two or three times, one should tie it.

Then, having grasped the enema bag with the right hand palm upwards, holding the nozzle with the middle finger and index finger of the left hand while closing the opening of the nozzle with the thumb;

and having taken the nozzle, whose tip has been smeared with ghee and which itself is smeared with ghee, one should administer it, saying: "Place the nozzle along the spinal column, level, facing upward, and reaching to the ear."
Having placed the enema bag in the left hand, one should squeeze it with the right;
with a single squeezing motion, neither too fast nor too slow.
Then, having removed the nozzle, one should wait for thirty mātrās from the time of squeezing and tell the patient, "Rise.
Then, for the sake of the enema's return, one should have the patient sit in a squatting posture (utkuṭuka).
The time for the return of the nirūha enema is one muhūrta.
An expert in enema therapy should administer the enema according to this procedure,
whether a second, a third, or a fourth time, as required by the circumstances.
Once the signs of proper absorption have been fully established, one should withhold the enema;
especially for those who are delicate, a mild procedure alone is beneficial.
One may indeed employ a mild procedure, but one must never employ an excessive one;
for he whose bladder is small, whose urges are weak, and whose waste and wind are diminished [should be treated thus].
That [condition] should be known as "ill-settled" (durnirūḍha), characterized by pain from urination, loss of appetite, and lassitude;
it possesses all those very symptoms previously mentioned by me regarding excessive purging.
These very [stages] should be understood by the wise even when they have become firmly established,
as the feces, bile, phlegm, and wind pass through them in succession.
When lightness arises, one should declare it well-established;
once it is well-established, one should then feed the person after he has bathed.
One should feed a patient afflicted by pitta, śleṣman, or anila with milk, vegetable soups, or meat broths respectively;
or, in all cases, one should feed them with the meat-broths of wild animals that do not provoke the humors.
Whether it be reduced by one-third, or by half, or even merely a little less—
Mātreya, this reduction of food is prescribed according to the severity of the digestive fire's impairment.
Immediately after that, one should administer an unctuous enema (snehabasti) according to the specific requirements;
[the signs of success are] solitude, mental contentment, unctuousness, and the subduing of the disease.
Regarding the signs of the correct administration of both non-unctuous and unctuous enemas:
on that very day, a powerful fear of the wind (vāta) is considered to exist for the patient.
On that day, rice with meat broth (rasaudana) is recommended, as well as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana);
thereafter, one should consider the strength of the digestive fire and the activity of the wind (pavana).
Once the abdominal cavity has been supported by food, an oil enema (snehabasti) is prescribed;
however, if the decoction enema (nirūha) does not emerge within a muhūrta, one should expel it with purificatory measures.
The wise physician should administer strong non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) combined with alkali, urine,
and sour substances for a Nirūha that has remained for a long time due to being obstructed by deranged Vāyu.
It may induce colic, distress, fever, flatulence, or even death;
therefore, it is the established rule that an asthāpana enema should not be administered to one who has eaten.
Or it may cause cholera, or even a most dreadful vomiting, or it may aggravate all the humors; therefore, one should not give [food] to one who is not eating.
When the food has been digested, the humors (doṣas) that have become manifest in a man's stomach depart completely and easily,
provided they are not oppressed by further eating.
When food has been scattered by the administration of an enema, the digestive fire runs away;
therefore, an enema should be administered by the wise physician to one who has fasted.
Having understood the sequential stages as well, one should administer the non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa);
for when the waste matter has been extracted, the strength of the humors (doṣas) is no longer present.
Milk products, sours, urines, fats, decoctions, meat juices,
as well as salts, fruits, honey, dill, mustard, and sweet flag;
Cardamom, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), rāsnā, sarala, and devadāru;
turmeric, madhuka, asafoetida, and kuṣṭha—these are the purifying agents.
Kaṭukā, sugar, musta, uśīra, candana, śaṭī, mañjiṣṭhā, madana, caṇḍā, trāyamāṇā, and rasāñjana.
The pulp of the bilva fruit, yavānī, phalinī, śakrajā, barley, kākolī,
kṣīrakākolī, and both jīvaka and ṛṣabhaka.
Likewise, Medā, Mahāmedā, Ṛddhi, Vṛddhi, and Madhūlikā—

When the patient is in a healthy state, there are four parts of the decoction and the fifth part is of the oil;
when vāta is provoked, the fourth part is used; when pitta is provoked, the sixth part; and when kapha is provoked, the eighth part.
In all these cases, one-eighth part of the medicinal pastes (kalka) should be used;
furthermore, honey, urine, fruit, milk, sour liquid, and meat-broth [are to be added in equal proportions].
The wise man should determine this through reasoning; such is the formulation for a Nirūha enema.

By the best of physicians, the excellent preparation of the enema (basti) is described through the proper combination of paste, oil/fat, and decoction; its administration is performed according to the correct method.
Having first given one akṣa of rock salt and two prasṛtas of honey,
one should stir it with the palm of the hand in a vessel, gradually adding the oil in the same manner.
After it has been thoroughly ground, one should then add the paste of the fruit;
thereafter, one should add the appropriate medicinal pastes, finely ground, in their respective proportions.
One should grind it in another deep vessel with a pestle,
or as one deems best, so that it is neither too thick nor too thin, but uniform.
Having observed the state of the humors (doṣas) regarding the tastes— bitter, sweet, sour,
and salty— one should administer five well-strained handfuls (prasṛtas) of decoctions therein.
Hereafter, we shall describe the twelve *prasṛta* formulations.
Having first given one *akṣa* of rock salt (*saindhava*) and two *prasṛta* of honey,
one should then churn it and add three *prasṛta* of oil or fat (*sneha*).
Then, when the oil has become unified, one should add one *prasṛti* of paste;
once it has thickened, one should add a decoction measuring four *prasṛtis*.
And at the end, one should add two prasṛtas of that powder;
thus prepared, the enema (basti) shall consist of twelve prasṛtas.
Indeed, this measurement has been declared for the maximum dose;
in cases of reduction, the physician should likewise decrease it by one *prasṛti*.
This formulation of non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), beginning with rock salt and ending with liquids, has been thus described according to age by the best of physicians who desire success.
Hereafter, the enemas (bastis) will be explained in their respective divisions; when administered according to the specific dosha, they destroy various kinds of diseases.
With śampāka, urubūka, varṣābhū, vājigandhā, and niśācchada;
and with the five roots (pañcamūlī), balā, rāsnā, guḍūcī, and suradāru.
These [drugs] should be boiled in one-pala portions each, combined with eight parts of madana fruit,
along with the pastes (kalkas) of māgadhikā, ambuda, hapuṣā, misi, and saindhava.
One should administer a lukewarm non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) prepared with vatsāhvaya, priyaṅgu, ugrā, yaṣṭyāhvaya, and rasāñjana, processed with honey and other appropriate ingredients.
It cures pain in the back, thighs, and sacrum, as well as urinary calculi, constipation, and retention of feces, urine, and flatus;
it destroys malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and wind-disorders, and it bestows blood, muscle, and strength.
With one pala each of guḍūcī, triphalā, rāsnā, daśamūla, and balā boiled together,
[one should mix] finely ground priyaṅgu, ghanasāra, and saindhava salt.
With *śatapuṣpā*, *vacā*, *kṛṣṇā*, *yavānī*, *kuṣṭha*, and *bilva*—
each weighing one *akṣa*— together with jaggery and half a *pala* of *madana*.
Having thoroughly stirred together honey, oil, ghee, milk, sour gruel, fermented rice-water,
and whey with urine, one should administer this as an excellent non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana).
It increases luster, complexion, strength, enthusiasm, vitality, digestive fire, and life-force;
it destroys all diseases caused by wind (vāta) and is the supreme means for maintaining youthfulness.
