With the five roots beginning with *kuśa*, *abda*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *utpala*, and *vāsaka*;
with *sārivā*, *uśīra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *rāsnā*, *reṇukā*, and *parūṣaka*.
With these substances properly boiled in water and then ground into a paste— namely, śṛṅgāṭaka, ātmaguptā, ibha, kesara, aguru, and candana— along with the pālikas...
With vidārī, misī, mañjiṣṭhā, śyāmā, indrayava, and saindhava salt;
with madana fruit, padmaka, and yaṣṭimadhu—these should be saturated with honey, milk, and ghee.
A cold non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana), administered with liquids that are devoid of sourness,
overcomes burning sensations, menorrhagia, hemorrhagic disorders, pitta-type abdominal tumors, and fevers.
With rodhra, candana, mañjiṣṭhā, rāsnā, anantā, balā, and ardhī;
with sārivā, vṛṣa, kāśmarya, medā, madhuka, and padmaka.
A decoction is prepared from three karṣas each of the roots of sthirā and other such grasses,
along with jīvaka, the two types of kākolī, ṛddhi, madhuka, and utpala, which have been ground into a paste.
With prapauṇḍarīka, jīvantī, medā, reṇu,
parūṣaka, abhīru, misi, sindhūttha, vatsaka, uśīra, and padmaka;
An enema that is very cold, administered with liquids containing kaseru and sugar, saturated with ghee, honey, and milk, and excluding substances that are sharp or sour; |||
It destroys abdominal tumors, menorrhagia, heart disease, anemia, and irregular fevers;
it also cures hemorrhagic disorders and diarrhea caused by pitta, as well as all diseases produced by pitta.
With bhadra, nimba, kulattha, arka, kośātakī, amṛtā, amara,
sārivā, bṛhatī, pāṭhā, mūrvā, āragvadha, and vatsaka;
A decoction and a paste should be prepared with vacā, madana, and mustard seeds;
with rock salt, amarakuṣṭha, elā, pippalī, bilva, and ginger.

For those suffering from jaundice, anemia, and urinary disorders, an asthapana enema should be administered immediately using a combination of pungent oil, honey, alkali, urine, oil, and sour substances.
For those who are corpulent, those who maintain no sacred fires, those afflicted by phlegm diseases or aversion to food,
and those suffering from goiter, throat-obstruction, exhaustion, elephantiasis, or abdominal enlargements;
With the ten roots (daśamūlī), turmeric (niśā), bilva, paṭola, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and amarā boiled together, along with a paste (kalka) of mustā, rock salt (saindhava), and devadāru;
One should properly administer a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) with pāṭhā, māgadhikā, and indrāhvā, saturated with oil, alkali, and honey, combined with urine, sour liquids, and fruit juices.
For those afflicted by phlegm, anemia, disease, lethargy, urinary disorders, or wind-related ailments;
for those suffering from undigested matter (āma), flatulence, apacī, phlegmatic tumors (gulma), or parasitic infections.
With vṛṣa, aśmabheda, varṣābhū, dhānya, gandharvahastaka,
daśamūla, balā, mūrvā, yava, kola, and the leaves of niśā;
With one pala each of *kulattha*, *bilva*, and *bhūnimba* boiled together as a decoction,
along with the pastes (*kalka*) of *madana*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, *amara*, and *sarṣapa*.
With pippalī root, rock salt, yavānī, miśi,
and vatsaka, saturated with honey, sugarcane juice, milk, cow urine, ghee, oil, and meat broth.
For those suffering from multiple combined diseases, an enema (āsthāpana) should be administered quickly;
it cures sciatica (gṛdhrasī), gravel-like stones (śarkarā), prostate enlargement (aṣṭhīlā), muscle-tendon pain (tūnī), and abdominal tumors (gulma).
With rāsnā, āragvadha, varṣābhū, kaṭukā, uśīra, vārida, trāyamāṇā,
amṛtā, raktā, pañcamūlī, and bibhītaka;
The decoction is made with the roots of *sabalā* and *pālikā*, while the paste (*kalka*) consists of *madana*,
*yaṣṭīmadhu*, *misi*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *phalinī*, and *indrayava*.
This enema, prepared with rasāñjana, juice, honey, grapes, and sauvīra,
and administered lukewarm, increases muscle mass, semen, strength, and ojas.
It is a promoter of longevity and digestive fire, and it quickly destroys these ailments:
abdominal tumors, menorrhagia, erysipelas, dysuria, chest wounds, and consumption.

It cures irregular fever, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), vātakuṇḍalī, stiffness of the knees, calves, head, and bladder, as well as upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and various types of wind disorders.
It cures disorders of wind and blood, urinary gravel, seminal concretions, colic in the abdomen, abdominal enlargements, and loss of appetite;
as well as internal hemorrhaging, pitta, kapha, insanity, urinary disorders, flatulence, and cardiac obstructions.
Decoctions of wind-alleviating herbs, combined with rock salt and trivṛt,
along with sour substances, should be administered as enemas when the vāyu is provoked, being pleasantly warm in temperature.
Enemas prepared from decoctions of the nyagrodhādi group combined with the kākolyādi group,
along with ghee and sugar, should be administered when pitta is predominant.
Decoctions of āragvadha and other such drugs, combined with pippalī and others,
along with honey and urine, should be administered as enemas when kapha is provoked.
Enemas that are very cold, combined with sugar, sugarcane juice, milk, and ghee,
and enriched with a decoction of milk-exuding trees (kṣīravṛkṣa), are beneficial for blood disorders.
Decoctions of purifying substances, combined with their pastes, fats, and rock salt,
and stirred with a churning rod, are known as purifying enemas (śodhana-vasti).
Enemas consisting of a decoction of triphalā combined with cow’s urine, honey, and alkali,
and containing a paste of the ūṣakādi group as an additive, are known as scraping (lekhanā) enemas.
Decoctions of nourishing substances combined with pastes of sweet drugs,
along with ghee and meat broth, are known as nourishing enemas (bṛṃhaṇa-basti).
Decoctions of sparrow eggs and *uccaṭā*, combined with milk, ghee, and sugar,
and with the addition of the seeds of *ātmaguptā*, are known to be aphrodisiacs for men.
The sprouts of *badarī*, *airāvatī*, *śelu*, *śālmalī*, and *dhanvana*,
boiled in milk and mixed with honey and ghee, are known as "slimy" (*picchila*).
In cases of slimy discharges from the bladder, fresh blood from a boar, a buffalo, a sheep, a cat, a deer, a cock, or a goat should be administered.
Enemas consisting of decoctions of the priyaṅgvādi group combined with the ambaṣṭhādi group,
along with honey and ghee, are known as astringent enemas (grāhi-basti).
In these very formulations,
the proven unctuous substances (snehas) may be administered individually or, alternatively, combined together as unctuous enemas (snehabasti) in the correct manner.
For women who have been purified by the hundred-fold decoction of *vandhyā*,
enemas should be administered in due order using *balā*-oil and *traivṛta*.
One should administer a sharp enema to a person of superior temperament,
a medium one to a person of medium temperament, and indeed a mild one to the opposite type.
Thus, one who understands disorders should administer enemas after carefully examining the time, the strength, the humor (doṣa), the disorder, and the potency of the enema substances.
A wise physician should first administer an enema that causes excitation, then one that eliminates the morbid humors (doṣas), and finally one that provides pacification.
Castor seed, licorice, long pepper, rock salt,
sweet flag, and the paste of hapuṣā fruit are known as a bladder-enema that induces distension.
A enema consisting of śatāhvā, madhuka, seeds of kuṭaja, and its fruit,
along with sour gruel (kāñjika) and cow's urine, is known to remove the bodily humors (doṣas).
A decoction enema (basti) containing priyaṅgu, madhuka, mustā,
and rasāñjana, along with milk, is highly recommended as the supreme pacifier of the doṣas.
[It is suitable] for kings, for those equal to them, as well as for very great persons;
for women, for the delicate, and even for children and the elderly.
For the purpose of eliminating the humors (doṣas) and for the increase of strength and complexion,
I shall briefly explain the procedure known as Mādhutailika.
In this matter, no restriction is prescribed regarding vehicles, women, food, or drink;
for an abundant fruit is seen, and there is also an absence of calamities.
Therefore, one who desires the procedure of non-unctuous enema (nirūha) should employ it with ease;
this should be administered by the wise practitioner whenever he so desires.
Honey and oil should be equal in quantity, along with a decoction of castor root;
half a pala of śatapuṣpā and half of that amount of rock salt [should be added].
Combined with one part of fruit and stirred with a ladle,
this preparation known as *mādhutailika* should be administered by the physician lukewarm.
Vacā-madhuka oil, a decoction with meat broth and rock salt,
combined with long pepper and madana fruit, is known as the Yuktaratha enema.
A decoction enema (basti) consisting of suradāru, excellent rāsnā, śatapuṣpā, vacā, honey,
asafoetida, and rock salt is known to eliminate the doṣas.
A decoction of the five roots (pañcamūlī), oil, Māgadhikā,
honey, Śatāhvā, and rock salt— this enema (basti) should be administered.
A decoction of barley, jujube, and horse-gram, combined with Pippali, honey, rock salt, and Yashtimadhu,
is known as the Siddha-basti.
Mustā, pāṭhā, amṛtā, tiktā, balā, rāsnā, punarnavā, mañjiṣṭhā,
āragvadha, uśīra, trāyamāṇā, and gokṣura.
One should boil eight madana fruits along with the five roots (pañcamūla) and pālikā measures in one āḍhaka of water until reduced to one-fourth; this decoction should then be boiled again.
Having added half an āḍhaka of milk and strained it thoroughly until no milk remains,
one should then add meat broth from wild animals, honey, and ghee in equal proportions.
An enema prepared with one karṣa each of śatāhvā, phalinī, yaṣṭī,
vatsaka, and rasāñjana, mixed with rock salt (saindhava), should be administered as a paste.
It cures disorders of wind and blood, urinary disorders, edema, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and urinary retention; it destroys erysipelas, fever, diarrhea, and internal hemorrhaging.
The Mustādi enema is considered a king among palliative treatments; it is strengthening, life-sustaining, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and a destroyer of colic.

Having examined the medicine and the disorder with his intellect, the knower of disorders and the expert in the scriptures may, by means of this fundamental principle, prepare even hundreds of enemas.
One should not administer it during indigestion and should avoid sleeping during the day;
all other aspects of diet and conduct may be followed as desired.
Because honey and oil are primarily administered [in this enema],
it is called the "mādhutailika" (honey-and-oil) enema by physicians.
Since he was not forbidden even when the chariots were yoked and the elephants and horses were prepared, he is therefore remembered as Yuktaratha (the one who mounted the chariot).
Since it brings about the success of strength, nourishment, complexion, and even the cure of a hundred diseases,
it is therefore considered a perfected enema (siddha-basti).
For those who are happy, have few afflictions, are always of a gentle disposition,
and possess a soft digestive tract, preparations made with honey and oil (mādhutailika) are prescribed.
Due to its mildness, the absence of foot-massage, the incomplete administration of the prescribed regimen,
and the application of a single enema, there is no restriction regarding the Siddha-basti.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of the Sequence of Non-unctuous Enemas (Nirūha)," in the Section on Therapeutics of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The thirty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of complications in patients.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
The digestive fire of an embodied being becomes weak after drinking oleaginous substances, after vomiting, after purging, after bloodletting, and after receiving a non-unctuous enema.
He is extinguished by fires that are exceedingly heavy when they are applied,
just as a small fire is quenched when covered by many great fuels.
And he grows by consuming even small and light foods,
like a fire kindled by tiny and sparse pieces of wood.
The rule for the quantity of food is always prescribed according to the measure of one's eliminated humors;
and in this regard, there are three measures: a prastha, half an āḍhaka, and an āḍhaka.
In that regard, the lowest dose is one *prastha*, while the remaining two—medium and superior—are two *prasthas* each;
when the liquid has been strained, a gruel made with very few grains of rice should be administered.
When two half-āḍhakas have been consumed, and three āḍhakas have passed,
one should then give a thick gruel made from a fourth part of the usual amount of cooked rice.
Then, according to the prescribed method, one should give it with soft rice grains and a non-slimy consistency,
along with clear green-gram soup that is neither burnt nor salty.
One should give well-steamed rice in a measure of two parts,
along with a savory dish that is pleasing to the heart and awakening to the senses.
The wise man should first offer three portions of soft boiled rice for the patient to eat;
thereafter, he should provide him with a meal as is appropriate.
One should administer well-prepared juices of the black buck, deer, and others;
this is prescribed for these mild, moderate, and strong purgations respectively.
This is the proper sequence for food in one-, two-, or three-fold portions:
[it applies] to those with a predominance of phlegm or bile, those who drink alcohol constantly, those who are emaciated, and those who have been purified.
For those whose [stools] are excessively moist, a regimen beginning with nourishing drinks (tarpaṇa) is beneficial;
this applies when [the condition] is caused by pain, lack of food, restrictive rules, grief, or mental distraction.
One should treat men who have fasted as if they were already purged;
for these are the measures—half an āḍhaka, an āḍhaka, and a prastha—prescribed for purgation.
Because purgation ends with the elimination of phlegm (śleṣman), those who know it do not desire that [second purgation];
there is only one purgation that ends with phlegm—there is no second whatsoever.
Since strength is said to be threefold, there are accordingly three stages therein;
among these, one who possesses strength may perform a single stage at a time.
One of middling strength should practice it twice, and one who is weak three times;
some authorities thus prescribe this sequence for those with weak, middling, and superior digestive fires.

When the digestive fire has increased through association with food, one should consume sweet and bitter tastes first, out of fear of provoking the humors; thereafter, one should take unctuous, sour, salty, and pungent tastes.
Then, like one in a state of health, he should consume sweet, sour, and salty tastes in abundance, followed by sweet and bitter ones,
and likewise unctuous and dry tastes, alternating them.
A person who has drunk only clarified butter, or who has vomited it out entirely,
should eat light food for seven nights.
The person for whom venesection has been performed, or for whom purification therapy has been administered,
should avoid [sexual intercourse] for one month, or until he regains his strength.
The patient should omit one enema every three days.
But in the third case of transgression, one should perform the expiation as appropriate.
Those suffering from ulcers are like earthen vessels filled with oil;
likewise those afflicted by diseases of the eyes, even when treated with unguents, as well as those suffering from fever and dysentery.
In one who is angry, the provoked pitta produces various complications;
in one who is fatigued or grieving, the mind falls into confusion.
Through the dread practice of sexual intercourse, the foolish man incurs diseases such as convulsions,
hemiplegia, and the stiffening of the limbs.
In the private parts there is swelling, as well as severe cough and dyspnea;
blood mixed with semen flows out, accompanied by a discharge of dust-like matter.
And from sleeping during the day, one incurs various diseases characterized by phlegm:
enlargement of the spleen, catarrh, jaundice, edema, and fever.
One who is overcome by *tamas* experiences a dullness of the limbs, a lack of digestion, and likewise a loss of appetite;
such a person delights only in sleep.
From speaking too loudly, the bodily air (vāyu) may cause pain in the head,
as well as blindness, numbness, loss of the sense of smell, deafness, and muteness.
It cures hanumokṣa, adhimantha, and the most severe ardita;
as well as stiffness of the eyes, involuntary blinking, thirst, cough, and insomnia.
He suffers from loose teeth and various other afflictions;
by traveling in vehicles, he experiences vomiting, fainting, vertigo, and exhaustion.
Likewise, from sitting for too long or remaining in one position, there occurs a seizing of the limbs, a terrible derangement of the senses, and pain in the hips.
From excessive walking, the bodily wind (vāyu) causes pain in the calves,
or emaciation of the thighs, or swelling, or even the tingling sensation known as pādaharṣa.
The consumption of cold and pleasurable waters leads to an increase of wind (vāta);
from that arise bodily aches, stiffness, colic, flatulence, and tremors.
From exposure to wind and sun, one may suffer discoloration and fever;
from eating incompatible foods or eating before the previous meal is digested, one meets with death or a terrible disease.
Unwholesome eating undoubtedly destroys strength and complexion;
for those lacking self-control who eat like beasts without moderation,
they indeed incur indigestion, which is the root of the host of diseases.
Having perceived the cause of calamities, a wise person, in the midst of these calamities,
should strive for the patient's recovery by means of an antidote.
For those who have undergone purgation or emesis, the meat of the hariṇa, eṇa, and lāvaka deer, as well as the śaśa rabbit, the peacock, and the tittiri partridge should be consumed;
likewise, ṣaṣṭika rice, aged śāli rice, mung beans, and whatever else is proclaimed to be light.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Complications in the Patient," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśrutasaṃhitā. ||39||
The fortieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of medicated smoking, nasal therapy, and gargling.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
Smoke is of five kinds, namely: that produced by application, that produced by oleation, and that produced by emesis.
It is a destroyer of cough and an emetic.

In that regard, with *elā* and other ingredients—excluding *kuṣṭha* and *tagara*—ground into a fine paste, one should wrap a twelve-finger-long reed stalk of finger-width circumference with eight fingers of linen cloth and apply it as a plaster; this is the *varti* for routine use (*prāyogika*).
For oleation (*snaihika*), it is prepared with fats, fruit-essences, beeswax, resin (*sarjarasa*), *guggulu*, and so forth, mixed with oil.
For purgation of the head (*vairecana*), it is prepared with drugs used for head-evacuation (*śirovirecana*).

In the *kāsaghna* [chapter], there are [drugs] such as *bṛhatī*, *kaṇṭakārikā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *kāsamarda*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *iṅguda* bark, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *chinnaruhā*, and *karkaṭaśṛṅgī*, which are used for curing coughs;
and in the *vāmanīya* [chapter], there are [substances] such as sinews, skin, hooves, horns, crab shells, dried fish, dried meat (*vallūra*), and worms, which are used for causing emaciation.
In this regard, the materials for the smoking pipe (*dhūmanetra*) are explained by means of the materials for the enema nozzle (*bastinetra*).

The smoking pipe, however, should have a circumference equal to that of the little finger at its tip, with an aperture the size of a *kalāya* pulse; at its base, it should have a circumference equal to that of the thumb, with an aperture for inserting the smoking wick (*dhūmavarti*). For routine use (*prāyogika*), it should be forty-eight finger-breadths in length; for oleation (*snehana*), thirty-two finger-breadths.
There are twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) for emesis; sixteen finger-breadths for the cure of cough and for inducing vomiting.
These also have apertures the size of a jujube stone.
The nozzle for the wound should be eight finger-breadths long, as large in circumference as a pea, and have a lumen that can admit a kulattha pulse.

Then, seated comfortably, with a serene mind, looking straight downward, and being vigilant, one should inhale the smoke by placing a wick—soaked in oil and with its tip held upright—into the passage of the eye.
One should first drink it through the mouth, and then drink it through both nostrils;
what is drunk through the mouth should be vomited through the mouth alone, and what is drunk through the nose [should be exhaled] through the nose.
Having taken in smoke through the mouth, one should not expel it through the nostrils;
for by that contrary method, the sight is destroyed therein.
Specifically, one should take the *prāyogika* (preparatory) [smoke] through the nose;
the *snaihika* (oleaginous) through both the mouth and the nose;
and the *vairecanika* (purgative/cleansing) through the nose alone.
The other two [are performed] by means of the mouth alone.

In that regard, for the *prāyogika* (habitual) smoke, one should remove the reed stalk from the wick, dry it in a place free from wind and sun, ignite it over charcoal embers, and instruct the patient: "Apply it to the opening at the base of the nozzle and inhale the smoke. In this same manner, one should perform the *snehana* (oleating) and *vairecanika* (purgative) procedures. For the other two types, one should place the wick into a stable, well-prepared earthen bowl from which the smoldering embers have been removed, cover it with another bowl that has a hole at its base, join the base of the nozzle to that hole, and then consume the smoke.

When the smoke has subsided, one should insert the remaining wick and cause the patient to inhale the smoke again until the purification of the *doṣas* is complete; this is the procedure for the method of smoking.

In this regard, those afflicted by grief, fatigue, fear, anger, heat, poison, blood-bile (*rakta-pitta*), intoxication, fainting, burning sensations, thirst, jaundice, dryness of the palate, vomiting, head injury, eructation, lack of nourishment, darkness before the eyes (*timira*), urinary disorders, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, upward-moving wind (*ūrdhva-vāta*), or those who are children, the elderly, weak, recently purged, or have undergone enemas; those who are awake at night, pregnant, dry, emaciated, or have chest injuries; and those who have consumed honey, ghee, curd, milk, fish, wine, or gruel, or whose *kapha* is depleted—these should not resort to smoking.
Taken at an improper time, it causes vertigo, fainting, headache,
and severe impairment of the nose, ears, eyes, and tongue.
The first three types of smoke-therapy (dhūma) should be employed during twelve occasions, namely:

after eating, cleaning the teeth, using nasal medication (nasya), bathing, sexual intercourse, vomiting, voiding urine, voiding feces, laughing, being angry, and at the conclusion of surgical procedures.
Regarding the classification therein, the unctuous (snaihika) type is indicated at the conclusion of voiding urine, voiding feces, sneezing, laughing, being angry, and sexual intercourse.
The purgative [smoke] is used at the end of bathing, vomiting, and daytime sleep;
the habitual [smoke] is used after cleaning the teeth, bathing, eating, and surgical procedures.

Among these, the unctuous (snaihika) pacifies vāta due to its unctuousness and its capacity for adhesion; the purgative (vairecana) excites and then eliminates kapha due to its dryness, sharpness, heat, and clarity;
and the habitual (prāyogika) excites kapha and then eliminates it once excited, while it pacifies vāta because it shares common properties with the former two.
And in this regard,
by the use of smoke, a man becomes one whose senses, speech, and mind are clear,
whose hair, teeth, and beard are firm, and whose face is fragrant and bright.

Likewise, cough, dyspnea, anorexia, coating of the mouth, hoarseness of voice, salivation, sneezing, vomiting, throat irritation, drowsiness, sleepiness, stiffness of the jaw and neck, chronic catarrh, diseases of the head, and pains in the ears and eyes—these oral diseases caused by vāta and kapha do not occur.
Its proper application (yoga), deficient application (ayoga), and excessive application (atiyoga) are to be understood. Among these, proper application alleviates disease;
deficient application does not alleviate disease.

Excessive application [of this treatment] produces dryness of the palate and throat, burning sensations, thirst, fainting, vertigo, intoxication, ringing in the ears, diseases of the eyes and nose, and debility.

The preparatory [breathing] consists of taking in three breaths through the mouth and nose alternately, or three or four times each. The unctuous [breathing] continues until the flow of tears occurs. The purgative [breathing] continues until the appearance of the humors (*doṣa*).
The emetic should be drunk after consuming a gruel made of sesame, rice, and barley;
it is a cure for cough when taken between mouthfuls of food.
One should apply smoke to the wound using a funnel-shaped pipe made from two joined earthenware bowls;
through the inhalation of this smoke, there occurs alleviation of pain, clarity of the wound, and cessation of discharge.
This procedure for medicated smoking has been briefly described by me;
hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for nasal medication (nasya) in its entirety.
Medicine, or oil prepared with medicinal herbs, administered through the two nostrils is called *nasya*.
It is of two kinds: head-purgative (*śirovirecana*) and oleating (*snehana*).
That [treatment] is of two kinds and each is fivefold; namely: nasal medication (nasya) and head-purgative therapy (śirovirecana).
Pratimarśa,
avapīḍa, and pradhamana.

Among these, nasal medication (nasya) and head-purgation (śirovirecana) are primary; the modification of nasal medication is the pratimarśa. The modifications of head-purgation are the avapīḍa and the pradhamana; thus, the term "nasya" is established as fivefold.

In this context, the specific term *nasya* is applied to that unctuous substance which is prescribed for the purpose of lubrication, for strengthening the head, neck, shoulders, and chest, or for producing clarity of vision.

It should be administered when the head is overcome by *vāta*, or in cases of the falling out of teeth, hair, or beard; severe earache, tinnitus (*karṇakṣveḍa*), visual impairment (*timira*), loss of voice, diseases of the nose, dryness of the mouth, *avabāhuka*, premature greying (*akālaja*), the appearance of wrinkles and grey hair (*valīpalita*), and painful awakening; as well as in *vāta-pitta* disorders of the mouth and other such conditions, using an unctuous substance prepared with drugs that alleviate *vāta* and *pitta*.

Head-purgation (śirovirecana) is indicated for those whose palate, throat, and head are pervaded by phlegm (śleṣman), and in cases of anorexia, heaviness of the head, headache, chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka), helminthiasis, coryza, epilepsy, loss of the sense of smell, and other disorders above the clavicle caused by phlegm; it is administered using drugs for head-purgation or with oil processed with such drugs.
In this regard, both of these [types of fasting] apply to one who has not eaten at the time of meals; specifically, in the forenoon for those with phlegm disorders,
at midday for those with bile disorders,
and in the afternoon for those with wind disorders.

Then, for a person who is to undergo head-purgation (śirovirecana), who has voided urine and feces, has eaten, and whose facial channels have been purified by the use of a tooth-stick and smoking at a time when the sky is cloudless; for one whose throat, cheeks, and forehead regions have been massaged after being fomented with the heat of his own palms; who is lying supine in a room free from wind, sun, and dust, with arms and legs extended, the head slightly tilted back, eyes covered with a cloth, the tip of the nose raised by the tip of the index finger of the left hand so that the channels are clear; [the physician] should, with the right hand, pour the oil—which has been heated with warm water and placed in one of these vessels: silver, gold, copper, gemstone, earthenware, or shell—using either a shell or a cotton swab, lukewarm and not agitated, in an unbroken stream, taking care that it does not reach the eyes.
While the oil is being poured, one must not shake the head;
nor should one become angry, nor speak, nor sneeze, nor laugh.
For when affection is impaired by these, one does not practice correctly;
consequently, there arises cough, catarrh, headache, and eye disease.
Its measure is eight drops emitted from two joints of the forefinger: the first is a *mātrā*,
the second a *śukti*,
and the third a *pāṇiśukti*.
These three measures should be administered according to one's strength.
A wise person should never, under any circumstances, swallow an oily enema.
Having overflowed the palate, it exits through the mouth;
out of fear of an excess of phlegm, one should expectorate it without holding it back.
Once he has recovered, one should again foment his throat, cheeks, and other areas, and have him inhale medicinal smoke. One should then feed him food that is slightly unctuous (abhiṣyandi).

After that, one should prescribe his regimen of conduct (ācārika), while he avoids dust, smoke, unctuous substances, sunlight, wine, the drinking of liquids, head-baths, excessive travel, anger, and so forth.
Regarding that, this is the knowledge concerning its proper application, excessive application, and lack of application.
Lightness of the head during yoga, pleasant sleep and awakening,
the subsiding of disorders, purity of the senses, and happiness of the mind.
Excessive salivation, heaviness of the head, and confusion of the senses are the symptoms of an over-oleated head; in that case, one should apply drying (rūkṣa) measures.

If there is improper application, one observes impairment of the vital breath (vāta), dryness of the sense organs, and lack of relief from disease; in such cases, one should administer nasal therapy (nasya) once again.
One should prescribe four, six, or eight drops as the dosage for oleation of the head, according to one's strength.
Three signs resulting from the application of nasal therapy (nasya) have been taught by those who contemplate the scriptures: namely, purity (śuddhi), deficiency (hīna), and excess (ati).
Lightness of the head, purity of the channels, conquest of disease,
and clarity of mind and senses are the signs of purification of the head.
Itching, coating, heaviness, and the discharge of phlegm from the channels are declared to be the signs when the head has been insufficiently purified.
When the head is strongly purged, there occurs the appearance of brain matter, an increase of wind (vāta), confusion of the senses, a sense of emptiness,
and even pain in the head.
If the head is insufficiently purified, one should administer treatments that subdue Kapha and Vata;
once the head is properly purified, one should instill medicated ghee as a nasal drop (nasya).
(Whether at intervals of one day, two days, or for seven days repeatedly;
or for twenty-one nights, or as long as one deems appropriate,) for that embodied being who is utterly overwhelmed by the wind-humor (vāta), [the following should be done].
The wise physician should also administer nasal drops (nasya) to him twice a day.

As for the pressed-out preparation (avapīḍa), one should administer it like a head-purgative (śirovirecana) to those with excessive secretions (abhiṣyaṇṇa), those bitten by snakes, or those who have lost consciousness; having crushed any one of the substances used for head-purgation, one should press it out.
For those who are emaciated or suffering from blood-bile (rakta-pitta), one should apply any one of the following: sugar-candy, sugarcane juice, milk, ghee, or meat broth.

For those who are emaciated, weak, timid, delicate, or women, medicated fats (snehas) boiled [with drugs] are for the purification of the head; among these, a paste (kalka) is beneficial according to the specific case.
One should blow powder into the nostrils of those afflicted by mental derangement, worms, or poison.

One should avoid administering nasal therapy (nasya) to those who have recently consumed food, those suffering from malnutrition, those with very acute coryza, pregnant women, those who have recently drunk unctuous substances, water, wine, or liquids, those with indigestion, those who have received enemas, those who are angry, those afflicted by artificial poison, the thirsty, those overwhelmed by grief, the exhausted, children, the elderly, those who have suppressed natural urges, and those desiring to bathe their heads. Furthermore, one should avoid nasal therapy and medicated smoking when the clouds do not appear at the proper season.

In that regard, complications arise from administering food that is too cold or too hot, or given with excessive force; or from drinking while the head is tilted back too far, or while sniffing, moving about, or eating; and from giving what is forbidden. These complications—such as thirst, eructation, and so forth—are caused by the humors (doṣa) or arise from depletion (kṣaya).
In this regard, two types of complications are recorded for nasal medication (nasya) and head-purgation (śirovireka):
they should be understood as arising respectively from the provocation of the humors (doṣotkleśa) and from depletion (kṣaya).
One should conquer those [pains] caused by the humors (doṣas) and the afflictions (kleśas) through pacifying (śamana) and purifying (śodhana) therapies;
however, when they are caused by depletion (kṣaya), nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) treatments appropriate to each case are beneficial.
Anointing the body with unguents should be practiced at fourteen times; namely:
when rising from bed, after cleansing the teeth, and when departing from the house.
By one exhausted by physical exercise, sexual intercourse, or travel; at the conclusion of urination, defecation, rinsing the mouth, or applying collyrium; and by one who has eaten.
By one who has vomited;
by one who has risen from sleeping during the day;
and in the evening.

In this regard, *pratimarśa* (nasal drops) practiced by one who has risen from bed destroys the impurities accumulated during the night that have entered the nasal passages and brings about clarity of mind.

When practiced by one who has cleansed his teeth, it produces firmness of the teeth and fragrance of the mouth. When practiced by one departing from the house, because the nasal passages are moistened, dust or smoke does not cause affliction.
When used by one exhausted by physical exercise, sexual intercourse, or travel, it destroys fatigue.
When used after voiding urine or feces, it removes heaviness of vision.
When used after gargling or applying collyrium, it clarifies the sight.
When used by one who has eaten, it brings about the purification of the channels and lightness of the body.
When used by one who has vomited, it removes the phlegm obstructing the channels and generates a desire for food.
When used by one who has risen from daytime sleep, it dispels the residual heaviness and impurity of sleep and produces one-pointedness of mind.
And when practiced in the evening, it results in pleasant sleep and awakening.
One should know that the quantity of oil for nasal administration (nasya) which, when poured in, reaches the mouth after being slightly sniffed, is the measure for a pratimarśa.
Through nasal medication (nasya), diseases of the regions above the clavicle in men are pacified;
it also brings about clarity of the sense organs and makes the mouth fragrant.
It bestows strength upon the jaws, teeth, head, neck, hips, arms, and thighs,
and brings about the non-appearance of wrinkles, graying hair, baldness, and freckles.
Oil should be administered in cases of kapha associated with vāta; muscle fat (vasā) in pure vāta; ghee always in pitta; and marrow in pitta combined with vāta.
Thus has the procedure for the four types of unctuous substances been proclaimed;
because it does not conflict with the sites of phlegm (kapha), oil is prescribed for those locations.
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for taking morsels (kavalagrahaṇa). A morsel is of four types: oleaginous (snehī), soothing (prasādī), purifying (śodhī), and healing (ropaṇa).
In the case of Vāta, an unctuous enema with warm, fatty substances is used; in the case of Pitta, a clarifying enema with sweet and cold substances;
and in the case of Kapha, a purifying enema with pungent, sour, salty, dry, and hot substances.
A healing agent for a wound consists of substances that are astringent, bitter, sweet, pungent, or hot;
this specific distinction regarding its fourfold nature has thus been proclaimed.

In that case, having mixed a paste of the three pungents (trikaṭu), vacā, mustard seeds, and harītakī with any one of oil, sour gruel (śukta), wine (surā), urine, alkali, or honey, and having added salt, one should apply it while it is heated; then, after the neck, cheeks, and forehead regions have been fomented and massaged, one should wear it.
That quantity which can be easily moved about is known as a *kavala*;
however, that quantity which cannot be moved about is proclaimed to be a *gaṇḍūṣa*.
It should be held with an undistracted mind and an erect body for as long as it takes for the cheeks to become full of saliva and for the nasal passages and eyes to overflow;
then it should be released, and another [drop] should be taken again.
Thus, gargles prepared with oil, milk, honey, meat-broth, urine, and sour liquids,
as well as with decoctions and warm water, are beneficial according to the specific dosha.
The reduction of disease, contentment, clarity, lightness of the mouth,
and serenity of the senses are the signs of purity in the kavala.
From deficient application, there arise dullness, an excess of kapha, and inferior cognition;
from excessive application, there is inflammation of the mouth, along with dryness, thirst, loss of appetite, and exhaustion.
For purification, these indeed become especially effective; there is no doubt:
sesame seeds, blue lotus, clarified butter, sugar, and milk.
A gargle with honey for one whose mouth has been burnt destroys the burning sensation;
thus, the procedure for gargling has been briefly proclaimed.
Having analyzed the medicine with his intellect, he should prepare the *pratisāraṇa* (local application) in four forms:
paste (*kalka*), medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*), honey (*kṣaudra*), and powder (*cūrṇa*).

Just as for those with diseases of the mouth, [medicines] are prescribed using the tips of the fingers according to their respective needs; in that regard, one should discern between the proper application and the improper application of what has been stated regarding gargles (kavala).
One should pacify those very diseases which a gargle (kavala) removes;
furthermore, one should feed the person food that subdues the humors (doṣa) and does not cause obstruction.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Smoking, Nasal Medication, and Gargling," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
Thus ends the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsā-sthāna) in the Suśruta-saṃhitā, taught by the Blessed Śrī Dhanvantari and composed by his disciple, the great sage Suśruta.

Now begins the section on pharmaceutical preparations (Kalpasthāna). Chapter One. Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparation for the protection of food and drink (annapānarakṣakalpa).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Dhanvantari, the lord of Kāśī and the best among those who uphold austerity and righteousness,
whose commands were unassailable, instructed his disciples, headed by Suśruta.
Enemies who have been overcome by your prowess, and those of your own kin who have become hostile,
are like those wishing to discharge the poison of their anger upon finding such an opening.
Evil-minded people might skillfully kill the king with poisons,
or women might sometimes employ various stratagems out of a desire for his fortune.
Or, through the administration of a poison-maiden, a man might lose his life in an instant;
therefore, the king must always be protected from poison by the physician.
And because the fickleness of the minds of men is as well known as that of horses,
a king should never place his trust in anyone at any time.
One who is of noble birth, righteous, affectionate, well-supported, ever-exerting,
free from greed, honest, devoted, grateful, and pleasant to behold.
One who is free from anger, harshness, envy, deceit, and laziness;
who has conquered the senses, is patient, pure, and endowed with good conduct and compassion.
One who is intelligent, tireless, devoted, and well-wishing;
one who is clever, bold, skillful, dexterous, and free from laziness.
In the kitchen, one should employ a physician who possesses the previously mentioned qualities, who is always attended by medicines, and who is honored by those learned in that science.
It was constructed in an auspicious direction and location, consisting of large, pure vessels;
it was provided with lattices, adorned with windows, and attended by a circle of trustworthy people.
The kitchen should also be free from the interference of women, provided with a canopy, kept clean, well-honored,
and its men and women thoroughly vetted.
In that regard, one should appoint as superintendent a person who generally possesses the qualities of a physician—
one who is pure, capable, skillful, disciplined, and pleasant to behold.
They were well-distributed, cheerful, with hair and nails kept short,
steadfast, bathed, firmly self-restrained, wearing turbans, and perfectly composed.
And various attendants shall be obedient to his command,
for living beings exist by means of food.
Therefore, the physician in the kitchen should be free from negligence,
as should the kitchen attendants, the carriers, the rice-cookers, and the flour-grinders.
And whoever else there may be who fall under the physician's power—
those men who understand intentions through the distortions of speech, gestures, and facial expressions.
A wise man should recognize the giver of poison by these signs:
when questioned, he does not give an answer, and though he wishes to speak, he falls into confusion.
He speaks much that is meaningless and confused, like a fool;
he snaps his fingers, scratches the ground without cause, and laughs.
Trembling arises within him, and terrified, he gazes at one another;
emaciated and with a pale face, he even scratches himself slightly with his nails.
Distressed, he repeatedly touches his hair with his hand;
and desiring to depart, he looks again and again toward the side doors.
But the poison-giver, being senseless, acts perversely;
some do so out of fear of the king, or others in haste by his command.
Even wicked men may perform the deeds of the virtuous;
therefore, kings who act with due respect must examine their servants.
In regard to food, drink, tooth-sticks, as well as oil-massage,
rubbing the body, bathing-powder, decoctions, sprinkling, and ointments;
Upon sacrificial ladles, garments, beds, armor, and ornaments;
upon sandals, footstools, and the backs of elephants and horses.
I shall now describe the symptoms of other substances mixed with poison, such as nasal drops, medicinal smoke, and collyrium, and immediately thereafter, their treatment.
Those flies, crows, and other such creatures that eat the poisoned offering set down by one devoted to the king perish right there.
With that food, the consumer of oblations crackles intensely with a *caṭacaṭā* sound,
and he becomes as unbearable as the throat of a peacock.
With its flames broken and thick smoke, it soon subsides;
indeed, the cakora bird’s aversion to it arises very quickly.
Seeing food mixed with poison, the jīvajīvaka birds die;
the cuckoo suffers a distortion of its voice, while the crane falls into a state of intoxication.
The peacock is excited, the parrot and the maina cry out,
the swan shrieks excessively, and the bhringaraja bird warbles.
The spotted deer sheds tears and the monkey voids excrement;
therefore, one should station these wild animals and birds in close proximity to the king.
Then, for the sake of adorning the house and for his own constant protection, as the steam from the food that had been set out rose upward; |||
Pain in the heart, wandering of the eyes, and headache arise;
in that case, *kuṣṭha*, *lāmajja*, *nalada*, and honey [should be used] as nasal drops and collyrium.
One should apply a plaster made of śirīṣa, haridrā, and sandalwood;
moreover, by applying sandalwood paste to the heart, one shall obtain comfort.
It causes the burning of the hand upon contact with it and the breaking of the nails;
for this, an ointment of śyāmā, indragopa, asoma, and utpala should be applied.
If he should consume that food through negligence or delusion,
his tongue thereafter becomes like a stone, incapable of perceiving flavors.
He is pricked and burned, and phlegm is discharged from his mouth;
in that state, the action of the tooth-stick is like that of one impelled by tears.
Having reached the stomach (āmāśaya), it causes fainting, vomiting, diarrhea, flatulence, burning sensation, tremors,
and impairment of the sense organs.
In that case, emesis should be induced quickly with the fruits of madana, alābu, bimbi, and kośātakī,
or else with curd, whey, or rice-water.
Having reached the colon (pakvāśaya), it causes burning, fainting, diarrhea, thirst, impairment of the sense organs,
flatulence, pallor, and emaciation.
In that case, a purgative with Nīlinī fruit mixed with ghee is prescribed;
or else, Dūṣīviṣāri should be drunk combined with curd or honey.
In all liquid substances— such as milk, wine, water, and the like—
various forms arise, including the production of foam and bubbles.
And here shadows are not seen, or if they are seen again,
they appear as pairs, or with holes, or thin, or likewise deformed.
Vegetables, soups, grains, and meats become sodden and tasteless;
they become as if stale overnight and acquire a foul odor.
All edible foods and fruits were devoid of fragrance, color, and taste;
those that were ripe quickly withered away, while those that were unripe turned rotten.
When the poison has entered the tooth-brushing twig, the brush-fiber disintegrates,
and swelling arises in the tongue, teeth, lips, and gums.
Then, once the swelling has been rubbed with honey and an ointment made from dhātakī flowers, pathyā, and the stones of jambū fruits, a rubbing (pratisāraṇa) should be performed.
Now, either the roots of aṅkoṭha, or the bark of saptacchada,
or even the seeds of śirīṣa, mixed with honey, constitute a medicinal paste for rubbing.
One should indicate the presence of poison in the tongue-scraper and the blade by the same signs as those for the tooth-stick;
likewise, an ointment that is slimy, excessive, greasy, or discolored is possessed of poison.
When poisoned oil is used for anointment, there occurs the bursting of boils, discharge from the skin caused by wind, inflammation of the skin, sweating, fever,
and even the tearing away of the flesh.
In that case, for one who has been sprinkled with cold water, an ointment should be applied,
consisting of sandalwood, tagara, kuṣṭha, uśīra, and veṇupatrikā.
Soma, valli, amṛtā, śvetā, padma, kālīyaka, and tvak—
this drink is administered with the juice of kapittha and cow's urine.
In the cases of rubbing the body, sprinkling, decoctions,
and ointments, as well as in beds, garments, and armor, one should recognize [the presence of poison] by the same signs as those for anointing the body.
When the ointment is tainted by poison, there occurs a falling out of hair, pain in the head, the flow of blood from the orifices,
and the formation of knots on the upper parts of the body.
In that place, there have been many applications of black earth mixed with the bile of a rishi,
ghee, śyāmā, pālindī, and taṇḍulīyaka.
Either the fresh juice of cow dung, or the juice of jasmine,
or the juice of *mūṣikaparṇī*, or smoke produced from a house [is beneficial].
Oil for anointing the head, a helmet, a bathing cloth, a turban,
and garlands contaminated with poison should be purified by scraping them clean.
When applied as a facial paste, the face becomes dark and exhibits the symptoms of an oil massage;
it is further covered with eruptions resembling the thorns of a lotus plant.
In that case, honey and ghee should be drunk, and sandalwood mixed with ghee should be applied as a paste;
[the herbs] payasyā, madhuka, phaṇijjhaka, bandhujīva, and punarnavā [are also to be used].
There is discomfort for elephants and other animals, salivation, redness of the eyes,
and the appearance of eruptions on the buttocks, anus, penis, and scrotum of the traveler.
In that case, the treatment for the rider and the vehicle is desired to be like that for an oil massage;
furthermore, there is the appearance of blood from the orifices, headache, and the discharge of phlegm.
When the medicinal smoke reaches the nasal passages, the symptoms include a distortion of the sense organs;
in that case, ghee boiled with the milk of cows and other animals and with ativiṣā should be administered.
In drinks and nasal drops, white madayantika is beneficial;
[otherwise] there would be loss of fragrance, discoloration, and wilting of the flowers.
For one who smells [the offering], there is pain in the head; for one whose eyes are filled with water, there is the shedding of tears;
and in that case, the rite is considered as if it were performed with the application of [impure] saliva upon the face.
When oil has entered the ear, there occurs impairment of hearing, swelling, and pain, as well as ear discharge;
in that case, one should immediately perform filling with [medicated] oil.
The expressed juice of the bahuputrā plant, combined with ghee and honey,
as well as the juice of the bark of the soma tree, is desired when well-cooled for therapeutic benefit.
When collyrium is mixed with poison, there occurs an accumulation of tears, a burning sensation, pain, confusion of vision,
and even blindness.
In that case, clarified butter should be drunk immediately as a satiating remedy along with *magadhā*;
likewise, the collyrium of a ram's horn and the resin of the *varuṇa* tree [are to be used].
The resin of the Muṣkaka or Ajakarṇa tree mixed with cow-bile,
or the flower of Kapittha, Meṣaśṛṅgī, or Bhallātaka [is used].
One should prepare each flower individually from both the Bandhūka and Aṅkoṭa;
[the symptoms are] swelling, discharge, numbness, and the eruption of blisters on the feet.
There is no doubt that [defilements] arise from sandals contaminated by poison;
one should treat shoes and footstools in the same manner as sandals.
The ornaments, their luster extinguished, do not shine as they did before;
moreover, they would destroy their own positions through burning, parching, and tearing asunder.
One should perform the procedure for anointing as prescribed for sandals and ornaments;
this includes the afflictions by poison, such as vapors and so forth, which are said to end with those of the ornaments.
Having carefully examined his complications, the physician should administer the treatment;
I shall now describe that great, fragrant medicinal compound.
One should administer strong purgatives and emetics in the form of drinks, ointments, nasal drops,
and collyriums.
If bloodletting is indicated, one should quickly pierce the veins;
or else, O King, a mouse or a lizard should be tied to the hand.
He renders all food mixed with poison free from its toxic effect;
moreover, when situated among friends, he should always maintain a protective shield over his heart.
The wise man should drink the ghee known as Ajeya and that called Amṛta;
or he may drink ghee, curd, milk, honey, or cold water.
One should constantly eat peacocks, mongooses, monitor lizards, spotted deer, and even antelopes, and one should also drink their juices.
Into the meat of the iguana, the mongoose, and the deer,
a wise man should add well-ground pālindī, madhuka, and sugar.
Sugar and ativiṣā should be given with peacock flesh and mahauṣadha;
likewise, long pepper and mahauṣadha should be administered with the meat of the spotted deer.
Soup made from legumes, combined with honey and ghee, is always beneficial;
furthermore, a wise person should consume foods and edibles that are antidotes to poison.
If poison has indeed been consumed, one whose heart is protected should induce vomiting with long pepper, licorice, honey, sugar, sugarcane juice, and water.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Protection of Food and Drink," in the Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Second Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of immobile poisons (sthāvara-viṣa).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Poison is said to be of two kinds: stationary and mobile.
The first has ten bases, while the second has sixteen substrates.
Root, leaf, fruit, flower, bark, milky sap, heartwood,
resin, minerals, and the bulb is recorded as the tenth.

Among these, there are eight root-poisons: *klītaka*, *aśvamāra*, *guñjā*, *sugandha*, *gargarakā*, *karaghāṭa*, *vidyucchikhā*, and *vijayā*; five leaf-poisons: *viṣapatrikā*, *lambā*, *avaradāru*, *karambha*, and *mahākarambha*; twelve fruit-poisons: *kumudvatī*, *veṇukā*, *karambha*, *mahākarambha*, *karkoṭaka*, *reṇuka*, *khadyotaka*, *carmarī*, *bhagandhā*, *sarpaghāti*, *nandana*, and *sārapāka*; five flower-poisons: *vetrakā*, *dambavallī*, *jāka*, *karambha*, and *mahākarambha*; seven resin-exudate poisons: *antrapācaka*, *kartarīya*, *saurīyaka*, *karaghāṭa*, *karambha*, *nandana*, and *nārācaka*; three milky-juice poisons: *kumudaghnī*, *snuhī*, and *jālakṣīrī*; two mineral poisons: *phenāśma* (or *bhasma*) and *haritāla*; and thirteen bulbous poisons: *kālakūṭa*, *vatsanābha*, *sarṣapa*, *pālaka*, *kardamaka*, *vairāṭaka*, *mustaka*, *śṛṅgīviṣa*, *prapuṇḍarīka*, *mūlaka*, *hālāhala*, *mahāviṣa*, and *karkaṭaka*. Thus, there are fifty-five stationary (*sthāvara*) poisons.
Four are said to be the size of a calf’s navel, two are proclaimed to be the size of a mustaka,
six are said to be the size of mustard seeds, and the remaining ones are each of a single [mustaka] size.
Twisting pain from root-poisons, delirium, and even fainting;
yawning, twisting of the limbs, and labored breathing are to be known as the effects of leaf-poison.
Swelling of the scrotum, burning sensations, and aversion to food result from fruits containing poison;
while vomiting, flatulence, and delusion result from flowers containing poison.
Indeed, when the resins, exudations, or poisons [of such trees] are consumed,
foul breath, roughness of the mouth, headache, and the discharge of phlegm occur.
The arrival of froth, diarrhea caused by milk-poisons, a heavy tongue,
pain in the heart, fainting, and a burning sensation in the palate are caused by metal poisons (dhātu-viṣa).
One should generally identify these as poisons that kill over time;
however, those produced from bulbs are sharp-acting, and I shall describe them in detail.
From contact with *kālakūṭa* poison, there is unconsciousness, trembling, and paralysis;
from *vatsanābha*, there is stiffness of the neck and yellowing of the feces, urine, and eyes.
In the *sarṣapa* [constellation], there is impairment of the bodily humors (*vāta*), constipation, and the formation of tumors;
in the *pālaka*, there is weakness of the neck and impediment of speech; these are the results recognized here.
From Praseka, known as Kardama, there occurs diarrhea and yellowness of the eyes;
from Vairātaka, bodily pain and diseases of the head arise.
From the *mustaka* poison, stiffness of the limbs and trembling arise;
from the *śṛṅgī* poison, there is exhaustion of the body, burning sensations, and enlargement of the abdomen.
By Puṇḍarīka there is redness of the eyes and enlargement of the abdomen;
by Mūlaka there is discoloration, vomiting, hiccups, swelling, and stupor.

A man bitten by the Hālāhala poison indeed breathes with difficulty after a long time; his complexion turns dark, and there is intense throbbing and the emergence of knots and piercing pain in the heart.
The *karkaṭa* leaps upward and, laughing, bites even the teeth;
these thirteen types of bulbous plants (*kandaja*) of fierce potency have been described.
All these [qualities] are to be known by the wise through ten virtues:
dryness, heat, sharpness, subtlety, speed, and pervasiveness; and likewise—
It is known to be expansive, clear, light, and non-digestive;
due to its dryness it provokes vāyu, and due to its heat, pitta along with blood.
Through its sharpness, it confounds the intellect and severs the vital joints;
through its subtlety, it enters the limbs of the body and causes them to malfunction.
Because of its swiftness, it acts quickly; because of its pervasiveness, it attains its natural state;
and because of its expansiveness, it diminishes the humors (doṣas), the tissues (dhātus), and even the wastes (malas).
Due to its clarity it may seem excessive, due to its lightness it is difficult to treat, and due to its lack of digestion it is hard to eliminate; therefore, it causes suffering for a long time.
Whatever poison is stationary, mobile, or even artificial— that should be known as possessing ten qualities which cause instantaneous death.
Whatever is stationary, moving, or artificial— whatever remains within the body without having emerged from it—
is either worn out, destroyed by anti-poisonous herbs, or withered by forest fires, wind, and heat.
For poison that is naturally devoid of its potency becomes a slow-acting poison (dūṣīviṣa);
due to its diminished strength, it does not cause immediate death, and being enveloped by phlegm, it persists for many years.
Afflicted by that [poison], with the color of his excrement altered, his mouth foul-smelling and tasteless, thirsty, fainting, vomiting,
with stammering speech and despondent, he becomes possessed of the symptoms of *duṣyodara*.
If it resides in the stomach, the person suffers from diseases of phlegm and wind; if it resides in the large intestine, he suffers from diseases of wind and bile.
His hair and limbs become withered, like a bird whose wings have been plucked out.
Alternatively, when it resides within the bodily fluids (rasa) and so forth, it produces disorders arising from the constituent elements (dhātu) as previously described;
furthermore, it quickly becomes provoked by cold winds and foul weather—first hear the symptoms thereof.

Drowsiness, heaviness, yawning, or else a sense of looseness in the joints, exhilaration, or bodily aching; thereafter, it causes indigestion from overeating, loss of appetite, circular eruptions, skin patches, and delusion.
It may cause the depletion of the bodily elements (dhātu-kṣaya), swelling of the feet, hands, and face, dropsy (dakodara), vomiting, diarrhea,
discoloration, fainting, irregular fevers, or it may produce intense and powerful thirst.
One [type] may produce madness, another may cause loss of self-awareness, and another may deplete the semen;
one may produce stammering, while others produce various kinds of skin diseases and many other types of disorders.
Because it is corrupted by place, time, food, and frequent daytime sleep,
and because it vitiates the bodily constituents (dhātus), it is known as dūṣīviṣa (corrupted poison).
When the first stage of the movement of ingested immobile (vegetable) matter occurs in men,
the tongue becomes dark and stiff, and fainting and labored breathing arise.
In the second stage, it causes trembling, exhaustion, burning sensations, and pain in the throat;
having reached the stomach, it produces distress in the heart.
In the third stage, however, there is dryness of the palate and intense pain in the stomach;
his eyes become discolored, greenish, and swollen.
In the fourth stage of the paroxysm, there occurs piercing pain in the stomach and the colon, hiccups, coughing, rumbling in the intestines, and excessive heaviness of the head.
In the fifth stage, there is excessive salivation, discoloration, aching in the joints,
aggravation of all the doṣas, and pain in the colon.
In the sixth [month], there is a loss of wisdom and one suffers from severe diarrhea;
in the seventh, there is a breaking pain in the shoulders, back, and waist, as well as a complete obstruction.
During the first stage of the poison's onset, once the patient has been made to vomit and sprinkled with cold water,
one should have them drink an antidote combined with honey and clarified butter.
In the second stage, one should administer a purgative as previously described;
in the third stage, however, the drinking of medicinal decoctions, as well as nasal drops and collyrium, is beneficial.
On the fourth day, the physician should administer the medicine mixed with unctuous substances;
on the fifth day, he should cause it to be given combined with honey and a decoction of madhuka.
In the sixth [case], success is like that of dysentery;
and in the seventh, having made a crow's foot-mark on the head, one should apply blood or flesh.
However, when one of the other stages has been reached after the action [of the poison], one should administer this cooling gruel,
mixed with ghee and honey, which destroys the poison.
Koṣātakī, agnika, pāṭhā, sūryavallī, amṛtā, abhayā,
śirīṣa, kiṇihī, śelu, giryāhvā, and the two types of rajanī.
A gruel prepared from the decoction of punarnavā, hareṇu, trikaṭu, sārivā,
and balā destroys both types of poison.
Madhuka, tagara, kuṣṭha, bhadradāru, hareṇu,
punnāga, elā, ilavālu, nāgapuṣpa, utpala, and sugar.
Viḍaṅga, candana, patra, priyaṅgu, dhyāmaka, the two types of haridrā, the two types of bṛhatī, sārivā, sthirā, and sahā.
Ghee prepared with the paste of these [herbs] is renowned as "Ajeya" (the unconquerable);
it destroys all poisons quickly and is never defeated by anything.
To one afflicted by dūṣīviṣa who has been well-sweated and purified through both upward and downward evacuations,
one should constantly administer this medicine which destroys dūṣīviṣa.
Long pepper, dhyāmaka, māṃsī, śāvara,
paripelava, suvarcikā, small cardamom, water, and golden ochre.
This medicine, combined with honey, indeed dispels dūṣīviṣa;
it is known by the name Dūṣīviṣāri, and it is not prohibited for use elsewhere either.
In fever, burning sensation, hiccup, flatulence, loss of semen,
swelling, diarrhea, fainting, heart disease, and abdominal enlargement as well.
In cases of insanity, trembling, and whatever other complications may arise,
one should perform treatment with anti-poisonous medicines according to their respective requirements.
In a person of self-control, [dūṣīviṣa] is immediately curable; if it has persisted for a year, it is palliable;
however, it is incurable in one who is emaciated and indulges in unwholesome things.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Knowledge of Stationary Poisons," in the Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||2||
The third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the ritual procedure for the diagnosis of moving (animal) poisons.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
The sixteen substrates of mobile poison have been stated by me in brief;
their detailed exposition shall now be told.
In that regard, [the sources of impurity are]: sight, breath, fangs, claws, urine, feces, semen, saliva, menstrual blood, the mouth, the bite, belching, the snout, bones, bile, bristles, and corpses.
In this regard, divine serpents have poison in their gaze and breath;
terrestrial ones, however, have poison in their fangs.
Cats, dogs, monkeys, crocodiles, frogs, pāka-fish, iguanas, snails, peacocks, house-lizards, four-footed insects, and others likewise have poison in their fangs and claws.

The *cipiṭa*, *picciṭaka*, *kaṣāyavāsika*, *sarṣapa*, *toṭaka*, *varcaḥkīṭaka*, and *kauṇḍinyaka* have poison in their excrement and urine. Mice have poison in their semen. Spiders (*lūtā*) have poison in their saliva, urine, excrement, mouth-bites, claws, semen, and menstrual blood.
Scorpions, centipedes, spiders, leeches, fish, and *ucciṭiṅga* insects, as well as sea-scorpions, possess immobile poison (*alaraviṣa*).
The *citraśiras*, *sarāvaka*, *kurdiśata*, *dārukārin*, *medaka*, and *sārikāmukha* have poison in their mouths, in their pincers (*mukhasandaṃśa*), in their vomit, and in their urine and feces.
Flies, *kaṇabha* insects, and leeches have poison in their mouths and in their pincers.
The bones of the *viṣaha* fish, the snake, the *varaṭī*, and the *matsya* fish are bone-poisons (*asthiviṣa*).
The *śakulī* fish, the *raktarājī* fish, the *varakī* (or *varaṭī*) fish, and the *matsya* fish possess bile-poison (*pittaviṣa*).
The minute-beaked *ucciṭiṅga*, the *varaṭī*, the centipede (*śatapadī*), the *śūka*, the *valabhikā*, the horned insects (*śṛṅgin*), and the bees possess stinger-poison (*śūkatuṇḍaviṣa*).

Those with the bodies of insects or snakes whose life-force has departed are poisons found in corpses; the remaining ones not mentioned here should be counted among those whose poison is located in the mouth or the fangs.
And there are verses on this subject:
"In a king's territory, enemies may corrupt the grass, water, roads, rivers, smoke, and winds with poison.
Having recognized these through their signs, one should purify those who are exceedingly wicked."
The water is foul, slimy, and of a pungent odor; it is covered with foam and streaked with lines.
Frogs and fish die, birds fall senseless, and those who frequent the marshlands wander about in confusion.
Those men, horses, and elephants who bathe therein suffer from vomiting, delusion, fever, burning sensations, and swelling;
therefore, one should strive to purify the corrupted water by removing those defects.
Having burned dhava, aśvakarṇa, āsana, pāribhadra, pāṭala, siddhaka, and mokṣaka,
along with royal trees and somavalka, one should scatter that cooled ash into lakes.
Having placed a handful of ashes into a jar, one may thus purify the desired water,
or likewise a patch of ground, a stone surface, a sacred bathing place, or even a barren wasteland that has been defiled by poison.
Whichever part of the body— whether that of a cow, a horse, an elephant, a camel, a donkey, or a human— is touched by it,
that part becomes swollen, burns, and likewise the hair and nails fall away.
There too, having ground an infinite amount [of the powder] together with all the fragrances and mixed it with wines,
one should sprinkle that path with water combined with excellent clay, or with the juices of viḍaṅga, pāṭhā, and kaṭabhī.
When grasses and grains are contaminated, some suffer, faint, or vomit;
others experience diarrhea or even die; one should administer their treatment as prescribed.
Or, having smeared [the drum] with poisons-removing medicinal herbs, one should play various musical instruments.
[The pigment] is made from equal parts of tāra, sutāra, sa-surā, indragopa, and a portion of kuruvinda.
An ointment for the ear prepared with bile from a tawny cow is prescribed and highly commended;
indeed, by the sound of such an instrument, even the most terrible poisons are destroyed.
When smoke or wind is contaminated by poison, birds fall to the ground afflicted by exhaustion;
moreover, there arise severe coughs, catarrhs, headaches, and diseases of the eyes.
Having placed lac, turmeric, ativiṣā, abhayā, rock salt, hareṇukā, elā, dala, vakra, kuṣṭha,
and priyaṅgu into fire, one should also purify the smoke and the wind.
While Brahmā was indeed creating these offspring from his own self,
a haughty demon named Kaiṭabha created an obstacle.
From the mouth of that Brahmā, the storehouse of splendor, as he was enraged, Wrath itself, having assumed a physical form,
fell forth most terrible.
He consumed that roaring, immensely powerful being who resembled Death itself;
then, having slain the asura, that wondrous splendor increased.
Then, upon seeing it, despair indeed arose among the gods;
and because it produced despair, it is called "viṣa" (poison).
Then, having created the subjects, the Lord deposited that remaining anger among all beings,
both the immobile and the mobile.
Just as water from the atmosphere, having reached the earth with its taste unmanifested, acquires this or that specific taste in various regions; so it is with the Self.
In the same way, whatever substance poison pervades and occupies,
it follows the taste of that very substance by its own inherent nature.
Since all qualities in poison are generally sharp,
therefore all poison should be known as an agitator of all the humors (doṣas).
But when provoked, they abandon their own functions; afflicted by poison, the poison does not reach its state of digestion, and thus it obstructs the vital breaths.
Because his passage is obstructed by phlegm, his exhalation is blocked;
thus, even while he still possesses life, the man remains unconscious.
The poison of all serpents pervades their entire bodies;
when they are enraged, it issues from their limbs like semen from the act of churning.
Their fangs are like fish-hooks; whatever comes near becomes caught in them, and because they are not agitated, those serpents do not release their venom.
Since poison is described as being exceedingly hot and sharp,
therefore, for all types of poison, a cold affusion is prescribed.
The venom of insects is mild, not excessively hot, and increases vāta and kapha;
therefore, even in the case of insect venom, fomentation (sveda) is not prohibited.
One should treat those bitten by insects with extremely potent venom as if they were snakes; however, the poison from the blow or the bite itself will subside of its own accord.

He who, out of greed, would eat the poisoned flesh of a snake that has been struck by a poisoned arrow or bitten by another snake, after it has pervaded the body with its parts and has just died; [he goes to the Raurava hell].
Just as he who consumes poison is afflicted by disease or even dies,
for this reason the flesh of these two is unfit to be eaten immediately after death.

Within a moment, one who suffers from diarrhea should take that excrement— provided it is free of blood, accompanied by wind, and resembles the smoke of a house-fire— and collect it after a blow has been struck [upon it].
One who is bloated, whose blood is excessively hot, who is discolored, afflicted by exhaustion, and vomits foam—
one should designate him as having drunk poison.
Moreover, even fire mixed with poison does not burn his heart;
for that is the seat of consciousness, which remains pervading it by its very nature.
Men bitten at the holy fig tree (aśvattha), in a temple, a cremation ground, an anthill, during the twilights, at crossroads,
under the constellation of Yama or the Pitṛs, or those bitten in the vital organs (marmans), must be avoided.
The venom of hooded snakes (darvīkara) acts with immediate destruction; moreover, all poisons are doubled in potency when the body is heated by indigestion, bile, or exposure to the sun.
They are likewise fatal in children, those suffering from urinary disorders (prameha), and in pregnant women.
In the case of the elderly, the sick, those who have not eaten, the hungry, the emaciated, the timid, or during foul weather;
or when one is wounded by a weapon, if the blood does not flow and the streaks do not appear like creeping vines, [one is to be known as dead].

There is no horripilation even when touched by cold water; one should avoid that person who is overcome by poison—whose tongue is white, whose hair falls out, and who suffers from the breaking of the nose as well as the breaking of the throat.
That bite which is blackish-red with swelling at the site, and where there is stiffness of the jaws, should be rejected;
likewise that from whose mouth a thick wick-like substance issues forth, or from which blood flows both upwards and downwards.
The physician should also avoid one whose fangs have all fallen out,
as well as one who is excessively deranged, afflicted by disease, has a feeble voice, or is discolored.
One should abandon a person whose fatal signs are extreme and whose breath is excessively rapid; in such a case, one should not perform any medical treatment.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Knowledge of Moving Poisons," in the Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||3||
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of the poison of snakebites.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Having clasped the feet of Dhanvantari, who was highly wise and proficient in all the sciences, Suśruta questioned him.
O Blessed One, you ought to speak of the number of snakes, their classification, the symptoms of being bitten, and the knowledge of the stages of the poison's onset.
Having heard those words of his, the best of physicians replied:
"Innumerable are the foremost among the Vāsukis, such as the renowned Takṣaka and others."
And there were great mountains and lords of serpents, whose splendor was equal to the sacrificial fire,
as well as those who incessantly roar, rain down, and scorch.
By them this earth, together with its oceans, mountains, and islands, is supported;
they could, when enraged, destroy the entire world with their very breath and glance.
Salutations to them; we have no need for any medical treatment from those who possess venom in their fangs, whether they be terrestrial or those that bite human beings.
I shall declare their number correctly and in due order:
the eighty [species] of serpents are divided into five groups.
The hooded snakes, the circular-spotted ones, and likewise the striped ones—these are further remembered as being of three types: those without venom and those with modified venom.
The serpents are of three types: hooded (darvīkara), circular-spotted (maṇḍalin), and striped (rājiman).
Among them, twenty-six serpents are to be known as hooded.
Twenty-two are known as maṇḍalina, ten as rājimat,
twelve as nirviṣa (non-venomous), and likewise three as vaikarañja.
The seven species arising from the Vaikarañja— namely the Citra, Maṇḍalin, and Rājila—
are dangerous when stepped upon, or when provoked, or even when seeking to devour [the victim].
Those great, fierce, and terrifying-looking [serpents] bite in three ways:
the "sarpita," the "radita," and thirdly, the "nirviṣa. Those who know the subject truly maintain that some bites are caused by the body of a snake.
Wherever footprints of tusks— whether one, two, or many—
are found deeply imprinted and slightly bloodied, he indeed creates them by uprooting [the trees].
The physician should recognize that as *sarpita* when it is accompanied by a fringe-like swelling at the edges, produces deformity, is contracted, and is characterized by edema.
Where the lines are reddish, blue, yellow, and likewise white, that should be known as *radita*; it should be understood as having little venom.
The physician should recognize as non-poisonous a bite— or multiple bites— on a person who is free from swelling, whose blood is not vitiated, and who remains in their natural state.
For in one who is afraid of a snake, the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated by that fear and produces a swelling in some part of the body;
however, that [swelling] which is struck by the snake's body is different.
Bites by those who are diseased, agitated, or bitten while already suffering from poison are known to have little venom;
likewise, a bite by one who is very old or a child is considered to contain little venom.
In a place frequented by Suparṇas, gods, brahmin-sages, yakṣas, and siddhas,
and endowed with poison-destroying herbs, poison does not take effect.
Those bearing the marks of a wheel, a plough, an umbrella, a svastika,
and a goad should be known as hooded cobras (darvīkara), which move swiftly.
Those snakes which have various circular spots, are variegated, large, and slow-moving, are to be known as Maṇḍalins; they possess a radiance equal to fire and the sun.
Those which appear glossy and variegated with stripes of various colors running both horizontally and vertically,
as if painted, are known as the Rājimantas.
Those serpents who possess the luster of pearls or silver, those who are tawny,
and those who are fragrant and golden-hued, are traditionally known as Brāhmaṇas by birth.
The Kṣatriyas, however, have a glossy complexion; they are like serpents and are exceedingly prone to anger.
Their emblems are the sun and moon, a parasol, and likewise the lotus.
Those snakes that are black, resembling a thunderbolt, or red in color,
as well as those that are smoke-colored or have the hue of a pigeon, are known as Vaiśyas among the serpents.
Those who have the color of buffaloes or elephants,
as well as those with rough skin and those of variegated colors— these, O Śūdra, are proclaimed to be such.
All serpents indeed agitate the wind (vāta) of a living being;
those with circular spots (maṇḍalin) agitate the bile (pitta), and those with many stripes (anekarājī) agitate the phlegm (kapha).
Offspring born from parents of different castes possesses the characteristics of two defects;
the specific defects of both husband and wife shall be explained here.
Indeed, during the last watch of the night, the variegated serpents roam;
those remaining are said to be the circular-marked ones, while the hooded snakes are known to move by day.
The *darvīkara* snakes are born young, the *maṇḍalins* old, and the *rājimants* in their middle age; they arise as causes of death.
Young snakes agitated by mongooses, those struck by water, emaciated ones,
those with sloughed-off skin, and those that are frightened are considered to have little venom.
Among them, the hooded snakes (*darvīkara*) are the black cobra (*kṛṣṇasarpa*),
the great black snake (*mahākṛṣṇa*),
the black-bellied snake (*kṛṣṇodara*), and the white pigeon snake (*śvetakapota*).
The Great Pigeon, Balāhaka, and the Great Serpent.
Śaṅkhakapāla, Lohitākṣa, and Gavedhuka.
Parisarpa,
Khaṇḍaphaṇa, and Kakuda.
Padmo, Mahāpadmo, Darbhapuṣpo.
Dadhimukha, Puṇḍarīka, and Bhrūkuṭīmukha.
The scattering bird;
the one strewn with flowers;
the mountain-serpent.
The straight serpent,
the white-bellied one,
and the large-headed one.
The *alagarda* is the "venomous snake" (*aśīviṣa*);
as for the *maṇḍalins*, they are the "mirror-circle" (*ādarśamaṇḍala*).
White maṇḍala; red maṇḍala; variegated maṇḍala.
Pṛṣata, Rodhrapuṣpa, Milindaka.
gonasa; vṛddhagonasa; panasa.
The great panasa;
the bamboo-leaved;
the young madana.
Pālindira,
Piṅgala,
Tantuka, and Puṣpapāṇḍu.
Possessing six limbs; fiery; tawny; astringent.
Kaluṣa, Pārāvata, Hastābharaṇa, and Citraka.
Regarding "eṇīpada" (2):
the Puṇḍarīka is striped; it has variegated stripes, such as stripes on the fingers.
Bindurāji,
Kardamaka,
and Tṛṇaśoṣaka.
The *sarṣapaka* has a white jaw;
the *darbhapuṣpa* is ring-shaped;
and the *godhūmaka*.
The *kikkisāda* is [so called]; however,
the *galagolī* and the *śūkapatra* are non-venomous (*nirviṣa*).
The python, the celestial serpent, and the rainy-season snake.
Puṣpaśakalī,
Jyotīratha, and Kṣīrikāpuṣpaka.
