The serpent-king Ahipātaka,
Andhāhika,
and Gaurāhika.
Regarding "tree-dweller" (vṛkṣeśaya):
the vaikarañjas, however, are born from the crossbreeding of the three [types of snakes], beginning with the darvīkaras;
for example, the mākuli.
The *poṭagala* is the "smooth-striped" snake.

Among these, the *mākuli* is born from a black cobra (*kṛṣṇasarpa*) and a *gonasī*, or vice versa; the *poṭagala* is born from a striped snake (*rājila*) and a *gonasī*, or vice versa; and the *snigdharājī* is born from a black cobra and a striped female (*rājimatī*), or vice versa.

Regarding these, some say that for the first [type of snake], the intensity of the venom is like that of a father, while for the other two it is like that of a mother; others say this applies to all three.

Furthermore, among the three *vaikarañja* types, there are seven: the *divyelaka*, *rodhra-puṣpa*, *kārāji*, *citrika*, *poṭagala*, *puṣpābhikīrṇa*, and *darbha-puṣpavellitaka*. Of these, the first three are like the *rājila* type.
The remaining ones are like those in the maṇḍala.
Thus, these eighty serpents have been explained.
In that regard, those with large eyes, tongues, mouths, and heads are males;
those with minute eyes, tongues, mouths, and heads are females;
and those possessing characteristics of both, who are dull, slow, and free from anger, are neuter.

In this regard, we shall describe the general symptoms of being bitten by all snakes alike. Why is this? For poison is like a sharpened sword, a thunderbolt, or a fire; it acts with extreme speed and, if neglected for even a moment, causes the patient to perish. There is no time to resort to a multitude of words, for even when the symptoms of each individual bite are stated, they are everywhere found to be of three types.
Therefore, we shall explain only the threefold classification; for this is free from weariness and causes no confusion.
Moreover, within this very framework, all the various manifestations of snakes are included.

Among these, the symptoms of *darvīkara* (hooded) snake venom are: blackening of the skin, eyes, nails, teeth, face, urine, and feces; dryness; heaviness of the head; pain in the joints; weakness in the waist, back, and neck; yawning; trembling; loss of voice; a rattling sound in the throat (*ghurghuraka*); stupor; dry eructations; cough and dyspnea; hiccup; upward movement of the vital air (*vāyu*); piercing pain and cramps; thirst; salivation; frothing at the mouth; obstruction of the channels (*srotas*); and various pains characteristic of *vāta*. The symptoms of *maṇḍalin* (ringed) snake venom are: yellowness of the skin and other tissues; desire for cold; a sensation of being smoked over; burning; thirst; intoxication; fainting; fever; discharge of blood from above and below; involuntary contraction of the muscles; swelling; putrefaction of the bite site; seeing yellow forms; rapid onset; and various pains characteristic of *pitta*. The symptoms of *rājimat* (striped) snake venom are: whiteness of the skin and other tissues; cold fever; horripilation; stiffness of the limbs; swelling at the site of the bite; thick expectoration of phlegm; vomiting; frequent itching of the eyes; swelling in the throat; a rattling sound in the throat; obstruction of breathing; entering into darkness; and various pains characteristic of *kapha*.
One bitten by a male looks upward;
in one bitten by a female, the veins on the forehead protrude;
one bitten by a neuter becomes a squint-eyed gazer.
One who is pregnant has a pale face and is bloated;
one who has recently given birth suffers from pain in the abdomen and passes blood in her urine, and she develops a ranula.
One who desires food longs for a meal.
In an old person, the impulses (vegas) are slow after a long time;
in a child, they are rapid and mild;
in one who is not poisoned, there are no symptoms of poison.
Some say that blindness results from the *andhāhika* snake.
It is called the *ajagara* because it swallows its prey; it takes away the life-force of the body, but not by means of its venom.
One bitten by a snake whose venom kills instantly falls to the ground like one struck by a thunderbolt from a scripture.
With his limbs drooping, he sleeps.
In that regard, there are seven stages of the venom for all snakes.
Among them, in the first stage of the hooded snakes (*darvīkara*), the venom vitiates the blood;
once vitiated, it turns black.
By that [first stage], blackness occurs in the limb, resembling the crawling of ants; in the second [stage], it vitiates the muscle tissue (*māṃsa*).
By that, extreme blackness, swelling, and nodules (*granthi*) appear in the limb; in the third [stage], it vitiates the fat (*medas*).

By that, there is discharge from the bite site, heaviness of the head, perspiration, and impairment of vision; in the fourth [stage], having entered the abdominal cavity (*koṣṭha*), it vitiates the humors (*doṣa*) dominated by phlegm (*kapha*).
By that, lassitude, salivation, and loosening of the joints occur; in the fifth [day], it enters the bones and vitiates the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the digestive fire (*agni*).
By that, there occurs splitting pain in the joints, hiccups, and a burning sensation; in the sixth [day], it enters the marrow and excessively vitiates the *grahaṇī*.

By that, heaviness of the limbs, diarrhea, cardiac distress, and fainting occur; in the seventh [day], it enters the semen and excessively agitates the *vyāna* wind, while displacing the phlegm (*kapha*) from the subtle channels.

By that, there occurs the appearance of phlegmatic eruptions, a breaking pain in the waist and back, obstruction of all physical movements, excessive flow of saliva and sweat, and suppression of the breath.
In the first stage of the Maṇḍalin variety, the poison vitiates the blood;
once vitiated, that blood assumes a yellowish hue.
In that regard, there is a burning sensation and a yellowish luster of the limbs; in the second stage, it vitiates the flesh.
Because of that, there is extreme yellowness, a burning sensation, and swelling at the site of the bite; in the third stage, it vitiates the fat.

Because of that, as before, there is visual impairment, thirst, moisture at the bite, and perspiration; in the fourth stage, having entered the internal cavity (*koṣṭha*), it brings about fever; in the fifth stage, it causes a burning sensation in all the limbs.
The sixth and seventh [stages] are as before.

In the first impulse of the *rājimant* [venom], the poison vitiates the blood; that vitiated blood turns pale. Because of this, the person experiences horripilation and appears white-complexioned; in the second [impulse], it vitiates the flesh.
By that [vitiation], extreme pallor, stupor, and swelling of the head occur; in the third stage, it vitiates the fat (*medas*).

By that, loss of vision, moistening of the bite site, perspiration, and discharge from the nose and eyes occur; in the fourth stage, having entered the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*), it produces stiffness of the neck (*manyāstambha*) and heaviness of the head; in the fifth stage, it causes obstruction of speech and a cold fever (*śītajvara*); in the sixth and seventh stages, it is as described previously.
And in this regard,
there are verses: "The seven stages (kalā) that have been fully described as existing within the different elements (dhātu)—
having passed through each one of them, the poison produces its impulse."
That interval by which one indeed pierces a minute fraction of time (kalā) is known as the "interval of velocity" (vegāntara), being carried along by the wind.
In the first stage, the animal, its limbs swollen, meditates in suffering;
in the second, however, with saliva flowing and its body turning black, it is tormented in the heart.
In the third stage, there is pain in the head and the neck and throat break;
in the fourth, the deluded man trembles, gnashes his teeth, and abandons his life-breaths.
Those who know these [stages] say there are three stages of speed, and among them, the end;
in the first stage of speed one meditates, but beyond that, the bird becomes deluded.
In the second stage he is said to be agitated, and in the third he meets death. Some indeed maintain that among birds there is but a single stage of the poison's onset;
the poison of cats, mongooses, and the like does not progress very far.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Knowledge of the Poison of Snakebites," in the Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||4||
The Fifth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the ritual procedure for the medical treatment of snakebite poisoning.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
In all cases, from the very beginning, one should bind a ligature four finger-breadths above the bite of a person whose limb has been bitten by a snake.
Poison does not enter the body when warded off by these auspicious substances, or by any one of the following: soot, leather scraps, or bark, combined with soft earth.
Having cut away the stinging part where no further binding occurs, suction,
excision, and cauterization are recommended in all such cases.
Having covered the mouth with cloths, suction should be applied beneficially;
or else, at that very moment, either a snake or even a clod of earth should be bitten.
Now, one who has been bitten by a maṇḍalī snake should by no means apply heat;
for due to the abundance of bile in its venom, the bite spreads further because of the application of heat.
An expert in mantras should also bind ariṣṭa with mantras;
when bound with cords and the like, it is considered a counteragent to poison.
The mantras proclaimed by divine and brahminical sages consist of truth and austerity;
they do not fail, and they swiftly destroy even the most difficult poison.
Poison is swiftly warded off by mantras consisting of splendor and composed of truth, sacred knowledge, and austerity, in a manner that cannot be achieved even by medicinal herbs when employed.
The acquisition of mantras should be performed by one who abstains from women, meat, and honey;
who eats moderately, remains pure, and sleeps on a bed of kuśa grass.
For the sake of attaining success in mantra, one should diligently worship the deities with perfumes, garlands, offerings, and oblations, as well as through recitation and fire-sacrifices.
Since mantras uttered according to improper rites, or deficient in vowels and consonants,
do not attain success, therefore the procedure for healing must be applied.
A skilled physician should pierce the veins all around the site of the bite;
or, once the poison has subsided, those [veins] at the tips of the limbs or on the forehead should be pierced.
When the blood is being drawn out, the entire poison is removed;
therefore, one should cause the blood to flow out, for that is the supreme treatment for this condition.
Having scarified the bite with all-around medicinal pastes,
one should apply an ointment and sprinkle it with water mixed with sandalwood and uśīra.
One should have them drink various antidotes with milk, honey, ghee, and so forth;
or, in their absence, long pepper (kṛṣṇā) and ant-hill earth may be beneficial.
One may eat kovidāra, śirīṣa, arka, or kaṭabhī;
however, one must not drink oil, kaulattha, liquor, or sauvīraka.
Whatever other liquid there may be, one should drink it repeatedly and then vomit it up;
for generally, by means of vomiting alone, the poison is expelled through the mouth.
In the first stage of the poison's onset from serpents, one should extract the blood;
in the second stage, the physician should cause the patient to drink an antidote mixed with honey and clarified butter.
One should employ nasal therapy and collyrium on the third day for the destruction of the poison;
once the patient has vomited, one should administer the previously mentioned gruel on the fourth day.
Having first applied cooling treatments, the physician should administer a sharp purgative on the fifth or sixth day, as well as the gruel (yavāgū) that has been prescribed.
In the seventh stage, however, one should cleanse the head with a sharp *avapīḍa* (pressed-out preparation);
one should also apply a sharp collyrium and [administer] a sharp instrument to the head.
Having made a "crow's foot" mark on the skin, one should apply blood or flesh;
first, during the onset of the Maṇḍalins, one should act as one would with Darvīkaras.
On the second day, one should have him drink an antidote with honey and ghee;
then, having induced vomiting, one should cause him to consume the previously mentioned gruel.
In the third stage, once it has been purified by strong [emetics], one should administer beneficial gruel;
in the fourth and fifth stages as well, one should act like a snake-charmer (using counter-irritants).
In the sixth month, the Kākolyādi group is beneficial, as is a sweet medicinal decoction;
in the seventh month, a medicinal expressed juice (avapīḍa) that destroys poison is beneficial.
In the first stage of the flow of blood from those with *rājimant* (lineated) hemorrhoids, one should remove the blood using a gourd-syringe;
furthermore, one should have the patient drink an anti-toxic medicine combined with honey and clarified butter.
On the second day, one should cause the patient to drink an anti-toxic medicine that destroys poison after it has been vomited;
on the third and subsequent days, this procedure using *dārvī* (daruharidrā) is beneficial.
In the sixth [month], the strongest collyrium is used, and in the seventh, the avapīḍa;
for pregnant women, children, and the elderly, these treatments are administered without venesection.
For those afflicted by poison, the prescribed mild treatment is recommended;
bloodletting and collyriums for goats and sheep are the same as those for humans.
For buffaloes and camels, it is threefold; for cows and horses, it is twice that;
for elephants, it is fourfold; and for all birds, it is simply the same as for elephants.
One should apply very cold sprinklings (pariṣeka) and plasters (pradeha). A māṣaka measure of the collyrium (añjana) is desired; twice that amount is beneficial for nasal administration (nasya);
four times that is wholesome for internal drinking (pāna), and eight times that again for emesis (vamana).

Having carefully considered the country, the individual's constitution, suitability, the season, the intensity of the poison, and the strength or weakness [of the patient], one should then perform the treatment with a discerning intellect.
This rite for the destruction of poison has been taught according to the sequence of its potencies. Now hear [the application] of both types of poison according to the specific stages of the disease.
When a limb is discolored, rigid, swollen, painful, or afflicted by poison,
one should promptly perform bloodletting according to the prescribed method.
Being composed, one should have the patient— who is afflicted by hunger, dominated by wind, and distressed by that poison—
drink meat broth, clarified butter, sour gruel, honey, and likewise curd.
In cases of thirst, burning sensations, and delusion caused by the dhatu of bile (pitta), or when one is afflicted by bile-based poison,
one should treat the patient with cooling massages, baths, and medicinal plasters.
One should cause a patient of the phlegmatic type, who suffers from cold-induced vomiting in the cold season and is afflicted by poison that increases kapha,
as well as one suffering from fainting and intoxication, to vomit using sharp emetic therapies.
A person afflicted by pitta, suffering from burning in the abdomen, pain, flatulence, retention of urine, and colic,
as well as obstruction of feces and flatus, should be purged with a strong laxative.
One should treat with collyriums a person whose eyelids and eye-sockets are swollen, who is afflicted by drowsiness, whose eyes are discolored and turbid, and who is pale in complexion.
In cases of headache, heaviness, lassitude, lockjaw,
and constriction of the throat, as well as in severe stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), one should quickly administer head-purgation (śirovirecana).
One should treat a person afflicted by poison who has lost consciousness, whose eyes are rolled back, and whose neck is broken,
by means of purgatives, powders, and sharp medicinal snuffs.
One should quickly venesect the vessels arising from his limbs and forehead;
while those [vessels] have not yet been bled, the one skilled in weapons should strike the head with a weapon.
One should make an incision in the shape of a crow's foot so that they may thus discharge;
one should then place blood-stained skin or flesh upon his head.
A skilled physician, having smeared a drum on both its sides with a decoction or a paste of *carmavṛkṣaka*, should cause it to be sounded with non-poisonous substances.
Once he has regained consciousness, one should again cleanse him from above and below;
in this manner, one should completely eliminate even the most invincible poison.
For even a small remnant [of the disease] leads to a recurrence with great force;
or it may produce pallor, discoloration, fever, cough, and pain in the head.
In cases of swelling, wasting, catarrh, visual impairment, anorexia, and chronic rhinitis,
one should likewise apply the appropriate therapeutic measures according to the specific dosha involved.
One should also treat complications arising from poison according to their respective [therapies].
Then, having quickly removed the *ariṣṭa* [ligature] and having scarified the area marked by it, [one should proceed].
Poison that has been spilled there might burn, yet it would again tend toward increasing its force;
even so, [the disease] may be countered with effort through medicines, mantras, and the application of therapeutic procedures.
When the poison has lost its potency and a disorder of the body arises,
one should then treat the aggravated wind with unctuous substances and other such remedies.

Pitta should be treated with decoction enemas (kaṣāya-basti) and oil enemas (sneha-basti) using drugs that alleviate pitta-fever, excluding oil, fish, horse gram (kulattha), and sour substances, while adding anti-toxic agents.
One should treat the kapha with the Māragvadha group of drugs mixed with honey,
as well as with anti-kapha medicinal formulations and bitter, dry foods.
One should treat as if they had lost consciousness those who have fallen from a tree or a precipice onto uneven ground, those who have died in water,
and those who have just hanged themselves.

When the poison has been tightly bound by an *ariṣṭa* ligature or extracted by sharp medicinal plasters or similar applications, yet the limb remains swollen, excessively moist, and putrid, one should know that this foul-smelling flesh is ruined by the poison; it is a grievous condition.

Immediately upon being pierced, it exudes blackish blood; it undergoes suppuration and is frequently burned with pain. The flesh becomes blackened, excessively moist, and extremely putrid, and it constantly sloughs away from the wound.
One should determine that a person who suffers from thirst, fainting, delusion, burning sensations, and fever has been struck by a poisoned arrow;
furthermore, one should recognize him as such if all the previously mentioned symptoms are present and his wounds are overwhelmed by poison.
Wounds caused by spiders, those pierced by poisoned arrows, or those afflicted by other poisons are generally characterized by putrefying flesh.
Having skillfully removed the putrid flesh from these and having drained the blood with water-soaked cloths;
Having quickly expelled the humors through both the upper and lower channels, one should properly sprinkle the area with decoctions of the bark of milk-exuding trees;
furthermore, one should apply poultices made of cooling, anti-venomous substances mixed with clarified butter, enclosed within a cloth.
In the case of a fracture by a malignant species [of snake], the previously mentioned procedure for bile-based poison should be employed;
likewise, the group consisting of trivṛt, viśalyā, madhuka, the two types of haridrā, raktā, narendra, and salt [is to be used].
One should place the three pungent substances (kaṭutrikam), well-powdered and mixed with honey, inside a horn;
this medicine, when administered through the methods of drinking, collyrium, anointing, and nasal drops, destroys poison.
Of irresistible power, the destroyer of the force of poison, it is called Mahāgada, possessed of great majesty;
it consists of viḍaṅga, pāṭhā, the three myrobalans, ajamodā, asafoetida, vakra, and the three pungents.
The entire group of salts, finely ground and mixed with citraka and honey, should be placed inside a cow's horn and covered with another horn; it should then be left to stand for a fortnight.
This is the medicine that conquers all poisons, both stationary and mobile; it is indeed invincible by name.
It consists of prapauṇḍarīka, suradāru, mustā, kālānusāryā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Sthauṇeyaka, dhyāmaka, guggulu, punnāga, tālīśa,
suvarcikā, kuṭannaṭa, elā, sitasindhuvāra, śaileya, kuṣṭha, tagara, and priyaṅgu.
Having made equal and fine powders of rodhra, water, golden ochre, māgadhī, sandalwood, and rock salt,
one should place them, mixed with honey, inside a horn.
This medicine, designated as "Tārkṣya," shall destroy even the poison of Takṣaka;
it consists of māṃsī, hareṇu, triphalā, muraṅgī, raktālatā, yaṣṭika, and padmaka.
Viḍaṅga, tālīśa, sugandhika, elā, cinnamon bark, kuṣṭha, patra, and sandalwood;
bhārgī, paṭola, kiṇihī, pāṭhā, mṛgādanī, karkaṭikā, and purā—these [are the ingredients].
One should place equal quantities of the fine powders of pālindī, aśoka, kramuka, the flower of surasī, and the flower produced from āruṣkara, along with bile, into a horn, together with honey.
The fat of the boar, the iguana, the peacock, and the porcupine, along with that of the cat, the panther, and the mongoose—
for whomsoever this well-prepared medicine is kept in the house, he shall be a bull among men, like the Bull among Men (the Buddha).
There, no snakes exist, much less insects; they abandon their vigor and their very poisons.
By this [power], even drums and kettledrums, when smeared with poison and resounded, would swiftly destroy all that is harmful.
Indeed, upon seeing banners smeared with poison, those who are not actually poisoned are instantly overcome by the fear of poison.
[The antidotes are: lac, harēṇu, nalada, priyaṅgu, the two types of śigru, yaṣṭikā, and pṛthvikā.

This powder, mixed with turmeric and combined with clarified butter and honey, should be placed in a cow's horn as previously described and covered; it is then to be employed as a collyrium, nasal drop, and potion.
This medicine named Saṃjīvana restores to life mortals here who are as if dead;
it consists of śleṣmātakī, kaṭphala, mātuluṅgī, śvetā, girihvā, kiṇihī, and sugar.
This "Sataṇḍulīya" is the foremost remedy against the poisons of the *darvīkara* and *rājila* snakes;
it consists of equal parts of *drākṣā*, *sugandhā*, *nagavṛttikā*, *śvetā*, and *samaṅgā*.
Two parts should be taken from the leaves of the *surasā*, as well as from the *kapittha*, the *bilva*, and the pomegranate;
likewise, half a part each from white *sindhuvāra*, the root of *aṅkoṭha*, and red ochre (*gairika*).
This medicine, combined with honey, especially destroys the poisons of the maṇḍalins;
it consists of moist bamboo bark, āmalaka, kapittha, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), haimavatī, and kuṣṭha.
The seeds of *karañja*, *tagara*, and *śirīṣa* flowers, combined with cow bile, destroy the poisons of spiders,
rats, and serpents, as well as *kaiṭa* poison, when applied as an ointment, collyrium, snuff, or potion.
Through the application of suppositories (varti), collyrium (añjana), and ointments (nābhilepa), it destroys the obstruction of feces, urine, flatus, and the fetus;
and through the use of collyrium and nasal drops (nasya), it cures severe cases of cataract (kāca), pterygium (armakotha), membrane formations (paṭala), and pupillary prolapse (puṣpa).
A decoction made from the roots, flowers, sprouts, bark, and seeds of the *śirīṣa* tree, heavily seasoned with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*),
mixed with salt and honey, when drunk, especially destroys the poison of insects.
Kuṣṭha, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), dārvī, madhuka, the two salts,
mālatī, nāgapuṣpa, and all the sweet substances.
This antidote, ground with the juice of wood-apple (kapittha) and combined with sugar and honey,
destroys all poisons, especially those of rats.
Soma-rājī fruit, its flower, kaṭabhī,
sindhuvāraka, coraka, varuṇa, kuṣṭha, sarpagandhā, and saptalā.
Punarnavā, the flower of Śirīṣa, and that produced from Āragvadha and Arka;
Śyāmā, Ambaṣṭhā, Viḍaṅga, as well as Āmra and Aśmantaka.
Bhūmī and kurabaka constitute the group known as Ekaśara;
it should be employed either singly or in groups of two or three to remove poison.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Poisoning from Snake Bites," in the Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Sixth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure (kalpa) concerning the sound of the drum.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Having collected the ashes of *dhava*, *aśvakarṇa*, *śirīṣa*, *tiniśa*, *palāśa*, *picumarda*, *pāṭali*, *pāribhadraka*, *āmra*, *udumbara*, *karahāṭaka*, *arjuna*, *kakubha*, *sarjaka*, *pītana*, *śleṣmātaka*, *aṅkoṭha*, *āmalaka*, *pragraha*, *kuṭaja*, *śamī*, *kapittha*, *aśmantaka*, *arka*, *cirabilva*, *mahāvṛkṣa*, *aruṣkara*, *āralu*, *madhuka*, *madhuśigru*, *śāka*, *gojī*, *mūrvā*, *bhūrja*, *tilvaka*, *ikṣuraka*, *gopaghoṇṭā*, and *irimeda*, one should strain them according to the procedure for alkaline preparation (*kṣārakalpa*) using cow's urine and cook [the resulting liquid].

And in this case, one should add equal parts of the powders of pippalīmūla, taṇḍulīyaka, varāṅga, coca, mañjiṣṭhā, karañjikā, hastipippalī, marica, viḍaṅga, gṛhadhūma, anantā, soma, saralā, bāhlīka, guhā, kośāmra, śvetasarṣapa, varuṇa, lavaṇa, plakṣa, niculaka, vañjula, vakrāla, vardhamāna, putraśreṇī, saptaparṇa, ṭuṇṭuka, elavāluka, nāgadantī, ativiṣā, abhayā, bhadradāru, kuṣṭha, haridrā, vacā, and of metals.
Then, having brought it to the desired consistency like a lye (kṣāra), one should remove it from the heat and place it in an iron jar.
With this [mixture], one should smear the drum, the banners, and the archways;
by hearing, seeing, or touching them, one is completely liberated from poison.
This is known as Kṣārāgada; it is used for gravel, urinary calculi, hemorrhoids, Vāta-gulma, cough, colic, and abdominal enlargements.
It should be administered in cases of indigestion, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, severe aversion to food, swelling,
generalized skin diseases (*sarvasara*), and even in severe dyspnea.
This medicine is always effective for all those afflicted by poison;
it is an iron hook for the mouths of even the foremost Takṣakas.
Viḍaṅga, triphalā, dantī, bhadradāru, hareṇu,
tālīśapatra, mañjiṣṭhā, keśara, utpala, and padmaka.
Pomegranate, jasmine flowers, the two types of turmeric, the two types of sārivā,
śrīparṇī, tagara, kuṣṭha, the two types of bṛhatī, and elavāluka;
This prepared ghee, known as Kalyāṇaka, which removes poison, is accomplished by means of these [plants] along with sandalwood;
for it destroys the influence of malevolent planets and epilepsy.
It cures anemia, poison, asthma, weak digestion, fever, and cough;
it is highly recommended for those suffering from consumption, those with scanty semen, and for infertile women.
One should grind the seeds of Apāmārga, the beans of Śirīṣa,
the two white [varieties], and Kākamācī with the urine of cows.
This supreme remedy for neutralizing poison, prepared with these very substances and ghee, is renowned by the name Amṛta; it can even restore the dead to life.
Sandalwood, agallochum, kuṣṭha, tagara,
tilaparṇika, prapauṇḍarīka, nalada, sarala, and devadāru.
Bhadraśrī, barley-seed, bhārgī, nīlī, sugandhikā,
kāleyaka, padmaka, madhuka, ginger, and jaṭāmāṃsī.
Punnāga, elā, ilavālu, gairika, dhyāmaka, balā, water,
sarjarasa, māṃsī, śatapuṣpā, and hareṇukā;
Tālīśapatra, small cardamom, priyaṅgu, kuṭannaṭa,
śilāpuṣpa, śaileya, patra, and kālānusārivā;
The three pungents (kaṭutrika), śītaśiva, kāśmarya, kaṭurohiṇī,
somarājī, ativiṣā, pṛthvikā, and indravāruṇī.
Uśīra, varuṇa, musta, kustumburu, and likewise nakha;
the two white varieties of haridrā, sthauṇeya, lac, and the salts.
The kumuda, utpala, and padma lotuses, as well as the flower born of the sun (the arka),
and the blossoms of the campaka, aśoka, sumana, and tilvaka;
Likewise, the flowers of the pāṭalī, śālmalī, śailu, and śirīṣa,
as well as the fragrant grasses and the blossoms of the sindhuvāra;
The flowers of the dhava, aśvakarṇa, pārtha, and tiniśa trees,
along with guggulu, saffron, bimbī, sarpākṣī, and gandhanākulī;
Having collected these ingredients, one should have them made into a fine powder;
mixed with cow-bile, honey, and clarified butter, one should place it inside a horn.
With this foremost of medicines, one may bring back to life a man whose shoulders are broken, whose eyes are staring wide, and who has fallen between the fangs of Death.
This [missile] would forcibly destroy even the fire-like, irresistible poison of the enraged Vāsuki, the lord of snakes, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
This king of all medicines, named Mahāsugandhi, endowed with eighty-five ingredients,
should always remain in the hand of the king.
A king who has bathed and anointed himself becomes beloved by all people;
he attains a radiant splendor even when situated in the midst of his enemies.
A wise physician should administer the prescribed treatment for those afflicted by poison, with the exception of heat;
for the venom of insects increases when treated with cold.
Having understood what is wholesome and unwholesome as stated in the rules for food and drink,
one should give what is wholesome to those afflicted by poison and prevent them from consuming incompatible substances.
One should avoid molasses, sugarcane juice, and sour gruel, as well as indigestion and overeating; in brief, one should also avoid the group of nine new grains and so forth.
One afflicted by poison should indeed avoid sleeping during the day, sexual intercourse, physical exertion, anger, exposure to the sun, as well as liquor, sesame, and horse-gram.

A physician should recognize a person as being free from poison by observing that their humors are clear, the bodily elements are in their natural state, there is no craving for food, the tongue is even and well-proportioned,
and the complexion, senses, mind, and movements are all serene.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Dundubhisvanīya Preparation," in the Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the pharmaceutical preparation of mice.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Previously, the eighteen species of *bhūṣika* spiders whose venom is semen were briefly mentioned; now, learn from me their names, symptoms, and remedies.
Lālana, Putraka, Kṛṣṇa, Haṃsira, Cikvira,
Chucchundara, Alasa, and Kaṣāyadaśana as well.
Kuliṅga, Ajita, Capala, Kapila, Kokila, Aruṇa by name, Mahākṛṣṇa, and Undura; |||
Together with the great Śveta and likewise the mouse Kapila,
and the pigeon-colored rat— these eighteen are traditionally recorded.
In whichever limb their semen falls, or which is touched by those whose semen has been discharged,
or by nails, teeth, and so forth, in that limb the blood becomes vitiated.
Knots, swellings, caruncles, and circular patches arise,
as well as severe clusters of pustules, erysipelas, and kiṭibha lesions.
Fracture of the joints, intense pain, fainting, lassitude of the limbs,
fever, debility, loss of appetite, dyspnea, vomiting, and horripilation [occur].
This has been stated in brief regarding the appearance of one who has been bitten; now hear it in detail:
from the licking [of the wound], salivation, hiccups, and vomiting arise.
In that case, one should lick the paste of Taṇḍulīyaka mixed with honey;
however, by means of Putraka, bodily exhaustion and a pale complexion arise.
The limbs become covered with nodules resembling young rats;
in that case, one should lick a paste of śirīṣa and iṅguda mixed with honey.
From the bite of a *kṛṣṇa* [scorpion], there is swelling at the site of the bite, vomiting of blood, and generally [occurrence] on a cloudy day;
one should drink *śirīṣa* fruit and *kuṣṭha* with the ash of *kiṃśuka*.
Aversion to food, yawning, and horripilation occur due to *haṃsira*;
in that case, once the person has been well-vomited, he should drink a decoction of the *āragvadha* group of drugs.
Headache, swelling, hiccups,
and vomiting caused by *cikvira* (or *cikkira*) should be treated by inducing emesis with a decoction of *jālinī*, *madana*, and *aṅkoṭha*.
In this case, one should administer the alkaline preparation of *yavānala* and *ṛṣabhī*, along with the two types of *bṛhatī*.
Vomiting induced by a muskrat, as well as fever and debility, [should be treated accordingly].
Stiffness of the neck, swelling of the back, loss of the sense of smell,
and cholera are treated with cavya, harītakī, śuṇṭhī, viḍaṅga, pippalī, and honey.
Likewise, one should drink the seed of the aṅkoṭha tree here as a remedy for poison.
Neck stiffness, lassitude, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), pain at the site of the bite, and fever [are the symptoms].
In that condition, one should lick a great medicinal compound (mahāgada) mixed with ghee and honey;
[otherwise there would be] sleep, astringent taste in the teeth, parching of the heart, and emaciation.
One should lick the heartwood, fruit, and bark of the śirīṣa tree mixed with honey;
this cures pain, swelling, and discoloration in the area of the bite caused by a kuliṅga insect.
One should lick sahe along with sindhuvāra mixed with honey;
by this, [the effects of] ajita—namely blackness of the limbs, vomiting, fainting, and cardiac oppression—are cured.
One should lick pālindī and mañjiṣṭhā ground with the milk of a female elephant along with honey;
[otherwise] vomiting, fainting, and thirst will arise due to instability.
One should lick a paste of Triphalā combined with the root of Bhadrakāṣṭha along with honey;
by using [the oil] of Kapilā, suppuration in a wound, fever, the appearance of tumors, and thirst are cured.
One should lick white Punarnavā mixed with honey;
it cures severe knots (tumors), fever, and agonizing burning sensations caused by the Kokila disease.
One should drink ghee prepared with the decoction and paste of *varṣābhū* and *nīlinī*;
for when the wind (*vāyu*) is provoked by *aruṇa*, it produces diseases born of wind (*vāta*).
Bile is [pacified] by Mahākṛṣṇa, phlegm by Śveta,
blood by Mahākapila, and the fourfold [humors] by Kapota.
And at their bites, there appear knots, circular patches, and callosities; there is a severe accumulation of pustules and an extremely agonizing swelling.
Three *prastha* measures each of curd, milk, and ghee are prescribed;
[along with] *karañja*, *āragvadha*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *bṛhatī*, *aṃśumatī*, and *sthirā*.
Having boiled these, one-fourth of the decoction should be set aside again;
[then add] trivṛt, gojihvā, amṛtā, vakra, sarpagandhā, and clay.
One should cause the bark of the *kapittha* and the *dāḍima* to be finely ground;
having combined all of that together, one should cook it slowly over a mild fire.
This [mixture] removes the poison of the five [species beginning with] Aruṇa;
or else, it may be prepared in the fresh juices of Kākādanī and Kākamācī.
One should bleed the veins as indicated and perform purificatory treatments;
this same procedure for all [the stages] should be followed in cases of rat poison.
Having cauterized the bite, one should drain it;
and having incised it, one should apply a plaster made of śirīṣa, rajanī, kuṣṭha, and kuṅkuma, combined with amṛtā.
Emetics are prepared from the decoctions of *jālinī*, as well as those of *śukākhyā* and *aṅkoṭha*;
also the roots of *śukākhyā* and *koṣavatī*, and *madana*.
Having drunk the fruit of *devadālī* with curd, one shall vomit poison;
this remedy brings relief to all those bitten by rats.
Phala, vacā, devadālī, and kuṣṭha, ground with cow’s urine, should be applied according to the previous method; they destroy all rat poisons.
For purgation, a paste of trivṛt, dantī, and triphalā is recommended;
for head-evacuation (errhines), the pith of śirīṣa and its fruits are used.
Cow-dung juice enriched with the three pungents (trikaṭu) is beneficial when used as an ointment;
one should also lick a mixture of wood-apple (kapittha) and cow-dung juice combined with honey.
Alternatively, one should lick a paste made from rasāñjana, haridrā, indrayava, and kaṭvī,
combined with ativiṣā and honey, in the morning.
A person should drink ghee prepared with the roots of taṇḍulīyaka,
or ghee prepared with the roots of āsphotā, or indeed the pañcakāpittha preparation.
The poison of rats generally becomes aggravated when it has not been expelled during cloudy weather;
in that case as well, this same procedure should be performed, which removes both corrupting poisons and ordinary poisons.
The physician, having incised the caruncle of ulcers that are either stable or painful,
should cleanse it like an ordinary ulcer according to the specific humor involved.
When the wind, vitiated by phlegm, resorts to the channels that carry consciousness and robs dogs, jackals, hyenas, bears, tigers, and other such animals of their consciousness; |||
Then, with his tail, face, and shoulders hanging down, excessively salivating,
and being utterly deaf and blind, he ran hither and thither.
In one bitten by a venomous fanged beast that is mad,
numbness arises at the site of the bite and black blood flows excessively.
One who has been pierced by a poisoned arrow is generally characterized by its specific symptoms;
furthermore, a person [should observe] the behavior and cries of the creature by which he was bitten.
One who attempts many remedies but lacks the proper action perishes;
so too does one who looks upon the very form of the fanged creature by which he has been bitten.
Whether in water or in a mirror,
one should predict misfortune for him who frequently trembles upon seeing or even touching water.
One should know that fear of water is indeed a fatal sign (riṣṭa), and it is proclaimed as such;
one who is bitten by a snake, or one who is afraid of water, will not succeed in any way whatsoever.
Whether asleep or awake, healthy or terrified, one does not recover from being bitten by them;
once bitten, the wound should be drained and cauterized with clarified butter.
One should apply medicinal pastes and cause the patient to drink old ghee;
furthermore, one should administer a purgative combined with the milky sap of the Arka plant.
Furthermore, one should give him white *punarnavā* combined with *dhattūraka*,
as well as minced meat, sesame oil, the milk of the *rūpikā* plant, and jaggery.
One karṣa of the root of śarapuṅkhā and half a karṣa of dhattūra destroy the poison of a venomous rat, just as the wind disperses a mass of clouds.
Taking rice-water, one should grind it together with the rice grains;
having wrapped it in the leaves of the *unmattaka* plant, one should cook it as a cake (*apūpaka*).
One afflicted by the poison of an *alarka* snake should eat that [medicine] at the time of taking medicine;
however, while that medicine is being digested, it produces the symptoms of a dog.
In the winter season, disorders are palliable when one stays indoors, away from water;
then, having bathed on the following day, his disorders are pacified.
One should feed him a meal of śāli or ṣaṣṭika rice with warm milk; this procedure is to be followed for three days or five days, using half a mātrā at a time.
The physician must certainly administer the antidote that destroys the poison of Alarka;
for that man whose own internal poison becomes provoked does not survive.
Therefore, one should quickly provoke [the earth] oneself as long as it remains unprovoked,
using jars filled with cool water containing seeds, jewels, and medicinal herbs.
One should bathe him on a riverbank or at a crossroads with mantras;
there too, one should offer an oblation consisting of oil-cake, minced meat, and curd.
And various garlands, as well as meat, both cooked and raw—
O Yakṣa, lord of Alakā, leader of the hosts of dogs!
"Make this [wound] of mine, which has been afflicted by the *alarka* [rabies], free from poison without delay.
One should administer a sharp purgative to the embodied being after he has bathed."
Even when a wound has fully healed, the poison of one who is impure flares up again;
as for the beasts of prey mentioned here, I have described them as those whose venom lies in their fangs.
Therefore, a man bitten by them performs their characteristic movements and cries out repeatedly while attempting to counteract the poison; he dies before long.
One should massage wounds caused by the nails and teeth of predatory beasts;
one should sprinkle them with lukewarm oil, for these indeed provoke the wind (vāta).
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Formulation of Mice," in the Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||7||
The eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmaceutical preparation of insects.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Snakes are born from semen, feces, urine, corpses, and putrid eggs;
likewise, various kinds of insects are known to have the nature of air, fire, and water.
Possessed by the natures of all defects due to their transformation,
they are all exceedingly terrible even in the state of insects, being of four kinds.
The kumbhīnasa, tuṇḍikerī, śṛṅgī, śatakulīraka,
ucciṭiṅga, agnināman, cicciṭiṅga, and mayūrikā;
Āvartaka, Urabhra, Sārikāmukha, Vaidala,
Śarāvakurda, Abhīrāji, Paruṣa, and Citraśīrṣaka.
Śatabāhu, and also the one celebrated as Raktarāji—
these eighteen are the Vāyavya insects, which provoke the wind humor.
By these, when people are bitten here, diseases caused by wind arise;
namely, the Kauṇḍinyaka, the Kaṇabhaka, the Varaṭī, and the Patravṛścika.
The vināsikā, the brāhmaṇikā, the bindula, the bhramara,
the bāhyakī, the picciṭa, the kumbhī, the varcaḥkīṭa, and the arimedaka.
The Padmakīṭa, the Dundubhika, the Makara, the Śatapādaka, the Pañcālaka, the Pākamatsya, the Kṛṣṇatuṇḍa, and the Gardabhī.
Klīta, Kṛmisarārī, and also Utkleśaka—
these indeed are the twenty-four types that have fire as their primary nature.
By these [snakes], when they bite here, diseases arising from the cause of bile (pitta) are produced.
They are Viśvambhara, Pañcaśukla, Pañcakṛṣṇa, and Kokila.
The saireyaka, the pracalaka, the valabha, the kiṭibha,
as well as the sūcīmukha, the kṛṣṇagodhā, and the one who is kāṣāyavāsika.
The Kīṭa, the Gardabhaka, and likewise the Troṭaka—
these thirteen mild insects aggravate the phlegm (śleṣman).
By them, diseases caused by phlegm (kapha) arise in those bitten here;
namely, Tuṅgīnāsa, Vicilaka, Tālaka, and likewise Vāhaka.
The Koṣṭhāgārī, the Krimikara, the Maṇḍalapucchaka,
the Tuṇḍanābha (or Tuṅganābha), the Sarṣapika, the Valguli, and likewise the Śambuka.
The Agnikīṭa should also be known; these twelve are destroyers of life.
For those bitten by them here on earth, the symptoms of the stages of poisoning are like those of a snake.
Those various intense pains are indeed like diseases arising from a derangement of the three humors (sānnipātika);
the bite is as if scorched by caustic fire, appearing red, yellow, white, and crimson.
Accompanied by fever, bodily aches, horripilation, and pain,
there are vomiting, diarrhea, thirst, burning sensations, fainting, and yawning.
Trembling, labored breathing, and hiccups; burning heat and severe cold;
a proliferation of pustules, swelling, glandular swellings, and circular eruptions.
Eruptions, carbuncles, erysipelas,
and kiṭibhas arise for those bitten by them, along with their respective complications.
Whatever other specific symptoms may arise from them, one should quickly prescribe their remedies;
likewise for those caused by the provocation of latent poison (dūṣīviṣa) or from the application of poisonous ointments.
This is the symptomatology for those with potent poisons; now hear that for those with mild poisons:
salivation, anorexia, vomiting, heaviness of the head, and coldness.

The origin of eruptions (piḍakā), urticaria (koṭha), and itching (kaṇḍū) is according to the specific division of the humors (doṣa). One should prescribe powders for these using various types of formulations, such as gara and others.
Having thus described the varieties of latent poisons (dūṣīviṣa) as well as those from ointments,
I shall hereafter speak of the insects according to their different species.
By means of the general symptoms of being bitten and according to the sequence of curability and incurability:
Trikaṇṭaka, Kariṇī, Hastikakṣa, and Aparājita—
these four are explained as "thorny" (kaṇabha) stings that cause intense pain.
In one bitten by them, there occurs swelling, aching in the limbs, heaviness of the body, and the bite site becomes black.
1. A reflection of the sun; appearing tawny; multicolored.
There is one called the *godheraka* which is incomparable [in its effects]; thus there are five types of *godherakas*. In one bitten by them, swelling, burning, and pain occur.
In the case of the *godheraka*, these same symptoms appear, along with the manifestation of nodules (*granthi*) and fever.
The *galagolikā* is white, black, or marked with red streaks.
There are six [types of spiders]: the Raktamaṇḍalā, the Sarvaśvetā, and the Sarṣapikā. When bitten by these, with the exception of the Sarṣapikā, there occurs burning, swelling, and discharge.
From *sarṣapikā* fever, there is pain in the heart and diarrhea;
among those [fevers], *sarṣapikā* is fatal.
The *śatapadī* is rough,
black,
and variegated.
Tawny; yellowish; red.
Śvetā and Agniprabhā—
these are the eight; when bitten by them, there is swelling, pain, and burning in the heart.
From the white [wind] and the fire [bile], there is precisely this: excessive burning and fainting, as well as the appearance of white pustules.
The frogs are Kṛṣṇa,
Sāra, and Kuhaka.
Green, red, and the color of barley.
Bhṛkuṭī and Koṭika—these are the eight [venomous creatures]. In one bitten by them, itching occurs at the site of the bite, and yellow froth issues from the mouth.
From Bhṛkuṭī and Koṭika, these same symptoms arise, along with excessive burning, vomiting, and fainting.
When bitten by *viśvambharā* snakes, the bite site is covered with painful pustules the size of mustard seeds,
and the person suffers from a cold fever.

When bitten by *ahiṇḍuka* spiders, there occurs piercing pain, burning, itching, swelling, and delusion. When bitten by *kaṇḍūmaka* spiders, the body becomes yellowish and the victim is afflicted with vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and other such symptoms. When bitten by *śūkavṛntā* spiders, itching and urticarial patches increase, and the bristle-like hair (*śūka*) of the spider is visible at the site.
The *pipīlikā* with a thick head;
the *saṃvāhikā*; the *brahmaṇikā*.
The *aṅgulikā* and the *kapilikā*.

There are six [species] of variegated color (*citravarṇā*); when bitten by them, there is swelling at the site of the bite, along with a burning sensation and inflammation like that caused by contact with fire.
Flies are of three kinds: the *kāntārikā*, the black, and the tawny.
Madhūlikā, Kāṣāyī,
and Sthālikā— thus there are six; in one bitten by them, itching, swelling, burning, and pain occur.
From these two—sthālikā and kāṣāyī—there arises this very same [condition], namely the eruption of dark pustules (śyāvapiḍaka), as well as complications such as fever and other ailments;
both sthālikā and kāṣāyī are life-threatening.
The Maśakas are from the ocean; they are circular;
[there is] the Hastimaśaka.

Kṛṣṇa: There are five types of mountain-dwelling [insects]; from being bitten by them, there arises intense itching and swelling at the site of the bite. However, the mountain-dweller is characterized by symptoms identical to those of life-threatening insects.
When excessively scraped with the nails, pustules, burning sensations, and suppuration occur.
The symptoms of being bitten by leeches and their treatment have been described.
And there are these verses on this matter:
"The Godheraka, the Sthālikā, those with a radiance like white fire,
Bhṛkuṭī, and Koṭika— these do not attain success within a single lifetime."
From contact with the urine or feces of a corpse, or with poisonous substances,
there may arise itching, burning, urticaria, eruptions, pustules, and piercing pain.
Furthermore, an exudation accompanied by excessive moisture causes the skin to suppurate intensely;
in such a case, one should duly apply the treatments prescribed for a poisoned arrow-wound.

A bite by an insect or similar creature that is neither depressed nor elevated, characterized by excessive agitation and pain, and where the discomfort is contrary to what is expected, is extremely distressing.
One should treat those bitten by insects with extremely potent venom in the same manner as one treats snakebites;
however, for the three aforementioned types [of bites], the threefold therapeutic measures are beneficial.
In this condition, one should apply warm fomentation, ointments, and affusions;
however, one must exclude cases where the bite has caused fainting, or is afflicted by suppuration and sloughing.
One should perform all the anti-venomous procedures and numerous purificatory treatments with *śirīṣa*,
*kaṭukā*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *rajanī*, and rock salt (*saindhava*).
A well-prepared *utkārikā* (medicated poultice) made from milk, marrow, fat, ghee, ginger, long pepper, and *dāru*,
or from the *sthirādi* group of drugs, is beneficial for inducing perspiration.
One should not apply heat to a bite that has no swelling; I shall now describe the fumigations for scorpion stings, and I shall explain the various types of antidotes individually.
Kuṣṭha, vakra, vacā, pāṭhā, bilva root,
suvarcikā, house-soot, the two types of haridrā, and the poison of the trikaṇṭaka are beneficial.
Rajanī, agāradhūma, vakra,
and kuṣṭha derived from the palāśa tree constitute an antidote that destroys poison for those bitten by a galagolika.
Saffron, tagara, drumstick tree, padmaka, and the two types of turmeric—
this medicinal powder, ground with water, destroys the poison of a hundred centipedes.
Meṣaśṛṅgī, vacā, pāṭhā, nicula, rohiṇī, and water—
this is an antidote that removes poison for all those bitten by frogs.
This antidote, consisting of dhava, aśvagandhā, atibalā, balā, sāti, guhā, and guhā—
the latter being synonyms for viśvambharā— is a destroyer of poison for those bitten by snakes.
Śirīṣa, tagara, kuṣṭha, śāliparṇī, sahā,
and the two types of niśā constitute an antidote that destroys the poison of those bitten by ahiṇḍukas.
For those bitten by *kaṇḍūmaka* insects, cooling treatments are beneficial at night;
during the day, they do not succeed at all, being overcome by the power of the sun's rays.
Vakra, kuṣṭha, and apāmārga constitute an antidote for poison from thorny stalks;
alternatively, black ant-hill earth ground with the juice of bhṛṅga may be used.
For those bitten by ants, as well as by flies and mosquitoes,
an ointment made of black ant-hill clay mixed with cow urine [is prescribed].
When a swelling arises from being scratched by a fingernail, the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* is beneficial.
For those bitten by a *pratisūryaka*, one should treat them as if they were bitten by a snake. Scorpions are said to be of three kinds: those with mild, moderate, and potent venom.
Those produced from the fermentation of cow dung are mild; those arising from wood or brick are middling;
those produced from the decomposition of snakes are sharp, as are others originating from poison.
The inferior [degrees] are twelve, the middling are three, and the superior are fifteen;
these are proclaimed by number as ten and twenty respectively.
Black, dark-brown, variegated, pale-colored, resembling cow-urine, rough, and dark-blue;
yellow, smoky, hairy, resembling green grass, red, and white with a white belly—these are the dull-witted.
And these scorpions are provided with many segments in their tail region compared to others;
when bitten by these, there is pain, trembling, stiffness of the limbs, and the discharge of black and red blood.
When bitten on a limb, pain spreads upward, accompanied by burning, sweating, swelling at the site of the bite, and fever;
the urine becomes red, yellow, or tawny, the abdomen darkens, and all three joints become smoky-colored.
These three types of snakes—born from urine, excrement, and putrid eggs—are to be known as the intermediate species among the three classes of serpents.
Whichever of these a person is born from their lineage shall produce a manifestation of the humors (doṣas) corresponding to its own nature.
When bitten by one of medium potency, there is swelling of the tongue, obstruction of food, and violent fainting.
[The snakes] are white, variegated, dark, reddish, red, white, and those with red and blue bellies.
One is yellow and not red; another is blue and yellow; likewise, one is red and blue, and another is blue and white.
One is red and tawny, and as before, there is one with a single joint, one without joints, and one that has two joints.
These scorpions, which are known as thieves of life-force, should be understood to be of various forms and colors, and even terrible;
their birth is declared to be from the decay of snakes, or from the bodies of those killed by poison.
When bitten by these, the onset of serpent-venom, the eruption of blisters, delusions, burning sensations, and fever occur;
black blood flows violently from the apertures, and consequently, one is swiftly deprived of life.
One should treat a bite by a venomous snake of fierce, moderate, or mild potency like a snake-bite.
Having fomented the site of the bite, one should scarify it and rub it with medicinal powders.
One should apply the tips of *surasā* leaves, ground with turmeric, rock salt, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), the fruits and flowers of *śirīṣa*,
and the sour juice of *mātuluṅga*, along with cow’s urine.
For massage and fomentation, cow dung that is pleasantly warm is considered beneficial;
for drinking, ghee mixed with honey or milk with plenty of sugar is recommended.
One should sprinkle the bite of those with mild venom with oil prepared from *cakra* seeds,
or alternatively, with lukewarm oil processed with the *vidārī* group of drugs.
One should apply *utkārika* fomentation and bandage the area with anti-venomous poultices;
or alternatively, one may give very cold molasses-water mixed with the four spices (*cāturjātaka*).
Drink should be given to him— either milk with jaggery or cold water—
as well as peacock feathers, chicken feathers, rock salt, oil, and ghee.
When applied as smoke, it quickly destroys the poison born of a scorpion;
likewise, safflower, turmeric, nightshade, or kodrava grass [may be used].
This incense, smeared with ghee and applied to the region of the anus,
will quickly destroy the poison arising from insects and that of the scorpion.
The poison of a spider is most terrible and most difficult to discern;
it is also the most difficult to treat for physicians of dull intellect.
When there is such doubt as to whether this [food] is poisonous or non-poisonous,
one should administer only an anti-poisonous medicine that is not incompatible [with the patient's condition].
Indeed, the application of medicines is appropriate for one afflicted by poison;
however, when applied to a man who is free from poison, that medicine results only in suffering.
Therefore, with every effort, the determination of poison must be known;
for by not knowing the true nature of poison, a physician may cause a person's death.
Just as a tree, when it is merely sprouting with a shoot, does not manifest its distinct species,
even so their poison, as soon as it is diffused through the body, is indeed most difficult to perceive.
On the first day, it may be slightly itchy, moving, accompanied by a small swelling, and of indistinct color;
on the second day, it becomes swollen at the edges, depressed in the center, and its form becomes clearly manifest.
Within three days it manifests its form here; on the fourth day, the poison reaches its peak of provocation.
Beyond that day, it produces in the living being the various disorders arising from the aggravation of the poison.
On the sixth day, it spreads and intensely envelops all the vital points (marmas). On the seventh day, having excessively pervaded the body and become fully developed, it destroys the mortal being.
Those spiders whose venom is sharp, fierce, and virulent kill a man within seven nights;
others, whose venom is said to be of medium potency, may kill him after even more than that time.
Those [insects] whose venomous potency is said to be minimal destroy [the victim] in merely half a month;
therefore, the physician should exert effort here with anti-venomous applications from the moment the bite occurs.
Spiders discharge poison in seven ways—through saliva, claws, urine, fangs, dust, feces, and their sexual organ; this poison is endowed with fierce, moderate, or weak potency.
They say that a bite by a nail-clawed [insect] is characterized by pustules and eruptions, is firm, has shallow roots, is caused by saliva, and involves mild pain;
furthermore, there is swelling, itching, horripilation, and a sensation of fuming at the site of the bite on the tip of the nail.
Know that the bite with blackness in the center and blood around the edges is torn;
know that the bite which is fierce, hard, discolored, and has a firm circular patch is caused by the fangs.
Know that the eruption born from the impurities of the skin and the organs is pale, like a ripe, pure *pīlu* fruit;
this much has been declared, and I shall now describe the ancient [diseases] originating from spiders.
The general symptoms of a bite— whether incurable or curable— and the treatment according to its specific characteristics have been described.
Once, it is said, Viśvāmitra, the best of kings,
went to the hermitage and provoked the anger of Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent of sages.
From the forehead of that enraged sage, drops of sweat fell at the mere sight [of him], possessing a brilliance equal to his own.
When the grass was cut by the great seer and gathered for the sake of the cow,
from that were born these terrible creatures of various forms and potent venom; they exist for the purpose of doing harm to men, their weapons, and their vehicles.
Because drops of perspiration from the Sage fell upon the grass as it was being cut, they are therefore called "lūtās"; and by number, they are sixteen.
Spiders (lūtā) are known to be of two kinds: those that are curable with difficulty and those that are incurable.
Therefore, eight of them are curable with difficulty, while an equal number—eight—are to be avoided.
Trimaṇḍalā, Śvetā, Kapilā,
Pītikā, Ālamūtraviṣā, Raktā, Kasanā, and the eighth is remembered as [Kṛṣṇā].
When bitten by them, there occurs pain in the head, itching at the site of the bite, and a sensation of distress;
furthermore, diseases characterized by phlegm (ślaiṣmika) and wind (vātika) arise specifically.
Sauvarṇikā, Lājavarṇā, Jālinyā,
Eṇīpadī, Kṛṣṇā, Agnivarṇā, Kākāṇḍā, and Mālāguṇā as the eighth.
When bitten by them, there occurs swelling at the site of the bite, discharge of blood,
fever, burning sensation, diarrhea, and diseases born of the three doṣas.
There are pustules of various forms, large circular patches,
and great swellings that are soft, red, dark-brown, and unstable.
This is the general characteristic of the bite of all spiders;
I shall now describe their specific characteristics along with their medical treatment.
When the *trimaṇḍala* [wind] is afflicted, black blood flows from the ear and it tears;
there is deafness, turbid vision, as well as a burning sensation in the eyes.
In that regard, the roots of arka, rajanī, nākulī,
and pṛśniparṇikā are recommended for use as a drink, as well as for nasal drops, ointments, and collyriums.
At the site of the bite of a Śvetā spider, there appears a white pustule that is itchy,
accompanied by burning, fainting, and fever, and it causes spreading inflammation, discharge, and pain.
In that case, sandalwood, rāsnā, cardamom,
hareṇu, nutmeg, kuṣṭha, lāmajjaka, vakra, and nalada constitute a beneficial anti-venom.
From the bite of a Kapilā spider, there arises a copper-colored, firm pustule;
furthermore, there is heaviness of the head, burning sensation, darkness of vision, and vertigo.
In that regard, the barks of padmaka, kuṣṭha, elā, karañja,
and kakubha, as well as sthirā, arkaparṇī, apāmārga, dūrvā, and brāhmī, are destroyers of poison.
In the case of a bite by a *pītikā* [female snake], there appears a firm yellow pustule;
furthermore, there will be vomiting, fever, pain in the head, and likewise in the eyes.
In that regard, the following are recommended: kuṭaja, uśīra, tuṅga, padmaka, and vañjula;
as well as the barks of śirīṣa, kiṇihī, śelu, kadamba, and kakubha.
When afflicted by the Alavi poison, there appear eruptions like mustard seeds on a bite that resembles a red mark,
accompanied by dryness of the palate and a burning sensation.
Therein were priyaṅgu, hrībera, kuṣṭha, lāmajja, and vañjula; agada, śatapuṣpā, along with pippala and the sprouts of the vaṭa tree.
It is putrid, with a discharge of urine and poison, spreading, and characterized by black blood;
it is accompanied by cough, dyspnea, vomiting, fainting, fever, and a burning sensation.
An ointment (agada) composed of realgar, red ochre, licorice, costus, sandalwood, and padmaka,
mixed with honey and the marrow of the *lāmajja* plant, is prescribed for that [condition].
A bite from a female snake is characterized by pale pustules, accompanied by burning and moisture;
it should be recognized as being red at its edges and associated with blood.
In that case, a medicinal preparation (agada) should be prepared with water, sandalwood, uśīra, padmaka,
as well as arjuna and śelu, and the bark of āmrātaka.
From the bite of a *kasana* spider, slimy and cold blood flows;
cough and dyspnea also occur there, and the treatment for a *raktalūtā* spider bite is prescribed in that context.
The bite of a black female [scorpion] has the smell of feces and little blood;
it is accompanied by fever, fainting, vomiting, burning sensation, cough, and dyspnea.
In that regard, the Pratyākhyāya-agada is prescribed with elā, vakra, sarpākṣī, gandhanākulī, and candana,
combined with mahāsugandhi.
In the case of the Agnivaktrā [venom], there is burning at the site of the bite, excessive discharge, and likewise fever,
accompanied by sucking pain, itching, horripilation, and eruptions with blisters.
In this case, having rejected the treatment for Kṛṣṇāpraśamana,
one should employ Sārivā, Uśīra, Yaṣṭyāhvā, Candana, Utpala, and Padmaka.
In all cases of poisoning, the physician should administer the bark of the *śleṣmātaka* tree,
as well as *akṣīva* and *pippalī*, in every possible manner.
Eight types of poison are said to be difficult to cure, and two are accidental;
learn from me the characteristics of those whose toxic potency is irresistible.
It is dark-colored, has the appearance of gold, is frothy, and smells like fish;
it is accompanied by dyspnea, cough, fever, thirst, and extremely severe fainting.
In the case of a bite by a lizard of the *lājavarṇā* species, dark-colored, putrid blood flows;
burning, fainting, diarrhea, and headache also arise.
The bite of the Jālinī is terrible; it is marked with stripes and spreads about.
Stiffness, labored breathing, an increase in darkness (loss of consciousness), and dryness of the palate arise.
The bite of an eṇīpadma is like a black sesame seed in shape;
it is accompanied by thirst, fainting, fever, vomiting, cough, and dyspnea.
A bite by a *kākāṇḍikā* spider causes a pale-red lesion accompanied by intense pain;
it further gives rise to excessive thirst, fainting, labored breathing, heart disease, hiccups, and cough.
The portion of the garland becomes red, its fragrance turns into smoke, and it causes intense pain;
it falls apart in many ways, accompanied by burning sensations, fainting, and fever.
Even in cases declared incurable, one should quickly reject them and apply treatment—
excluding cauterization and excision— according to the specific aggravation of the humors.
As soon as a living being has been bitten by these spiders, which are characterized by their specific symptoms,
the wise physician should properly extract the fang-mark with a lancet.
One who knows the procedure should perform the excision of a bite that is not on a vital spot, which is free from fever and other complications,
and characterized by only slight swelling.
Then one should apply medicinal ointments mixed with honey and rock salt,
as well as those made from priyaṅgu, rajanī, kuṣṭha, samaṅgā, and madhuka.
One should cause [the patient] to drink sārivā, madhuka, drākṣā, payasyā, kṣīramoraṭa,
or alternatively, vidārī, gokṣuraka, honey, and madhuka.
One should sprinkle [the patient] with well-cooled decoctions of the bark of milky trees;
one should treat the complications according to the specific dosha using anti-poisonous remedies alone.
In this condition, one should administer nasal drops, collyrium, ointment, potions, medicated smoke, as well as pressed-out juices (avapīḍa), gargles,
strong purificatory therapies for both the upper and lower tracts, and even venesection.
A physician skilled in treating vitiated [wounds] should treat all wounds caused by insect bites as well as those caused by snake bites, from the onset of burning and suppuration.
Once the swelling has subsided, the removal of the *karṇikā* (plug) is beneficial;
[this is done with] neem leaves, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, safflower, and honey.
Having abandoned guggulu, rock salt, yeast, the excrement of a pigeon,
and food that increases poison, a communal meal is beneficial.
Indeed, for a stable abscess caused by all types of poisons,
one should treat it by first scarifying it and then applying purificatory agents mixed with honey.
Thus, the symptoms of being bitten by each of the one hundred and sixty-seven types of insects have been described in detail, followed immediately by their medical treatment.
These one hundred and twenty chapters have been declared according to their divisions; hereafter, I shall speak of the matters indicated but not yet fully described in this Uttara-khaṇḍa.
Because the Vedas are eternal and likewise imperishable,
and because their fruits are perceived and they are beneficial to embodied beings.
Because it expands upon the meaning of a collection of words and because it is honored by embodied beings,
we have heard of nothing more meritorious than medical science.
Having upheld the stainless doctrine, highly esteemed by the seer Indraprabhāva— the source of immortality and the teacher of physicians—
one rejoices both in this world and after passing away, provided one follows the prescribed diet and conduct.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, named the Chapter on Insects, in the Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||8||
Thus ends the fifth section, the Kalpasthāna, in the Suśruta Saṃhitā composed by the great sage Suśruta, the disciple of the Blessed Lord Śrī Dhanvantari, as instructed by him.
Now begins the Uttaratantra. Chapter One.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on complications (aupadravika).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
In the twentieth century of chapters,
I have repeatedly stated that I shall fully explain these matters in various ways in the subsequent [sections].
Now I shall proclaim that supreme and most excellent tantra,
wherein various kinds of diseases are taught in their entirety.
Those causes of diseases in children which have been mentioned in the Śālākya-tantra, those proclaimed by the Lord of Videha, and those seen in detail elsewhere; [all these are here described].
Those diseases which were described by the supreme sages within the six branches of medical treatment, as well as those known as afflictions and adventitious disorders;
The sixty-three combinations of tastes, as well as the regimen for maintaining health,
the appropriate applications and methods, and likewise the classifications of the humors (doṣas).
In this [work], various topics concerning the causes and means of treating diseases have been declared;
it is a great treatise, as difficult to fathom as the ocean.
First, I shall describe the diseases located in the head,
according to their number, their symptoms, and in the order of those that are curable and incurable.
The physician should know that the eyeball is two fingers in thickness, equal in size to the belly of one's own thumb,
and measures two and a half fingers in diameter on all sides.
Well-rounded and shaped like a cow’s udder, it is the source of the qualities of all beings;
its flesh arises from the earth, its blood from fire, its blackness from wind, and its whiteness from water.
From space, the tear-ducts and the eyeball arise;
and herein I shall describe vision just as an expert would explain it.
The black circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) is said to be one-third of the length of the eye;
those expert in vision maintain that the pupil (dṛṣṭi) is located at the seventh part from the black circle.
One should understand that the circles, the joints, and the membranes of the eye are five, six,
and six respectively.
The circles of the eyelashes, the eyelids, the white [sclera], the black [iris], and the pupil—
these four middle ones increase in size in regular succession, while the final one increases even more than the preceding.
The junction located at the eyelashes and eyelids is one; another is located at the eyelid and the white of the eye (śukla);
yet another is located at the white and the black of the eye (kṛṣṇa); another is located at the black of the eye and the pupil (dṛṣṭi);
then the sixth is known to be located at the inner corner (kanīnaka) and the outer corner (apāṅga).
One should know that there are two layers of the path [of vision] and four others in the eye;
in these, the disease known as timira arises, which is extremely terrible.
The external [element] rests upon fire and water; among those, another rests upon flesh;
the third layer rests upon fat, and the bone rests upon the other.
It is held that the abundance of these— of the vessels (sirās), the tendons (kaṇḍarās), the fat (medas), and the temporal muscle (kālakā)— is equal to one-fifth part of the vision.
The humors (guṇas) are superior to time; phlegm (śleṣman), joined with the vessels, is located in the binding of the eyes.
It is caused by the humors (doṣas), which have become disordered and moved upward, following the course of the vessels.
Extremely dreadful diseases arise in the regions of the eyes;
therein, there is turbidity, agitation, tearing, itching, and discharge.
It is afflicted by itching, piercing pain, redness, and other symptoms with unmanifest characteristics;
it is accompanied by pain in the eyelid margins and resembles being filled with bristles.
Just as one might previously have seen the eye impaired in its functions regarding forms,
so too the wise man, upon seeing it, would realize that it is indeed possessed by a defect.
Having identified the origin [of the disease] therein, one should administer medical treatment according to the specific dosha;
otherwise, eye diseases will become powerful.
In brief, the yoga of action consists of avoiding the primary causes and the counteracting of [the imbalances of] wind and the other humors; this will be explained again in detail.
From entering water when tormented by heat, from gazing at distant objects, and from the reversal of dreams;
from the impact of afflictions such as excessive weeping, anger, grief, and suppression [of natural urges], and from excessive sexual intercourse.

Due to the consumption of fermented gruel, sour liquids, horse gram, and black gram; from the suppression of natural urges; from sweating or the inhalation of smoke; from the obstruction of vomiting or excessive emesis;
and from the suppression of tears or intense staring, the bodily humors (doṣas) produce disorders in the eyes.
From wind (vāta) there are ten, likewise from bile (pitta) ten, and from phlegm (kapha) thirteen;
from blood (rakta) sixteen are to be known, and those born from all [three] together are twenty-five.
Likewise, there are two more external diseases; thus, seventy-six diseases are recorded.
These include hatādhimantha, nimiṣa, and gambhīrikā of the vision.
Furthermore, those eyelid diseases caused by Vāta that have been struck down by Vāta do not succeed [in being cured];
however, Kāca (cataract) caused by that [Vāta] is palliable, while those associated with other forms of Māruta are curable.
Dry ophthalmia (śuṣkākṣipāka), adhimantha, syanda, and disorders arising from vāta;
as well as the condition known as hrasvajāḍya and bilious (paittika) lacrimation—these are incurable.
Parimlāyin, Nīla, Yāpya, Kāca, as well as those consisting of that [Kāca], Abhiṣyanda, Adhimantha, Amlādhyuṣita, and Śuktikā;
A vision impaired by pitta and the condition of seeing smoke are curable;
however, a discharge born of kapha is incurable, and cataract (kāca) caused by that same humor is palliable.
Abhiṣyanda, adhimantha, balāsagrathita,
dṛṣṭi afflicted by phlegm, pothakya, and lagaṇa;
Krimigranthi, pariklinna, vartmaśukla, arma, piṣṭaka,
and śleṣmopanāha are declared to be curable among those diseases arising from kapha.
The discharge of blood, resembling the secretion of a goat, accompanied by hemorrhoids and ulcers,
as well as cataract (kāca) arising from that [condition], are declared to be incurable or merely manageable (yāpya).
Furthermore, avraṇaśukra, śoṇitārma, and arjuna— these are indeed curable among the disorders born of blood when occurring on the day of the moon's change (parvan).
Pūyāsrāva, nākulāndhya, akṣipākātyaya, and alajī are incurable when caused by all three doṣas; kāca and the disorder of the eyelashes (pakṣmakopa) are palliable.
The disease known as vartmāvabandha, the pustules that appear on the vessels, and those which are prastāryarma, adhimāṃsārma, snāyvarma, and utsaṅginī; |||
Pūyālasa, arbuda, śyāva, kardama-vartman, as well as arśo-vartman, śuṣka-arśas, and śarkarā-vartman; these indeed [are the diseases].
Pāka with swelling and without swelling, Bahalavartma,
Aklinnavartma, Kumbhīkā, and Bisavartma are curable.
The two types arising from external causes—the one with signs and the signless—are incurable;
this is declared to be the summary of the seventy-six disorders.
Among them, nine are dependent on the junctions (sandhi), twenty-one are born from the paths (vartman),
eleven are in the white portion (śuklabhāga), and four are born in the black portion (kṛṣṇabhāga).
All seventeen types arise from the internal substratum (āśraya), while twelve indeed arise from the external;
two diseases are declared to be produced by external factors and are extremely terrible.
I shall explain these further by way of their number, symptoms, and treatments.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "On Complications," within the Śālākyatantra, which is part of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||1||
The Second Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of diseases located in the joints.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Pūyālasa, Sopanāha, the various discharges (srāvas), Parvaṇikā, Alajī,
and Krimigranthi— these nine diseases are to be known as located in the joints.
A suppurated swelling arising from the joints that discharges thick, foul-smelling pus is called *pūyālasa*.
A small, non-suppurating glandular swelling (*granthi*) at the junction of the pupil, characterized primarily by itching and lacking pain, is known as *upanāha*.
Having entered through the path of the lacrimal ducts, the humors (doṣas) may produce painless discharges from the inner corner of the eye;
some indeed call these discharges "netranāḍī" (eye-duct), and I shall describe its fourfold symptoms.

That which flows as pus from a joint during suppuration is designated as *pūyāsrāva*, which is of many forms. That which flows as white, thick, and slimy, and is painless, is designated as *śleṣmāsrāva*.
The discharge of blood arising from the blood is bloody, hot, not small in quantity, and not too thick;
the discharge of bile flows from the middle of the joints, appearing yellowish-blue, hot, and watery.
Parvaṇī should be known as copper-colored, thin, accompanied by burning and pain, reddish, and characterized by circular swellings at the joints;
alajī occurs at the junction of the black and white parts of the eye, manifesting with the same symptoms previously described.
Worms born in the junction cause *krimigranthi* (worm-nodules) and itching of the eyelids and lashes;
appearing in various forms and moving at the junction of the eyelid and the white of the eye, they corrupt the interior of the eye.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Diseases Affecting the Joints," in the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||2||
The third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of diseases located in the eyelids.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
When the individual or combined humors (doṣas),
having increased excessively, occupy the eyelids and pervade the vessels, they remain there localized within the eyelids.
Then, having increased the flesh and the blood, they quickly produce disorders localized in the eyelids; learn their names from me.
Then there are Utsaṅginī, Kumbhīkā, Pothakī, Vartmaśarkarā,
as well as Arśovartma, Śuṣkārśas, and Añjananāmikā.
Thick eyelid (bahalam vartma), as well as the disease that binds the eyelid (vartmāvabandhaka),
those known as afflicted and muddy eyelids (kliṣṭa-kardama-vartman), and likewise dark-brown eyelids (śyāva-vartma).
The moistened eyelid, the non-moistened eyelid, that which is struck by Vāta, as well as the tumor (arbuda), the nimesha, and that which is known as the blood-piles (śoṇitārśas); |||
Lagaṇa, viśanāman, and likewise pakṣmakopa—
these twenty-one disorders are located in the eyelids (vartman).
Having indicated them by their names, we shall now describe them by their characteristics:
that which is inward-facing, situated on the outer fold, and located below the path.
The condition known as Vijñeyotsaṅginī is characterized by a mass of pustules resembling the seeds of the Kumbhīka plant appearing on the eyelids.
Those pustules which, when burst, cause swelling are called *kumbhīkā-piḍakās*. Those that are exuding, itchy, heavy, resembling red mustard seeds,
and painful are known by the name *pothakīs*.
Covered with very fine and dense pustules,
that which consists of coarse and large pustules is to be known as *vartma-śarkarā*.
When small, rough, slightly painful pustules resembling the seeds of the *ervāru* gourd appear on the eyelid,
that condition is called *darśavartma*.
Long, hard, stiff, and harsh, arising along the path [of the rectum],
this disease is declared to be known by the name "dry hemorrhoid" (śuṣkārśas).
A copper-colored,
soft, and minute pustule arising on the eyelid, accompanied by burning and pricking sensations and mild pain, is to be known as *añjananāmikā*.
One should recognize Bahala-vartma as that condition in which the eyelid is thickened all around by pustules that are equal in color and uniform in appearance.
When a person's eyelid is itchy, slightly painful, and swollen,
