and cannot close evenly over the eye, that is known as bandha-vartman (eyelid closure).
When the eyelid is copper-colored, slightly painful, and even,
yet suddenly becomes red, one should designate that as *kliṣṭavartman*.
Furthermore, when the vitiated blood, joined with bile, causes a burning sensation,
it then reaches a state of moistness and is called Vartmakardama.
When the external eyelid is dark-brown, swollen, painful,
burning, itchy, and exuding moisture, that condition is known as Śyāvavartman (dark-brown eyelid).
Painless, swollen on the outside, moist and oozing within,
and characterized by excessive itching and pricking— this is called klinnavartman.
When the eyelids, though washed again and again,
continue to stick together because they have not yet ripened, one should know that condition to be *aklinna-vartman*.
One should recognize this as *vātahata* (paralysis due to wind), whether it is painful or painless, characterized by loosened joints, lack of movement, and an eyelid that does not close.
An irregular, painless, knotted growth situated at the edge of the eyelid,
reddish and hanging down, is to be recognized as an arbuda in men.
When the Vayu enters the nimeṣaṇī veins located within the eyelids, it excessively agitates the lids;
this condition is known as the disease Nimeṣa.
The soft sprouts located on the anal folds, though cut and sliced, continue to grow;
these hemorrhoidal growths arising from blood are accompanied by burning, itching, and pain.
A painless, unripened, hard, thick, itching,
and slimy nodule arising on the eyelid, measuring the size of a jujube fruit (kola), is called a lagaṇa.
When the eyelid is swollen and covered with many minute holes,
like a lotus stalk submerged within water, it is known as bisavartman.
The humors, having reached the follicles of the eyelashes, produce lashes that are sharp-tipped and rough;
irritated by them, the eye suffers pain.
Peace is produced by repeatedly lifting [the lashes];
that which hates wind, heat, and fire is called *pakṣmakopa*.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Diseases of the Eyelids," in the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||3||
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of diseases affecting the white part of the eye (śukla).
Then the Blessed One Dhanvantari spoke.
Indeed, there are five diseases known as prastāri, śukla, kṣataja, adhimāṃsa, and snāyvarma;
as well as śuktikā, arjuna, piṣṭaka, sirājāla, and those which are piḍakas.
There are indeed eleven diseases in the white portion (śuklabhāga) of the eye along with balāsagrathita;
among them, prastāri is well-known here as a thin, widespread growth in the white portion that has a blood-like luster and is slightly blue.

They describe the one called *śukla* as soft and white; it increases slowly and evenly here in the white portion. That flesh which undergoes accumulation in the white portion and resembles a lotus in appearance is taught as *lohitārma*.
One should recognize as *māṃsārma* that which is extensive, soft, thick, resembling the color of the liver, or dark-brown;
whereas that which is white, consists of flesh that has increased, is rough, and very pale, is declared to be *snāyvārma*.
Those spots which are dark-brown, resembling flesh, and have the luster of a mother-of-pearl shell on the white of the eye are called *śukti*.
That single spot which resembles the blood of a hare and is located upon the white of the eye, they call *arjuna*.
That which is sunken, resembling water, and then becomes a white, ground-like speck that is well-rounded is called *piṣṭaka*.
That which has the appearance of a web, is hard, nodular, large, and reddish is known here as *santāna*, bearing the designation "web."
One should recognize those white pustules, covered with veins and arising near the black portion [of the eye], as *sirājā*.
When the white portion becomes like the luster of bell-metal, resembling a drop of water, it should be known as the condition called *balāsaka*, which is neither soft nor painful.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Diseases Affecting the Semen," in the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||4||
The Fifth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the diagnosis of diseases affecting the black part of the eye (kṛṣṇagatarogavijñānīya).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Whether it be ulcerated or non-ulcerated, as well as pākātyaya and ajakā—
these four disorders located in the black portion (kṛṣṇa) have been previously described in summary.
Indeed, when the form appears sunken and feels as if pierced by a needle,
and if it exudes a warm discharge accompanied by excessive pain, they call that wound *śukra* (white).
That which is not near the vision, nor deeply penetrated, nor does it flow, nor is it painless,
nor is the semen double— that never attains success.
A swelling that has a gap in its center, or is covered with flesh, or is mobile yet attached to vessels, or causes loss of vision;
one that involves two layers of skin, or is red at the edges, or has been present for a long time—these should be rejected as incurable.

That [eye disease] in which there is the falling of hot tears and pustules on the black part (kṛṣṇa), and the white part (śukra) resembles a mung bean, is declared by some to be incurable; so too is that which is like the wing of a partridge.
When a white, flowing discharge appears on a dark area, not excessively painful and free from tears,
resembling a clear cloud in the sky, they say that such an unscarred ulcer is most easily curable.
They say that when the *śukra* (vitreous humor) has become deep-seated, thick, and long-standing, it is difficult to treat;
for in such a case, the entire black circle (*asitamaṇḍala*) is covered by a vitiated humor that resembles white.
They call that *akṣipākātyaya* (suppuration of the eye) arising from *akṣika*, characterized by intense pain.
It resembles the dung of a goat, is painful, reddish, and has blood-streaked, slimy tears.
Having burst open the black part (*kṛṣṇa*), a swelling (*pracaya*) develops; one should diagnose that as *ajāka*.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Diseases Affecting the Black Part [of the Eye]," in the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||5||
The Sixth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of diseases affecting the entire body.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Four types of syanda (blepharitis) are taught here, and likewise four types of adhimantha;
together with the two types of pāka—those accompanied by swelling and those without swelling—these ten are thus fully described.
Hatādhimantha, anilaparyaya, śuṣkākṣipāka, and likewise anyataḥ-vāta; as well as dṛṣṭi, amlādhyuṣita, and both utpāta and harṣa—these are all varieties [of vāta].
Generally, all eye diseases have their root cause in *abhiṣyanda* (ocular congestion);
therefore, a wise person should promptly treat the manifesting *abhiṣyanda* for the sake of well-being.
Pricking pain, stiffness, horripilation, a sensation of rubbing, roughness, headache, dryness,
and cold tearing occur when the eyes are afflicted by Vāta.
Burning, suppuration, a longing for cold, smoking, an overflow of tears,
hot lacrimation, and yellowness of the eyes occur when the eyes are afflicted by pitta.
A desire for warmth, heaviness, swelling of the eyes, itching, exudation, whiteness,
excessive coldness, and frequent slimy discharge— these occur when the eyes are afflicted by phlegm (kapha).
A coppery hue of the ears, redness of the eyes, and the surrounding regions of the eyes being excessively red,
as well as whatever symptoms belong to pitta, occur when the eyes are affected by blood (rakta).
From these aforementioned morbid humors (abhiṣyandas) occurring in men who do not undergo treatment,
there arise as many types of adhimantha, accompanied by intense pain in the eye.
One should recognize Adhimantha by its specific symptoms as being like the eyes being excessively torn out or churned,
and likewise affecting half of the head.
It was as if his eye were being plucked out or churned like a fire-drill;
agitated by the friction, pressure, and tearing of the flesh, it became turbid.
That condition by which half of the head is accompanied by contraction, bursting pain, distension, trembling, and aching is Adhimantha caused by Vāta.
Covered with red streaks and discharging fluid, it feels as if it is being scorched by fire;
resembling a lump of liver, it burns as if wounded and smeared with caustic alkali.
When the eyelids are swollen and ripened at their edges, accompanied by perspiration and a yellowish vision,
and the patient suffers from fainting and a burning sensation in the head, the eyes are afflicted with Adhimantha caused by Pitta.
It is characterized by swelling, though not excessively inflamed, accompanied by discharge and itching,
and possesses coldness, heaviness, sliminess, impurities, and horripilation.
One sees forms with pain, as if turbid and filled with dust;
accompanied by nasal congestion and headaches, it is afflicted by an excess of phlegm.
Resembling the bandhujīva flower, it throbbs and is intolerant to touch;
accompanied by a bloody discharge and piercing pain, the patient sees the quarters of the sky as if they were ablaze with fire.
When a black portion is observed like a ripe *ariṣṭa* fruit submerged in blood,
and that which is radiant has red margins, it is known as *raktādhimanthita*.
Adhimantha arising from phlegm destroys vision within seven nights; that born from blood does so within five nights;
those two arising from wind destroy it within six nights; and that caused by bile destroys it immediately due to improper conduct.
Accompanied by itching, exudation, and tearing, it resembles a ripe udumbara fruit;
it is characterized by burning, horripilation, copperiness, swelling, pricking pain, and heaviness.
In Netrapāka with swelling (Śophaja), blood flows repeatedly and copiously, being hot, cold, or slimy;
it is accompanied by intense irritation and suppuration.
In cases of non-inflammatory ophthalmia (aśophaja-netrapāka), the symptoms are devoid of swelling;
however, if neglected, when a wind-natured Adhimantha forcibly afflicts the eye with intense pains,
it becomes incurable— this disease is indeed known as Hatādhimantha.
When the wind (vāyu), situated within the vessels, strikes and distorts the vision, it produces Hatādhimantha; the wise know this to be incurable.
When the vitiated wind does not circulate through the eyelashes, the eyes, and the eyebrows,
but instead causes pains in these areas alternately, they call that condition *vātaparyāya*.
That eye which is contracted, whose eyelids are harsh and cruel, whose vision is blurred when looking,
and which is extremely painful upon opening— it is an eye afflicted by *śuṣkākṣipāka* (dry ophthalmia).
If the Vāyu (wind) located in the hollows of the ears, the head, the jaw, or the nape of the neck, or elsewhere,
should cause excessive pain in the eyebrows or the eyes, they call that condition Anyatovāta.
When the eye is completely covered by sour food that causes a burning sensation,
becoming swollen and reddish-blue, such a condition is said to be afflicted by sourness (amlādhyuṣita).
Whether painless or accompanied by pain, if the lines of the iris become copper-colored and repeatedly fade away on all sides, this disease is designated as *sirotpāta*.
If sirōtpāta is neglected due to delusion, it becomes the disease known as sirāpraharṣa;
blood flows profusely from the vessels, appearing coppery and clear, and the patient is unable to see properly.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Diseases Affecting All Parts of the Body," in the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||6||
The Seventh Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the diagnosis of diseases affecting the eye.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
It is the size of a marura leaf, born from the refinement of the five elements,
blazing with imperishable splendors like the light of a firefly or a spark.
Those who contemplate the eye state that the vision of humans is covered by an external film in the form of a cavity, and is naturally adapted to cold.
We shall now describe the twelve terrible diseases residing therein,
as well as the symptoms of *timira* that has entered the layers of the eye.
When a deranged humor, having reached the interior through the channels,
becomes excessively aggravated and is localized in the first layer of the pupil (paṭala) of the eye;
One perceives all forms as if unmanifest;
when the second layer [of the eye] is affected, vision becomes utterly confused.
She sees flies, mosquitoes, hairs, and cobwebs;
she sees circles, banners, rays of light, and earrings.
He perceives various flickering rain-clouds and darknesses,
and he regards forms that are at a distance as being nearby.
Due to the confusion of the visual field, one does not see what is nearby nor what is far away;
even with great effort, one may fail to perceive the loop of a needle.
When it has entered the third layer, one sees above and below;
even great forms appear as if covered by a cloth.
One perceives ears, nose, and eyes as distorted;
and the vision becomes colored according to whichever humor (doṣa) is most powerful.

When the fault is situated below, one does not perceive what is nearby or what is far away; when it is situated above, one does not perceive what is at the side; and likewise, when the fault is at the side, one does not perceive things situated at the side.
When a defect is present all around, one sees things as if they were crowded together;
when a defect is located in the center of the vision, one perceives a single object as double.
When [the object] is situated in two ways, one sees it as threefold, and when it is not fixed, one sees it as manifold;
this is indeed the defect called *timira*, which has reached the fourth layer [of the eye].
That which obstructs vision from all sides is called liṅganāśa;
even when that great disease has not yet fully developed and has become characterized by darkness.
He beholds the moon and the sun together with the stars in the firmament,
as well as the stainless splendors and radiant luminaries.
That very loss of vision is designated as *nīlikā* and *akāśa*;
therein, due to the derangement of *vāta*, one perceives forms as if they were spinning.
Due to bile (pitta), a person perceives the sun, fireflies, Indra’s bow (the rainbow), and lightning as turbid, reddish, and distorted.
One sees forms variegated with peacock feathers, as well as blue and black;
through phlegm (kapha), one sees forms that are glossy and white.
One may see things exceedingly subtle, white as a cow's tail-whisk or like white clouds, and even a mass of clouds in a cloudless sky.
Just as a person's states of numbness are washed away by water.
Likewise, by means of blood, various kinds of darknesses are produced.
One sees [visions] that are green, dark-brown, black, and smoke-colored;
due to the derangement of the humors (sannipāta), one perceives them as variegated and distorted.
He sees all the luminaries everywhere, either in many ways or in pairs, or else with deficient or redundant limbs.
The pitta, becoming faint and intensified by the fiery energy of the blood, causes the directions to appear yellow;
likewise, one perceives the rising sun as if it were [yellow].

I shall describe the sixfold destruction of the signs [of the self] through passions, as well as trees scattered by fireflies and by their very splendors; hereafter, I shall speak of the destruction of the marks.
Redness is declared to be caused by wind (vāta), while from bile (pitta) it becomes faded or blue;
from phlegm (kapha) it is white, but that born from blood (rakta) is red; when all the humors (doṣas) are involved, its form is variegated.

In the disease arising from blood (raktaja), a circular patch (maṇḍala) appears in the vision with the appearance of thick glass or fire; in the case of the parimlāyin disease, the circular patch becomes faded and blue.
Due to the subsidence of the humors (doṣas), there may sometimes be a spontaneous vision therein;
the orb appears reddish, flickering, and rough due to the influence of wind (vāta).
From bile (pitta), the circular patch is bluish, resembling the color of bell-metal or yellow;
from phlegm (śleṣman), it is thick, oily, and as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.
Like a white drop of water resting upon a moving lotus petal,
it contracts excessively in the heat and expands in the shade.
And as the eye is being pressed, that circle spreads forth—
a circle consisting of blood, resembling coral and the petals of a lotus.
In the destruction of the vision (liṅganāśa) caused by the three doṣas, there occurs a variegated affection of the sight;
indeed, the specific symptoms of each respective doṣa manifest in all of them.
There are six types of loss of vision (liṅganāśa), these six diseases, and likewise six others based on the visual faculty;
among them, one man has a vision scorched by pitta, another by kapha, and yet another is a "smoke-seer" (dhūmadarśin).
Short-sightedness, blindness like that of a mongoose, a perception of depth, and likewise [distorted] vision—
these occur when the bile is corrupted and has reached the eye, such that the vision of a person becomes yellow.
That person who perceives yellow forms has a vision impaired by bile;
when the disorder reaches the third layer, he does not see by day but sees at night.
At night, one whose vision is assisted by cold may see those [objects] even due to the paucity of bile;
likewise, a person whose vision is impaired by phlegm indeed perceives those very same things as white.
When the humors are diminished in three layers [of the eye], it forcibly causes night-blindness;
however, by day, one whose vision is favored by the sun may perceive forms due to the scarcity of phlegm (kapha).
If a person’s vision is afflicted by the distress of grief, fever, or headaches,
and they perceive all objects as if enveloped in smoke, they say that disease is called "smoke-vision."
That [wind], when diminished and sluggish, causes one to see short forms with difficulty during the daytime;
when the person's vision is afflicted by this disorder, it flashes like that of a mongoose.
If one sees variegated forms during the day, that is indeed the disorder known as *nakulāndhya*;
the vision becomes distorted, afflicted by wind, and the eye contracts and recedes inward.
When pain is deeply seated, those who know it call that eye disease "gambhīrika" (deep-seated);
furthermore, two external types are specified here: that caused by a specific cause and that which occurs without a manifest cause.
In that case, it should be known by signs such as a headache and the symptoms of *abhiṣyanda* (ophthalmia),
as well as by the vision of radiant gods, sages, gandharvas, and great serpents.
The vision of that man is destroyed; this is known as *liṅganāśa* caused by no apparent external cause.
In that condition, the eye appears quite clear, and the sight is stainless with the color of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*).
But the vision of men, struck by an assault, is either torn asunder, fails, or perishes.
Thus, these seventy-six disorders located in the eyes have been enumerated by me here separately;
following this, I shall explain their entire treatment in detail, each according to its proper method.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Diseases Affecting the Vision," within the Śālākyatantra, which is part of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||7||
The Eighth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of the classification of medical treatment.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari spoke to Suśruta.
Listen now to the treatment, both in brief and in detail, for those seventy-six diseases that have been described according to their names and characteristics.
Among these, eleven are declared to be excisable (chedya), nine are to be scraped (lekhyāḥ),
five morbidities are to be incised (bhedya), and fifteen are indeed to be punctured (vyadhya).
Twelve diseases are incurable by surgery, while seven are indeed palliable; fifteen diseases should be avoided by the wise,
though two of those designated as exogenous may either be incurable or palliable.
The eyelid affected by hemorrhoids (arśas), as well as dry hemorrhoids, tumors (arbuda), pustules (piḍakā), and varicose veins (sirāja);
likewise, the five types of vascular webs (sirājāla) and the five types of cataracts (arma), along with the disease of the eyelid-fold (parvaṇikā)—these are the conditions that require excision.
Those eyelids which are characterized by a pouch, a path of thick exudate, or a dark-brown discoloration; those described here as *baddhavartman*;
those that are *kliṣṭa* (afflicted) or accompanied by *pothakī* pustules; and those with *kumbhīkinī* and *śarkarā*—these indeed are to be scarified.
The two types of *śleṣmopanāha*, the *gaṇa* [of diseases], *bisa*, those *granthi*s caused by worms, and *añjananāmikā*—
these are first declared to be treatable by venesection (*sirā*), as are the two types of ocular inflammation (*pāka*) caused by Vāta and the other [humors].
Indeed, suppuration, lachrymation, disorders caused by vāta, and the condition known as mantha are pacified by venesection;
so too are dry ophthalmia (śuṣkākṣipāka), disorders of kapha and pitta, corrupted vision (vidagdhadṛṣṭi), the condition called amlādhyuṣita, cataract (śukra), arjuna, and piṣṭaka.

Experts declare that surgical intervention with a blade is not advised when the eyelids are unscarred, or when they are scarred by the fire of inflammation, or likewise in conditions known as *balāsa* characterized by excessive tearing;
nor is it advised when the vision is impaired by either exogenous factors or a pair of endogenous diseases.
Of the six types of *kāca* that have been described for one who observes [the objects], those accompanied by irritation of the eyelids (*pakṣmakopa*) are palliable.
Four arise from wind (*pavana*), two from bile (*pitta*), and one from phlegm (*kapha*).
There are four diseases born of blood (*rudhira*), as many as those (four) spoken of as arising from the three *doṣas*, and two more are said to be external (*bāhya*).
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Knowledge of the Classification of Treatments," within the Śālākyatantra, which is part of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The Ninth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for vāta-abhiṣyanda (wind-induced ocular congestion).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
For those afflicted by syanda, adhimantha, or pīḍita, once they have been lubricated with aged ghee and fomented according to the prescribed rule, one should apply venesection.

One should properly restore the patient who has been correctly treated with oleation and purgation by means of enemas, as well as saturating drinks, *puṭapāka* preparations, medicinal smokes, and eye-drops.
By means of nasal drops (nasya), oleation (sneha), affusions (pariṣeka), and head-pouches (śirobasti),
as well as by sprinkling decoctions of Vāta-subduing meat from marshy and aquatic animals and sour liquids.
By means of the four unctuous substances, warm liquids, the wearing of yellow garments,
milk, vesavāra, sālvaṇa plasters, and likewise milk-rice (pāyasa), [the fever is pacified].
The physician should prepare these two with honored poultices (upanāha) consisting of the fatty meat-juices of domestic,
marshy, and aquatic animals, combined with the juices of fruits.
Their diet is prescribed with well-refined milks,
and likewise, the drinking of clarified butter after a meal is highly commended.
Milk that has been processed with a decoction of triphalā, or milk that is simply aged,
or milk prepared with drugs that alleviate vāta or with the first group [of drugs].
Oils prepared with Vata-alleviating drugs, excluding sesame oil, are beneficial for nourishing therapy;
likewise, oleaginous *puṭapāka*, medicated smoke (*dhūma*), and nasal medication (*nasya*) of that same type are recommended.
For nasal administration and similar procedures, oil cooked with stable, milky, and sweet plants is desired;
likewise, goat's milk boiled with castor leaves, roots, or bark may be used.
A lukewarm infusion of Kaṇṭakārī roots is beneficial for irrigation;
likewise, milk boiled with Saindhava salt, Udīcya, Yaṣṭimadhu, and Pippalī is beneficial.
Half-watered *hrīvera* is beneficial for sprinkling as well as for eye-drops;
it should be prepared with *hrīvera*, *vakra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and the bark of the *udumbara*.
One should administer goat's meat or even goat's milk as an excellent wash for the ulcer;
furthermore, one should grind together madhuka, rajanī, pathyā, and devadāru.
This collyrium, prepared with goat's milk, is excellent for treating excessive lacrimation;
it consists of red ochre, rock salt, long pepper, and dry ginger, each succeeding ingredient being superior to the one preceding it.
The flour, ground with water in a two-to-one ratio, is intended for use as a pill-ointment (guṭikāñjana);
furthermore, an unctuous ointment (snehāñjana) beneficial in this condition will now be described according to the prescribed method.
The physician should treat both the disease caused by *anyatovāta* and that which is a transformation of *māruta* according to this very same procedure.
Clarified butter taken before a meal, or milk during a meal, is beneficial;
likewise, [decoctions] made from vṛkṣādanī, kapittha, and the great five roots (mahat-pañcamūla) are also beneficial.
In this condition, one should drink ghee prepared with milk and crab juice;
or they say that ghee prepared with *pattūra*, *ārtagala*, and *agni* is beneficial here.
Or ghee with milk from the meṣaśṛṅgī plant, or with vīratara;
or rock salt, devadāru, ginger, citron juice, and ghee.
When the inflammation has become dry, that collyrium should be prepared with breast milk and water;
furthermore, the drinking of ghee and the saturation of the eyes with it are highly recommended in this case.
Nasal drops (nasya) made with ghee mixed with life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs and with Aṇu oil are beneficial here;
likewise, cold milk with rock salt is recommended for pouring over the head (pariṣeka).
Alternatively, an ointment prepared with *rajanī* and *dāru*, combined with rock salt (*saindhava*),
or *mahauṣadha* ground with breast milk and mixed with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).
Alternatively, fat from marsh-dwelling or aquatic animals, combined with rock salt and slightly mixed with ginger,
when cooked until dry, constitutes that collyrium.
Whatever diseases arise from wind (vāta) that destroy vision,
a wise person should apply the ritual treatment for them using this seed-mantra.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vata-type Ophthalmia," within the Shalakya-tantra, which is part of the Uttara-tantra of the Sushruta Samhita. ||9||
The Tenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment for the obstruction of the eyes caused by pitta (pittābhiṣyanda).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
In cases of biliary discharge (pittasyanda) and biliary ophthalmia (paittika-adhimantha), bloodletting and purgation should be performed;
furthermore, eye-washes, plasters, and collyriums should be applied, as well as whatever regimen is prescribed for biliary erysipelas (paitta-visarpa).
Gundrā, śāli rice, śaivala moss, śailabheda, dārvī, elā, utpala,
rodhra, abhra, lotus leaf, sugar, darbha grass, ikṣu, tāla, another rodhra, vetasa, and padmaka.

Having ground grapes, honey, sandalwood, liquorice (yaṣṭikāhva), women’s milk, turmeric (rātri), and costus (ananta), ghee prepared with these is recommended for satiation, sprinkling, and nasal administration; likewise, goat’s milk prepared with these same ingredients is also praised.
This group of drugs may be applied as a nasal medication (nasya) either individually or combined, and it is always appropriate even when the count is four (eight divided by two).
All actions that pacify pitta are recommended; furthermore, after three days, milk and ghee may also be used as a nasal application.
For the purpose of collyrium, there should be blood from the Palāśa tree, or [blood] from the Śallakī mixed with sugar and honey;
or one may prepare a Rasakriyā (medicated extract) from Pālindī or Madhuka, likewise mixed with sugar and honey.
One should prepare an ointment by grinding together Musta, the foam of the ocean, Utpala, Kṛmighna, Elā, Dhātrī seeds, the juice of Ādra, Tālīśa, Elā, Gairika, Uśīra, and Śaṅkha with breast milk.
One should prepare a powder for the purpose of collyrium, or a juice mixed with breast milk from the *dhātakī* and *syandana* trees;
or likewise, women’s breast milk rubbed with gold, combined with honey and the flowers of the *kaiśuka* tree.
Having ground together rodhra, grapes, sugar, blue lotus, yaṣṭimadhu, and vacā in milk,
as well as the bark of the varṇaka tree in milk, and sandalwood and udumbara mixed with water;
Sea-foam should be prepared for the purpose of collyrium by rubbing it with woman’s breast-milk and honey;
likewise, liquorice, lodhra, grapes, sugar, and blue lotus should be kept steeped in woman’s breast-milk.
Clarified butter rubbed with liquorice (yaṣṭikāhva), red sandalwood (rodhra), and bound in linen cloth is beneficial for eye-drops;
likewise, they say that kāśmarī, dhātrī, and pathyā mixed with water, as well as kaṭphala with water alone, are similarly effective.
This entire sequence, with the exception of venesection, should also be applied to the condition known as *amlapitta* (acid gastritis) and to *śukti*.

Ghee should be drunk, or Traiphala or Tailvaka oil should be drunk, or simply aged ghee. When the morbid humor has been expelled downward in cases of Shuktika, collyrium should be applied immediately with cooling substances.
This collyrium— consisting of finely ground powder of vaidūrya, crystal, coral, pearl, conch-shell, silver, and gold,
mixed with sugar and honey— quickly destroys cataracts (śukti).

A person who perceives smoke from clarified butter should employ it; furthermore, one should carry out the remaining regimen for raktapitta, as well as everything else that subdues pitta, and indeed all the treatments prescribed for paittika visarpa.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Pitta-type Ophthalmia," within the Śālākya-tantra, which is part of the Uttaratantra of the Śrī Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The eleventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the suppression of phlegm-induced ophthalmia (śleṣmābhiṣyanda).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
One should conquer the increased *syanda* and *adhimantha* caused by *kapha* by means of venesection,
as well as through the application of sudation, pressed-out collyria (*avapīḍa*), medicinal smokes (*dhūma*), washes (*seka*), ointments (*pralepa*), and gargles (*kavalagraha*).
Likewise, with dry applications such as eye-drops and similarly with dry *puṭapāka* formulations,
and at the conclusion of each three-day period of fasting, bitter ghee is recommended for those two [eyes] every morning.
One should indeed consume that food and drink which does not increase phlegm;
[this may be done] with the decoctions of *kuṭannaṭa*, *āsphoṭa*, *phaṇijjña*, *bilva*, *pattūra*, *pilu*, *arka*, and *kapittha*.
One should apply sudation or an ointment made of barhiṣṭha, śuṇṭhī, surakāṣṭha, and kuṣṭha;
or with saindhava, hiṅgu, triphalā, madhūka, prapauṇḍarīka, añjana, tuttha, and tāmra.
Collyrium-sticks may be prepared from these powders mixed with water; alternatively, they may be made from pathyā, haridrā, madhuka, and añjana.
Or, the three pungents (trīṇyūṣaṇāni), triphalā, haridrā, and the essence of viḍaṅga should be taken in equal parts.
One should grind together barhiṣṭha, kuṣṭha, kāṣṭhāmara, śaṅkha, pāṭhā, āmalaka, vyoṣa, and manaḥśilā with water,
or one may employ the flowers of jātī, karañja, and śobhāñjana ground with water.
Alternatively, the fruit of the *śigru* tree or its flower is equal [in potency] to the two types of *bṛhatī*;
likewise, *rasāñjana*, rock salt, sandalwood, realgar, orpiment, and garlic are all equal [in their application].
Having ground these for the purpose of collyrium, the wise physician should apply them as wicks for eye diseases born of phlegm;
in the case of the disease known as *balāsagrathita*, this collyrium should be administered by the learned after the body has been thoroughly purified.
Having burned blue barley grains that have been soaked in cow's milk, which are stalked, dry, and shriveled,
as well as the flowers of arjaka, āsphota, kapittha, bilva, nirguṇḍī, and jātī;

One should then place that—consisting of alkali, rock salt, tuttha, and gorocanā—which has been cooked in an iron tube, as a collyrium for a condition of knotted phlegm (balāsagrathita); this is the secondary procedure for cases involving phaṇijjñaka and other such plants.
Mahauṣadha, māgadhikā, mustā, rock salt (saindhava), and white marica— these,
ground with the fresh juice of mātuluṅga and used as an eye-salve, quickly destroy piṣṭaka.
At the time of fruit ripening, one should place a paste made from *bṛhatī* and those originating from Magadha into the fruit;
having extracted it once it is joined with *srotoñjana*, this same procedure applies as well to ground [substances].
In the fruits of vārtāka, śigru, indrasurā, paṭola, kirātatikta, and āmalakī,
as well as in kāsīsa, sāmudra, rasāñjana, jāti, and also kṣāra (or koraka), [one should prepare the collyrium].
For the condition of *praklinna-vartman* (moistened eyelids), the following medicinal collyrium (*yogāñjana*) is prescribed, ground with honey:
equal parts of the finest *nādeya* (rock salt), white pepper (*marica*), and Nepalese realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
This formulation with the juice of *mātuluṅga* destroys itching with a single application as an ointment;
likewise [is the use of] *śṛṅgavera*, *suradāru*, *musta*, rock salt (*sindhuprasūta*), and jasmine buds (*jātimukula*).
Indeed, this collyrium ground with wine is said to be beneficial for itching and swelling;
one should always follow the treatment regimen for syanda and adhimantha, remaining ever vigilant in all these cases.
"In particular, one should perform eye-bathing (*nāvana*) and also the *saṃsarga* treatment as instructed.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Kaphaja Abhiṣyanda," within the *Śālākyatantra* contained in the *Uttaratantra* of the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*. 11.
The twelfth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment for the prevention of *raktābhiṣyanda* (blood-induced ocular inflammation).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
One should treat these four diseases arising from blood— mantha, syanda, sirotpāta, and sirāharṣa— with a single therapeutic regimen.
One should treat these four types of persons afflicted by disease with unctuous ghee from a jar,
or with excellent meat-broths, or by means of venesection.
And for those who have been thoroughly purged,
one should cleanse their heads with clarified butter prepared with purgative drugs and mixed with sugar.
(Or with marrow mixed with that [fat], or with fat cooked with it;
thereafter, plasters, sprinklings, nasal medications, and fumigations should be administered according to their respective indications;
likewise, eye-drops, massages, saturations, oleaginous treatments, and the applications of *puṭapāka* should be performed.
One should apply a plaster all around the eyes using blue lotus, ushira, katankateri, kaliya, licorice, musta, and rodhra, along with padmaka, mixed with washed ghee.
In cases of extremely intense pain as well, mild sudation is beneficial;
furthermore, leeches should be applied all around the eyes.
A large dose of ghee, when drunk, alleviates pain;
furthermore, the therapeutic procedure for pacifying *pittābhiṣyanda* has been prescribed.
Alternatively, a powder made from Kaśeru and Madhuka, enclosed within a cloth and placed in rainwater,
serves as a beneficial eye-drop (āścyotana).
One should take equal quantities of the flowers of pāṭalī, arjuna, śrīparṇī, dhātakī, dhātrī, bilva, the two types of bṛhatī, bimbī, and loṭa.
This collyrium, prepared by grinding mañjiṣṭhā with honey or sugarcane juice,
is prescribed for the pacification of redness and ocular discharge (raktābhiṣyanda).
Sandalwood, white water-lily, leaves, bitumen with saffron,
iron and copper dust, blue vitriol, neem resin, and collyrium;
Having ground tin, brass, and impurities with the juice of flowers,
large wicks were made and always worshipped for use as collyrium.
Collyrium made of ghee and honey is a remedy for headache;
likewise, rock salt and ferrous sulfate (kāsīsa) rubbed with breast milk is highly esteemed.
Honey, conch-shell, rock-salt, Tuttha, and Darvi; the juice of Śirīṣa flowers, along with wine, black pepper, and honey.
Gairika mixed with honey is beneficial for use as an eye-salve;
in the case of irritation of the vessels (sirāharṣa), one should apply an eye-salve consisting of treacle combined with honey.
Or honey with *tārkṣya-ja* (guggulu), or *kāsīsa* with rock salt;
or molasses with rock salt, combined with cane-sour (*vetrāmla*) and breast milk.
One should perform the entire Pitta-pacifying regimen for the sake of pacifying Arjuna [fever],
using sugarcane juice, honey, sugar, breast milk, Darvī, Madhuka, and Saindhava salt.
In this condition, eye-drops (sekāñjana) are beneficial, as well as eye-washes (āścyotana) prepared with sour substances;
likewise, [a collyrium] made from sugar, madhuka, kaṭvaṅga, whey, honey, sour liquids, and rock salt.
Combined with the sour fruits of the citron, the jujube, and the pomegranate—
either individually, in pairs, or all three together— in the appropriate manner.
Rock crystal, coral, conch shell, madhuka, and sugar candy,
combined with conch shell, honey, and white sugar— or indeed, sea foam alone— [are used for purification].
These two formulations have been prescribed for the purpose of clearing and destroying the *arjuna* disease:
*rasāñjana* combined with *saindhava*, honey, and *kataka*; or *rasāñjana* combined with honey.
In this collyrium, kasīsa should always be combined with honey;
likewise, all iron powders, metallic ores, and salts [may be used].
Jewels, ivory, horns, and a multitude of suppressive substances;
hen’s eggs, potsherds, garlic, and the three pungents.
The seeds of *karañja* and *melā* should be applied; this is known as *lekhya-añjana*.
It is administered following *puṭapāka* and concludes with the draining of blood and similar procedures.
A skilled physician should extract the pure semen, free from injury, by means of this entire procedure which has been duly performed and which stops the flow.
Whether it be superficial or deep-seated, hard or even ulcerated,
[it is treated] with the seeds of śirīṣa, black pepper, long pepper, and rock salt.
One should perform the rubbing of the semen with rock salt,
or one may prepare it with copper powder, conch-shell, realgar, black pepper, and rock salt.
By doubling these [numbers] starting from the last, one should perform the collyrium that destroys semen;
or else, one may properly apply these two half-verse formulations as collyriums.
[One may cleanse the teeth] with conch shell, kola fruit, kataka nut, grapes, licorice, and honey; or likewise with honey, tooth-wood, sea-foam, and śirīṣa flowers.
One should administer alkaline collyrium to remove the hardened phlegm, or alternatively,
roasted dehusked mung beans mixed with conch-shell powder, honey, and sugar.
One should always mix the pith of the Madhūka tree with honey for use as an ointment;
alternatively, the marrow of the Bibhītaka seed with honey destroys the discharge of semen.
Conch shell, pearl-oyster, honey, grapes, licorice, and kataka seeds— these,
or a Vata-alleviating and satiating (tarpaṇa) preparation, are beneficial when [the disease] has reached the second layer of the skin and is accompanied by pain.
One should burn bamboo, *jāruṣkara*, palmyra palm, and coconut;
having extracted the alkali, one should powder it and saturate it with the bone of a camel.
This ointment, when applied frequently, destroys the discoloration of semen;
having pierced an *ajakā* tumor on its side with a needle, one should drain the fluid.
One should fill the ulcer with powdered beef along with clarified butter;
furthermore, if the eyelid has become involved, one should scrape it repeatedly.
Regarding the two types of suppuration that have been described— those with swelling and those without swelling—
the physician, having prepared the patient with oleation and sudation, should then venesect.
One should administer washes, eye-drops, nasal drops, and puṭapāka treatments;
furthermore, this collyrium should be applied to one who is purified in every respect.
Clarified butter mixed with rock salt, kept for one month in a copper vessel;
or likewise, *maireya* liquor, or curd, or even *dadhyuttara*.
Clarified butter placed in a brass vessel, or breast milk mixed with rock salt,
or the essence of Madhūka flowers in equal parts with honey, or [milk] with red ochre (gairika).
One should administer clarified butter with rock salt and copper,

combined with breast milk; or a medicinal extract (rasakriyā) made from pomegranate, ārevata, aśmantaka, and kola, along with sour substances and rock salt, in order to properly eliminate the morbid heat.
For one month, ginger mixed with rock salt should be kept in clarified butter;
this is to be applied as an eye-drop and collyrium combined with the milk of a female elephant.
The flower of the *jāti* plant, rock salt (*saindhava*), ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), the seeds of long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), and the essence of the "enemy of insects" (*kīṭaśatru*)—
this ground mixture, combined with honey, should be applied without hesitation as a collyrium for the inflammation of the eyes (*netrapāka*).
In the case of pūyālasi (suppuration), bloodletting is beneficial, as is poulticing;
the entire therapeutic procedure that prevents suppuration of the eye should be applied by the physician according to the prescribed rules.
In this case, an ointment made of green vitriol (kāsīsa), rock salt (saindhava), and fresh ginger (ārdraka) is beneficial;
one should employ these mixed with honey, or alternatively, combined with the powders of copper and iron.
Having properly eliminated the humors (doṣas) by means of oleation and other therapies, and having then provided nourishment according to the specific requirements,
one should treat a patient with moistened eyelids using affusions, collyriums, eye-drops, nasal drops, and medicated smokes.

In this case, an eye-drop (āścyotana) should be prepared from Musta, Haridrā, Madhuka, Priyaṅgu, Siddhārtha, Rodhra, Utpala, and Sārivā, all ground together; and the collyrium (añjana) should be made of honey (mākṣika).
One should prepare a medicinal preparation by cooking the leaf and fruit of the āmalaka, or else use it for the purpose of collyrium;
or one may prepare a medicinal extract (rasakriyā) from the root of the bamboo, or a wick (varti) cooked in a copper vessel.
Or one may administer a medicinal preparation (rasakriyā) cooked with triphalā and palāśa flowers, or with svaramañjarī;
or having ground the soot of a bell-metal vessel together with goat’s milk and cloth fibers.
This counter-collyrium should be used together with black pepper,
copper powder, sea-foam, the best salt (rock salt), conch-shell, mung bean, and white pepper.
This powdered collyrium quickly overcomes dullness of vision, itching, and inflammation of the eyelids;
these same formulations should also be employed for cases of excessive tearing from the eyelids, after carefully considering the specific dosha involved.
Collyrium mixed with soot, rubbed in a copper vessel along with ghee and sulphur.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Raktābhiṣyanda," within the Śālākyatantra, which is part of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||12||
The thirteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diseases of the eyes.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
This general procedure applies to those nine [substances] which have been declared as being written [on the tongue]:
for one who has undergone oleation, emesis, and purgation, in a room free from wind and sunlight.
For one who has been firmly secured by trusted attendants in the house and laid down on his back, the physician,
being well-composed, should foment the eyelid with a cloth heated by warm water;
having everted the lid, it should be held between the left thumb and finger.
With the index finger and the thumb,
one should carefully evert the eyelid so that it does not move or slip away between the two cloths.
Then, having wiped the wound with a cloth to clear the marks of the surgical instrument,
one should incise it again with a blade or with leaves once the blood has settled.
Having fomented [the area], one should rub it with a fine paste of realgar, green vitriol, the three pungents (vyoṣa), fresh añjana, and rock salt,
mixed with honey and washed with warm water.
Having washed it and sprinkled it with clarified butter (havis), one should treat it like a wound;
after three days have passed, one should apply fomentation (sveda), pressing-injections (avapīḍa), and other such measures.
The procedure for the act of painting has been described to you in detail:
it should be free from the discharge of blood and tears, and devoid of itching and swelling.
The eyelid should be incised evenly, resembling the surface of a fingernail; this is considered the correct method.
If it is cut too deeply by the instrument, blood will certainly flow from the wound and the eye will discharge its contents.
There is redness, swelling, discharge, darkness of vision, and failure to overcome disease; the eyelid is dark-brown, heavy, stiff, and characterized by itching, horripilation, and exudation.
Or one may cause a severe inflammation of the eye to arise in a patient who does not provide treatment;
this should be known as "badly scratched," and one should scratch again after applying an unctuous substance.
When the eyelid turns back and the eyelashes become disoriented,
and there is pain with excessive discharge, that condition is known as *atisrāvita* (over-bleeding).
In those cases, the sequence beginning with oleation and sudation is desired as it subdues the wind (vāta).
This applies to the conditions described as vartmāvabandha, kliṣṭa, and bahala.
Having first gently scarified the skin, the wise physician should then slowly incise the pustules;
he should mark the path of the disease on both the dusky and the muddy types of skin with equal care.
Having treated the kumbhīkinī, the śarkarā, and likewise the utsaṅginī with an instrument,
one should then incise them without weariness.
Those pustules on the eyelids which are very hard, short, and copper-colored should be incised when suppurated;
once incised, one should also scarify them.
Having recognized that these small, slightly inflamed pustules arising from the external eyelid (bāhyavartma) belong to a young person,
one should treat them with fomentation, medicinal plasters, and purificatory procedures.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases Requiring Excision," within the Śālākyatantra, which is part of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||13||
The fourteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diseases requiring incision.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Having fomented the lotus-root knot (bisagranthi) until its cavities are devoid of moisture,
one should split it open with a sharp instrument once cooked and dust it with rock salt (sindhava).
Then, having applied kāsīsa, māgadhī flowers, nepālī, and elā,
one should add honey and ghee and properly perform the bandage.
Rocanā, alkali, tuttha, pippalī, and honey—
each one of these is recommended as a rubbing agent (pratisāraṇa) when a lagana has burst open.
Even in a severe case, the physician skilled in procedure should apply alkali and cautery;
having fomentated and incised it, he should squeeze out the discharge from the eye, including the eyelashes.
One should rub [the area] with rock salt, cardamom, and rock crystal mixed with honey;
or, having incised it, one skilled in surgical procedures should treat it with *rasāñjana* and honey.
One should apply warm rubbing-collyriums produced from the flame of a lamp;
once the worm-tumor has been properly fomented and incised, the rubbing-collyrium should be administered.
A medicinal paste (rasakriyā) made from triphalā, tuttha, kāsīsa, and saindhava salt should be applied;
having burst open the kapha-born upanāha, one should treat it with pippalī, honey, and saindhava salt.
One should apply [the paste] with the edge of a blade all around and scrape it off;
having softened it with leaf-cuttings and having steamed it as desired.
In all these cases, once the treatment has been prescribed with affection,
one should, having become purified and being certain that the wound is fully healed, perform the healing of the ulcer.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases Requiring Incision," within the Śālākyatantra section of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of diseases requiring excision.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
For one who has eaten unctuous food and is seated with effort,
the physician should cause the eye to contract by means of saline powders.
Then, once it has been quickly incensed, well-sweated, and thoroughly rubbed,
the physician should apply this [ointment] to the ulcer where folds have formed.
While he gazes at the corner of his eye,
the wise man, being composed, should extract it with a hook, or else with a small forceps, or again with a needle and thread.
One should not raise it too quickly, for that would cause the wound to swell;
moreover, out of fear of injury from the weapon, one should keep the two eyelids firmly closed.
Then, once it has become loose and remains suspended by only three [teeth],
one should clean it by scraping with the sharp edge of a mandala-agra instrument.
Having led [the gaze] free from all things, as well as from the black and white circles,
to the edge of the pupil, one should cut [the connection] without going too far into the pupil.
When a quarter of the flesh has been removed, the eye does not suffer injury;
however, from the destruction of the *kanīnaka* (the pupil), either hemorrhage or a sinus may arise.
Furthermore, after its base has been cut away, it quickly attains growth again;
even that net-like web which spreads across it is wiped away and hangs down.
One should cut with a curved instrument the affected area extending from the eyelid margin to the edge of the white of the eye;
immediately thereafter, an application for rubbing the eyes should be performed.
After fomenting it with the powder of bamboo pith, the three pungents (trikaṭu), and salt,
the skilled physician should then apply a bandage.
Having administered the unctuous substance as is beneficial, according to one's knowledge of the humors, seasons, strength, and time,
one should thereafter provide for its management just as one would for a wound.
After three days, having released the patient from hand-sudation (karasveda) and administered purification therapy,
one should administer milk prepared with karañja seeds, āmalaka, and madhuka.
For pain, a beneficial eye-drop mixed with honey should be applied twice a day;
and a paste made from madhuka, utpala, kiñjalka, and dūrvā should be applied to the head.
A cold plaster made of milk-ground [herbs] mixed with ghee is recommended;
if any remnant of the disease should remain, one should remove it with scraping collyriums.
One should treat that ulcer which is small, resembles curd, or is blue, red, grey, thin,
or white like semen.
That which resembles leather, is extensive, covered with dense sinews and flesh,
and located in the black portion (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala), is indeed an arma and must be excised.
When the catararact is removed, the eye becomes pure in color, free from affliction, its functions unimpaired,
and it remains perfectly healthy, just as it was naturally intended to be.
Among the network of vessels, those that are hard, the wise physician should scrape with a circular blade after they have been secured with a hook.
When pustules have formed on the veins that do not heal with medicines,
their excision is desired using a circular blade, as in the case of an armakośa.
For these two diseases, the treatment prescribed for the vital points (marmas) is scarification (pratisāraṇa),
along with a procedure involving scraping agents (lekhanadravya) prepared according to the specific dosha.
Having moistened the junction with warm water, the skillful physician should, with a probe,
locate the *varṇikā* (the opening) in the upper third [of the vessel] and hold it steady with a hook.
One should then cut half of that [portion] at the tip, for otherwise the tear-duct (aśru-nāḍī) would be damaged;
in this case as well, the application of rock salt and honey (saindhava-kṣaudra) is desired as a rubbing agent (pratisāraṇa).
Powders to be written down are the remedy for the remnant of the disease:
conch-shell, sea-foam, and *maṇḍūkī* produced from the ocean.
Crystal, kuruvinda, coral, and aśmantaka,
as well as vaidūrya, pulaka, pearls, iron, copper, and gold dust.
Having ground these ingredients in equal proportions together with antimony (srotoñjana),
one should have a powdered collyrium prepared and placed in a vessel made from the horn of a medicinal animal.
Having applied it at both times, the wise man should constantly massage;
by that means, he shall indeed destroy ulcers, pustules, and networks of veins.
Likewise, regarding hemorrhoids— namely dry hemorrhoids (śuṣkārśas) and arbuda—
as well as internal growths located within the eyelids (vartmaśayas), their treatment shall now be described.
Having fomented the eyelid, everted it, and carefully lifted it with a needle,
the best of physicians should incise it at its base with a sharp circular blade.
Then one should rub [the area] with rock salt, black sulphate of iron, and long pepper;
once the bleeding has ceased, one should properly cauterize the eyelid with a probe.
If a remnant of the disease should remain, one should also scrape it away with an alkaline agent;
thereafter, one should expel the morbid humors (doṣa) by means of strong drugs that act on both parts of the body.

One should also apply the procedure for managing excessive secretions according to the specific dosha involved; and once the surgical procedure has ceased, the patient should remain strictly disciplined for one month.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases Requiring Excision," within the Śālākyatantra section of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The sixteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the disorder of the eyelashes (pakṣmakopa).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Regarding that curable disorder arising from the eyelid which was previously described as *pakṣmaprakopa*,
for a man seated thereon, the skin above the eyelid [is to be treated] precisely along its length.
Having set aside two parts below the eyebrows and one part resting on the eyelashes, one should then trim [the hair] all around,
level with the inner corner of the eye and the outer corner, in the shape of a barley grain for a person of smooth body.
Having cut [the growth] with a blade to the size of a barley grain, the vigilant physician should sew it with a hair;
then, having applied ghee and honey, he should perform whatever procedure is prescribed for a wound.
Having tied a bandage over the forehead and having also secured another that was previously stitched there,
once stability has been attained in the surgical track, the skilled physician, having carefully observed, should release the sutures.
If it does not heal in this manner,
the wise physician, having carefully examined it, should excise the path and the fold corrupted by the humors, and then cauterize it with fire or with alkali.

Having evenly cut away the row of eyelashes, one should grasp [the foreign body] correctly with three hooks and then properly extract it with a fruit of *pathyā* or with *tūvaraka* powder that has been ground smooth.

These four procedures—purgation, eye-drops, fumigation, and nasal medication—are each separately recommended to remove the obstruction of the eyelids; as are ointments, collyriums, oleation, and meat-juice preparations.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases Affecting the Eyelashes," within the Śālākyatantra section of the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The seventeenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diseases affecting the vision.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Three are curable, three are incurable, and six are indeed palliable;
among these, the remedy for one has been proclaimed by Dhūmadarśin.
When the vision is impaired by the vitiation of pitta or by kapha,
one should employ a treatment that removes pitta and kapha, with the exception of surgical intervention.

In the first stage, one should employ nasal drops, irrigations, collyriums, ointments, and puṭapāka applications along with nourishing therapies (tarpaṇa); in the latter stage, however, the triphalā decoction and trivṛt ghee should be consumed.
Tailvaka is wholesome for both [types of hemorrhoids], whether taken alone or simply when aged;
likewise, red ochre, rock salt, long pepper, and the soot of cow's teeth [are beneficial].
Cow flesh, black pepper seeds, śirīṣa, realgar,
the stalk of a wood-apple, and the fruits of svayaṅguptā, [mixed] with honey.
These four formulations, made from kubjaka, aśoka, śāla, āmra, priyaṅgu, nalina, and utpala, are beneficial for the application of both [the eye-salve and the collyrium].
With powders composed of *puṣpa*, *hareṇu*, *kṛṣṇāhvā*, *pathyā*, and *āmalaka*,
combined with clarified butter and honey, placed within a bamboo tube;
The physician should also apply an ointment prepared from the flowers of the *āmra* and *jambū* trees, which have been processed with bile and phlegm, along with *hareṇukā* mixed with their juice.
Alternatively, one should apply a collyrium made by grinding the filaments of the red and blue lotuses along with red ochre and the liquid from cow dung,
mixed with honey and clarified butter.
This pill or collyrium is beneficial for those with day-blindness and night-blindness;
it consists of rasāñjana, juice, honey, tālīśa, and golden ochre (svarṇagairika).
For one whose vision is impaired by bile,
one should grind either cold *sauvīraka* salt or *rasāñjana*, mixed with cow dung juice and saturated with that same juice.
The wise person should saturate this with the bile of a tortoise or that of a Rohita fish;
this powdered collyrium should be used daily for the pacification of pitta.
An eye-salve made from the flowers of *kāśmarī*, *madhuka*, *dārvī*, *rodhra*, and *rasāñjana*,
combined with honey, is likewise always beneficial for this disease.
One should grind together srotoñjana, saindhava salt, and reṇukā;
these, made into wicks with goat's urine, are beneficial as an ointment for night-blindness.
One should add kālānusārivā, kṛṣṇā, nāgara,
madhuka, tālīśapatra, kṣaṇadā, and gāṅgeya to the juice of the liver.
These wicks, made from ground realgar, yellow myrobalan, the three pungents (vyoṣa), balā, and kālānusārivā, dried in the shade, provide great comfort when applied.
One should cook foamy, rolled balls made from ground [medicinal herbs] combined with goat’s milk,
in cow urine, bile, wine, liver, and the juice of *dhātrī*.
Another minor collyrium may be prepared with the juice [of the drugs], or with the three myrobalans (triphalā) boiled in water;
or it may be made from cow’s urine, clarified butter, sea-foam, long pepper, honey, and kaṭphala.
One should administer goat's fat, liver, ghee, long pepper, rock salt, and honey, placed within a hollow bamboo tube and mixed with Saindhava salt.
One should also properly cook the juice of āmalaka and store it in a vessel made of khadira wood;
likewise, this is beneficial as a minor collyrium (kṣudrāñjana).
For one whose vision is impaired by phlegm (kapha), an ointment should be applied consisting of hareṇu, the marrow from the bones of the Magadha goat,
and cardamom, combined with the juice of liver.
Having cooked half-sliced ox liver, well-filled with *māgadhikā* peppers, and roasted over a fire,
its consumption as a collyrium undoubtedly destroys night-blindness.
Likewise, goat's liver, properly cooked in fire with the addition of *magadha* salt,
when applied as before, undoubtedly conquers night-blindness in men through a single application as an ointment.
Having prepared both the spleen and the liver from an animal that has been fed on *upabhākṣita* [herbs], and having roasted them on spits with ghee and oil—
or combined them with mustard oil— if this collyrium is applied, it instantly destroys night-blindness (*naktāndhya*).

Nadīja, śimbī, the three pungents (trikaṭu), añjana, manaḥśilā, the two types of niśā, and the liver (or dung) of cows— this pill, or this collyrium mixed with candana, is highly recommended for those who cannot see during the daytime.
Indeed, those six diseases which are palliable should always have their blood removed by venesection,
and the patient should also be purged with aged ghee prepared with purgative adjuncts.
In cases arising from Vāta, they say that oil of Pañcāṅgula mixed with milk is beneficial;
however, Traiphala ghee is especially a purifying agent for diseases of blood and bile (rakta-pitta).
In cases of cataracts caused by Kapha, a triple-purging (trivṛt) enema is recommended; in those caused by all three Doshas, they prescribe oil prepared with that [trivṛt].
For all types of cataracts, aged ghee kept in an iron vessel is beneficial in every respect.
One should know that Triphalā-ghṛta is always beneficial, as is that which is prepared with the substances known by the names of "ram's horn" (meṣaviṣāṇa);
furthermore, in cases of Pittaja Timira, one should always lick well-powdered Triphalā mixed with a profusion of ghee.
In cases caused by Kapha, one should appropriately administer oil mixed with honey when the wind is mild;
however, oil prepared by boiling it in a decoction of cow dung is excellent and beneficial for nasal drops (nāvana) in cases of Timira.
Clarified butter alone is beneficial in the case of Pitta; likewise, goat's or sheep's ghee processed with sweet drugs is beneficial.
Oil prepared with the Sthirādi group or the Madhura group is beneficial, as is Aṇu-taila in cases arising from Vāta and blood (Rakta).

Ghee prepared with a decoction of aśvagandhā, atibalā, and varī is beneficial when used as a nasal drop (nasya), as is the ghee mentioned for trivṛt; likewise, ghee produced from milk processed with the meat of aquatic and marsh-dwelling animals should be administered.
The *puṭapāka* preparation made from the meat of carnivorous animals and the *eṇa* deer, combined with rock salt, clarified butter, and honey, is beneficial.
Furthermore, fat derived from vultures, snakes, and cocks, when mixed with *madhuka*, is always praised for use as an ointment.
This counter-collyrium, which has arisen in a stream and has been successively infused in juice, milk, and ghee,
should be kept for three periods of ten days inside the mouth of a black cobra that has been wrapped with kuśa grass.
Collyrium combined with jasmine buds and rock salt, used constantly, is effective for night-blindness (timira) and colored vision;
likewise, experts in the scriptures declare that [collyrium] well-soaked in milk for three days removes cataracts (kāca).

In the case of Pitta-type [diseases], they say that oblations derived from milk and prepared with sweet medicinal herbs are beneficial for nasal therapy (nasya). That same preparation is also beneficial when employed as a saturating drink (tarpaṇa), as well as meat from wild animals; among these, that which is called "puṭapāka" is also recommended.

Experts in this matter recommend that *kṣudrāñjana*—consisting of *rasāñjana*, honey, sugar, and realgar—or *samāñjana* derived from a gold mine, should be finely powdered and combined with licorice (*madhuka*). This is considered the best.

Sprinkling with water infused with the fragrance of bhillōṭa is beneficial here, as is the application of *tutthaka* as an eye-salve; when combined in equal parts with *meṣaśṛṅga* and *añjana*, it removes the impurities of *kāca* arising from the eyes.
The juices of *palāśa*, *rohitaka*, and *madhūka*, combined with honey and mixed with the first portion of wine (*madirāgra*),
should be cooked with *uśīra*, *lodhra*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *priyaṅgu* to be used as a nasal medication (*nasya*) for the pacification of diseases caused by *kapha*.
One should employ viḍaṅga, pāṭhā, kiṇihī, and the bark of iṅgudī combined with dhūma and madhuśīra;
likewise, ghee cooked with a decoction of vanaspati along with haridrā and nalada is beneficial as a satiating (tarpaṇa) remedy.
A puṭapāka preparation should consist of samāgadha, enriched with honey and rock salt, along with meat from wild animals;
furthermore, procedures should be performed using realgar, the three pungents (tri-ūṣaṇa), conch-shell, honey, rock salt, iron sulfate (kāsīsa), and rasāñjana.
They likewise say that green vitriol (kāsīsa) and rasāñjana are beneficial when combined with jaggery and ginger;
or that collyrium which has been repeatedly steeped in cow's urine or in water boiled with the three myrobalans (triphalā) is wholesome.
One should place this collyrium, which has resided within the bones of a night-walker (niśācara), in unstable water for one month;
then, combined with the flowers of a ram and with madhuka, that collyrium should be employed for every purpose.

All therapeutic measures beneficial for wounds arising from blood are likewise beneficial when the eye is withered; furthermore, the regimen that removes *pitta* is beneficial when applied after carefully considering the specific humors (*doṣas*) according to their respective natures, as it alleviates *syanda*.
When the humors have arisen and have not yet reached a state of extreme derangement, the wise physician should administer medicinal substances as nasal drops (nasya) and other such treatments;
furthermore, another auspicious and detailed procedure for collyrium (añjana) will be explained later in the Kalpa section, and that too should be employed here.
For a man who diligently consumes aged ghee, triphalā, śatāvarī, paṭola, mung beans, āmalaka, and barley,
there exists no fear whatsoever from the most terrible timira.
Milk-rice prepared solely with śatāvarī, or likewise milk-rice made with āmalaka fruits,
or barley-rice with abundant ghee and an abundance of triphala water, dispels timira.
Jīvanti, suniṣaṇṇaka, sataṇḍulīya, and excellent vāstuka;
likewise cillī, mūlaka, and kapotikā, as well as the meat of birds and wild animals, are beneficial for the eyesight.
The vegetables derived from the paṭola, karkoṭaka, kāravella, vārtāku, tarkārī, karīra, and ja,
as well as those from śigru and ārtagala, when prepared with ghee, are beneficial for the eyesight.
One should avoid bloodletting when redness has appeared in the case of *timira*;
for the *doṣa*, being forced out by the instrument, would swiftly destroy vision.
Timira that is colorless (arāgi) and located in the first layer (paṭala) is curable;
it becomes difficult to treat in the second layer, while in the third it is said to be palliable (yāpya).
Even when blood is stained by rāga (redness) or affected by timira (darkness),
those leeches should be employed as prescribed for the purpose of draining, and they should be utilized according to the instructions given.
In the case of a loss of vision caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika), I shall describe the procedure for its successful treatment,
provided that the lesion is stable and shaped like a crescent moon, a drop of sweat, or a pearl.
Whether it is uneven, thin in the middle, marked with streaks, or very radiant;
whether the defect is located in the pupil, painful, or blood-red—it is thus observed.
Then, for that person who has been lubricated and fomented, at a time that is neither too hot nor too cold,
while he is restrained and seated, looking straight at his own nose;
The wise man, having avoided the two dark portions at the outer corners,
should properly open his eyes, which are free from the network of veins.
Then, neither too low nor too high, nor from the sides,
he should carefully insert a trusty probe shaped like a barley grain into the opening made by fate.
With the right hand, the physician should pierce the left [eye], and with the left hand, the other, holding the hand steady by means of the middle finger and the thumb.
The arrival of water droplets should be correctly indicated by sounds during the piercing;
then, as soon as it has been pierced, the expert should sprinkle it with breast milk.
Whether the humor (doṣa) is stable or mobile, one should foment the eye externally by properly inserting a probe and applying decoctions that destroy Vāta.
Then, one should scrape the circle of the pupil with the tip of a probe;
while piercing, one should block the nostril on the side opposite to the eye being pierced.
Phlegm located within the circle of vision should be removed by means of suction;
when the vision shines forth clearly like the sun in a cloudless sky, [the task is accomplished].
Then that [letter] which is written correctly and without error should be understood as such;
likewise, this applies when a fault is impossible to remove or when it has already returned.
Once it has been treated with oleation and other such measures, the extraction is performed again;
then, when the forms [of the foreign body] are visible, one should slowly withdraw the probe.
Having anointed the eye with clarified butter, one should wrap it with a cloth bandage;
then, in a place free from disturbances, the patient should lie down on his back.
At that time, one should not perform belching, coughing, sneezing, spitting, or shaking; nor should one engage in any restrictive postures, as in the case of one who has drunk medicated oil.
Every three days, one should wash the eye with decoctions that pacify Vāta;
after three days, out of fear of Vāta, one should foment the eye as previously described.
Having thus restrained oneself for ten days for the benefit of clarifying the vision,
one should thereafter engage in ritual acts and consume light food in moderation.

In the procedure for venesection, a physician should not perform venesection on the nīlikā vein of those persons previously excluded from the ritual verses (ṛc), except in cases specifically prescribed otherwise.
The eye becomes filled with blood spreading from the venesection;
in that case, ghee cooked with breast milk and liquorice is beneficial for irrigation.
If the arrow is lodged near the outer corner of the eye (apāṅga), there will be swelling, pain, lacrimation, and redness;
in that case, one should apply a poultice between the eyebrows and perform irrigation with warm clarified butter.
When a wound is caused by a black insect (vyādha) that is near the black [part of the eye], redness occurs and the black part is afflicted;
in that case, purification from below, affusion with clarified butter, and bloodletting are prescribed.
Moreover, if it is pierced from above, a painful pain arises;
in that case, sprinkling with lukewarm clarified butter is recommended.
The discharge (āsava) there is extremely slimy due to the downward piercing of the sharp-pointed probe;
its treatment is the same as previously described.

When there is excessive tearing, pain, stiffness, and horripilation, the application of unctuous substances and sudation is beneficial; in that condition, an oil enema (anuvāsana) is also recommended.
Even if the humors have been drawn downward, if they are still immature,
they may move upward again and cause the eyes to become white and reddish, accompanied by intense pain and loss of vision.
There, one should perform an irrigation of the eyes with sweet, prepared ghee,
apply a head-poultice (śirovasti) with that same [ghee], and provide a meal consisting of meat.
But when the dosha has gained strength, become dense, and filled the entire circle,
it perishes upon reaching the tip of the probe, like a thin cloud before the wind.
The dosha returns through trauma to the head, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, fainting, anger, and in the case of one who has been pierced or is very young.
A probe that is rough causes pain; one that is coarse leads to an overflow of the humors;
one with a broad tip produces a wide wound; and one that is sharp may injure in many ways.
However, a purgative that is irregular in its action, or associated with improper treatment, or unstable, causes a discharge of watery matter when it is devoid of the [proper] qualities;
therefore, it should be beneficial when free from these defects.
Eight finger-breadths in length, wrapped in the middle with thread,
it is equal in thickness to the joint of a thumb and shaped like a bud at its two ends.
The probe should be made of copper, iron, or gold, and be faultless.
Redness, swelling, a tumor, sucking pain, vesicles, and the appearance of a boar’s eye [are signs of infection].
Other diseases such as *adhimantha* and the like may arise from the defects of surgical wounds or from unwholesome conduct; one should treat them according to their respective [causes].
Learn from me further formulations for pain or redness of the eyes:
red ochre, sārivā, dūrvā grass, barley flour, clarified butter, and milk.
This pleasant ointment should be applied for the pacification of the passion of sensation;
it may also be made with sesame seeds that have been lightly roasted and combined with white mustard seeds.
An easy-to-apply plaster composed of these along with the juice of *mātuluṅga* accomplishes that purpose;
likewise, one made from *payasyā*, *sārivā*, leaves, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *madhuka*.
An application of goat's milk, lukewarm, is said to be beneficial;
likewise, an application made with *dāru*, *padmaka*, and *śuṇṭhī* is also recommended.
Or likewise with grapes, licorice, and costus combined with rock salt;
or goat's milk with lodhra, rock salt, raisins, and licorice.
Milk boiled with madhuka,

utpala, and kuṣṭha, or with grapes, lac, and sugar, along with rock salt, should be applied as a sprinkling (seka) to alleviate pain and redness. This boiled milk is a destroyer of both pain and inflammation.
Ghee boiled with śatāvarī, pṛthakparṇī, mustā, āmalaka, and padmaka,
along with goat’s milk, destroys burning sensations and pain.
Ghee prepared with four times as much milk that has been processed with Vātaghna drugs,
and with the addition of the Kākolyādi group as a paste, should be employed in all therapeutic procedures.
If the pain does not subside in this manner, one should administer oleation and sudation and then perform venesection;
thereafter, the wise physician may also apply cauterization, as has been prescribed.
Therefore, O auspicious lady, listen to me regarding the collyrium for the purpose of clarifying the vision:
[use] the flowers of the Meṣaśṛṅga, as well as those of the Śirīṣa and Dhava.
Having ground together *sumanā* flowers, pearls,
and lapis lazuli with goat’s milk, one should place them in copper for seven days.
Having prepared those substances, the physician should apply them as a collyrium,
using antimony, coral, sea-foam, and realgar.
One should also prepare pills of long pepper (marica) as before;
this beneficial collyrium should be applied for the sake of stabilizing the vision.
I shall further describe the principal collyriums in detail;
one should also employ those of various kinds mentioned in the ritual manual (kalpa) here.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Diseases Affecting the Vision," within the Śālākyatantra section of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||17||
The eighteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the ritual procedure for the rites.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:

Then the sage, the lord of Kāśī, who knew the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, whose vision was penance, and who possessed noble intellect, instructed his disciple, the son of Viśvāmitra.
Tarpaṇa, puṭapāka, seka, āścyotana, and añjana—
learn from me their detailed exposition as they have been taught in their respective places.
On an auspicious day, when the body and head have been thoroughly cleansed and food has been digested,
the saturation of the eyes should be performed either in the forenoon or in the afternoon.
In a dwelling free from wind, sun, and dust, lying on his back,
he should apply circular supports made of moistened bean flour.
The two eye-sockets should be made even, firm, and free from obstruction;
they should be filled with the scum of clarified butter that has been melted in lukewarm water.
Then, having positioned it from the tip of the eyelashes, one should apply five hundred applications for a healthy person;
six for kapha, eight for pitta, and ten for vāta, which is the best.
Some declare that death occurs according to the specific location of the disease:
in three, one, five, or seven [days], as taught in their respective order.
Then one should contemplate ten hundred views and eight hundred words;
thereafter, having caused affection to flow from the outer corner of the eye, one should purify the eye.
Then, having applied a poultice of steamed barley flour stimulated by the potency of fats,
one should purify his phlegm with the appropriate inhalation of medicated smoke.
It is desired that [the treatment] last for one day, or three days, or at most five days;
during the satiation (tarpaṇa), one should observe these signs of satisfaction regarding the eye.
Easy sleep and awakening, clarity, proficiency of speech,
contentment, the destruction of disease, and lightness of action.
An eye that is turbid, heavy, excessively unctuous, and characterized by tearing, itching,
and discharge should be known as "over-satiated" (atyarthatarpita), being afflicted by the provoked humors (doṣas).
An eye that is rough, turbid, full of tears, intolerant of the sight of forms,
and characterized by an increase in disease should be known as an eye that has been under-nourished.
Because of the abundance of defects in the incurable type,
the expert in application should strive for treatment with medicated smoking, nasal drops, collyria, and sprinklings— both dry and unctuous.

That which is extremely parched and withers away, that which is dry and exceedingly harsh, that whose eyelashes are shriveled and turbid, that which is distorted, and that which is severely afflicted by disease; |||
By the mere act of satiating that eye, one shall undoubtedly obtain vigor,
even amidst foul weather, excessive heat or cold, and the confusion of anxiety and fatigue.
When the affliction of the eye has not subsided, saturation therapy (tarpaṇa) is not recommended;
likewise, in these cases, surgical excision (puṭapāka) and nasal medication (nasya), which are otherwise prescribed, are forbidden.
Those who have not been declared fit for the tarpaṇa procedure, and those who are unable to drink medicated fats—
