once their humors have been pacified and they are capable of undergoing puṭapāka— [then [the treatment should be applied].]
The physician should apply puṭapāka to the eyes;
it is of three types: emollient (snehana), scraping (lekhanīya), and healing (ropaṇīya).
One [type of collyrium] is beneficial and unctuous for those who are excessively dry, while another is scraping even for those who are already unctuous;
yet another is for the sake of strengthening the vision and alleviates pitta, blood disorders, wounds, and vāta.
The *puṭapāka* prepared with fats, meat, muscle fat,
marrow, fat, and sweet medicinal herbs should be retained for two hundred words.
With the liver and meat of wild animals combined with scraping substances,
along with black iron filings, copper, conch-shell, coral, and products from the sea;
By means of sea-foam, green vitriol, antimony,
and the whey of curdled milk, one who practices this as a linctus attains the supreme retention of a hundred words.

A *puṭapāka* prepared with breast milk, meat from arid regions (*jāṅgala*), honey, clarified butter, and bitter substances should be retained for three times the duration of a scraping (*lekhana*) treatment; it is curative of healing (*ropaṇa*).
One should perform the treatments prescribed for *tarpaṇa*, excluding fumigation; however, one should omit the healing (*ropaṇa*) treatment.
Oleation and sudation should be applied in both cases, but they must never be used during the healing stage.
Whether it be for one day, two days, or even three days,
the period of confinement is prescribed to be double the time required for the performance of the ritual act.
One should not look at flames, wind, the sky, a mirror,
or bright objects after the eyes have been satiated by the performance of *puṭapāka*.
Whatever disease arises from improper application of these two [collyrium and eye-drops] should be treated with appropriate collyrium, eye-drops, and sudation.
It possesses a clear complexion, is bright, endures wind and heat, is light,
and is endowed with the qualities of easy sleep and awakening, as well as the therapeutic benefits of *puṭapāka*.

From excessive application (atiyoga) there arise pain, swelling, pustules, the onset of darkness before the eyes, suppuration, lacrimation, and irritation; likewise, from deficient application (hīna), there is the emergence of the humors (doṣas).
Henceforth, I shall explain the preparation of *puṭapāka*:
two smooth, ground balls of meat, each the size of a *bilva* fruit.
The quantity of solid substances should be the size of a bilva fruit, while that of liquid substances is considered to be one kuḍava;
having mixed these together and thoroughly wrapped them with leaves.
One should coat it with clay containing *kāśmarī*, *kumuda*, castor plant, lotus, and plantain, and then line the interior with charcoal from *khadira* wood.
One should prepare [the site] using kataka, aśmantaka, eraṇḍa, pāṭala, vṛṣa, and bādara,
or with the wood of milk-exuding trees, or even with cow dung, according to the proper method.
Having extracted the steamed [substance], squeezed it, and taken its juice,
one should administer it to men according to the prescribed method for *tarpaṇa*.
The Kanīnaka (the inner corners of the eyes) should always be sprinkled while the patient lies on their back;
these two [corners] are cold when blood and bile are present, and warm for removing wind and phlegm.
Excessive heat and sharpness are always known to cause burning and suppuration;
when not washed, they cause coldness, obstruction of the lacrimal ducts, pain, and friction.
Excessive [humors] cause astringency, contraction, and throbbing;
those of deficient measure greatly generate the agitation of the bodily humors.
When properly prepared and applied, they destroy burning, swelling, pain, itching, and discharge;
they also eliminate itching, skin eruptions, dūṣīkā, and red streaks (raktarājī).
Therefore, avoiding these defects, one should administer those two [therapies] which bring about well-being;
and one should overcome complications according to the specific dosha by means of nasal drops, medicated smoke, and collyrium.
At the beginning and end of these two [therapies], fomentation with warm water and cloth is beneficial;
likewise, at the conclusion, when phlegm is predominant, the application of smoke is recommended.
When applied according to the specific disorder, eye-drops (āścyotana) that are not excessively strong in potency destroy disease; however, irrigation (seka) is even more powerful.
These two [types of collyrium] are employed in diseases in three ways, like the *puṭapāka* preparation:
seven or eight drops for the scraping (*lekhanīya*) type, and ten drops for the oleating (*snaihika*) type.
Twelve [applications] should be employed for āścyotana, while twelve are prescribed for ropaṇa;
the time for seka is considered twice that of puṭapāka.
Alternatively, the application for the accomplishment of the task is according to the sequence:
in the forenoon, the afternoon, at midday, and during the times of pain for both.

By means of appropriate or inappropriate applications of oleation and affusion, they describe the treatment of the diseases arising in the head as being like those of *tarpaṇa* (satiating therapy), having destroyed even the most powerful [symptoms] through their specific qualities.
The head enema (śirobasti) is prescribed for those ailments of the head known as mūrdhatailika;
it should be administered in the evening to one whose body has been purified and who has eaten according to the requirements of the disease.
Then, while the patient is sitting upright, one should firmly bind the bladder sac;
having secured it, one should hold it filled with oil boiled according to the specific disease.
One who knows the ritual procedure should perform the libation ten times as prescribed, according to the specific dosha.
When the faults have become manifest, [the state] of the pure body alone [remains].
When the dosha is located specifically in the eye, one should apply collyrium (añjana) as required—
whether it be scraping (lekhanam), healing (ropaṇam), or soothing (prasādanam).

In that regard, one should diligently employ the five types of scraping (lekhana) treatments using the five tastes individually— excluding the first taste (sweet)— according to the specific dosha involved.
One should cause that morbid humor (doṣa), which has taken refuge in the eyelids, vessels, cavities, channels, and the śṛṅgāṭaka, to flow out through the mouth, nose, and eyes by means of ojas.
A paste that is either astringent or bitter, yet unctuous, is considered healing;
due to its unctuousness and coldness, it improves the complexion and increases the strength of the eyesight.
An ointment that is sweet and rich in unctuousness is clarifying;
it is beneficial for the purpose of clarifying defects of vision and for the purpose of providing lubrication.
These collyriums, as prescribed, should be applied by those skilled in diseases according to the specific disorder, during the morning, evening, or night.
Pills, medicinal powders, and collyriums are of three kinds;
the wise say that their efficacy increases in the order mentioned, with the former being superior to the latter.
The wick for scraping should be the size of a mustard seed;
for soothing, it should be one and a half times that size, and for healing, twice as large.
The dose of *rasāñjana* is considered to be measured according to its consistency;
for the powder, it is likewise progressively two, three, or four *śalākās*.
One should provide vessels for them that correspond in quality to their respective recipients,
whether they be made of gold, silver, horn, copper, lapis lazuli, or bell-metal.
And iron probes should be applied in due order;
they should be shaped like buds at their two ends and be as thick as a pea.
A staff eight finger-breadths thick at the middle, well-fashioned and effective for restraining the wicked—
whether made of udumbara wood, stone, or even from a human bone— shall be beneficial.
Having well-composed himself, he should open his left eye with his hand and apply the collyrium for the maiden with a stick using his right hand.
Or one may perform the movement back and forth along the outer corner of the eye as appropriate;
or whatever is to be rubbed upon the eyelid, that one should apply with the finger alone.
A physician, even while treating, should not apply collyrium to the inner corners of the eye;
nor should he employ irrigation in an eye whose morbid humors have not been expelled.
When the disorder has subsided, it likewise destroys the strength of vision;
one should see clearly with water that is free from defects and devoid of tears.
After washing the eye according to the specific disorder, counter-collyrium (pratyañjana) should then be applied;
[this is contraindicated] in cases of exhaustion, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), weeping, intoxication, anger, fear, or fever.
Collyrium is not recommended for those suffering from disorders caused by the suppression of natural urges or diseases of the head,
because it may give rise to redness, pain, cataracts, discharge, aching, and inflammation.
Upon the waning of sleep, there arises the impairment of the power of action; when afflicted by wind, the loss of the power of vision;
when struck by dust and smoke, the onset of ocular inflammation caused by the discharge of passion.
Headache at the end of nasal therapy when it is accompanied by agitation and pain, headache during head-bathing when it is excessively cold, and [headache] when the sun has not yet risen; |||
Due to the stability of the humors (doṣas), it would be ineffective and instead causes an aggravation of the humors;
even so in the case of indigestion (ajīrṇa), the same occurs because of the obstruction of the channels (srotas).
If applied when the force of the humors (doṣas) has arisen, it will produce various complications;
therefore, one should skillfully apply the collyrium while avoiding the humors.
This specific time for applying the medicinal paste has been proclaimed;
one should overcome these complications by means of irrigation, instillation, and ointments.
When [the doshas] have been aroused by their respective applications of medicinal smoke (dhūma) and nasal drops (nasya),
the sense organs become clear, light, non-secretory, efficient in their function, and perfectly pure.
One should declare the eye to be properly purged when its afflictions have been completely pacified; whereas an eye that is distorted, harsh, discolored, drooping, or excessively dry is not so.
In the event of excessive purgation, the eye flows excessively;
in that case, nourishing therapy and measures that subdue Vāta should be employed.
If the eye is insufficiently purged and possesses excessively aggravated doshas,
then the elimination of those doshas through fumigation, nasal medication, collyrium, and bloodletting is beneficial.
When the soothing treatment has been properly administered, the eye should be known as being endowed with moisture, color, and strength; it is clear, free from defects, and at rest.
If, after excessive satiation has been performed, there should be even a slight morbid transformation,
then mild, parched medicine that removes the humors (doṣas) is recommended.

Even though it is common to all, the characteristic of ropana (healing) should be understood in this way; when that [ropaṇa] is applied excessively, one describes it as being like prasādana (soothing).
Whether it be for emollience or healing, an application that is deficiently administered is useless;
therefore, one who desires success must apply the collyrium with the proper measure.
In procedures such as the *puṭapāka* (herbal steaming), this very same method of preparation applies;
and thousands of ointments have been honored by means of the seed-syllable previously mentioned.
For the purpose of strengthening the power of vision and for the alleviation of chronic diseases,
learn from hereafter these foremost ointments worthy of kings.
One should take eight parts of collyrium with the luster of a blue lotus,
along with copper, gold, and silver, in equal proportions.
A skilled physician should then add these eleven ingredients;
it is then cast into a crucible, blown with a bellows, and covered within the fire.
With twigs of Khadira and Aśmantaka, or even with cow-dung;
or in the liquid of cow-dung, in urine, in curd, in clarified butter, or in honey.
And in oils, wines, muscle fat, marrow, and water infused with all kinds of fragrant substances;
and in grape juice, sugarcane juice, the juice of the three myrobalans, and very cold liquids.
One should sprinkle this [substance], having heated it again and again, separately with a decoction of the sārivādi group and with a decoction of the utpalādi group.
Then, having remained for seven days in the water tied to a raft in the open air,
one should dry and powder pearls, crystal, and likewise coral.
Having also obtained black aloe-wood through yoga,
this excellent powder-collyrium should be placed in a beautiful vessel.

Having performed worship with [substances] processed a thousand times, one should employ it for the king upon a throne made of ivory, crystal, lapis lazuli, or conch-shell, or on a well-prepared seat of gold, horn, or silver.
With eyes anointed by that, the king shall become beloved by all people,
invincible to all beings, and free from diseases of the eye.
Kuṣṭha, sandalwood, cardamom, cinnamon leaf, madhuka, añjana,
the flowers of meṣaśṛṅga, vakra, and the seven gems.
The filaments of the blue lotus, the large lotus, and the red lotus;
nāgapuṣpa, uśīra, long pepper, and excellent tuttha.
One should take hen’s eggs, potsherds, dārvī, pathyā, rocanā, black pepper,
the marrow of an elephant, and an equal amount of gṛhagopikā.
Having made this into a fine powder, one should place it there after worshipping as before;
this is called Bhadrodaya, which a king always deserves.
Take equal parts of vakra, marica, māṃsī, and śaileya;
then, with all these combined in equal proportions, add an amount of manaḥśilā equal to the total.
Four parts of *patra*, twice as much *añjana* on all sides, and the same amount of *yaṣṭīmadhuka*; this collyrium is prepared as previously described.
Realgar, devadāru wood, the two types of turmeric, the three myrobalans, black pepper,
lac, garlic, mañjiṣṭhā, rock salt, cardamom, and honey.
Powdered rodhra, sāvaraka, iron, and copper,
as well as kālānusārivā and the petals of the kukkuṭāṇḍa plant.
The wise physician, having ground these in equal parts with milk,
should prepare pills for the alleviation of itching, blindness, cataracts, and vascular streaks in the eye.
Bell-metal polish, soot, madhuka, rock salt,
and castor root, taken in equal parts, combined with twice as much bṛhatī;
Having ground [the ingredients] with goat's milk, one should smear a copper vessel;
those wicks, rolled seven times and dried in the shade, destroy pain.
Equal parts of harītakī, tuttha, and yaṣṭimadhu, with sixteen parts of marica—
this suppository, ground with cold water, is used for all disorders.
One who is skilled in the prescribed methods of processing mercury should,
being diligent, prepare medicinal pills and collyria according to the appropriate procedures as described.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Treatment," within the Śālākyatantra, which is part of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The nineteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment for injuries to the eyes.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
When the eyes of men are struck in various ways by pains tumultuous with agitation and redness,
the wise physician should again prescribe nasal drops, facial ointments, affusions, saturations, and so forth, which are beneficial for the pain arising from blood and bile.
The physician should quickly employ procedures that generate clarity of vision using unctuous, cold, and sweet applications;
likewise, he should treat even those cases afflicted by perspiration, fire, smoke, fear, grief, disease, or injury in that same manner.
This procedure is for an eye injury sustained immediately; beyond that, it should be performed after considering the specific dosha involved.
Furthermore, an eye that has been struck should be slightly moistened with tears; thus, it becomes free from pain in an instant.
A single injured *paṭala* is curable; two are difficult to treat; one should avoid [surgery for] three injured *paṭalas*.
Furthermore, the eye that is crushed (*piccita*), excessively sunken (*avasanna*), prolapsed (*srasta*), displaced (*cyuta*), or has its vision destroyed (*hatadṛk*) is only palliable (*yāpya*).

When the eyes have entered too deeply, they should be raised quickly by means of obstructing the breath, inducing vomiting, or tickling the throat; this restores the wide field of vision, removes the redness, shows what was previously seen as unreal, and brings about a clear perception of the object as it truly exists.
Drooping eyelids, snoring, and the discharge of water from the head were ordained by Fate long ago;
these sixty-six diseases born of the eyes are said to afflict both the small and the great.
Another disease, Kukūṇaka, arises from the corruption of breast milk by kapha, vāta, pitta, and blood, affecting the eyelids;
it causes excessive itching of the eyes and the eye-sockets, as well as the nose and forehead, and the infant is constantly afflicted by it.
If [the child] cannot endure the light of the sun, has a continuous discharge, one should quickly extract its blood and scrape it away.
One should rub the area with pungent substances mixed with honey, and one should carry out the prescribed procedure for both the mother and the infant.
One should indeed cause that [milk] to be vomited by drinking milk mixed with honey, rock salt, and the fruits of the *kharamañjarī*.
Alternatively, one may use [the powder] combined with long pepper (pippalī), salt, and honey; however, one should not attempt to induce vomiting even if the patient is already vomiting.
Once the patient has eaten food and drunk milk mixed with *vacā*, those knowledgeable in the procedure should subsequently administer an emetic containing the *phala* fruits.
A decoction should be prepared from the fine leaves of Jambu, Āmra, and Dhātrī for the purpose of washing and for irrigation;
furthermore, ghee processed with Guḍūcī is beneficial here as an eye-drop, and they also say that ghee cooked with Triphalā is likewise effective.
Nepalese black pepper, conch shell, and *rasāñjana*, combined with rock salt, jaggery, and honey, constitute an ointment;
or alternatively, iron filings burnt together with *madhurasā*, *madhuka*, and mango, or even burnt ghee, milk, and honey, may serve as an ointment.

Physicians desire that *vyoṣa*, onion, *madhuka*, the best salt (*saindhava*), lac, and red ochre combined, should be made into a pill or an ointment; or they prefer an ointment consisting of equal parts of neem leaves, *madhuka*, *darvī*, copper, and *lodhra*.

The physician skilled in diseases, desiring to destroy the eye ailment of an infant, should administer collyrium prepared from *srotoja*, conch-shell, curd, and rock-salt for half a fortnight; this removes the *śukra* (milk-haze) caused by phlegm (*kapha*), and one should follow the prescribed regimen for *syanda* (ophthalmia).
As deep as the ocean, it is impossible to provide a complete medical treatment for it,
even with tens of thousands of verses.
Even if it is explained by the thousands, a man of small intellect,
unlearned and devoid of the meaning of the treatises on logic, does not grasp it at all.
This seed of medicine, which contains many hidden meanings,
when taken up by a skilled practitioner, grows forth in many ways.

Therefore, a wise person who perceives the meaning of various scriptures and possesses an understanding of the traditional teachings should always infer the entire scripture whose meaning is unfathomable.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Ocular Trauma," within the Śālākyatantra of the Uttaratantra in the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||19||
The twentieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the diagnosis of diseases affecting the ear.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Earache, ringing in the ears, deafness, and a roaring sound;
ear discharge, itching of the ear, and likewise wax in the ear.
Kṛmikarṇa, Pratināha, the two types of Vidradhi,
Karṇapāka, Pūtikarṇa, and likewise the four types of Arśas.
There are seven types of ear-tumors (karṇār-buda) and four types of swellings (śopha);
these twenty-eight diseases located in the ear have been described.
When the wind (samīraṇa) reaches the ears and acts abnormally, it causes an intense piercing pain in both ears on all sides;
when obstructed by the humors (doṣas) according to their respective natures, this is described as the difficult-to-treat earache known as karṇaśūla.
But when that very [wind], having entered a wrong path, remains within the sound-carrying channels, then a man hears various sounds; they call this condition "praṇāda" and declare it a disease.
When that very [wind], accompanied by kapha and following the channels, persists by pervading the auditory passages,
then deafness will undoubtedly occur for the man who fails to seek treatment.
Due to fatigue, wasting, or the consumption of dry and astringent foods, the wind (vāyu) becomes established in the pathway of sound;
furthermore, in one who has undergone head-purgation or who indulges in cold things, it indeed produces an excessively loud ringing in the ears.
Due to a blow to the head, or from submerging in water, or even from the suppuration of an abscess, pus may flow from the ear when it is obstructed by Vāyu;
this is proclaimed as Karṇasaṃsrāva (discharge from the ear).
When phlegm (kapha) is excessively accumulated in the passage known as the ear, intense itching occurs.
When that phlegm is dried up by the heat of bile (pitta), earwax (karṇagūthaka) forms in the ear passages of men.
When that earwax, having become liquid and dissolved, reaches the nostrils and the mouth,
then it becomes the disorder known as *karṇapratināha*, which causes distress throughout the head.
When living creatures become encrusted, or when maggots are produced [in the ear],
that disease of the ear is designated by the ancient physicians as *kṛmikarṇaka* (ear-worm) because of its appearance like collyrium.
An abscess (vidradhi) arises either from injury to a wound or, alternatively, from the humors (doṣas).
It discharges blood that is reddish, yellowish, or crimson, accompanied by pricking pain, a sensation of fuming, burning, and swelling.
Indeed, due to the provocation of pitta, there may be suppuration in the ears, causing putrefaction and moistening;
when the heat of pitta remains in the channel where kapha is situated, it causes intense burning as it dissolves that kapha.
Whether painless or accompanied by pain, when pus flows thickly and with a foul odor, it is called Pūtikarṇaka.

The symptoms of Arśas (ear polyps) have been described in truth, and likewise those of Śopha (swelling) and Arbuda (tumors) were previously stated by me; having carefully examined them, the diligent and excellent physician should apply them here as well.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Diseases of the Ear," within the Śālākya-tantra of the Uttara-tantra in the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diseases affecting the ear.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
In cases of ear-obstruction, the general treatment consists of drinking ghee as a rejuvenative (rasāyana),
abstaining from physical exertion, avoiding bathing the head, practicing celibacy, and refraining from boastfulness.
In cases of earache, ringing in the ears, deafness, and tinnitus,
they know this to be the general remedy for all four diseases.
One should treat a person who has been unctuated and purged with oleaginous substances by means of Vata-alleviating sudations,
both through tube-sudation (nāḍīsveda) and likewise through bolus-sudation (piṇḍasveda).
With bilva, eraṇḍa, arka, varṣābhū, badhī, unmatta,
śigru, bastagandhā, aśvagandhā, tarkārī, yava, and veṇu;
When this nāḍī-sveda (tube-fomentation) is applied using these boiled fermented gruel decoctions,
it dispels earache arising from the provocation of kapha and vāta.
One should apply fomentation using boluses made from the meat of fish, chicken, or quail, or even with milk,
to alleviate earache.
Having prepared a basket of many leaves made from the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree,
one should place it, well-filled with its charcoal, upon the ear.
Whatever oil drips from that pan heated by charcoal reaches the auditory canal and immediately causes intense pain.
One should fumigate it with linen, guggulu, and aguru mixed with clarified butter;
clarified butter applied over the food is beneficial, as is the administration of enema therapy (bastikarma).
Having fasted at night and drunk that clarified butter, one should drink milk afterwards;
it is used for head-purgatives, nasal drops, brain-massages, and affusions.
Balā oil processed a hundred times is also recommended for food;
likewise, having boiled Kaṇṭakārī in goat’s milk, one should use that milk [for the preparation].
One should cook chicken fat and fill the ears with it;
likewise, one may use the roots of *taṇḍulīyaka* and the fruit of *aṅkola*.
The root of the ahiṃsā-kiṇvuka, sarala, devadāru,
garlic, ginger, and likewise bamboo scrapings.
One should cook the four kinds of fats with the pastes of these [drugs] as well as with sour substances;
this filling of the ear is beneficial for the alleviation of pain.
The fresh juice of garlic, ginger, śigru, muraṅgī, radish,
and plantain is excellent when used as a warm ear-drop.
The juice of ginger, honey, rock salt, and oil—these, when lukewarm, should be poured into the ears;
this indeed removes the pain.
The physician should cook ghee with goat or sheep urine mixed with bamboo scrapings;
he should then fill the ear of one suffering from earache with that preparation.
Having wrapped an eighteen-finger-length section of the great five-roots (pañcamūla) with linen cloth and sprinkled it with oil, one should then set it on fire.
The oil that drips from those wicks onto the vessel should be known as dīpikā-taila; it causes immediate pain.
In this same manner, a wise person should prepare lamp-oil from Bhadrakāṣṭha, Kuṣṭha, and Sāralakāṣṭha to destroy earache.
One should place sprouts of the *arka* plant, ground with sour liquids, smeared with oil, and mixed with salt,
inside a hollowed-out stem of the *sruhī* plant that is covered by its own leaves.
One should squeeze the [medicinal paste] that has been steamed by the process of *puṭapāka* until the juice is extracted;
one should then apply that lukewarm juice into the ear for the alleviation of pain.
One should fill the ear with the auspicious, pleasantly warm juices of wood-apple (kapittha), citron (mātuluṅga), and ginger (śṛṅgavera) for the cessation of that pain.
One suffering from earache should fill the ear with lukewarm sour gruel (cukra),
and one should also skillfully dust it with the powder of sea-foam (samudraphena).
For the alleviation of earache, one should fill the ear with any one of these eight urines, made lukewarm.
The physician should cook the four kinds of fat (sneha) in sour urines and in a decoction of the Vata-subduing group (vātaghna-gaṇa); that should then be used for filling the ears.
One should perform these very same procedures with pitta-alleviating substances when the condition is associated with pitta;
in this case, ghee prepared with the Kākolyādi group, ten parts of milk, and bitter herbs is beneficial.
It is best prepared by cooking the paste and decoction of the tender shoots of milk-exuding trees, as well as madhuka and sandalwood, together with sugar, madhuka, and ghee.
The oils of *iṅgudī* and mustard are beneficial for filling [the ear] when phlegm is present;
likewise, soups of bitter herbs and sudation therapies that destroy phlegm are recommended.
Oil prepared with the *surasā* group of drugs and also with the great *pañcamūla*,
as well as the juice of *mātuluṅga*, fermented gruel (*śukta*), and the juices of garlic and fresh ginger;
Each one of these is beneficial when used as a filling (pūraṇa), or oil prepared with them may be used;
furthermore, strong head-purgatives (mūrdhavireka) and gargles (kavala) are highly recommended in this condition.
This entire procedure for earache is curative of pitta in cases involving obstructed blood;
however, it is specifically proclaimed for the treatment of piercing pain, ringing, deafness, and roaring sounds in the ears.
Listen now to the general and specific treatment for deafness:
having ground bilva fruits with cow urine, one should cook oil [with them].
For deafness, one should fill the ears with water mixed with milk;
or alternatively, with goat's milk processed with sugar, licorice (madhuka), and the bimba fruit.
One should churn warm water in a decoction of *bimbi* fruit; once it has cooled, that liquid is removed and boiled again with ten parts milk and with sugar, *madhuka*, and sandalwood.
That oil, saturated with bilva water, used as an ear-drop for deafness, is recommended;
furthermore, the procedure prescribed for catarrh shall also be honored here.
The regimen prescribed for diseases of the wind (vātavyādhi) is also beneficial in cases of ear discharge (karṇasrāva),
putrid ear (pūtikarṇa), and likewise in worm-infested ears (kṛmikarṇaka).
One should perform the same treatments, as well as specific yogic applications,
such as head-purgation (śirovirecana), fumigation (dhūpana), and filling the ears (pūraṇa).
Having repeatedly inspected the vessel for cleaning and washing,
one should administer it with water from the *rājavṛkṣa* group or with the *surasā* group of decoctions.
One should perform the cleansing of the ear and fill it with these powders;
furthermore, one should administer a decoction of the five astringents (pañcakaṣāya) combined with the juice of wood-apple (kapittha).
In cases of otorrhoea (discharge from the ear), they praise filling it with honey combined with the juice of cotton seeds mixed with the powder of Sarja bark.
Or, combined with honey, it is recommended for ear discharge;
likewise, lac, rasāñjana, and sarja resin, ground into a powder, are used as an ear-filling.
Oil prepared with śaivala, large trees, jambu, and mango blossoms, along with kulīra, honey, and maṇḍūkī, is highly esteemed.
Tinduka, abhayā, rodhra, samaṅgā, āmalaka, and honey— this filling,
when combined with the juice of kapittha, would be wholesome in this case.
The juices of mango and wood-apple, or oil extracted from madhūka, dhava, and śāla,
or oil cooked with these, are recommended for the purpose of filling the ear cavity.
With priyaṅgu, madhuka, ambaṣṭhā, dhātakī, śilaparṇī,
mañjiṣṭhā, lobhra, and lākṣā, or with the juice of kapittha;
One should cook oil; by filling [the cavity] with it, it arrests the discharge.
Ghee, combined with rasāñjana, honey, and the milk of a woman, [should be used].
This is recommended even for long-standing, suppurating, and purulent ear-ache:
the fresh juice of nirguṇḍī, oil, rock salt, soot-dust, and jaggery.
Pūraṇa (filling) combined with honey is a pacifier for pūtikarṇa;
for the destruction of kṛmikarṇaka, one should employ a vermifuge procedure.
The smoke of eggplant is beneficial, as is mustard oil;
likewise, an anthelmintic treatment with yellow orpiment combined with cow's urine is effective.
For foul odor of the ears, fumigation with guggulu is said to be the best remedy;
likewise, emesis, inhalation of medicinal smoke, and the holding of gargle-water are recommended.
In cases of ear-ache, mustard oil is beneficial for filling the ear;
furthermore, one should apply the treatment prescribed for abscesses (vidradhi) in cases of an abscess as well.
Having moistened it with oil and softened it by means of fomentation,
the wise physician should properly clear away the earwax using a probe.
Nasal fomentation, emesis, medicated smoking, head-purgation,
and all procedures that remove phlegm (kapha) alleviate itching of the ears.
Now, in cases of ear-obstruction (karṇapratīnāha), one should employ oleation and sudation;
thereafter, once the head has been purged, one should perform the appropriate therapeutic measures.
One should treat the medicinal remedy for karṇapāka (ear-inflammation) as one would for pitta-visarpa (pitta-type erysipelas).
Regarding an insect, moisture, or impurities residing within the ear canal:
The wise physician should extract it with a horn or even with a probe;
as for the remaining disorders, their treatment has already been described.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Ear," within the Śālākyatantra of the Uttaratantra in the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The Twenty-second Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of diseases affecting the nose.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Chronic catarrh, putrid nose, as well as nasal suppuration,
and likewise hemorrhaging from the nose, and even pus and blood [discharges].
Sneezing, discharge, inflammation, nasal obstruction,
and discharge— these eleven diseases are said to arise along with dryness of the nose.
There are four types of hemorrhoids (arśas), four types of swellings (śopha), seven types of tumors (arbuda),
and five types of chronic catarrh (pratiśyāya) that will be described along with their treatments;
these thirty-one diseases of the nose have thus been proclaimed.
One should diagnose as being afflicted by apīnasa (chronic rhinitis) that person whose nose becomes stuffed, emits a foul odor, becomes moist, and also becomes dry;
who does not perceive smells or tastes; and who is thus possessed by the disease.
One should describe that disorder arising from wind and phlegm as having symptoms identical to those of chronic catarrh (pratiśyāya),
occurring when the wind is obstructed at the root of the palate by the vitiated humors.

When putrid matter flows out from both the mouth and the nostrils, they call that disease *pūtināsa*. When pitta is located in the nose, it produces ulcers (*arūṃṣi*) in that disorder, along with intense suppuration.
One should diagnose that as *nāsikāpāka* (nasal suppuration) where both moisture and putrefaction are observed.
I shall now further describe the four types of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), which have two origins.
When a person's forehead is struck by the humors (doṣas) that have become inflamed, or by foreign objects, the nose may discharge pus mixed with blood;
this disease they call Pūyarakta.
When the vital point (marman) dependent on the nose is thoroughly afflicted, the wind (anila) exits through the nostrils.
Those who know the medical method call that disease *kṣavathu* (sneezing), which is frequently accompanied by phlegm and sound;
it arises from the excessive use of pungent substances, smelling strong odors, or from gazing at the sun.
Alternatively, when the joints of the young bones and vital points (marman) are opened by means of sutures and the like, another discharge flows out;
that which issues from the nose itself is thick, putrid, and salty phlegm (kapha).

When pitta, previously accumulated at the crown of the head, becomes heated, they declare that disease to be *bhraṃśathu*. When the nose is intensely inflamed with a burning sensation, the wind (breath) issues forth as if it were smoke.
When the nose of a person feels as if it were on fire, they declare that disease to be "Dipta" (burning).
This occurs when the Vayu known as Udāna, covered by Kapha, remains disordered in its own channel.
When that disease obstructs the sense of smell as it were, it is designated as nasal obstruction (nāsāpratīnāha);
in this condition, the nose constantly discharges clear, water-like, and colorless fluid.
One should specifically diagnose that disorder as *nāsāparisrāva* (nasal discharge), especially when it occurs at night;
this happens when the phlegm residing in the nose has been thoroughly dried up by the wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*).
One who breathes with difficulty, gasping both upward and downward, suffers from what is called the drying up of the nose;
one should likewise describe hemorrhoids and swellings as being caused by those same three doshas, either individually or collectively.

Having also examined the principles of Śālākya, the seventh [chapter], which is universal in nature, concerns the disease arbuda; meanwhile, pratiśyāya (catarrh) is taught here, and it will be described as fivefold later on.

Thirty-one diseases are proclaimed to be located in the nasal passages (*nāsāsrotas*). Among them, an *arbuda* (tumor) occurs in the path of the passage as a large growth resembling a pouch (*kośa*). Furthermore, swellings (*śopha*) characterized by the knowledge of swelling are situated within the nasal passages.
Hemorrhoids have been described in the Nidāna [section]; thus one should analyze them.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Diseases Affecting the Nose," within the Śālākyatantra section of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of diseases affecting the nose.
Then the Blessed One Dhanvantari spoke.
In the case of a person suffering from the previously mentioned putrinasya, oleation, sudation, emesis, and purgation are appropriate;
the food should be sharp, small in quantity, and light, along with warm water and the timely inhalation of medicinal smoke.
Asafoetida, the three pungents (vyoṣa), vatsaka, śivāṭī, lac, the seeds of saurabha,
kaṭphala, ugrā, kuṣṭha, tīkṣṇagandhā, viḍaṅga, and karaja— these are always considered the best ingredients for an avapīḍa.

With these substances, a wise person should cook mustard oil mixed with urine for the purpose of nasal medication (nasya). In cases of inflammation of the nose (nāsāpāka), all Pitta-alleviating measures should be employed, both externally and internally.
Having extracted the blood, decoctions and ointments made from the bark of milk-exuding trees mixed with clarified butter (ājya) should be applied.
Hereafter, I shall describe the pacification of blood and bile; the treatment for pus-filled blood should be like that for a sinus tract (nāḍī).
When vomiting has been properly induced, they prescribe a sharp avapīḍa, as well as purifying smoke and nasal medication (nasya).
In cases of sneezing and drooping of the head, powder should be administered through a tube by means of head-purgative (mūrdhavairecanīya) nasal medications.
One should apply sudations to the head that destroy Vata disorders, as well as unctuous medicated smokes and whatever else is beneficial;
however, when the disease is aggravated by Pitta, one should employ all Pitta-alleviating measures, including everything sweet and cold.

In the constriction of the nose, the primary treatment is the internal administration of fats (sneha-pāna), along with unctuous medicated smokes (snigdha-dhūma) and daily cranial enemas (mūrdha-basti).
Bala-taila should be employed in every way, as well as whatever else has been prescribed for vāta diseases.
In cases of nasal discharge, one should administer powder through the nose via a tube, as well as a sharp *avapīḍa* (pressed snuff).
They prescribe strong smoke made from *devadāru* and *agni* (citraka), or goat meat prepared with salt and other seasonings.
In cases of nasal dryness (nāsāśoṣa), milk-ghee is the primary remedy; oil prepared according to the "aṇu" method should be used as a nasal drop (nasya).
One should also drink ghee, eat meat from wild animals (jāṅgala), and employ oleation, sudation, and unctuous medicinal smoking (snaihika-dhūma).
One should restrain the remaining diseases arising from the nose according to the specific treatment for each that has been described to you.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Nose," within the Śālākya-tantra, which is part of the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-fourth chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the prevention and cure of catarrh (pratiśyāya).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Excessive indulgence with women, heat in the head, exposure to smoke and dust, cold, excessive heat,
and the suppression of urine and feces are said to be the immediate causes of catarrh.
When the Vāyu and the other [humors], both individually and collectively, have reached the head, and likewise the blood,
being provoked by various provocative factors, they indeed cause catarrh (pratiśyāya) in human beings.
Heaviness of the head, the onset of sneezing, as well as body aches and horripilation—
these and various other complications are known to precede catarrh in men.
The nostrils become obstructed and covered, with only a thin discharge flowing;
there is dryness of the throat, palate, and lips, as well as a piercing pain in the temples.
In the case of a wind-natured (vātika) coryza, there is impairment of the voice;
in the bile-natured (paittika) type, warm and yellowish discharge flows from the nose.
The person becomes emaciated, extremely pale, and feverish, oppressed by thirst;
he feels as if he is suddenly vomiting smoke along with fire.
In the case of a disorder caused by phlegm (kapha), white and cold secretions flow repeatedly from the nose;
the patient appears pale, has swollen eyes, and feels heaviness in the head and face.
Excessive scratching of the head, neck, lips, and palate, and a catarrh that repeatedly occurs and then suddenly subsides; |||
Whether fully matured or immature, that [type] is considered the source of all;
and such are the symptoms of all types of chronic catarrh (pīnasa) arising from the combination of all [doshas].
In the case of a blood-born catarrh (raktaja pratiśyāya), a discharge of blood occurs;
the person's eyes become copper-colored, and he is afflicted by a constriction in the chest.
With a foul-smelling breath and face, he likewise no longer perceives odors;
moreover, white, glossy, and minute worms infest him there.
Its symptoms are similar to those of the disorder of the head caused by worms;
furthermore, the nose becomes moistened and then dries up again.
It contracts again and again, and likewise expands;
there is the foul odor of exhalation and inhalation, and one no longer perceives other fragrances.
Thus one should recognize malignant coryza as difficult to cure;
indeed, all types of coryza become incurable for a man who fails to provide treatment.
When occurring at the improper time, malignant cases of pīnasa (chronic rhinitis) arise,
producing deafness, blindness, loss of smell, and terrible eye diseases; furthermore, when aggravated, these pīnasas cause cough, loss of digestive fire, and swelling.
Having dispelled all cases of acute coryza, one should treat the patient with the drinking of ghee,
various types of sudation, appropriate emetics, and timely applications of nasal drops.
For one whose food is not being digested, sudation is beneficial for the purpose of promoting digestion, along with sour foods and non-cold meals;
or, ginger taken with milk, or combined with preparations of sugarcane products, will bring about complete digestion.
One should eliminate that which is matured, thickened, and hanging down by means of head-purgatives (śirovireka),
while considering the specific doshas, using purgatives, non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), medicinal smoking (dhūmapāna), and gargles (kavalagraha).
One should resort to a bed, seat, and movements that are free from drafts; likewise, the head should be kept heavy and warm, as should one's clothing.
Strong purgatives for the head, medicated smokes, dry barley-based food, and Vijayā (harītakī) should be utilized.

One afflicted by the disease of chronic catarrh (pīnasa) should avoid cold water, women, immersion in cool baths, anxiety, excessively dry food, suppression of natural urges, grief, and fresh alcoholic liquors.
One should properly treat a patient suffering from chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) who is afflicted by vomiting, weakness of the limbs, fever, heaviness, anorexia, restlessness, and diarrhea,
using fasting, digestive, and appetizing therapies as appropriate.
One who suffers from chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) and is of middle age, when afflicted by vāta and kapha with an abundance of secretions, should be made to vomit.

Furthermore, one should overcome the complications according to the instructions, using specific medicines and dietary regimens. Once the initial symptoms have become mild, one should apply the treatments previously described.
In the case of a vātika catarrh,
one should drink ghee prepared with the five salts and the first group [of drugs] in the prescribed order.
One should observe the entire procedure for nasal therapy (nasya) and other treatments as proclaimed by Ātreya;
for those conditions arising from pitta and blood, ghee boiled with drugs of the sweet group should be drunk.
One should also apply cooling sprinklings and plasters;
[specifically using] śrī, sarjarasa, pattaṅga, priyaṅgu, and honey-sugar.
In this condition, gargles (kavala) should be prepared with grapes, madhūlikā, gojī, śrīparṇī, and honey;
likewise, purgation may also be induced using sweet substances.
One should cook [the paste] with dhava-bark, triphalā, śyāmā, tilvaka, and madhuka,
mixed with śrīparṇī and the two types of rajanī, in ten times the amount of milk.
Oil obtained at the appropriate time should be used as a nasal drop (nasya) for these two;
in the case of the kaphaja type, one should first administer oleation with ghee prepared with sesame and māṣa.
One should cause emesis with gruel; once vomited, one should follow the regimen that subdues Kapha.
[The drugs include] both types of Bala, the two Bṛhatīs, Viḍaṅga, and Trikaṇṭaka.
One should collect the roots of śvetā, sadābhadra, and varṣabhū here;
oil cooked with these should be prepared for use as a nasal medication (nasya).
Wicks prepared from *saralā*, *kiṇihī*, *dāru*, *nikumbha*,
and *iṅgudī* should be employed for the practice of smoking according to the prescribed rules.
Clarified butter, pungent and bitter substances, sharp medicinal smokes,
and acrid drugs, when employed, destroy [the disease] born from the provocation of all [three humors].
In this case, a wise physician should administer oil cooked with rasāñjana, ativiṣā, mustā, and bhadradāru for the purpose of nasal therapy (nasya).
Mustā, tejovatī, pāṭhā, kaṭphala, kaṭukā, vacā,
sarṣapa, pippalīmūla, pippalī, saindhava, and agnika.
One should employ a decoction made from *tuttha*, *karañja* seeds, salt, and *bhadradāru* as a gargle.
Oil cooked with these [drugs] is beneficial for head-purgation;
likewise, milk boiled with half its quantity of water and the meat of wild animals and birds should be prepared.
Having carefully prepared ghee from this milk that remains after being boiled with snow, mixed with water-born flowers and wind-dispelling medicinal herbs;
Having added all-fragrant substances, sitā, anantā, madhuka, and likewise candana,
one should boil that ghee again with ten parts of milk.
When administered as nasal drops (nasya), it dispels aggravated cases of coryza;
furthermore, one should diligently prepare oil with pacifying agents for each respective dosha.
The wise physician should apply the aforementioned treatments for urine and bile,
as well as anthelmintic medicines, to cases of worms for the purpose of their suppression.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Pratiśyāya (Coryza)," within the Śālākya-tantra of the Uttara-tantra in the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||24||
The twenty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the diagnosis of diseases of the head.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
The head of mortals aches due to the three— wind, bile, and phlegm—
as well as from their combination (sannipāta), from blood, from wasting, and likewise from worms.
The characteristics of the eleven types [of head diseases], namely Sūryāvarta, Anantavāta, Ardhabhedaka, and Śaṅkhaka, will now be fully described.
When there is causeless pain in the head that is intense and excessive at night,
and which is characterized by a particular aggravation from binding or pressure, that is headache caused by Vāta.
That headache in which the head feels as if covered with hot coals, such that it burns and emits smoke up to the eyebrows and nose,
and which is especially aggravated by cold at night, arises from the provocation of pitta.
He whose head and throat are smeared with phlegm, heavy, constricted, and cold;
whose temples and face are swollen; he suffers from headache due to the provocation of phlegm.
When the three [doshas] are involved in a fever affecting the head, all their symptoms manifest;
that which is characterized by blood has symptoms identical to those of pitta, and there is an inability to tolerate touch of the head.
Due to the depletion here of fat, phlegm, and blood located in the head, a headache arising from such depletion occurs;
it is a painful affliction, characterized by intense and excessive suffering.
It increases through fomentation, emesis, fumigation, nasal therapy, and bloodletting;
he whose head is excessively pricked as if being devoured and feels as if it is bursting within [suffers from this].
If water mixed with blood flows from the nose, there is a severe headache caused by worms;
and for one who faces the rising sun, a deep pain gradually comes upon the eyes and eyebrows.
A living being increases along with the moon and likewise ceases when the sun turns away;
sometimes he finds relief through cold, and at other times he attains happiness through heat.
They call that condition Bhāskarāvarta, a most painful disorder involving the entire body;
it occurs when the three vitiated humors (doṣas) compress the nape of the neck (manyā), causing extremely intense pain in the carotid regions (ghāṭā).
It causes twitching in the eyebrows and quickly brings about a stiffening in the region of the temples;
moreover, it causes trembling at the sides of the cheeks, lockjaw, and diseases of the eyes.
They describe that disorder of the head arising from the three humors as *anantavāta*,
in which half of the person's head is excessively afflicted by piercing pain, throbbing, dizziness, and aching.
One should diagnose this as "Half-Splitting" (ardhameda) if it occurs after a fortnight, ten days, or even suddenly;
in this condition, the wind, having taken refuge in the conch-shell (the head), rises with great force, accompanied by phlegm, bile, and blood.
It spreads extremely intense pains in the head and especially in the temples;
indeed, the great sages of old, learned in the Vedas, call this very painful condition by the name Śaṅkhaka.
They call this disease like risen death, difficult to ward off even by thousands of physicians.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Diseases of the Head," within the Śālākyatantra section of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment for diseases of the head.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
The procedure prescribed for Vātavyādhi should be performed for head diseases caused by Vāta;
one should consume ghee or oil with milk as an after-drink.
One should eat mung beans, horse gram, and black gram alone at night;
these should be pungent, hot, and mixed with ghee, and one should drink lukewarm milk afterwards.
A person should drink either oil with milk or the paste of that [herb] with milk;
furthermore, one should perform affusion with lukewarm milk processed with Vata-alleviating drugs.
One should apply a warm plaster of milk-porridge prepared with those [medicinal herbs],
or alternatively, of steamed fish flesh or kṛśara (rice and pulse porridge) mixed with rock salt.

For one who has been lubricated, an unctuous nasal medication (nasya) consisting of very finely ground sandalwood, blue lotus, and kuṣṭha, combined with māgadhī and prepared with crab broth, should be administered.
When the group beginning with Varuṇa has been crushed, one should cook milk with half as much water;
once only the milk remains, it should be churned while cold, and the essence (the cream) should be extracted.
Then, that clarified butter (havis) prepared with Madhuraka drugs is recommended for use as a nasal drop (nasya). Once that milk has been cooked, the ghee should be drunk along with sugar.
The physician should also administer oleaginous smoke to the patient at the appropriate time,
through drinking, anointing, nasal medication, enemas, and affusion.
The wise physician should administer Traivṛta or Balā-taila;
he should also feed the patient with unctuous meat broths or well-prepared milk preparations.
One should ward off diseases of the head arising from bile and blood by means of head-poultices mixed with ghee and by cool affusions.
