One should apply head-poultices (śiraḥpralepa) consisting of vaṃśa, śaivala, yaṣṭyāhva, mustā, and ambhoruha, combined with ghee; likewise, similar applications for erysipelas (vaisarpa) should be used.
By means of sweet mouth-washes,
nasal therapies (nasya), non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), purgatives, and wholesome unctuous enemas (snehabasti).
Milk and ghee are beneficial as nasal medication (nasya), or the pure fat of wild animals is likewise;
an non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) prepared with milk boiled with the utpala group of drugs is also beneficial.
The diet should consist of meat juices from wild animals and clarified butter;
for unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), sweet substances, milk, and ghee should be used, along with sugar for the purpose of oleation.
Whatever has been prescribed as a destroyer of pitta and blood is also beneficial;
one should conquer head diseases arising from kapha by means of kapha-alleviating treatments.
One should treat [the patient] with head-purgatives (śirovireka), strong emetics, and the holding of gargles (gaṇḍūṣa);
one should also cause [the patient] to drink clear clarified butter (sarpiḥ) and apply fomentation (sveda) repeatedly.
The physician should lubricate the head with the essence of *madhūka* and then administer a purgative using either the bark of *iṅguda* or *meṣaśṛṅga*.
One should employ a wick prepared from these very two for the inhalation of smoke;
likewise, powdered kaṭphala should be used as snuff, and gargles that remove kapha should be administered.
One should apply a warm, comfortable paste to the head, ground with alkaline water and mixed with salt, consisting of *saralā*, *kuṣṭha*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *devadāru*, and *rohiṣa*.

One should feed [the patient] food consisting of barley or sixty-day rice combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali, along with soups made from patola, mung beans, and horse-gram, in the proper quantities.
In cases of head disease arising from the three doṣas, a regimen that pacifies the three doṣas is beneficial;
indeed, they specifically prescribe the drinking of ghee, or even aged ghee.
In the case of a wasting disorder (kṣayaja), once the state of depletion has been reached, a nourishing regimen should be adopted;
ghee processed with Vata-subduing and sweet drugs should be used for drinking and as nasal drops.
In this condition, they know that ghee which cures wasting and cough is most wholesome;
now, the treatment for a head being eaten by worms shall be described.
For one should apply blood as a nasal drop; by that, the creatures swoon, and being intoxicated by the smell of blood, they come from here and there.
Their extraction should then be performed by means of head-purgatives (mūrdhavirecana),
or with the seeds of the short-leafed śigru mixed with bell-metal ash and indigo.
One should treat the condition with worm-destroying nasal drops (avapīḍa) ground with urine,
and one should employ fumigations containing putrid fish as well as other anthelmintic substances.
Worm-destroying foods and various kinds of drinks,
as well as medicinal treatments such as nasal administration (nasya), should be prescribed for one suffering from sūryāvarta.
The diet should consist primarily of meat from wild animals, preparations of milk and rice, and ghee;
likewise, in the case of the disease known as ardhabhedaka, whatever else may be appropriate should be administered.

An expressed juice (avapīḍa) made from the roots and fruits of the śirīṣa is beneficial for these two; an expressed juice made from the roots and fruits of the bamboo (vaṃśa) is also beneficial for these two.
In this case, an *avapīḍa* (nasal drop) combined with *vacā* and *māgadhikā* is beneficial; or an *avapīḍa* made from *madhuka* mixed with honey is likewise recommended.
Alternatively, a nasal medication (nasya) consisting of a paste of realgar (manaḥśilā) mixed with honey and sandalwood,
or at the end of those [treatments], a beneficial nasal drop containing ghee and sweet juices should be administered.
A plaster consisting of *sārivā*, blue lotus, *kuṣṭha*, and *madhuka*,
ground with sour liquids and mixed with ghee and oil, brings relief to both [types of wounds].
This very [treatment] should be employed for diseases of the head caused by phlegm;
in the case of Anantavāta, the procedure that removes Sūryāvarta should be performed.
Venesection should be performed for the pacification of Ananta-vāta,
and a diet that destroys vāta and pitta must be prescribed.
A meal consisting of honey, *mastaka*, *saṃyāva*, and *ghṛtapūra*,
as well as milk and clarified butter, are recommended for both nasal administration and internal consumption in cases of *śaṅkhaka*.
In this condition, a diet consisting of the unctuous juices of wild animals is recommended,
along with śatāvarī, black sesame seeds, madhuka, and blue lotus.
One should properly apply a plaster of dūrvā and punarnavā,
or alternatively, mahāsugandhā and pālindī ground with sour gruel (amlapeṣita).
In this condition, one should apply cold affusions and plasters;
furthermore, an expressed juice (avapīḍa) that wards off sūryāvarta should be administered here.
In cases of head diseases caused by the destruction of worms, the wise physician, having avoided [other treatments],
should perform strong head-purgation using substances combined with honey and oil.
Afterwards, one should then administer a nasal medication (nasya) with mustard oil;
if they still do not attain relief in this way, the physician should then treat them with oleation and sudation.
Thereafter, one should properly treat [the patient] by means of venesection.
There are seventy-six diseases of the eyes and eighteen of the ears.
Thirty-one are located in the nose, and eleven indeed in the head;
thus have they been described in detail, along with their characteristics and treatments.
To this extent, according to their gross characteristics,
the diseases located in the head have been described in this treatise by way of enumeration, symptoms, and treatment.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Head," within the Śālākya-tantra of the Uttara-tantra in the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the knowledge of the forms of the nine planets.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
O Suśruta, listen with a focused mind to the knowledge of the child-seizing spirits (bālagraha), their ritual accomplishment, as well as their origin and cause, which follows immediately hereafter.
The first is Skandagraha, as well as Skandāpasmāra;
then Śakunī, Revatī, Pūtanā, and Andhapūtanā.
Pūtanā, Śītanāmā, and likewise Mukhamaṇḍikā;
the ninth is Naigameṣa, who is designated as Pitṛgraha.

Due to the previously mentioned misconduct of the nurses and mothers, or because the children have fallen from purity, or lack auspicious conduct, or are frightened, excited, threatened, or beaten— these [demons] may indeed harm the boys for the sake of receiving worship.
Established in their sovereignty, those of universal form cannot be seen by human beings as they enter the body;
having considered that authoritative statement, I shall describe the signs which manifest within the body.
With swollen eyes, smelling of blood, loathing the breast, with a distorted face and one eyelid flickering while the other is motionless;
agitated, with rolling eyes, weeping little, suffering in his shoulders, and possessing the strength of a firm grip—such is the child afflicted by Skanda.
He becomes unconscious and then conscious again; agitated, he seems to dance with his hands and feet.
Yawning and crying out, he voids excrement and urine, and when seized by that [demon], he emits froth.
With drooping limbs, trembling with fear, smelling of birds, and tormented on all sides by oozing wounds;
his body covered with eruptions accompanied by burning and suppuration—such a child is to be recognized as one afflicted by Śakunī.
With a red face, greenish excrement, and an extremely pale or dark-complexioned body, the child suffers from fever, inflammation of the mouth, and pain;
his body is tormented by Revatī, and he certainly rubs his ears and nose while being afflicted.
With drooping limbs, the child sleeps happily by day but not at night; he passes loose stools that smell like a crow's excrement;
afflicted by vomiting, his body hair stands on end, and he becomes thirsty—such is the child seized by Pūtanā.
The physician should declare that a child who hates the breast, is afflicted by diarrhea, cough, hiccup, and vomiting accompanied by fever,
who is discolored, constantly lying on his back, and has a sour odor, is here tormented by Andhapūtanā.

The physician should recognize that patient here as afflicted by Śītapūtanā who is extremely agitated, trembles violently, weeps, sleeps in a state of contraction, suffers from rumbling in the intestines, has limbs that emit a foul odor, and is severely afflicted with diarrhea.

One whose limbs are withered, yet whose hands, feet, and face are very beautiful; who eats excessively, has a belly covered with foul veins, is agitated, and possesses an odor like that of urine—he is to be known here as a child afflicted by *vaktra-maṇḍikā*.
He who vomits froth, bends at the waist, laments with agitation while looking upward,
suffers from constant fever, has a smell of fat, and loses consciousness, is indeed possessed by Naigameṣa.
The child who is rigid, who hates the breast, and who repeatedly faints while being possessed—
such a child, exhibiting all these symptoms, the graha kills before long.

One should treat a child afflicted by recent [fever] with measures opposite to those [prescribed for chronic cases]. Being pure oneself, one should anoint the child with old clarified butter (havis) inside a clean house.
One should scatter mustard seeds for them and cause a lamp to be lit with their oils;
furthermore, one should always keep the sacrificial fire present and offer oblations into it.
Adorned with all kinds of fragrant herbs, seeds, perfumes, and garlands,
he should continuously offer oblations, saying "Svāhā to Agni" and "Svāhā to the Kṛttikās."
Salutations to the god Skanda, the lord of the planetary spirits; salutations!
I bow to you with my head; please accept this offering from me.
May a healthy child, free from all defects, be born to me quickly.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter (the first in the Kumāra-tantra section) from the beginning, titled "Knowledge of the Forms of the Nine Planets," within the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The twenty-eighth chapter:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the affliction by Skandha-grahas.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
For boys afflicted by seizure-demons (skandagraha),
a decoction of the leaves of wind-alleviating trees is recommended for sprinkling.
Oil prepared from their roots is beneficial for massage;
it is recommended with the addition of all fragrant substances, the scum of wine (surāmaṇḍa), and kaiḍarya.
One should administer to him a drink of ghee prepared with devadāru, rāsnā, and sweet trees, along with milk.
Mustard seeds, sloughed snake skin, *vacā*, *kākādanī*, ghee,
and the hair of camels, goats, sheep, and cows constitute the incense for the child.
One should wear Somavallī, Indravallī, Śamī, the thorns of the Bilva,
and the roots of Mṛgādanī, strung together as a garland.
Red garlands, red banners, red perfumes, and various kinds of edible foods,
as well as a bell and a fine cock, should be offered as a sacrifice to the god for the benefit of one seized by Skanda.

One should perform ablutions for three nights at the crossroads at night; one should fill the city with fresh rice and barley, and sprinkle it with water consecrated by the Gāyatrī mantra, while kindling the fire with the Vyāhṛtis.
Therefore, I shall proclaim this protective rite which destroys the sins of children;
it should be performed day after day by physicians who are free from sloth.
May that immutable God Skanda be gracious to you— he who is the treasury of austerities, of splendors, of glories, and of forms.
May the blessed Guha— the god who is the commander of the grahas, the all-pervading lord of the divine army, and the destroyer of the hosts of the gods' enemies— protect you.
May he who is the son of the great god of gods, of Pāvaka, of Gaṅgā, Umā, and the Kṛttikās, grant you protection.
May the glorious god, the destroyer of Krauñca, who wears red garlands and garments, who is adorned with red sandalwood,
and whose divine body is crimson, protect you.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter from the beginning, titled "The Treatment of Skanda," within the Kumāra-tantra of the Uttara-tantra in the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||28||
Chapter Twenty-nine:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the prevention of Skandāpasmāra (epilepsy caused by the deity Skanda).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
The bilva, śirīṣa, golomī, and the group beginning with surasā should be employed for sprinkling to pacify skandāpasmāra.
Oil processed with all types of fragrant substances is beneficial for massage,
as is oil prepared with a decoction of milk-exuding trees and the Kākolyādi group of drugs.
Clarified butter that has been processed with milk, as well as water mixed with milk,
and an ointment prepared with *vacā* and asafoetida are beneficial for the seizure of Skanda.
The excrement of vultures and owls, hair, elephant claws, clarified butter,
and the hair of a monkey should also be employed as an incense fumigation.
One should also carry an endless supply of hen, bimbi, and markaṭī fruits,
as well as meat both cooked and raw, fermented liquor, blood, and milk.
Having offered cooked rice (bhūtaudana) into a pit at a crossroads for Skanda and Apasmāra,
one who is self-restrained should perform his ritual bath there.
May he who is known as Skandāpasmāra, the beloved friend of Skanda,
and he who is named Viśākha, the child with the deformed face, be auspicious.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter (the third from the beginning), titled "The Treatment of Skandāpasmāra," within the Kumāratantra, which is part of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirtieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the prevention of *śakunī*.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
For one who is overwhelmed by *śakuni*, a knowledgeable physician should administer a decoction of cane,
mango, and wood-apple for sprinkling.
Oil prepared with astringent and sweet substances,
along with madhuka, uśīra, hrībēra, sārivā, utpala, and padmaka, should be used for the infant's massage.
One should smear the child with rodhra, priyaṅgu, mañjiṣṭhā, and gairika;
furthermore, the various powders and wholesome remedies mentioned for wounds are beneficial.
One should also employ these fumigants here for the seizure of the aggregates (skandha-graha):
śatāvarī, mṛgairvāru, nāgadantī, and nidigdhikā.
One should also wear Lakṣmaṇā, Sahadevā, and Bṛhatī;
likewise, a garland of sesame and rice, yellow orpiment, and red arsenic.
This offering should be presented by one of self-restraint among the *karañja* trees;
and his ritual bath should be performed in the pleasure garden according to the prescribed rules.
Ghee that pacifies Skanda and Apasmāra is also honored here;
one should perform various worship of Śakunī with auspicious flowers.
May the goddess who moves through the atmosphere, adorned with every ornament,
the iron-faced one with a sharp beak, the bird— may she be gracious to you.
May Śakunī— difficult to behold, large-bodied, tawny-eyed, with a terrifying voice,
pendulous-bellied, and spike-eared— be gracious to you.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter from the beginning, titled "The Prohibition of Śakunī," within the Kumāra-tantra of the Uttara-tantra in the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||30||
The thirty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the prevention of Revatī.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Aśvagandhā, śṛṅgī, sārivā, punarnavā, the two sahe, and vidārī— these decoctions are beneficial for sprinkling.
Oil should be used for anointing in cases of leprosy (kuṣṭha), as well as with resin (sarjarasa),
bdellium (palaṅkaṣā), nalada, and girikadambaka.
Water and ghee are recommended for use with dhava, aśvakarṇa, kakubha, dhātakī, tindukī,
and also with the kākolyādi group of drugs.
A poultice consisting of horse gram (kulattha), conch-shell powder, and the "all-fragrant" (sārvagandhika) group of drugs;
or vulture and owl excrement, barley, the yavaphala fruit, and clarified butter.
This fumigation of the child should be performed during both twilights;
likewise, one should provide a necklace made of varuṇa, ariṣṭaka, rucaka, and sinduka wood.
One should also constantly maintain [this practice], or provide for one's livelihood through one's grandson;
likewise, white flowers, parched grain, milk, and rice cooked with milk.
One who is self-restrained should offer an oblation to Revatī at Gotīrtha;
and at the confluence, a physician should perform the ritual bath for the nurse and the child.
May the dark-complexioned goddess Revatī, who wears various garments, is adorned with variegated garlands and ointments, and has swinging earrings, be gracious to you.
May that goddess be pleased with you—she whom the goddesses adorned with various ornaments constantly worship: Lambā, Karālā, Vinatā, and likewise Bahuputrikā; Revatī, and she who is named Śuṣkā.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter (the fifth in the Kumāra-tantra) within the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Repelling of Revatī."
The thirty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the prevention of Pūtanā.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said:
Kapota-vankā, aralu, varuṇa, pāribhadraka,
and āsphotā should be employed for the sprinkling of children.
Vaca, vayasthā, golomī, yellow orpiment,
realgar, kuṣṭha, and resin of the sarja tree— this group is prescribed for the purpose of oil.
Clarified butter prepared with *tugākṣīrī* and the drugs of the sweet group (*madhuraka*),
as well as with *kuṣṭha*, *tālīśa*, *khadira*, *candana*, and *syandana*, is likewise beneficial.
Devadāru, vacā, hiṅgu, kuṣṭha, girikadamba, elā,
and hareṇu should always be employed for fumigation.
The resin of the *nākulī* and *kumbhīka*, the marrow of the jujube (*badara*),
crab shells, clarified butter, and mustard seeds together constitute an incense fumigation.
One should carry *kākādanī*, *citraphalā*, *bimbī*, and *guñjā*;
one should prepare fish-rice, *kṛśarā*, and likewise minced meat;
having placed these in a hollowed-out pair of earthen bowls, one should offer the oblation in an empty house.
The bathing of the child is desired with the remains of the consecration;
and the goddess Pūtanā is to be worshipped with offerings and oblations.
Clad in soiled garments, with filthy and coarse hair,
the goddess Pūtanā, dwelling in an empty house, may she protect the child.
May the goddess Pūtanā— difficult to behold, foul-smelling, formidable, dark as a cloud, and dwelling in a broken house— protect the child.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter (from the beginning), the sixth in the Kumāra-tantra, within the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the prevention of Andhapūtanā.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
A decoction of the leaves of bitter trees should be used for pouring over [the wound];
likewise, liquor, sour gruel, kuṣṭha, yellow orpiment, and realgar [should be applied].
Likewise, resinous exudate (sarjarasa) is prescribed for the purpose of oil;
as are long pepper (pippalī), the root of long pepper, the group of sweet drugs (madhuraka), and honey.
Śālaparṇī and the two types of Bṛhatī are prescribed for the preparation of ghee;
furthermore, an external application (pradeha) made with all fragrant substances, cooled, should be applied to the limbs and the eyes.
One should prepare smoke for fumigation using cock excrement, hair, leather, snake skin,
and a worn-out monk’s outer robe.
One should carry a hen, a monkey, a legume, and also the Anantā plant;
likewise, one should carry raw meat, cooked meat, and blood at a crossroads.
One should offer oblations within the house for the sake of protecting the child,
and one should perform the ritual bathing of the child with auspicious waters scented with all kinds of fragrances.
May the goddess Andhapūtanā— fierce, tawny-eyed, shaven-headed, and clad in saffron robes—
protect this child with affection.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter (the seventh in the Kumāra-tantra) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Andhapūtanā."
The thirty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the prevention of Śītapūtanā.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
One should employ kapittha, suvahā, bimbī, as well as bilva,
pracīvala, nandī, and bhallātaka for the purpose of irrigation.
One should employ goat's urine, cow's urine, musta, devadāru,
kuṣṭha, and all the fragrant substances for the purpose of preparing the oil.
Having boiled the barks of the Rohiṇī, Sarja, Khadira, Palāśa, and Kakubha trees,
one should cook ghee with milk in that decoction.
One should employ vulture and owl droppings, the skin of a goat, the skin of a snake,
nimba leaves, and madhuka for the purpose of fumigation.
One should also wear a long guñjā and likewise a kākādanī;
one should propitiate Śītapūtanā with offerings of food made from mung beans at a river.
An offering of liquor and blood is to be given to the Goddess;
furthermore, the ritual bathing of the child at the edge of a body of water is prescribed.
May the goddess Śītapūtanā— who eats cooked mung beans, who drinks wine and blood,
and whose abode is a reservoir of water— protect you.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter from the beginning, titled "The Treatment of Śītapūtanā," within the Kumāratantra section of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta Saṃhitā. ||34||
The thirty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the prevention of facial eruptions (mukhamaṇḍikā).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Kapittha, bilva, tarkārī, vāṃśī, gandharvahastaka,
and kuberākṣī should be employed for the ritual sprinkling of children.
Having combined the juices of *bhṛṅga* trees with the oils and fat of *aja* and *hari-gandha*, one should cook it for the child’s anointing.
One should cook ghee with Madhūlikā, milk, Tugākṣīrī, the [Madhura] group,
and the smaller Pañcamūla.
Vacā, sarjarasa, kuṣṭha, and clarified butter are beneficial as an inhalation;
one should also apply the tongues of blue jays, chīralli birds, and snakes.
One should likewise offer unguents, powders, garlands, collyrium, mercury, and realgar,
as well as a sacrificial oblation in the middle of the cow-pen.
One should offer milk-rice together with sacrificial cakes for the purpose of the bali-oblation;
and it is beneficial to perform a ceremonial bath right there with waters purified by mantras.
Adorned, beautiful, fortunate, able to assume any form at will,
and delighting in dwelling in the midst of the cow-pen— may Mukhamaṇḍikā protect you.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter (the ninth in the Kumāra-tantra section) of the Uttaratantra within the Suśruta-saṃhitā, entitled "The Treatment of Mukhamaṇḍikā."
The thirty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the prevention of Naigameṣa.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Bilva, agnimantha, and pūtīka should be used for sprinkling;
likewise, liquor containing seeds and fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) are recommended for sprinkling.
One should cook oil with priyaṅgu, saralā, anantā, śatapuṣpā, and kuṭannaṭa, along with cow’s urine, curd-whey, and sour kāñjika.
A wise person should cook ghee in a decoction of the two groups of five roots, in milk, in the drugs of the sweet group,
or even in the juice of the top of the date palm.
One should also employ vacā, vayaḥsthā, golomī, and jaṭilā;
in this condition, massage is beneficial and destroys Skanda-disease and epilepsy.
Siddhārthaka, vacā, hiṅgu, kuṣṭha, along with unbroken grains (akṣata),
bhallātaka, and ajamodā— this fumigation is beneficial for an infant.
When a child is seized by a new graha, one who desires the welfare of the child should perform an incense ritual with the excrement of monkeys, owls, and vultures while the people are asleep.
One should offer sesame seeds, rice, garlands,
and various kinds of edible foods at the foot of a tree to Kumāra, the father of Meṣa.
The ritual bathing beneath the banyan tree is thus instructed;
one should present an offering to the banyan trees on the sixth lunar day.
May the god Naigameṣa, who is unborn, whose eyes and brows are restless, who can assume any form at will, and who possesses great glory—
may he, the father of Bāla, protect Bāla.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter (the tenth in the Kumāratantra section) of the Uttaratantra within the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Prohibition of Naigameṣa."
The thirty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the origin of the Grahas (seizing spirits).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
These nine classes of spirits and others, who are said to be the "seizers" (grahas) of children,
are glorious, possess divine bodies, and take the forms of women and men.
These were created by Kṛttikā, Umā, Agni, and Śūlin for the protection of Guha while he was staying in the Forest of Reeds,
being guarded by his own splendor.
Those grahas which have female forms and various shapes described by me are portions of Gaṅgā, Umā,
and the Kṛttikās, characterized by the qualities of rajas and tamas.
Naigameṣa, however, was created by Pārvatī as a ram-faced graha;
he is the bearer of Kumāra and a friend to the god Guha equal to his own self.
He who was known as Skandāpasmāra, possessing a radiance equal to fire due to his fiery nature,
is called by the names Skandasakha and Viśākha.
Skanda was created by the Lord, the divine enemy of Tripura;
that planet also bears the other name Kumāra.
This Lord Rudra, born from fire, who assumes the playfulness of a child,
does not himself engage in false practices.
Because of his similarity to Skanda, some unwise people of little understanding, who contemplate the body, declare that the Kumāra takes [the embryo].
Then, when the Blessed Skanda had been appointed as the commander-in-chief of the celestial army,
all the planetary deities approached Guha, who wielded a blazing spear.
With palms joined in reverence, they said to him, "Please provide for our livelihood.
For their sake, Skanda then invoked the auspicious god Śiva.
Then the Blessed One, the destroyer of the eyes of Bhaga, spoke to those planets:
"The three worlds consist of the animal realm and the human realm."
They exist and are sustained through mutual assistance;
the gods gratify human beings, and likewise those of the animal realm.
By means of the seasonal cold, rain, heat, and wind occurring in their proper time,
and through sacrifices, reverential salutations with joined palms, silent recitations, burnt offerings, vows, and so forth;
Men, by means of properly performed [rites], gratify the lords of the third heaven;
for the sacrificial portion has been distributed, and not even a trace of a remnant remains.
Therefore,
your virtuous livelihood shall exist only among those families where neither the gods nor the ancestors are worshipped.
Even Brahmins who are virtuous, as well as teachers and guests,
[are not honored] when they live upon the food of others while having abandoned proper conduct and purification.
In those houses where offerings and alms have ceased and where broken bronze vessels are used for eating,
seize the children who dwell there without hesitation.
Therein you shall have abundant livelihood and honor;
thus the planets are produced, and from this they seize children.
Children afflicted by planets are considered most difficult to treat;
in the case of Skanda-graha, deformity or even death is certain.
Since the seizure known as Skandagraha is declared to be the most violent of all,
any other seizure that manifests in every form is said to be incurable.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter (the eleventh in the Kumāra-tantra) from the beginning, titled "The Origin of Grahas," within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment for the disorders of the female reproductive tract (yonivyāpad).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
When a woman who is dry, weak, or young excessively indulges with a man whose virile organ is greatly enlarged, her bodily wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated.
That vitiated [semen], having reached the womb,
leads to disorders of the womb according to the specific characteristics of each of the three doshas.
Twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract have been described in the compendium of diseases,
which arise from the improper conduct of women and from vitiated menstrual blood.
They are born due to defects in the seed and due to fate; hear of them individually:
the Udāvartā, the Vandhyā, the Viplutā, and the Pariplutā.
The *vātalā* is caused by wind; the *pittotthā* arises from bile; the *rudhirakṣarā*, *vāminī*, and *snāṃsinī* are also [caused by blood]; and the *putraghnī* is caused by bile.

The *atyānandā* womb is characterized by excessive pleasure; the *karṇinī* is known to have two feet; the *śleṣmalā* should be understood as arising from *kapha*; and the one called *ṣaṇḍā* is likewise *phalinī*.
The mahatī, sūcivaktrā, and sarvajā types arise from the three doṣas;
in these, the woman discharges frothy menstrual blood with difficulty due to upward movement (udāvarta).
One should know that a woman who has ceased menstruating is "barren" (vandhyā), while one who suffers from constant pain is "disordered" (viplutā).
In the case of a woman who is "overflowing" (pariplutā), there is intense pain during sexual intercourse.
It is characterized by wind, roughness, stiffness, and is afflicted by piercing and pricking pains;
moreover, in all four of these [types], there are sensations caused by Vāyu.
She from whom blood constantly flows is called Lohitakṣarā;
she who vomits seed mixed with menstrual blood is called Vāminī.
The *prasraṃsinī* flows when agitated, as does the *duḥprasū*;
the *putraghnī*, however, destroys every embryo that has taken root due to the discharge of blood.
The excessively bilious (pittala) vagina is characterized by burning, suppuration, and fever;
furthermore, in all four of the aforementioned types, there is an aggravation of the symptoms of pitta.
Excessive pleasure does not lead to satisfaction through vulgar sexual intercourse;
it is produced by the phlegm and blood within the ear-like cavity of the womb.
If she does not engage in sexual intercourse, she excels the man;
but by excessive indulgence, she may fail to conceive a seed.
The kapha-type vagina is slimy, itchy, and excessively cold;
moreover, in all four of these [types], there is an increase of the symptoms of kapha.
A woman who has not reached her menses, one who is a eunuch, or one whose touch is harsh during sexual intercourse,
as well as a young woman possessed by a giant demon, may become pregnant.
The atimahāyoni is wide open, while the sūcīvaktrā is extremely constricted;
the former arises from the emergence of all [sexual] organs, and the latter is born from the provocation of all the bodily humors (doṣas).
In all four of these initial types, there is an elevation of all the genitalia;
these five types of origins are incurable and arise from all the humors.
In diseases that are curable, the sequential procedure beginning with oleation (sneha) is prescribed according to each specific dosha;
one should especially administer urethral/vaginal enemas (uttarabasti) as previously described.
If the vagina is rough, cold, stiff, or has diminished sensation during sexual intercourse,
one should treat it with Kumbhī-sveda (pot-fomentation) combined with the meat of marshy and aquatic animals.
One should diligently insert vesavāra mixed with sweet medicinal herbs into the vaginal canals,
and one should also apply picu-taila.
The physician should prescribe purgatives and enemas,
and when there is burning and heat, he should apply cold measures as prescribed.

One should fill the vagina, which is foul-smelling and slimy, with powders derived from the five astringents (pañcakapāya) and also with decoctions of the Rājavṛkṣa group for the purpose of cleansing.
In the case of a vagina that discharges pus, purification with substances collected for cleansing,
combined with cow's urine and salt, is desired as beneficial.
One should fill and likewise fumigate an itchy, slightly sensitive area with a paste of *bṛhatī* fruit combined with the two types of *haridrā*.
In the case of Karṇinī, one should insert a wick prepared with cleansing substances;
in the case of Prasraṃsinī, one should insert a wick smeared with ghee and steamed in milk.
Having covered it with veśavāra, one should then perform the binding;
the physician should prepare surā, ariṣṭa, and āsava according to the specific disorder.
Every morning, one should consume the juice extracted from garlic,
and one's diet should consist primarily of milk and meat broth.
The defects of semen, menstrual blood, and so forth, as well as diseases of the breasts, have been described;
likewise, the causes of impotence, the management of a malpresented fetus, and its procedures.
The treatment for diseases occurring during pregnancy has also been described;

a wise physician should apply that in all cases of disorders of the female genital tract. Furthermore, the physician should treat diseases resulting from difficult delivery using the subsequent [sections].
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter (the twelfth from the beginning), titled "The Prevention of Vaginal Disorders," within the Kumāra-tantra of the Uttaratantra in the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The second [chapter], the Kaumāra-tantra, is completed in the Uttaratantra. ||2||
The thirty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of fever.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
By him, in a previous birth, the nectar was drawn from the midst of the waters,
from which the thirty gods obtained immortality from the Lord of the Three Heavens.
Then the disciples, Suśruta and the others, questioned that seated deity:
"The complications of wounds have been described; hereafter, [describe] those of the wounded as well."
O best of physicians, tell us both in brief and in detail how a wound afflicted by a complication (upadrava) is cured with difficulty.
Complications arising in a patient with an ulcer are declared to be difficult to cure,
especially when the patient's strength and flesh have wasted away due to the depletion of the remaining bodily tissues.
Therefore, tell us all the afflictions along with their treatments—
those which were observed by the supreme seer in the entire science of bodily medicine.
Having heard those words of theirs, the best of physicians spoke:
"I shall first describe fever; it is remembered as the king of the host of diseases."
Born from the fire of Rudra’s wrath and scorching all beings,
he is celebrated under various names by other sentient beings.
At birth and likewise at death, it mostly enters the embodied being;
therefore, this [wind] is proclaimed the king of all transformations.
Except for gods and humans, no one else can endure it;
for by means of action, one attains even divinity from the human state.
Furthermore, having fallen from heaven, one follows the human state;
therefore, as humans, you endure fever by virtue of your divine nature.
All other animals afflicted by fever perish;
likewise, there is obstruction of perspiration, a burning sensation, and a seizing pain throughout all the limbs.

That fever in which the various morbid transformations (vikāras) occur simultaneously is thus described; it arises from the humors (doṣas) individually, collectively, in pairs, or even as an exogenous (āgantu) cause.
Fever is known to arise from many causes and is of eight types;
it occurs when the humors (doṣas), provoked by their respective aggravating factors at their specific times, become disturbed within their own locations.
Indeed, the vitiated humors (doṣas), provoked by their respective causes and reaching the stomach (āmāśaya) along with the heat (ūṣman), pervade the entire body and bring about fever.
Having come together with the *rasa*, it obstructs the channels that carry the flow of *rasa* and sweat,
and diminishes the digestive fire.
Having expelled the external heat from the site of digestion alone,
it pervades the entire body and manifests as the onset of fever at its own appointed times.
Furthermore, through the improper or excessive application of oleation and other such therapies to people, it produces disorders of growth or abnormal pigmentation in the skin and other tissues.
From various types of trauma, from the onset of disease, from suppuration,
from exhaustion, from depletion, from indigestion, from poison, and from the seasonal reversal of what is wholesome;
From the scent of medicinal herbs and flowers, from grief, from the affliction of the stars,
from malevolent magic and curses, and from mental apprehension caused by spirits;
In women who have given birth to stillborn infants, as well as those who have given birth to living children,
fever arises due to the humors (doṣas) along with unwholesome factors and the cessation of breast milk.
By those [winds], which are forceful, wandering in many directions, and moving along wrong paths,
the internal fire is quickly dispersed and becomes external.
And because it obstructs the watery element (ap-dhātu), one afflicted by fever becomes extremely hot-bodied;
for that reason, he is called "jvarita" (one with fever).
Fatigue, restlessness, discoloration of the complexion, a bad taste in the mouth, watering of the eyes,
and frequent desire and aversion toward cold, wind, heat, and so forth;
Yawning, aching of the limbs, heaviness, horripilation, loss of appetite,
darkness of vision, lack of joy, and coldness occur when fever is about to arise.
Generally, from the specific [humors], excessive yawning arises from vāta;
burning of the eyes from pitta; and a lack of desire for food from kapha.
The combination of all symptoms occurs when all the doṣas are provoked;
however, they know that which is mixed with the characteristics of two [doṣas] to be born from a pair (dvandvaja).
Trembling, an uneven surge [of energy], dryness of the throat and lips,
loss of sleep, suppression of sneezing, and roughness of the limbs as well.
In fever born of Vāta, there occurs pain in the head, heart, and limbs; a bad taste in the mouth; constipation; yawning; flatulence; and likewise colic.
A sharp impulse, diarrhea, scantiness of sleep, as well as vomiting,
inflammation of the throat, lips, mouth, and nose, and perspiration arise.
In the Pitta-type [fever], there is incoherent speech, pungency in the mouth, fainting, burning sensation,
intoxication, thirst, yellowness of the feces, urine, and eyes, as well as giddiness.
Heaviness, coldness, nausea, horripilation, excessive sleepiness,
obstruction of the channels, weakness of the digestive fire, salivation, and a sweet taste in the mouth [are the symptoms].
In the case of fever born of phlegm (kaphaja), there is a lack of excessive heat in the body, vomiting, lassitude of the limbs,
indigestion, catarrh, loss of appetite, cough, and whiteness of the eyes.
Loss of sleep, vertigo, labored breathing, drowsiness, numbness of the limbs,
loss of appetite, thirst, delusion, intoxication, stiffness, burning sensation, coldness, and pain in the heart.
The digestion of the humors is slow, insanity occurs, the teeth become blackish,
the tongue becomes rough and dark, and there is pain arising in the joints, the head, and the bones.
The eyes are distorted and turbid; the ears are afflicted with pain from sounds;
there is delirious speech, suppuration of the orifices, moaning, and loss of consciousness.
In the case of the type caused by all three doshas (sarvaja), there is a slow and slight discharge of sweat, urine, and feces;
it exhibits all the symptoms, so hear from me the specific features regarding this.
Neither too hot nor too cold, possessing little consciousness, with wandering glances and a ruined voice,
he has a rough tongue, a parched throat, and is devoid of sweat, feces, and urine.
Tearful, with a broken heart, hating those who served him, his luster destroyed,
he lies fallen, gasping for breath, overwhelmed by a multitude of lamentations.
Some call this "Abhinyāsa," while others describe it as "Hataujas"; others know it as "Sannipāta-jvara," which is difficult to cure and considered incurable.

One should recognize as "sannyāsa" that fever which is characterized by sleepiness, prostration, emaciation, loss of vitality, and the sinking of the limbs, occurring in one who is subject to all its manifestations.
He whose vitality (ojas) fails due to the aggravation of bile (pitta) and wind (anila) becomes unconscious,
desiring to lie down because of stiffness in his limbs and coldness.
Whether awake, sleeping, or drowsy, the person becomes talkative;
his hair stands on end, his limbs become flaccid, and the sensation of heat is diminished.
A skilled physician should recognize that [the fever] arises from the suppression of *ojas* when the seventh,
tenth, or even the twelfth day has arrived.
Becoming even more severe, it either subsides or kills;
those arising from a combination of two [humors] are known as the three types of dual-origin fevers, characterized by the symptoms of the elevation of both defects.
Thirst, fainting, vertigo, burning sensations, loss of sleep, headache,
dryness of the throat and mouth, vomiting, horripilation, and likewise loss of appetite.
Splitting pain in the joints, yawning, the symptoms of fever caused by vāta and pitta,
numbness, breaking pain in the joints, drowsiness, and heaviness— these are the signs.
Headache, catarrh, cough, perspiration,
and moderate internal heat are the symptoms of fever caused by vāta and śleṣman.
A coated and bitter-tasting mouth, drowsiness, delusion, cough, anorexia, thirst,
alternating sensations of heat and cold— these are the clinical features of fever caused by kapha and pitta.
Yawning, flatulence, intoxication, trembling, breaking pain in the joints,
emaciation, thirst, delirium, and burning sensations occur in a fever caused by wind and bile.
Pain in the chest, cough, nausea, coldness,
shivering, catarrh, heaviness, loss of appetite, and constipation arise from the provocation of Vāta and Kapha.

In the fever caused by kapha and pitta (kaphapaittika), there occur coldness, burning sensations, anorexia, stiffness, perspiration, delusion, intoxication, vertigo, cough, malaise of the limbs, and nausea.
[This occurs] in those who are emaciated, those recently freed from fever, or those who indulge in improper diet and lifestyle.
Even a very small fault, when increased and fanned by the wind, [destroys] embodied beings.
Indeed, [the physician] administers chronic, daily, tri-dosic, and quartan fevers, along with those accompanied by a coating,
respectively according to the divisions of the seats of phlegm (kapha).
Moving from place to place day by day and night by night,
the dosha reaches the stomach (āmāśaya) and thereby causes fever in human beings.
Likewise, the Pralepaka type should be known as fatal to those suffering from wasting diseases;
it is most difficult to treat, mild in onset, extremely painful, and causes the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Or, when the dosha remains in two, three, or four of the seats of kapha,
it produces disorders known as viparyaya, which are irregular and difficult to treat.

Some have stated that the cause of irregular fever (viṣamajvara) is either an external factor or a constitutional trait; for generally, an exogenous factor is indeed the persistent underlying condition in irregular fever.
Those who know the truth declare that the tertian and quartan fevers arise from a predominance of wind (vāta);
in the case of the quotidian fever and that born of wine, they state the cause to be produced by bile (pitta).
Experts declare that *pralepaka* and *vātabalāsaka* fevers arise from a predominance of *kapha*;
those irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*) which are accompanied by fainting (*mūrchā*) generally originate from a combination of two [humors].
When kapha and vata are located in the skin, they first produce coldness in fever;
once those two have subsided, pitta causes burning at the end.
Likewise, pitta located in the skin first produces an intense burning sensation;
once that has subsided, both of them (kapha and vāta) subsequently produce coldness.
These two types of fever, characterized by heat and cold respectively, are known to arise from the combination [of doshas].
Of these two, the one preceded by heat is considered more severe and is difficult to cure.
Furthermore, that which arises from physical impact and that which originates from consciousness have been previously described as occurring during the six periods of day and night.
A violent and irregular fever assails a person in many ways,
and that irregular fever never leaves the body.
Since he is not freed from illness, heaviness, and emaciation,
it is observed that "this [fever] has passed" only when its paroxysm has subsided.
Abiding in another realm, it is not perceived due to its subtlety and its state of dissolution,
like a fire whose fuel consists of slight defects that has been extinguished when the fuel is spent.
A small dose of morbidity arising from unwholesome factors, or that of one who has recently recovered from a fever,
reaches one of the bodily constituents (dhātu) and produces irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
On the first day it resides in the lymph and blood; on the next day, it takes refuge in the flesh;
on the third day, it reaches the fat; and then again, on the fourth day, it enters the bones and marrow.
It may produce the terrible quartan fever, the end-maker, or a combination of diseases;
some describe this irregular fever as arising from possession by malevolent spirits (bhūta).
Whether for seven days, ten days, or even twelve days,
he who maintains the continuity without interruption is called "one of continuous practice" (santata).
The *satataka* fever persists continuously throughout day and night;
the *anyedyuṣka*, however, occurs once every twenty-four hours.
The tertian fever occurs on the third day, and the quartan fever on the fourth day;
provoked by wind and subsiding from all sides,
these fevers of mortals caused by one or two humors arise on those very same days.
They repeatedly bring about that very same time during the onset of a fever,
just as the ocean, being tossed by the wind, becomes filled again and again.
In the same way, the humors (doṣas), impelled by the wind, indeed produce fevers,
just as at the onset of the tide, the waves of the great ocean cover the shore.
Just as water, when its momentum is exhausted, subsides back into that very place from which it arose,
so too, upon the rising of the force of the humors (doṣa), fever indeed manifests in this person.
Just as water subsides in the ocean when its momentum is lost,
so too does the fever that has arisen through various types of trauma subside once its force is spent.
One should identify that fever according to the provocation of its respective doshas;
in the case of one caused by poison (viṣa), there is a darkened countenance, burning sensations, diarrhea, and cardiac oppression.
Loss of appetite, thirst, piercing pain, fainting, and loss of strength [occur];
from the smell of medicinal herbs, there is fainting, headache, vomiting, and sneezing.
From desire arises the derangement of the mind, as well as drowsiness, laziness, and loss of appetite;
moreover, there is pain in his heart and his body becomes parched.
From fear arises incoherent speech, and from grief comes trembling;
from anger arises trembling as well, while delusion and thirst are born from malevolent magic and curses.
In embodied beings, the wind (vāyu), provoked by possession by spirits, by fatigue, loss of strength, or injury, causes agitation, laughter, trembling, and weeping.
Having filled the entire body, it produces intense fever;
this arises from the emergence of diseases as well as from internal burning sensations and external (āgantu) causes.
Another fever arises from various other causes;
however, it never transcends the symptoms of the [three] humors (doṣas).
Heaviness, distress in the heart, lassitude, vomiting,
and loss of appetite— these, along with a sense of wretchedness, arise as signs when fever is located in the rasa-dhatu.
Spitting of blood, burning sensations, perspiration, vomiting, giddiness,
delirium, pustules, and thirst occur in men when fever has reached the blood.
In fever located in the muscle tissue (māṃsaga), there is swelling of the calves, thirst, discharge of urine and feces,
internal heat, a burning sensation within, restlessness, and exhaustion.
Excessive perspiration, thirst, fainting, delirium, and vomiting;
foul odor, loss of appetite, exhaustion, and intolerance—these occur when [the poison] resides in the fat.
Pain in the bones, contraction of the limbs, labored breathing, purging, vomiting,
and tossing of the body— these occur when fever has entered the bones.
When the fever has reached the marrow, there is entry into darkness, hiccups, coughing, coldness, vomiting,
internal burning, labored breathing, and a cutting pain in the vital organs; in that state,
when the fever has reached the seat of the semen, one meets with death.
The stiffness of the penis and, especially, the discharge of semen—
just as fire consumes fuel or as poison destroys the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Having accomplished its purpose, the fever departs for peace after having struck down the body;
such is the characteristic of fevers arising from wind, bile, and phlegm.

Likewise, the wise physician should speak to them regarding the tastes and so forth; he should also diagnose [the disease] as being located in the bodily constituents (dhātu) through the combination of all [factors], that is, by means of a derangement of the humors (sannipāta).
One should also declare that fever born of the combination of two [humors] is caused by the defects arising from those very two;
furthermore, a deep-seated fever is to be recognized by internal burning and thirst.
With his body extremely emaciated, suffering from the onset of labored breathing and coughing,
his radiance and senses destroyed, he was wasted away and tormented by a loss of appetite.
One should avoid treating a patient afflicted by a fever that is deep-seated, acute, and characterized by intense force,
especially when it is caused by the humors (doṣas) in their low, moderate, or excessive states, and lasts for three, seven, or twelve days respectively.
The onset of the fever becomes intense, yet it remains as easy to manage as before;
for this is Time itself, as well as Yama, Niyati, and Death.
When that [fever] has departed from the body, birth here again is said to occur;
thus the fevers have been fully described, and now karma will be explained.
When the premonitory symptoms of fever are present, a wise person should drink clear clarified butter; thereby, he attains relief.
This is the procedure for those caused by Vāta; for those caused by Pitta, purgation is prescribed;
and likewise, mild emesis is ordained for those caused by Kapha.
In cases arising from all two-fold combinations of doshas, one should apply the treatment according to the specific dosha involved;
such a patient should not be given oleation nor purification, but should be treated with fasting and similar measures.
One should know the difference between form and its precursor, as between fire and smoke;
for those whose forms are clearly manifest, fasting is exclusively beneficial.
When the doshas are located in the stomach (āmāśaya) and are agitated, emesis is the best treatment;
for as long as the patient remains bound by the stagnant doshas, [the condition persists].
One should first practice fasting and thereafter adopt a restricted diet;
however, one should not employ this regimen in cases born of wind (vāta), depletion (kṣaya), or mental origin (mānasa).
Furthermore, those who were previously declared in the chapter on the two types of wounds to be unfit for fasting— namely,
those with unstable humors (doṣas) and digestive fire (agni)— for them, fasting serves to digest the humors.
It destroys fever, stimulates digestion, produces appetite, relish, and lightness; it facilitates the passage of flatus, feces, and urine, overcomes hunger and thirst, and is light.
One should recognize a man whose mind and senses are clear but who is emaciated as one who has successfully undergone the ordeal.
[The symptoms include] loss of strength, thirst, wasting, drowsiness, sleep, vertigo, and exhaustion.
Complications such as dyspnea and others may arise from excessive fasting;
[light food], however, stimulates digestion, breaks up phlegm, and facilitates the downward movement of pitta and vata.
Warm water is beneficial for those afflicted by fever caused by kapha and vāta, as it relieves thirst;
for it softens the doṣas and the channels, whereas cold water acts otherwise.
Fever arising from bile, alcohol, or poison increases when treated with cold water;
for these types, cold water boiled with bitter herbs is beneficial.
This [decoction] made with Gāṅgeya, Nāgara, Uśīra, Parpaṭa, Udīcya, and Candana is digestive,
carminative, light, and a fever-destroyer for those afflicted by fever.

When the time for solid food arrives in a fever lasting more than seven nights, a beneficial gruel prepared with appropriate digestive drugs should be given to one who has abundant morbid humors and weak digestion.
When the morbid humor (doṣa) is not digested by means of fasting, water, or barley gruel,
then it [should be treated] with remedies that eliminate bad taste in the mouth, thirst, and anorexia.
One should treat [the patient] with astringent decoctions that are digestive, pleasing to the heart, and fever-destroying;
specifically, a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūlī) is a digestive remedy for fever caused by Vāta.
In the case of Pitta-type fever, a decoction prepared with Musta, Katuka, and Indrayava along with honey should be administered;
however, in Kaphaja fever, a decoction of the Pippalyadi group serves as a digestive (pācana) agent.
In cases arising from dual humors, one should either administer a combined treatment or avoid it altogether;
likewise, one who has drunk water, undergone fasting, eaten, suffered from indigestion, is emaciated, or is thirsty [should not be treated].

(One should recognize fever as having undigested humors [sāmadoṣa] when the fever is intense, the body is heavy, and the waste products [malas] are obstructed; conversely, one should know it as digested [pakva] when these conditions are absent. When the fever is mild, the body is light, and the waste products are mobile, [it is considered digested].
One should recognize that the morbid humor (doṣa) has ripened; at that time, the medicine for fever should be administered.
According to some, the signs of ripening due to the morbid transformation of the humors and constitution are:
a twisting sensation in the heart, drowsiness, salivation, and loss of appetite.
Non-activation of the humors, laziness, constipation, excessive urination, heaviness of the abdomen,
absence of perspiration, indigestion, and a lack of interest in stool [are the symptoms].
Drowsiness, stiffness, heaviness of the limbs, dullness of the digestive fire,
impurity of the mouth, lack of fatigue, and a persistent, powerful fever.
By these signs, the wise physician should recognize the fever as being of the undigested (āma) type;
some authorities maintain that medicine should be administered after seven nights have passed.
Some authorities have determined that after ten nights, [the medicine] should be administered;
or it may be given in the case of a Pitta-type fever that has arisen within a short period of time.
Medicine should be administered even to one who has recently developed a fever, once the morbid humors have ripened;
for medicine given while the humors are still undigested causes the fever to flare up even more.
One should administer purification or pacification for irregular fever;
however, one should always disregard the morbid humor when it is being expelled or is excessively provoked by the fever.
If it flows excessively, one should treat it like dysentery;
this occurs when the impurities of the channels have reached the digestive tract, become digested, and are obstructed.
Even for one who has recently suffered from fever, one should then administer a purgative;
for a morbid humor (doṣa) that has been ripened but not expelled remains in the body and causes great harm.
It may cause irregular fever as well as the impairment of strength;
therefore, the elimination of the humors (doṣas) must be performed by means of emesis and other such methods.
One should perform the preliminary treatment for him, namely emesis, as well as non-unctuous enema;
likewise, one should administer purgation and head-evacuation.
In a fever characterized by an excess of phlegm (kapha), emesis should be administered gradually once the patient has gained strength;
however, when pitta predominates and the internal organs are softened, purgation should be performed.
In cases of pain arising from Vāta accompanied by downward movement (udāvarta), a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) should be administered;
for one suffering from stiffness of the waist and back with a stimulated digestive fire, an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) is indicated.
Head-purgatives (mūrdhavirecana) should be administered when the head is afflicted by phlegm; they alleviate heaviness and pain in the head and awaken the sensory faculties.
In a weak patient, one should pierce the abdomen when it is distended and painful with wood-apple (dāru),
Himalayan gentian (haimavatī), costus (kuṣṭha), dill (śatāhvā), asafoetida (hiṅgu), and rock salt (saindhava).
When Vata has ascended upwards, for one whose urine and feces are obstructed, one should insert a suppository into the anus made from sour substances ground with a pleasant warmth.
Or one should cause him to drink a gruel prepared with long pepper, long pepper root, yavānī, and cavya,
which facilitates the downward movement of wind and other humors.
If the fever of one who has been purified on both counts does not subside,
it should be conquered with clarified butter (ghṛta), as that person remains dry due to residual morbid humors (doṣas).
One should treat a patient who is emaciated and has few symptoms with palliative (śamana) measures;
however, if the fever arising from over-nutrition (santarpaṇa) occurs in a strong person, one should treat it with fasting.
One should give a person with weak digestion and suffering from thirst a lukewarm gruel to drink;
however, for one who drinks alcohol and suffers from thirst, vomiting, burning sensations, or heat, a parched grain (lāja) satiation is appropriate.
Afterwards, when it has been digested, one should take rice with broth and meat-soup along with honey and water;
this is for fever caused by fasting or physical exertion, which is diminished and characterized by a predominance of Vāta.
A wise man should feed one with a stimulated digestive fire rice with meat broth;
rice with mung bean soup is also beneficial when [the disease] arises from phlegm.
That same [gruel], when combined with sugar, is cooling and beneficial for pitta-type fever;
likewise, a soup made of pomegranate, emblic myrobalan, and green gram is beneficial for vata-pitta-type fever.
Soup made from small radishes is beneficial when wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman) predominate;
soup made from patola and nimba is wholesome when pitta and kapha are present.
To one who is afflicted by burning sensations and vomiting, emaciated, abstaining from food, and tormented by thirst,
one should administer a satiating drink of parched grain mixed with sugar and honey.

For one afflicted by kapha and pitta, as well as for one suffering from blood-pitta (raktapitta) in the summer, or for one who is habitually addicted to wine, gruel is not beneficial; one should treat such a person accordingly.
For one with weak digestive fire, aged wine served with beneficial soups— whether sour or non-sour— or with the meat broths of wild animals, along with barley-based foods, is wholesome.
One afflicted by phlegm and loss of appetite should be given buttermilk mixed with the three pungents (savyoṣa).
A man who is emaciated, has few remaining humors, is dejected, and is suffering from chronic fever [should also be treated thus].
One who has obstructed or expelled the doshas, is dry, suffers from fever caused by pitta and vata,
and is afflicted by thirst and burning sensations, shall find relief through milk.
That very [food], if consumed by a young person, kills a man like poison;
however, in all fevers, a light meal taken in the proper measure is beneficial.
For otherwise, when the force [of the fever] has subsided, it increases the intensity of the fever;
therefore, one suffering from fever should eat what is wholesome, even if he has no appetite.
For at the time for food, one who does not eat perishes or dies;
being thus wasted away, he falls into a state of misery and even reaches a condition beyond remedy.
Therefore, one should protect the strength of men, for life exists only when strength is present;
moreover, one suffering from fever should by no means consume heavy, obstructive, or unsuitable food at the wrong time.

But for one who is emaciated and has been ill for a long time, even food that is wholesome, continuous, or balanced may not lead to longevity or happiness if it is unwholesome or taken at the wrong time.
One should treat fever with wholesome, light, and well-prepared foods,
such as mung beans, lentils, chickpeas, horse gram, and wild kidney beans.
At the time of eating, one should cause these to be given to the fever patient for the sake of soup:
the leaf of *paṭola*, eggplant (*vārtāka*), *kaṭhilla*, and *pāpacailika*.
One should provide *karkāṭaka*, *parpaṭaka*, *gojihvā*, young radish,
and the leaves of *guḍūcī* as vegetables for those suffering from fever.
