For those who are accustomed to meat and who suffer from fever, one should provide the flesh of the crane,
the curlew, the peacock, the cock, and likewise the partridge.
Some physicians do not recommend warm treatments for fever;
however, when the wind (vāyu) reaches a state of provocation in those afflicted by fever, [warmth is required].
At that time, these [medicines] are also recommended when administered according to the proper measure and timing:
affusions, plasters, oleation therapies, and purification treatments.
Bathing, oil massage, sleeping during the day, exposure to cold, physical exercise, women,
as well as astringent, heavy, and dry foods, and likewise anger and other such [afflictions].
One suffering from acute fever should avoid substantial foods and edibles;
likewise, in brief, one should avoid newly harvested grain and similar items.
The fever, fanned by these fires of unstable humors,
attains depth, sharpness, and rapid onset, as well as incurability itself.
One who has been released from fever should not indulge in cold water, sleeping during the day, anger, physical exercise,
or sexual intercourse until he has regained his strength.
Even for one who has been freed from fever, if it returns quickly while still weak due to unwholesome things,
the fever will consume the body just as fire consumes a dry tree.
Therefore, precautions must be taken by those freed from fever, as by one who has undergone purgation,
until they have returned to their natural state in terms of both the humors and the vital breaths.
In fever, confusion arises even from slight exertions;
therefore, one should feed the patient while he is seated and assist him in passing urine and feces.
In cases of anorexia, bodily lassitude, discoloration, or impurities of the limbs, a person—
even if their fever has subsided— should be purged out of fear of a relapse.
A wise person should never suddenly cause one emaciated by fever to bathe;
for the fever, being aggravated by that act, would surely return to him once again.
One should treat all fevers by applying remedies contrary to their causes;
however, in cases arising from fatigue, wasting, or injury, one should treat the underlying primary disease.

For women who have given birth to defective offspring and for those whose breast milk has become vitiated, the physician who knows the prescribed rules should administer a pacifying treatment according to the specific dosha involved.
Therefore, learn from me the decoctions that pacify [diseases],
which should be administered by a learned physician in all types of fevers.
A decoction prepared from pippalī, sārivā, drākṣā, śatapuṣpā, and āhareṇu,
taken with jaggery, destroys fever born of vāta.
One should indeed drink either boiled or cold decoction of *guḍūcī*,
or a decoction of *balā*, *darbha*, and *śvadaṃṣṭrā* reduced to one-fourth its original volume.
One should drink [this] combined with sugar and ghee to remove vāta-fever;
[the ingredients are] śatapuṣpā, vacā, kuṣṭha, devadāru, and hareṇukā.
One should prepare a decoction of kustumburu, nalada, and musta in water;
this decoction, combined with honey and sugar, is used when vāta is predominant.
Having boiled grapes, guḍūcī, kāśmarya, trāyamāṇā, and sārivā together,
one should drink that decoction with treacle for fever caused by vāta.
The fresh juice of *guḍūcī* should be taken, along with an equal amount of that of *śatāvarī*;
when drunk together with jaggery, it immediately destroys fever caused by *vāta*.
One should employ [this] in the states of ghee massage, sudation, and external applications;
it is derived from śrīparṇī, candana, uśīra, parūṣaka, and madhūka.
A decoction sweetened with sugar cures fever caused by pitta;
when drunk with sugar, the sārivādi group destroys pitta-type fever.
Likewise,
a decoction or a cold infusion of yaṣṭīmadhuka, utpala, and other [lotus parts], combined with sugar, shall destroy [the disease].
A cold decoction of gudūcī, padmaka, rodhra, sārivā, and utpala,
sweetened with sugar, removes fever caused by pitta.
Alternatively, one may use decoctions made from grapes (drākṣā) and āragvadha, or from kāśmarya— these being sweet,
bitter, and astringent— mixed with sugar.
One should pacify excessive thirst and burning sensations with very cold [substances];
or, for one who is thirsty, one should drink cold water mixed with honey up to the throat.
One should induce emesis after administering these [drugs], for by that means thirst is pacified;
likewise, with very cold milk, decoctions of milk-yielding trees, and sandalwood water.
In cases of internal burning, one should administer these and other cooling substances:
Padmaka, Madhuka, Drākṣā, Puṇḍarīka, and Utpala.
One should place roasted barley, uśīra, samaṅgā, and the fruit of the kaśmarī tree into water,
stir it, and let it stand overnight.
For one drinking this mixed with honey, fever and burning sensations are pacified;
it should be administered when there is dryness of the tongue, palate, throat, and kloma, as well as in the head.
The filaments of the citron fruit, combined with honey and rock salt,
or likewise with sugar and pomegranate, or with grapes and dates.
In cases of loss of taste, one should apply a paste and likewise use a gargle;
saptacchada, guḍūcī, nimba, and sphūrjaka are beneficial for this purpose.
In fever caused by Kapha, one should drink the decoction after boiling it with honey;
[the ingredients are] Trikatu, Nagapushpa, Haridra, and Katurohini.
The fruit of *kauṭaja*, when consumed, destroys fever born of *kapha*;
likewise, *haridrā*, *citraka*, *nimba*, *uśīra*, *ativiṣā*, and *vacā*.
One should drink a decoction prepared from kuṣṭha, indrayava, mūrvā, and paṭola,
combined with marica and honey, in cases of fever caused by kapha.
A decoction prepared with sārivā, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, purākhya, durālabhā,
and musta, when drunk, destroys fever caused by kapha.
A decoction of Musta, Vṛkṣakabīja, Triphalā, Kaṭurohiṇī,
and Parūṣaka destroys fever caused by Kapha.
The decoction of the group of trees beginning with rājavṛkṣa, when combined with honey and administered at the proper time,
quickly destroys fever caused by kapha and vāta.
Nāgara, dhānyaka, bhārgī, abhayā, and suradāru;
vacā, parpaṭaka, musta, bhūtīka, and then kaṭphala.
In cases arising from phlegm and wind, this should be boiled and administered with honey and asafoetida;
it destroys asthma and cough, and is indicated for excessive phlegm and constriction of the throat.
In cases of hiccups, swelling of the throat, and pain in the heart and flanks,
[one should use] a decoction of balā, paṭola, triphalā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and vṛṣa.
A decoction made from kaṭukā, vijayā, drākṣā, musta, and parpaṭaka, when drunk mixed with honey, destroys fever caused by pitta and kapha.
This decoction, when drunk, destroys fever arising from phlegm and bile (kapha-pitta).
[It is prepared] with bhārgī, vacā, parpaṭaka, dhānya, hiṅgu, abhayā, and ghanā.
A decoction of *kāśmarya* and *nāgara*, mixed with honey, [is used] for disorders born of *kapha* and *pitta*.
One should take one *akṣa* measure of *kaṭukā* with warm water along with sugar.
Having drunk [this], a person may conquer fever arising from phlegm and bile:
kirātatikta, amṛtā, drākṣā, āmalaka, and śaṭī.
Having decocted these for disorders arising from vāta and pitta, one should drink that decoction with jaggery (guḍa),
along with rāsnā, vṛṣa, triphalā, and the fruits of rājavṛkṣa.
A decoction prepared and drunk conquers fever caused by vāta and pitta;
however, in cases arising from all the doṣas combined, one should administer a combination of these.
One should treat all fevers according to the predominance of the specific dosha,
using vṛścīva, bilva, varṣābhū, milk, and water.
One should cook it until only the milk remains, for that indeed removes all fevers;
three parts water and one part milk, combined with the essence of *śiṃśapā* wood.
That decoction, boiled down until only the milk remains, should be drunk to remove all fevers.
[One should also use] the roots of *nala* and *vetasa*, *mūrvā*, and *devadāru*.
Having prepared this decoction according to the prescribed method, it should be drunk to dispel fever;
it consists of turmeric, bhadramusta, triphalā, and katurohiṇī.
A decoction of picumanda, paṭolī, devadāru, and nidigdhikā,
when drunk, conquers fever caused by the combination of all three doṣas (sannipāta-jvara).
In cases arising from all three doṣas, a decoction of the three fruits (triphalā) mixed with ghee should be drunk to treat indigestion, excessive salivation, swelling, cough, and loss of appetite.
One should administer one akṣa each of anantā, bālaka, mustā, nāgara,
and kaṭurohiṇī with lukewarm water before sunrise.
This destroys all fevers, quickly kindles the digestive fire,
and likewise promotes substances that are appetizing and purgative.
One should employ these fever-destroying remedies either singly or in pairs;
this linctus of ghee, honey, abhayā, and oil cures fever of all origins.
A decoction of trivṛt combined with honey should be administered to bring even a severe fever to peace;
however, in the case of irregular (viṣama) fever, purification by means of emesis and purgation must be performed both upwards and downwards.
Or, the ghee mentioned for splenic enlargement (plīhodara) may destroy irregular fever;
or one afflicted by irregular fever should drink triphalā mixed with a large quantity of jaggery.
One should consume the decoction of guḍūcī, nimba, and dhātrī mixed with honey,
or one should take garlic with ghee every morning.
One should drink the decoction prepared with three, four, or five ingredients combined:
namely, madhuka, paṭola, rohiṇī, and mustaka.
This entire threefold formulation of harītakī is prescribed,
or else ghee, milk, sugar, honey, and māgadhī (long pepper) should be taken according to one's strength.
One should administer either Magadha-pippalī with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī),
or one should drink the "increasing dose of pippalī" (pippalī-vardhamāna) while subsisting on milk and meat broth.
One may drink excellent wine with the meat of a cock;
or one should cook ghee in a decoction of kola, agnimantha, and triphalā, along with curd.
This Tilvaka-avapa indeed destroys irregular fevers (viṣamajvara),
[prepared] with long pepper (pippalī), ativiṣā, grapes (drākṣā), arivā, bilva, and sandalwood (candana).
With kaṭuka, indrayava, uśīra, siṃhī, tāmalakī, and ghana;
with trāyamāṇā, sthirā, dhātrī, viśvabheṣaja, and citraka.
Ghee cooked with these [drugs], when drunk, overcomes irregular digestive fire (visamāgni),
chronic fever, headache, abdominal tumors (gulma), enlargement of the abdomen (udara), and halīmaka.
Guḍūcī, triphalā, vāsā, trāyamāṇā, and yavāsaka dispel consumption-cough accompanied by fever and pain in the flanks.
These [drugs], having been made into a paste in equal parts and boiled according to the prescribed method,
are cooked with raisins, pippalī, musta, nagara, utpala, and candana.
Ghee processed with *kalaśī*, *bṛhatī*, *drākṣā*, *trāyantī*, *nimba*, and *gokṣura* conquers wasting disease, dyspnea, cough, and chronic fever.
Clarified butter should be cooked with the decoction of bala, parpaṭaka, ambhoda, śālaparṇī, and yavāsa,
combined with the paste (kalka) of these same ingredients.
A decoction made with śaṭī, tāmalakī, bhārgī, medā, āmalaka, and pauṣkara,
combined with twice the amount of milk, cures chronic fever.
This is the supreme remedy for alleviating headache, pain in the sides, cough, and wasting,
[prepared] with paṭolī, parpaṭa, ariṣṭa, guḍūcī, triphalā, and vṛṣa.
With kaṭukā, ambuda, bhūnimba, yāsā, yaṣṭyāhvā, candana, dārvī,
śakrayava, uśīra, trāyamāṇā, kaṇa, and utpala;
Ghee prepared with the juices of dhātrī, bhṛṅgarāja, abhīru,
and kākamācī quickly cures apacī, skin diseases, fever, śukra, arjuna, and wounds.
Viḍaṅga,
triphalā, musta, mañjiṣṭhā, dāḍima, and utpala destroy diseases arising in the eyes, face, ears, and nose.
With priyaṅgu, vella, elavāluka, candana, and amaradāru;
with barhiṣṭha, kuṣṭha, rajanī, parṇinī, and the two types of sārivā;
One should cook ghee with twice its amount of milk along with hareṇukā, trivṛt, dantī, vacā, tālīśa, kesara, and mālatī flowers.
This supreme and auspicious medicated ghee, known as Kalyāṇaka, cures chronic fever, dyspnea, cough, abdominal tumors, insanity, and the effects of poisons.
It removes misfortune, planetary afflictions, demons, fire, sluggish digestion, epilepsy, and sin;
it is highly recommended for those whose semen has failed and is the supreme bestower of offspring to barren women.
It is moderate, beneficial for the eyes, conducive to longevity, and a purifier of the seminal passage;
it is prepared with these very same substances as well as all types of fragrant aromatics.
Having prepared one prastha of ghee from a tawny cow, combined with gold and gems,
and having processed it together with her milk using these flowers;
It was covered with *sumana*, campaka, *aśoka*, and *śirīṣa* flowers,
as well as with the filaments of *nalada*, lotuses, and pomegranates.
On an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation,
the rite for the human deity was performed by Brahmins and consecrated with mantras for the sake of the practitioner and the patient.
When administered, this Mahākalyāṇaka indeed destroys all fevers.
Through both sight and touch, it is auspicious, removing all diseases;
one becomes invincible to all beings and free from wrinkles and grey hair.
By practicing this here with ghee, one shall live for three hundred years;
[the six substances are] cow's curd, urine, milk, clarified butter, the liquid of dung, and [cow's] urine.
These should be cooked in equal parts, and one should add the following as a paste (kalka):
triphalā, citraka, musta, haridrā, ativiṣā, and vacā.
Viḍaṅga, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), cavya, and likewise devadāru—
this "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya) destroys irregular fever when drunk.
Except for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), it should be cooked with vṛṣa while still in the vessel;
thereafter, it should be cooked with balā, and likewise with guḍūcī.
This is highly esteemed for chronic fever, swelling, and jaundice. By this very same method, one should cook the "fivefold goat ghee" (pañcāvika-ghṛta),
as well as the fivefold goat ghee, the fivefold buffalo ghee, and likewise the fourfold camel ghee.
With triphalā, uśīra, śampāka, kaṭukā, ativiṣā, ghanā, śatāvarī,
saptaparṇa, guḍūcī, and the two types of rajanī;
With *citraka*, *trivṛt*, *kaṭukā*, *viśālā*, *paṭola*, *ariṣṭa*, and *vālaka*;
and with *kirātatiktaka*, *kaṭukā*, *viśālā*, *padmaka*, and *utpala*.
With the two types of sārivā, yaṣṭyāhva, cavika, red sandalwood,
durālabhā, parpaṭaka, trāyamāṇā, and ṭarūṣaka;
Clarified butter (havis) prepared properly with rāsnā, saffron, mañjiṣṭhā, māgadhī, and ginger, along with twice as much of the juice of āmalaka fruits; |||
This is the supreme remedy for the prevention of erysipelas, fever, dyspnea, abdominal tumors, and leprosy;
it is also most beneficial for anemia, splenic disorders, and impaired digestion.
One pala each of paṭola, kaṭuka, dārvī, nimba, vāsā, triphalā, durālabhā, parpaṭaka, and trāyamāṇā [are taken].
One should boil one prastha of āmalaka fruits in one ārmaṇa of water;
with that decoction reduced to one-fourth, one should cook one prastha of ghee.
This [oil], prepared with the pastes of *kuṭaja*, *bhūnimba*, *ghana*, *yaṣṭyāhvā*, *candana*, and *pippalī*,
is beneficial for the eyes and is wholesome for the two white parts (the sclera).
It cures diseases of the nose, ears, eyes, mouth, and eyelids, as well as ulcers;
it dries up blood, bile, phlegm, sweat, moisture, and pus.
Milk boiled with sugar, long pepper, honey, and ghee is a supreme remedy for removing jaundice, fever, erysipelas, and scrofula.
This "Five-essence" drink, when churned, is prescribed for irregular fever,
as well as for chest wounds, emaciation, wasting diseases, dyspnea, and heart disease.
Oil prepared with lac, viśvaniśā, mūrvā, mañjiṣṭhā, and svarjikā,
along with six times the amount of buttermilk, is a destroyer of fever.
With milk-exuding trees, āsana, ariṣṭa, jambu, saptacchada, and arjuna;
with śirīṣa, khadira, āsphoṭā, amṛtavallī, and āṭarūṣaka;
Oil prepared with kaṭukā, parpaṭa, uśīra, vacā, tejovatī, and ghanā,
when used for massage, quickly removes chronic fever.
He should frighten him at the time of arrival with non-venomous snakes, tame elephants, or disguised thieves; on that day, he should not feed him.
If the patient suffers from excessive secretions or heaviness, one should induce vomiting repeatedly;
or one should administer strong wine or fever-destroying ghee.
On that same day, the wise physician should administer either old ghee, or a generous purgative, or a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) to the person who has been well-fomented.
One should cause an incense fumigation to be administered for him, consisting of the skin and hair of a goat or a sheep, vacā, kuṣṭha, palaṅkaṣā, and nimba leaves, mixed with honey.
Cat excrement should be applied as an ointment, or it may be used as an incense for one who is trembling;
long pepper, rock salt, oil, and Nepalese antimony should be used as an eye-salve.
The medicated ghees mentioned previously by me for abdominal ailments,
as well as the unconquerable ghee (Ajita-sarpiḥ) prescribed in the Kalpa, will overcome fever when consumed.

One should conquer the affliction arising from possession by spirits through the binding, invocation, and worship prescribed in the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā), and mental affliction through higher knowledge and other such means.
One should eat rice with meat broth after being anointed with ghee when the fever arises from exhaustion;
one should conquer fevers arising from curses or malevolent spells through burnt offerings (homa) and other such rites.

In cases of fever caused by portents, planetary afflictions, or injuries, one should perform remedial rites consisting of charity, auspicious ceremonies, and hospitality, while avoiding all heating measures.
One should administer a decoction that is sweet and unctuous, according to the specific dosha involved;
furthermore, for those caused by medicinal herbs or poison, one should use remedies that pacify poison and bile.
One should conquer the bitter taste with that which is beneficial and prepared from all fragrant substances;
likewise, a decoction of neem and deodar is beneficial, as is the saumanasa flower.
Barley, its preparations, clarified butter, and wine are beneficial in cases of irregular fever.
One should honor the twice-born, cows, and the deities Īśāna and Ambikā.

In cases of fever arising from kapha and vāta, when the patient is afflicted by cold, one should apply a warm poultice with the [appropriate] group of drugs; furthermore, the subsequent warm regimen is beneficial.
One should sprinkle [the area] with lukewarm sour gruel, fermented rice water, cow urine, or whey;
or one should apply a plaster made from the ground leaves of *palāśa*, *surasā*, *arjaka*, or *śigru*.
Anointing with alkaline oil mixed with sour gruel (śukta) is prescribed,
as is especially the drinking of the decoction of the āragvadhādi group of drugs.
An immersion bath that is pleasantly warm and mixed with decoctions that subdue Vata,
having thus overcome the cold through these gradual steps, should be followed by sprinkling with pleasantly warm water.
Having brought him inside, one should have him— whose body is emaciated and adorned with black aloe-wood— lie down, covered with garments of wool, cotton, and silk.
Abounding in breasts, endowed with beauty, skillful, and in the bloom of youth—
auspicious women who dispel cold and dejection should attend upon him with their limbs.
With faces like the autumnal moon and eyes like blue lotuses,
they caused the surface of their foreheads to tremble with the graceful arching of their quivering creeper-like eyebrows.
Their lower lips resembled hanging, swaying bimba fruits;
they had slender waists and were languid from the weight of their broad hips.
Their limbs were smeared with saffron and agallochum; they possessed thick, lofty breasts;
and they were adorned with smooth garments and ornaments, which were perfumed by fragrant incense.
They would embrace him firmly, like forest creepers clinging to a tree;
then, perceiving Prahlāda's joy, they should remove those women once again.
One should feed them wholesome food that wards off the fever caused by the cold of their embrace, so that they may attain happiness.
But when one is overcome by burning sensations, one should perform the rite for the destruction of that burning,
either with water infused with honey and molasses, or even with water infused with nimba leaves.
A wise physician should quickly induce emesis in one afflicted by burning fever;
or, having anointed the patient with ghee washed a hundred times, he should apply a plaster made of barley flour.
With kola and āmalaka combined with vinegar and fermented grain-liquor (dhānyāmla), ground with sour substances,
and likewise with very cold, frothy sprouts;
One should apply a plaster made of the leaves of the *palāśa* tree ground with sour liquids while still very cold,
or a foam produced from *badarī* sprouts and *ariṣṭaka*.
When applied as an ointment to the limbs, burning sensations, thirst, and fainting are entirely pacified;
likewise, having ground half a kuḍava of barley and half a pala of mañjiṣṭhā.
One should cook one *prastha* of oil mixed with one hundred *prasthas* of sour gruel;
this "Pralhādana" oil destroys fever and burning sensations.
One should apply a paste made from the nyagrodhādi group, the kākolyādi group,
or the utpalādi group, ground together.
Oils prepared with those decoctions and sour substances are beneficial for massage;
or, one should have the patient suffering from the pain of burning sensations immerse themselves in a cold decoction of those same herbs.
When the force of the burning fever has passed, one should lift the person out of that [liquid],
sprinkle him with cold water from the ocean, and anoint him with sandalwood and other cooling substances.
Or let excellent women, clad in delicate silken garments with breasts moistened by sandalwood paste, embrace him when he is sick or dejected in spirit.
Bearing variegated lotus garlands and adorned with jewels and gems,
may they attend upon him, touching him with their cool breasts and with the pleasant touch of their lotuses.
Having ascertained that he is Prahlāda, one should again remove those women and feed him wholesome food; thus he attains great happiness.
The pacifying treatments prescribed for pitta-fever, purgation, and whatever else is beneficial should be employed;
when the humors are combined, one should first eliminate the pitta itself.
For that [thirst] is indeed most difficult to ward off, especially for those afflicted by fever,
because it is not opposed by vomiting, fainting, thirst, and other such symptoms of fever.
One should also conquer the complications by means of an antidotal cause;
hear now another specific method for the destruction of complications.
Madhuka, rajanī, musta, dāḍima, amlavetasa,
añjana, tintiḍīka, nalada, patra, and utpala.
One should smear the head of one afflicted by fever with these— tvak, vyāghranakha, and the juice of mātuluṅga mixed with honey— or with honey and fermented vinegar (madhuśukta).
This medicinal plaster destroys headaches, delusion, hiccup, and trembling— these complications of those afflicted by fever.
Then [he offered] madhūka, hrīvera, utpala, and madhūlikā.
Having licked these powders with honey and ghee, one shall conquer vomiting,
excessive salivation due to phlegm, hemorrhagic disorders, Pitta-related ailments, hiccups, and severe dyspnea.
One afflicted by fever should lick a compound of triphalā and pippalī with honey;
in cases of cough and dyspnea, one shall find relief by taking them with honey and ghee.
One should apply a medicinal paste made from vidārī, pomegranate, lodhra, dadhittha,
and bījapūraka to the head of a person suffering from thirst and burning sensations.
In cases of a bad taste in the mouth, one should hold a paste of pomegranate, sugar, grapes, and emblic myrobalan, as well as perform gargling with these substances as appropriate.
In the case of an empty head, nasal medication (nasya) with milk, sugarcane juice, sour gruel, ghee, oil, or warm water, or ghee boiled with the drugs of the jīvanīya group, is beneficial.
A purgative consisting of powdered triphalā, śyāmā, trivṛt, and pippalī,
combined with honey and sugar, is highly recommended.
In a mature pitta-fever, in upward-moving hemorrhage,
and likewise in shivering caused by kapha and vāta, one should purify the patient with oleation and massage.
One whose humors have been removed but who suffers from the affliction of dizziness should lick honey, sugar, and *abhayā*.
In fever born of Vāta, non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*) should be administered combined with Vāta-alleviating and sweet substances.
Having considered the morbidity and the vital breath (prāṇa), the oil enemas (anuvāsana) should be prepared according to the specific requirements,
enriched with decoctions such as those of the utpalādi group, and combined with sandalwood and uśīra.
Sweetened with sugar, they are considered cooling and effective in removing pitta-type fever.
[One should take] the bark of mango and other such fruits, conch shell, sandalwood, licorice, and blue lotus.
Then, red chalk, collyrium, madder, lotus stalks, and lotuses,
finely ground with milk and combined with sugar and honey—
One should administer a well-purified and cool enema to one suffering from burning sensations;
likewise, an oil enema (anuvāsana) prepared with those same [decoction] ingredients is effective for removing fever and burning.
Decoctions of the āragvadha group, combined with the pippalyādi group and administered with honey and urine,
should be given to destroy fever born of kapha.
Enemas prepared with substances that specifically pacify kapha are also effective;
in cases of dual humors (saṃsarga) and the triad of all three (sannipāta), enemas compounded from a combination of these are beneficial.

All the oleation therapies (snehas) that have been properly described as removing diseases of Vata— whether administered alone or combined with other substances— are effective when used for non-unctuous enemas (anuvāsana).
In fever born of Vata, those same [medicines] should be used without oil;
they should be employed in their entirety for applications such as massage and the like.
In the Pitta-type [fever], ghee prepared with sweet and bitter substances is esteemed;
in the Kapha-type, with pungent and bitter substances; and in the combined types, with those that are mixed.
When the bile remaining in the heart has moved to the skin, it produces fever;
in that case, one should drink cold sugarcane juice or sugar-water.
One should eat rice of the *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* varieties mixed with milk;
indeed, one should employ sudation and oil massage specifically for those [afflictions] arising from *kapha* and *vāta*.
Clarified butter should be administered in all fevers after twelve nights have passed; for by that interval, the humors indeed return to their own respective seats.
Agitating the bodily constituents (dhātus), the affliction (doṣa) becomes more powerful at the time of liberation;
by that, one whose mind is agitated behaves as if dying even here.
Lightness of the head, perspiration, a pale face that improves with digestion,
sneezing, and a desire for food are the signs of one who has been freed from fever.
Born from the wrath of Śambhu, terrible, and capable of destroying strength, complexion, and fire, he is the king of diseases,
a mass of afflictions, and is designated as fever (jvara).
Because of its pervasiveness, because of its contact with all things, because of its difficulty to endure, and because of its occurrence at the end,
this fever is taught to be the very ender of living beings.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter (the first from the beginning), titled "The Prohibition of Fever," within the Section on Internal Medicine contained in the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The fortieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diarrhea (atisāra).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

By foods that are excessively heavy, unctuous, dry, hot, liquid, or bulky; by those that are extremely cold; and by meals that are incompatible, consumed before the previous meal is digested, or eaten while undigested, as well as by unwholesome foods.
From the excessive application of oleation and other therapies,
from improper administration, from poison or fear, from grief, from drinking contaminated water or alcohol in excess, and from the sudden change of habitual diet or season;
Due to excessive indulgence in water, the obstruction of natural urges, or from the disorder of parasites, diarrhea occurs in men; its symptoms will now be described.
When the watery element (ap-dhātu) is suppressed within by fire, and that fire— mingled with bile and impelled by wind—
increases excessively and flows downward, they call that terrible disease *atisāra*.
"He is said to be caused by each of the humors individually, by all of them together, by grief, and a sixth by undigested matter (āma).
Some say it is of many forms and types, but the King of Kāśī declared that it is not so."
The various states of his humors arise from time to time as he is afflicted by disease:
depression of the heart, navel, bladder, abdomen, and flanks; distension; exhaustion of the limbs; and obstruction of the vital breaths.
Attachment to unwholesome food, flatulence, and indigestion will be its precursors;
he will be afflicted by colic, suffer from obstructed urination, experience rumbling in the intestines, and feel a sense of weakness in the anus, waist, thighs, and feet.
Accompanied by wind, the stool is released in small, frequent amounts, frothy, dry, and dark-brown;
it is foul-smelling, hot, forceful, resembling meat-washings, broken up, and the body is perspiring with an intense heat.

Due to bile (pitta), the stool is yellow, blue, or reddish; the patient is afflicted by thirst, fainting, burning sensations, suppuration, and fever; he suffers from drowsiness, sleepiness, heaviness, nausea, and frequent urges; and even after passing stool, he feels as though there is more to come.
The stool is white and thick, associated with phlegm; the patient has an aversion to food, passes soundless excrement, and has horripilation.
Accompanied by drowsiness, delusion, exhaustion, and dryness of the mouth, and afflicted by thirst, he voids stools of many colors.

When it arises from all [causes], there is the manifestation of all symptoms; this *kṛcchra* fever is incurable in children and the elderly, as it enters the person by means of various conditions, having pervaded the state of digestion (*pakti*).
Having reached the stomach, it agitates his blood, which then flows downward like the *kākaṇantī* plant;
mixed with feces, either with or without stool, and either with or without odor, it is discharged with great difficulty by that [disease].
Born of grief, this exceedingly difficult-to-cure disease has been declared by physicians to be a painful affliction;
the vitiated humors, agitated along with the food, have become corrupted and are afflicting the stomach with indigestion.
They repeatedly expel various-colored matter with great difficulty; this is called the sixth [type of vomiting].
When mixed with these humors (doṣas) and cast into water, it sinks;
it is extremely foul-smelling feces, broken up and known as *āmavarcas*.
However, when these very signs are reversed in a person and there is lightness [of the body], one should declare that it is digested.
If the discharge flows in the form of clarified butter, vesavāra, water, oil, marrow, milk, or honey;
or if it resembles mañjiṣṭhā, or is like brain matter, or is foul-smelling, cold, has the odor of a corpse, or resembles collyrium—[then it is fatal].
If it is streaked with lines, covered with spots, resembles pus, looks like mud, or is hot;
or if it flows in the opposite direction, or is diminished—these conditions kill the patient, as do numerous complications.
One should abandon a patient who has a prolapsed anus, who is emaciated, difficult to fill with food, afflicted by complications, whose rectum is suppurated,
whose body heat has departed, and who bears the scars of chronic diarrhea.
Diarrhea that has arisen in embodied beings from whatever cause never transcends the symptoms of the [three] humors (doṣas).
That caused by indigestion due to unctuous substances (sneha) is characterized by excessive colic and dysentery;
that caused by indigestion due to visūcikā is another type arising from indigestion;
and that produced by poison, hemorrhoids, or worms exhibits the specific symptoms of their respective doshas.
Since there is no specific treatment for diarrhea that disregards the sequence of undigested (āma) and digested (pakva) stages,
all cases of diarrhea should therefore be understood by means of the signs of the undigested and the digested states.
In that regard, first, fasting (laṅghana) should be performed for embodied beings suffering from diarrhea;
thereafter, a regimen beginning with gruel (yavāgū) combined with digestive (pācana) agents is beneficial.
Alternatively, when the *āmadoṣa* is afflicted by colic and flatulence,
one should administer emesis and then treat the patient with fasting and other such measures, along with water mixed with long pepper (*pippalī*) and rock salt (*saindhava*).
At the conclusion of emesis, one should prescribe light food that is easily digestible;
furthermore, one should employ the Pippalyādi group of drugs in conjunction with meat broth, vegetable soup, or gruel.
If one's diarrhea does not subside by this method,
that person should drink a decoction of haridrā and other drugs, or vacā and other drugs, in the morning.

In persons suffering from diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātīsāra), astringent therapy (saṃgrahaṇa) should not be administered at the outset; for their obstructed humors (doṣas) may first produce these following diseases: The patient develops a burning sensation (dāha), thirst, fever, vomiting, fainting, and a sense of heaviness in the head, as well as pain in the sides, the back, and the waist. Furthermore, there occurs a discharge of feces that is foul-smelling, mixed with mucus, and accompanied by blood. This condition is known as pravāhikā (tenesmus). If the treatment is applied improperly, the humors become excessively aggravated and, being obstructed, produce these complications: a burning sensation, thirst, fever, vomiting, fainting, and heaviness of the head; pain in the flanks, the back, and the waist; and a discharge of stool that is foul-smelling, mixed with mucus, and containing blood. This is called pravāhikā. It cures splenic disorders, anemia, abdominal distension, urinary diseases, skin diseases, abdominal enlargements,
fevers, edema, abdominal tumors, malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, colic, lassitude, and cardiac oppression.
In one who suffers from diarrhea that is painful, frequent, difficult,
and obstructed, one should cause the accumulated doshas to be expelled by means of purgatives (pathyās).
For one who passes excessively frequent and copious stools in diarrhea,
one should first administer emesis, followed by fasting and digestive treatments.
One who suffers from diarrhea that is either scanty, intermittent,
or accompanied by pain should be purged with lukewarm pastes of *abhayā* and *pippalī*.
In the case of undigested matter (āma), fasting is recommended at the outset, or else digestive treatment alone;
furthermore, formulations for the destruction of āmātisāra will now be described.
Kaliṅga, ativiṣā, hiṅgu, sauvarcala, vacā, and abhayā;
devadāru, vacā, mustā, nāgara, ativiṣā, and abhayā.
Abhayā, dhānyaka, musta, pippalī, nāgara, and vacā;
or nāgara, dhānyaka, musta, vālaka, and bilva.
Musta, parpaṭaka, śuṇṭhī, vacā, prativiṣā, and abhayā;
likewise, abhayā, ativiṣā, hiṅgu, vacā, and sauvarcala.
Citraka, the root of Pippalī, Vacā, Kaṭukarohiṇī, Pāṭhā, the seeds of Vatsaka, Harītakī, and Mahauṣadha.
Mūrvā, nirdahanī, pāṭhā, tryūṣaṇa, gajapippalī, siddhārthaka,
bhadradāru, śatāhvā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Cardamom, *sāvaraka* costus, the two types of turmeric, *kauṭaja* seeds, barley, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, cinnamon, cardamom, *kṛmighna*, and *vṛkṣaka*.
Vṛkṣādanī, vīrataru, the two types of bṛhatī, the two types of saha,
aralu-bark, tindukī, dāḍimī, kauṭajī, and śamī.
Pāṭhā, tejovatī, musta, pippalī, fruit of kuṭaja,
paṭola (or paṭolī), dīpyaka, bilva, the two types of haridrā, and devadāru.
Viḍaṅga, abhayā, pāṭhā, śṛṅgavera, ghana, vacā;
vacā, seeds of vatsaka, saindhava, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Asafoetida, seeds of vatsaka, vacā, unripe bilva fruits,
ginger, ativiṣā, musta, long pepper, and vatsaka fruit.
Mahauṣadha, prativiṣā, and musta are the ingredients for these digestive (āmapācana) formulations;
these twenty recipes are prescribed in half-verses.
One should drink either fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), warm water, or wine;
or one should drink well-prepared, comfortably warm decoctions of these same substances.
Having boiled twenty mustā roots in three times the amount of water with milk until only the milk remains,
drinking that [milk] destroys undigested matter (āma) as well as colic.
This entire procedure for the pacification of fever has been taught;
[it consists of] *harītakī*, *ativiṣā*, asafoetida, *sauvarcala* salt, and *vacā*.
A person afflicted by diarrhea with fever should drink [a decoction of] paṭola,
dīpyaka, bilva, vacā, pippalī, and nāgara, along with lukewarm water.
One should drink Musta, Kuṣṭha, and Viḍaṅga with lukewarm water,
or one should drink Śṛṅgavera and Guḍūcī with warm water.
Salt, long pepper, viḍaṅga, harītakī,
citraka, śiṃśapā, pāṭhā, śārṅgeṣṭā, and salts.
The seeds of the Hiṅgu and Vṛkṣaka trees, the various salts in equal parts, elephant-castor root, and long pepper— these two pastes (kalkas) are each remembered as being one akṣa in measure.
Vaca and the stalks of Guḍūcī—this formulation is considered supreme. These five formulations are held by the wise to be administered with lukewarm water.
When the acute colic has subsided, if one's wind (vāyu) is not restored to its natural state,
and he suffers from slight, intermittent pain and passes stools accompanied by colic, [this is known as Anila-śūla].
One with weak digestive fire should drink ghee prepared with alkaline salts and combined with milk,
ginger, cāṅgerī, jujube, and sour curd.
Or one should drink clear ghee for the pacification of colic and diarrhea;
likewise, ghee cooked with curd, oil, and the three pungents (vyoṣa), costus (ajāti), and leadwort (citrika).
Or, for those afflicted by pain, this entire procedure described may be performed with bilva, pippalī root, and pomegranate for the pacification of vāta and śleṣman.
In the case of a Pitta-born [fever], the physician should administer this [diet] excluding sharp and hot substances;
at the end of the fast, gruel as described is recommended.
These are prepared from bala, aṃśumatī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, bṛhatī, and śatāvarī;
they are perfectly cooled and mixed with honey.
Soups made from mudga and other pulses should be well-prepared with these substances;
they should be mild, digestive-stimulating, and bitter, serving as a means to digest undigested matter (āma).
Haridrā, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, vatsabīja, and rasāñjana;
rasāñjana, the two types of haridrā, and the seeds of kuṭaja.
Pāṭhā, guḍūcī, bhūnimba, and likewise kaṭurohiṇī—
decoctions made from these, as indicated by this half-verse, serve to digest pitta.
Musta, kuṭaja seeds, bhūnimba, rasāñjana, dārvī,
durālabhā, bilva, vālaka, and red sandalwood.
Sandalwood, vālaka, musta, bhūnimba, along with durālabhā;
lotus stalk, sandalwood, rodhra, nāgara, and blue water-lily.
Pāṭhā, musta, the two types of haridrā, pippalī, fruit of kuṭaja,
the bark of vatsaka, śṛṅgavera, ghana, and vacā.
These six formulations have been described as destroyers of pitta-type diarrhea. A decoction prepared from bilva, śakrayava, ambhoda, bālaka,
and ativiṣā cures diarrhea accompanied by undigested matter (āmātisāra) arising from pitta.
A decoction prepared from Madhuka, Utpala, Bilva, Abda, Hrībera, Uśīra, and Nāgara,
combined with honey, destroys Pittaja diarrhea.
When diarrhea, even if matured, continues to recur frequently due to the weakness of the patient's *grahaṇī*, then astringent therapy (*saṃstambhana*) is beneficial.
Samaṅgā, dhātakī flowers, mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, mustaka,
the mucilage of śālmalī, rodhra, and the barks of the vṛkṣa and pomegranate;
The pulp from the middle of a mango stone, lodhra, the pulp of a bilva fruit,
priyaṅgu, madhuka, ginger, and the bark of the dīrghavṛnta tree;
These four formulations are destroyers of chronic diarrhea (pakvātīsāra);
they have been described as those which should be used mixed with honey and taken with rice-water.

One should drink either a decoction of *lodhra* alone or a single astringent decoction mixed with honey; in this same manner, one should employ the groups of drugs beginning with *ambaṣṭhā* and *priyaṅgu*.
One should drink padmā, samaṅgā, madhuka, and the tender fruits of bilva and jambū with rice-water, along with honey and agadaṅkara.
Or one may take a paste of *kacchūrā* root the size of an *udumbara* fruit,
along with *payasyā*, sandalwood, *padmā*, sugar, *mustā*, and lotus filaments.
This formulation, when drunk, conquers chronic diarrhea (pakvātisāra) accompanied by blood;
it also cures that which is free from undigested matter (nirāmam), afflicted with colic, and emaciated by fasting and other such depletive therapies.
Having observed that the person is dry, one should have them drink ghee prepared with alkali and boiled with the roots of balā,
bṛhatī, aṃśumatī, and kacchurā.
One afflicted by colic should drink ghee mixed with honey and madhuka;
[or] ghee prepared with dārvī, bilva, kaṇā, drākṣā, kaṭukā, and indrayava.
This preparation, cooked with sour curd and combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa), cumin (ajājī), and leadwort (citraka), destroys diarrhea caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha.
One afflicted by pain or assailed by colic should drink milk, ghee, and honey, along with saca, pippalī-mūla, and pomegranates.
Sprinkled with the powder of sugar, ajamoda, kaṭvaṅga, and madhuka, it is painless,
well-cooked, and suitable for one with a strong digestive fire who has suffered from chronic diarrhea.
One should treat diarrhea characterized by various colors with *puṭapāka* preparations,
using a ball of bark from the *dīrghavṛnta* tree combined with lotus filaments.
Having wrapped it firmly with threads using *kāśmarī* leaves and lotus petals,
and having well-prepared it by coating it with clay, one should heat it in glowing embers.
Having steamed it, extracted it, and squeezed out the juice,
one should then cool it, add honey, and administer it for abdominal diseases.
One should prepare [the medicine] in this manner using substances such as *jīvantī* and *eṣaśṛṅgī*.
Then, one should properly pluck a partridge, remove its entrails, and fill it [with the preparation].
One should cause it to ferment as before with the pastes of the barks of the Nyagrodha and other trees;
then, having extracted the juice of that well-sweated substance, one should take it together with honey.
One should administer a cold drink mixed with sugar for abdominal diseases,
containing lodhra, candana, yaṣṭyāhvā, dārvī, pāṭhā, and white utpala.
Having ground rice with water and mixed it with long-stalked bark,
one should take the cool liquid from that previously boiled decoction.
One should have this, mixed with honey, drunk in cases of abdominal diseases caused by kapha and pitta;
likewise, one should prepare it from the sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree and others according to the prescribed method.
One should administer auspicious *puṭapāka* preparations as appropriate, combined with the meat of wild animals,
for cases characterized by excessive phlegm, blood, mild wind, and long-standing onset.
The inspissated juice (phāṇita) of *kauṭaja* also destroys diarrhea by its vital potency,
when combined with honey and the *ambaṣṭhādi* group, and accompanied by the *pippalyādi* group.
A patient suffering from abdominal diseases should drink a gruel prepared with *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *bilva*, *vālaka*, blue lotus (*utpala*), coriander (*dhānyaka*), and *nāgara*.
Having added and ground together aralu bark, priyaṅgu, madhuka, and pomegranate sprouts,
one should prepare a thin gruel (yavāgū) with curd.
This undoubtedly destroys all types of diarrhea when prepared:
rasāñjana, ativiṣā, and likewise the bark and seeds of kuṭaja.
One should cause [the patient] to drink dhātakī and nāgara with rice-water;
these, when combined with honey, destroy blood-born [fever] accompanied by pain.
Madhuka, bilva pulp, combined with sugar and honey,
as well as the grains of śāli and ṣaṣṭika rice, destroy diarrhea.
Likewise, the root of the Badarī tree mixed with honey should be licked;
as should the bark of the Badarī, Arjuna, Jambu, Āmra, Śallakī, and Vetasa trees.
Taken with sugar and honey, these [decoctions] destroy abdominal diseases;
with these same [ingredients], one should prepare gruels, milk-porridges, and soups.
When these substances are thirsty for water,
the wise man prepares a decoction from the fibers of the śālmali tree known as "the cold one."
One who suffers from obstructed flatus and feces, colic pain, and dysentery should drink a potion that has stood overnight, mixed with honey and Madhuka.
One suffering from raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders) accompanied by thirst should drink milk;
for milk is as honored as nectar in cases of diarrhea.
This should be drunk when the [fever] has been long-standing, boiled with three parts of water;
for it removes the remnants of the humors (doṣas), and therefore it is considered most wholesome.
An unctuous purgative, slimy enemas, or those prepared with a slimy decoction are beneficial;
likewise, ghee cooked with a slimy decoction is said to be wholesome.
When blood mixed with feces is passed,
either before or after the stool, accompanied by pain and cutting sensations;
One should drink ghee boiled with milk and the sprouts [of the kṣīrin plant], mixed with honey and sugar;
or ghee prepared with the bark of dārvī, pippalī, śuṇṭhī, lākṣā, and śakrayava.
When combined with Bhadrarohiṇī, cooked and mixed with gruel or similar liquids,
it destroys even the most severe diarrhea caused by the three humors (tridoṣa) when drunk.
In cases of nausea where kapha is predominant, emesis is beneficial;
likewise in fever accompanied by burning sensations and constipation due to vāta, as in the case of raktapitta.
When the doshas are fully ripened, abundant, and obstructed, one should promptly administer an asthāpana enema with urine-purifying agents,
as well as an anuvāsana enema.
In cases of dysuria, prolapse of the rectum, urinary obstruction,
and stiffness of the waist, oil or ghee boiled with sweet and sour substances should be administered as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
If internal suppuration (gudapāka) occurs due to pitta in one who eats unwholesome food,
then pitta-alleviating affusions and oil enemas prepared with those same [pitta-subduing] ingredients should be administered.
Oil prepared with whey, wine, and bilva is beneficial for disorders associated with wind (vāta);
likewise, milk boiled with the roots of kacchurā is wholesome as a food.
When blood is discharged in very small quantities frequently, accompanied by pain during defecation,
and when the wind (vāyu) is obstructed, then the picchā-basti is beneficial.
Generally, weakness of the anus occurs in those suffering from chronic diarrhea;
therefore, the application of oil to the anus is beneficial for them.
The wood-apple, silk-cotton tree, phañjī, banyan, cotton-plant, pomegranate, jasmine, kacchurā, śelu, hemp, cuccū, and dādhika; these are the [plants] belonging to the dadhika group.
Śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī,
kaṇṭakārikā, balā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, bilva, pāṭhā, nāgara, and dhānyaka.
This is beneficial for all those suffering from diarrhea when combined with food;
likewise, a paste of sesame seeds and the juice of mung beans are beneficial in this condition.
That mortal suffering from bilious diarrhea who excessively indulges in bilious substances will have his bile quickly vitiated,
leading to the onset of bloody diarrhea.
Fever, colic, thirst, burning sensations,
and severe inflammation of the anus occur in one who passes blood either before or after the stool.
He should drink milk prepared with the sprouts of the banyan tree and other such trees, along with ghee, sugar, and honey; or alternatively, he may churn that same milk.
Then one should lick fresh butter and subsequently drink buttermilk;
[one should also take] the barks of priyāla, śālmalī, plakṣa, śallakī, and tiniśa.
Madhuka, sugar, lodhra, payasyā, and sāriva, when crushed in milk and drunk with honey, destroy [excessive] blood.
One should drink [this] with goat's milk and honey to destroy hemorrhaging:
mañjiṣṭhā, sārivā, lodhra, padmaka, kumuda, and utpala.
One should drink lotus with goat's milk for the pacification of hemorrhage;
likewise, sugar, blue water-lily, lodhra, samaṅgā, madhuka, and sesame seeds [should be used].
Black sesame seeds with yaṣṭyāhvā, samaṅgā, and blue lotuses;
likewise, sesame seeds, mocarasa, lodhra, madhuka, and utpala.
Kacchurā, sesame paste, and the four formulations should be drunk with goat's milk,
combined with honey, in cases involving blood.
When there is a discharge of fluid mixed with blood, one should first lick young bilva fruit with treacle, honey, and oil; for that is quickly beneficial.
Cocoanut kernel fried in ghee, along with parched rice powder, sugar, and honey,
when licked, destroys abdominal disease arising from blood and bile accompanied by pain.
The combination of the pulp of bilva with madhuka,
mixed with sugar and honey and taken with rice-water, conquers disorders arising from pitta and blood.
One should drink other unifying (sāṃgrāhika) yogas mixed with honey and sugar,
and one should prepare puṭapākas from the nyagrodhādi group as previously described.
The procedures prescribed for anal inflammation (gudapāka) are also remembered as applicable here;
furthermore, when pain does not subside, a picchā-vasti is beneficial.
One who has hard stools and an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas), yet suffers from diarrhea despite a stimulated digestive fire,
should be purged with decoctions of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and kṛṣṇā.
Alternatively, one should administer gruel made with milk alone processed with castor seeds,
or prepared with vāta-alleviating and digestive-stimulating ingredients.
One whose digestive fire is kindled and who has no fecal matter, yet passes frothy stools,
should drink molasses along with ginger, curd, oil, milk, and ghee.
One should eat jujubes that have been steamed with molasses and oil,
or likewise, those that have been steamed and ground into a paste together with the tender fruits of the bilva.
Having consumed boiled barley with curd, one should drink Śvetā-Surā;
likewise, one may take the meat of a hare with its blood, along with *samaṅgā*, ghee, and curd.
When there is a depletion of feces, one should consume easily digestible food and take mild nourishment;
a well-prepared broth made from black gram, barley, and jujube is beneficial when combined with the two (sour and salty) tastes.
For the purpose of food, one should provide curd prepared with pomegranate,
along with viḍa salt, unripe bilva fruits, and ginger, all ground together with sour liquids.
The cream of curd, prepared as a Yamaka preparation and fried [in ghee], is beneficial for the loss of luster (varcas).
One who has diminished luster and suffers from diarrhea accompanied by colic, even with a stimulated digestive fire,
should drink ghee combined with digestive stimulants (dīpana) and astringents (saṃgrāhaka).
When the wind is aggravated, it drives the accumulated phlegm downward in one who eats unwholesome food and strains repeatedly;
those who know the truth call that condition *pravāhikā*.
Pravāhikā caused by Vāta is characterized by pain; that from Pitta is accompanied by a burning sensation; and that from Kapha is associated with phlegm.
That arising from blood, however, is marked by blood in the discharge; these are considered to originate from either unctuous or dry conditions.
One should indicate their symptoms, the sequence of treatment, and the state of undigested or digested matter as being like those of diarrhea;
for if the disease does not find relief through fasting or digestive formulations when it has become aggravated, [then other measures must be taken].
That [blood] is quickly destroyed by boiled milk, sesame oil, sesame seeds, and slimy enemas;
likewise, the fresh stalks of the *śālmalī* tree, when thoroughly wrapped in moist *kuśa* grass, [achieve the same].
Having thoroughly crushed the fruits by means of the *puṭapāka* method, one should extract the juice from them;
or else, milk boiled and mixed with oil and clarified butter, along with a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhuka*.
The physician, remaining vigilant, should administer an enema in cases of dysentery accompanied by the retention of urine and feces;
or, when there is pain during straining, an enema prepared with a decoction of the two panchamulas mixed with honey.
Non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) with milk is declared the best; one should employ unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with oil.
Oil prepared with the group of vāta-alleviating drugs and the salts is beneficial when used for food and drink.

One afflicted by diarrhea (niścāraka) should lick a paste of *lodhra*, *viḍa* salt, and unripe *bilva* fruits, enriched with the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*) and mixed with oil; furthermore, he should eat with curd that has its whey removed, combined with honey.
One afflicted by colic pain should be fed for his benefit with milk that has been boiled with well-refined copper, or with cold milk mixed with honey,
or with milk processed with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and vidārigandhā.
One should also consume six types of gruels prepared with wind-alleviating, astringent, and digestive-stimulating ingredients;
one should eat fish and enjoy meat broth prepared with wind-alleviating herbs, along with ghee and oil.
One should eat the prepared meat of the black antelope or the goat together with the tender sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree;
or else, one may consume the prepared blood of a fatty goat, mixed with curd, ghee, and oil.
One should eat them with medicinal pastes or with preparations from peacock and lizard; one may also eat them with excellent soups and curds.
One should consume well-cooked mung beans mixed with the scum of clarified butter, or eat them with curd accompanied by black pepper as a side dish.
In cases of severe pain and dysuria,
the physician should administer an enema prepared with licorice and blue lotus, mixed with milk, honey, and ghee.
That enema pacifies his hemorrhage, as well as burning sensations and fever;
furthermore, an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) prepared with sweet medicinal herbs is beneficial for him.
Whether by night or by day, for whatever man is constantly afflicted by pain,
the more he possesses oil, the more his wind (vāta) is pacified.
When the wind has been pacified, the dysentery (pravāhikā) also attains peace;
therefore, in the disease of dysentery, the physician should pacify the wind.

Pāṭhā, ajamodā, kuṭaja, utpala, śuṇṭhī, and equal parts of māgadhikā, ground together and drunk with lukewarm water, pacify disease; or milk boiled with the seeds of medhyāṇḍa and mixed with ghee [is likewise effective].
Having cooked ginger, ghee, kṣavaka, and oil together, one should lick the preparation; it will quickly destroy disease.
[This should be prepared] with the juices of gajāśana, kumbhika, and pomegranate, along with oil, ghee, and curd.
A gruel prepared with bilva is most wholesome, as is the drinking of warm, freshly drawn milk;
furthermore, light, wholesome, digestive-stimulating, and unctuous foods are beneficial in cases of abdominal diseases.
For the constant benefit [of the patient], the vigilant physician should administer those various medicinal applications after having properly analyzed them.
The gruel (yavāgū) removes thirst, is light, stimulates digestion, and cleanses the bladder;
it is always beneficial in cases of fever and diarrhea.
When [a disease] arises from dryness, the treatment should be unctuous; when it arises from the cause of unctuousness, the treatment should be dry.
When it arises from fear, it is preceded by consolation; when it arises from grief, it is that which destroys grief.
It is beneficial for the arising of poison, hemorrhoids, and worms, and it bestows well-being upon both [the patient and the physician];
furthermore, it should be used without contradiction to treat vomiting, fainting, thirst, and other such conditions.
In a combination of humors, however, one should first treat the pitta in cases of fever and diarrhea,
but in all other instances, one should treat the vāta.
If urine and flatus pass properly even without straining,
and if the digestive fire is kindled and the abdomen is light, then the abdominal disease has been cured.
Some diseases are born of karma, others are born of the humors (doṣas), and still others arise from both karma and the humors;
among these, those born of karma alone are without [visible] causes.
They perish through non-action when karma is exhausted by those actions;
those born of the humors are pacified by the causes for the exhaustion of the humors.
Among those, those that have slight causes and are severe,
or those that are mild but possess many defects, arise from the defects of karma.
Their success is ordained through the destruction of the defects of karma;
the grahaṇī of a living being becomes impaired by causes that extinguish the digestive fire.
Even when the diarrhea has ceased, if the digestive fire is weak and the patient eats unwholesome food,
the fire becomes further impaired and will vitiate the grahaṇī.
Therefore, in the case of diarrhea, one should avoid [heavy foods] just as in the case of one who has been purged,
until the patient has returned to their natural state in terms of both the humors (doṣas) and the vital strength (prāṇa).
The sixth constituent, which is proclaimed as the bearer of bile (pitta), is situated between the stomach and the small intestine; it is known as the *grahaṇī*.
For the strength of the grahaṇī is indeed the digestive fire (agni), and that fire is likewise dependent upon the grahaṇī;
therefore, when the fire is impaired, the grahaṇī becomes thoroughly deranged.
Whether individually or all at once, due to excessively aggravated humors,
that corrupted [wind] frequently causes the discharge of food that has been eaten in an undigested state.
Those learned in Ayurveda call that disorder of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-roga) which is either cooked, painful, or putrid, and which alternates between being constipated and liquid.
Upon its manifestation, there is a burning sensation in the stomach, as well as exhaustion, lethargy, thirst, fatigue,
loss of strength, anorexia, cough, ringing in the ears, and rumbling in the intestines.
Furthermore, if a creature is born with swollen hands and feet and is emaciated,
it will suffer from pain in the joints, restlessness, thirst, vomiting, fever, loss of appetite, and burning sensations.
Afflicted by excessive salivation, a bad taste in the mouth, fainting, and loss of appetite, one should vomit up substances that are sour, bitter, acidic, metallic, smoky, or foul-smelling.
From Vata, there is pain predominant in the anus, heart, flanks, abdomen, and head;
from Pitta, with a burning sensation and heaviness; from Kapha, with heaviness; and from all three combined, with the symptoms of all three.
Likewise, by the color of the humors (doṣas) appearing on the nails, as well as on the feces, urine, eyes, and face,
a person may be suspected of heart disease, anemia, abdominal enlargement, tumors, hemorrhoids, or splenic disorders.
According to the specific aggravation of his doshas, one should properly administer, in the correct sequence,
a diet beginning with liquid gruel (peyā), well-prepared with digestive stimulants (dīpanīya).
Then, one should drink in the morning the three groups of drugs— purgatives, astringents, and digestive stimulants— with wine, fermented liquor (ariṣṭa), oil, fat, urine, or lukewarm water.
Either buttermilk with water or buttermilk alone is said to be beneficial;
one should also employ treatments that destroy worms, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and hemorrhoids in this condition.
In this case, a powder of hingu and other such ingredients, or ghee prepared with the paste of pippalī and the fresh juice of cāṅgerī, destroys splenic enlargement.
Ghee prepared with four times the amount of curd is beneficial;
furthermore, one should treat fever and other complications with their respective specific therapies.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diarrhea," within the Section on Internal Medicine of the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. [From the beginning: 40.
The forty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment for wasting diseases (śoṣa-pratiṣedha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Accompanied by many diseases and preceded by many ailments,
consumption is a disease of great power, difficult to diagnose and difficult to ward off.
Because it dries up the bodily fluids (rasa) and the rest, it is designated as "drying" (śoṣa);
and because it causes the destruction of functional activity (kriyā), it is further called "depletion" (kṣaya).
Since this disease befell King Candramas,
some people, moreover, call it "rājayakṣma" (the king's consumption).
Indeed, some say that it arises from the doshas individually,
because of the presence of one among the eleven according to the principles of tantra.

Because the functions [of the humors] are undivided and because they arise simultaneously, depletion (śoṣa) is considered to be one alone; for it consists of the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).
Indeed, due to their excess, the signs of the humors fall there [upon the fetus],
resulting from depletion, the obstruction of natural urges, injury, or irregular eating.
It arises in an embodied being whose body is pervaded by aggravated doshas,
when the channels of rasa are obstructed by doshas dominated by kapha.
Furthermore, for one who indulges excessively in sexual intercourse, when the semen is exhausted, all the bodily constituents (dhātus) are subsequently depleted; thereafter, human beings wither away.
Loss of appetite, aversion to food, fever, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis,
and hoarseness of voice arise in the sixfold form of rājayakṣman.
From pitta arise hoarseness of voice, pain from wind, aching in the shoulders and sides,
fever, burning sensation, diarrhea, and the discharge of blood.
Fullness of the head, a complete lack of desire for food,
coughing, and a hoarseness of the throat are to be known as arising from the provocation of phlegm (kapha).
Or else, it is endowed with these eleven or even six [symptoms]:
cough, diarrhea, pain in the flanks, hoarseness of voice, loss of appetite, and fever.
Or, if afflicted by these three symptoms— fever, cough, and blood disorders—
one who desires very great fame should abandon a person stricken by consumption.
Indeed, others say that wasting diseases (śoṣa) arise from excessive sexual indulgence, grief, old age, physical exercise, travel, fasting,
and from the affliction of wounds or chest injuries.
One who is emaciated by excessive sexual indulgence is afflicted by the symptoms of seminal depletion;
his body becomes pale, and his bodily tissues (dhātus) waste away as they did before.
He was habitually lost in deep thought, with drooping limbs and emaciated by grief,
appearing as such even without the physical disorders caused by the depletion of semen.
Wasted by old age, emaciated, with his vigor, intellect, strength, and senses diminished;
trembling, lacking appetite, and possessing a broken voice like that of a cracked bronze vessel.
Afflicted by heaviness and loss of appetite, he spits out phlegm that is deficient [in quantity];
his mouth, nose, and eyes are constantly discharging, and his complexion is numb, rough, and covered in dirt.
His limbs were withered by the journey, his body was drooping, and his skin was parched and rough;
the parts of his body were as if asleep, and his palate, throat, and mouth were dried up.
One who is emaciated by excessive physical exertion,
being endowed with these very same symptoms produced by chest injury, yet devoid of the actual wound, [is said to have a wasting due to exertion].
From the depletion of blood, from painful sensations, and likewise from the restrictive nature of the diet, consumption (śoṣa) occurs in one who has been wounded;
and that is considered most incurable.
Due to physical exercise, carrying heavy loads, study, trauma, excessive sexual indulgence,
or even by exertion involving the chest, the chest of one whose [thoracic] cavity is thus torn becomes wounded;
consequently, blood, pus, and phlegm are discharged from that wound in the chest.
Coughing, he vomits yellow, red, black, or reddish-brown matter;
with his chest excessively inflamed, he faints from the intense piercing pain.
A man whose breath from his mouth has a foul odor and whose complexion and voice have become altered—
such wasting away (śoṣa) indeed arises in some cases due to various causes.
In that state, there is no simultaneous manifestation of all the signs of the doshas;
rather, they should be understood as specific depletions (kshaya), each designated by the name of its respective constituent element (dhatu).
Indeed, their medical treatment has already been described previously in the section on the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu).

In one who is about to succumb to consumption (śoṣa), there occur labored breathing, weakness of the limbs, excessive salivation, dryness of the palate, vomiting, loss of digestive fire, intoxication, catarrh, anemia, and excessive sleep; furthermore, such a person has white eyes, is devoted to meat, and is desirous of giving.
In his dreams, crows, parrots, gallinules, peacocks, vultures, as well as monkeys and lizards carry him away;
he sees rivers devoid of water, and trees withered and afflicted by wind, smoke, and forest fires.
One should avoid a patient of consumption who eats excessively, is emaciated, is afflicted by diarrhea, and has swollen scrotum and abdomen.
One should treat a self-controlled person who has a strong digestive fire,
who is not emaciated, and who is young, with ghee prepared from the milk of goats or sheep and processed with the drugs of the Sthirādi group.
For one who has been oleated, mild purification should be performed both upward and downward;
likewise, non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) and head-purgatives (śirovirecana) should be administered.
Once purified, the person should eat barley, wheat, and rice with meat broths;
when the digestive fire has been strengthened and complications have subsided, one should further nourish the individual.
Diseases born of Vata generally afflict one who is emaciated by sexual excess;
for such a person, a nourishing regimen that is unctuous and pacifies Vata is beneficial.
One should offer crows, owls, mongooses, cats, earthworms, snakes,
hole-dwelling rats, and vultures, fried in mustard oil with rock salt and accompanied by various incantations.
The meats of wild animals, as well as soups of mung beans and *āḍhakī* pulses, are pleasing to the heart;
the well-prepared meats of the donkey, camel, elephant, mule, and horse should also be served.
One should drink fermented liquors (ariṣṭas) with meat as an accompaniment, and wines blended with grapes (mārdvīka) should be consumed;
likewise, various kinds of foodstuffs should be prepared from barley that has been soaked in water containing the ashes of *arka*, *amṛtā*, and *kṣāra*.
One who is emaciated should eat or drink ghee, or that of goats or sheep, along with barley gruel at the time of meals;
one afflicted by wasting disease (kṣaya) should lick a paste of the three pungents (trikaṭu) combined with cavya and viḍaṅga, mixed with ghee and honey.
Ghee prepared with the meat of carnivorous animals, combined with honey and Pippali, cures emaciation;
likewise, a linctus made of grapes, sugar, and Pippali, mixed with honey and oil, destroys the disease of consumption (kṣaya).
One should lick a powder made of *turaṅgagandhā*, sesame, and black gram, along with ghee, goat’s milk, and honey;
or a powder of sugar, *aśvagandhā*, and *magadhodbhavā* (long pepper), combined with ghee and honey.
Or one may drink milk boiled with *vājigandhā*; in this way, one attains nourishment of the limbs.
Alternatively, one may drink in the morning the ghee extracted from that milk, enriched with sugar, followed by a draught of milk as an after-drink.
For massage, one should apply horse-urine, *yava*, and *punarnavā*;
furthermore, one who eats wholesome food should drink ghee prepared with the entire *vṛṣa* plant and its flowers, mixed with honey.
This [preparation] destroys severe consumption, cough, dyspnea, and even jaundice;
likewise, equal parts of the meat-juices of cow, horse, elephant, goat, and sheep, as well as their decoctions, should be used in those same proportions.
One part each of the milky sap of the mūrvā, haridrā, and khadira trees, and another part of ghee—
these ten parts the knower of the ritual should cook together, having added the three groups [of drugs] and the entire sweet group.
The three pungents (kaṭutrika) along with bhadradāru and excellent ghee are for the warding off of consumption (yakṣman);
likewise, the two groups of five roots (pañcamūlī), varuṇa, karañja, bhallātaka, bilva, and punarnavā.
Having prepared a decoction of barley, horse gram, jujube, bhārgī, pāṭhā, citraka, and mahīkadamba,
one should cook one measure of ghee with six measures of that decoction.

Vyoṣa, the juice of mahāvṛkṣa, abhayā, cavya, that which is called surā, and the best of salts— this indeed destroys wasting diseases, abdominal enlargements, and urinary disorders (prameha) along with wind.
Ghee prepared with the dung, juice, milk, meat-juice, and blood derived from cows, horses, sheep, goats, deer, donkeys, and camels,
along with grapes, *aśvagandhā*, *pippalī*, and sugar, cures the disorders of consumption (*yakṣma*).
Elā, ajamodā, āmalaka, abhayā, akṣa, gāyatrī, ariṣṭa, asana, sārasa, viḍaṅga,
bhallātaka, citraka, ugrā, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), ambhoda, and surāṣṭrajā.
Having boiled [the ingredients] in water, one should cook ghee in that [liquid];
once it is well-cooked and removed from the heat, one should add thirty palas of white sugar and six palas of tugākṣīrī.
One should add twice as much honey to a prastha of ghee, then churn it with a churning-stick;
having licked it, one pala at a time, in the morning, one should thereafter drink milk without weariness.
For this is supremely pure, holy, beneficial for the eyes, conducive to longevity, and brings fame;
it quickly dispels consumption, as well as jaundice and fistula.
It destroys dyspnea, hoarseness of voice, cough, and diseases of the heart, spleen, abdominal tumors, and malabsorption;
moreover, while this elixir is being practiced, there is nothing whatsoever that must be avoided.
The medicated ghee prescribed for splenic enlargement (plīhodara) should be administered, as well as three other beneficial [fats] mentioned here;
furthermore, one should overcome complications such as disorders of the voice by carefully consulting the scriptures according to their specific requirements.
By habitually consuming the dung, urine, milk, ghee, blood,
and flesh of goats, and by performing various rites such as ritual bathing, one gradually and completely dries up the body through disciplined practice.
One afflicted by consumption should duly employ garlic preparations, or the application of *nāgabalā* with milk,
or the regimen for *māgadhikā*, as well as the use of bitumen (*jatunī*) derived from stone.
One should abandon grief, women, anger, and envy;
one should cultivate noble objects of sense, physicians, the twice-born, the gods, and teachers, and one should listen to sacred words from the learned.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter from the beginning, the third chapter in the section on internal medicine within the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The forty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of abdominal tumors (gulma).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
When the humors (doṣas) are provoked by the aforementioned aggravating factors and reach the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha), they produce gulma in humans; that is said to be of five types.
A mass located between the heart and the bladder, whether mobile or immobile,
characterized by fluctuation in size and being round in shape, is designated as gulma.
The five sites of the Gulmas in men are the sides, the heart, the navel, and the bladder;
this is because they have their root in the vital air (vāyu) and because they arise from deep-seated roots.
Or rather, it is called a "gulma" because of its vastness, like a thicket;
for it accumulates within itself, just as bubbles form in water.
Because it moves internally and therefore does not undergo digestion,
it is produced by the humors (doṣas) both individually and when all are aggravated together.
Likewise, another [type of discharge] from men and women should be known by its blood;
it causes a sinking sensation, burning, flatulence, and rumbling in the intestines.
Obstruction of feces, urine, and flatus, intolerance to satiety, aversion to food, and upward movement of wind— these are the premonitory symptoms of those afflicted with gulma.
Pain in the heart and abdomen, dryness of the mouth and throat, suppression of flatus, and irregularity of digestion—
these various disorders of a windy nature arise when the gulma is caused by vāyu.
Perspiration, fever, burning from food, a burning sensation, thirst, discoloration of the limbs, and a bitter taste in the mouth—
all the symptoms that belong to pitta are present in a gulma caused by pitta.
In a gulma arising from kapha, there is heaviness of the body, loss of appetite, lassitude, vomiting, excessive salivation, sweetness in the mouth,
and whatever other symptoms are characteristic of kapha.

That which possesses all [symptoms] and is associated with all complications is said to be incurable. Now I shall describe [the causes of] blood-born [diseases]: a woman who has recently given birth, one who eats unwholesome food, or one who discharges an immature fetus during her menses; |||
For the Vayu, having seized her blood, produces a Gulma accompanied by pain and burning;
it possesses symptoms identical to those of the Pittaja type, but listen now to another distinguishing characteristic.
When there is no throbbing, no enlargement of the abdomen, yet the signs of pregnancy appear,
and this persists beyond the normal time for gestation, those who know the truth call that blood-born gulma, which requires medical treatment.
One should treat a patient afflicted by vātagulma who has been oleated with appropriate unctuous purgatives,
using non-unctuous enemas (nirūhas) and oil enemas (anuvāsanas) at the proper time.
One who suffers from a pitta-type gulma should first be treated with oleation using Kākolyādi-ghṛta;
once purged, he should be managed with sweet formulations and non-unctuous enemas (nirūhas).
One who suffers from a phlegmatic gulma (abdominal tumor) should first be treated with oleation using *pippalyādi-ghṛta*,
and once purged with sharp [emetics], should then be treated with non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*) of a similar nature.
In a case of Gulma arising from the combination of all three Doshas (Sannipāta), a therapeutic procedure that subdues the three Doshas is beneficial;
for a woman suffering from Raktagulma, the same course of treatment as prescribed for Pittaja Gulma should be administered.
Listen now to another specific distinction regarding this [treatment] for the differentiation of blood:
one should employ clarified butter prepared with the alkaline water of palāśa.
One should administer an uttarabasti (urethral/vaginal enema) with pippalyādi-ghṛta;
or, if it has burst, one should cause it to burst with warm [substances], for the regimen prescribed for asṛgdara (menorrhagia) is beneficial in that case.
The marrow of marshy or aquatic animals, muscle fat, oil, ghee, and curd— these,
when cooked together, are recommended as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) for vātagulma.
In the case of a Pitta-type Gulma, the fat and ghee of wild animals with uncloven hooves are used;
likewise, in a Kapha-type Gulma, the oil and marrow of wild animals are employed.
One should cook six-fold medicated ghee with the fresh juice of āmalaka fruits, combined with sugar and rock salt; this is beneficial for one suffering from vāta-gulma.
With equal parts of citraka, vyōṣa, saindhava salt, pṛthvīkā, cavya, dāḍima,
dīpyaka, granthika, jīraka, hapuṣā, and dhānyaka;
One should drink ghee prepared with the fresh juices of curd, aragvadha, jujube, and radish;
it cures vata-type abdominal tumors (gulma), weakness of the digestive fire, flatulence, and colic.
With asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, cumin, viḍa salt, pomegranate,
dīpyaka, puṣkara, trikaṭu, coriander, sour vetasa, alkali, and citraka;
Ghee cooked with śaṭī, vacā, jagandhā, elā,
and surasa, along with curd, removes colic and constipation for those suffering from vāta-gulma.
With feces, pomegranate, rock salt, fire (citraka), the three pungents (vyoṣa),
cumin, asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, alkali, ginger, wood sorrel, and sour vetasa;
Clarified butter prepared with the juice of citron and four times as much curd,
known as *dādhika*, cures abdominal tumors and overcomes splenic disorders and colic.
Clarified butter (sarpiḥ) should be prepared with the juice of garlic (rasona), combined with the decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla),
along with the juices of wine (surā), fermented rice water (āranāla), sour curd (dadhyamla), and radish (mūlaka).
With equal parts of the three pungents (vyoṣa), pomegranate, wood sorrel (vṛkṣāmla), yavānī, cavya, rock salt (saindhava), asafoetida (hiṅgu), amlavetasa, cumin (ajājī), and dīpyaka;
This proven formulation conquers abdominal tumors, chronic diarrhea, hemorrhoids, asthma, insanity, consumption,
fever, cough, epilepsy, weak digestion, splenic disorders, colic, and wind disorders.
One should cook five āḍhakas of curd, sauvīraka, ghee, and the decoctions of mung and kulattha beans, having added two palas each of the following:
Ghee prepared with sauvarcala, sarjikā, devadāru,
and saindhava salt is a digestive stimulant that cures vāta-gulma.
One should cook ghee in a decoction of grass roots along with the vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs,
or likewise in a decoction of the nyagrodhādi group or the utpalādi group.

These medicated ghees undoubtedly destroy disorders arising from rakta-pitta (bleeding diseases). One should cook ghee with the drugs of the āragvadha group combined with digestive stimulants (dīpanīya).
One should cook another [type of] ghee in the group of alkaline substances, and another in the group of urines;
these ghees undoubtedly destroy gulma arising from phlegm.
