One should treat the sānnipātika type according to the predominance of the specific doṣas,
using either the hiṅgvādi powder or the clarified butter that destroys splenic enlargement (plīhanāśana).
At the appropriate time, one should drink ghee that cures gulma, or indeed Tilvaka-ghee, or ghee prepared with sesame,
Ikṣuraka, Pālāśa, mustard, and barley.
And also with the ashes produced from radishes, and from cows, goats, sheep,
donkeys, elephants, and buffaloes, mixed with their urine and ground into fine powder.
Combined with ten palas each of kuṣṭha, saindhava salt, yaṣṭīmadhu, nāgara, viḍaṅga, ajamoda, and rock salt (sāmudra).
Having cooked it in an iron vessel over a small fire until it becomes a linctus, one should then remove it;
one should drink a dose of that with curd, wine, or even clarified butter.
This alkali, taken with sour gruel, warm water, or the juice of *kaulattha* beans,
undoubtedly destroys abdominal tumors and disorders of the wind (*vāta*).
Alkali derived from *ketakī* seeds, combined with *svarjikā* and *kuṣṭha*,
when drunk with oil, pacifies a gulma arising from wind (*vāta*).
Alternatively, one may drink a mixture of svarjikā, kuṣṭha, and saindhava salt with warm water;
or likewise, vṛścīva, urubūka, varṣābhū, and the two types of bṛhatī.
Having boiled Citraka in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth,
one should place it in a jar smeared with Māgadhī, Citraka, and honey.
Having added a prastha of honey mixed with half a part of powdered harītakī,
a person who has finished his meal should drink it after letting it stand for ten days.
This ariṣṭa conquers gulma, indigestion, and anorexia;
it consists of pāṭhā, nikumbha, rajanī, trikaṭu, triphalā, and agnika.
Salt and the seeds of the *vṛkṣaka* tree should be taken in equal parts, along with sugar and *pathyā* fruits;
this powder should be cooked together with cow’s urine.
One who has become weary of those [other] pills should eat this pill on an empty stomach;
it will completely destroy abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and loss of digestive fire.
It cures heart disease, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), and severe anemia (pāṇḍuroga), as well as conditions characterized by pain,
swelling, lack of pulsation, and accompanied by burning, suppuration, and agony.
In cases of gulma with blood, one should remove the blood by means of leeches or venesection;
[the patient should also take] lukewarm meat-broths of wild animals, well-oleated and seasoned with rock salt.
For those suffering from gulma, drinks prepared with the three pungents (kaṭutrika) are beneficial;
likewise, gruels (peyā) processed with vāta-alleviating herbs and well-prepared soups made from horse gram (kaulattha) are recommended.
Pulses along with the five roots are beneficial for those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) when consumed in food;
however, milk with fresh ginger is recommended for those with constipated feces and suppressed wind.
A skilled physician should administer treatments involving jars, boluses, bricks, and fomentation; for all those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) are said to be extremely difficult to purge.
Therefore, once these [limbs] have been well-fomented, one should treat them with emollients,
as well as with measures for softening, anointing, and cauterization.
Poultices such as *sālvaṇa* and others, which are pleasantly warm, should be applied;
likewise, the medicated ghees mentioned for abdominal diseases and the application of medicinal suppositories with urine should be employed.
And the salts that have been prescribed for wind-diseases (vāta) should be employed;
however, in cases of the suppression of flatus and feces, [one should use] sea salt, fresh ginger, and mustard seeds.
One should prepare suppositories (varti) with a predominance of black pepper,
using the roots of dantī and citraka, as well as other vāta-alleviating herbs, and insert them into the anus.
One should perform all the propitiatory rites (ariṣṭas) as prescribed in the section on verses;
or one may eat the roasted sprouts of the pūtīka and nṛpavṛkṣa trees.
One should not administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) to a person suffering from upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta) or one afflicted with abdominal tumors (gulmin).
Instead, such a person should drink trivṛt and ginger, or harītakī with jaggery (guḍa).
Having considered the relative strength [of the patient], one should administer guggulu, trivṛtā, dantī, dravantī, rock salt (saindhava), and vacā with urine, wine, milk, or grape juice.
In this manner, one should drink fried *pīlu* fruits with salt,
along with long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), *cavya*, *citraka*, and rock salt (*saindhava*).
Surā, when administered at the proper time, quickly destroys gulma. A patient suffering from gulma with obstructed feces and flatus should eat barley with milk.
Or he may eat boiled grains with plenty of oil and an abundance of salt;
then, a complication such as colic pain may somehow arise in him.
That by which one experiences discomfort as if a stake has been driven into him is called *śūla*;
in that condition, there is obstruction of feces and urine, labored breathing, and stiffness of the limbs.
Thirst, burning, giddiness, undigested increase of food,
horripilation, loss of appetite, vomiting, increase after eating, and numbness of the limbs [are the symptoms].
Having observed [the condition], one should administer it mixed with wind (vāyu) and the other [doshas] according to their respective order, or with all combined;
[using] pathyā, the three salts, alkali (kṣāra), asafoetida (hiṅgu), tumburu, and pauṣkara.
Yavānī, haridrā, viḍaṅga, amlavetasa,
vidārī, triphalā, abhīru, śṛṅgāṭī, jaggery, and sugar.
Kāśmarī fruit, yaṣṭyāhva, parūṣaka, and himā;
likewise ṣaḍgranthā, ativiṣā, dāru, pathyā, marica, and vṛkṣaja.
One should take the roots of black turpeth, chavya, ginger, alkali, and citraka,
[administered] with warm sour gruel, milk, or water, as concluded by the verses.

In cases of combined disorders, they should be applied in their respective order; in cases of dual disorders, they should be mixed accordingly; and in cases arising from all three doshas, all measures should be employed.
Likewise, this applies to affusion, immersion, ointments, massages, and diet.
The holding of vessels filled with cold water,
as well as the practices of emesis, massage, sudation, fasting, and depleting therapies.
All preparations involving fats and the like are specifically prescribed;
likewise dried meat, radish, fish, dried vegetables, and pulses.
One suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) should not eat sweet fruits or tubers such as the potato;
for that pain which arises in the locations of the tumor even without a tumor is caused by these.
I shall describe its cause, its symptoms, and its treatment:
[it arises] from the suppression of flatus, urine, and feces, and from overeating.
From indigestion, overeating, fatigue, and the consumption of incompatible foods;
from drinking water at times of hunger, and from the consumption of sprouted grains;
From the consumption of flour-based foods and dried meat,
as well as from the use of other such substances, [the following occurs].
The wind (vāyu), aggravated within the abdominal cavity, produces intense colic;
afflicted by that pain, the man becomes breathless.
Because intense pains are experienced by one stuck on that [spit], like the bursting of a wooden pin,
it is therefore called a "śūla" (dart/pain) here.
When intense pain arises in one who has ceased eating,
his limbs become rigid and he breathes with great difficulty.
A person passes flatus, urine, and feces with difficulty;
by these symptoms, one should recognize colic arising from wind (vāta).
Thirst, burning heat, intoxication, fainting, and likewise intense pain occur;
he becomes desirous of cold and is relieved by cold itself.
By these signs one should recognize colic arising from pitta:
nausea arises in one who is being tormented by the colic.
Excessive fullness of the abdomen as well as heaviness of the limbs—
this is stated to be the diagnostic indication of colic arising from phlegm (kapha).
Having observed all the symptoms, one should designate it as a sannipātika [fever];
one should declare that fever arising from the combination of all three humors to be incurable.
The symptoms of colic pains have been declared; now learn from me their treatment.
For the wind (vāyu) acts with great speed; therefore, one should conquer it with haste.
For one afflicted by colic, sudation alone is a source of relief;
likewise, milk-rice, boluses of kṛśara, or unctuous meats are beneficial.
One should eat a meal that is unctuous and warm, prepared with the three-foliate śāka vegetable;
or alternatively, one may consume sprouts of cirabilva fried in oil.
One afflicted by colic (śūla) should consume unctuous meat juices of birds and wild animals,
as well as the flesh of burrow-dwelling creatures, according to their availability.
Wine, fermented gruel, sour gruel, whey, buttermilk, and curd,
taken with black salt, should be drunk in cases of colic arising from Vata.
A soup of horse gram (kulattha), prepared with sour ingredients, seasoned with the broth of common quail (lāvaka),
and containing rock salt and black pepper, destroys wind-related colic.
One should drink viḍaṅga, śigru, kampilla, pathyā, śyāmā,
amlavetasa, surasā, and aśvamūtrī, combined with sauvarcala salt.
Alcohol quickly pacifies colic born of Vāta.
[The following paste consists of: Pṛthvīkā, Jīraka, Cavya, Yavānī, Vyōṣa, and Citraka.
One should powder long pepper (pippalī), the root of long pepper (pippalīmūla), and rock salt (saindhava);
these powders should be drunk with milk or with kāmbalika wine.
With honey-wine (madhvāsava), sour gruel (cukra), wine (surā), or fermented barley-water (sauvīraka);
or else, these same powders may be taken with the juice of citron (mātuluṅga).
Likewise, one should drink those [seeds], which have been repeatedly infused with jujube (badara) decoction,
seasoned with asafoetida (hiṅgu), along with sugar.
A medicinal wick (varti) should be prepared with pomegranate marrow by the physician;
that wick quickly dispels colic caused by Vāta.
Alternatively, when colic arises from hunger, it is beneficial to consume a light nourishing diet after licking [the medicine] with jaggery and oil, or drinking it with wine.
When wind-pain (vāta-śūla) has arisen, one should treat it with warm milk, gruels (yavāgū), unctuous preparations, and likewise with meat broths;
one should nourish the patient with unctuous food.
Well-prepared offerings should be presented, especially *ghṛtapūra* cakes;
and if the person drinks *vāruṇī* liquor, he likewise becomes happy.
Thus has been described the treatment for colic arising from Vāta;
hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for that arising from Pitta.
Having vomited comfortably and drunk cold water,
that man should resort to all cooling things and avoid all hot things.
One should place vessels made entirely of jewels, silver, and copper,
filled with water, upon this stake.
Jaggery, śāli rice, barley, milk, the drinking of ghee, purgatives,
and the meat of wild animals are the remedies for those suffering from pitta-type colic.
One should consume tastes that pacify pitta and avoid those that increase it;
one may drink either a soup made from the leaves of the palāśa tree or a wild vegetable broth, mixed with sugar.
One should drink parūṣaka fruits, as well as grapes, dates, and those grown in water, combined with sugar; this alleviates pitta-type colic.
If a kapha-type disorder becomes aggravated immediately after eating,
the physician should induce emesis with water infused with long pepper (pippalī).
Dry sudation should be employed, as well as other heating treatments which are beneficial;
pippalī and ginger are the physician’s remedy for pain caused by kapha.
One should drink a broth made from pāṭhā, vacā, trikaṭu, and kaṭukarohiṇī,
along with arjaka, in a decoction of citraka.
The fruits and roots of castor, the root of gokṣuraka,
śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā;
One should give śṛgālavinnā and likewise sahadevā,
mahāsahā, kṣudrasahā, and the root of ikṣuraka.
Having collected these ingredients, one should boil them in a droṇa of water;
when reduced to a quarter part, one should drink it combined with yavakṣāra.
Whether it be caused by wind (vātika), bile (paittika), phlegm (ślaiṣmika), or a combination of all three (sānnipātika),
it forcibly destroys the pain, just as the wind scatters a broken cloud.
Having taken long pepper, the alkali of svarjika salt, barley, and citraka,
the wise man should prepare their ashes.
That [medicine], when drunk with warm water, is the physician’s remedy for phlegmatic colic;
for phlegm situated in the belly and the sides obstructs the vital air (vāyu).
Being thus obstructed, that man quickly experiences flatulence and a rumbling sound in the abdomen;
he suffers piercing pains as if from needles and breathes with great difficulty.
One who, afflicted by pain, desires neither food nor sleep,
should be known as suffering from pārśvaśūla (side-ache), which arises from kapha and vāta.
In that case, one should administer a powder made from Puṣkaramūla, Hiṅgu, Sauvarcala, Viḍa, Saindhava, Tumburu, and Pathyā.
In cases of pain in the sides, the heart, or the bladder, one should administer clarified butter mixed with a decoction of barley,
or the ghee prescribed for splenic enlargement (plīhodara), or ghee combined with asafoetida (hiṅgu).
Or the essence of citron fruit prepared with milk,
or castor oil, or liquor, curd-whey, milk, and the juice [of fruits].
One should also feed [the patient] with milk or with the broth of wild game when the wind (māruta),
having assailed the digestive fire, becomes aggravated in the abdomen.
Then, the food he has eaten does not digest properly due to that obstruction;
he breathes heavily with undigested feces and is repeatedly struck by sharp pains.
Neither on a seat nor on a bed, nor while standing, does one find comfort;
this is known as *kukṣiśūla*, arising from undigested food (*āmaja*) due to wind (*vāta*).
In that condition, one should administer emesis or induce fasting according to the patient's strength;
one should also perform digestive treatments for associated disorders using sour substances combined with digestive stimulants.
Nāgara, dīpyaka, cavya, hiṅgu, sauvarcala, viḍa,
the seeds of mātuluṅga, as well as those of śyāmā and urubūka.
One should drink a decoction of *bṛhatī* and *kaṇṭakārī*, which removes colic;
as well as *vacā*, *sauvarcala*, *hiṅgu*, *kuṣṭha*, *ativiṣā*, and *abhayā*.
The seeds of *kuṭaja* are indeed instant removers of colic;
one should employ them for purgation after having ascertained the relative strength and weakness of the *doṣas*.
One should administer oil enemas (snehabasti) and decoction enemas (nirūha) that eliminate the doshas,
as well as poultices (upanāha), oleation affusions (snehaseka), and sprinkling with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla).
Immersions are recommended, as are whatever other things are beneficial;
for when the wind (vāyu), obstructed by phlegm and bile, becomes saturated with the essence of food (rasa), [it causes disease].
When it resides in the heart, it produces a severe pain that obstructs the breath;
this condition, arising from the derangement of the rasa and vāta, is known as hṛcchūla (heart-pain).

In that regard as well, the action has been stated as follows: "Due to the suppression of those things that cause agitation of the heart, the provoked wind (vāyu), having enveloped the bladder, remains there."
Thereafter, a piercing pain arises for him in the bladder, groin, and navel;
obstructing feces, urine, and flatus, that is bladder-pain caused by Vāta.
When it obstructs the urine at the navel, the groins, the sides, the abdomen, or the penis,
causing pain in the intestines, that condition arising from Vāta is called Mūtraśūla.
When the wind is provoked in an embodied being who consumes dry food,
it obstructs the waste matter situated in the abdomen, having first weakened the digestive fire.
Indeed, producing intense pain and obstructing his channels,
it arises by seizing either the right or the left side of the abdomen.
Then, wandering everywhere with a roaring sound, it increases rapidly;
intense thirst grows, and dizziness and fainting arise.
If it is vomited and passed as urine, yet finds no relief,
the physician should recognize this as the most dreadful *viṭśūla*.
A physician who knows well must quickly perform the removal of the humors (doṣas) through sudation,
pacification, non-unctuous enemas, and unctuous enemas.
One should administer the previously mentioned formulations that cleanse the digestive tract,
as well as all other therapeutic measures that alleviate upward-moving wind (udāvarta), which bring about comfort for the patient.
When food is eaten in excess and the digestive fire has become weak, that food remains stagnant in the stomach,
and the vital air, becoming obstructed, stays there.
For food that has not undergone digestion causes intense colic,
as well as fainting, flatulence, burning sensations, nausea, and vilambikā.
One suffers purging, vomiting, trembling, and then fainting;
furthermore, a colic arising from the defects of food occurs due to indigestion.
Emesis, fasting, sudation, digestive stimulants,
medicinal suppositories, alkalis, powders, and pills are recommended for the destruction of colic pain.
For all those suffering from colic, medical treatments appropriate for the stage of *gulma* should be performed according to the rules.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter (the fourth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Gulma."
The forty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of heart disease (hṛdroga).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

By the suppression of natural urges, by the consumption of hot and dry foods in excessive amounts, by incompatible foods, eating before previous meals are digested, by indigestion, and by unwholesome or excessive eating;
When the humors (doṣas), having vitiated the vital essence (rasa) and become disordered, reach the heart, they cause affliction in the heart;
that is designated as heart disease (hṛdroga).
That [disease] is of four types, arising separately from the humors (doṣas) and from worms;
I shall describe its symptoms and the treatment immediately thereafter.
In a fever born of wind (vāta), the heart is stretched,
pierced, churned, torn asunder, burst open, and even split apart.
In the Pitta-type [fever], there may be thirst, burning heat, parching, exhaustion of the heart,
a sensation of fuming, fainting, perspiration, and dryness of the mouth.
Heaviness, expectoration of phlegm, loss of appetite, stiffness, weakness of the digestive fire,
and a sweet taste in the mouth occur when the heart is pervaded by balāsa (phlegm).
In the case of worms, there occurs nausea, spitting, pricking pain, colic, heartburn, darkness of vision,
loss of appetite, darkening of the eyes, and emaciation.
Dizziness, fatigue, exhaustion, and dryness should be known as their complications;
in the case of that born of worms, those symptoms which are considered characteristic of the types born of worms and of the kapha-type are present.
When the heart is afflicted by Vāta, one should cause the patient, who has been treated with oleation,
to vomit using a decoction of the two Pañcamūla groups mixed with unctuous substances and salt.
Long pepper, cardamom, sweet flag, asafoetida, barley ash, rock salt,
black salt, ginger, and ajamoda— all these should be made into a powder.
Once the patient has been purified, one should have them drink fruit-acid, sour gruel, horse gram, curd, wine, fermented liquors, or any other kind of unctuous substance.
One should feed him aged śāli rice with meat juices of wild animals prepared with ghee;
and one should administer an enema in the proper measure using oil processed with vāta-alleviating drugs.
One should induce vomiting with a decoction of śrīparṇī, madhuka, honey, white lotus, and water;
when the heart is afflicted by pitta, one should consume that which has been boiled with sweet drugs.
The physician should administer ghee and the aforementioned decoctions that destroy pitta-fever to one who has been satiated with excellent, sweet meat-juices mixed with ghee.

One should administer oil prepared with madhuka and mixed with honey into the enema (basti) for a heart disease caused by kapha; or, for one who has vomited after administering decoctions of vacā and nimba, [the same treatment should be applied].
One should cause the patient to drink the prescribed powder for the Vata-type [fever], and have him eat that [diet];
furthermore, the person should drink the Phaladi, Mustadi, or Triphala [decoctions].
Alternatively, a purgative consisting of ghee mixed with the paste of Śyāmā and Trivṛt should be administered;
furthermore, one skilled in enemas should apply an enema using Balā oils.

One suffering from heart disease caused by worms should be treated with oleation and then fed meat and rice along with curd and minced meat for three days; thereafter, one should administer a purgative.
Immediately thereafter, one should also have him drink fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) mixed with fragrant substances, salt, cumin, sugar, and a large quantity of viḍaṅga.
In this way, worms residing in the heart of men fall downward;
thereafter, one should give him barley-food along with viḍaṅga.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter (the fifth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Heart Disease."
The forty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
As the Blessed One Dhanvantari has said:
In one who excessively indulges in sexual intercourse, sour foods, salts, wine, clay, daytime sleep, and extremely pungent substances,
the humors (doṣas), having vitiated the blood, produce a pale discoloration on the skin.
Pāṇḍvāmaya is declared to be of four types, caused by the doṣas individually, collectively, or simultaneously;
and because the state of pallor (pāṇḍubhāva) is predominant in all of these, it is indeed called pāṇḍuroga.
Cracking of the skin, spitting, weakness of the limbs, eating earth, observing swelling on the forehead,
yellowish discoloration of the feces and urine, and indigestion— these are the premonitory symptoms of that which is about to occur.

That disease known as *kāmalā*, *pānaka*, *pāṇḍuroga*, *kumbha*, *lāgharaka* (or *lāghavaka*), and *alasākhya*—its complete characteristics are now explained; listen, for I shall describe them in due order.

One should diagnose a person as afflicted by Vāta when he has black eyes, is covered with black veins, and possesses black-colored feces, urine, nails, and face; furthermore, he is pale and possessed of other such complications.

One should diagnose a person as suffering from pāṇḍu caused by pitta when they have yellow eyes, are covered with yellow veins, and possess yellow-colored feces, urine, nails, and face, as well as being afflicted by other complications associated with that condition.

One should diagnose a person as having *pāṇḍu* due to *kapha* by observing white eyes, veins covered with white, and a complexion, stool, urine, nails, and face of that same color, as well as by the presence of other associated complications.
One should understand that all this exists within the universal self; now I shall describe the symptoms of jaundice (kāmalā).
For when a person at the end of an illness suddenly consumes sour food and unwholesome substances, his pitta [is provoked].
It makes the face especially pale, and causes excessive drowsiness and loss of strength on the preceding day;
its specific characteristic is indeed a swelling called *kumbhasāhva*, and in that condition there is a breaking pain in the joints.
Accompanied by fever, body ache, vertigo, exhaustion, drowsiness, and wasting, this condition known as *lāghavaka* (or *lāgharaka*) and designated as *alasa*—
which appears yellowish-green or blue due to the predominance of *vāta* and *pitta*— is called *halīmaka* by those who know it.
Their complications are: aversion to food, thirst, vomiting, fever, headache, loss of digestive fire, swelling in the throat, debility, fainting, exhaustion, and a pressing sensation in the heart.
Having examined the patient suffering from anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya) who has been oleated with ghee and purified through both emesis and purgation,
the physician should treat him with formulations consisting of powdered harītakī mixed with copious amounts of honey and ghee.
One should drink ghee processed with turmeric, or oil prepared with triphalā and trivṛt;
or one may drink preparations made from purgative substances, or purgative formulations combined with ghee.
Having boiled half a pala of nikumbha in urine, one should drink it frequently in a dose of half a kuḍava;
or one may eat jaggery cooked with abhayā, or drink a decoction of the āragvadhādi group.

One should lick a powder of iron filings, trikaṭu, and viḍaṅga, or haridrā combined with triphalā, mixed with ghee and honey; or one may also employ the formulations prescribed in the relevant sections of the medical treatises.
One should eliminate the humors (doṣas) many times in small quantities, for if the humors are expelled in excess, one may suffer from swelling;
therefore, while eating wholesome food, one should drink the juice of *dhātrī* fruits, sugarcane juice, or a churned drink (*mantha*) mixed with honey.
Having boiled both types of *bṛhatī*, *rajanī*, *śukākhyā*, *kākādanī*, along with *kākamācī*,
*ādārī*, *bimbī*, and *kadambapuṣpī*, one should cook ghee in that decoction.
When used, it destroys that paleness, or alternatively, Magadhika taken with milk according to one's digestive fire;
and one should lick a decoction or powder of Yaṣṭīmadhuka mixed with honey, or both in equal parts.
Having administered iron powder mixed with cow’s urine along with the leaves of *triphalā* for a considerable time,
one should likewise lick the powder of coral, pearl, collyrium, and conch-shell, as well as that derived from golden ochre.
One *kuḍava* measure of goat dung, along with *viḍa* salt, turmeric, and the best of salts (*sauvarcala*)—
each weighing one *pala*— this entire powder should be licked with honey by one who eats wholesome food.
This electuary, consisting of equal parts of maṇḍūra, iron, agni, viḍaṅga, pathyā, and vyoṣa, with an amount of tāpya equal to the whole mixture,
processed in urine and taken with honey, destroys even severe anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya) in a short time.
A bolus prepared from the powders of *bibhītaka*, iron filings, and *nāgara*, along with sesame seeds and primarily jaggery,
taken with buttermilk as an after-drink, destroys even the most severe cases of jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*).
One should lick sauvarcala salt, hiṅgu, and kirātatikta, each in the measure of a kalāya, with warm water;
or one should lick mūrvā, haridrā, and āmalaka, which have been kept for seven days in cow urine.
One afflicted by jaundice (pāṇḍu-roga), while adhering to a wholesome diet, should drink one akṣa each of the roots of balā and citraka;
or, one who subsists on milk should consume the fruit of śigru mixed with an equal amount of salt and warm water.
One who eats wholesome food should drink the cooled decoction of the Nyagrodha group mixed with sugar and honey;
or else, one should lick the powder of the heartwood of the Śāla group or Āmalaka fruit with honey.
Having made powders of viḍaṅga, musta, triphalā, ajamoda, parūṣaka, vyoṣa, and vinirdahanī,
as well as jaggery, sugar, ghee, honey, and the two auspicious [substances], [one should administer them].
Having prepared this medicinal compound in water infused with heartwood from a tree of excellent quality,
the wise man, recognizing that it has reached the consistency of a paste, should place it in a casket made of mokṣaka wood.
Indeed, this electuary destroys anemia (pāṇḍuroga) along with swelling, as well as even severe jaundice (kāmalā).
For those suffering from jaundice, Tribhaṇḍī with sugar, Gavākṣī with jaggery, and Śuṇṭhī are beneficial.
Ghee cooked with kāleyaka and mixed with turmeric (rajanī) is also beneficial;
or, in the case of kumbha, one should drink mercury (dhātu), realgar (nadīja), lac (jatu), or bitumen (śailaja) combined with cow's urine.
Or indeed, one may drink iron rust (loha-kiṭṭa) mixed with rock salt, kept in urine for a month;
or one may drink iron dross that has been burnt with Akṣa wood and quenched in cow's urine eight times.
Having powdered it and licked it with honey, it quickly destroys Kumbha-type jaundice;
or likewise, having made rock salt as hot as fire and cast it once into urine while it is boiling hot.
Having repeatedly heated iron dross and likewise repeatedly quenched it in urine,
one should combine these, grind them with cow’s urine, and cook the resulting mixture together in a cauldron.
One should drink that [powder] thoroughly dried and pulverized with buttermilk so that it does not burn;
by eating rice with buttermilk, one shall conquer the disease of jaundice and likewise kindle the digestive fire.
Ghee prepared with the juices of grapes, guḍūcī, and āmalakī is beneficial for lāghavaka (lightness/convalescence).
Likewise, one should consume gauda-ariṣṭas, honey-sugar preparations, urine-based asavas, and those made from alkalis.

A patient suffering from jaundice should regularly consume unctuous juices mixed with āmalaka or kola fruits, as well as the meat of wild animals; he should also follow the formulations prescribed for swelling and consume śāli rice and barley daily.
One should overcome dyspnea, diarrhea, anorexia, cough, fainting, thirst, vomiting, colic, fever, edema, burning sensations,
as well as indigestion, hoarseness, and malaise, by carefully consulting the scriptures and applying the appropriate remedies for each.
Swelling at the extremities with the middle diminished, or likewise with the extremities faded and the middle swollen;
swelling of the anus, the penis, and the scrotum; and fainting, as if losing consciousness.
One who desires fame should avoid a patient suffering from jaundice, as well as one afflicted by diarrhea and fever.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter (the sixth from the beginning), titled "The Treatment of Anemia," within the Section on Internal Medicine of the Uttaratantra in the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The forty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Anger, grief, fear, fatigue, incompatible food,
sunlight, fire, pungent, sour, salty, alkaline, sharp, hot, and excessively burning things;
Constantly consumed, the corrupted taste provokes the pitta;
the vitiated pitta, by its own qualities, quickly causes the blood to burn.
Thereupon the blood flows upwards, downwards, or in both directions;
it proceeds upwards from the stomach (āmāśaya) and downwards from the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya).
The flow of blood from two inflamed [organs] proceeds in two directions;
some authorities declare that its course originates from the liver and the spleen.
The upward-moving [vāyu] is curable, the downward-moving is suppressible, and that which moves simultaneously is incurable.
[Its symptoms are] exhaustion, a desire for cold, a sensation of smoke rising from the throat, and vomiting.
In this condition, the breath acquires an iron-like odor;
through external signs such as the appearance of blood, the wise recognize its number, defects, and increase.
Weakness, dyspnea, cough, fever, vomiting, intoxication, lassitude, burning sensations, fainting, a burning sensation after eating, constant instability, and pain in the heart as if from a blow;
thirst, hoarseness of the throat, heaviness in the head, spitting of foul matter, aversion to food, indigestion, and loss of sexual desire—these are the complications of *raktapitta*.

That which resembles the washing of flesh, or appears as if boiled, or like muddy water; that which is similar to fat, pus, or blood; or like liver, or has the luster of a ripe jambū fruit; that which is black or blue, excessively putrid, or where such morbid changes are described—that rakta-pitta is to be avoided, as is that which shines like the bow of the Lord of the Gods (Indra).
Blood that is excessive should not be drawn at the outset from a strong person who is eating;
for that [blood-letting] brings about anemia, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors (gulma), and fever.

One should conquer blood that has flowed downward with emetics, and that which moves upward with purgatives; or, in the case of a weakened patient, one should treat it with palliative measures according to whichever of the two [channels] is affected.
In one whose humors (doṣas) have become excessively aggravated and who suffers from internal hemorrhage (lohitapitta),
depleting therapy (apatarpaṇa) should first be administered, provided that his strength, muscle mass, and digestive fire (agni) have not diminished.
After the patient has undergone the leaping therapy (laṅghana), one should then prescribe thin gruel (peyā) with a very small amount of rice;
meat broth and vegetable soup, prepared with fragrant substances and fats, should be administered,
along with various types of satiating drinks, digestive elixirs, linctuses, and medicated ghees.
A purgative combined with grapes, licorice, kāśmarya, and sugar is beneficial,
as is an emetic combined with liquorice and honey.
Cool waters, the juices of wild animals, wholesome soups, rice and sixty-day grain;
and [preparations] derived from patola, śelu, suniṣaṇṇaka, yūthikā, vaṭa, sprouts of atimukta, and sinduvāra.
Beneficial vegetables prepared with ghee, likewise accompanied by emblic myrobalan and pomegranate,
as well as broths made from pigeon, conch, and tortoise, and gruels prepared with an abundance of ghee, are always prescribed.
Barley gruel prepared with milk processed with the *utpala* group of drugs is recommended, as are those enriched with honey and sugar;
likewise, cold poultices, the sweet groups of drugs, medicated ghees, and wholesome diets are beneficial for those suffering from *raktapitta*.

A skilled physician should prepare four honeyed electuaries (lehas) for the benefit of the patient and for the pacification of hemorrhage, using the powdered flowers of Madhuka, Śobhāñjana, Kovidāra, and Priyaṅgu.
One should lick the tender leaves of dūrvā grass, the vaṭa tree, and the white karṇikāra flower, accompanied by honey;
likewise, dates mixed with honey are beneficial, as are other fruits possessing similar qualities.
One should also employ here the formulations prescribed for blood-dysentery;
having crushed a pure stalk of sugarcane in a new jar with cold water, [one should use it].
Having prepared it, one should throw that [mixture] along with blue lotuses into the sky at night;
in the morning, the patient suffering from raktapitta (hemorrhagic disease) should drink what has flowed down, combined with honey.
Or one should drink a cold decoction derived from the jambu, mango, and arjuna trees;
or, having ground the fruit of the udumbara tree, one should drink its juice.
One should drink either a paste of cucumber and radish with honey and rice-water,
or a paste of liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka) in the measure of one akṣa.
One should likewise drink equal parts of candana, madhuka, and rodhra;
or one may drink karanja seeds combined with sugar and honey.
One should drink the marrow of the iṅguda fruit mixed with madhuka in this manner;
likewise, one may drink the seeds of the karañja tree, salted and made lukewarm, along with the whey of curd.
Or a mortal afflicted by raktapitta may drink it for three days;
these six excellent formulations are praised as the best remedies for curing raktapitta.
In cases of excessive bleeding from the nose, one should employ wholesome errhines (avapīḍa);
or, if the blood flows excessively, one should drink blood mixed with honey;
or one may consume raw goat's liver combined with bile.
One should drink ghee prepared by cooking it in the fresh juice of the Palāśa tree, well-cooled and mixed with honey;
or one may drink milk and ghee processed with the fresh juices of various trees, combined with sugar.

One should throw one pala each of raisins, uśīra, padmaka, and sugar into water and let it stand overnight; when drunk by one who eats wholesome food, this—either with milk or mixed with an equal amount of water—conquers blood diseases.
One should drink the fresh juice of the horse-gram (*turaṅgavarcas*) with honey, or that of the *vṛṣa* plant mixed with sugar and honey;
likewise, one should lick the powder of *vāstuka* seeds or of *taṇḍulīyaka* combined with honey.
One should lick either parched grain mixed with the powder of añjana alone, or likewise tugākhyā combined with sugar and honey;
or else, one may take grapes, sugar, and tiktarohiṇī, or madhuka, with cold water.
A patient suffering from raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders) should likewise lick pathyā, ahiṃsrā, rajanī, and ghee at night.
[One should also employ] a decoction of vāsā, utpala, mṛttikā, priyaṅgu, rodhra, añjana, and the filaments of ambhoruha.

Having drunk [the decoctions] of gāyatrī, jambu, arjuna, kovidāra, śirīṣa, rodhra, aśana, and śālmalī combined with sugar and honey, one shall quickly abandon the violent onset of bile-born hemorrhaging.
The flowers of the *śigru* tree, ground into a powder and taken as a linctus with honey, [cures] the disease of *rakta-pitta*.
Likewise, the ash of the *indīvara* mixed with water and honey, *karañja* seeds, or honey and clarified butter [are effective].

Water boiled with *jambu*, *arjuna*, and *āmra*—these three combinations destroy *pitta* and blood disorders. One should also drink the roots and flowers of the *mātuluṅgī* ground together with rice-wash water.
If the nosebleed persists, water mixed with sugar should be given quickly, or milk through the nostrils;
alternatively, one should drink grape juice, milk, ghee, sugared sugarcane juice, or cold water with sugar.
In cases of blood-bile (rakta-pitta) disease, one should especially provide cooling treatments that are sweet in nature,
prepared with *vidārigandhādi* [drugs] boiled together with grapes, ghee, honey, and sugar.
Non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) with milk is declared the foremost, and ghee is beneficial for the purpose of unctuous enema (anuvāsana),
prepared with priyaṅgu, rodhra, añjana, gairika, utpala, suvarṇa, kālīyaka, and red sandalwood.

Having administered a Nirūha enema with milk mixed with honey and saturated with ghee— prepared from white Aśvagandhā, Ambuda, Yaṣṭikāhvaya, Mṛṇāla, and Saugandhika, ground together in equal proportions— he should then be sprinkled with cold water.
One should then feed him milk-rice and administer an unctuous enema with ghee prepared with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhu).
This will eliminate the downward-flowing blood as well as difficult-to-cure dysentery of blood.
In the case of excessive purgation, emesis is indeed recommended; and when blood has been conquered, one who is endowed with strength [should be treated].
Such measures as the *uttarabasti* should be administered when blood is located in the bladder;
furthermore, in cases of hemorrhoids with active bleeding, one should indeed apply the treatment prescribed for *raktapitta*.
This same procedure should be performed by a knowledgeable physician for women suffering from menorrhagia,
as well as for those who bleed excessively following surgical intervention.
Having observed the symptoms of all three humors as well as those present entirely in the blood, the medical treatment must be administered immediately thereafter.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter (the seventh in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Raktapitta."
The forty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment for fainting (mūrcchā).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

In one who is emaciated, whose humors are greatly aggravated, who consumes incompatible food, or who, having suppressed natural urges, suffers a physical injury or possesses diminished vital strength; |||
When the fierce humors enter the sense organs, both external and internal, then human beings fall into a swoon.

Pain in the heart, yawning, exhaustion, loss of consciousness, and loss of strength—these are the premonitory symptoms of all [the fevers]; one should recognize them according to their respective [causes].
When the channels that carry perception are blocked by the vital airs and other humors,
darkness suddenly overcomes one, bringing about the cessation of both pleasure and pain.
Due to the removal of pleasure and pain, a person falls like a piece of wood;
they say that delusion (moha) swoons there, and it is proclaimed to be of six kinds.
In all six of these— wind and the others, blood, wine, and poison—
it is indeed pitta that prevails by its predominance.
The symptoms of those [seizures] have been truly described as being identical to those stated for epilepsy (apasmāra).
Earth and water are of the nature of tamas, and blood has that [tamas] as its essence.
Therefore, human beings on earth faint from the scent of blood;
some maintain that this is due to the inherent nature of substances, as in the case of poison and wine.
Since the qualities (guṇas) exist in a state of extreme intensity in both poison and liquor,
delusion arises from them in the manner described.
Lamenting through intoxication, with his mind ruined and bewildered,
he lies tossing his limbs upon the ground until he reaches old age.
Trembling, sleepiness, thirst, and rigidity occur when one is poisoned and unconscious;
it should be understood that these are more intense according to the specific characteristics of the poison involved.
Immersion in water, gems with their strings, cooling plasters, the breeze from fans,
and fragrant cooling drinks— these are prescribed without exception for all types of fainting.
Drinks prepared with sugar, milk, and sugarcane juice, combined with the fresh juices of grapes and madhūka,
boiled with the juices of dates and kāśmarya, as well as life-sustaining medicated ghees (sarpis).
In the category of sweet [tastes], milk and the juices of wild animals prepared with pomegranate are always proven effective;
likewise, barley, red śāli rice, and satīna peas are always wholesome in cases of fainting.

One should drink equal parts of *bhujaṅgapuṣpa*, black pepper, *uśīra*, and the pulp of *kola* with cold water; likewise, one may take *bisā* and *mṛṇāla* with honey, or *kṛṣṇā* with sugar, or *pathyā*.
One should not obstruct her nose or mouth, nor should she drink the milk of human women;
however, if fainting persists, one should overcome it with frequent head-purgatives (śirovireka) and sharp emetics.
Ghee boiled with a decoction of harītakī, or ghee prepared with the fresh juices of āmalaka fruits;
or [drinks] that are cool, containing grapes, sugar, pomegranate, and parched grain, along with blue and red lotuses.
One should drink fragrant decoctions which pacify Pitta-fever;
however, he whose humors are excessive and who is overwhelmed by an abundance of darkness (tamas) does not awaken from his stupor at all.
O men, one whose consciousness has thus been cast away should be known by the wise as being extremely difficult to treat;
he is like a raw lump of clay dropped into water that dissolves instantly upon being lifted out.
In that same way, the best of physicians should treat with haste one who has not sweated and is approaching the power of death,
using applications of sharp collyrium, ointments, and medicinal smoke, as well as by striking with sharp instruments beneath the nails.

One who does not regain consciousness despite unprecedented musical performances, songs, conciliatory words, physical manipulations, and the rubbing of secret parts with fruits, and who merely snorts, drools, and pants, should be abandoned.
Once the patient has regained consciousness, been purified by sharp emetics and purgatives, and has eaten light, wholesome food,

one should treat him for a month with preparations of the three fruits (triphalā), citraka, and ginger, as well as with applications of mineral pitch (śilājatu) mixed with sugar; in particular, he should be made to drink aged ghee.
One should administer appropriate decoctions that alleviate fever,
and for those overcome by all types of fainting, one should use anti-toxic remedies in cases of fainting caused by poison.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter (the eighth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Syncope."
The forty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment for the disorders resulting from excessive drinking (pānātyaya).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Alcohol is hot, sharp, subtle, clear, dry,
quick-acting, pervasive, and expansive.
Due to its heat, it counteracts cold; due to its sharpness, it destroys the movement of the mind;
due to its subtlety, it enters the minute parts [of the body]; and due to its clarity, it destroys phlegm and semen.
Due to its dryness and rapidity, it provokes the wind (māruta) and performs swift actions;
due to its exhilarating nature and expansive quality, it spreads throughout the body.
That is declared to be sour in taste, light, appetizing, and digestive-stimulant;
indeed, some authorities prescribe all tastes here except for the salty.
When consumed together with unctuous foods, meats, and edibles,
it leads to the prolongation of life, as well as to strength and physical growth.
Desirability, satisfaction of the mind, fortitude, splendor, and great prowess—
these qualities are present when wine is consumed according to the prescribed rules.
That very same food, when consumed by an ignorant person without moderation,
produces intoxication upon meeting with the fire of the stomach, which is itself like fire.
When intoxication causes a transformation of the senses,
one is rendered powerless and reveals even one's own hidden disposition.
Intoxication (mada) should be understood as having three stages: initial, middle, and final. In the initial stage, there is an increase in vigor, pleasure, attachment, joy, and talkativeness.
In the middle state there is delirious speech and delusion regarding what is appropriate and inappropriate action;
in the final state, one lies unconscious, with the qualities of action and performance lost.

Drinking does not cause excessive affliction for those who have a predominance of phlegm (śleṣman), little bile (pitta), who are unctuous, and who consume [liquids] in moderation; however, it afflicts those whose constitution is the opposite.
If liquor is consumed constantly by a person in a state of total abstinence,
it will produce most grievous disorders and may even bring about the dissolution of the body.
By one who is angry, afraid, thirsty, tormented by grief, or hungry;
by one exhausted by physical exertion, heavy loads, or travel; and even by one afflicted by the suppression of natural urges.
When consumed by one whose stomach is distended with excessive food and unwholesome edibles, who has eaten before the previous meal is digested, who is weak,
and who is scorched by heat, liquor produces various disorders.
I shall now describe the symptoms of excessive drinking (pānātyaya), extreme intoxication (paramada), indigestion from alcohol (pānājīrṇa), and the severe disorder of drinking (pānavibhrama).
In alcoholism caused by vāta, there is stiffness, limb pain, cardiac distress, palpitations, tremors, and headaches;
in that caused by pitta, there is sweating, delirium, dryness of the mouth, burning sensations, fainting, and yellowness of the face and eyes.
In a fever of the phlegmatic type, there is vomiting, coldness, and excessive salivation; when all three humors are involved, there is a combination of all these symptoms.
There is a burning sensation, heaviness of the limbs, a distaste in the mouth, an excess of phlegm, loss of appetite, and retention of feces and urine.
Those who know the truth say that the signs of excessive intoxication are thirst and pain in the head, as well as a splitting sensation in the joints.
They say that flatulence, belching, a sour taste, and a burning sensation are the signs of indigestion caused by drinking.
In that regard, the physician should recognize with certainty the symptoms produced by the provocation of pitta:
pricking pain in the heart and limbs, nausea, fever, a sensation of smoke in the throat, fainting, discharge of phlegm, headache, and a burning sensation.
The wise declare that aversion toward various kinds of wine, food, and their derivatives constitutes the entirety of the disorder of drinking.
One who has been destroyed by excessive drinking—characterized by a sunken upper lip, extreme coldness, intense burning, and an oily luster of the eyes—should be abandoned.
One whose tongue, lips, and teeth are blackish or even blue, whose eyes are yellow and who discharges blood,
and who suffers from hiccups, fever, vomiting, trembling, pain in the flanks, cough, and vertigo— such a person is afflicted by alcohol.
Listen now in its entirety to this method being declared by me for their prevention, with its explicit terminology:
liquor mixed with *cukra*, black pepper, fresh ginger, *dīpyaka*, *kuṣṭha*, and *sauvarcala* salt is sufficient for the pacification of wind (*vāta*).
For the sake of comfort, one should administer [the medicine] combined with pṛthvīkā, dīpyaka, mahauṣadha, hiṅgu, and sauvarcala salt;
and one should also prepare auspicious ṣaḍava drinks using āmrātaka, mango fruit, pomegranate, and mātuluṅga.
One should consume soups and other liquids mixed with fruit juices, as well as fragrant meats from marshy regions;
in cases of a pitta constitution, wine mixed with the sweet group of substances and astringents, along with honey, sugar, and pleasant scents, is beneficial.
Having drunk wine thoroughly saturated with sugarcane juice until it is completely finished, one should wait for a moment and then vomit it up.
For the sake of comfort, one should drink the meat-broths of quail, deer, and partridge that are not sour, as well as soups made of mung beans mixed with ghee and sugar.
In the event of intoxication caused by phlegm (kapha), one should induce vomiting with wine mixed with the water of *bimba* and *vidula* fruits;
for the sake of recovery, one should consume excellent soups of bitter and pungent tastes, as well as broths seasoned with bitter and pungent ingredients.

One should prescribe barley-based foods and preparations, meat from wild animals, and whatever else is Kapha-subduing and harmless. Furthermore, in cases arising from all three Doshas (Sannipāta), one should apply the treatment for each; in cases arising from two Doshas (Dvandvaja), one should observe both and act according to whichever is predominant.
I shall now describe another general formula which is complete and foremost, as well as that which produces exhilaration for the mind and provides pleasure:
take equal parts of *tvak*, *nāgapuṣpa*, *magadhaila*, *madhūka*, *dhānya*, *ślakṣṇa*, *jīraka*, and *marica*.
In cases of intoxication from excessive drinking, one should duly offer a drink consisting of wood-apple juice, water, and emblic myrobalan, strained through a cloth;
and having anointed [the patient] with flowers of *hrīvera*, lotus, *paripelava*, *karavīra*, and aquatic species.
One should also administer sprinklings with pure, very cold water mixed with the powders of padmaka, sārivā, and other [herbs], combined with cinnamon-bark,
leaves, bamboo-skin, black pepper, elā, tagara, the flower of śleṣmātaka, and jaggery.
Grape juice that has been strained to remove impurities should be consumed by those afflicted by alcoholism; it is pure and fragrant and fit for human use.
Furthermore, one should repeatedly drink a paste made of madhuka, kaṭurohiṇī, grapes, and the root of trapuṣī.
Having drunk equal parts of *kārpāsinī*, *nāgabalā*, and *suvarcalā*, one becomes well;
likewise, there is the refreshing drink prepared with water from *kāśmarya*, *dāru*, *viḍa*, *dāḍima*, *pippalī*, and *drākṣā*.
When drunk quickly with the juice of *bījapūraka*, it brings about supreme peace very soon in cases of *paramada*.
Likewise, one should drink [the powder] prepared from grapes, sugar, *madhuka*, cumin, coriander, and black pepper, along with *trivṛt*.
An abundant sprinkling with water boiled with Bhārgī, mixed with Sauvarcala salt, sour fruit juices, and a generous amount of broth, is beneficial.

Having boiled the seeds of *ikṣvāku*, *dhāmārgava*, and *vṛkṣaka*, along with *kākāhvā* and *udumbarikā*, one should drink it from the hollow of the hand; one should drink the liquor when the day has passed and [the previous meal] is not yet digested.
One should consume sour fruits combined with asafoetida, black pepper, cardamom, and *viḍa* salt, along with cinnamon, long pepper, *bhujaṅgapuṣpa*, and *viḍa*.
Alternatively, one may take *viḍa*, cinnamon, *cavya*, cardamom, asafoetida, long pepper, long pepper root, and dry ginger, mixed with hot water and rock salt.
In this case, a meal consisting of palatable meats is recommended, as well as a beverage made from grapes, wood-apples, and pomegranates;
furthermore, a drink enriched with honey and sugar, or a juice-drink made from āmrātaka and kola fruits, removes the complications arising from excessive drinking.

One should drink these— prepared from dates, rattan, karīra, and parūṣaka, along with grapes and trivṛt, mixed with sugar, or as a cold infusion— or else one may drink them combined with śrīparṇī, mixed with liquorice, blue lotus, and cold water.
Milk, sprouts, lotus root, cumin, nagapuṣpa, patra, elavāluka, white sārivā, padmaka;
āmrātaka, bhavya, karamarda, kapittha, kola, vṛkṣāmla, vetra-fruit, jīraka, and pomegranate.

Or one may consume meat juices prepared with black pepper, cumin, nagapuṣpa, cinnamon, cardamom, ginger, long pepper, and elā; when these fragrant-smelling juices have been strained through fine cloth and cooled, they dispel all seven types of diseases arising from drinking without exception.
Objects of the five senses, served with mild drinks, pleasing and always agreeable to the mind, should be enjoyed;
likewise, women with broad thighs and hips, whose waists are bent by the weight of their full and elevated breasts, should be attended to in cases of alcoholism.
Mature women with limbs full of fresh youth, who are to be enjoyed and whose very nature consists of the excellence of the five sense-objects.
One should drink the juice derived from flowers or fruits, combined with sugar, madhūka, and the three aromatics (trisaugandhya),
having ground and mixed them together with equal parts of nāgakeśara, cumin, long pepper, and black pepper.
One desiring well-being should stir together varṣābhū, yaṣṭyāhva, madhūka, lakṣā, the bark of karbudāra, sprouts of jīraka, drākṣā, kṛṣṇā, and keśara in milk, and then drink it.

If one has been cast down by the excessive drinking of any intoxicant, such as liquor or spirits, one should cause that very substance to be administered to him according to the prescribed rule; otherwise, he will certainly suffer ruin.
Just as someone who has been struck down by a king might find favor through that very person and no other,
so too a living being struck down by liquor will surely find favor through that very thing and no other.
For one who has suddenly indulged in excessive intoxication after abstaining from liquor,
the disorders specified under the heading of *pānātyaya* (alcoholism) indeed arise.
The fiery (āgneya) and airy (vāyavya) qualities of alcohol dry up the water-carrying channels;
by that means, thirst is produced.
One should drink water cooled by ice, prepared with the roots of pāṭala and utpala, along with mudgaparṇī and mixed with māgadhikā.
Combined with ghee, oil, muscle fat, marrow, curd, and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*,
along with a decoction of *bilva* and barley, and ground with all the fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*).
Cooked [medicinal substances] are best for massage, while a cold decoction is best for sprinkling;
one should also administer flavorful foods according to their respective requirements.

Drinks that are very cold, pleasing to the heart, and fragrant [are beneficial]. However, when the heat of the drink reaches the skin, being intensified by the combination of pitta and blood, it produces a terrible burning sensation; in that case, the remedy is the same as for pitta disorders.
Henceforth, I shall describe the cooling regimen that brings peace to the burning sensations of accomplished men;
therein, first of all, an application of sandalwood paste—cool as moonbeams, pearl necklaces, and snow-water—is beneficial.
While he lies thus, let the women touch him with necklaces cooled by cold water and bracelets of lotus stalks;
or let him lie upon a bed bright with blooming blue lotuses and frost, or upon the leaves of the lotus-plant dripping with water-drops.
Inhaling the breeze brought by women, being caressed by the lovely forest breezes amidst clusters of white and red lotuses and water-moss,
he shall be able to wander through the palace groves and long ponds.
Or, if overcome by burning sensations, one should sprinkle [the patient] with waters of *lāmajjaka*, lotus, and sandalwood;
or with water that has been strained and cleared of impurities, filled with fresh water, containing the waters of lotuses and blue lilies, and infused with fragrant scents.
Adorned with yellow sandalwood paste, his body’s pores bristling from the rough touch of his beloved’s hands, he should frequent the pond;
there, women shall touch him with their cool lotus-petal-like faces, thighs, and firm breasts.

when exhausted, he should lie down in a fountain-house that resembles a dark, rainy day, its interior cooled by the spray of water and breezes.
