one should sleep— recollecting the Hemanta season, the Vindhya, Himavat, and Malaya mountains, their cool waters, and their verdant trees with plantain groves.
One should listen to delightful stories of the rising moon and of lakes filled with blossoming blue and white lotuses—

stories that are pleasing to the mind for one whose heart is withered and dejected— as well as [the company of] women with full breasts, thighs, and hips, their limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood paste.
Then those weak women, with their garments wet and their girdles and strings of pearls loosened, should lie down together with him, embracing him closely.
Women situated in private may delight a man with their own qualities;
through their coolness, they may also pacify the internal excess of bile caused by drinking.
This therapeutic regimen should be employed for thirst, burning sensations, and raktapitta; now hear in detail the specific treatment for all types of burning sensations without exception.
When the blood, pervading the entire body, becomes excessively aggravated, it indeed causes a burning sensation;
the patient feels as if being sucked dry and burned, appearing copper-colored with copper-colored eyes.
With his limbs and face smelling of iron, he is as if scorched by fire;
having overcome that state through the prescribed method, one should partake of mixed food.
If the burning sensation does not subside even when the patient is satiated with meat juices from wild animals,
one should duly puncture the *rohiṇī* veins located in the extremities.
It is like a fever caused by pitta, and the treatment prescribed for that [fever] is beneficial for this [condition] as well;
for when the watery element is diminished due to the suppression of thirst, the internal heat (tejas) becomes excessively aggravated.
Indeed, one of dull intellect burns the body both internally and externally;
with his throat, palate, and lips completely parched, he moves about, having thrust out his tongue.
In that case, one should pacify the fiery element (tejas) and increase the watery element (ap-dhātu);
one should drink water as desired, or even milk enriched with sugar.
If one follows the prescribed procedure, one should administer cold sugarcane juice or a churned drink (mantha);
for one whose abdominal cavity is filled with blood, an unbearable burning sensation occurs.
The procedure and its symptoms have been described in the chapter on acute wounds (sadyovraṇīya).
The burning sensation mentioned in the context of the depletion of the bodily tissues (dhātu-kṣaya) is accompanied by fainting and thirst.
One whose voice is weak, who has failed in his activities, and who suffers greatly from affliction,
should be treated with the regimen for raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders) that is unctuous and pacifies vāyu.
Another, while eating or even while grieving in many ways, consumes his own blood;
by that he is intensely consumed within, afflicted with thirst, fainting, and delirium.
Provided with desired objects and surrounded by friends,
he should prepare a diet of milk, meat, and broth according to the prescribed rule.
There is also that which arises from injury to a vital point (marman), and that is considered most incurable;
indeed, all [types] should be rejected in embodied beings whose limbs are cold.
One who is afflicted by such a disease as alcoholism should undergo purification even when the complications have subsided.
Liquors containing cumin, ginger, *ārdraka*, *śṛṅgavera*, and *sauvarcala* salt, soaked in half their volume of water—
being heart-pleasing and fragrant— immediately quench thirst when drunk.
One who is immersed in water, whose limbs are adorned with sandalwood paste, and who wears a garland, may drink liquor accompanied by meat as a side dish along with devotion;
such a person will certainly not incur diseases, nor will his mind be disturbed, nor will he fall into intoxication.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter (the ninth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Alcoholism."
The forty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the prevention of thirst (tṛṣṇā-pratiṣedha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
One who constantly drinks water yet finds no satisfaction,
and who craves water once more, should be designated as one afflicted by thirst.
Due to agitation, grief, fatigue, and the drinking of alcohol; from the excessive use of dry, sour, parched, hot, and pungent substances;
from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu), fasting, and exposure to the heat of the sun—both pitta and vāta become greatly increased.
For when the two [wind and bile] together vitiate those channels of embodied beings that carry water, then,
because the water-carrying channels have been corrupted, an exceedingly powerful thirst arises.
Three types are traditionally recognized; the fourth arises from injury (kṣataja), another from wasting (kṣaya), and the sixth from undigested matter (āma).
Know now the seventh to be that caused by food (bhakta-nimitta); learn their symptoms in due order.
Dryness and burning of the palate, lips, throat, and mouth, along with feverish heat, delusion, vertigo, and incoherent speech—
these are the premonitory symptoms that especially appear at the time of their onset.
In the condition arising from Vāta, there is dryness of the mouth as well as a pricking pain in the temples and the head;
there is obstruction of the channels, a bad taste in the mouth, and the symptoms increase with cold water.
Fainting, delirium, loss of appetite, dryness of the mouth, yellowness of the eyes, constant burning sensation,
a desire for cold things, bitterness in the mouth, and a feeling of being enveloped in smoke— these are the symptoms of the Pitta-type [fever].
When the wind (vāyu) and fire (agni) are obstructed by phlegm (kapha), the phlegm itself becomes dried up and produces thirst;
one afflicted by this condition experiences drowsiness, heaviness, and a sweet taste in the mouth, and becomes excessively parched.

In the kaphaja type, there is a coating of the throat, sliminess of the mouth, cold fever, vomiting, and loss of appetite; furthermore, there is heaviness of the limbs, swelling in the extremities, and indigestion. These are its symptoms; one afflicted by it desires water but does not drink it.
The fourth type of thirst is considered to be born of injury (kṣatajā), arising from both the pain of a wound and the loss of blood;
for one overcome by it, days and nights pass in suffering even while drinking water.

That which arises from the depletion of the bodily fluids (rasa) is considered "born of depletion" (kṣayaja); one afflicted by it withers and feels a burning sensation, and moreover, craves water excessively. Some say that this [condition] arises from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta).
The physician should diagnose that condition in its entirety by the symptoms described for the depletion of the bodily fluids (rasakṣaya);
it possesses the signs of the three doṣas, arises from undigested matter (āma), and is accompanied by chest pain, spitting, and loss of voice.
Likewise, the consumption of unctuous, sour, salty, or heavy food causes excessive thirst;
one should quickly avoid a patient who is emaciated, unconscious, deaf, afflicted by thirst, or whose tongue has protruded.
When thirst has increased and the stomach is full, one should induce vomiting with water mixed with māgadhikā;
in this case, it is beneficial to provide appetizers made from pomegranate, āmrātaka, and mātuluṅga.
In this case, the three [doshas] should be properly restrained through applications consisting of substances possessing cold rasa and vīrya;
furthermore, when the mouth has lost its natural taste, one should perform gargles with sour liquids and with the auspicious powders of āmalaka.
One should quench thirst with lukewarm water made from gold, silver, or the like heated by fire, or with clods of earth, or with sand and such; or one may use cold water mixed with sugar and honey.
Regarding the five groups of five-fold formulations that have been described, if water is prepared with the first group,
a person who drinks it lukewarm will indeed be freed from thirst born of wind (vāta) before long.

A decoction prepared with the Pitta-subduing group of drugs, mixed with sugar and honey, and taken well-chilled, destroys thirst caused by Pitta; or likewise, boiled milk processed with the Jīvanīya (vitalizing) drugs may be used.
A decoction prepared with bilva, āḍhakī, kanyaka, pañcamūlī, and darbha overcomes vomiting born of kapha;
furthermore, emesis induced here by warm water infused with nimba blossoms is beneficial.
In all types of thirst, or even in that caused by pitta, one should employ this procedure, for by it they do not exist;
[one may use] the juice of ripe udumbara fruit with sugar, or water boiled with that [juice].
Those afflicted by thirst should drink cool water prepared with the *sārivādi* group of herbs once it has been processed;
likewise, water boiled with *kaśeru*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, lotus stalks, lotus roots, and sugarcane cures diseases born of blood.
Having added parched grain, blue lotus, ushira root, and sandalwood, one should let it infuse overnight in a well-ventilated place;
they say that this excellent water, possessing a noble fragrance, when mixed with sugar and honey, is the best.
And for the benefit of men afflicted by thirst, the physician should administer grape-juice thickened with sugar;
likewise, [he should prescribe it] when the Sārivādi, Tṛṇapañcamūla, Utpalādi, or the first group [of drugs] is used.
One should prepare a decoction according to the prescribed method from madhūkapuṣpa and other such ingredients;
furthermore, six types of syrups made from rājādana, kṣīrī, and pītana are beneficial in this case.
Alternatively, one should drink the ground seeds of *satuṇḍikera* or those derived from cotton;
by quelling the pain arising from the wound, one may conquer [the disease] through the drinking of meat juices and blood.
One should cure hemorrhage arising from *kṣaya* (consumption) with milk-ghee, or meat-broth, or liquorice-water;
however, one should conquer that arising from *āmadoṣa* (undigested matter) with decoctions containing *bilva* and *vacā*, along with digestive stimulants (*dīpanīya*).
One should drink digestive (dīpana) decoctions prepared with āmrātaka, bhallātaka, and balā;
furthermore, one should overcome thirst caused by heavy food through emetics, except for that arising from wasting (kṣaya), which is produced by all [the aforementioned causes].
Meat broth, or molasses water, or even a stirred drink (mantha) overcomes thirst born of physical exertion.
One who is thirsty from the obstruction of food should drink warm gruel, or else a cold stirred drink.
If a person who has drunk an unctuous substance (sneha) experiences thirst, he should drink warm water;
however, for one who drinks alcohol, half-watered liquor cures the thirst arising from that liquor, as does liquor itself for a habitual drinker.
Well-cooled water with sugar, as well as sugarcane juice and water, destroy thirst arising from [bile].
For those [vomiting disorders], emetics with their respective decoctions, as well as digestive (pācana) remedies prescribed for fever, should be administered.
One should administer medicinal plasters, immersions, and affusions, as well as cool rooms;
furthermore, purification therapies, milk, meat broths, ghees, and sweet, cooling linctuses in all [the stages].
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter from the beginning, titled the tenth chapter within the section on internal medicine (*kāyacikitsā*) contained in the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā.
The forty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the prevention of vomiting.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

By foods that are excessively liquid, excessively unctuous, unpalatable, or excessively salty; by those consumed at the wrong time, in excessive quantity, or which are unsuitable to one's constitution.
Due to fatigue, depletion, agitation, indigestion, or the presence of worms;
in the case of a pregnant woman, or likewise for one who eats too quickly.

For one who is not utterly overwhelmed, the occurrence of vomiting is certain; [it arises] when one is forcibly and suddenly provoked by loathsome causes or others. Covering the mouth with its forceful onsets, it afflicts the body with breaking pains.
It is defined as *chardi* (vomiting) when the bodily humors (*doṣa*) issue forth from the mouth.
Aggravating the increased doshas and becoming obstructed by vyāna,
udāna moves forcefully upward due to the consumption of incompatible food.
Excessive salivation, distress in the heart, and a lack of desire for food are considered the premonitory symptoms of vomiting;
one should further discern them according to their specific characteristics.
Vomiting that is frothy, scanty, and frequent; accompanied by pain, with the sides and back afflicted;
occurring when exhausted, with a sound, and repeatedly bitter; and which increases after digestion—this vomiting is born of Vāta.
That [vomiting] which occurs with an excessively sour taste in the mouth, or a pungent and bitter one; where one vomits yellow, blood-stained, or green matter;
accompanied by burning, sucking pain, fever, dryness of the mouth, and fainting—that is born from the cause of *pitta*.
He whose hair stands on end and who vomits sweet, copious, white, cold, and thick phlegm-laden matter,
while suffering from loss of appetite, pain, heaviness, and exhaustion— such vomiting arises from the provocation of phlegm (kapha).

That [condition] in which all forms [of vomiting] occur is considered to arise from all the *doṣas* (humors). It is born of loathing (*bībhatsaja*), born of pregnancy-longing (*dauhṛdaja*), and born of indigestion (*āmaja*). Furthermore, that which arises from the provocation of what is unwholesome (*sātmyaprakopa*) and that which is born of worms (*kṛmija*)—this is the fifth; one should discern it precisely by the predominance of the *doṣas*, as previously stated.
It is characterized by excessive piercing pain and nausea, especially when caused by worms,
and is marked by symptoms identical to those of heart disease caused by worms.

A skilled physician should not undertake the treatment of persistent vomiting that is accompanied by complications, contains blood and pus, and is associated with a "moon-like" (milky) appearance, occurring in a patient who is already emaciated.
For all [these disorders] arise from an agitation of the stomach; therefore, fasting alone is beneficial for them.
In cases of vomiting characterized by an excess of the humors (doṣas), emesis is said to be beneficial;
or the physician should administer purgation according to the predominance of the specific humor.
One should gradually follow a regimen of light, dried, and wholesome foods combined with appropriate medicinal herbs.
One should administer appropriate astringent decoctions that destroy fever;
milk and ghee, when drunk, will cure vomiting caused by Vata.
One should drink ghee with rock salt to ward off vomiting caused by Vata;
or a soup of Mudga and Āmalaka with ghee and rock salt;
or one should drink gruel prepared with the five roots (pañcamūlī) mixed with honey.
Or one should drink the meat broth of gallinaceous birds, made sour with fruits and mixed with clearly visible rock salt;
in this condition, an unctuous purgative that is lukewarm and salty is beneficial.
Decoctions that pacify pitta, those prepared by boiling, and cold substances,
when employed as astringents, destroy vomiting caused by pitta.
In this condition, purification with sweet substances combined with grape juice is recommended;
furthermore, when the disease is strong, they praise the use of *tailvaka* ghee.

In the case of [fever] born of phlegm, the physician should cause the patient to drink either a decoction of āragvadha and other such drugs, or the ten-ingredient formulation (daśāṅga-yoga), mixed with honey.
A decoction of guḍūcī prepared according to the rules and known as "the cold infusion" (himasaṃjñita) is beneficial in all three stages when combined with honey.
One should treat nausea born of disgust with pleasant things, that born of pregnancy-longings (dauhṛda) with desired fruits,
that born of fasting with emetics, and that born from the provocation of one's own constitutional suitability (sātmya) with things that are suitable.
One should treat vomiting caused by worms in the same manner as heart disease caused by worms,
and subsequently administer the recommended treatment according to the specific dosha involved.
By repeatedly licking long pepper mixed with the juice of wood-apple and combined with honey,
a person is liberated from vomiting.
Honey mixed with rice-water, or sweet juice drunk with rice-water,
or a refreshing drink (tarpaṇa) combined with honey— these are the remedies for all three [types of vomiting].
One should drink a gruel prepared with *svayaṃguptā*, *yaṣṭyāhvā*, rice-water, and honey;
or alternatively, one may drink a gruel prepared with the leaves of the *karañja* tree.
Alternatively, cumin seeds ground with a proper amount of sour and salty substances are beneficial;
or one should eat wood-apple (kapittha) with rice-water or with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa).
One should lick honey mixed with white sandalwood and the excrement of a fly,
or drink milk that has been heated over a fire and then extinguished by the body of a house-lizard.
Or likewise, one should drink parched grain flour mixed with ghee and honey;
or similarly, one should lick Pippalī (Māgadhī) combined with ghee, honey, and sugar.
One should either rub sandalwood with the juice of dhātrī or with the water of split mudga beans,
or one should lick the marrow of kola and āmalaka along with the three aromatics (trisugandhika).
A person should drink gruel made of rice and parched grain with honey,
and one should also present fragrant substances that are pleasing to the mind and pleasant to the sense of smell.
He should, without weariness, provide at all [ceremonies] auspicious meats from wild animals, refreshing drinks, and various kinds of foods.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter (the eleventh within the section on internal medicine) contained in the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Prohibition of Vomiting. ||49||
The fiftieth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of hiccup.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
By means of foods that cause burning, heaviness, constipation, dryness, and excessive secretions;
and by cold drinks, sitting or standing in cold places, dust, smoke, wind, and fire;
Through physical exertion, labor, carrying heavy loads, travel, suppression of natural urges, fasting, the disorder of undigested food (āmadoṣa), injury, women, wasting diseases, and afflictions;
From irregular eating, from fasting, and likewise from eating in moderation,
hiccups, dyspnea, and cough arise in men.
The wind repeatedly rises with a sound, as if ejecting the liver, spleen, and intestines from the mouth;
because it quickly destroys the vital breaths while making that noise, it is therefore called "hikkā" (hiccup) by physicians.
Indeed, the wind, accompanied by phlegm, produces five types of hiccups: those born of food, the twin hiccups, the minor, the deep, and the great.
Astringent taste in the mouth, lack of appetite, heaviness of the throat and chest,
abdominal distension, and flatulence are the premonitory symptoms of hiccup.
Furthermore, for one who eats food while hurrying,
or while it is very cold, the wind, overspread by the foods and greatly afflicted by pungent substances, becomes intensely provoked.
The physician should recognize that as the "food-born" (annajā) hiccup when it moves upward and causes a choking sound;
it is that hiccup which proceeds with slow and double (yamala) impulses.
One should designate that as Yamalā when it causes the head and neck to tremble and proceeds with slow velocities over long intervals of time.
That hiccup which has issued from the base of the collarbones is called *kṣudrikā*;
that hiccup which originates in the navel is terrible and deep-sounding.
That which causes dryness of the lips, throat, tongue, and mouth, as well as labored breathing and pain in the sides,
and is accompanied by numerous complications, is known as Gambhīrā.
That which proceeds constantly as if piercing the vital points (marmas),
stretching the body with force and causing one who is excessively thirsty to cry out,
and making all the limbs tremble, should be known as Mahāhikkā.
One whose limbs are stretched out while hiccuping, whose vision is intensely fixed upward,
who is emaciated, who loathes food, and who coughs— these two types of hiccuping patients at the end stage should be abandoned.
In this condition, breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma), causing agitation, and frightening with the stings of needles are recommended;
likewise, a nasal squeeze (avapīḍa) with liquorice and honey, or long pepper mixed with powdered sugar, is advised.
For one who is not excessively emaciated, lukewarm ghee, milk, or sugarcane juice should be administered for the sake of pacification;
likewise, non-white sandalwood ground with breast milk, along with ghee, rock salt, and warm water, may be used.
Saindhava salt ground into a powder and administered with water, or used as a nasal drop (nasya), destroys hiccup;
one should also employ smoke produced from the resin of the Śāla tree, or from Nipāla, or from cow horns.
Alternatively, fomentation (sveda) should be applied to the site of the hiccup using leather or hair treated with clarified butter;
or one should lick a powder of red ochre (gairika), or of the mineral called kāñcanāhva, or of the bone of domestic animals, mixed with honey.
Similarly, in this case, the hair of a dog, sheep, goat, or *gośallaka*— burnt by internal smoke—
as well as ashes produced from the leaves of *barhi* grass smeared with honey and clarified butter, or ashes from *udumbara* or *tilvaka* wood, [are used].
Svarjikṣāra, taken with honey and the juice of bījapūra, quickly destroys hiccup when licked.
Warm gruels (yavāgū) made smooth with clarified butter, or lukewarm milk-rice (pāyasa), taken in small morsels, also cure hiccup.
Goat’s milk boiled with ginger-water, or likewise drunk mixed with sugar,
or consumed until satiety, or even the urine of goats and sheep when smelled, quickly destroys hiccup.
Having well-pounded together the sapūtikīṭa, garlic, asafoetida, and the lotus,
one should drink that well-processed powder with honey and sugar, along with the juice of elephant-keśara, sugarcane, and madhūka.
One should drink one pala of the best salt, or the entire amount of two palas of clarified butter;
or one should drink harītakī with lukewarm water as an after-drink, followed by ghee mixed with alkali and honey.
One should drink a śukti-measure of the juice of wood-apple with honey and long pepper for one's well-being.
Black pepper, white pepper, and āmalaka, licked with ginger and honey;
or else the powder of the marrow of the jujube stone, collyrium, and parched rice flour, licked with honey—these destroy hiccup.
The fruit and flower of the pāṭalā, red ochre (gairika), kaṭurohiṇī, the core of the date palm, māgadhī, kāśīśa, and the substance called dadhi.
These four formulations,
shown according to their respective verses, should be prepared with honey as the second ingredient by one who understands them for the treatment of hiccup.
One should drink the juices derived from pigeons, doves, sparrows, śvadaṃṣṭra,
monitor lizards, and jackals— sour with fruit, cooled, mixed with rock salt, and unctuous— as well as those produced by the peacock, the deer, and the bird.
Purgation is considered the most wholesome treatment; likewise, lukewarm ghee mixed with rock salt and sugar is beneficial.
Some authorities state that for those suffering from hiccups, an oil enema (anuvāsana) is also beneficial when the upward-moving vital air (sadāgati) has become deranged.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter (the twelfth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Hiccough."
The fifty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment for the prevention of dyspnea.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
By the very same causes through which hiccough is produced in many ways,
by those same causes a terrible asthma arises in embodied beings.
Having left its natural state, the wind (vāyu), joined with prāṇa and kapha, moves upward and causes one to breathe; that they call "śvāsa" (asthma/dyspnea).
That great disease, dyspnea (śvāsa), is specifically divided into five types: kṣudraka, tamaka, chinna, mahān, and ūrdhva.
Its premonitory symptoms are cardiac pain, aversion to food, extreme restlessness,
distension of the abdomen, colic in the sides, and a bad taste in the mouth.
He whose breath continues to flow while he undertakes some activity,
yet comes to rest when he is seated, is designated as "trifling."
Accompanied by thirst, perspiration, vomiting, and a gurgling sound in the throat, and especially distressed during cloudy weather— that breathlessness is considered Tamaka-shvāsa.
A man who is overwhelmed by a great sound, whose chest is congested with phlegm,
who breathes heavily while lacking strength, who has an aversion to food, and who sleeps without being afflicted by any other pain— [he is in the grip of death].
It subsides when phlegm is diminished, but it increases in one who sleeps;
that should be known as *pratamaka*, occurring in one overcome by fainting and fever.
A person whose bladder is distended and being burnt by pain,
and who breathes with all his vital strength in broken gasps, should be designated as having "interrupted" (ucchinnam) breath.
One who is unconscious, afflicted by pain in the sides, has a dry throat and an excessively loud breathing sound,
with eyes wide open and gasping after stretching out the body, is known as *mahān* (the great).
One who breathes while the vital points (*marmans*) are being stretched and is repeatedly delirious is also [known as such].
One who looks upward, whose voice is destroyed, and whose breath flows upward, one should declare to be dead.
Among these, the minor type is the most easily curable; Tamaka is said to be difficult to treat.
Three types of dyspnea are incurable, as is Tamaka occurring in a weak person.
Indeed, some authorities prescribe mild purification both upward and downward for those suffering from asthma, even without the use of unctuous enemas (snehabasti),
as it is the best treatment for those with chronic respiratory ailments.
This well-prepared aged ghee, processed with abhayā, viḍa salt, and asafoetida, is highly esteemed for treating dyspnea, cough, hiccups, and heart disease.
Alternatively, one may take fresh ghee prepared with sauvarcala salt, abhayā, and bilva;
or ghee processed with the drugs of the first group (vīrarasa) as a paste.
Ghee prepared with the five salts and [the following]— hiṃsrā, viḍaṅga, pūtīka, triphalā, vyoṣa, and citraka— dispels both asthma and cough.
One should drink ghee prepared with two parts milk and four parts water, along with [the paste of] drugs in the measure of a kola;
for this indeed dispels asthma and cough.
One should cook clarified butter with four times as much of the entire decoction of vṛṣaka to treat hemorrhoids, anorexia, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, and wasting.
One should add the powder of its root-flower to cold water and mix it with honey,
along with kaṇṭakārī, madhūlikā, bhārgī, śuṇṭhī, tārkṣya, sugar, and ambuda.
The wise physician, having added equal parts of yellow sandalwood and liquorice, should cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much cold water according to the prescribed method.
This ghee cures dyspnea, cough, and hiccups;
[the ingredients are] suvahā, kālikā, bhargī, śukākhyā, and the fruit of naicula.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with two kuḍavas of water and these ingredients— kākādanī, śṛṅgavera, varṣabhū, and the two types of bṛhatī— in quantities equal to a kola each.
Indeed, this pungent and hot [mixture],
when drunk with sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra, kaṭukā, vyoṣa, and citraka, destroys the disease of asthma.
Ghee prepared with vacā, abhayā, and viḍaṅga is for the pacification of dyspnea;
another [preparation] is ghee cooked with double the amount of water from gopavallī.
These five oblations are said by physicians to be for asthma and cough:
tālīśa, tāmalakī, ugrā, jīvantī, kuṣṭha, and saindhava.
Ghee should be cooked with bilva, puṣkara, bhūtīka, sauvarcala salt, kaṇā, agni, pathyā, and tejovatī, along with four times the amount of water.
This prepared Vāsā-ghṛta (Vāsā ghee) combined with asafoetida is an excellent remedy for all types of dyspnea; alternatively, the Ṣaṭpala-ghṛta or simply ghee would also be beneficial in this case.
Oil prepared with ten times as much of the auspicious juice of Bhṛṅgarāja,
when used according to the prescribed method, dispels asthma and cough.
Sour fruits, the meat-juices of gallinaceous birds, unctuous preparations with clearly added rock salt,
or well-prepared dishes of horse-gram served with the heads of deer and other such animals.
Milk prepared with these,
as well as powdered seeds of *timira* and the substance called *karkaṭa*, destroy both asthma and cough.
Dūrvā grass, pippalī, the one called kaṭukā, harītakī,
the hair of a porcupine and a peacock, kola, māgadhikā, and kaṇā.
Bhārgī, tvak, śṛṅgavera, sugar, and the powder derived from the limbs of the śallaka plant,
along with the seeds of nṛttakauṇḍaka— all these should be ground into a fine powder.
These five half-verses describe the linctuses that have been correctly expounded;
they are to be licked with ghee and honey by men afflicted by cough and dyspnea.
One should drink the flowers of the saptacchada and long pepper, having powdered them with buttermilk and honey; or else, one should eat parched grain.
One afflicted by dyspnea should drink a well-prepared satiation of barley grains that have been repeatedly processed with *arka* sprouts, mixed with honey.
Having drunk the flowers of śirīṣa, kadalī, and kunda, combined with māgadhikā and rice-water, one shall conquer all forms of dyspnea without exception.
One should lick kola-majjā, tāla-root, ṛṣya-hide, and asī with honey; or one may take bhārgī combined with ghee and honey.
Or one may take the seed of the *nīcaiḥkadamba* with honey and rice-water;
or else, grapes, *harītakī*, *kṛṣṇā*, *karkaṭa*, and *durālabhā*.
By licking together ghee and honey with haridrā, marica, drākṣā, guḍa, rāsnā, kaṇā, and śaṭī, one destroys even the most dreadful forms of asthma.
One afflicted by dyspnea, while following a wholesome diet, should lick equal parts of cow-dung juice,
honey, ghee, and long pepper (kaṇā).
One should lick the juice of horse dung in cases of dyspnea and cough;
those formulations which have been proclaimed for use in cases of anemia and edema [are also applicable].
Those which are renowned as cures for cough and those that remove dyspnea and cough include bhārgī,
bark, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), oil, haridrā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
One should cook a beneficial poultice (utkārikā) consisting of long pepper (pippalī), black pepper (marica), caṇḍā, and the juice of cow dung,
using the seeds of the talakoṭa plant.
When consumed, this [diet] quickly destroys even those most difficult-to-cross dyspneas;
likewise, aged ghee, long pepper, horse-gram, and the meat-broths of wild animals [are beneficial].
Wine, fermented gruel, asafoetida, the juice of citron, honey, grapes,
emblic myrobalan, and bilva fruit are recommended for those suffering from labored breathing and coughing.
One should treat a patient afflicted by dyspnea and hiccups with unctuous sudations;
once anointed with salt and oil, the patient's congealed phlegm [is loosened] by them.
Remaining in the stomach, it undergoes dissolution and the wind subsides;
then, knowing it has been digested, one should feed him rice with broth.
Or, in cases of obstruction caused by Vāta and Kapha, the physician should administer medicated smoke using realgar,
deodar, turmeric, cinnamon bark, and meat.
Having prepared wicks according to the prescribed method from lac, the root of the *uruvūka*,
ghee, oil-cake, beeswax, and the resin of the *śāla* tree;
The horns, hair, hooves, sinews, and skin of cows— all of these—
as well as those of the Turuṣka, Śallakī, Guggulu, and Padmaka trees.
All these medicated smokes mixed with clarified butter should be administered by one who understands [the treatment].
In cases of severe affliction by phlegm, emesis along with purgation should be performed.
For one who is weak and emaciated, nourishing therapy (tarpaṇa) is said to be beneficial,
using well-prepared meats from wild animals, sheep, or marshy creatures.

A man afflicted by dyspnea, indeed, conquers even severe breathlessness within three days by simply licking a dose of *nidigdhikā* the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, combined with an increased amount of asafoetida and well-mixed with honey.
Just as a blazing fire fanned by the wind, or like the thunderbolt released by the king of the gods,
so indeed are these diseases— asthma, cough, and chronic dyspepsia— difficult to ward off.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter (the thirteenth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Hiccups and Dyspnea."
The fifty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of cough.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
The causes that have been stated for the two diseases of dyspnea and hiccough should also be understood as the causes of the origin of cough.
Likewise, from injury by smoke or dust, from physical exertion, from the consumption of dry food,
from food taken at improper times, and likewise from the suppression of the urges of vomiting and sneezing;

When the *prāṇa* wind, followed by the *udāna*, becomes vitiated, it issues suddenly from the mouth with a sound resembling that of a cracked bell-metal vessel; accompanied by the bodily humors (*doṣa*), this is described as *kāsa* (cough) by the learned.
That [fever] arises from wind and bile, from phlegm, likewise from injury, and another from wasting;
thus described by physicians as being of five types, when aggravated, it becomes the disorder known as *yakṣman*.

For one who will suffer from this, these symptoms arise: itching of the throat, obstruction of the food passage, coating of the palate and throat, abnormality of one's own voice, loss of appetite, and a decline of the digestive fire.
Suffering from pain in the heart, temples, head, abdomen, and sides, with a wasted face and diminished strength, voice, and vitality,
he coughs repeatedly and dryly due to the internal phlegm being stirred by wind, accompanied by a hoarseness of voice.

Afflicted by burning pain in the chest, fever, and dryness of the mouth, with a bitter taste in the mouth and tormented by thirst, one vomits yellow and pungent matter due to pitta; such a person, pale and suffering from a burning sensation, coughs.
With a face smeared [with mucus], sinking down, afflicted by headache, and with the body filled with phlegm;
suffering from loss of appetite, pain, heaviness, and exhaustion, he coughs up thick phlegm due to the excess of *kapha*.
But that man whose chest has been excessively injured by physical exertion, heavy loads, study, or trauma, being one with a split chest, spits blood repeatedly; they call him *kṣataja*.
The patient suffering from cough may experience body aches, fever, burning sensations, and delusions, as well as the loss of vital strength;
becoming emaciated and weak with wasted flesh, he spits out blood mixed with pus.
Physicians declare that cough arising from wasting (kṣayaja) exhibits all symptoms and is extremely difficult to treat;
however, they say that when it occurs in one who has reached old age, it is merely palliable.
Having drunk śṛṅgī, vacā, kaṭphala, kattṛṇa, abda, dhānyā, abhayā, bhārgī, amarāhvā, and viśva,
combined with hiṅgu and warm water, one quickly overcomes even a cough characterized by a constricted throat.
A linctus made from equal parts of the three fruits (triphalā), the three acrids (vyoṣa), viḍaṅga, śṛṅgī, rāsnā, vacā, padmaka,
and devadāru, mixed with honey, sugar, and ghee, quickly destroys even severe cough.
One suffering from cough should lick a powder made of pathyā, sugar, āmalaka, parched grain, pippalī, and śuṇṭhī,
along with saindhava salt and black pepper, mixed with ghee and honey, using warm water.
One should eat jaggery with ginger and long pepper, or lick grapes with ghee and honey;
likewise, one may take equal parts of grapes, sugar, and long pepper, along with fresh ginger, licorice, and tugākṣīrī.

One should lick sugar-candy in equal parts mixed with ghee and honey, or combined with a portion of black pepper; or one should drink the powder of āmalakī, pippalī, viśva, and sugar-candy along with the scum of curd.
One afflicted by the disease of cough should drink equal parts of *hareṇukā* and *māgadhikā* with curd;
or one should drink equal parts of the two types of *haridrā*, *suradāru*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *gāyatrisāra*.
One should consume dantī, dravantī, and that which is called tilvaka, fried in goat's urine or lukewarm water;
then one may eat jujube leaves fried in ghee along with rock salt.
One should drink a kola-measure of asafoetida with sour gruel (sauvīraka) or with a sour juice;
or one should lick black pepper with honey; or a medicinal wick (varti) made of bhārgī, vacā, and asafoetida [should be used].
For the purpose of fumigation (dhūma), it is recommended to use either ghee mixed with bamboo bark, cardamom, and salt;
or a paste made from musta, ingudi bark, madhuka, māṃsī, and realgar, ground with goat's urine.
One suffering from cough caused by Vāta and Balāsa should prepare a wick (varti) and inhale medicated smoke with milk as a post-drink;
or he should drink Sidhu wine mixed with black pepper, for by this means he quickly and forcefully conquers the cough.
One should drink milk boiled with grapes, water, mañjiṣṭhā, and purāhvaya, combined with honey;
and one should eat well-prepared mung beans with honey, along with nidigdhikā, ginger, and pippalī.
Having cooked a bolus (utkārikā) enriched with ginger in ghee along with the roots of *truti* and *kola* leaves,
one should consume this prepared as a thin gruel (*peyā*), well-cooled and mixed with honey.
The six-ingredient ghee prepared for splenic disorders (plīha) overcomes vāta-type cough by force;
likewise, ghee prepared with the vidārigandhādi group or cooked with the juice of vāsaka is effective.
In this condition, purgation with unctuous substances, as well as non-unctuous and unctuous enemas, are prescribed;
one should carefully inhale unctuous medicated smoke and drink lukewarm clarified butter.
Beneficial gruels prepared with meat broths, milks, and electuaries likewise combined with ghee;
as well as emetics, purgatives for the body and head, medicinal smokes, and gargles.
Warm linctuses that are pungent specifically destroy kapha through their drying action;
they say that the three pungents (kaṭutrika) are also wholesome, as is ghee cooked in the juice of kṛmighna.
Ghee cooked in the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍī* leaves cures cough arising from *kapha*.
[Likewise, ghee prepared with] *pāṭhā*, *viḍaṅga*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *viḍaṅga*, rock salt (*sindhu*), *trikaṇṭaka*, *rāsnā*, *agni*, and *balā* [achieves the same].

Having decocted the group beginning with Vidārigandha, Utpala, and Sārivā, along with the entire group of sweet (madhura) drugs, one destroys the five types of cough— even those aggravated by dyspnea, loss of digestive fire, and hoarseness of voice.
One should cook ghee with sugarcane juice, water, milk, and the Kākoli group of drugs, along with sugar;
one should drink this in the morning for cough caused by pitta, for cough resulting from sexual excess, and for cough born of chest injury.
A powder made from equal parts of kharjūra, bhārgī, magadhā, priyāla, madhūlikā, elā, and āmalaka,
when consumed with sugar, honey, and plenty of ghee, destroys the three types of cough.

One should lick equal parts of red ochre, turmeric, antimony, *pāṭhā*, *mūrvā*, and *upakulyā* with honey for coughs arising from chest wounds or wasting. One should also drink ghee cooked in sugarcane juice.
Or one who eats wholesome food should drink the powder of *āmalaka* with milk, or that which is cooked with ghee;
likewise, the powders derived from wheat and barley, and the *kākolī* group of drugs, should be made into a very fine paste.
In cases of the three types of cough, those suffering from cough should drink the Peya prepared with milk, honey, and ghee;
or indeed, they should drink boiled jaggery-water, cooled and mixed with honey, accompanied by black pepper.
Having added three *prasthas* of pure *āmalakī* juice and half a *tulā* of jaggery,
along with the powders of *granthika*, *cavya*, *jīra*, *vyoṣa*, *ibhā-kṛṣṇā*, *hapuṣā*, and *ajamoda*;
Having added one *picu* each of viḍaṅga, rock salt, triphalā, yavānī, pāṭhā, agni (citraka), and dhānya,
along with eight palas of trivṛt powder and eight palas of oil, one should cook it according to the prescribed method.
One should consume that [medicine] in the size of a jujube fruit, combined with the three aromatics (trisugandhi), acting as one pleases;
by this, all disorders of the *grahaṇī*, along with asthma, cough, hoarseness of voice, and swelling, are cured.
This renowned jaggery known as Kalyāṇaka pacifies chronic internal fever, serves as a cause for increasing virility,
and acts as a destroyer of sterility and disease in women.
The two pentads of roots, Ela, Pippalī, Ātmaguptā, Bhārgī, Śaṭī, Puṣkaramūla,
Viśvā, Pāṭhā, Amṛtā, Granthika, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Rāsnā, Agni, Apāmārga, Balā, and Yavāsa.
Having placed two *pālikās* [of each], one *āḍhaka* of barley, and one hundred heavy *harītakīs*,
and having prepared a decoction in one *droṇa* of water combined with one *āḍhaka*, when it has been reduced to a purified fourth part;
One should cook one tulā of pure jaggery, adding separately one kuḍava each of oil and ghee;
an equal amount of powdered Pippalī should be added to it, and once it has been prepared and cooled, honey should be mixed in.
One should regularly lick one karṣa of this elixir along with two abhayā fruits;
it quickly destroys consumption (rājayakṣman), disorders of the grahaṇī, edema, weak digestion, hoarseness of voice, and cough.

The venerable Agastya prepared this [medicine], which bestows intelligence, strength, energy, and wisdom, and cures anemia, dyspnea, disorders of the head, heart disease, hiccup, and irregular fevers.
Having decocted the group consisting of crab, pearl oyster, sparrow, antelope, and quail, along with the entire sweet category [of herbs], one should cook ghee in it;
when consumed, that ghee cures cough arising from chest wounds as well as that born of wasting (kṣaya).
Ghee cooked with *śatāvarī* and *nāgabalā* should be administered for the benefit of those suffering from cough.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter (the fourteenth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Cough."
The fifty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of hoarseness of voice.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

When the bodily humors—wind and the others—are provoked by speaking too loudly, grief, excessive study, loud singing, cold, and so forth, they enter the channels that carry the voice and destroy its stability; thus, the voice becomes sixfold [in its disorders].
Due to Vāta, the eyes, face, urine, and feces become black; he speaks slowly with a stammering voice, and his throat is accompanied by a burning sensation.
Due to Pitta, the face, eyes, feces, and urine are yellowish; he speaks with a throat afflicted by intense heat.

Due to kapha, one constantly speaks with difficulty, with the throat perpetually obstructed by phlegm, speaking slowly and softly, especially during the day; when all three doshas are involved, there is a combination of all symptoms and indistinctness of speech—this they call incurable due to tamas.
His speech may falter and he shall suffer loss of his voice; such a person, whose speech is impaired, should be avoided.
With his throat, lips, and palate coated with fat, he speaks slowly, his voice choked within his throat and his words indistinct.

A disease of the voice that arises in one who is emaciated, aged, or thin, whether it has been long-standing or is newly arisen; or one that occurs in a person of great fatness and originates from all [the humors]—such a disease does not attain success (cure).
One should treat those patients who are unctuous and whose morbid humors have been eliminated by appropriate means, using emesis, purgation, and enemas,
as well as nasal drops, pressed-out drops, mouth-washes, medicinal smokes, electuaries, and various types of gargles.

One should endeavor to apply in its entirety that entire procedure for dyspnea and cough which was taught at the very beginning; furthermore, I shall hereafter describe the specific treatment—learn all of that which is beneficial for those afflicted by disorders of the voice.
In cases of hoarseness caused by Vāta, one should drink ghee after a meal;
or ghee boiled with the expressed juices of *kāsamarda*, *vātārka*, and *mārkava*.
Ghee prepared with the juice of *ārtagala*,
or with *yavakṣāra* and *ajamodā*, or with *citraka* and *āmalaka*, when drunk, destroys *vāta*.
Or goat's meat prepared with devadāru and agnika, accompanied by honey; or jaggery-rice with ghee, followed by a drink of warm water.
In the case of pitta, however, one should diligently drink ghee with milk as an after-drink,
and should eat milk-porridge (pāyasa) mixed with ghee and licorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka).
Or one should lick the powder of the sweet fruits (madhuraka) saturated with honey and ghee;
likewise, a formulation of śatāvarī powder or even balā powder may be used.
In cases of hoarseness caused by phlegm, one should drink pungent substances with urine;
or one should lick them with honey and oil, or eat pungent substances after a meal.

In cases of hoarseness caused by fat (medas), the procedure prescribed for phlegm (kapha) is desired; however, in cases arising from all three doshas or from wasting (kshaya), one should perform treatment only after informing the patient that the prognosis is unfavorable.
One whose voice is impaired when speaking loudly should drink boiled milk mixed with sugar and honey, along with sweet substances.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter (the fifteenth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Prohibition of Vomiting."
The fifty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the prevention and treatment of diseases caused by parasites (krimi).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Through indigestion, overeating, unwholesome, incompatible, or impure food;
through lack of exercise, sleeping during the day, and the consumption of heavy, excessively unctuous, or cold substances.
With bean flour, split grains, lotus stalks, water-lilies, and kaseruka;
with leaf-vegetables, wine, fermented gruel, curd, milk, molasses, and sugarcane.
Kapha and pitta become aggravated by the consumption of straw, marshy meat, oil-cakes, parched grain, and the like, as well as by sweet, sour, and liquid drinks.
It produces worms of many forms that inhabit various locations;
the birth of those born from phlegm and feces occurs in the stomach and the large intestine,
while the birth of those born from blood is generally recorded as occurring in the vessels (dhamanīs).
The origin of the twenty species of worms is recorded as being threefold;
I shall now describe them in detail according to their respective sources: feces, phlegm, and blood.
Ajavās, vijavās, kipyās, cipyās, as well as gaṇḍūpadās,
cūravas, and dvimukhas— these seven are to be known as born of excrement.
These white and minute worms pierce [the body] and crawl toward the anus;
others among them indeed become broad with tails.
From those born of feces arise colic, impaired digestion, anemia, constipation, loss of strength,
excessive salivation, anorexia, heart disease, and diarrhea.
Long red earthworms cause itching and discharge from the anus;
they produce colic, flatulence, diarrhea, and destroy the power of digestion.
The darbhapuṣpas, mahāpuṣpas, pralūnas, and cipiṭas,
as well as the dreadful pipīlikās, arise from the provocation of phlegm (kapha).
They were hairy, with hair on their heads, possessed of tails, and marked with dark circles;
they resembled the sprouts of grown grain, and were white and slender.
They cause diseases of the marrow, the consumption of the eyes, and afflictions of the palate, ears, head, heart, vomiting, and catarrh.
The Keśaromanakha, Dantāda, Kikkīśa,
Kuṣṭha, and Parīsarpa are to be known as arising from blood.
Those [vātas] which are reddish, black, unctuous, and likewise broad,
generally produce disorders arising from the seat of blood (raktādhiṣṭhāna).
Those born from feces arise from black gram flour, split pulses, and leafy vegetables;
those arising from phlegm arise from meat, black gram, molasses, milk, curd, and oil.
Indeed, blood-born [fevers] arise from incompatible foods, indigestion, leafy vegetables, and the like;
their symptoms are fever, discoloration, colic, heart disease, lassitude, and vertigo.
Aversion to food, diarrhea, and the symptoms of worms have arisen;
thus, thirteen types of worms are proclaimed at the outset.
The first group, beginning with Keśāda, are invisible; one should avoid the first two.
Having identified any one of these as being about to strike, one should act toward that affectionate and distressed person.
One who has first been made to vomit with ghee cooked with *surasā* and other herbs should be purged with very potent formulations and then administered an enema.
With a decoction of barley, jujube, horse-gram, and the group of herbs beginning with *surasā*,
combined with *viḍaṅga*, oil, and salt.
Once the enema has returned, the excellent physician should have the man bathe with lukewarm water and then promptly administer anti-parasitic foods.
One should treat him with an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) prepared with unctuous substances;
thereafter, he should drink the juice of śirīṣa and kiṇihī mixed with honey.
Or likewise, one who eats pungent food as before may take the juice of *kevuka* or the juice or paste of *palāśa* seeds with rice-water.
One should drink the fresh juice of *pāribhadraka* leaves with honey,
or likewise drink the fresh juice of *pattūra*, or that produced from the *surasā* group of herbs.
One should lick the powder of horse dung or that of the *vaiḍaṅga* tree mixed with honey,
or [the powder] of well-ground *mūṣikaparṇī* leaves mixed with flour.
One should eat cooked cakes (pūpalikā) and drink fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) afterwards;
or, oil cooked with the group of drugs beginning with surasa is desired as a drink.
Or one should have foodstuffs prepared with flour mixed with powdered viḍaṅga;
or likewise, the oil of sesame seeds that have been saturated with its decoction.
The powder of the dung of a porcupine, well-impregnated seven times with a decoction of viḍaṅga as well as with a decoction of triphalā;
Having licked it with honey, one should drink the juice produced from āmalaka;
or likewise, the juice of akṣa and abhayā—this is the procedure for iron preparations as well.
Or one may drink the fresh juice of pūtīka together with honey;
or one may drink the root of pippalī combined with goat’s urine.
Or, for seven nights, the physician should have the patient drink powdered tin with curd-whey;
in this way, he shall surely destroy worms born of feces and those arising from phlegm.
One should specifically treat various disorders localized in the head, heart, nose, ears, and eyes by means of collyriums, nasal drops, and pressed-out medicinal extracts.
One should thoroughly saturate well-dried horse dung juice with a decoction of viḍaṅga;
that powder is indeed used as a nasal insufflation (pradhamana).
The physician should administer iron powders according to this very same procedure;
furthermore, oil boiled with kāṃsya, nīla, and the drugs of the surasādi group should be used as a nasal medication (nasya).
The procedure for alopecia (indralupta) should also be applied to those who consume the body hair;
the treatment for tooth-eaters has been specified as the protocol for diseases of the mouth.

One should apply the remedies for blood-born [diseases] as described in the treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha); however, one should employ the group beginning with surasā in all cases by every possible means.
Food that is well-cooked and extremely pungent is beneficial,
as is the drinking of alkaline water mixed with the alkali of horse gram (kulattha).
One who wishes to destroy worms should, in brief, avoid milks, meats, clarified butters, curds, and leafy vegetables, as well as those that are sour, sweet, or cold.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter (the sixteenth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Worms."
The fifty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of udāvarta (upward movement of wind).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
A wise person who desires to live should not forcibly restrain the natural urges of the bodily humors, such as wind and the rest, whether they arise from below or above.
When wind, feces, urine, yawning, tears, sneezing, eructation, vomiting, or the sense organs are obstructed or excited,
it is called udāvarta.
From the suppression of hunger, thirst, breath, and sleep arises udāvarta;
I shall describe its symptoms and treatment in detail.
This [disease] is of thirteen types when divided by these causes;
furthermore, another type will be described as resulting from the consumption of unwholesome food.
It causes flatulence and colic, constriction of the heart, headache, excessive dyspnea and hiccup,
cough, catarrh, throat obstruction, and the terrible spreading of phlegm and bile.
If the apāna vāyu is obstructed in its own path, it may strike the feces, causing them to be expelled through the mouth;
or it may cause flatulence, colic, cutting pain, retention of feces, and upward movement of flatus.
When the urge for feces is suppressed, feces may even emerge from the mouth of a man;
when the urge for urine is suppressed, however, the man voids urine with difficulty, drop by drop.
In the penis, anus, groin, bladder, scrotum, or the region of the navel, or even in the head,
there occurs a distended bladder accompanied by intense pains, as if one's very form were being torn apart by colic.
From the impairment of yawning, disorders of the neck, throat, and head arise due to the wind (pavana);
likewise, severe disorders affecting the ears, mouth, nose, and eyes occur.
For one who does not release the tears that have come— whether born of joy or arisen from grief—
there occurs heaviness of the head, severe eye diseases, along with catarrh.
From the suppression of a forceful sneeze, diseases arise intensely in the head, eyes, nose, and ears;
there is a sensation of the throat and mouth being filled, excessive pricking pain, a wheezing sound, or even the non-passage of wind.
When the force of eructation is suppressed, terrible disorders born of the wind (vāta) arise;
and by the obstruction of vomiting, leprosy (kuṣṭha) may occur through whichever humor the food has been improperly digested.
Swelling, pain, and retention of urine occur in the bladder, the anus, and the scrotum;
furthermore, seminal calculi may form, or there may be discharge of semen, and various other disorders arise when the semen is impaired.
From the impairment of hunger (kṣudh) arise lassitude, body aches, loss of appetite, and confusion of vision, as well as emaciation.
From the impairment of thirst (tṛṣṇā) arise dryness of the throat and mouth, obstruction of hearing, and pain in the heart.
For one who is exhausted, by the suppression of the breath there may arise heart disease, delusion, or even abdominal tumors (gulma);
or from the suppression of sleep, yawning, body ache, stiffness of the limbs, head, and eyes, or even lethargy (tandrā) may occur.
A wise physician should abandon a patient suffering from upward-moving wind (udāvarta) who is afflicted by thirst, exhausted, emaciated, tormented by colic pains,
and vomiting feces.
In all these types of udāvarta, without exception, treatments for the vital air (vāyu) must be administered according to the rules, so that it may return to its own proper path.
Now listen further from me regarding the specific treatment for each type in general:
for a disorder born of Vāta, the administration of an Asthāpana enema is especially recommended after the patient has been treated with oleation and sudation.
In the case of a rectal obstruction caused by feces (purīṣaja), the procedure for intestinal distension (ānāhika) should be performed;
however, if the urine is obstructed, one should drink wine enriched with sauvarcala salt.
Or else, a man should drink cardamom with wine, or milk;
or he should drink the fresh juice of *dhātrī* fruits mixed with water for three days.
One should drink the juice of horse dung or that of a donkey;
or one may drink honey with meat as a side dish, or rum distilled from molasses.
One should drink deodar, ghanasāra, mūrvā, turmeric, and madhuka,
each in the size of a jujube fruit, with rainwater.
Or one may drink a decoction of saffron that is rough to the touch and tasteless,
or one may drink the seed of the bottle-gourd with water, having made it salt-free.
One should administer milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī) or even grape juice;
furthermore, one should apply here the previously mentioned formulations that break up urinary calculi (aśmarī).
One should also perform the entire procedure for dysuria without exception;
furthermore, I shall describe those formulations for the pacification of urinary obstruction.
One should treat udāvarta caused by suppressed yawning with oleation and sudation;
in the case of that born from suppressed tears, the person's body should first be lubricated and fomented, and then the shedding of tears should be induced.
One should induce the discharge of nasal mucus by means of sharp collyriums and pressed-out juices, by inhalation of strong-smelling substances,
or by the application of medicinal wicks.

In cases of hoarseness due to upward-moving wind (udgāra-ja), one should administer unctuous smoke in a gradual sequence, either by means of inhalations of sharp medicinal herbs or by the rays of the sun.
One should properly overcome vomiting caused by injury to the throat with wine mixed with sauvarcala salt and the juice of bījapūra,
employing oleation and other therapies according to the specific doṣa involved.
In this case, one should administer an oil massage (abhyaṅga) mixed with alkali and salt,
along with milk that has been boiled with four parts water and the medicinal additives for purifying the bladder.
When a man has vomited semen due to its upward movement, beloved women should delight him by drinking from his cup as much as he desires after it has been boiled and cooled.
For the alleviation of hunger, food that is unctuous, warm, and small in quantity is beneficial;
for the alleviation of thirst, one should drink either a stirred drink (mantha) or even cold gruel (yavāgū).
A man who has eaten with relish, one exhausted by fatigue and labored breathing,
or one whose sleep has been interrupted, should drink milk and engage in pleasant conversation before sleeping.
In diseases such as flatulence (ādhmāna) and others, one should indeed apply remedies according to their respective requirements;
whatever is appropriate for a particular condition, that one should employ in that case.
The bodily air (vāyu), moving within the digestive tract, being provoked by foods that are dry, astringent, pungent, or bitter, indeed immediately causes upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
It indeed causes the channels that carry wind, urine, feces, blood, phlegm,
and fat to become obstructed, and it causes the feces to be expelled excessively.
Then, afflicted by pain in the heart and bladder, and oppressed by heaviness and loss of appetite,
the person voids flatus, urine, and feces with great difficulty.
It cures dyspnea, cough, catarrh, burning sensations, delusion, fainting,
fever, thirst, hiccup, diseases of the head, and disorders of the mind and hearing.
And he suffers from many other disorders arising from the provocation of Vāta;
one should administer a Nirūha enema to him after he has been anointed with oil and salt, lubricated, and fomented.
If the stool is broken up by the doshas after eating, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana);
if even then this most dreadful upward movement of wind (udāvarta) does not find relief, [further measures must be taken].
Then, once he has been sweated profusely, one should administer oleation-purgatives;
one should have him drink Trivṛt, Pīlu, and Yavānī, along with sour digestive stimulants.

Either asafoetida, kuṣṭha, vacā, svarjikā, and viḍaṅga, or these same ingredients with each subsequent one added in double quantity— these two formulations destroy upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and pain born of vāta.
One should boil devadāru, agnika, kuṣṭha, śuṇṭhī, pathyā, palaṅkaṣā,
and the roots of puṣkara in half an āḍhaka of water.
That [mixture], when drunk with only a quarter part remaining, dispels udāvarta;
likewise, dried radish, fresh radish, varṣābhū, and the five roots (pañcamūla).
Having boiled *ārevata* fruit in water, one should cook ghee with it;
when that is drunk, it completely subdues even severe upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*).
One should drink vacā, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, yavakṣāra,
harītakī, kṛṣṇā, and nirdahanī with warm water.
One should drink equal parts of ikṣvākumūla, madana, viśalyā, ativiṣā, vacā, kuṣṭha, kiṇva, and agnika, as before.
One should drink Devadāru, Agni, Triphalā, and Bṛhatī with urine;
likewise, one prastha of barley along with the fruits of Kaṇṭakārī should be boiled in one āḍhaka of water.
Having boiled it down until half a prastha remains, one should drink it mixed with asafoetida,
along with the seeds of madana and alābu, long pepper, and nidigdhikā.
Having powdered these—
nikumbha, kampilla, śyāmā, ikṣvāku, and agnika— one should blow the powder into the rectum with a tube so that it enters as far as the anus.

One should prepare *kṛtavedhana*, *māgadhī*, and the salts with cow’s urine; one should then make suppositories (*varti*) from these to be inserted into the rectum. These two formulations provide immediate relief and are considered equal to nectar.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter (the seventeenth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Udāvarta."
The fifty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of visūcikā (colic).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
From that which is described as indigestion— whether undigested (āma), obstructed (viṣṭabdha), or burnt (vidagdha)—
there arise visūcī, alasaka, and also vilambikā.
When the wind remains lodged, piercing the limbs as if with needles due to indigestion,
that condition is called *tiviṣūcikā* by physicians.
Those who have mastered the scriptures and observe moderation in food do not obtain that [state];
rather, it is the deluded, those who have not conquered themselves and possess turbid intentions, who obtain it.
Fainting, diarrhea, vomiting, thirst, colic, vertigo, cramps, yawning, burning sensations, discoloration, tremors,
pains in the heart, and a splitting sensation in the head occur during that [fever].
The abdomen becomes excessively distended; he faints and groans;
and the obstructed wind also rushes about within the belly.
When there is severe suppression of flatus and feces in the abdomen,
accompanied by thirst and suppression of eructation, one declares that to be alasaka.
When corrupted food, due to the aggravation of phlegm and wind, neither moves upward nor downward,
those ancient experts in the scriptures call that condition *vilambikā*, which is extremely difficult to treat.
Wherever the undigested matter (āma) causes pain, that very region is especially afflicted by various types of disorders;
one should identify it by the specific symptoms of the involved humor (doṣa) as well as those arising from the presence of āma.

The man who has blackish teeth, lips, and nails; whose consciousness is faint; who is afflicted by vomiting; whose eyes are sunken inward; whose voice is weak; and whose joints are all loosened—he shall depart never to return.
For curable cases, cauterization of the heels is recommended, as well as the application of fire-heat and strong emetics;
once the food is digested, fasting, digestive stimulants, and purgatives should be administered.
For one whose body has been purified, fainting, diarrhea, and other such ailments are pacified immediately;
they also declare that non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) are wholesome, so learn now of other formulations for all [conditions].

A powder made from *pathyā*, *vacā*, *hiṅgu*, *kaliṅga*, *gṛñjana*, *sauvarcala*, and *ativiṣā*, when drunk with lukewarm water, immediately destroys indigestion, colic, choleraic disorders (*visūcī*), and loss of appetite.
Alternatively, one may use alkaline anti-poison (kṣārāgada), salt, or poison; or mustard seeds mixed with molasses;
or the two groups of three [substances] combined with sour liquid, rock salt, asafoetida, bīja-pūra fruit, and ghee.
One should drink either the three pungents combined with salts and mixed with the milky sap of Snuhī,
or one should drink the "Kalyāṇaka" salt, which was previously mentioned in the treatment of wind disorders.
One should drink either black ajamoda and kṣavaka in equal parts, or māgadhā and nikumbha in equal parts;
or one should drink a paste of māgadhodbhavā combined with dantī, using the juice of koṣavatī as the vehicle.
One should drink the paste of plants grown in Magadha mixed with the paste of ginger and warm water;
likewise, one may take equal parts of the three pungents (vyoṣa), the fruit of karañja, the two types of haridrā, and the root of mātuluṅgī.
These pills, dried in the shade and prepared as an ointment for the eyes,
would destroy visūcī (cholera-like dysentery) once it is known that the person has been properly vomited, well-purged, or has undergone a successful fast.
One should properly treat the patient afflicted by hunger with digestive stimulants (dīpana) and carminatives (pācana), such as peyā and other gruels,
especially when undigested matter (āma) or feces have accumulated and become further obstructed by vitiated vāyu.
When this [wind] flows improperly, they describe its transformation as "I-am-ness" (ahaṃkāra). However, when it arises excessively, there occur thirst, catarrh, and a burning sensation in the head.
There is pain in the stomach, heaviness, nausea, suppression of belching, stiffness in the waist, back, feces, and urine, as well as colic and fainting; moreover, he vomits feces.
In the case of *ānāha* arising from the colon (*pakvāśaya*), symptoms similar to those of *alasaka* occur;
when it arises from the stomach (*āmaja*), one should treat the patient with emesis followed by the sequential administration of food and digestive stimulants (*dīpanīya*).
Now, as for the other case where one cannot vomit even once, one should conquer that undigested matter (āma) through sudation and digestive treatments,
using those substances prescribed for visūcikā which are purgative in nature.
One should prepare wicks by pulverizing those very same [substances] with the urine of a buffalo, a goat, or a ewe;
having inserted these into the anus of one who has been fomented, one should blow the powders of these [substances] into it through a tube.
Having prepared the medicinal substances that move upwards and downwards according to the prescribed method in urine,
one should quickly administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) with that decoction, combined with half as much urine and honey.
Having administered a handful of salt together with the three medicinal groups (tribhaṇḍī), one should follow the procedure for purgation;
and if it has occurred while these very [medicines] were being prepared with oil, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter (the eighteenth in the section on internal medicine) of the Uttaratantra within the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Visūcikā."
The fifty-seventh chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of anorexia (arocaka).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Due to the humors (doṣas) individually or combined, and due to mental derangement, [the disease] spreads deeply into the channels of food and the heart;
there is no relish for food—physicians call this fivefold disorder "Bhaktopaghāta" (loss of appetite).
In the case of anorexia caused by Vāta, the symptoms are a piercing pain in the heart, distress, and a distasteful facial expression;
likewise, when caused by Pitta, there is excessive burning and sucking pain in the heart, bitterness in the mouth, fainting, and thirst.
In the case of an anorexia caused by phlegm (kapha), there is itching, a sense of constriction in the skin, salivation, exhaustion, drowsiness, and a sweet taste in the mouth.
However, when all three humors are involved, the wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) provoke many symptoms within the heart.
But for one whose mind is overwhelmed by passion, grief, and fear, that [vomiting] occurs through anxiety and from the sight of impure things.
One should induce vomiting with wind-inducing substances, or drink a medicinal powder with fats, wines, or warm water.

In cases of pitta-type vomiting, emesis induced by *kṛṣṇā*, *viḍaṅga*, barley ash, *hareṇu*, *bhārgī*, *rāsnā*, *elā*, asafoetida, rock salt, and ginger, mixed with jaggery, water, and sweet substances, is recommended; likewise, an unctuous enema (*sneha*) containing rock salt, sugar, honey, and ghee is desired.
In cases of [cough] born of phlegm (kaphaja), the post-drink (anupāna) for one who has swallowed [the medicine] with nimba-water should be the water of rājadruma mixed with honey and dīpyaka;
or else, that same powder which was prescribed for the wind-born (vātaja) type should be used. Thus, one should treat [the condition] caused by all [three humors] with all these measures.

One should properly prepare a linctus by grinding together grapes, *paṭola*, sprouts of *vetra*, *karīra*, neem, *mūrvā*, *abhayā*, *akṣa*, jujube, emblic myrobalan, and *indravṛkṣa*, along with the seeds of *karañja* and *nṛpavṛkṣa*, combined with the urine of a cow.
Having ground mustā, vacā, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), the two types of rajanī, bhārgī, kuṣṭha, and nirdahanī, one should cook them in cow’s urine;
or alternatively, one may cook pāṭhā, tugā, ativiṣā, and the excellent rajanī in elephant urine.
One who knows the proper procedure should cook maṇḍūkī, arka, amṛtā, and the plant called lāṅgalā in the urine of a buffalo.
For one who consumes these four medicinal electuaries (lehas), abdominal tumors, loss of appetite, dyspnea, and diseases of the throat and heart shall cease to exist.
One should eat various foods suited to one's constitution and prepared in one's own country, as well as drinks, roots, fruits, syrups, and seasoned condiments;
and one should consume various juices in diverse ways that are light, dry, and pleasing to the mind.
In this condition, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) according to the prescribed rules, as well as purgation and mild head-purgatives (errhines).
The three pungent spices (trikaṭu), turmeric, and triphalā, combined with the awns of barley, should be reduced to a powder.
One should administer other bitter and pungent medicines mixed with honey for the purpose of clearing the mouth;

furthermore, one should conquer [the disease] with various decoctions prepared from the *mustādi* group, the *rājataru* (bark-tree) group, and the *daśāṅga* formula, combined with honey, as well as with various electuaries (*lehāḥ*).

Likewise, with fermented liquors made from urine, molasses, and *ariṣṭas*, as well as alkaline spirits whose fragrance is equal to honey and *mādhava* wine—this same procedure should be employed when the fire has been struck by phlegm and wind; and once it has subsided, this is for its pacification.
When the internal fire has been struck by the blows of desire, fear, and grief, one should indeed offer objects that are within one’s power for the sake of worldly existence;
and when those objects have again diminished, one should seek to restore them through hundreds of traditional scriptures.
When the mind has fallen into despondency, awakening is recommended here; however, in the case of anorexia, whatever is pleasing should be indulged in.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter (the nineteenth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Anorexia."
The fifty-eighth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Vātakuṇḍalika, aṣṭhīlā, and likewise vātabasti;
mūtrātīta along with jaṭhara, mūtrotsaṅga, and kṣaya.
Urinary calculus, seminal urine, and hot wind (uṣṇavāta),
as well as the two diseases beginning with urinary gravel (mūtraukasāda)— these twelve are proclaimed.
Due to dryness or the suppression of natural urges, the wind, having entered the internal space, becomes disordered and coiled; it then obstructs the urine and causes it to flow with difficulty.
One should know that disease to be the most dreadful *vātakuṇḍalikā*, which produces very small amounts of stool or stool mixed with mucus, gradually and slowly.
Residing in the space between the rectum and the bladder,
it forms a firm, immobile, and elevated knot like a stone (ashṭhīlā).
There, obstruction of feces, urine, and flatus occurs, as well as distension;
and when there is intense pain in the bladder, they know that condition as Vātāṣṭhīlā (urinary stone due to wind).
If an unskilled man forcibly suppresses the urge to urinate,
the Vayu (wind) located in the bladder obstructs the opening of that bladder.
By that, there occurs an obstruction of urine accompanied by pain in the bladder and the abdomen;
this should be known as Vatabasti, a disease difficult to cure.
If one who has suppressed the urge to urinate desires to void it again,
yet the urine does not come forth or only flows out with great difficulty, [it leads to disease].
One should recognize that condition as *mūtrātīta*, born from the suppression of the urge to urinate, which occurs repeatedly in very small amounts with little pain during the flow.
When the urge to urinate is suppressed,
the apāna vāyu becomes aggravated by that cause of upward movement (udāvarta) and fills the abdomen excessively.
One should recognize that condition, which causes distension below the navel accompanied by intense pain and obstructs the downward channels,
as *mūtrajaṭhara*.
If the urine of a person, once it has begun to flow, becomes obstructed at the base of the penis, or in the urethra, or at the glans, or is passed with blood while straining;
When urine flows slowly, in very small quantities, and either with pain or without pain,
that disease produced by vitiated Vāyu is known as Mūtrotsaṅga.
In one who is dehydrated and whose body is exhausted, pitta and vāta located in the bladder cause a painful, burning,
and difficult suppression of urine accompanied by a decrease in its volume.
Located within the opening of the enema nozzle, it is round, small, and firm;
it is painful, does not subside, and obstructs the urinary passage.
That condition in which a stone-like knot suddenly arises,
characterized by pain and other symptoms, is called *mūtragranthi* (urinary knot).
But he who, when urination has already begun, takes pleasure in sexual intercourse,
his semen suddenly flows forth mixed with urine.
Whether appearing before or even after the urine,
that which resembles ash-water is called *mūtraśukra*.
When pitta, obstructed by vāyu, reaches the bladder due to physical exertion, travel, or exposure to the sun,
it causes a burning sensation in the bladder, penis, and anus, and discharges downward.
When the urine of a person is discharged with difficulty, appearing either yellowish, reddish, or even purely red,
they call that condition Uṣṇavāta.
The urine becomes clear, yellowish, burning, and thick;
it also becomes dry and resembles the powder of yellow pigment (rocanā).
The wise physician should recognize that disease as *mūtraukasāda* (urinary gravel), caused by *pitta*,
characterized by sliminess, thickness, whiteness, and painful discharge.
That which is dry, as white as powdered conch-shell,
and accompanied by the sediment of urine, one should know to be the twelfth disease arising from phlegm (kapha).
Decoctions, medicinal pastes, clarified butter, solid foods, electuaries,
milks, alkalis, wines, fermented liquors, sudation, and enemas known as uttarabasti;
In that case, the wise physician should apply the procedure for the destruction of urinary calculi,
and he should employ here in its entirety the formulations for the upward displacement of urine (mūtrāvarta).
By drinking one akṣa measure of the paste of ervāru seeds along with rock salt and fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), one is indeed liberated from dysuria.
A man suffering from dysuria should drink wine mixed with sauvarcala salt;
or he may drink honey-wine with meat as an accompaniment, or even molasses-based liquor.
Or one should drink one karṣa of saffron mixed with honey and water, having let it stand overnight;
thus, in the morning, one shall obtain well-being.
Having drunk wine that is sour with pomegranate and mixed with cardamom, cumin,
and ginger, along with salt, one is liberated from dysuria.
One should boil the roots of the group beginning with pṛthakparṇī and those of gokṣuraka with half a prastha of water and four times as much milk.
A person should drink that milk when it is cooled and mixed with sugar and honey;
this prevents urinary obstruction arising from wind and bile.
Having properly squeezed out the excrement of a donkey and a horse with a cloth, one should drink one *kuḍava* of that liquid; it removes pain caused by urine.
One should drink a paste of Musta, Abhayā, Devadāru, Mūrvā, and Madhuka,
each equal to one Akṣa in measure, to ward off disorders of the urine.
One should drink a paste of *abhayā*, *āmalaka*, and *akṣa*, equal in quantity to a jujube fruit,
mixed with water and salt, to alleviate the pain of urinary disorders.
One should drink a paste of *udumbara* equal [in weight] to the fruit, combined with grape juice and left to stand overnight; when cooled, it removes the pain of dysuria.
One should drink one kuḍava of the fresh juice of Nidigdhikā in the early morning to remove urinary disorders, or alternatively, it may be taken mixed with honey.
Having squeezed out a *kuḍava* measure of the juice of *āmalaka* fruits and drunk it,
