a person afflicted by diseases of the urinary tract shall become free from disease.
In this manner, a person should drink either small cardamom with the juice of āmalaka fruit,
or having ground it, with very cold rice-water.
One should drink the fresh root of the palmyra palm, the juice of the trapusa fruit,
and white crab, together with milk, in the morning.
A person should drink milk boiled with sweet (madhura) drugs and mixed with ghee for the purpose of purifying urinary disorders as well as for the destruction of calculi.
Balā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, krauñca bones, kokilākṣa seeds,
śataparvaka roots, devadāru, and citraka;
A person should drink the seeds of Aksha ground into a paste with wine for the purpose of purifying urinary disorders; likewise, it is a destroyer of stones.
Having obtained the alkali of the *pāṭala* flower and strained it seven times, one should drink it mixed with a measured amount of oil; this destroys disorders of the urine.
One should drink the seeds of *nalā*, *aśmabheda*, *darbha*, *ikṣu*, *trapusa*, and *ervāru*,
boiled in milk and mixed with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).
The wise man [should prepare] a powder of cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper with alkaline water from the *pāṭalī*, *yavaśūka*, *pāribhadra*, and sesame.
One should drink it mixed with jaggery, or lick various electuaries separately.
Hereafter, I shall describe the beneficial regimen for urinary disorders (mūtradoṣa).
For those who have undergone oleation and sudation, purgation is beneficial;
thereafter, for those whose bodies have been thoroughly cleansed, uttarabasti enemas are beneficial.
If blood is seen in one who has excessive indulgence with women,
cessation of sexual intercourse and a nourishing regimen are prescribed for him.
The fat of a cock and oil are beneficial for urethral enemas (uttarabasti);
the procedure for this has indeed been described previously in detail.
Having given half a vessel of honey, a vessel of milk and ghee,
as well as powder of sugar and an equal amount of powdered grapes;
One should prepare half a portion of the fruit of *svayaṅguptā* and likewise of *ikṣuraka*,
combined with the powder of *pippalī*.
Then, having brought these together into a single mass, one should churn them with a churning-stick.
Thereafter, having licked a palmful of the powder, one should drink milk.
A man whose body is always purified by the regular use of this ghee shall conquer all urinary disorders, even those that are very difficult to overcome by other formulations.
It conquers disorders of the blood, and a barren woman shall obtain a child;
a woman employing this [remedy] is liberated from defects of the womb.
Balā, kola-stone, madhuka, śvadaṃṣṭrā, śatāvarī,
lotus stalk, kaśeru, and the seeds of ikṣuraka.
Sahasravīryā, Aṃśumatī, Payasyā with Kālā,
Śṛgālavinnā, and Atibalā constitute the group that is nourishing (bṛṃhaṇīya).
A wise person should prepare these in equal parts together with four times as much milk and one *tulā* of jaggery.

One should cook that purified liquid remaining from the decoction until it is reduced; with that, one should prepare an āḍhaka of ghee. Once prepared, it should be placed in a jar together with a prastha of honey.
One who employs this ghee is liberated from urinary disorders;
likewise, one may use the powders of tugākṣīrī and sugar.
Having stirred these together with an equal amount of honey, one should have them licked on an auspicious day;
thereafter, one should eat a dose according to one's capacity and drink milk.
A mortal who is well-restrained, having properly consumed [this], shall conquer defects of the semen;
moreover, one whose semen is depleted by sexual intercourse immediately regains his vigor and attains happiness.
A mortal who drinks this becomes vigorous and strong, and indeed rejoices;
it consists of Citraka, Sārivā, Balā, and Kālānusārivā.
One should take grapes, viśālā, long peppers, and likewise citraphala;
similarly, one should give madhuka, pathyā, and āmalakas.
One should cook one āḍhaka of ghee with these pastes, each weighing one karṣa, in one droṇa of milk and one droṇa of water; once it is prepared, one should remove it from the fire.
The wise man should thoroughly mix all of that— both the cooled and strained liquid combined with one prastha of sugar, along with the milk of the Tugākṣīrī plant.
Then, at the proper time, one should drink [the medicine] in measured doses according to the specific humor (doṣa) and according to one's strength—
whether one has vāta-semen, kapha-semen, or pitta-semen.
One desiring freedom from disease should drink this blood-semen gland-essence;
this clarified butter is vitalizing, aphrodisiac, and bestows strength.
This ghee, which is beneficial, auspicious, the remover of all diseases,
and propitious— by using it, a woman will conceive a child before long.
It also conquers disorders of the blood and combined disorders of the female reproductive tract;
this treatment should be applied in all disorders of the urine.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter (the twentieth in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, entitled "The Prohibition of Urinary Obstruction."
The fifty-ninth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Obstruction of urine caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, or all three combined, as well as by trauma, feces, and urinary stones—
and likewise another extremely painful type caused by gravel— is declared to be the eighth.
Having compressed it very slightly with the testicles, penis, and bladder,
he voids urine with great difficulty, as if by the impact of wind, like fruit being squeezed out.
Due to an affliction of pitta, one passes urine that is yellow, hot, or red, as if the testicles, urethra,
and bladder were being scorched by fire.
Due to an affliction by phlegm (kapha), one passes urine that is unctuous, white, and not hot, with the scrotum, penis,
and bladder feeling heavy and the body hair standing on end.
Afflicted by the pains of burning and cold, fainting repeatedly, he passes urine of various colors with great difficulty due to the derangement of the humors (sannipāta).
When the urine-carrying channels are injured by a foreign body, or are otherwise afflicted or struck,
urinary obstruction accompanied by intense pain arises.
One should observe that its symptoms are identical to those of vātabasti;
for the vāyu, having become disordered due to the obstruction of feces, [produces these effects].
Indeed, it causes flatulence along with pain and retention of urine;
this is described as the first type of urinary obstruction caused by calculi (aśmarī).
Aśmarī (urinary calculi) and śarkarā (gravel) are identical in their origin and symptoms;
however, listen as I describe the specific characteristics of śarkarā.
The fragmented particles of phlegm (śleṣman), being cooked by bile (pitta) and split apart by wind (vāyu),
are designated by the name "gravel" (śarkarā).
There is pain in the heart, trembling, colic in the abdomen, and the digestive fire becomes extremely weak;
by these [symptoms], fainting occurs as well as severe obstruction of urine.
When those [seeds] are expelled by the urge of urine, the pain subsides,
provided that another pill does not again reach the opening of the channel.
This is the symptom of mūtrāghāta arising from sugar;
now the treatment for all eight of these will be described.
Having carefully considered what has been stated regarding urinary calculi (aśmarī),
one should apply it as well as the sequential regimen beginning with oleation (sneha) according to the specific dosha involved.
Śvadaṃṣṭrā, aśmabhida, kumbhī, hapuṣā, kaṇṭakārikā,
balā, śatāvarī, rāsnā, varuṇa, and girikarṇikā;
Likewise, having collected the drugs beginning with Vidārigandhā, one should cook oil or ghee with the three sweets (traivṛta); that should be drunk, or used for an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
One should administer an urethral enema (uttarabasti) for the pacification of dysuria caused by Vāta;
likewise, oil prepared with the fresh juice of Śvadaṃṣṭrā, along with jaggery, milk, and ginger [should be used].
Having boiled that [milk], it should be applied as before; therein, it removes the pain caused by Vāta when prepared with the Tṛṇotpalādi, Kākoli, and Nyagrodhādi groups [of drugs].
Drinking ghee or even milk will destroy the distress caused by pitta;
one should also administer an uttarabasti for the pacification of pitta-induced dysuria.
Oil prepared with these very same [substances] is beneficial for all three types of enemas;
likewise, purgation combined with the juices of sugarcane, milk, and grapes is beneficial.
The oil prepared from the group beginning with surasā, uśīra, and mustā, as well as that from the group beginning with varuṇa,
along with gruels (yavāgū) and similar preparations, are recommended for the affliction caused by kapha.
One should apply these same measures according to the predominance of the specific doshas, and in cases arising from all three combined (sarvaja),
one should administer a powder of phalgu, vṛścīra, darbha, and aśmasāra with water.
The drinking of cow's urine, sugarcane juice, and darbha-water removes the pain of urinary distress (kṛcchra);
likewise, in cases born of injury, one should employ the treatment for fresh wounds (sadyovraṇa).
In cases of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) and the retention of feces (śakṛjjāta), treatments that alleviate Vāta should be administered,
such as sudation (sveda), immersion baths (avagāha), massage (abhyaṅga), enemas (vasti), and the application of medicinal powders (cūrṇa).
But for those others who are likewise in distress, the procedure for their ritual action has been declared for those two.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter (the twenty-first in the section on internal medicine) within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, titled "The Treatment of Dysuria."
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the prevention of non-human afflictions.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
"One who is afflicted by a wound must always be protected from night-stalkers"—
this which was previously stated shall now be explained in detail.
In which there is secret knowledge of the future, instability, intolerance,
or superhuman activity— that is proclaimed to be possessed by a graha.
Whether impure, or having transgressed the bounds of propriety, or wounded, or even unwounded,
they would harm him for the sake of sport or for the sake of honor.
The innumerable hosts of planets and those who are lords of the planets manifest in various forms; they are likewise divided into eight classes.
The gods, as well as the hosts of their enemies, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Pitṛs, Bhujaṅgas, Rākṣasas,
and the species of Piśācas— this is the eightfold host of deities known as the Grahas.
Contented, pure, fond of pleasant perfumes and garlands, free from drowsiness, speaking truthful and refined speech,
radiant, with steady eyes, a bestower of boons, and devoted to Brahmanas— such a man becomes beloved by the gods.

Sweating profusely, speaking ill of Brahmins, preceptors, and gods, with squinting eyes, devoid of fear, and looking toward evil paths; such a person is not satisfied with various kinds of food and drink, and being wicked-souled, he is possessed by the enemies of the gods.
With a joyful soul, frequenting the interiors of sandy banks and forests, well-behaved, and fond of songs, perfumes, and garlands,
a man afflicted by the Gandharva-graha dances and laughs beautifully with soft sounds.
One who has copper-colored eyes, wears pleasant red garments, is profound yet quick-witted, speaks little, is patient, radiant, and says,
"What shall I give to whom?", is a person afflicted by the Yakṣa-graha.
With a tranquil mind, he offers rice-balls upon the sacrificial grass to the pretas, while wearing his garment over the right shoulder;
one who is desirous of meat, or longing for sesame, molasses, and milk-rice, becomes possessed by a paternal spirit (pitṛ-graha) after consuming that [offering].
He who sometimes crawls on the ground like a serpent, or likewise scrapes his corners of the mouth with his tongue,
being drowsy and desiring molasses, honey, milk, and rice-pudding, should be known as one possessed by a snake-spirit.
Desirous of flesh, blood, and various preparations of liquor, shameless, exceedingly cruel,
and over-bold, prone to anger, possessed of great strength, wandering at night, and hating purity— he who is thus becomes one seized by a *rākṣasa*.

With disheveled hair, emaciated and harsh, talking incessantly for a long time, foul-smelling, extremely impure, and very restless; eating voraciously, dwelling in solitary places, cold, water, or at night; agitated, he wanders about weeping—one possessed by a *piśāca*.
One who has large eyes, a quick gait, licks his own froth, is drowsy, falls down, and trembles excessively;
and one who, having fallen from a mountain, an elephant, or a tree, does not survive, or is afflicted by old age.
The planetary spirits (devagrahas) seize on the full moon day, the asuras also during the two twilights;
the gandharvas mostly on the eighth day, and the yakṣas on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
The ancestors enter on the new moon day, the serpents on the fifth,
the Rakṣasas at night, and the Piśācas on the fourteenth.
Just as a reflection enters a mirror and the like, just as cold and heat enter living beings,
just as the rays of the sun enter its own gem, and just as the embodied soul enters the body,
so too do the planets enter the embodied being, yet they are not seen.
Austere penances, as well as charity, vows, righteousness, observances, truth,
and likewise the eight qualities, are eternally present within them, both individually and collectively, according to their respective power.
They do not dwell together with human beings, nor do they ever enter into human beings;
those who say that they enter them do so out of delusion and must be excluded from the domain of the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā).
The attendants of those planets, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of padmas—
terrible beings who feed on blood, fat, and flesh, and who roam by night— enter into him.
Among those night-stalkers, indeed, those who have taken refuge with the hosts of gods should be known as "añjanas" because of their association with that [divine] nature.
Furthermore, those who are impure are called "god-seizers" (devagrahas);
they are honored like gods and supplicated like gods.
This sequence of masters, virtues, actions, and conducts applies to the gods and the others;
that which are the daughters of Nirṛti are known as their offspring.
Because they are established in truth, their conduct was ordained by the hosts [of gods];
for those who take pleasure in violence, whatever they may be, have attained the state of deities.
The designation "bhūtas" was assigned to them by those who first proclaimed their names; for by this term, the physician recognizes those entities known as grahas.
For this very reason, it is defined as the "science of beings" (bhūtavidyā) by means of knowledge;
therefore, the physician, being well-composed, seeks [this science] for the sake of their pacification.
One should begin the treatment with recitations, observances, and burnt offerings;
[one should also employ] red fragrances, garlands, seeds, honey, and clarified butter.
All things are edible for all; this is declared to be the general rule regarding garments, perfumes, garlands, meats, and blood.
One should cause those things to be given to each person that they desire;
however, on those days during which men generally commit acts of violence, [one should avoid such gifts].
During those days, offerings should be given to avert the influence of that spirit;
having offered oblations into the fire in a temple of a deity, one should cause a bali-offering to be presented.
One should, at the appropriate time, place offerings consisting of kusa grass, svastikas, cakes, clarified butter, umbrellas, and milk-rice for the Asura at crossroads and similar locations.
In the midst of the cows of a Gandharva, there is wine, meat, and the flesh of water-fowl;
in the heart-pleasing mansion of a Yakṣa, there are boiled grains, blood, liquor, and so forth.
One should offer the bali-oblation with flowers such as the atimuktaka, kunda, and lotus;
and for the ancestors, one should prepare a desired offering on a riverbank adorned with a bed of kuśa grass.
In that very place, one should also offer various kinds of oblations to the Naga at a crossroads,
or to the Rakshasa in fearsome thickets.
In an empty house, one should offer a potent oblation to the Piśāca,
using the mantras previously practiced as shown in the Bhūtavidyā.
They cannot be conquered by force; one should treat them with yogic methods.
[One should employ] the hair from the skin of a goat and a bear, as well as that of a porcupine and an owl.
One should administer the smoke of asafoetida and goat's urine;
by this, even a powerful seizure is quickly pacified.
One should grind together the roots of *pippalī* called "gaja," the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *āmalaka*, and mustard seeds,
along with the bile of a monitor lizard, a mongoose, a cat, and a ruru deer.
One who knows the true principles of yoga should employ [the fat] derived from a swan, a horse, a mule, an owl, a camel, a dog, or a jackal for nasal medication, massage, and affusion.
One should grind the excrement of vultures, crows, and boars with goat's urine;
oil prepared with these ingredients would be beneficial as previously described.
One should grind śirīṣa seeds, garlic, ginger, white mustard,
vacā, mañjiṣṭhā, turmeric, and black pepper with goat's urine.
These, made into a wick and dried in the shade, along with bile, form an ointment for the eyes;
likewise, the fruit of *naktamāla*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and the roots of *śyonāka* and *bilva*.
One should prepare wicks from the two types of *haridrā* as before for use as an eye-salve (*nayanāñjana*).
Likewise, rock salt (*saindhava*), *kaṭukā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *vayaḥsthā*, and *vacā*,
ground with goat's urine or fish bile, should be applied as previously described.
For whatever planetary spirits (grahas) do not yield, eye-salve is the remedy for all:
aged ghee, garlic, asafoetida, white mustard, and vacā.
Golomī, ajalomī, bhūtakeśī, jaṭā, kukkuṭā,
sarpagandhā, as well as kāṇavikāṇike.
Vajraproktā, vayaḥsthā, śṛṅgī, mohanavallikā,
the root of arka, trikaṭuka, latā, and añjana from a stream (sroto'ñjana).
Nepalese yellow orpiment, those substances proclaimed as destroyers of Rākṣasas,
and likewise the skins of lions, tigers, bears, cats, leopards, horses, and cows;
The excrement, skin, hair, fat, urine, blood, bile, nails, and so forth of the porcupine, the hedgehog, the iguana, the camel, and the mongoose [are used].
In this section, the physician should prepare oils and clarified butters;
the wise one should employ them for drinking, massage, and nasal administration.
One should administer it as a pill for nasal compression and for collyrium;
likewise, one should administer it as a decoction for sprinkling and as a powder.
One should apply this as a fine powder for dusting or as a paste for external application;
thus, O Aparājita, it overcomes all mental disorders.
Even the procedure beginning with oleation (sneha) may be accomplished in a short time;
however, one should not employ an impure application when seizing a deity.
One should not act in opposition to anyone except a Piśāca;
for if angered, physicians and patients will surely destroy one's vital energy.
Whatever has been stated in the chapter on the beneficial and the harmful, the physician should always practice accordingly; thereby he shall attain success and abundant fame.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter from the beginning, titled [Chapter One], within the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||60||
The sixty-first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of epilepsy (apasmāra).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Memory is the cognition of things as they truly are; its absence in the context of avoiding [harmful things] is called apasmāra (epilepsy), and therefore this disease brings about the end.
From the improper or excessive indulgence in the objects of the senses and in activities,
and by the humors (mala) provoked by incompatible and unclean food and lifestyle, [disease arises].
For those whose conduct consists of cruelty, who eat unwholesome and impure food,
who are overcome by passion and darkness, and who approach women in their menses;
Likewise, when the minds of men are violently struck by desire, fear, agitation, anger, grief, and the like, epilepsy arises.
Trembling of the heart, emptiness, perspiration, meditation, fainting,
bewilderment, and loss of sleep— these will indeed occur for him at that time.
A person, deluded by a wandering mind, is carried away by the streams of perception which are filled with defects and enveloped by passion and ignorance.
Waving his hands and feet, with knitted brows and rolling eyes,
gnashing his teeth and vomiting foam, he falls to the ground with wide-open eyes.
And after a short time, he regains consciousness again;
this is called apasmāra (epilepsy), and it is observed to be of four types.
In men, [the seizure] arises from wind, bile, and phlegm, and a fourth from the combination of all three (sannipāta);
it is characterized by trembling, gnashing the teeth, labored breathing, and even vomiting foam.
If one should say, "A deformed black creature is pursuing me," then my mind would perish; that is epilepsy of a windy nature.
Afflicted by thirst, heat, perspiration, and fainting, and trembling with his limbs in a state of agitation, he who says, "A transformed being is pursuing me; I have been drunk!"—that man is lost.
From that, there would be a loss of consciousness for me; that is said to arise from bile (pitta).
Afflicted by coldness, nausea, and sleepiness, one falls to the ground vomiting phlegm (kapha).
He who says, "A deformed being, white in color, is pursuing me;
because of that, my mind shall perish"—that is epilepsy (apasmāra) caused by phlegm (kapha).
In each of these three [types of fever], there occurs, respectively, piercing pain in the heart, thirst, and excessive salivation;
furthermore, delirium, moaning, and distress should each manifest individually here.
When all symptoms are present together in a disease arising from the provocation of all the doṣas,
it is incurable because the disease arrives without apparent cause and departs even when no treatment has been administered.
Furthermore, others declare that epilepsy (apasmāra) arises from scripture (āgama) and is not born of the [three] humors (doṣaja),
because of the sequential application of the humors and likewise because of their momentariness.
That [Self], however, is described by the wise through scripture and through its manifold forms;
just as when it rains upon the gods, only certain seeds on the earth [germinate].
Just as [plants] sprout in autumn, so too do diseases arise;
some that have been persistent increase rapidly in a short time.
They manifest transformations of universal form by their very nature;
therefore, epilepsy is indeed a great disease born solely from the humors (doṣas).
For that condition, every treatment prescribed for cases of insanity (unmāda) should be performed;
moreover, the drinking of aged ghee and its application as an oil massage are highly recommended.
The application of the formulations mentioned for the planets is especially effective;
through them, all those [ailments] are cured, and one may also effect a cure by other formulations.
[Oil] prepared with the juice of drumstick (śigru), belleric myrobalan (kaṭvaṅga), ferment (kiṇva), and the bark of neem (nimba) [is used].
Anointing with oil mixed with four times the amount of cow urine is beneficial;
likewise for the meat of the iguana, mongoose, elephant, spotted deer, bear, and cow.
Oil prepared with pitta-alleviating drugs is highly recommended for both internal consumption and external massage;
furthermore, one should cleanse the head using strong emetics and purgatives.
One should constantly perform worship of Rudra and his attendants;
furthermore, one should treat the wind-disorder (vātika) with enemas and the bile-disorder (paittika) with purgatives.
The wise physician should treat epilepsy caused by phlegm (kapha) with emetics,
using horse-gram, barley, jujube, hemp seeds, and *palaṅkaṣā*.
Having carefully decocted the two types of *pañcamūla* along with *jaṭilā* and *pathyā*, one should cook ghee with goat's urine; this is beneficial for the vātika type [of dysuria].
Ghee prepared with the first group of drugs (the vidārigandhādi gaṇa) with the addition of the kākolyādi group,
combined with milk, honey, and sugar, is beneficial for the pitta-type [fever].
Ghee prepared with the first group of drugs (the Vidārīgandhādi group) as a decoction base,
with the addition of the Kākolyādi group as a paste, and combined with milk, honey, and sugar, is beneficial for the Pitta-type fever.
With devadāru, vacā, kuṣṭha, siddhārtha, vyoṣa, and hiṅgu;
with mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of rajanī, samaṅgā, triphalā, and ambuda.
Clarified butter prepared with karañja seeds, śairīṣa, girikarṇī, and hutāśana,
along with four times as much urine and known as siddhārthaka, [is effective].
It destroys worms, skin diseases, poisons, asthma, catarrh, and irregular fevers; it also eliminates all afflictions caused by spirits, planetary influences, insanity, and epilepsy.
With the ten roots, the bark of the indravṛkṣa, mūrvā, bhārgī, the three fruits (triphalā),
śampāka, śreyasī, saptaparṇa, apāmārga, and phalgu;
With the boiled pastes (kalkas) of bhūnimba, pūtīka, vyoṣa, and citraka,
along with trivṛt, pāṭhā, the two types of niśā, the two types of sārivā, and pauṣkara;
Ghee should be prepared with kaṭukā, āyasa, dantī, ugrā, nīlinī, and krimiśatru,
along with cow’s milk, curd, urine, and the liquid of cow dung.
This preparation known as pañcagavya, when accomplished, destroys all forms of epilepsy and possession by spirits;
it also subdues quartan fever, consumption, asthma, and insanity.
One should cook a milk-porridge (pāyasa) made with śāli rice in milk boiled with bhārgī;
for three days, one should provide this to the boar to eat once it has been purified.
Having ascertained that it has become sweet, one should slaughter the animal and extract the meat;
then, one should mix three parts of that powder with one part of fermenting agent (kiṇva).
For the purpose of the consecrated water (maṇḍodaka), a well-cooled decoction of bhārgī should be given;
one should then place that collection of ingredients along with the liquor into a purified jar.
The physician should administer the medicine that has acquired its characteristic odor and taste to the patient;
then he should venesect at the appropriate site and have the patient wear auspicious amulets.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter (the second in the Uttaratantra section) of the Suśruta Saṃhitā, within the Bhūtavidyātantra, entitled "The Prohibition of Apasmāra. ||61||
The sixty-second chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of insanity (unmāda-pratiṣedha).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
Because the defects (doṣas), having become agitated and deviated from the right path, cause intoxication,
this mental affliction is therefore proclaimed as "insanity" (unmāda).
It is said to be fivefold: [arising] from each of the defects individually, from all of them combined when they are excessively intensified, and from mental suffering.
The sixth [type] arises from poison; its remedy is according to the specific nature [of that poison].
And when it is not fully developed and is young, it bears the designation "mada" (intoxication).
Delusion and agitation, ringing in the ears, a sense of heaviness in the limbs,
excessive enthusiasm, aversion to food, and eating unclean things in dreams [are the symptoms].
Furthermore, one who experiences agitation by the wind or a whirling sensation as if on a turning wheel will very soon fall into insanity.
With rough skin, harsh speech, and prominent veins, or afflicted by cold, with a thin body and throbbing joints, one who slaps his limbs,
wanders about, sings, is prone to dancing, cries out, and even staggers, does so from the provocation of wind (vāta).
Abounding in thirst, perspiration, and burning heat, frequently suffering from insomnia, and seeking relief in shade, cold winds, and the vicinity of water;
though fierce even amidst a mass of snow and ice, he suspects it to be fire; and due to the derangement of bile (pitta), he perceives stars even in the sky by day.

One afflicted by the provocation of *kapha* becomes prone to vomiting, loss of digestive fire, exhaustion, anorexia, and cough; one who delights in solitude with women, whose mental activity is diminished, who is intent on sleep, speaks little, eats sparingly, and seeks warmth, especially at night.
In that which is the essence of all, wind, bile, and phlegm, as if mutually excited according to their own nature, manifest their respective symptoms.
When the mind is severely wounded by being terrified by thieves, royal officers, enemies, or others, or by the loss of wealth and kinsmen,
or when one desires to sport with a beloved woman, a most intense mental transformation arises.
He speaks incoherently, following the dictates of his mind; then, losing consciousness, he sings, laughs, and weeps with a bewildered intellect.
With bloodshot eyes, his strength, senses, and luster destroyed, utterly dejected and with a dark-complexioned face, one afflicted by poison may then become lifeless.
One should purify a person afflicted by insanity who has been anointed with unctuous substances and fomented,
using sharp emetics and purgatives, as well as head-evacuants.
Having combined that powder with various types of pressed oils mixed with mustard oil, one should apply it to his nose.
One should constantly fumigate it with the highly putrid flesh of dogs and cows;
furthermore, nasal drops and anointing with mustard oil are always beneficial.
He should show him wonders, or speak of the destruction of a beloved one,
using men of terrifying appearance, tamed elephants, and non-venomous serpents.
One should frighten him while he is restrained with nooses or strike him with whips;
or, having secured him well-guarded, one should terrify him with a grass fire.
One may threaten him with water or cause him to experience fear through blows from ropes;
one who is powerful should also guard him and keep him submerged within the water. One should prick him with a sharp instrument, avoiding, however, a blow to a vital organ.
Having entered the interior of his house, he should protect him while setting that house on fire.
One should cause her to dwell constantly in a covered well that is not very deep,
or provide her with barley-gruel or nourishing drinks every three days.
The learned physician should feed him wholesome food that is pleasing and digestive-stimulating— either plain water or gruel made of kulmāṣa beans.
With viḍaṅga, triphalā, musta, mañjiṣṭhā, dāḍima, and utpala;
with śyāmā, elavāluka, elā, candana, and amaradāru.
With *barhiṣṭha*, *rajanī*, *kuṣṭha*, the two types of *parṇinī*, and the two types of *sārivā*;
with *hareṇukā*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *vacā*, *tālīsaka*, and *kesara*.
Ghee prepared with two parts milk and mālatī flowers cures abdominal tumors,
cough, fever, asthma, consumption, and insanity.
This very same preparation, when fully cooked and combined with vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs and four times its quantity of milk, is called Mahākalyāṇaka.
This ghee quickly destroys epilepsy, possession by spirits, consumption, impotence, emaciation, and seedlessness, as well as those diseases mentioned previously.
With barhiṣṭha, kuṣṭha, mañjiṣṭhā, kaṭuka, elā, and niśā;
with tagara, triphalā, hiṅgu, vājigandhā, and amaradruma;
Clarified butter cooked with four times its quantity of milk and with vacā, ajamodā, kākolī, medā, madhuka, and padmaka, along with sugar, is beneficial.
This celebrated *phalaghṛta* (fruit-ghee) is for children afflicted by planetary spirits, for men with vitiated or scanty semen, and it quickly bestows pregnancy upon barren women.
[It contains] *brahmī*, *aindrī*, *viḍaṅga*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), wine (*surā*), and *jaṭā*.
Viṣaghnī, garlic, rāsnā, viśalyā, surasā, and vacā;
One should grind jyotiṣmatī, nāgara, anantā, abhayā,
and saurāṣṭrī in equal parts with the urine of an elephant.
One skilled in the procedure should employ those wicks, dried in the shade,
for pressing out [medicines], collyrium, massage, nasal drops, fumigation, and external application.
One should release the veins on his chest, limbs, and forehead,
and one should also perform the treatments prescribed for epilepsy and those indicated for seizure by planetary spirits (graha).
One should treat [the patient] with unctuous enemas (snehabasti) once the defects have been pacified and the body purified;

in all cases of insanity (unmāda), one should effect the calming of the mind (citta-prasādana). In cases of intoxication (mada) as well, one should employ mild treatment, beginning with gentle measures.
In the fifth type of insanity caused by grief, the physician should extract the thorn of sorrow;
in that caused by poison, he should first employ mild measures and then administer anti-poisonous treatments.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter (the third in the section on the treatment of mental disorders) within the Bhūtavidyā-tantra, which is part of the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, entitled "The Prevention of Insanity."
The sixty-third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the classification of the variations of tastes.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
The purpose for which the fifteenfold movement of the *doṣas* was described is now stated by means of the sixty-three varieties of *rasa*.
They are divided into sixty-three types, both the unrefined and the refined;
having repeatedly observed these sixty-three varieties of rasa, one should apply them accordingly.
Regarding that which was described as the sequential treatment of each individual humor part by part,
the wise physician should apply sixty-three methods therein.
Among the pairs proceeding in their respective order, the sweet taste follows five combinations, while the sour taste follows four.
The salty taste follows three [tastes], the pungent follows two, and the bitter follows the astringent;
thus these are ten and five in pairs.
For example: sweet and sour;
sweet and salty;
sweet and pungent.
Sweet-bitter;
sweet-astringent.
These five are preceded by the sweet [taste]; sour-salty.
Sour and pungent; sour and bitter; sour and astringent.
These four have been enumerated as sour; [the others are] salty-pungent,
salty-bitter,
and salty-astringent.
These three are traversed by the salty [taste]: pungent-bitter, pungent-astringent.
These two are traversed by the pungent; bitter-astringent is the single one traversed by the bitter. Thus, these fifteen combinations of pairs have been explained.
We shall now describe the triads:
the sweet taste, when employed first, proceeds through ten [qualities];
the sour, six; the salty, half of that [three]; and the pungent, one.
For example: sweet, sour, and salty;
sweet, sour, and pungent;
sweet, sour, and bitter.
Sweet, sour, and astringent;
sweet, salty, and pungent;
sweet, salty, and bitter.
Sweet, salty, and astringent;
sweet, pungent, and bitter;
sweet, pungent, and astringent.
Sweet, bitter, and astringent.
Thus, among these ten combinations of three, sweet is employed first: sour, salty, and pungent;
sour, salty, and bitter.
Sour, salty, and astringent; sour, pungent, and bitter; sour, pungent, and astringent.
Sour, bitter, and astringent.
Thus, among these six, sour is employed first; then salty, pungent, and bitter;
and then salty, pungent, and astringent.
Salty, bitter, and astringent:

thus, among these three, salt is administered first; pungent, bitter, and astringent: thus, among these, pungent is administered first. In this manner, these twenty combinations of triads have been explained.
We shall now describe the groups of four.
Through combinations of four tastes, the sweet taste proceeds with ten;
the sour follows four, while the salty follows only one.
Sweet, sour, salty, and pungent;
sweet, sour, salty, and bitter;
sweet, sour, salty, and astringent.
Sweet, sour, pungent, and bitter;
sweet, sour, pungent, and astringent;
sweet, sour, bitter, and astringent.
Sweet, salty, pungent, and bitter;
sweet, salty, pungent, and astringent;
sweet, salty, bitter, and astringent.
Sweet, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Thus, among these ten [tastes], the sweet is employed first; then sour, salty, pungent, and bitter;
and [finally] sour, salty, pungent, and astringent.
Sour, salty, bitter, and astringent;
sour, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Thus, among these four, sour comes first: salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Thus, for one [ingredient], there is first the salty; in this way, these fifteen combinations of four tastes have been proclaimed.
We shall speak of the groups of five:
among the five [tastes], the sweet consists of five, while the sour consists of one.
Sweet, sour, salty, pungent, and bitter;
sweet, sour, salty, pungent, and astringent;
sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and astringent.
Sweet, sour, pungent, bitter, and astringent;
sweet, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Thus, among these five, the sweet is employed first; [then] sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Thus, for one [element], there is first the sour [taste]; in this manner, these six combinations of five [elements] have been explained.
We shall describe one group of six; however, there is only one combination of six [tastes]: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. This is the sole combination of six.
And each one of these six becomes sweet, sour, or salty.
Pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Thus [it is said].
And here it is said: "This sixty-threefold [classification] of tastes has been explained by those who contemplate tastes;
however, it should be applied by the wise according to the sixty-three variations of the humors (doṣas)."
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter (the first in the section on the classification of tastes) within the chapters titled "Ornaments of the Treatise" in the Uttara-tantra of the Suśruta-saṃhitā. ||63||
The sixty-fourth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the regimen for those in good health (Svasthavṛtta).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
As has been described in the Sūtrasthāna,
the nature of one who is healthy is such that the preservation of that state is indeed the purpose of medical treatment.
Indeed, whatever has been previously stated by me regarding his conduct and protection from the beginning—
the meaning therein has been expressed in brief, and it shall now be told here in detail.
In whichever season whatever humors become aggravated in embodied beings,
those specific tastes should be administered by one who possesses knowledge.
Indeed, because the bodies are excessively moist during the rainy season,
all the humors, beginning with Vāta, become aggravated in everyone when the digestive fire is weak.
Therefore, for the purpose of cleansing through moistening and for the removal of the humors (doṣas),
one should employ a preparation that is free from harmful substances and endowed with astringent, bitter, and pungent tastes.
Food that is neither too oily nor too dry, warm, and digestive-stimulating should be given to the king; as for the water, it is as described previously.
Or one may drink water that has been heated and cooled, mixed with honey,
when the day is pervaded by clouds and winds and filled with excessively cold rainwater.
At that time, medicinal herbs undergo a burning sensation due to their youthfulness;
therefore, a wise person should not engage in excessive physical exertion for that reason.
One should avoid excessive drinking of water, exposure to dew, sexual intercourse, and the heat of the sun;
and one should sleep in the open air to prevent the body from being affected by the vapors of the earth.
In the cold, he should go about adorned with excellent agallochum, accompanied by female elephants, in a house provided with fire and sheltered from the wind, and well-furnished with heavy coverings.
One should diligently avoid sleeping during the day and indigestion during that season; in autumn, one should carefully consume substances that are astringent, sweet, and bitter.
Dairy products, sugarcane preparations, honey, rice, mung beans, and the like; meat from wild animals; white garlands; moonbeams at twilight; and light clothing.
And because the water was so clear, it was entirely beneficial at that time;
likewise, bathing in the lakes amidst the lotuses, blue lilies, and fragrant water-lilies was likewise wholesome.
At dusk, one should apply the rays of the moon and sandalwood ointment,
and employ the drinking of bitter ghee and the controlled draining of blood according to the proper method.
One should also eliminate the pitta accumulated during the rainy season by means of purgatives;
furthermore, one should avoid sharp, sour, hot, alkaline substances, as well as sleep during the day and exposure to the sun.
One should avoid staying awake at night and sexual intercourse as well;
[one should drink] sweet, cool water, which is pure and as clear as crystal.
At that time, all the water was beneficial, being washed by the rays of the autumn moon and rendered free of poison by the rising of the star Agastya, owing to its clarity.
One should wear light, clean garments scented with sandalwood and camphor,
enjoy autumnal garlands, and drink sidhu liquor in moderation.
One should practice everything that pacifies pitta.
Winter is cold, dry, characterized by weak sunlight, and turbulent with wind.
Then, upon encountering cold, the wind becomes aggravated there;
the fire situated within the digestive tract, through contact with the cold, becomes condensed within.
It quickly dries up the bodily fluids; therefore, unctuous food is beneficial then.
In the winter, food that is intensely salty, alkaline, bitter, sour, and pungent is recommended.
A diet consisting of ghee, oil, and meat is said to be beneficial;
one should also drink strong liquors while adorned with aguru.
He should bathe in a large water-vessel filled with pleasantly warm water mixed with oil,
and lie upon a great couch provided with glowing coals and spread with a silken coverlet.

Surrounded by various women whose thighs, hips, and breasts were full, and who were richly perfumed with the smoke of aguru incense, he should lie upon his bed within the inner chamber of the womb-like room.
And when satisfied, the king should indulge in sexual intercourse to his heart's content,
as well as foods that are sweet, bitter, pungent, sour, and salty.
Food and drink, sesame seeds, mung beans, leafy vegetables, curds,
as well as products of sugarcane, rice, and fragrant, fresh [grains].
One should consume the meat of carnivorous animals, those that dwell in holes, those of marshy lands, aquatic creatures, birds that float on water, and those that walk upon their toes.
One who desires nourishment at the onset of winter may, according to his desire, consume intoxicating liquors, clear spirits, and whatever else provides strength.
One should diligently avoid sleeping during the day and indigestion;
this very same regimen is prescribed for the winter season.
The phlegm accumulated during the winter remains in the bodies of those who have become cold;
then, provoked by the heat of spring, it produces many diseases.
Thereafter, one should avoid sour, sweet, unctuous, salty, and heavy foods,
and one should also perform treatments such as emesis and the like.
One should appropriately serve sixty-day rice, cooled barley, mung beans, wild rice, and kodrava,
along with the juices of birds such as the common quail and various soups.

At the end of winter, one should drink preparations of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *vārtāka*, and other bitter herbs, along with honey-wine (*madhvāsava*), fermented liquors (*ariṣṭa*), rum (*sīdhu*), honey-mead (*mādhvīka*), and *mādhava* wine.
One should enjoy physical exercise, collyrium, medicinal smoke, and strong gargles, as well as all things with lukewarm water, at the arrival of spring. [One should avoid] that which is sharp,
dry, pungent, alkaline, astringent, slightly warm, or non-liquid.
In the spring, a diet consisting primarily of barley, mung beans, and honey is beneficial.
In this context, physical exertion consists of wrestling, walking, and striking stones;
likewise, it includes massage, bathing, women, and forest groves.
One should treat and eliminate the phlegm accumulated during the winter by means of head-purgatives,
emetics, non-unctuous enemas, gargles, and other such therapies.
One should avoid sweet, unctuous, heavy, and liquid foods; daytime sleep, physical exercise, heat, exertion, sexual intercourse, and drying substances.
In the summer, one should avoid foods with an abundance of the fiery quality (agni-guṇa),
as well as lakes, rivers, ponds, and beautiful forests.
There were most excellent sandalwood woods, garlands with lotuses and water-lilies,
fans cooled by the breeze, and likewise cool chambers.
During the hot season, one should wear very light garments that are scented with sugar-candy and other sweets, fragrant, and cool.
One should consume beverages and also churned drinks mixed with sugar;
likewise, one's food should be wholesome, cool, accompanied by ghee, and sweet in its liquid consistency.
At night, on a bed situated within the palace and strewn with fresh flowers, he should drink boiled milk sweetened with sugar.
At the end of the heat, one should sleep with limbs moistened with sandalwood paste while being touched by pleasant breezes;
for at that time, the three heavy tastes are always beneficial.
Milk, meat broths, lukewarm oils, and clarified butters—
whatever is nourishing as well as obstructive to the channels (abhiṣyandi).
One skilled in the prescribed methods should subdue the wind that has been accumulated during the summer heat and has become provoked, by means of a procedure that pacifies the wind.
In this state, one should avoid river water, parching food, hot substances, stirred-up gruel, as well as exposure to the sun, physical exertion, sleeping during the day, and sexual intercourse.
One should avoid newly harvested grain, dry food, cold water, and parched flour; likewise, one should avoid barley, ṣaṣṭika rice, wheat, and non-newly harvested śāli rice.
In the middle of a palace, in a place sheltered from the wind, one should resort to a bed that is soft on top;
[one should avoid] the excrement, urine, saliva, spittle, and so forth of venomous creatures.
Then the water, which had been submerged [in the lake], became like poison in the atmosphere,
corrupted by the monsoon wind tainted with venom.
Therefore, at that time, one should avoid all such indulgences;
however, one may appropriately partake of *ariṣṭa*, *āsava*, and *maireya* liquors along with their accompanying snacks.

One should drink [the decoction] during the rainy season when the previous meal is digested; however, one should avoid drinking it at night. Furthermore, one should treat the patient with purgatives, enemas, and other remedies that alleviate Vata.
One should pacify the provoked wind and observe the regimen prescribed for the rainy season;
that man who conducts himself according to this rule in every season [attains well-being].
He never contracts diseases caused by severe or untimely seasons.
Hereafter, we shall describe the twelve types of dietary conduct.

Among these, there are those involving cold, hot, unctuous, dry, liquid, or solid foods; those taken once or twice a day; those combined with medicinal substances; and those characterized by proper or deficient quantity for the purpose of pacifying the bodily humors.
One should treat those suffering from the burning heat of thirst, those afflicted by blood-bile (raktapitta) or poison,
those distressed by fainting, and those emaciated from sexual indulgence with cool foods.
One should treat with warm foods those people afflicted by diseases of phlegm and wind, those who have undergone purgation, those who have consumed oleaginous substances,
and those whose bodies are not yet moistened [by the treatment].
One should treat those with vāta disorders, those with dry bodies, those impaired by sexual excess,
and those who engage in physical exercise with unctuous foods.
One should treat those who are overwhelmed by fat, as well as those suffering from urinary disorders (meha) characterized by unctuousness,
and those whose bodies are afflicted by phlegm, with dry foods.
One should treat those with emaciated bodies and those afflicted by thirst with liquids, even if they are weak;
likewise, those with excessively moistened bodies, those with ulcers, and those suffering from urinary disorders (mehin) with dry substances.
Food should be given at a single time for the sake of increasing a weak digestive fire;
likewise, food taken twice a day is highly recommended for one with a balanced digestive fire.
To one who hates medicine, it should be given mixed with other medicines;
for a patient with weak digestion, it is recommended when administered in a small dose.
Food given according to the season is traditionally held to pacify the bodily humors (doṣas).
Beyond this, for the sake of the maintenance of those who are healthy,
one should employ all these twelve types of foodstuffs in the following manner.
Henceforth, we shall describe the ten times for administering medicinal herbs:

1) before food (abhakta), before the meal (prāgbhakta), after the meal (adhobhakta), during the meal (madhyebhakta), between meals (antarābhakta), with food (sabhakta), as a bolus (sāmudga), repeatedly (muhurmuhuḥ), at every morsel (grāsa), and between morsels (grāsāntara). These are the ten times for administering medicinal herbs.
Among those, that which is taken as medicine alone, without any food, is called *abhakta*.
Medicine that possesses superior potency and is not deficient in its ingredients undoubtedly and swiftly destroys disease;
however, children, the elderly, women, and those of delicate constitution, having drunk it, suffer extreme exhaustion and a loss of strength.
That which is to be consumed before a meal is called "prāgbhakta."
Medicine taken before a meal undergoes digestion quickly, does not harm the bodily strength as it is shielded by food, and does not repeatedly emerge from the mouth due to vomiting;
therefore, this very same medicine should be administered to the elderly, children, the timid, the emaciated, and women.
That which is below the meal is called *adhobhakta*.
That which is drunk in the middle of a meal is called *madhyebhakta*.
When consumed after eating food, it destroys various diseases in the upper body and bestows strength;
when drunk in the middle [part of the meal], it removes those diseases which, due to their non-dispersive nature, have overcome the middle part of the body.
"Between-meals" (antarābhakta) refers to that which is drunk between the two meals, namely the morning and the evening.
That which is together with food is called "sabhakta."
Indeed, wholesome food accompanied by other meals is always beneficial for women and the weak, as well as for those who dislike it, and likewise for children and the elderly;
moreover, that which is pleasing to the heart, strength-giving, and digestive-stimulating becomes wholesome when taken as an "antara-bhaktaka" (between-meal) snack.
That which is drunk at the beginning and at the end of a meal is called *sāmudga*.
When the doshas have spread in two directions, that which is consumed at the beginning and end of a meal is known as "samudga."
1. Repeated administration: when a medicine, whether it be palatable or unpalatable, is administered repeatedly at intervals.
They say that this should be employed in cases of excessive and frequent respiration, coughing, hiccups, and vomiting.
But the morsel is that which is mixed with the funeral ball (piṇḍa).
But the interval between morsels is that which occurs between the morsels.
In the case of weak digestive fires, one should endeavor to administer digestive stimulants and aphrodisiacs with the morsels of food;
between the morsels, one should provide emetics and medicinal smokes, as well as electuaries whose efficacy in treating dyspnea and other ailments is well-known and proven.
Thus, these are the ten times for medicinal herbs.
When stool and urine have been discharged, when the sense organs are clear and the body is light,
when eructations are pure and the heart is very clean, when wind moves freely,
and likewise when there is a desire for food, when exhaustion has passed and the belly has become relaxed.
That time is considered by physicians to be the proper occasion when food is to be administered.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter (the second in this section) from the beginning, titled "The Chapter on Their Respective Functions," within the chapters that adorn the treatise in the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
The sixty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the methodological formulations (tantrayukti).
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.
There are thirty-two methodological principles (*tantrayukti*) in the treatise. They are as follows: the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*), the connection (*yoga*), and so forth.
The meaning of the term;
the meaning of the reason; the enunciation.
Exposition; instruction; designation.
A specific instance;
an extension; an exception.
The remainder of the sentence; presumptive testimony;
and contrariety.
The consequence;
the absolute;
the non-absolute.
The prima facie argument;
the final decision;
the assent.
The rule;
the anticipation of what is yet to come; the review of what has passed.
Doubt;
explanation;
one's own technical term.
Etymological explanation;
illustration; injunction.
Alternative; conjunction; that which is to be inferred.
Thus [it is said].
What is the purpose of these tantrayuktis? It is said: the construction of sentences and the construction of meanings.
And there are verses on this subject:
"The refutation of statements employed by opponents who speak falsely,
as well as the establishment of one's own position, is accomplished through the methodological principles of the treatise."
Furthermore, those meanings which have not been explicitly stated, those that are implicit, those that are impure, and whatever has been mentioned only in brief— all these shall now be established.
Just as the sun is for the lotus grove, and just as a lamp is for the interior of a house,
so too are the logical arguments (yuktis) for the purpose of illuminating the awakening to the system (tantra).
In that context, the subject matter with reference to which something is stated is the *adhikaraṇa* (locus); for example, "taste" or "humor."
That by which a statement is logically connected is *yoga*.

For example: "One should drink oil prepared with *amṛtavallī*, *nimba*, *hiṃsrā*, *abhayā*, *vṛkṣaka*, *pippalī*, and the two types of *balā*, along with *devadāru*, for the constant benefit of those suffering from the disease of goiter (*galagaṇḍa*)."
In this context, although "one should drink the prepared oil" (tailaṃ siddhaṃ pibet) ought to have been stated first, the word "prepared" (siddham) is employed in the third quarter [of the verse].
Thus, the unification of even words situated at a distance is *yoga*.

The meaning expressed in a *sūtra* or a word (*pada*) is the "meaning of a word" (*padārtha*). The meaning of a single word, two words, or multiple words is the *padārtha*. And the meanings of words are infinite.
For example, when *sneha*, *sveda*, and *añjana* are mentioned, the application of two or three meanings is observed.

In such cases, that meaning which is established through its connection with what precedes and follows should be accepted. For instance, when it is said, "We shall explain the chapter on the origin of the Vedas," the intellect hesitates, wondering which Veda he will speak of regarding its origin.
Since the Vedas, such as the Ṛgveda and others, derive from the two verbal roots *vid*— meaning "to investigate" (*vicāraṇe*) and *vidl*—

meaning "to obtain" (*lābhe*), both of which possess multiple meanings, one arrives at the understanding that the author intends to speak on the origin of Āyurveda by observing the connection between what precedes and what follows; this is the meaning of the word.
That which has been stated otherwise and serves to establish another meaning is the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*).
For example: "Just as a lump of clay is moistened by water, so too is a wound moistened by things such as black gram and milk."
A brief statement is an enumeration (uddeśa),
such as "the arrow-head" (śalya).
Detailed explanation is exposition;
for example, "bodily" and "adventitious."
"Thus" is the instruction:
"In such a manner one should not wake [at improper times] at night, and one should avoid sleeping during the day."
"By this reason" is the designation (apadeśa);
for example, as it is designated: "sweet [substance] increases phlegm."
Pradeśa (application by analogy) is the proof of the subject at hand by means of what has already been established.
For example: "Just as this [man] extracted the thorn from Devadatta, so too will he extract it for Yajñadatta."
1. Extension (*atideśa*) is the application of what has been stated regarding a future [case].
For example: "Since his wind rises upward from this [place], he would be one suffering from upward-moving wind (*udāvartin*)."
Apavarga (exclusion) is the removal [of something] after having pervaded it;
for example, "the poison-tainted [substances] are not to be sweated,
except for insect-poison."
That word by which a sentence is completed when it has not been explicitly stated is the "sentence-complement" (vākyaśeṣa).
For example, when it is said, "of the head, hands, feet, sides, back, belly, and chest," even without the mention of "man," it is understood that these belong to "the man."
Presumption (arthāpatti) is that which is understood by implication from what has been stated;
for example, when it is said, "I shall eat rice," it is understood by implication that this person is not thirsty and does not wish for barley-gruel.
The opposite of what has been stated here is its reversal (*viparyaya*).
For example, when it is said that those who are emaciated, weak, or timid are difficult to treat, the opposite—that those who are robust and so forth are easy to treat—is understood.
*Prasaṅga* is the conclusion by means of another context;
or rather, it is that matter which, having been interrupted by another context and stated more than once, is finally concluded.

For example, after stating in the *Vedotpatti* [chapter] that "the person (*puruṣa*) is the collection of the five great elements and the embodied soul; action resides in him; he is the locus [of action]," [it is concluded here].
Furthermore, regarding the consideration of the elements, it has been stated that the person (*puruṣa*) is the aggregate of the five great elements and the embodied being;
indeed, this very person of action (*karmapuruṣa*) is the subject of medical treatment.
(1. Sarvatra) That which is stated with a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is an absolute rule (*ekānta*). For example: "The *trivṛt* purges;
the *madana* fruit emetics."
That which is "so in some cases and otherwise in others" is the non-absolute (anekānta).
For example, some teachers assert that substance (dravya) is primary, while others assert that taste (rasa) is.
Some [say it is] vigor; some [say it is] maturation.
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is a question preceded by an objection;
for example: "In what way do the four types of prameha caused by wind become incurable?"
The resolution to this is as follows:
just as the wind, having compressed the body and subsequently moved downward, releases urine permeated by fat, marrow, and lymph, so too are those diseases born of Vata considered incurable.
And so it has been said: "When the wind, joined with fat, marrow, and muscle-fat, compresses the entire body and becomes aggravated below, those diseases born of wind (vāta) are incurable."
An opponent's view that is not refuted is accepted;
for example, if another were to say, "There are seven tastes," that is somehow consented to by virtue of its not being refuted.
The procedure has been explained according to the sequence of the chapters;
for example, the eleven vital points (marmans) of the thighs have been explained according to the sequence of the chapters.
"Thus he will speak" refers to looking toward the future;
for example, as one might say in the *Ślokasthāna*, "I shall explain [this] in the *Cikitsitasthāna*."

That which was previously mentioned is "overlooking what has passed," as for example when one says in the section on therapeutics (Cikitsā-sthāna), "as it was stated in the Section on General Principles (Śloka-sthāna)."
Doubt arises from the perception of two opposing causes;
for example, that a blow to the chest is fatal,
whereas the severing of hands and feet is not fatal.
In the *tantra*, there is an explanatory description of excellence;
for example, here the twenty-fifth principle, the *puruṣa*, is explained. In other *tantras* of Āyurveda, the consideration begins with the primary elements (*bhūta*) and so forth.
A technical term is one not common to other treatises;
for example, the term *mithuna* (pair) refers to honey and clarified butter, or it may be an example well-known in common usage.
A definitive statement is a *nirvacana* (etymological derivation).
For example: "Ayurveda" [is so called] because life (*āyus*) exists in it, or by means of it one finds (*vindati*) life.
An illustration (nidarśana) is the manifestation of an example;
for instance, just as fire accompanied by wind increases in dry grass, so too does a wound aggravated by the derangement of wind, bile, and phlegm.
An injunction is the determination that "this alone must be done," such as:
"One should eat only wholesome food."
"Both this and that" is a collective aggregate (*samuccaya*).
For example, in the category of meats, the *eṇa* deer, *hariṇa* deer, and so forth, as well as the *lāva* partridge, *tittiri* partridge, and *śāraṅga* partridge, are the principal ones.
The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is "this" or "that," such as [the thought]:
"Let there be rice with sauce, or barley-gruel with ghee."
That which is not explicitly stated but is understood by the intellect is to be inferred (*ūhya*).

For example, in the section on the rules for food and drink, four kinds of food are taught: that which is to be chewed (*bhakṣya*), that which is to be eaten (*bhojya*), that which is to be licked (*lehya*), and that which is to be drunk (*peya*).

Although four kinds should have been mentioned, only two are stated; this is what must be inferred here: that when the two specific categories of food and drink are included, all four are thereby included. Furthermore, food consisting of all four types is rare.

For the most part, there are only two [types]; therefore, duality is well-established. Furthermore, that which is to be chewed is included within the category of "food" (anna) due to its similarity to solid substances, and that which is to be licked is included within the category of "drink" (peya).
Because of the commonality of fluidity.
And on this point there are verses:
"The systematic arrangement of these has been demonstrated by means of a general overview;
however, the specific details should be discerned by the wise according to their application."
Indeed, these thirty-two methods,
endowed with linguistic, semantic, and logical principles, have been correctly set forth by me for the purpose of investigating the essence of the Tantra.
For that wise physician who knows these [sciences] according to the prescribed rules, having become like a lamp, is worthy of honor; this is the opinion of Dhanvantari.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter (the third from the beginning), titled "The Methodology of the Treatise" (*Tantrayukti*), within the chapters on the Adornments of the Treatise (*Tantrabhūṣaṇa*) in the Uttara-tantra of the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*.
The sixty-sixth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the classification of the variations of the *doṣas*.
As the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari has said.

The illustrious Suśruta, son of Viśvāmitra, questions the highly energetic Divodāsa, who is learned in the eight branches of the Veda, who has severed all doubts regarding the meaning of the scriptures, and who is an ocean of subtle and profound traditional knowledge.
The sixty-two varieties of faults which were previously proclaimed;
"How many are to be known therein—individually, in pairs, or even in threes?
Having heard those words of his, the one of great asceticism cut through his doubt.
With a joyful heart, that tiger among kings spoke truly to Suśruta:
"The three humors (doṣas), the tissues (dhātus), as well as feces and urine."
For these maintain the body with beneficial juices without causing it harm;
the person consists of sixteen parts, and there are eleven vital breaths.
There are one thousand two hundred and twenty diseases,
and one hundred and seventy-five medicinal substances.
For that has been proclaimed in detail: the three qualities (guṇas) are indeed divided into faults (doṣas), and it is certain that these become sixty-two in their most numerous form.
There are exactly three distinct doshas; taken two at a time, there are nine combinations with the superior one added;
and taken three at a time, there are thirteen combinations according to whether one, two, all three, or the middle one is predominant.
Thus, there are exactly fifty [types] together with those that have reached exhaustion;
likewise, there are others consisting of those with diminished middling [faculties], those with excessive diminishment, and those with diminished increase.
Thus, the twelve [types] are declared; the three doshas become sixty-two-fold.
When mixed with the impurities of the dhatus, the doshas again reach an innumerable state.
Therefore, having restrained the tendency toward excessive proliferation through conceptualizations of various defects,
one should treat the disease after diagnosing it, using the various tastes as prescribed.
The physician is the agent, the instruments are the tastes, and the humors are the causal factors;
health alone is the effect, while ill-health is the opposite.
Thus, this entire and prosperous Uttara-tantra is composed with the sequence of words and meanings woven together through sixty-six chapters.
The knowledge of both the manifest and the hidden meanings has been proclaimed by you according to the rules and according to your questions, for those whose minds are not deeply dull.

Having studied all this together with its supplements according to the prescribed rule as declared, one does not fall away from the goals attained by the mind; these words regarding Brahman are exceedingly true.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Classification of Variations of the Doshas," in the Uttaratantra of the Suśruta Saṃhitā.
Thus ends the Uttarasthāna in the Śuśruta Āyurvedaśāstra.
